title: NQ Futures Review & 1st Presented Reflection FVG
head: First Presented Fair Value Gap (FPFVG)
body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:** The very first candlestick gap that forms after 9:30 AM ET on any trading day. Identified by the candlestick close and next candlestick open not aligning (either up-close gap or down-close gap). Crucial marker for intraday structure. Does NOT need displacement (breaking prior swing highs/lows) to be valid, but FPFVG with displacement is emphasized more heavily.
- **How to identify:** Start observing candles at 9:30 AM ET; mark the first candlestick that creates a gap (body doesn't fill the space between prior close and current open).
- **How to use:** If FPFVG is up-close (buy-side imbalance, sell-side inefficiency), look for the first opposing down-close gap (SIBI) formed afterward — this becomes the Reflection FVG, equally important for understanding the market's structure.
- **Example in this video:** Friday's FPFVG was an up-close gap at open (29,681 close to 29,681 next open); Monday's action used this to define targets for the day.
- **Timestamps:** [0:00:52](https://youtu.be/9W4YpyAg5RY?t=52) "first presented fair value gap," [0:02:26](https://youtu.be/9W4YpyAg5RY?t=146) "buy-side imbalance, sell-side inefficiency."
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Not every gap after 9:30 is the FPFVG; only the very first one counts. Confusion arises when FPFVG-D exists (see below).

title: NQ Futures Review & 1st Presented Reflection FVG
head: First Presented Fair Value Gap with Displacement (FPFVG-D)
body:
- **Kind:** definition (refinement)
- **What ICT says:** When the FPFVG is part of a move that ALSO breaks the prior swing high or low (displacement), it becomes "FPFVG with displacement" and receives significantly more emphasis in future trading. This gap is more significant because it represents a true breakout, not just an opening gap. If both a plain FPFVG and an FPFVG-D exist in the same session, extend the FPFVG-D forward for higher probability targeting.
- **How to identify:** Identify the FPFVG; check if the candlestick that created it (or subsequent candles in that run) broke above or below the prior day's swing high/low. If yes = FPFVG-D.
- **How to use:** Prioritize FPFVG-D for targeting and support/resistance; it's more likely to be referenced intraday by price action. Plain FPFVG still has value but secondary emphasis.
- **Example in this video:** Friday had a plain FPFVG (up-close, no displacement); later a FPFVG-D formed (up-close gap WITH breakout of prior day's highs). The FPFVG-D is carried forward with higher conviction.
- **Timestamps:** [0:01:39](https://youtu.be/9W4YpyAg5RY?t=99) "first presented fair value gap with displacement," [0:03:15](https://youtu.be/9W4YpyAg5RY?t=195) "much more significant... much more emphasis."
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Distinguish between plain FPFVG and FPFVG-D in your chart annotations; don't confuse them.

title: NQ Futures Review & 1st Presented Reflection FVG
head: First Presented Reflection Fair Value Gap (Reflection FVG)
body:
- **Kind:** definition (derived concept)
- **What ICT says:** After identifying the FPFVG (especially if it's an up-close gap), search for the very first down-close gap (SIBI: sell-side imbalance, buy-side inefficiency) that forms after it. This SIBI is the "reflection" of the FPFVG — it's the mirror-image, opposite characteristic. Named "reflection" because it's the reverse of the FPFVG, just as a mirror reverses an image. CRITICAL: If the FPFVG is NOT an up-close (buy-side) gap, the reflection concept doesn't apply; there's no significance to the first SIBI.
- **How to identify:** (1) Confirm FPFVG is an up-close gap. (2) Scan forward through candlesticks for the first down-close gap (SIBI). (3) That SIBI becomes the Reflection FVG.
- **How to use:** The Reflection FVG acts as a secondary reference level for support/resistance intraday; price often retraces into it or respects its high/low/midpoint boundaries.
- **Example in this video:** Friday's FPFVG was up-close; the first SIBI that formed (down-close gap at 10:01 AM) became the Reflection FVG. Monday and Tuesday, price traded into this Reflection FVG multiple times.
- **Timestamps:** [0:06:29](https://youtu.be/9W4YpyAg5RY?t=389) "first presented reflection fair value gap," [0:06:29](https://youtu.be/9W4YpyAg5RY?t=389) "mirror image of the very first presented fair value gap."
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Only applies if FPFVG is up-close (buy-side); if FPFVG is down-close, no Reflection FVG concept applies.

title: NQ Futures Review & 1st Presented Reflection FVG
head: Displacement (Gap Definition)
body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:** When a candlestick gap is part of a run that also breaks the prior swing high or swing low, it has "displacement." Displacement signifies a true breakout or breakdown, not just a routine opening gap. Gaps with displacement are much more significant for future use.
- **How to identify:** Identify a gap; check if the candle(s) forming that gap also clear the prior session's swing high (for upside displacement) or swing low (for downside displacement).
- **How to use:** Prioritize gaps with displacement; they're more likely to serve as reference levels and liquidity magnets throughout the day.
- **Example in this video:** A gap on Friday had displacement because price broke above prior highs; this makes it an FPFVG-D (more significant) vs. plain FPFVG.
- **Timestamps:** [0:01:39](https://youtu.be/9W4YpyAg5RY?t=99) "displacement is where it's part of a run that takes out the high or low," [0:18:29](https://youtu.be/9W4YpyAg5RY?t=1109) "displacement here."
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Displacement adds conviction to a gap's validity and future use.

title: NQ Futures Review & 1st Presented Reflection FVG
head: Wick Consequent Encroachment (Midpoint as Support/Resistance)
body:
- **Kind:** refinement
- **What ICT says:** The midpoint of a wick (high + low)/2 acts as a critical support/resistance level. When a candlestick wicks above or below a level but the body closes far from it (not touching or closing in upper/lower half of the wick), the wick's midpoint becomes the next friction point. Price often respects the midpoint for one or two candles before breaking further.
- **How to identify:** Identify a wick; calculate its midpoint; observe candlestick bodies relative to that midpoint on subsequent candles.
- **How to use:** Use wick midpoint as short-term support/resistance for exits and reversal prediction. Bodies failing to close above/below wick midpoint = weakness/strength depending on direction.
- **Example in this video:** Friday's Reflection FVG wick midpoint was monitored; Monday's open wicked above it but bodies stayed below it, signaling weakness (bearish). ICT used this as a signal to go short.
- **Timestamps:** [0:12:08](https://youtu.be/9W4YpyAg5RY?t=728) "I'm watching this wick's consequent encroachment, its middle point," [0:12:56](https://youtu.be/9W4YpyAg5RY?t=776) "trading just to consequent encroachment."
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** More granular than full wick support; used for precise short-term reversals.

title: NQ Futures Review & 1st Presented Reflection FVG
head: Half-Wick Run (50% of Prior Wick Retracement)
body:
- **Kind:** refinement
- **What ICT says:** When price retraces from an extreme (high or low) and reaches exactly 50% of the prior wick's range, that 50% point often acts as a stall point or signal of weakness/strength. If price goes to half-wick and reverses, that's a strong reversal signal. If price reaches half-wick and continues through, the move has strength.
- **How to identify:** Identify a wick (high to low); calculate 50% of its range; mark that level; observe price interaction at that point.
- **How to use:** Half-wick as a micro-target or reversal zone; if price stalls at 50%, expect pullback; if price pierces 50%, expect acceleration.
- **Example in this video:** Post-open, price wicked up through wick midpoint but only reached half of that wick's range upward before reversing, signaling weakness.
- **Timestamps:** [0:16:54](https://youtu.be/9W4YpyAg5RY?t=1014) "half of that wick's run up here," [0:16:54](https://youtu.be/9W4YpyAg5RY?t=1014) "that's just one of the sweetest little things."
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Micro-level precision; best used in conjunction with macro directional bias.

title: NQ Futures Review & 1st Presented Reflection FVG
head: Gradient Levels (Pre-Market Session Structure)
body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:** The 7:00–9:00 AM ET pre-market session has its own high and low; these act as "gradient levels." When divided into octants and quarters (using Fibonacci), these pre-market levels become support/resistance anchors for the RTH session. Price often gravitats back to these levels intraday.
- **How to identify:** Mark the 7:00 AM and 9:00 AM ET boundaries on a 1-minute chart; identify the high and low between those times; divide using Fibonacci.
- **How to use:** Use gradient levels as secondary targets (after main RTH targets); if price runs and misses RTH target, look for pullback into gradient level octant.
- **Example in this video:** 7:00–9:00 AM gradient levels were used as targets and support zones throughout the day; price repeatedly touched them.
- **Timestamps:** [0:23:24](https://youtu.be/9W4YpyAg5RY?t=1404) "7:00 to 9:00 in the morning pre-market session," [0:30:36](https://youtu.be/9W4YpyAg5RY?t=1836) "Sibby. Trade up. Bodies stopping dead in its tracks... goes down into the low of 7:00 to 9:00 range."
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Pre-market can vary in strength/volatility; post-holiday pre-market is especially weak.

title: NQ Futures Review & 1st Presented Reflection FVG
head: Post-Holiday Volume Trading Caution
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:** The trading day immediately after a holiday (e.g., day after Labor Day) tends to have "funky" or erratic price behavior due to pent-up aggression, fear, and behavioral uncertainty. New traders should reduce contract size, avoid chasing the best exit, and target low-hanging fruit (nearest support/resistance) rather than maximum profit. Don't be greedy; take easy wins and exit early.
- **How to identify:** Identify holidays in the trading calendar (Labor Day, Thanksgiving, etc.); mark the trading day immediately after as "caution day."
- **How to use:** Reduce position size by 50–80% on post-holiday days. Target nearest support/resistance only. Exit early rather than holding for optimal profit. Avoid leverage.
- **Example in this video:** Day after Labor Day Monday (trading resumed Tuesday); ICT traded only 1 contract instead of 6, and exited at the first easy target rather than chasing the bigger move lower that materialized.
- **Timestamps:** [0:17:41](https://youtu.be/9W4YpyAg5RY?t=1061) "post holiday... can be a little funky," [0:29:00](https://youtu.be/9W4YpyAg5RY?t=1740) "low-hanging fruit objective."
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Not a rule against trading; rather, a risk-management rule for elevated uncertainty.

title: NQ Futures Review & 1st Presented Reflection FVG
head: Macro Time Delivery of Gaps
body:
- **Kind:** refinement
- **What ICT says:** When a gap (especially FPFVG) forms at a macro time (1:00 AM, 10:50–11:10 AM, etc.), it gains additional significance because it's delivered during a scheduled algorithmic clustering window. This makes the gap more likely to be referenced intraday.
- **How to identify:** Identify the time a gap forms; check if it aligns with a known macro time window.
- **How to use:** Higher conviction when gap forms at macro time; extend it forward with greater emphasis.
- **Example in this video:** Reflection FVG formed at 1:01 AM (macro window boundary); ICT notes it's "macro delivered" and therefore more significant.
- **Timestamps:** [0:04:52](https://youtu.be/9W4YpyAg5RY?t=292) "it's also part of a macro time," [0:07:18](https://youtu.be/9W4YpyAg5RY?t=438) "It also makes it stronger when it is a macro delivered inefficiency."
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Macro delivery is a filter/confirmation, not a standalone signal.

title: How To Engage Price After Holiday Volume Days
head: Post-holiday engagement rule  (aliases: "how to start back after a holiday")
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - After a holiday, go in light — "like one contract" — even if you are trading paper, to test price. It helps you get into alignment: either you're offside or onside with your initial expectation.
  - Post-holiday volume is thin and the market can be "a little wonky" with a slow start while participants return; "people tend to not want to move the market too much after a holiday." So "why throw good money after a gamble? Let it work out the kinks."
  - He lets the morning session go and wants a "pulse" on what the market does. It's "not about the money; it's about getting in sync with price action and not trying to force a will." There are plenty of days in the rest of the week to capture money.
  - Because of the holiday, the new week opening gap high was not his default objective as it normally would be (he mentions he would otherwise aim for it), but it ended up as a reference.
  - Paper trading disclosure: he says he's in paper trading this morning so viewers can stop worrying about "counting pennies."
- **How to use:** First session after a holiday: reduced size (1 contract/micro or paper), look for reasons the market agrees with your expectations, scale up only after price confirms.
- **Timestamps:** [0:03:31](https://youtu.be/VBgfJRMVCaI?t=211) — one contract, paper trade, aligning with price; [0:06:58](https://youtu.be/VBgfJRMVCaI?t=418) — why paper trade after a holiday; [0:15:30](https://youtu.be/VBgfJRMVCaI?t=930) — rule of thumb: after holidays go in light.
- **Nuance / caveats:** A sizing/process rule, not a PD-array rule; he explicitly says the information (gap/FVG logic) stays the same.

title: How To Engage Price After Holiday Volume Days
head: Premium Opening Range Gap + Friday's First Presented FVG as framing for a short
body:
- **Kind:** entry model (applied)
- **What ICT says:**
  - At the 9:30 open there was a premium opening range gap of roughly 100 handles (open above the prior RTH settlement). He frames it from the RTH settlement to the 9:30 open, mid gap marked, with half-gap and full gap closure levels.
  - He also uses last Friday's (Aug 28) first presented FVG as a key reference ("we're using Friday's first presented fair value gap").
  - Plan: look for a reason for price to want to get down to the mid gap; place the short; stop above the second wick high; aim for the sell-side liquidity beneath.
  - After price traded "premium gap opening ... pull down half the gap" and then "just past half the gap" into a sell-side liquidity pool and the suspension block (below), full gap closure and the new week opening gap lie further down. He states he is not demanding the full closure.
- **How to use:** Short a premium gap on a reason (premium PD array), target the half gap first, then liquidity under it; keep a stop just above the high that invalidates the premium array (here the second wick high).
- **Example in this video:** NQ 1m, first morning after Labor Day: open ~100 handles above settlement; price first runs buy side, then pulls down to half the gap; a short entered into the upper part of the SIBI wick; stop just above the second wick high; half gap hit; risk removed; down into the suspension block and then below its low (sell side).
- **Timestamps:** [0:00:00](https://youtu.be/VBgfJRMVCaI?t=0) — premium gap ~100 handles, Friday's first presented FVG, mid gap; [0:01:55](https://youtu.be/VBgfJRMVCaI?t=115) — stop above second wick high, aim for sell side; [0:06:10](https://youtu.be/VBgfJRMVCaI?t=370) — buy side first, then half the gap, sell-side pool, full gap closure, NWOG below.

title: How To Engage Price After Holiday Volume Days
head: Suspension block  (new coinage / label, caption partly unclear)
body:
- **Kind:** new coinage
- **What ICT says:** A wick range with a volume imbalance at both ends: "inside that wick, and volume imbalance at both ends, so that's a suspension block." He treats it as a discount array when price reaches the lower part/low of it and says liquidity rests just below its low. He also divides the SIBI "with the volume imbalance low" for a consequent encroachment and remarks "there's liquidity resting right below that low."
- **How to identify:** Candle wick range bounded by volume imbalances at both its top and bottom (per his words; no further definition given in this clip).
- **How to use:** Short from the upper half / sell the premium side and expect the lower half (discount) to be tested and a sell-side pool just under it to be the target; remove risk once the half gap/block high is traded.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 1m: down into the suspension block high after the half gap fill; below its low there is a sell-side pool that is cleared.
- **Timestamps:** [0:02:42](https://youtu.be/VBgfJRMVCaI?t=162), [0:05:20](https://youtu.be/VBgfJRMVCaI?t=320).
- **Nuance / caveats:** Definition is thin and the caption is noisy; later he mentions a "semi mouse hole" (caption unclear — possibly the same structure). Needs confirmation from a dedicated lecture.

title: How To Engage Price After Holiday Volume Days
head: Premium sensitivity of a bearish FVG (SIBI): bodies in the lower half, upper half untested
body:
- **Kind:** rule | refinement
- **What ICT says:** For a SIBI (bearish FVG), the upper half is premium; if price trades into it but the BODIES do not close above the midpoint (CE) and the upper half is not tested at all, that is a sign of bearish order flow ("it's allowing for the market to want to pull up into this deeper" only if a close above CE happens). A close above the consequent encroachment means price is likely to trade back up toward 9:30's opening price again (reasonable, not unusual). He wants "some of that stay open ... remain completely untested at all" — the portion he wants untested is the upper part of the SIBI. When price goes into the lower half and looks "heavy," expect sells in the next few candles toward the new week opening gap high; if it goes into the upper half, treat it with caution. At the end he re-states: "premium sensitivity: not seeing the upper half of that SIBI traded to or even tested ... and we sold off."
- **How to identify:** Draw the SIBI, find its CE; track closes of bodies relative to CE; note whether the upper half was touched.
- **How to use:** Hold or add to shorts while bodies stay below CE; stop just above the high of the premium array; a body close above CE changes the expectation (back to 9:30 open). If price rallies only into the lower half of the gap and gets heavy, add to the sell.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 1m, post-Labor Day: price rallies into the lower half of the SIBI/suspension block, bodies never close at or above its midpoint, "got heavy," and drops to new lows into the new week opening gap high (caption "NWOG high for this week").
- **Timestamps:** [0:08:53](https://youtu.be/VBgfJRMVCaI?t=533) — bodies didn't close above/below the midpoint; [0:09:40](https://youtu.be/VBgfJRMVCaI?t=580) — lower half, "heavy"; [0:15:30](https://youtu.be/VBgfJRMVCaI?t=930) — premium sensitivity restated; [0:16:17](https://youtu.be/VBgfJRMVCaI?t=977) — final rule review.
- **Nuance / caveats:** The wording about "upper/lower half" conflates the SIBI with the suspension block in the captions; the rule (bodies below CE, upper half untested = continuation lower) is clear.

title: How To Engage Price After Holiday Volume Days
head: Scaling out: "running down equity" / partial at every new low
body:
- **Kind:** rule (trade management)
- **What ICT says:** Remove risk when the half gap is filled. Any position still open: stop just above the high. Anytime price creates a new low and you haven't taken a partial yet, it's a good idea to "pay yourself" — especially if sell-side liquidity rests below the low and has just been cleared. He calls this "running down equity": pursue new increases in your account balance rather than demanding that your entire "terminus" (final target) be the only way you get paid. He says this matters while you're developing and working out your model.
- **How to use:** Partial at the low where sell-side was just cleared; move stop above the high; leave the remainder for the final objective.
- **Timestamps:** [0:02:42](https://youtu.be/VBgfJRMVCaI?t=162) — remove the risk at half gap; [0:10:29](https://youtu.be/VBgfJRMVCaI?t=629) — partial at new low; "running down equity."
- **Nuance / caveats:** "Terminus" is the term he uses for the ultimate target (also the name of one of his models; here used generically).

title: How To Engage Price After Holiday Volume Days
head: Overnight Asia long: new week opening gap + Friday's first presented FVG (recap of his own trade)
body:
- **Kind:** example only
- **What ICT says:** Last night in Asia he traded: price dropped into the new week opening gap for the present week; the bodies stayed above ("they weren't interested in exploring any lower"); one candle opened below it, the next opened at it and rallied; "discount sensitivity" was visible. Price rallied into Friday August 28th's first presented FVG, retraced back down into it; he elected highs to the left as the draw. Entry was inside Friday's first presented FVG (caption: 595.25), stop under the low of a candle; price came close to the stop but did not reach it ("a little bit of heat" — lowest low against him around 75 per caption, roughly 10–20 handles on three contracts, which he called insignificant). Then price rallied through the highs, kept going, and "gave up the ghost" at 12:46 a.m. ET with a sell-off back down to the new week opening gap, then to Thursday's first presented FVG, then taking out lows (this morning).
- **How to use:** Illustrates using a weekly/daily-gap PD array (NWOG) plus prior day's first presented FVG as discount arrays in a long, with a draw to the highs to the left.
- **Example in this video:** NQ, overnight (Asia) into the morning: long in Friday Aug 28 first presented FVG with stop below a candle low and a draw to prior highs; hit; reversed at 12:46 a.m. ET.
- **Timestamps:** [0:11:33](https://youtu.be/VBgfJRMVCaI?t=693), [0:12:20](https://youtu.be/VBgfJRMVCaI?t=740) — NWOG/discount sensitivity and first presented FVG; [0:13:06](https://youtu.be/VBgfJRMVCaI?t=786) — entry, stop, heat; [0:13:53](https://youtu.be/VBgfJRMVCaI?t=833) — 12:46 a.m. reversal.
- **Nuance / caveats:** Price digits are unreliable in captions (595.25, 75, 1825).

title: NFP Review & New Student Encouragement
head: TGIF (Thank God It's Friday) — weekly range retracement  (aliases ICT uses: "TGIF", "20 to 30% of the weekly range")
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:** When a week has a lot of range, or moves in one direction, price tends to retrace 20–30% of that weekly range late in the week. Draw a fib from the weekly low to the weekly high and mark the 20% and 30% levels. The retracement can begin as early as 1:00 p.m. ET Thursday or in the later stages of Friday trading. There is no single specific time, so you must know what direction the market should be going to agree with that retracement.
- **How to identify:** One-directional or large-range week. Fib from the week's low to its high (for a bearish retracement; the reverse for an up retracement) with 20% and 30% levels annotated. He also keeps a weekly candle on the right-hand side of the chart to see the week's high, low, open and close.
- **How to use:** Use 20% and 30% as retracement targets or reaction zones on Thursday afternoon and Friday. He publicly tweeted "TGIF" early Friday before NFP and 9:30. He says he has a separate short video on TGIF on his channel.
- **Example in this video:** NQ, week ending Fri Aug 28. 20% level = 29,549.00 and 30% level = 29,471.25. After NFP, price dropped through the low and hit the 20% level "handsomely" on the number. Later in the day it fell to Thursday's first presented FVG low and the 30% level.
- **Timestamps:** [0:00:00](https://youtu.be/-Qag-99u_BM?t=0) — TGIF set-up with the weekly candle; [0:00:49](https://youtu.be/-Qag-99u_BM?t=49) — the 20–30% retracement rule and its timing window; [0:01:37](https://youtu.be/-Qag-99u_BM?t=97) — the two price levels; [0:18:32](https://youtu.be/-Qag-99u_BM?t=1112) — 30% hit, tweeted in advance.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Given as a tendency, not a trigger. Direction still has to come from your read of what the market should do.

title: NFP Review & New Student Encouragement
head: Regular trading hours (RTH) opening range gap  (aliases: "opening range gap", "RTH ORG")
body:
- **Kind:** definition + example
- **What ICT says:** The gap between the RTH settlement (4:14 p.m. ET the previous day) and the 9:30 a.m. ET open the next day. This is not the electronic overnight data, which he distinguishes from regular trading hours. The 9:30 open price is the high of the gap (here a gap-down), the prior close is the other edge, and the midpoint is the consequent encroachment (CE).
- **How to identify:** Mark Thursday's 4:14 p.m. ET RTH settlement, mark Friday's 9:30 opening price, and shade between them (he used bright yellow).
- **How to use:** If price trades back inside the gap, use it as a premium array on the way up, expecting premium-sensitive selling. The expected path is a run up into the 9:30 opening price (the high of the gap), then a move lower that takes out the CE. The gap's high edge acts as resistance.
- **Example in this video:** NQ Fri Aug 28. Thursday RTH settlement = 29,521.25 (4:14 p.m.). Friday 9:30 open sits above it. After price traded back below the low formed in the NDOG, he looked for a run up into the 9:30 open and then a move lower through the CE.
- **Timestamps:** [0:07:17](https://youtu.be/-Qag-99u_BM?t=437) — Thursday 4:14 p.m. ET settle and 9:30 Friday open explained; [0:08:05](https://youtu.be/-Qag-99u_BM?t=485) — shades the gap and defines it; [0:08:53](https://youtu.be/-Qag-99u_BM?t=533) — premium-array expectation, CE, targets.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** He says it is "inside the gap", so it uses that area as a premium array. Tied to his conviction after the low was taken out. The 4:14 settlement time is as heard in the captions (caption slightly unclear).

title: NFP Review & New Student Encouragement
head: NDOG used as a liquidity reference (new day opening gap)  (aliases: "orange box")
body:
- **Kind:** example only
- **What ICT says:** The low that price ran through on NFP "formed randomly" inside Thursday's new day opening gap (the orange box on his chart). Price took that low out and then continued lower.
- **How to use:** Marked in advance, the NDOG low was a visible liquidity point.
- **Example in this video:** NQ, Thursday's NDOG low taken on NFP after the 8:30 move, then price kept falling toward the 20% retracement level.

title: NFP Review & New Student Encouragement
head: First Presented FVG (FPFVG) of Mondays / Fridays / days  (aliases: "first presented fair value gap")
body:
- **Kind:** refinement
- **What ICT says:** The first FVG formed after 9:30 ET is the "first presented" FVG of the day. He tracks Monday's and Friday's first presented FVGs for the last two weeks. The market "many times" makes significant intraday or daily highs at them, and sometimes a weekly or monthly high. He asks students not to take his word for it but to keep records.
- **How to use:** Keep the prior two weeks of Monday and Friday FPFVGs on the chart as reference levels for reversals and targets. You can also keep several separate layouts: one for FPFVGs only, one for NWOG only, one for NDOG only, one for RTH opening range gaps. How you split them is up to you.
- **Example in this video:** NQ Friday Aug 28: the first FVG after 9:30 formed on the rally up. Price failed to take the highs of the wicks. Thursday's (Aug 27) FPFVG low was later a target on the way down. During the lunch-macro pullback, price rallied into a prior Friday's FPFVG ("last Friday's", caption unclear which Friday) and then dropped.
- **Timestamps:** [0:03:16](https://youtu.be/-Qag-99u_BM?t=196) — Friday's first presented FVG formed; [0:13:41](https://youtu.be/-Qag-99u_BM?t=821) — Monday/Friday FPFVGs of the last two weeks marking highs; [0:14:28](https://youtu.be/-Qag-99u_BM?t=868) — layout suggestions.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** The claim "many times" is a tendency.

title: NFP Review & New Student Encouragement
head: Run on liquidity does not need to take the wicks  (aliases: "run on old high / old higher low")
body:
- **Kind:** refinement
- **What ICT says:** At 8:30 the wicks rallied above the short-term high without a candle body closing above it. After 9:30, price rallied again and failed to take the highs of the wicks. A run on liquidity or an old high does not necessarily need to take out the wicks. If the bodies of the recent candles are significantly higher than the close of the earlier candle, that can be enough (caption partly unclear).
- **How to identify:** Compare bodies, not just wicks, against the old high.
- **How to use:** Do not insist on a wick-through of every old high before treating the liquidity as taken. But on NFP Friday he still did not trust a short here, for the event-risk reason below.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 8:30 NFP: wicks poked above the short-term high without a body above it; the post-9:30 rally again fell short of those wick highs.
- **Timestamps:** [0:02:29](https://youtu.be/-Qag-99u_BM?t=149) — 8:30 wicks above, no body above; [0:03:16](https://youtu.be/-Qag-99u_BM?t=196) — rally fails to take the wick highs and the "run does not need the wicks" idea.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** He frames this as something "taught in the past".

title: NFP Review & New Student Encouragement
head: NFP / event-day risk: abstain or reduce  (aliases: "don't trade Mondays and Fridays" joke)
body:
- **Kind:** rule / psychology
- **What ICT says:** He normally abstains from trading NFP Thursday and Friday. On this NFP Friday before a long weekend he did not trust shorting the inversion FVG or the immediate rebalance, as he did not want to be caught in a quick run-up that took out the highs. If it had not been NFP day, he says he would have shorted the inversion FVG, the immediate rebalance, and pyramided into more entries on the SIBI-type bounce that later became an inversion FVG. The "don't trade Mondays and Fridays" line is a running joke of naysayers. He used his model and a few factors rather than blanket rules.
- **How to identify:** NFP day, long weekend, price near a short-term high with unresolved buy-side above.
- **How to use:** Respect event risk; either stand aside or wait for a clean confirmation (here, the low being taken out) before engaging.
- **Example in this video:** NQ Fri Aug 28. Price rallied into a short-term high after 9:30, creating an inversion FVG and immediate rebalance he skipped. Only after the low was taken out did he treat it as a market maker sell model that would not run up to take out the buy side at 29,704.50 (his words: "that's not weakness. That's knowing what I want to see").
- **Timestamps:** [0:04:05](https://youtu.be/-Qag-99u_BM?t=245) — why he did not trust shorting on NFP / long weekend, and what he would have done on a normal day; [0:05:42](https://youtu.be/-Qag-99u_BM?t=342) — MMSM conviction once the low is taken, buy side 29,704.50.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Says he is teaching students to respect risk on NFP Friday, so he should behave the same way himself.

title: NFP Review & New Student Encouragement
head: Short entry management in the video (manual close)
body:
- **Kind:** example only
- **What ICT says:** A short recorded live in the premium of the gap, with the targets Thursday's first percent FVG (Aug 27) and 30% of the weekly range. During the recording he said it was a last-chance type of area: if price did not get there, he would be stopped out, and it was "not likely to pan out". He closed it manually before the stop, which would have been hit ("stopped in the black", i.e. not a loss). Price later went lower after the recording, in the afternoon, to the Aug 27 FPFVG low and the 30% level. He admits he could have been "all over this" with much larger profit but says that is not the point.
- **Timestamps:** [0:09:40](https://youtu.be/-Qag-99u_BM?t=580) — manual close, later target reached; [0:12:55](https://youtu.be/-Qag-99u_BM?t=775) — short taken at the first 10:00-hour high, covered there.

title: NFP Review & New Student Encouragement
head: Lunch macro (11:30 latest start) and the 10:00-hour first high  (aliases: "lunch macro")
body:
- **Kind:** rule / refinement
- **What ICT says:** 11:30 a.m. ET is the latest time at which you should anticipate a delayed lunch macro starting. At that time price tends to pull back into the range built earlier. To find the target: take the 10:00 hour (10:00–11:00), and from the 11:00 line scan left to the first high you hit inside the 10:00 hour. That high is what the lunch macro retracement reaches. Order flow: if bullish, price stays in the upper half of the PD array / inefficiency and the bodies stay in the upper half. In this example, price did not reach the full high and respected the midpoint (CE) of the area before dropping.
- **How to identify:** (1) Draw a box across the 10:00 hour; (2) from 11:00 go left to the very first high in that hour; (3) check time is about 11:30; (4) check bodies are respecting the upper half.
- **How to use:** Used to time a short and to place a stop just above the first 10:00-hour high; or to expect a retracement, then continuation to lower targets (here 30% of the weekly range).
- **Example in this video:** NQ Aug 28: price traded lower into 11:30 without retracing; at 11:30 it pulled up into the first high of the 10:00 hour (where his short was taken and covered) and into a prior Friday's FPFVG, then dropped to the 30% level.
- **Timestamps:** [0:11:18](https://youtu.be/-Qag-99u_BM?t=678) — 11:30 lunch macro latest start, go back in the 10:00 hour; [0:12:06](https://youtu.be/-Qag-99u_BM?t=726) — blue box 10:00–11:00 and "first high to the left" method; [0:16:09](https://youtu.be/-Qag-99u_BM?t=969) — upper half order flow and the 11:30 repeat; [0:20:07](https://youtu.be/-Qag-99u_BM?t=1207) — "at 11:30 it's got to start following its script".
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** This is the clearest statement of the "first high of the 10:00 hour" lunch-macro target in this batch; ICT specifies 11:30 as the last line, not the standard start.

title: NFP Review & New Student Encouragement

body:
- **Kind:** refinement
- **What ICT says:** In the lunch-macro rally, the candle bodies did not trade all the way to the high of the area; they respected its midpoint. He also states the general order-flow rule that bullish order flow keeps the bodies in the upper half of the PD array / inefficiency. (Which area exactly he means is not fully clear from the captions; the "bearish" reading here is my inference from the context of the short.)
- **Timestamps:** [0:16:09](https://youtu.be/-Qag-99u_BM?t=969) — upper half rule; [0:17:45](https://youtu.be/-Qag-99u_BM?t=1065) — bodies respect the midpoint.

title: How New Students Should Start Part 4 \ Pillars Of Daily Log Entries
head: The three-pillar daily logging routine  (aliases ICT uses: "logging key phenomenon daily", "three primary pillars", "daily log entries")
body:
- **Kind:** rule / study method
- **What ICT says:** Do not try to learn everything fast; new students who rush learn nothing. Start with three things, but do not look for all three at once. Weeks 1–2: pick one pillar. Weeks 3–4: add a second. Weeks 5–6: add the third. After that make it a steady diet, logged every single day. A more advanced student who has never done this can do all three from the start. Without this, he says you will not be consistent and will hop from one thing to the next. He says people who call his material over-complicated are trying to discourage you.
- **How to use:** Three screenshots per day (one per pillar), chart centered and zoomed so that the highest high to lowest low fill the screen, leaving empty space to write observations. Takes about 20 minutes a day for all three. Review all screenshots on Saturday or Sunday when the market is not moving, because you will see details you missed live. Do it on one market only, NASDAQ, even if you will trade something else (so that his NASDAQ references will resonate). Go back six weeks of old data and do the same, then walk forward six weeks: 12 weeks of data in total. Start day 1 "next Tuesday" after the US Labor Day Monday. This is logging only, not backtesting; the next video covers backtesting.
- **Example in this video:** n/a (method). Instrument for the examples is not named in the captions on screen; he tells students to use NASDAQ.
- **Timestamps:** [0:01:58](https://youtu.be/L81eMQhmXmc?t=118) — three things to start with and the two-week stagger; [0:05:12](https://youtu.be/L81eMQhmXmc?t=312) — six weeks, or all three if more advanced; [0:24:46](https://youtu.be/L81eMQhmXmc?t=1486) — six weeks back plus six weeks forward on NASDAQ; [0:26:21](https://youtu.be/L81eMQhmXmc?t=1581) — about 20 minutes a day, start the Tuesday after Labor Day.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** He says the principles work in all markets, including CFDs and forex, but he uses futures (regulated, not CFD) because it allows many examples; CFD traders must match things up.

title: How New Students Should Start Part 4 \ Pillars Of Daily Log Entries
head: Pillar 1 — Pre-market session (7:00–9:00 a.m. ET) range and character  (aliases: "pre-market hours phase", "relative equal lows / relative equal highs", "highest high and lowest low")
body:
- **Kind:** rule / study method
- **What ICT says:** Every trading day except Sunday has a pre-market window of 7:00 a.m. to 9:00 a.m. Eastern. Draw a vertical line at 7:00 and one at 9:00, and mark the highest high and lowest low between them (draw a box around the range). Also mark any relative equal highs/lows inside it. These are the specific pools of liquidity for the day; it removes the ambiguity of "which high or low matters". Then note whether price between 7 and 9 is trending (small range vs one-way movement; could be up or down) or consolidating (sideways). For a brand-new student, reduce it to trending or consolidating. A more advanced alternative is the four phases/conditions of the market (expansion, reversal, consolidation, etc.) from the first video of the 2016 paid mentorship playlist, not necessary here.
- **How to identify:** (1) lines at 7:00 and 9:00; (2) highest high and lowest low in between; (3) relative equal highs/lows; (4) character: trending or consolidating.
- **How to use:** The 7–9 character is a precursor ("crystal ball") for how the market tends to book after 9:30 ET: expansion/trend or chop. He says "it's not a panacea" and will not work every day. The stated example is a trend between 7 and 9 that was followed by a small expansion at 9:30 and then consolidation the rest of the day. (The rule for what a consolidating pre-market implies is cut off in the captions: caption unclear.) The simplest trade shown: after price trades below the relative equal lows (a sweep), aim for the opposite end of the 7–9 range (the high); hitting it is a "bread-and-butter" setup and "you're done for the day".
- **How to log:** The screenshot, plus notes on: the phase/condition, the raw numbers (highest high, lowest low, relative equal levels), how those levels were traded to (if at all), and the time elapsed from 9:30 until price reacted off a key liquidity level. ICT himself logs these by hand in leather journals (not electronically) and says he has done this every day for about 34 years.
- **Example in this video:** 1-minute chart. Price trended up in the 7–9 window from a low to a high. A pair of relative equal lows formed in the window. After 9:30 price swept below the equal lows and then rallied to the 7–9 high ("hit it right here"). A little expansion at 9:30, then consolidation for the rest of the day.
- **Timestamps:** [0:05:12](https://youtu.be/L81eMQhmXmc?t=312) — pillar 1 introduced; [0:06:03](https://youtu.be/L81eMQhmXmc?t=363) — 7:00 and 9:00 vertical lines, highest high/lowest low; [0:07:44](https://youtu.be/L81eMQhmXmc?t=464) — trending vs consolidating (and 2016 four conditions); [0:10:08](https://youtu.be/L81eMQhmXmc?t=608) — "crystal ball" for post-9:30; [0:10:55](https://youtu.be/L81eMQhmXmc?t=655) — sweep of equal lows then run to opposite end of 7–9 range; [0:11:44](https://youtu.be/L81eMQhmXmc?t=704) — how ICT journals it by hand.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** This is a study/logging exercise first; he is not telling students to trade it yet.

title: How New Students Should Start Part 4 \ Pillars Of Daily Log Entries
head: Pillar 2 — RTH opening range gap and consequent encroachment delivery  (aliases: "regular trading hours opening range gap", "RTH ORG", "CE", "middle of the inefficiency")
body:
- **Kind:** rule / study method
- **What ICT says:** On TradingView, use a 1-minute chart and switch the lower-right toggle from ETH (electronic trading hours) to RTH. The gap is between the previous day's 4:14 p.m. ET final print (the close of that 1-minute candle) and the 9:30 a.m. ET opening price. Draw a rectangle across the gap with the "mid level" option turned on (set it in the favorites) so the middle (consequent encroachment, CE) is shown. Log how price pulls back to half the gap and how quickly. In the example it does it almost immediately (the 9:31 candle open trades right down to it, "second minute after 9:30"). He estimates roughly a 70% likelihood it reaches the CE by 10:00 a.m. but says "don't hold me to that": keep daily records and calculate your own statistics at year-end.
- **How to identify:** RTH-only view; previous 4:14 p.m. close; 9:30 open; rectangle with mid-line.
- **How to use:** Anchor a target at the CE. If looking for lower prices, take any old fair value gap or bearish order block (once you learn them) and target the CE; no need to expect the whole gap to close. Annotate the screenshot with observations such as "third time this week it went to the RTH ORG CE by 10 o'clock", and the entry idea (e.g. an inversion fair value gap higher up selling down to the CE).
- **Example in this video:** 1-minute chart; the gap lies below the open (a gap-down); price opens at 9:30 and by 9:31 trades down to the CE; short idea from an inversion FVG up top to the CE.
- **Timestamps:** [0:12:33](https://youtu.be/L81eMQhmXmc?t=753) — pillar 2 introduced; [0:13:22](https://youtu.be/L81eMQhmXmc?t=802) — ETH/RTH toggle, 4:14 p.m. final print; [0:14:13](https://youtu.be/L81eMQhmXmc?t=853) — rectangle with mid level; [0:15:50](https://youtu.be/L81eMQhmXmc?t=950) — pullback to half the gap, 70% by 10:00 claim; [0:16:40](https://youtu.be/L81eMQhmXmc?t=1000) — anchor a target, annotate observations.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** The 4:14 p.m. time and the "70%" are his stated figures; the 70% is explicitly not to be trusted without your own stats.

title: How New Students Should Start Part 4 \ Pillars Of Daily Log Entries
head: Pillar 3 — Silver Bullet first presented FVG after 10:00 a.m. ET  (aliases: "Silver Bullet", "first presented fair value gap in the 10:00 hour")
body:
- **Kind:** entry model (study version) / rule
- **What ICT says:** On a 1-minute chart, look at 10:00 a.m. ET. The 10:00 candle itself can be part of an FVG, or the next candles. The first FVG that forms inside the 10:00 hour is the one to log. Include volume imbalance: when candle bodies don't meet in a potential FVG, include that gap. Draw a rectangle for the FVG and extend it to the right at first; when annotating, turn extending off and drag it to the first time price returns into it. The pattern: price creates the FVG, drops lower after 10:00 and forms a short-term low, rallies back up into the FVG, then from the FVG goes down below that low where sell-side liquidity sits. It tells you what time it forms, how it forms, and you only need to determine where the high/low is that it aims for.
- **How to identify:** (1) 10:00 ET start on a 1-minute chart; (2) the first FVG (incl. volume imbalance) in the 10:00 hour; (3) price returns into it; (4) price takes the short-term low (or high) created after the FVG formed.
- **How to use / log:** In the first four to six weeks, do not try to predict direction; record it after the fact. Record the time the FVG formed (example: 10:01 ET), how many minutes before price came back into it, and the range in handles from the return high to the low it took (highest high to lowest low). Over time you will see the formations, and where it goes (sell side or buy side). Keep an electronic log if possible with keywords.
- **Example in this video:** 1-minute chart: 10:00 candle then 10:01 candle leaves a sell-side imbalance / buy-side inefficiency gap (SIBI) with a volume imbalance; price drops lower after 10:00 to a short-term low, rallies back up into the FVG, then sells down through that low (sell side). Earlier in the day price came far from a high, rallied, broke the lows, and traded back up.
- **Timestamps:** [0:18:17](https://youtu.be/L81eMQhmXmc?t=1097) — pillar 3 introduced; [0:19:06](https://youtu.be/L81eMQhmXmc?t=1146) — first FVG in the 10:00 hour, 10:01 SIBI example; [0:19:54](https://youtu.be/L81eMQhmXmc?t=1194) — volume imbalance, rectangle extension tip, sequence of the setup; [0:23:09](https://youtu.be/L81eMQhmXmc?t=1389) — what to record (time, minutes, handles).
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** This pins the Silver Bullet to the 10:00 hour first FVG only, as a "streamlined" version; the entry/stop/target rules are not covered here.

title: How New Students Should Start Part 4 \ Pillars Of Daily Log Entries
head: Journaling / logging method  (aliases: "silver bullet log 10 a.m.", "pre-market session condition or phase", "pre-market liquidity pools")
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:** Store entries in a searchable electronic format with keywords, by date and topic. Suggested tags: "silver bullet log 10 a.m."; "pre-market session condition or phase and pre-market liquidity pools"; "regular trading hours opening range gap consequent encroachment delivery". Be neat, organized and concise, as if a professor were grading neatness: it is "a sign of character" and in 10 years the notes are a time machine of what you learned that day. He lacks that benefit because his journals are leather books.
- **Timestamps:** [0:27:09](https://youtu.be/L81eMQhmXmc?t=1629) — neatness and organization; [0:28:42](https://youtu.be/L81eMQhmXmc?t=1722) — electronic keyword tags.

title: My Model On NQ NFP Friday
head: Short from the RTH opening range gap high (9:30 open) with stacked PD arrays  (aliases: "high of the opening range gap", "daily volume imbalance", "daily bias on the balance sell side inefficiency", "new week opening gap high")
body:
- **Kind:** example only (entry model application)
- **What ICT says:** Price traded up into the high of that day's RTH opening range gap, i.e. the 9:30 opening price. That level coincides with (a) the high of a daily buy-side imbalance / sell-side inefficiency (as heard: "daily bias on the balance sell side inefficiency", caption unclear), (b) the upper portion of a daily volume imbalance he shaded gray and has been discussing for about three weeks, and (c) the high of the new week opening gap (purple shaded area). Price "didn't want to take the liquidity out of up here" (the relative equal highs stayed intact), so he expected it to come down for the stops below. He later notes it was also the high of the daily volume imbalance (blue area) and gets "a lot of reaction there".
- **How to identify:** RTH ORG high at the 9:30 open; overlapping higher-timeframe imbalance (daily volume imbalance / daily inefficiency) and NWOG high; relative equal highs left untouched above.
- **How to use:** Short from the premium array, stop above, target the sell side below and the first presented FVG of the previous day. See stop/management below.
- **Example in this video:** NQ Fri Aug 28 after 9:30. Price rallies to the 9:30 open (gap high) and stalls; relative equal highs above remain untouched. Price then declines through the NWOG low and the RTH ORG low, into the NFP low and the NDOG.
- **Timestamps:** [0:04:58](https://youtu.be/Khj1veL49r8?t=298) — expects to take out the ORG low and the NFP-formed low in Thursday's NDOG; [0:05:46](https://youtu.be/Khj1veL49r8?t=346) — ORG high / daily imbalance / liquidity left up above; [0:06:34](https://youtu.be/Khj1veL49r8?t=394) — NWOG high (purple) and aggressive acceleration wanted; [0:19:22](https://youtu.be/Khj1veL49r8?t=1162) — also the high of the daily volume imbalance (blue).
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** The video begins mid-trade (captions start 0:03:54), so the exact entry price is not given. Video 13 states the short was taken at the first high of the 10:00 hour.

title: My Model On NQ NFP Friday
head: Market maker logic: why would they leave the longs' stops?  (aliases: "think like a market maker")
body:
- **Kind:** refinement / reasoning
- **What ICT says:** Ask why, if you were the market maker, you would let longs keep their stop loss right below here after taking price down past the ORG low and to the low of the NWOG. The relative equal highs were left intact above, and longs are trying to hold for the whole day with stops sitting just below. So the expectation is a run down for those stops ("hot knife through butter") rather than a bounce. He adds that there is NFP liquidity resting just below 29,500, and that a "last kiss" retest of the ORG low before going lower is typical.
- **How to identify:** Price has already gone through the gap low and a prior-week gap low, longs' stops sit just below, equal highs are untouched.
- **How to use:** Hold the short for the stop run rather than expect a bounce; keep the stop on the gap side. When price breaks a prior low, lock in profit with a tighter stop, but not immediately, in case of a stop-hunting pop.
- **Example in this video:** NQ: price drops through ORG low, hits NWOG low ("banging the low of the new week opening gap"), clears the NFP low, retests the ORG low once more as the "last kiss before the train leaves", and then keeps dropping.
- **Timestamps:** [0:08:57](https://youtu.be/Khj1veL49r8?t=537) — "hot knife through butter", longs holding with stops below, equal highs left intact; [0:12:54](https://youtu.be/Khj1veL49r8?t=774) — "think you're the market maker" argument; [0:13:42](https://youtu.be/Khj1veL49r8?t=822) — repeated; [0:17:57](https://youtu.be/Khj1veL49r8?t=1077) — touches the ORG low again, "last kiss".
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Presented partly as banter, but it is the logic behind the sell-side-first expectation.

title: My Model On NQ NFP Friday
head: Nested PD arrays / full gap closure
body:
- **Kind:** refinement
- **What ICT says:** At a shaded array he sees "discount sensitivity" and describes nesting PD arrays (a gap inside a gap). He prefers that price tear through aggressively rather than "bop a pop" off a full gap closure. When the RTH ORG gap was fully closed he still wanted it to crush through and continue, because NFP liquidity sits just below 29,500. Expects the ORG low to give premium sensitivity (retail "resistance") as price retests it from below, with the middle of the NWOG (CE) in play.
- **Timestamps:** [0:08:09](https://youtu.be/Khj1veL49r8?t=489) — discount sensitivity, nesting PD arrays; [0:11:18](https://youtu.be/Khj1veL49r8?t=678) — full gap closure but wants it to crush through; [0:12:06](https://youtu.be/Khj1veL49r8?t=726) — ORG low as premium sensitivity, middle of the NWOG CE.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Caption quality is poor in this segment (partly unclear which gap he refers to at each point).

title: My Model On NQ NFP Friday
head: Targets: NFP sell-side, Thursday's first presented FVG, TGIF 20% / 30%  (aliases: "sell side right below that low", "30% retracement")
body:
- **Kind:** example only
- **What ICT says:** Primary objective: an acceleration down to take out the sell side right below the NFP low (which formed inside Thursday's NDOG; "find that" is his hint that the turning point lines up with an NDOG). Further: Thursday Aug 27's first presented FVG ("first minute of pre-market gap", caption unclear; he calls it Thursday of last week's first presented FVG at one point), and the TGIF 20% and 30% levels. The 20% level was reached in the NFP delivery (just over 25% retracement at one point). 30% of the weekly range = 29,471.25 (he says it is "still in contention"). A limit order sat near the high of Thursday's FPFVG.
- **How to use:** Layer targets from liquidity (NFP sell-side below 29,500), then first presented FVG, then the TGIF percent levels.
- **Timestamps:** [0:07:22](https://youtu.be/Khj1veL49r8?t=442) — acceleration to take the sell side below the low; [0:09:55](https://youtu.be/Khj1veL49r8?t=595) — 20% hit on NFP delivery, over 25% retracement, 30% below; [0:15:37](https://youtu.be/Khj1veL49r8?t=937) — Thursday Aug 27 FPFVG and 30% retracement 29,471.25; [0:27:13](https://youtu.be/Khj1veL49r8?t=1633) — limit order near Thursday's FPFVG high.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Matches the TGIF rule in video 13 (20–30%).

title: My Model On NQ NFP Friday
head: Trade management: ratcheting the stop, partial give-back tolerance, manual close
body:
- **Kind:** rule / example
- **What ICT says:** As price drops, he lowers the stop in steps, "take the starch out of those pants". He plans to move the stop to 29,543 once the low at 29,502 is taken (as heard, "bring the stop down to 543"; he waits so a weird pop does not sting him). He says he is fine being stopped out with large open profit ("You want 10 grand, you got to risk being stopped out"; no reason to give up more than about 5,000 of unrealized profit). Eventually he closes manually for about 6,470 (dollars, as stated) rather than let the stop be hit, and if price goes on to the target, he treats it as a coincidence. He puts the final target "just below" (as heard, six handles below some level; caption unclear) to cover.
- **How to use:** Lock profit in stages; take the manual exit when the structure that supported the idea stops working; use a limit order for the target. Accept missing the exact target.

title: Trading NFP Thursday High Resistance Liquidity Runs
head: New Week Opening Gap (High Resistance Liquidity Run)
body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:** The gap between Friday's RTH close and Monday's RTH open (similar to daily RTH gap, but spans the weekend). This gap is a significant liquidity magnet. On NFP week Thursdays (high volatility days), price often runs from intraday highs down to this new week gap low, targeting stop-losses above the gap high. This is called a "high resistance liquidity run" because price must overcome significant resistance (prior highs, relative equal highs) to reach the target.
- **How to identify:** Mark Friday's RTH close; mark Monday's RTH open; the void between is the new week opening gap.
- **How to use:** Use the low of this gap as a short target; use the high of this gap as stop-loss placement (just above it) for shorts.
- **Example in this video:** Monday's gap was targeted for a short entry; price ran from intraday highs down to this gap low throughout the day.
- **Timestamps:** [0:00:02](https://youtu.be/xpH0wDANtmM?t=2) "new week opening gap low," [0:00:52](https://youtu.be/xpH0wDANtmM?t=52) "relatively equal lows."
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** NFP week Thursdays see aggressive liquidity runs; use caution (position sizing, early profit-taking).

title: Trading NFP Thursday High Resistance Liquidity Runs
head: Quadrant Level (1/4 Gap Division)
body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:** Divide any gap (new week, daily RTH, etc.) into 4 equal parts using Fibonacci. The quadrant level (1/4 or 3/4 point) acts as short-term friction. For shorts below a gap, the upper quadrant is a retracement resistance; price often wicks to this level and reverses back down. This is a "kiss level" — price touches and respects it.
- **How to identify:** Identify gap high and low; measure distance; divide by 4; mark the 1/4 and 3/4 points.
- **How to use:** Shorts: expect retracement into upper quadrant on wicks; don't panic when price spikes there. Longs: use upper quadrant as breakout resistance confirmation.
- **Example in this video:** Quadrant level of the new week gap was identified; price spiked to this level, wicked, and reversed lower (confirmed weakness).
- **Timestamps:** [0:08:29](https://youtu.be/xpH0wDANtmM?t=509) "quadrant level," [0:09:17](https://youtu.be/xpH0wDANtmM?t=557) "Spiked up to that quadrant level. And look at the reaction."
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Quadrant is a friction level, not a reversal guarantee; context (bodies, other support) must confirm.

title: Trading NFP Thursday High Resistance Liquidity Runs
head: Octant Level (1/8 Gap Division)
body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:** Divide any gap into 8 equal parts using Fibonacci. Octant levels (1/8, 2/8, 3/8, etc.) are micro support/resistance points. An octant level is more precise than a quadrant for identifying weakness (bodies failing to close below an octant = weakness; bodies below = strength). Often used as "key gradient level" (especially 2/8 octant of major gaps).
- **How to identify:** Gap high and low; divide by 8; mark all 8 points.
- **How to use:** Shorts: bodies must close below target octant to confirm continuation. Failure = reversal. Longs: bodies closing above octant = strength.
- **Example in this video:** Octant level at 29,291.25; bodies closing below this level confirmed the short thesis; failure to reach this level would have signaled weakness.
- **Timestamps:** [0:10:06](https://youtu.be/xpH0wDANtmM?t=606) "octant level," [0:22:41](https://youtu.be/xpH0wDANtmM?t=1361) "I'm watching every little detail."
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** More granular than quadrant; requires precise charting.

title: Trading NFP Thursday High Resistance Liquidity Runs
head: Inversion Fair Value Gap (Short Entry Mechanics)
body:
- **Kind:** entry model (for shorts)
- **What ICT says:** When shorting from a high, identify an inefficiency (gap or volume imbalance) just below the entry point. This inefficiency becomes the "inversion FVG" for shorts — the equivalent of a long entry into an iFVG. Shorts should see the inversion FVG close below its low (bodies not floating in upper half) to confirm the move down.
- **How to identify:** Identify high; scan downward for the first gap or imbalance (low close, high open on next candle).
- **How to use:** Short entry should be at or above the inversion FVG; stop loss above it; target below; confirm by watching bodies stay in lower half of the gap.
- **Example in this video:** Inversion FVG identified at ~29,292–29,250 range; bodies needed to close below this range to confirm the short; when they did, continuation was confirmed.
- **Timestamps:** [0:01:48](https://youtu.be/xpH0wDANtmM?t=108) "I want to see this little gap in here behave like an inversion fair value gap," [0:02:51](https://youtu.be/xpH0wDANtmM?t=171) "weakness."
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Opposite of long iFVG entry; bodies must stay below the gap (not above) for confirmation.

title: Trading NFP Thursday High Resistance Liquidity Runs
head: Market Maker Sell Model (Three Stages)
body:
- **Kind:** definition (advanced)
- **What ICT says:** A market maker sell event typically unfolds in three distinct stages:
  1. **First Stage Distribution** — Institutional selling begins; price moves down steadily.
  2. **Second Stage Redistribution** — Main sell-off; most animated, fastest price movement; longest duration.
  3. **Third Stage Accumulation** (implied) — Sellers have left; price consolidates near lows before resuming or reversing.
  The second stage is the most violent; stop-losses are typically placed at the boundary between stage 1 and stage 2 to preserve capital if the model fails.
- **How to identify:** Track candlestick patterns and volume/bodies; early stage = steady decline + retracements touching prior highs; second stage = aggressive decline with minimal retracement; final stage = consolidation near lows.
- **How to use:** Identify which stage you're in; in stage 2, expect minimal pullback — hold position. In stage 1, be ready to add on weakness. Exit at the end of stage 2 or early stage 3.
- **Example in this video:** ICT identified transitioning from first stage distribution (early sell-off) to second stage redistribution (main acceleration); he did NOT lower stops during second stage to let price breathe and find larger move.
- **Timestamps:** [0:16:57](https://youtu.be/xpH0wDANtmM?t=1017) "first stage distribution," [0:16:57](https://youtu.be/xpH0wDANtmM?t=1017) "second stage redistribution," [0:20:07](https://youtu.be/xpH0wDANtmM?t=1207) "second stage redistribution, which means it's going to be the biggest, the most animated portion."
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Not to be confused with Wyckoff distribution; ICT's model is his own specific categorization.

title: Trading NFP Thursday High Resistance Liquidity Runs
head: First Presented Fair Value Gap (FPFVG) as Daily Reference
body:
- **Kind:** definition (context-specific)
- **What ICT says:** Each day, the FPFVG (first gap after 9:30 AM) serves as a daily reference level. If that gap forms on a 1-minute scale, the midpoint and boundaries of that gap (especially its consequent encroachment) act as support/resistance throughout the day. On multi-day reviews, prior days' FPFVGs are extended and monitored.
- **How to identify:** Mark the first gap that forms after 9:30 AM on the 1-minute chart for each day; extend those levels forward to future days.
- **How to use:** Use FPFVG boundaries to confirm or negate short/long thesis. Bodies respecting these levels = confirmation; bodies breaking = shift in bias.
- **Example in this video:** Wednesday's FPFVG, Tuesday's FPFVG, and Monday's FPFVG were all extended and monitored; price interactions with their boundaries confirmed the short bias throughout the multi-day sequence.
- **Timestamps:** [0:08:29](https://youtu.be/xpH0wDANtmM?t=509) "Tuesday of August 25th first present fair gap," [0:10:56](https://youtu.be/xpH0wDANtmM?t=656) "Wednesday of last week, August 26th. First presented fair value gap."
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Multiple days of FPFVGs create a framework; each one is a potential inflection point.

title: Trading NFP Thursday High Resistance Liquidity Runs
head: Daily Volume Imbalance (as Support/Resistance)
body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:** On the daily chart, gaps (high to low over daily candle) represent imbalances. These imbalances attract intraday price; they act as magnets. An imbalance low acts as support; an imbalance high acts as resistance. When price reaches a daily chart imbalance zone intraday, expect a reaction or consolidation.
- **How to identify:** Look at daily chart; identify gaps (wicks not filling the full range between open and close on consecutive days).
- **How to use:** Intraday, when price approaches a daily imbalance zone, anticipate friction or a bounce (even if overall trend is down, expect intraday hiccup).
- **Example in this video:** A daily chart volume imbalance (shaded blue area) was identified from Wednesday; when intraday price approached this zone, it reacted (bounced) before continuing lower.
- **Timestamps:** [0:15:12](https://youtu.be/xpH0wDANtmM?t=912) "daily chart volume of balance... blue box shaded area," [0:24:18](https://youtu.be/xpH0wDANtmM?t=1458) "reaction right off of that."
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Daily imbalances override intraday moves in terms of friction; they slow down intraday price.

title: Trading NFP Thursday High Resistance Liquidity Runs
head: Body Placement as Order Flow Confirmation
body:
- **Kind:** refinement
- **What ICT says:** For shorts, bodies MUST close below target levels (FPFVG low, octant level, etc.). If bodies close above or in the upper half of these levels despite price wicking below, it signals weakness in the downside move (indecision, potential reversal). Bodies in lower half = strength (institutional conviction). No bodies = best case (pure continuation).
- **How to identify:** After each candlestick close, note where the body sits relative to key level. Upper half = weakness; lower half = strength.
- **How to use:** Shorts: bodies in lower half = continue holding; bodies in upper half = start thinking of exits. Longs: opposite.
- **Example in this video:** Bodies consistently closed in lower half of FPFVG ranges, confirming the short thesis throughout the move. One retracement where bodies floated in upper half = warning signal, but ICT understood it was a stage-1 event, not a reversal.
- **Timestamps:** [0:13:22](https://youtu.be/xpH0wDANtmM?t=802) "we don't want to see any bodies in the upper half," [0:18:31](https://youtu.be/xpH0wDANtmM?t=1111) "That's bearish."
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Bodies are the most precise order flow indicator; use them above everything else.

title: Trading NFP Thursday High Resistance Liquidity Runs
head: NFP Week Trading Caution (High Manipulation)
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:** Non-farm payroll (NFP) weeks — especially Thursday and Friday post-release, and Wednesday post-11 AM ET — see high market manipulation from dealers and real market makers. Manual intervention is heavy. As an educator, ICT recommends new traders avoid these days entirely. Experienced traders can trade NFP days, but should expect adversity (whipsaws, stop-runs). Position sizing should be reduced 50–80%; take early partials rather than holding for full moves.
- **How to identify:** Check the economic calendar for NFP release dates (typically first Friday of each month); treat that week (Wed–Fri) as high-risk.
- **How to use:** New traders: don't trade. Experienced: reduce size, take partials early, expect adversity, don't be shocked by stopped-outs.
- **Example in this video:** ICT states he "wouldn't do any executions on a day I said I wouldn't do any" (NFP Thursday), but a sincere student's question prompted him to demonstrate on this high-risk day. He traded 3 contracts but took partials early due to the risk.
- **Timestamps:** [0:03:40](https://youtu.be/xpH0wDANtmM?t=220) "non-farm payroll weeks post 11:00 a.m. Eastern time on Wednesday," [0:03:40](https://youtu.be/xpH0wDANtmM?t=220) "high degree of manipulation."
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Not a rule against trading, but a risk acknowledgment; manipulation can hurt even correct setups.

title: Trading NFP Thursday High Resistance Liquidity Runs
head: Selling into Market Maker Weakness (Narrative Reversal)
body:
- **Kind:** refinement
- **What ICT says:** When retail narrative is primed to expect strength (e.g., "good" employment data), smart money (dealers, real market makers) often sell into that narrative to clean out buy-side stops. The setup that ICT trades often contradicts the retail narrative; employment data was used to prime bullishness, but ICT sold, knowing dealers would rug-pull retail and run the market down.
- **How to identify:** Read morning news/narrative; note retail expectation; check daily chart structure to see if it aligns or contradicts.
- **How to use:** Use narrative as contrarian filter; if retail is bullish but chart is set up for shorts, shorts are likely the smart move.
- **Example in this video:** Employment data (released 8:30 AM ET) primed retail to expect strength; but ICT had already identified new week gap low as target, implying downside intent.
- **Timestamps:** [0:00:02](https://youtu.be/xpH0wDANtmM?t=2) "market's reacting off of some bogus number," [0:24:18](https://youtu.be/xpH0wDANtmM?t=1458) "retail wants to see it go higher, which is wonderful because that's juxtaposed to what I believe smart money is anticipating."
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Not always applicable; context matters.

title: How New Students Should Start Part 3
head: Information management: separate layouts/matrices, no clutter  (aliases: "be a good manager of the data", "workspace/layout")
body:
- **Kind:** rule | process
- **What ICT says:**
  - Heat maps, liquidity maps and busy indicators make charts unreadable; what you need is key levels, PD arrays and a higher-timeframe/macro perspective, handled as a daily/weekly/monthly regimen: "you do X, Y, Z to get A, B, C data."
  - These reference points are used to "call price moves" and measure the strength/weakness and continuity of a price run.
  - Use layouts/workspaces (in TradingView, or any platform with saved layouts) and keep each layout to one family of data; avoid dragging all annotations onto one chart. His own cluttered chart equals what's on his notepad; he does most of his data management with journals and "piece of paper 99% of the time," annotating charts for students to follow his logic.
  - Everything he teaches is stored as levels you can toggle; tap into monthly keys anytime via the "monthly keys" layout; copy layouts by quarter.
  - He insists this is not complicated and tells those who think it is to leave; the stated cost of not managing data: "if you mishandle the data, you're not going to do well."
- **Timestamps:** [0:00:54](https://youtu.be/MB7clEZvF7s?t=54) — manage key levels, PDAs, HTF macro; [0:03:21](https://youtu.be/MB7clEZvF7s?t=201) — notepad equals chart; layouts; [0:39:12](https://youtu.be/MB7clEZvF7s?t=2352) — copy per quarter; "be a very good manager of the data".

title: How New Students Should Start Part 3
head: Monthly Macro Keys layout  (aliases: "monthly keys", "HTF macro perspective")
body:
- **Kind:** definition | rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - On the monthly chart mark the high, low, open and close of each of the last THREE months (here June, July, August 2026, labeled e.g. "August 2026 monthly high/low/opening/closing price"). Optionally extend to 12 months for a full calendar year.
  - Also keep the previous week's high and low (Monday–Friday range) as one reference; he is not tracking more than that: only monthly OHLC (three months) and previous week's high and low. (Sunday data: some platforms compress or omit Sundays; figure it out for your platform.)
  - Style he uses: highs and lows in blue; opening prices in black dashed lines.
  - Nothing else on this layout: no FVGs, order blocks, breakers, first presented FVGs, NWOGs or NDOGs.
  - Use: determine where price sits relative to the three-month range (here June's high to July's low) and the last month / year: premium (above 50%) or discount (below 50%) vs equilibrium. On 2 Sep 2026 (second trading day of September) price was sitting at about the midpoint of the three-month range, "right inside equilibrium," so the weekly and daily charts must give more information. Also measure where price is relative to the previous week's high/low (here the lower portion, a discount) and where the week opened relative to that range (it opened in the premium side).
  - "Quarterly shifts" tie to seasonal tendencies: the big swing-trader moves (he points to the 2016/2017 mentorship for quarterly shifts); understanding where the next quarterly shift is likely to go provides a daily edge.
  - Traders using a short-term mentality (1–3 days, "one shot one kill") use this logic of premium/discount over the last three months/previous week to frame their trade.
  - Write the levels, measure the previous week's range, and grade it (fib, "gradient levels and octants"); then take the fib off. Result: "key information about premium vs. discount relative to previous week's high/low, last month's high/low, last three months' range."
- **How to use:** Build the layout once per month/week, record the fib/gradient levels in your journal, remove the clutter afterwards.
- **Example in this video:** NQ monthly, 2 Sep 2026: June high and July low frame the 3-month range; price at 50%; weekly: opened in the premium of the previous week's range but now in a discount; daily: also at equilibrium of the relevant range.
- **Timestamps:** [0:05:14](https://youtu.be/MB7clEZvF7s?t=314) — last three months OHLC on the monthly chart; [0:06:52](https://youtu.be/MB7clEZvF7s?t=412) — where are we relative to the three-month range, nothing else on the chart; [0:08:30](https://youtu.be/MB7clEZvF7s?t=510) — halfway/equilibrium; [0:10:06](https://youtu.be/MB7clEZvF7s?t=606) — colors/styles, previous week high/low; [0:14:08](https://youtu.be/MB7clEZvF7s?t=848) — summary: key levels in reference to the real dealing range by time.
- **Nuance / caveats:** "Open, high, low, and close in deference to time" (his phrase) is his substitute for heat maps/liquidity maps.

title: How New Students Should Start Part 3
head: Premium / Discount / Equilibrium relative to the dealing range (macro version)
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:** Upper portion of the range is premium, below 50% is discount; at the 50% line is equilibrium. For short-term traders (1–3 days or "one shot one kill") use this to frame the trade. He applies it simultaneously to three months, previous week and daily ranges.
- **Timestamps:** [0:09:18](https://youtu.be/MB7clEZvF7s?t=558), [0:12:33](https://youtu.be/MB7clEZvF7s?t=753), [0:14:08](https://youtu.be/MB7clEZvF7s?t=848).

title: How New Students Should Start Part 3
head: Seasonal tendency for index futures (September–February)
body:
- **Kind:** rule (context)
- **What ICT says:** September is usually a weak, bearish month for index futures: they usually trade down into a low in September or October; rarely the seasonal low is made in November; then a flurry of action into year-end and up into the first week of February is the usual catalyst. In the last week of August it can already begin. He cautions it is a general rule of thumb, not a "must": "they can twist this thing around and go against the grain." He had told students the previous week that price would enter this seasonal sell-off.
- **Timestamps:** [0:12:33](https://youtu.be/MB7clEZvF7s?t=753), [0:16:32](https://youtu.be/MB7clEZvF7s?t=992).

title: How New Students Should Start Part 3
head: Daily PD array grading: volume imbalance, octants/quadrants, "no support in open air"
body:
- **Kind:** refinement | example
- **What ICT says:**
  - He had told students for a week that the sell-side objective was a daily volume imbalance (shaded blue) with a SIBI/volume imbalance and the consequent encroachment of a wick as an impact level. Price reached the high of that gap on one day and closed outside of it, a confirmation of lower prices; it then failed to reach the volume imbalance that day.
  - Treat a slightly up-close candle's tiny body as part of one big volume imbalance when the open/close difference is small: his example candle opened 288.00 and closed 289.50 (1.5 handles, six ticks), so he treats the whole range as the volume imbalance: draw it to the body with no extension, and include all levels graded inside.
  - Question he poses: what should price do trading down through a daily area with only a wick and open space (no bodies to build support)? Answer: not staggered/struggling; "there isn't a whole lot of opposition or obstruction," so price travels quickly through. Monday it traded down through once and then absorbed; on Tuesday at about 3:00 a.m. it "cascaded" through the whole gap in the overnight session with no support at any of the usual support/resistance spots.
  - Grade the PD array (the blue daily gap) from low to high with a fib: split into eighths: highest octant at the high, then upper quadrant, the second octant above CE (midpoint), CE, lower octant below midpoint, lower quadrant, lowest octant, and lowest (his wording on octant/quadrant is loose in captions; the structure is eighths with quarter levels marked). On the 1-minute chart the market then used these levels precisely: it broke below the highest octant, came down to the upper quadrant, back up to the upper octant, sold off to the lower octant, back up to the upper quadrant, broke lower to and through CE "as you would expect"; with weak order flow it does not return to CE once broken; it then traded to the lower quadrant, back up to the octant, down to the lowest octant/quadrant and out of the gap, using the low of the daily FVG, the middle (dotted CE of the big gap), and the lowest octant "bang" as the lowest volume imbalance on the daily.
  - He argues the algorithm "really uses these levels because it's algorithmic, it's scripted" (floor pivots mentioned as other levels).
  - Having reached this objective during non-farm payroll week, price was "gyrating in no man's land" at CE.
- **How to use:** Grade any PD array you are interacting with (daily range of the gap) in octants/quarters; use CE and octants as intraday support/resistance in the direction of order flow; expect fast delivery through areas with no bodies.
- **Example in this video:** NQ daily and 1m, 31 Aug–2 Sep 2026: daily blue volume imbalance (price traded down through it Tuesday around 3:00 a.m.); graded levels interact precisely on 1m through Wednesday.
- **Timestamps:** [0:16:32](https://youtu.be/MB7clEZvF7s?t=992) — SIBI/CE reaction and close outside; [0:17:19](https://youtu.be/MB7clEZvF7s?t=1039) — treating a small-body candle's range as a volume imbalance; [0:19:05](https://youtu.be/MB7clEZvF7s?t=1145) — open space = no obstruction; [0:22:21](https://youtu.be/MB7clEZvF7s?t=1341) — grading with fib low to high; [0:24:44](https://youtu.be/MB7clEZvF7s?t=1484) — octant/quadrant walk-through on 1m; [0:27:08](https://youtu.be/MB7clEZvF7s?t=1628) — lowest octant and CE of the daily gap.
- **Nuance / caveats:** The octant/quadrant terminology is inconsistent in the captions ("octant", "quadrant", "percentile"); treat as eighths/quarters of a PD array. Price values are caption-derived.

title: How New Students Should Start Part 3
head: Transposing higher-timeframe levels into lower timeframes (time is the most important)
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:** Take higher-timeframe reference points and transpose them to the lower timeframe, think in premium/discount, grade levels and inefficiencies, then know key levels and TIME ("time is the aspect that's most important"). He says he is condensing the entire 2016/2017 mentorship focus in this video. OHLC "in deference to time" gives the highest degree of where big moves come from, so heat maps and liquidity maps are unnecessary. Everything he teaches is designed to be used "the way I designed it."
