title: How New Students Should Start Part 3
head: New Week Opening Gap (NWOG) matrix: definition and how to build it
body:
- **Kind:** definition | how-to
- **What ICT says:**
  - NWOG = difference between the Sunday 6:00 p.m. ET open (every Sunday) and the previous Friday's last print (ETH 4:59 p.m. on the 1-minute chart). If a holiday prevents trading on Friday, use Thursday.
  - Keep a rotating display of at least the last five weeks' NWOGs on a layout with nothing else on it; label each gap by its date and keep colors consistent. (He suggests labeling with the date, e.g., "NWOG Aug 30", any format works.)
  - How to draw (TradingView): switch to electronic trading hours (ETH); use the calendar "go to date" to jump to the previous Sunday at 18:00 (military time 1800 = 6 p.m. ET); zoom in; anchor the rectangle at the Friday close at 4:59 p.m. (the last print, down-close candle: anchor to the close) and drag up to the Sunday 6:00 p.m. opening price. Repeat going back week by week (example weeks: Sunday Aug 30; Friday Aug 21 4:59 p.m. close to Sunday Aug 23 open).
  - Manage the objects via the object tree: rename each (e.g., "NWOG Aug 23"), toggle visibility, copy the layout for each quarter and delete old ones; hiding old ones keeps them in the list for later.
  - Reading the matrix: hovering over a gap highlights it; use consequent encroachment of the gap; price "meandering around an empty space between two key PD arrays" can be read relative to the nearest NWOGs.
- **Example in this video:** Layout with five NWOGs and first presented FVGs; on 2 Sep price was in no-man's land between a previous Monday first presented FVG and Tuesday's first presented FVG (and Wednesday's), far from an NDOG and with another far below.
- **Timestamps:** [0:31:57](https://youtu.be/MB7clEZvF7s?t=1917) — NWOG definition, Sunday 6 p.m. vs Friday close, holiday rule; [0:32:46](https://youtu.be/MB7clEZvF7s?t=1966) — keep five rotating weeks; [0:33:35](https://youtu.be/MB7clEZvF7s?t=2015) — drawing via ETH + calendar; [0:35:12](https://youtu.be/MB7clEZvF7s?t=2112) — anchor to Friday 4:59 p.m. close, Sunday 6 p.m. open; [0:37:36](https://youtu.be/MB7clEZvF7s?t=2256) — object tree, rename; [0:39:12](https://youtu.be/MB7clEZvF7s?t=2352) — quarterly copies.
- **Nuance / caveats:** Reconciles with Oct 2024 videos in this batch (NWOG = Friday ETH settlement to Sunday 6 p.m. open). He says the matrix is for students; he himself uses paper journals.

title: How New Students Should Start Part 3
head: RTH Opening Range Gap matrix: marking, grading, nesting, and "shadow"  (aliases: "regular trading hours opening range gap matrix", "shadow")
body:
- **Kind:** definition | how-to | new coinage (shadow)
- **What ICT says:**
  - Make a layout containing only RTH opening range gaps. Toggle to regular trading hours (not electronic). The previous day's final print is the 4:14 p.m. ET 1-minute candle (RTH close); the 9:30 a.m. ET open is the other side of the gap. Example: Tuesday 1 Sep 2026's RTH opening range gap runs from Monday's 4:14 p.m. close (its high, since the market opened lower) down to Tuesday's 9:30 open (caption misspeaks "Wednesday's"). The "consequent encroachment" is the midpoint; "I don't care if you don't like the name."
  - How to grade an older gap: on the RTH ORG matrix chart use the calendar to jump to the date at 9:30 (e.g., Aug 26 at 9:30), drag a fib from the previous day's 4:14 p.m. close to the very first tick of the 9:30 open, and keep it consistent.
  - Nesting: in consolidation you will have many overlapping RTH ORGs (and overlapping first presented FVGs, NDOGs or NWOGs). Of the nested gaps, look at the largest/widest one that price is inside (the pink shaded gap for Tuesday Sep 1 here); "if there's ever a doubt of what I would be using" (rule statement is truncated in the caption).
  - Price behavior on 2 Sep: price opened low, meandered, went up into a proportion of last Wednesday (Aug 26)'s RTH opening range gap; the retracement went only to half of Tuesday's RTH opening range gap (CE) and the candle bodies showed bearish order flow, so the low was taken; then price came back up into the lowest octant/lower quadrant of Wednesday Aug 26's RTH ORG, tagged it, took out the low and went lower; later, "chopping wood but reacting off key levels."
  - SHADOW (new coinage): where Wednesday Sep 2's RTH opening range gap overlaps Tuesday's pink Sep 1 RTH opening range gap, the overlap region (a different hue) is a "shadow" — a shared space of nested gaps. A down-close candle (order block) anchored inside the shadow is valid; price respected that area repeatedly. "This is for order block lovers." Two RTH ORGs bleeding together make a very strong support or resistance level; far more precise than classic support/resistance or trend lines, where you would have had to guess whether to buy a high.
  - Order block stack: consecutive down-close candles count as ONE order block; the change in state of delivery is at the opening price (of the first candle in the stack); extend that level; price rallying and not trading back to it signals bullish; it then rallied to the lower quadrant of Wednesday Aug 26's RTH ORG.
  - He says he can find setups even in "slop" like this but you "have to be very nimble," and he teaches students not to require these setups.
- **How to identify:** Overlap of two (or more) RTH ORG boxes; look for an order block (down-close for support) anchored in the overlap; check bodies' behavior vs CE and octant levels.
- **How to use:** Treat the shadow/anchored order block as a precise support/resistance; use CE and lowest/lower octants of larger nested gaps as buy/sell reactions; use as context for journaling.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 1m, Wed 2 Sep 2026: Tuesday 1 Sep RTH ORG (pink) with CE hit by a retracement only; Wed Sep 2 ORG overlap = shadow; an order block (down-close candle) anchored in the shadow supports the rally back to the lower quadrant of Aug 26's RTH ORG; a later stack of consecutive down-close candles forms one order block whose opening price is the CISD level.
- **Timestamps:** [0:47:16](https://youtu.be/MB7clEZvF7s?t=2836) — RTH ORG matrix, nesting; [0:49:38](https://youtu.be/MB7clEZvF7s?t=2978) — 4:14 p.m. final print, 9:30 open; [0:51:15](https://youtu.be/MB7clEZvF7s?t=3075) — grading Aug 26 gap via calendar; [0:53:42](https://youtu.be/MB7clEZvF7s?t=3222) — retracement only to half the gap; [0:54:32](https://youtu.be/MB7clEZvF7s?t=3272) — shadow defined; [0:55:20](https://youtu.be/MB7clEZvF7s?t=3320) — order block anchored in shadow validated; [0:58:33](https://youtu.be/MB7clEZvF7s?t=3513) — shadow precision vs classic support/resistance; consecutive down-close candles = one order block, CISD at opening price.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** "Shadow" and "nested PDAs" are new in this video. The caption fuses a few sentences; the nested-PDA selection rule (use the widest the market is inside) is partially inferred.

title: How New Students Should Start Part 2
head: RTH Opening Range Gap (settlement vs 9:30 open) — large-gap handling  (aliases: ORG, "opening range gap", overnight gap, RTH OG)
body:
- **Kind:** rule / refinement (re-application of the concept from [[L26-019]])
- **What ICT says:**
  - The gap runs from the prior day's regular-trading-hours settlement (captioned "4:14 p.m. Eastern", cash session end; the transcript garbles it as "9:14 p.m." on the open side) to the 9:30 ET open. Here Monday's settlement was about 29,511.5 (caption "0.9511 and a half") and price opened far below, a discount gap of "400 handles or more".
  - He grades the gap with fib levels from the 9:30 open up to the settlement: lines are counted off from the open ("one, two, three, four") with the fourth being the gap's midpoint / consequent encroachment. Normally price trades to the gap midpoint "with 70% likelihood by 10:00 a.m."; on this day it had not happened yet, so he treated it as "deferred delivery" and said price could skip it entirely.
  - On days with a huge gap you "always" should at least give price an attempt to trade into the gap. It may be moot (the market can be too weak and keep selling), but if you try and get stopped out that is okay, because a stop-out is usually followed by an easier setup.
  - Because of the size of the gap and "a lot of open air space up there", he says he is "heavier-handed on the longs": long entries are more likely to yield an exaggerated run in your favor than shorts on a day with that big a gap. He says this does not mean it cannot go lower.
  - The ORG and the 9:30 open line are drawn on the chart so that opening-range-gap levels can be compared directly with the daily array levels.
  - Alternative scenario he voiced pre-open: price could first run higher to sweep the early buy side (the stops of breakout sellers), then drop to try the lower octant of the daily array and bounce.
- **How to identify:** prior RTH settlement line; 9:30 open; measure open-to-settlement; midpoint (CE) = target price is statistically drawn to by 10:00.
- **How to use:** a gap above price after a big overnight drop is a bias toward long entries; use ORG fib levels as objectives; if the gap closure does not get a chance to start by mid-morning, do not fade it blindly ("I don't want to fade that on a day like today").
- **Example in this video:** NQ, open below Monday's ~29,511.5 settlement after an overnight run of about 500 handles lower; hypothetical longs from ~29,0xx–29,13x with the buy-side pools (initial intraday high, equal/"smooth" highs) and 29,212 as objectives; ORG midpoint not reached in the first hour.
- **Timestamps:** [0:01:50](https://youtu.be/djabvhihIM8?t=110) settlement and gap size · [0:26:32](https://youtu.be/djabvhihIM8?t=1592) always attempt the gap · [0:40:34](https://youtu.be/djabvhihIM8?t=2434) why heavier on longs · [0:56:42](https://youtu.be/djabvhihIM8?t=3402) gap midpoint, 70% by 10:00
- **Nuance / caveats:** The 70% figure is the same as in [[L26-019]] (it says half the gap fills by 10:00 about 70% of the time); here he phrases it as the CE of the gap.

title: How New Students Should Start Part 2
head: Confluence of daily array grading with ORG levels → "low hanging fruit" objective  (aliases: layered key levels, octant / quadrant grading)
body:
- **Kind:** rule / refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - If there is an inefficiency on the daily timeframe (here the gray BISI box from Part 1) and you grade it with fib levels (quadrants = 25%, octants = 12.5%), and one of those levels agrees exactly with a level on the opening range gap grading, that level becomes an obvious objective: "two levels lining right up at 29,212".
  - He cares more about reaching that shared level than about reaching the gap midpoint, even though the midpoint is also likely, because of NFP week, a day after significant consolidation, and a big overnight run lower: "I want to have a low hanging fruit objective because it's part of a consolidation profile day."
  - Once at that level: partial there, then watch whether price shows "unction" (interest) to keep going or gives up and breaks lower.
  - At the end he stresses you do not need order-flow tools or "inside the candle" data: open, high, low, close and time form the whole story ("you can read that book by its cover").
- **How to identify:** daily BISI graded in 8 parts; ORG graded from open to settlement; look for a price where one level from each lines up. He describes it as the "lowest octant / lower quadrant" of the ORG coinciding with the daily array's level; caption mapping of which octant is which is unclear. 29,212 is the same number as the 50% line of the daily BISI in [[L26-019]] (29,211.25) and sits inside the upper half of that array per this video.
- **How to use:** target = the shared level; stop = below the structure of the entry; first partial at or just before it; trail the remainder to the next level (here Wednesday Aug 26's first presented FVG and the octant inside it).
- **Example in this video:** hypothetical longs from 29,067.5 onward targeting 29,212; the runner partial was filled at 29,213 (~1:05:51) and the last contract went to the octant within Wed Aug 26's first presented FVG.
- **Timestamps:** [0:54:17](https://youtu.be/djabvhihIM8?t=3257) two things layer at same level · [0:57:30](https://youtu.be/djabvhihIM8?t=3450) why 29,212 is the objective · [1:05:51](https://youtu.be/djabvhihIM8?t=3951) partial at 213 · [1:22:23](https://youtu.be/djabvhihIM8?t=4943) "no-brainer", read the candle
- **Nuance / caveats:** Reinforces that stacking higher-timeframe PD array levels with the RTH gap levels is the high-probability filter he taught in [[L26-019]].

title: How New Students Should Start Part 2
head: First Presented FVG (of a prior day) as support/resistance and entry zone  (aliases: "first presented fair value gap", FPFVG)
body:
- **Kind:** refinement / example only (definition not restated in this video)
- **What ICT says:**
  - He carries forward the first presented FVGs of Monday Aug 24, Tue Aug 25 and Wed Aug 26 as key levels on the chart. Price runs toward the high of Monday's gap and into Tuesday's.
  - For a long using a prior day's first presented FVG as a discount array: no candle bodies in the lower half of it ("it can wick into it, preferably it doesn't"); that is enough to start "ripping higher". He repeats the same condition many times (no bodies below the 50% of the gap/wick area).
  - Today's own first presented FVGs (several formed after the 9:30 open) are "your entries" for a return into the opening range gap, with a further chance to pyramid at an order block (see below).
  - He shades a gap orange when it must be watched as a potential iFVG (see next concept).
- **Example in this video:** price dips into Monday Aug 24's first presented FVG, wicks in but bodies stay in the upper half; a push above clears the intraday high and runs toward the equal highs and 29,212. Later Wed Aug 26's first presented FVG low is the final partial and its inner octant is the last draw.
- **Timestamps:** [0:04:37](https://youtu.be/djabvhihIM8?t=277) run into Tuesday's first presented FVG · [0:17:35](https://youtu.be/djabvhihIM8?t=1055) Monday's gap, no bodies in the lower half · [1:07:29](https://youtu.be/djabvhihIM8?t=4049) today's first presented FVGs as entries · [1:12:51](https://youtu.be/djabvhihIM8?t=4371) Wednesday's low as final partial
- **Nuance / caveats:** The exact rule that defines which FVG is "first presented" is not given here; check L26-019/other videos.

title: How New Students Should Start Part 2
head: Wick consequent encroachment: close confirmation rules  (aliases: wick CE, "dash line", mile marker)
body:
- **Kind:** rule / refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - When price stutters inside an array it "needs to close above this wick's halfway point (consequent encroachment)". A close above the dashed midpoint line is confirmation that price is likely to clear the buy-side above.
  - If a wick sits just above and a candle fails to close above its CE, price needs to build a close above it with the next candle or the very next one after: "That wick needs to be completely overtaken by this candle or the very next. Preferably this one. If it's this candle, that means it's really strong."
  - For longs, bodies should stay in the upper half of the wick's range; a down-close candle sitting in that zone is watched for rejection. Mirrors the short-side logic from Part 1 (bodies stay below the wick midpoint).
  - A wick high of a candle that is taken out (price closes above it) is also read as proof price can reach the pools above.
- **How to use:** the CE of a recent prominent wick is a checkpoint; failure to close above (long) tells you to tighten risk rather than hope.
- **Example in this video:** at ~9:35-9:40 price wicks up to a prior wick, rejects; he waits for a body close above the wick; the next candle closes above the wick and above the high (the intraday high at "43"), then runs to the 29,118.5 buy-side level.
- **Timestamps:** [0:16:42](https://youtu.be/djabvhihIM8?t=1002) close above the CE dash line · [0:18:54](https://youtu.be/djabvhihIM8?t=1134) not yet confirmed · [0:19:46](https://youtu.be/djabvhihIM8?t=1186) overtaken by this candle or the next · [0:21:25](https://youtu.be/djabvhihIM8?t=1285) confirmed
- **Nuance / caveats:** Time labels are approximate (he does not announce clock time); the example price is described only relatively.

title: How New Students Should Start Part 2
head: Inversion FVG — validity requires a close; not-yet-inverted as information  (aliases: iFVG)
body:
- **Kind:** rule / refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - A first presented FVG formed on a down close is treated as potential iFVG: "we don't want to see it behave as a premium array to sell off and go lower". He wants price to go above it, come back down into it, treat it as a foothold (support) and run into the buy-side pools above.
  - It becomes an inversion fair value gap only if price closes below it after having taken out a high: "the close below is what warrants it". Price moving (wicking) below the gap on a candle or two without a close below does not count.
  - If it does not invert, "it didn't tell us it wants to go lower based on the rules I got", which supports favoring the long side.
  - Also noted pre-trade: if a candle's low is left partly open (price does not completely close back into that candle's low), the next candle could open up, trade down and use that void as a "foothold" to launch higher.
- **How to use:** use the iFVG/no-iFVG status as the tiebreaker for direction; an unconfirmed iFVG keeps the "mode" you were in.
- **Example in this video:** shaded orange block from the first presented FVG; price traded below it twice without a close below; he stayed long at 29,132.
- **Timestamps:** [0:15:40](https://youtu.be/djabvhihIM8?t=940) orange gap as potential iFVG · [0:43:26](https://youtu.be/djabvhihIM8?t=2606) "becomes a potential iFVG if we close below it" · [0:44:48](https://youtu.be/djabvhihIM8?t=2688) "close below is what warrants it" · [0:45:39](https://youtu.be/djabvhihIM8?t=2739) stays long
- **Nuance / caveats:** Reinforces "close, not wick" as the inversion criterion, a point readers who already know iFVGs should double-check in their own definition.

title: How New Students Should Start Part 2
head: Volume imbalance (one-tick) as support; keep it open  (aliases: "buy side of balance outside efficiency", institutional order flow entry drill)
body:
- **Kind:** refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - A volume imbalance is the space between one candle's close and the next candle's open. Example: close 29,133.25, next open 29,133.50, a one-tick (0.25) difference, still a real volume imbalance.
  - If order flow is bullish the imbalance should stay open and not be filled; price only "dips its toe" into the zone (a partial, institutional reference gap closure) and moves on. He does not want a full closure.
  - Price that did not trade down to the candle's close produced "this nice little reaction": the leftover void is where buyers defend.
  - He treats such an entry as an "institutional order flow entry drill": get long as it touches that open space.
  - This array layers with the opening range gap's 9:30 open level, giving two reasons at the same level.
- **How to use:** entry/hold zone for longs; stop just below the candle low.
- **Example in this video:** the 29,133.25 close / 29,133.50 open pair; long at 29,132, stop about 21 handles below, two minis; a partial at ~29,135 (cost-covering stop).
- **Timestamps:** [0:48:10](https://youtu.be/djabvhihIM8?t=2890) bounce on a buy-side balance array · [0:48:57](https://youtu.be/djabvhihIM8?t=2937) don't want full closure · [0:51:04](https://youtu.be/djabvhihIM8?t=3064) one-tick imbalance explained
- **Nuance / caveats:** Uses the caption phrase "buy side of balance outside efficiency" (= BISI); I read it as BISI with "bounce" in the caption being "balance".

title: How New Students Should Start Part 2
head: Order block (open = low example) and pyramiding  (aliases: "action block" in captions)
body:
- **Kind:** example only
- **What ICT says:** Late in the session he adds contracts ("last chance for adding on a pyramid") at an order block: a candle whose open is 29,116.00 and low is exactly 29,116.00. He insists "that's an order block, that's not a demand zone". Extension off (he does not show an extension).
- **How to use:** add-on location while the run continues; stop under the candle's low.
- **Timestamps:** [1:07:29](https://youtu.be/djabvhihIM8?t=4049) · [1:08:30](https://youtu.be/djabvhihIM8?t=4110) open equals low
- **Nuance / caveats:** The precise candle direction/type is unclear from captions (open = low describes an up-close candle, which differs from the textbook "last down-close candle" definition). Treat his criteria here as an observation, not a full definition. An earlier fragment ("up close candles, closing price", [0:38:28](https://youtu.be/djabvhihIM8?t=2308)) suggests he marks the closing price of up-close candles as an accumulation reference (caption unclear).

title: How New Students Should Start Part 2
head: Retracement range re-delivery (measured projection) for partials and stop trailing  (aliases: "range redelivering the same range"; ICT calls it an "advanced topic")
body:
- **Kind:** refinement / new idea
- **What ICT says:**
  - Take the small rally-then-pullback range (high to the pullback low). Project that same range upward from the new high: if price trades up to that projected level it is "this range redelivering that same range".
  - Rules he gives: if price trades to the projected level, bring the stop to just below the low of the pullback; if it does not, stay where you are (stop at that candle's low). The projected line is also used as the partial level (e.g. "partial just below this line, which is simply this range of retracement projected above").
  - Why: from that level a deeper retracement is more likely; do not give back more than that. Worst case: you raise the stop, price spikes to the level and then immediately reverses in one candle: "rare, but it can happen".
- **Timestamps:** [1:09:30](https://youtu.be/djabvhihIM8?t=4170) projection explained · [1:10:18](https://youtu.be/djabvhihIM8?t=4218) deeper retracement risk · [1:12:51](https://youtu.be/djabvhihIM8?t=4371) used for partial
- **Nuance / caveats:** He eyeballs the lines ("I'm just eyeballing it"); no exact number given.

title: How New Students Should Start Part 2
head: Consolidation profile after a trending overnight; the 10:00 news and the 10:30 one-hour dealing range
body:
- **Kind:** rule / context
- **What ICT says:**
  - After a seriously trending overnight (about 500 handles lower), "it's reasonable to anticipate this session to be consolidation in the morning session"; it would clear the buy side and rip into the next level, and that is about as far as he sees the AM going. He is not talking about Market Profile, rather his own schematic of how price books.
  - In a consolidation you must be "really nimble and very forgiving to yourself" if chopped; new traders should let that experience happen while only watching price, so they learn the danger of chasing a move.
  - News: a medium-impact release (ISM at 10:00 ET) was minutes away. He expected a "whipsaw" that would easily hit a tight stop (29,100); he wanted price a bit higher first. When it hit he sat out and waited. Later: "that news didn't really have all that much impact."
  - At 10:30 ET there is "1 hour's dealing range" in place; it becomes much more likely that the gap stays open for a while, price begins to "animate", and "proprietary algorithms will start firing off now after 10:30". He tells students to watch for the 10:30 candle close to see more movement.
- **Timestamps:** [0:26:32](https://youtu.be/djabvhihIM8?t=1592) wait after stop-out for news · [0:29:46](https://youtu.be/djabvhihIM8?t=1786) consolidation expectation · [0:31:27](https://youtu.be/djabvhihIM8?t=1887) be nimble and forgiving · [0:42:32](https://youtu.be/djabvhihIM8?t=2552) 10:30 one hour dealing range · [1:00:55](https://youtu.be/djabvhihIM8?t=3655) algorithms fire after 10:30
- **Nuance / caveats:** The "10:30 = one hour dealing range, gap stays open longer, animation" idea is new phrasing; compare with his hourly-macro talk in [[L26-019]].

title: How New Students Should Start Part 2
head: Trade management used in the session: cover-cost stops, partials, trailing under candle lows
body:
- **Kind:** rule / management
- **What ICT says (as practiced):**
  - Enter small to "test the water"; initial stop just below the structure low (e.g. long at 29,067.5, stop 29,050 = 17.5 pts; a long near 29,132 with ~21-handle stop; the shorts used a 130-ish stop, ~35 handles, with two then four minis).
  - Move the stop to "cover costs" (entry plus a few points for commissions; e.g. up to 29,070 or 29,135) as soon as the trade is working or at the first partial.
  - Partials at buy-side levels (e.g. 29,118.5 ≈ 49-51 handles on a first partial); after a partial, trail the stop to just below the low of the current candle or the hypothetical "29,100" (locking about 32.5 handles).
  - Roll the stop up only when a candle closes with the body in the upper half of a key wick, or when price reaches a defined partial level.
  - Do not hold a stop that is tied to an invalid reference: when a reference line is no longer valid, delete it and place the stop under the new reference.
  - Final runners are exited at named levels (Wed Aug 26 first presented FVG low; then the octant inside it).
  - Day tally (his): one losing transaction (about 20 handles) against about 50 gained at the 1:03 mark, net about 125-130 handles on the day by that point, with more partials after.
- **Timestamps:** [0:05:24](https://youtu.be/djabvhihIM8?t=324) first hypothetical long with stop · [0:13:45](https://youtu.be/djabvhihIM8?t=825) second entry 29,067.5 stop 29,050 · [0:21:25](https://youtu.be/djabvhihIM8?t=1285) partial / 29,100 stop idea · [0:24:57](https://youtu.be/djabvhihIM8?t=1497) 49 handles on a partial · [1:03:17](https://youtu.be/djabvhihIM8?t=3797) day tally
- **Nuance / caveats:** His arithmetic and captioned prices are inconsistent (29,118.5 minus 29,067.5 = 51, he says 49; he also quotes both "33 and a half" and "32 and a half"). Treat the exact numbers as approximate; the structure of the management is the lesson.

title: How New Students Should Start Part 2
head: Regular trading hours versus electronic trading hours significance
body:
- **Kind:** rule / nuance
- **What ICT says:** Even if price traded these levels overnight (before 9:30 ET), it is more likely and more significant when price books at the same prices in regular trading hours. What you see in the electronic session "should be by context and confirmation delivered also in regular trading hours; otherwise it's just something that happened overnight during globex".
- **Example in this video:** the post-9:30 trading reached 29,212 after overnight trade there.
- **Timestamps:** [1:18:16](https://youtu.be/djabvhihIM8?t=4696)

title: How New Students Should Start Part 2
head: Contract math (NQ micros and minis)
body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:** 1 handle = 1 point = one full-figure move = 4 ticks. Micro NQ: $2 per point, $0.50 per tick. Mini NQ: $20 per point, $5 per tick. Beginners should keep records in micro terms, and graduate to minis once comfortable with the volatility.
- **Timestamps:** [1:13:46](https://youtu.be/djabvhihIM8?t=4426) · [1:14:36](https://youtu.be/djabvhihIM8?t=4476)

title: How New Students Should Start Part 2
head: Seasonal tendency (lower prices)
body:
- **Kind:** example only
- **What ICT says:** "We are definitely in our seasonal tendency for lower prices", something he mentioned two weeks earlier. Used as a supporting reason that price was falling into the lower quadrant of the daily array.
- **Timestamps:** [0:12:33](https://youtu.be/djabvhihIM8?t=753)
- **Nuance / caveats:** Appears to sit in tension with [[L26-019]], where he said seasonal months from September into year-end deliver cleanly; the direction (lower) is stated here, the cleanliness there.

title: How New Students Should Start Part 1
head: Weekly preparation and economic calendar filter  (aliases: "news drivers", weekend prep)
body:
- **Kind:** rule / process
- **What ICT says:**
  - Do the weekly prep on Saturday evening or Sunday afternoon before the market opens; it takes little time.
  - Use the Forex Factory calendar (he blocks ads by zooming). Toggle only the currency relevant to what you trade; for NQ/futures that is USD only. If trading a forex pair, toggle the currencies of that pair.
  - Impact filter: low impact (yellow) and gray (speeches etc.) are not a concern; the orange (medium) and red (high) folder events are "where the big waves of interference with normal price delivery occur". Note the day and the time of each one.
  - Week shown: Mon (Aug 31) light calendar, so pure price action; Tue 10:00 ISM Manufacturing PMI and JOLTS (medium); Wed 8:15 employment-change release (caption unclear which report); Thu 8:30 unemployment claims and 10:00 ISM; Fri 8:30 average hourly earnings, NFP, unemployment rate.
  - He says he does not care about the actual numbers because the data is later revised (he considers it unreliable); what matters is that the 8:30 report creates volatility.
- **How to use:** see the next two concepts for the trade/no-trade rules.
- **Timestamps:** [0:00:02](https://youtu.be/BWEPtHZ1Y2Y?t=2) calendar setup · [0:04:48](https://youtu.be/BWEPtHZ1Y2Y?t=288) reading the week's red/orange events · [0:05:37](https://youtu.be/BWEPtHZ1Y2Y?t=337) Thursday/Friday NFP week
- **Nuance / caveats:** He also notes "seasonal tendency months" are starting (September into year-end) when price delivery "gets very clean" because of holiday/end-of-year spending economic drivers; his expectation is better price action from here.

title: How New Students Should Start Part 1
head: NFP-week rules for new students and the "Monday" clarification  (aliases: day-of-week tendencies)
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - NFP is the first Friday of the month at 8:30. The volatility is "like a flame" and new traders are the moths.
  - Teach students to avoid trading Thursday and Friday of NFP week, and on Wednesday to be done by 11:00 ET. Monday through Wednesday-until-11:00 is the "safe spot" for finding setups.
  - Monday of an NFP week: be in your seat and expect to find a setup, because traders will want to take their profit early in the week to avoid Thursday/Friday. "Every Monday of non-farm payroll [week]" is a day to be drilled in.
  - Any other Monday is "potluck": it can be good or not, depends on experience. A new trader should not be demanding a setup every Monday.
  - He explicitly rejects the rumor that "ICT says never trade Mondays"; the above is the real statement. He, and experienced students, can find a Monday setup every week, but he is being practical for beginners.
  - Thursday of NFP week is a day a new student should be studying price, not engaging it. A student not yet ready for even a demo account should not touch Thursday/Friday.
  - Why patience matters early: habits formed at the start tend to stick; rushing and being "toxic" in reaction when wrong (which is normal at the beginning) can lead to talking yourself out of trading altogether.
- **Timestamps:** [0:03:11](https://youtu.be/BWEPtHZ1Y2Y?t=191) Monday of NFP week · [0:06:25](https://youtu.be/BWEPtHZ1Y2Y?t=385) avoid Thu/Fri, Wed until 11:00 · [0:07:12](https://youtu.be/BWEPtHZ1Y2Y?t=432) the "never trade Mondays" myth
- **Nuance / caveats:** This clarifies a commonly mis-quoted ICT line; it is framed as guidance for brand-new students, not a universal ban.

title: How New Students Should Start Part 1
head: Handling a 10:00 ET news release
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:** On a day with a 10:00 driver (e.g., Tuesday ISM/JOLTS), wait for the first 30 minutes of trading (9:30–10:00) and let liquidity or inefficiency set up before the news. Let the news hit, then work with whatever is left in its wake.
- **Timestamps:** [0:08:48](https://youtu.be/BWEPtHZ1Y2Y?t=528)

title: How New Students Should Start Part 1
head: Marking previous-month high / low / close on every timeframe  (aliases: monthly high/low, HTF levels)
body:
- **Kind:** process
- **What ICT says:**
  - On the monthly chart note the previous month's high, low and where it settled (the monthly close is only known after the Friday-session end of the month; he says the month closes at 5:59 pm ET). Label them (e.g., "July monthly high", "July monthly low"). Very high timeframe labels: bold, black, right-justified.
  - Set each line's visibility to show on every timeframe: every minute setting (and the seconds tab if you trade sub-1-minute), hourly, daily, weekly. Then no matter what lower timeframe you drop to, the macro levels are visible and you do not need to flip between monthly and weekly charts.
  - Copy a line by hovering until the end handle appears, hold Ctrl, and drag; then double-click to rename (July became August).
  - He does not bother to mark the monthly open: a monthly open eventually gets "baked in" to a new week opening gap (NWOG), and NWOG is what he tracks.
  - A buy-side liquidity label is unnecessary on a monthly high ("you already know that is the high of the month") but he labels the monthly low as sell-side liquidity.
- **How to use:** these are the first levels of the draw-on-liquidity map; a monthly high implies resting buy stops above it (breakout buyers, and swing shorts with stops above).
- **Timestamps:** [0:10:53](https://youtu.be/BWEPtHZ1Y2Y?t=653) previous month high/low · [0:13:21](https://youtu.be/BWEPtHZ1Y2Y?t=801) show on all timeframes · [0:15:49](https://youtu.be/BWEPtHZ1Y2Y?t=949) why no monthly open
- **Nuance / caveats:** Contradicts nothing, but explicitly deprioritizes the monthly open versus NWOG.

title: How New Students Should Start Part 1
head: Chart layouts / workspaces and labeling conventions
body:
- **Kind:** process
- **What ICT says:**
  - Keep a "naked" working layout (the one he teaches and executes from) plus separate saved layouts for specific lists: new week opening gaps, new day opening gaps, first-presented FVGs, and a layout with only RTH opening range gaps and a running tally. Toggle between layouts instead of putting everything on one chart (clutter and overload).
  - Anything you only need once, write down the numbers on a notepad.
  - Right-justify labels for higher-timeframe levels. If a label is left-justified on a daily chart, on a 15-minute chart it sits far off-screen and you see a price on the axis but do not know what it is.
  - Lines anchored to the right and extended to the right; otherwise they disappear as new data prints. Save the layout after editing.
  - For intraday or minor levels, place the label just above where it is anchored (not right-justified) so you can find it by compressing the chart (drag the time axis).
  - Colors: buy-side liquidity in blue, sell-side liquidity in deep red, always the same so viewers know what he is highlighting even without understanding his language. Tiny liquidity levels can be drawn as short trend lines.
  - Hierarchy of line thickness: higher-timeframe-anchored lines should be thicker, but not the very boldest (daily-anchored: one notch below the thickest; weekly: same logic) so they stand out among lower-timeframe noise.
  - Add the context to the label (e.g., "daily SIBI") so you keep things framed.
  - Do not show the high/low or midpoint tool lines he doesn't use; each extra line is something to babysit or explain.
- **Timestamps:** [0:18:11](https://youtu.be/BWEPtHZ1Y2Y?t=1091) layouts · [0:26:14](https://youtu.be/BWEPtHZ1Y2Y?t=1574) right-justify labels · [0:33:09](https://youtu.be/BWEPtHZ1Y2Y?t=1989) line thickness by timeframe

title: How New Students Should Start Part 1
head: Dealing range, premium/discount and equilibrium on the daily chart
body:
- **Kind:** definition / process
- **What ICT says:**
  - First order of business on the daily: where are we relative to the most recent range? Anchor range lines to the highest high so they are visible on the daily (he dislikes overhang).
  - Example: the July high-to-low range's equilibrium is the midpoint; price (Aug 31) is in the upper half of July's range, but in the middle of August's range, slightly in discount (just below that midpoint).
  - Look for where liquidity sits in close proximity to current price.
- **Example in this video:** NQ Sept contract (NQU2026) daily: July monthly high above, August low below; price oscillating around the August midpoint, inside a daily SIBI/BISI zone (below).
- **Timestamps:** [0:21:28](https://youtu.be/BWEPtHZ1Y2Y?t=1288) · [0:23:05](https://youtu.be/BWEPtHZ1Y2Y?t=1385)

title: How New Students Should Start Part 1
head: Grading a daily PD array in eighths (quadrants and octants)  (aliases: fib grading, "octant")
body:
- **Kind:** refinement / new coinage (octant)
- **What ICT says:**
  - He shades the daily "buy-side imbalance sell-side inefficiency" (BISI; caption "buy side of balance sell side efficiency") zone gray, from a candle's low down to the low of a volume imbalance, and grades it with fib levels in eight equal parts.
  - A quadrant is a quarter of the range; an octant is half of a quadrant (12.5%). The first line from the top is the 0.125 level (upper octant); the next is 0.25 (first quadrant line); 0.5 is halfway.
  - He turns off the extension and does not show the midpoint line while building it (to avoid student confusion about extra lines); the midpoint line colored black for contrast, the other levels dark but not black.
  - Price tends to use these levels as stepping stones: it traded sideways, then used the daily gray box's upper octant.
- **Example in this video:** 0.125 level = 29,451 ("the first line you would come to"); 0.5 midpoint = 29,211.25; the 0.25 (lower quadrant) line = 29,371 (derived: caption calls it "the lower quadrant at 29,371"). Price came down to the 0.125 and 0.25 lines the same morning.
- **Timestamps:** [0:27:57](https://youtu.be/BWEPtHZ1Y2Y?t=1677) shading and grading · [0:45:46](https://youtu.be/BWEPtHZ1Y2Y?t=2746) the 0.125 and 0.5 numbers · [0:53:15](https://youtu.be/BWEPtHZ1Y2Y?t=3195) "upper octant" as a target
- **Nuance / caveats:** If price closes above the top of the daily array, that changes the whole interest in dropping into it (stated as the invalidation).

title: How New Students Should Start Part 1
head: Suspension block  (aliases: SIBI with volume imbalance at its high and low)
body:
- **Kind:** definition (as ICT describes it here; caption quality limited)
- **What ICT says:**
  - A sell-side imbalance buy-side inefficiency (caption "cibby") that has a volume imbalance (two bodies not touching) at its high and its low is a "suspension block".
  - It sits above price here and acts as a premium array; he shades it red and gives the lines a red hue.
  - He uses the volume imbalance at its top as a place a short would have been taken; price trading into the lower half of it was "the lower half of this suspension block".
- **How to identify:** a daily SIBI whose boundaries include volume imbalances (gaps between bodies) at both ends. (Exact geometry not fully clear from captions.)
- **Example in this video:** the red daily SIBI/suspension block above market, with the gray BISI zone below; price is between them, "waiting and seeing" whether it will use the high as a high or stay in the upper half.
- **Timestamps:** [0:30:20](https://youtu.be/BWEPtHZ1Y2Y?t=1820) · [0:31:18](https://youtu.be/BWEPtHZ1Y2Y?t=1878)
- **Nuance / caveats:** A recent coinage; treat the exact definition as provisional.

title: How New Students Should Start Part 1
head: RTH Opening Range Gap (previous settlement) and the half-gap statistic  (aliases: RTH OG, regular trading hours opening range gap)
body:
- **Kind:** definition / rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - Before the 9:30 open, draw a line at the previous regular-trading-hours settlement (Friday's close here), labeled "RTH opening range gap settlement". Keep chart time on New York time.
  - At 9:30: if the open is above that price, the line becomes "RTH OG low"; if the open is below it, the line becomes "RTH OG high". So the word "settlement" turns into low or high depending on the opening price.
  - If price opens below the settlement it is a discount gap (premium gap if it opens above); the gap generally tries to fill.
  - Stated statistic: if there is a gap, half the gap gets filled by 10:00 AM about 70% of the time (the first 30 minutes after the open).
  - Plan: draw a fib from the open to the settlement; half gap is the 50% point of that range. Alternative path: price first runs the nearby sell-side (a minor low), then tries half gap, and a trader might leave a runner for full closure.
  - Keep a template/workspace that holds only RTH opening range gaps and a running tally.
- **Example in this video:** Friday's RTH settlement was about 29,487.5 ("487 half"); at ~8:39 price was ~29,420 (caption says "47 handles higher" — digits unclear). At 9:30 price opened below settlement (discount gap) and rallied immediately through the gap, past full closure ("gap closure and more"), heading to the high of the daily BISI box.
- **Timestamps:** [0:41:46](https://youtu.be/BWEPtHZ1Y2Y?t=2506) annotation rule · [1:36:58](https://youtu.be/BWEPtHZ1Y2Y?t=5818) 70% half-gap by 10:00 · [1:42:51](https://youtu.be/BWEPtHZ1Y2Y?t=6171) the 9:30 move
- **Nuance / caveats:** Two draws "in contention" for the opening range (9:30–10:00) were: the minor sell-side low and the RTH OG high. A new student will not know which one; the job is to observe which one price goes to at 9:30.

title: How New Students Should Start Part 1
head: Draw on liquidity — step-by-step mapping  (aliases: DOL)
body:
- **Kind:** process
- **What ICT says:**
  - "Flesh out the chart" with no entries: know what you are looking for, why it should be there, which levels are important, and what would change it. This is "the first part of what you are supposed to learn".
  - Layers used: monthly high/low, daily range equilibrium, daily BISI/SIBI zone graded in eighths, relative equal highs on the hourly, minor sell-side lows, RTH OG settlement.
  - Draw hierarchy: price moves from the nearest key level to the next (e.g., from the daily gray box's upper octant down toward the 0.25 line, then a minor sell side). He wants to see the candles "book" with interest to keep going lower, not just reach the level.
  - The more PD arrays and levels you can anchor to the daily chart, the more probable the setup; "probable" does not mean guaranteed or no losing trades; it means never feeling confused. If your read is wrong, that is "a transactional operating error" and the operator owns it.
- **Example in this video:** at 8:39 price sits inside the daily gray zone after a 8:09 buy-side raid (relative equal highs taken on Friday at 10:00, then a drop). He labels the lowest low as sell-side liquidity (deep red, potential draw). He tracks whether price will reach the 0.25 level (29,371) and then the minor sell side.
- **Timestamps:** [0:53:15](https://youtu.be/BWEPtHZ1Y2Y?t=3195) · [0:54:05](https://youtu.be/BWEPtHZ1Y2Y?t=3245) "how to arrive at draw on liquidity step by step" · [0:56:43](https://youtu.be/BWEPtHZ1Y2Y?t=3403) why setups are reliable only if you know why price should go there

title: How New Students Should Start Part 1
head: Big prominent wicks: consequent encroachment as a "mile marker"  (aliases: wick CE, premium sensitivity)
body:
- **Kind:** refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - Whenever a big, prominent wick forms, grade it in half (its consequent encroachment) and measure what price does around that halfway point. "Wicks are wonderful little mile markers for measuring continuation."
  - If short: you want to see bodies stay below the wick's midpoint; the upper half is "premium sensitivity" and, preferably, price does not trade there at all. A wick that price has moved below (even if the wick itself is the lower portion of an individual candle) is a premium array relative to where price is now.
  - A close above the midpoint is a concern, not a reason to bail out completely; it means more information to manage.
  - The more candles and distance price gains away from where an entry would have been, the more it builds an "onside narrative" (encouragement versus fear).
- **Example in this video:** after a lower low in the macro, he grades the big wick above it, watches the body stay below, and later notes price took the buy side briefly but the body "stayed inside" (not a close above).
- **Timestamps:** [0:48:15](https://youtu.be/BWEPtHZ1Y2Y?t=2895) · [0:58:20](https://youtu.be/BWEPtHZ1Y2Y?t=3500) wicks as mile markers · [0:59:08](https://youtu.be/BWEPtHZ1Y2Y?t=3548) premium sensitivity

title: How New Students Should Start Part 1
head: Macro (hourly 20-minute window)  (aliases: algorithmic time window)
body:
- **Kind:** definition / rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - Every hour: the last 10 minutes of the hour ending and the first 10 minutes of the new hour (a 20-minute window, e.g., 8:50–9:10, 9:50–10:10). In the video the 8:50–9:10 macro is marked between two vertical lines.
  - A macro gives no directional information at all. It only gives a time at which price should start "spooling": a decisive run toward inefficiency or liquidity, "like a micro start of a new race". You want to see it animate in the direction your analysis expects.
  - If price consolidates through the macro (as seen here), that is problematic for the idea. In recent years he has observed that the consolidation is often followed by a burst right after the 10-minute mark of the new hour (e.g., 10 minutes after 9, 10, 11, 12); he calls this a recent observation, not something he saw in prior decades. Reasons he offers: manipulation, news-driven volatility spikes.
  - If a move expected in the macro does not arrive, that is cause for concern; lower your stop.
- **Example in this video:** 8:50–9:10 macro on NQ 1m: price fell ~half an hour, ranged inside the macro, made a new low around 9:00 (a ~55–60 handle drop from the volume imbalance), consolidated, then took the highs and animated upward after 9:10 (hypothetical stop out).
- **Timestamps:** [1:02:46](https://youtu.be/BWEPtHZ1Y2Y?t=3766) macro defined · [1:05:12](https://youtu.be/BWEPtHZ1Y2Y?t=3912) no directional info · [1:29:37](https://youtu.be/BWEPtHZ1Y2Y?t=5377) consolidation then burst
- **Nuance / caveats:** The "last 10 minutes of the hour + first 10 of the next" definition is stated in his own words here; the "burst after consolidation" idea is explicitly labeled a recent personal observation.

title: How New Students Should Start Part 1
head: Event horizon (partial-profit level)  (aliases: halfway to the draw)
body:
- **Kind:** new coinage / rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - Grade the distance between the most recent low (price just made) and the next draw-level (e.g., a daily quadrant line). The midpoint of that is the "event horizon" and the place to take a partial. "How can I make sure I take something away and reward myself for participation?"
  - For a beginner on a demo or paper trade: if you hold three micros, take one off at that level; the partial "pays" the transaction and removes the need to be right about the final target.
  - Rationale: price has been moving continuously one way for about half an hour with no significant run on the short-term opposite liquidity, so halfway is a reasonable place.
- **Example in this video:** hypothetical short from the volume imbalance in the daily SIBI above; low taken; draw level 29,371; partial at the halfway point (event horizon). After that, as price retraced, he watched the wick midpoint and rolled the stop down.
- **Timestamps:** [1:08:22](https://youtu.be/BWEPtHZ1Y2Y?t=4102) · [1:09:11](https://youtu.be/BWEPtHZ1Y2Y?t=4151) "event horizon" · [1:10:00](https://youtu.be/BWEPtHZ1Y2Y?t=4200) three micros · [1:27:06](https://youtu.be/BWEPtHZ1Y2Y?t=5226) answering "partials are stupid"
- **Nuance / caveats:** He counters people who say taking partials is stupid: here two partials plus a lowered stop paid roughly 30 handles (stop lowered to 29,412 locks ~30 handles from the hypothetical entry) and later "32 more handles" (caption).

title: How New Students Should Start Part 1
head: Trade management: partial, then roll the stop to fund the position
body:
- **Kind:** rule / management
- **What ICT says:**
  - Once a partial is taken, roll the stop down (for a short) to just above the nearest short-term high; if stopped out, the trade has been "funded" by the partial and you were paid for your time.
  - Managing the psychology of holding is tied to reward and consequence: we are motivated by reward and fearful of consequence (what if I held too long, didn't take profit). A stop lowered after a partial removes the need to be right about the final target.
  - If you leave the stop at the original level and ignore what price is doing, you only have a small unrealized profit and live in fear ("a horror movie"); instead, take a shot at the target, then protect the exit ("Top Gun").
  - If a retracement closes above the wick/array that "should never" be closed above, that is a concern: partially exit or cancel the transaction; but the decision is about information, not panic.
  - He teaches students not to depend on being right; they should aim for consistent execution of a model and measure its statistical behavior in their own hands.
- **Example in this video:** hypothetical short from the volume imbalance; partial near event horizon; stop moved to ~29,412; price retraced into a minor buy-side run and stopped the hypothetical remainder with a profit.
- **Timestamps:** [1:11:36](https://youtu.be/BWEPtHZ1Y2Y?t=4296) · [1:12:25](https://youtu.be/BWEPtHZ1Y2Y?t=4345) reward vs consequence · [1:26:17](https://youtu.be/BWEPtHZ1Y2Y?t=5177) stop at 29,412 locks ~30 handles · [1:31:15](https://youtu.be/BWEPtHZ1Y2Y?t=5475) Top Gun analogy

title: How New Students Should Start Part 1
head: Inversion FVG and "immediate rebalance" used as feedback  (aliases: iFVG, immediate rebalance, discount/premium sensitivity)
body:
- **Kind:** refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - Watch whether a PD array "continuously supports the idea of the transaction you're in or watching". A bearish FVG (formed in a bearish market) is a premium array: price should respect its lower half as premium sensitivity and push lower; if instead price trades above it, comes back down into it and respects it from above, it has inverted and now acts as a discount array (bullish iFVG), and the low beneath it becomes an intermediate-term low (possibly the session/day/week low).
  - If price closes above the gap but cannot hold, and price then trades through it, that gap has lost its sensitivity.
  - Two PD arrays nested together (an FVG's consequent encroachment lying on a wick's CE) give "immediate intel" on the strength or continuity of a run.
  - Immediate rebalance: after a big up-close candle that cleared the RTH settlement high, if the very next candle (or the one after) trades back to the high of that candle with no volume imbalance or FVG left behind, that is one of his strongest PD arrays because the feedback is immediate. He says it is consistent and that nothing beats it: narrative from market structure plus a clear draw plus an unhideable footprint.
  - Journal it: whenever you see an immediate rebalance, record it.
- **How to use:** In the hypothetical 9:30 short: after the big up-close candle that cleared the RTH settlement, watch whether the next candle reaches the high of that up-close candle; if it trades there, sell short; the stop one tick above the mean threshold (50%) of the up-close candle (caption unclear on exactly which candle); targets the sell side below; take 50–65% off below the low with a partial halfway between that low and the next level, and leave the rest for the sell side.
- **Example in this video:** at 9:30 price opened at a discount and rose through the RTH OG high, with a bearish FVG on the 1m acting as sensitivity; price then dropped, took the low, closed back above the wick, wicked and rejected. The immediate-rebalance candle, then the sell-side delivery ("look how fast it was").
- **Timestamps:** [1:16:05](https://youtu.be/BWEPtHZ1Y2Y?t=4565) iFVG discussion · [1:18:30](https://youtu.be/BWEPtHZ1Y2Y?t=4710) nested PD arrays · [1:56:55](https://youtu.be/BWEPtHZ1Y2Y?t=7015) immediate rebalance · [1:57:44](https://youtu.be/BWEPtHZ1Y2Y?t=7064) stop, size
- **Nuance / caveats:** He also says if the up-gap is too large in points for your size, use a micro; if a micro can't pay you, "you're a gambler". Some of the candle references are ambiguous in captions.

title: How New Students Should Start Part 1
head: Short / intermediate / long-term highs and lows

  - A low formed by an inverted FVG getting respected after the macro can be an intermediate-term low (and the session/day/week low).

head: Learning method: observation lab / tape reading and journaling
body:
- **Kind:** process / psychology
- **What ICT says:**
  - Do this every day with no risk: map the chart, state expectations ("it should do this, shouldn't do that"), then watch how price books; this is how you build a skill set. It is not copy-trading: "watching trades live in front of you is entertainment".
  - Screenshot the inflection points in his videos (e.g., the candle that closed and the next that opened), type your own notes on why price should have behaved that way, and keep them in your journal.
  - For people with day jobs: screen-record a 1-minute chart all day (he mentions Ctrl+Alt+R on Windows, unsure), then in the evening replay it, pause and state what should happen, unpause; do it for the first hour (9:30–10:30).
  - "Not market replay" — he is using the live recording approach.
  - Don't take funded-account challenges or demo-trade with pressure early: "That's all gambling"; no one gives a final exam on day one. You need enough experience before you can measure performance.
  - He does not teach people to trade with real money (not licensed); students should use paper trading or tape reading and hypothetically note the entry, partial, stop.
  - Confidence for beginners comes from seeing predictions play out ("I saw something, I observed something and measured its delivery").

title: NQ Trade Review Jackson Hole Symposium Day #2
head: Seek and Destroy Model
body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:** Market maker pattern of taking out buy-side and sell-side liquidity in alternating runs. Price runs up to take out buy-side stops (above prior highs), then reverses to take out sell-side stops (below prior lows), then reverses again upward. This back-and-forth pattern — low, higher high, lower low, higher high, etc. — is the "seek and destroy" where institutions systematically collect both long and short stop-losses. Occurs frequently on event-driven weeks (Jackson Hole, FOMC, NFP).
- **How to identify:** Mark the highs and lows on a 1-minute chart; look for alternating pattern where each swing extends beyond the prior swing. Example: Low → Higher high → Lower low (below first low) → Higher high (above second high).
- **How to use:** Anticipate the pattern; expect multiple "second runs" (reversals to take out the other side's stops). Don't panic on reversals; they're part of the pattern. Hold through reversals if your original thesis (direction) is intact on larger timeframe.
- **Example in this video:** Price ran low (took out sell-side), then higher high (took out buy-side), then lower low (took out new sell-side), then higher high (took out new buy-side) — classic seek and destroy on an event-driven day.
- **Timestamps:** [0:11:04](https://youtu.be/iSWZOe3aUFE?t=664) "second runs," [0:11:56](https://youtu.be/iSWZOe3aUFE?t=716) "that is the seek and destroy model. That's it."
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** More pronounced during event-driven weeks (Jackson Hole, FOMC, NFP); less common in quiet weeks.

title: NQ Trade Review Jackson Hole Symposium Day #2
head: Discount Wick as Target / Reference Level
body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:** The prior day's wick (high to low), especially if it's a "discount wick" (below the body, indicating weakness), serves as an intraday target on the following day. Price often runs to touch the upper half or midpoint of the prior day's discount wick before continuing or reversing. This wick acts like a magnet or friction level.
- **How to identify:** Look at the prior day's candlestick; if it has a significant wick (body doesn't fill entire range), mark the wick high and low; note if it's below the body (discount wick).
- **How to use:** On the following day, anticipate price to gravitate toward the upper half or midpoint of the prior wick. Use as a target zone or reversal level.
- **Example in this video:** Thursday's 9:55 AM ET discount wick was targeted on Friday; price ran down to touch its upper half and midpoint, then reversed.
- **Timestamps:** [0:02:24](https://youtu.be/iSWZOe3aUFE?t=144) "Thursday's 9:55 a.m. Eastern time discount wick," [0:03:12](https://youtu.be/iSWZOe3aUFE?t=192) "Look where the body stopped."
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Upper half or midpoint is target, not full wick range.

title: NQ Trade Review Jackson Hole Symposium Day #2
head: Displacement Lower (SIBI Entry Mechanics)
body:
- **Kind:** entry model (for longs after downside displacement)
- **What ICT says:** When a candlestick opens lower and closes lower (down-close candle), it creates "displacement lower" = sell-side imbalance, buy-side inefficiency (SIBI). This candlestick is NOT the FPFVG; it's a separate inefficiency. If price later trades down to the low of this displacement and reverses back up into the inefficiency zone, that becomes an inversion FVG long entry opportunity.
- **How to identify:** Identify a down-close candle (close below open); mark its range (high to low); this is the displacement lower.
- **How to use:** When price trades down into the low of this displacement and bounces back up, enter long into the inefficiency zone (between the wick low and body close). Stop below the wick low. Target upward.
- **Example in this video:** 9:30 AM ET showed a displacement lower; later, price pulled back into it, qualifying it as an inversion FVG entry for longs.
- **Timestamps:** [0:04:44](https://youtu.be/iSWZOe3aUFE?t=284) "displacement lower... sell side imbalance buy side inefficiency," [0:04:44](https://youtu.be/iSWZOe3aUFE?t=284) "potential inversion fair value gap."
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Don't confuse displacement lower with FPFVG; displacement is a separate inefficiency.

title: NQ Trade Review Jackson Hole Symposium Day #2
head: Fibonacci Projections (Half-Wick as Target)
body:
- **Kind:** refinement
- **What ICT says:** Identify a range (wick high to wick low); use Fibonacci to measure the distance. The midpoint (50% level) or other Fibonacci ratios (like 0.618, 0.382) act as target levels for price retracements and continuations. Especially useful for identifying where price is likely to stall or reverse.
- **How to identify:** Mark a wick or range; measure high to low; apply Fibonacci tool; identify 50%, 61.8%, 38.2% levels.
- **How to use:** Use these levels as micro-targets for exits, stops, or trend confirmation. Bodies respecting these levels = confirmation of direction.
- **Example in this video:** Fibonacci levels of prior wicks were used to identify exact price targets (e.g., 29,757.25 as next target, then 830s as extension target).
- **Timestamps:** [0:02:24](https://youtu.be/iSWZOe3aUFE?t=144) "grab our fib and anchor it to that range," [0:03:59](https://youtu.be/iSWZOe3aUFE?t=239) "29,757 and a quarter uh that would be the next upside draw."
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Multiple Fibonacci levels on same chart require discipline to avoid clutter; prioritize key levels only.

title: NQ Trade Review Jackson Hole Symposium Day #2
head: Jackson Hole Symposium Week Impact (Event-Driven Volatility)
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:** Jackson Hole Symposium week (typically late August, featuring Federal Reserve economic discussions) produces extreme market volatility and manipulation. Institutions push agendas; dealers actively intervene; second runs (seek-and-destroy patterns) are frequent and violent. New traders should NOT trade with real money during this week; demo or tape reading only. Experienced traders can trade but must anticipate whipsaws and high stop-runs. Volatility can be profitable for experienced traders but devastating for new ones.
- **How to identify:** Check economic calendar for Jackson Hole Symposium dates; mark that week as high-risk.
- **How to use:** New traders: observe only, don't trade with real money. Experienced: reduce position size, anticipate seek-and-destroy, expect volatility, don't over-leverage.
- **Example in this video:** ICT's Friday execution faced volatility; he didn't perfect it (could have closed earlier) but demonstrated mechanics. Multiple livestreamers and traders got hurt on this week.
- **Timestamps:** [0:11:04](https://youtu.be/iSWZOe3aUFE?t=664) "Jackson Hole Symposium... effect on the marketplace," [0:19:50](https://youtu.be/iSWZOe3aUFE?t=1190) "Respect Jackson Hole Symposium Week. Anticipate it."
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Not "never trade"; rather, scale appropriately and expect adversity.

title: NQ Trade Review Jackson Hole Symposium Day #2
head: Trader Development Three-Stage Model
body:
- **Kind:** rule (process)
- **What ICT says:** New traders should develop through three stages:
  1. **Stage 1: Observation & Logging (1+ months)** — Study price action, screenshot key levels, annotate, journalize. Do NOT trade (not even demo). Focus on seeing repeating patterns.
  2. **Stage 2: Demo/Paper Trading (minimum 2–3 months)** — Trade using only the patterns you observed. Use no leverage or minimal leverage. Measure like a scientist; don't chase money.
  3. **Stage 3: Live Trading** — Only when you're no longer excited or scared about outcomes; when you know the process repeats; when you're certain you're not impulsively chasing.
  Never rush through these stages; they cannot be skipped. Each stage builds courage and conviction through repetition.
- **How to identify:** Self-assess: Are you still impulsive? Still chasing? Still afraid? If yes, you're not ready for the next stage.
- **How to use:** Follow the progression rigorously. Use observation phase to understand price action mechanics, not to find trade opportunities. Spend time in demo before committing real money.
- **Example in this video:** ICT emphasizes avoiding demo trading during Jackson Hole week; instead, use it for observation of the seek-and-destroy model.
- **Timestamps:** [0:23:47](https://youtu.be/iSWZOe3aUFE?t=1427) "It's a matter of collecting information, data," [0:24:33](https://youtu.be/iSWZOe3aUFE?t=1473) "Minimum, 3 months... demo or paper trading," [0:25:20](https://youtu.be/iSWZOe3aUFE?t=1520) "you're probably going to be ready to trade... no longer excited or scared."
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** These stages are not negotiable; many traders skip them and blow accounts.

title: NQ Trade Review Jackson Hole Symposium Day #2
head: Trader Independence & Mentality
body:
- **Kind:** rule (psychology)
- **What ICT says:** As a trader, you owe no one your results or schedule. Don't feel obligated to trade every day (even Mondays or Fridays) just because content creators, live streamers, or social media expect it. The strongest traders close profitable weeks early (take 3-day weekends) rather than chasing more money. Trading every day when you're already profitable is greed, not discipline. Conversely, don't skip trading just to please followers. Make decisions based on YOUR risk/reward, not external pressure.
- **How to identify:** Ask yourself: "Am I trading this setup because I genuinely see it, or because I feel pressured to be active?"
- **How to use:** Build decision-making independence. Close winners early if risk isn't worth it. Skip days if necessary. This communicates maturity and self-control, which is more valuable than constant activity.
- **Example in this video:** ICT stated he wouldn't trade Friday (Jackson Hole vol); when a student's sincere question prompted execution, he did it but with caution and early partials. He didn't feel obligated to "perform" for audience.
- **Timestamps:** [0:14:18](https://youtu.be/iSWZOe3aUFE?t=858) "every single day... every report day," [0:15:06](https://youtu.be/iSWZOe3aUFE?t=906) "if you've been very profitable, take a 3-day weekend," [0:17:27](https://youtu.be/iSWZOe3aUFE?t=1047) "you're not the influencer, you're the influenced."
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Discipline isn't trading more; it's having the courage to do less.

title: NQ Trade Review Jackson Hole Symposium Day #2
head: Inversion FVG on Multi-Day Structures
body:
- **Kind:** refinement
- **What ICT says:** Inversion FVG logic isn't limited to intraday charts. When reviewing multi-day price action, an inefficiency (gap or imbalance) formed on a prior day can become an inversion FVG target on the current day. Example: If Friday shows a gap down (displacement lower), price on Monday may run down into that Friday gap zone and reverse back up — that Friday gap becomes a multi-day inversion FVG.
- **How to identify:** Review prior day(s) for inefficiencies (gaps, imbalances); identify the range (high to low); mark that range.
- **How to use:** On the current day, if price reaches the low of that prior inefficiency, anticipate a reversal back into the inefficiency zone for long entries. Stop below; target above.
- **Example in this video:** Friday's inefficiency (displacement lower at 9:30 AM) was used as a multi-day reference; price action throughout the day interacted with this level.
- **Timestamps:** [0:04:44](https://youtu.be/iSWZOe3aUFE?t=284) "inversion fair value gap... trades below it... goes like one or two ticks below it, that's fine."
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Extend these levels forward; they retain validity across multiple days.

title: NQ Trade Review & Deep Dive Into Price Delivery
head: Daily BISI graded in octants (upper octant 29,451) and "following the leftmost anchor down"  (aliases: buy-side imbalance sell-side inefficiency, gray box, octant, quadrant)
body:
- **Kind:** refinement (re-application)
- **What ICT says:**
  - The gray box on his intraday charts is the daily BISI, graded from one candle's close up to the low of the candle that created it, including the volume imbalance at the low. "Entirety of the range" = the gray box.
  - Levels inside a graded array, from the top: the high (where the gray turns white), upper octant, upper quadrant, then the first octant above consequent encroachment, CE/midpoint (blue), then octant, lower quadrant, octant, and the lowest percentile at the bottom. The uppermost octant is 0.125 = 29,451 here.
  - Price dropped into the gray area at the high and stopped at the upper octant 29,451 at the first drop of the day: "It's not random. It's bullish and it's going to use that level." The bodies did not close at or below it, which marks it as a key level.
  - Tracking tip: to read any anchored fib, find the leftmost anchor point and look straight down; all the levels line up that way.
  - In the afternoon, price traded back into the gray area near its high with a lot of energy and reacted again ("daily PDA, it will have a reaction, it's tradable").
- **How to use:** upper octant is the first line you come to; if price drops into the array but bodies do not close beyond that line, the level is respected and favors longs from it.
- **Example in this video:** NQ Thursday Aug 27, 9:30 open: price opened, traded down to take sell-side, rallied to take buy-side (leaving a slightly lower buy-side high), then dropped into the gray box and stopped at 29,451 (upper octant). From there it rallied, took the shorts' stops and the highs, and ran into the inefficiency above.
- **Timestamps:** [0:00:49](https://youtu.be/MD1Ts09dkYs?t=49) what the gray area is · [0:06:36](https://youtu.be/MD1Ts09dkYs?t=396) drop into upper octant · [0:07:32](https://youtu.be/MD1Ts09dkYs?t=452) levels named, 29,451 · [0:23:39](https://youtu.be/MD1Ts09dkYs?t=1419) find leftmost anchor and go straight down
- **Nuance / caveats:** Same 29,451 as in [[L26-019]] (0.125 level); consistent.

title: NQ Trade Review & Deep Dive Into Price Delivery
head: Suspension block (SIBI with volume imbalance at both ends); BISI vs suspension block  (aliases: "cibby" = SIBI in captions)
body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:**
  - A suspension block is a SIBI that has a volume imbalance at its high AND a volume imbalance at its low. The SIBI above price here was one.
  - The daily BISI he uses (gray box) has a volume imbalance only at the low, so it is not a suspension block: "just simple buy side of balance sell side efficiency".
  - Price trading up into the volume imbalance at the SIBI's high, then into the CE of a wick, then through to the gap above, was the sequence of "orders of business" he laid out for longs.
- **How to use:** the sequence of levels (volume imbalance, wick CE, gap, old high) is the ordered list of draws on liquidity above.
- **Timestamps:** [0:01:37](https://youtu.be/MD1Ts09dkYs?t=97) · [0:03:24](https://youtu.be/MD1Ts09dkYs?t=204) · [0:52:58](https://youtu.be/MD1Ts09dkYs?t=3178) afternoon recap, "two volume imbalances make this SIBI a suspension block"
- **Nuance / caveats:** Confirms the provisional definition in [[L26-019]].

title: NQ Trade Review & Deep Dive Into Price Delivery
head: Failure to reach an objective as a directional clue ("return to premium")  (aliases: reading the daily narrative)
body:
- **Kind:** rule / reasoning
- **What ICT says:**
  - On Monday Aug 24 he wanted price to trade to the high of the daily volume imbalance; how it behaved there would show whether it wants to go lower or run higher. Price traded lower but did not get to the objective it could have easily reached. Using his PDAs and key levels at key times, that "indicates... the market is undergoing a return back to premium", so he looks for price to go higher.
  - Targets once long: the wick CEs above, the volume imbalance at the SIBI's low then high, the remainder of the SIBI, with an intraday gap used as a place to go long on the way.
  - Intraday, shorts exist "if the market was going to go lower all through here" via an iFVG, but now that price showed unwillingness to drive lower into the volume imbalance, "we have to change gears and go likely higher".

title: NQ Trade Review & Deep Dive Into Price Delivery
head: Seek & destroy day (megaphone / expanding price delivery), Jackson Hole day one  (aliases: seek and destroy, broadening pattern, "megaphone")
body:
- **Kind:** rule / definition
- **What ICT says:**
  - Day one of the Jackson Hole Symposium (here Thursday Aug 27, 2026) is the highest-likelihood day for a seek and destroy; it can still occur on day two. The speakers' commentary is "thrown out to the ether" and used as a smoke screen that affects what you believe is buying and selling pressure; the whole week can be wild.
  - Behavior: up, down, up (clear stops), down (clear stops), in a widening pattern (he half-recalls "megaphone"), "everybody trying to position gets knocked out". Look back to the left and you see exactly what each swing is sweeping. You must trade it "very nimbly".
  - Target logic for the long: "High, low, higher high, lower low, then reach for that high": the old high to the left is a likely draw.
  - If a body will not close through a key level during such a run, the level is a low that builds the narrative of higher prices, though it can still be subject to a stop run / raid after the rally.
  - He advises students to avoid the Jackson Hole Symposium, especially day one ([0:30:08](https://youtu.be/MD1Ts09dkYs?t=1808)), even though he traded it with real risk.
- **Example in this video:** 1m: rally, break lower to make relative equal lows, rally into an FVG, aggressive sell-off ("nice little short", a scalp he did not take); he instead expected another run below those lows into Friday Aug 21's first presented FVG, then a rally.
- **Timestamps:** [0:05:01](https://youtu.be/MD1Ts09dkYs?t=301) day one likelihood · [0:08:20](https://youtu.be/MD1Ts09dkYs?t=500) up-down-up-down, megaphone · [0:09:58](https://youtu.be/MD1Ts09dkYs?t=598) relative equal lows then FVG sell-off · [0:21:13](https://youtu.be/MD1Ts09dkYs?t=1273) high-low-higher high-lower low
- **Nuance / caveats:** Ties the "seek and destroy" label to a scheduled news event (Jackson Hole), not just to a price pattern.

title: NQ Trade Review & Deep Dive Into Price Delivery
head: Buying below a low (sell-side raid) with minimum criteria and wick-midpoint confirmation  (aliases: false break below a low, buying sell stops, "turtle soup" logic)
body:
- **Kind:** entry model / rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - Minimum criterion for buying sell-side liquidity: price must trade below the low. "Anything at that price or lower you're buying where smart money buys", buying the breakout sellers' stops ("I'm standing in front of them saying you're wrong").
  - His planned path: from the low (relative equal lows) down toward last Friday Aug 21's first presented FVG (the first FVG after 9:30 ET). He watched the candle going down and wanted a close below the midpoint of the range between the low and the high of that first presented FVG. If it closed below that midpoint he would wait for price to touch the high of that gap and buy there. It could not close below the midpoint, and neither could the next candle, so he bought earlier: "I can't hold any longer, I've got to get in now because once it starts going above here, it's going to take off".
  - He verbalizes his concern in real time. If a low is pierced while he is talking about going long, he is treating it as a false break; and "the middle of that wick" is where he wants price to get above.
  - Once price rips back above the low quickly, he needs to see a close above the CE of the wick, then a close above an inverted gap (see below).
- **How to identify:** a swing/relative equal low being traded through; a candle that cannot close below the 50% of the range to the discount array below; fast reclaim of the low.
- **How to use:** buy below the low; first target a nearby buy-side high (limit order one tick under the high to be sure of a fill); extend the terminus to the old high to the left if the run is strong.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 1m Thu Aug 27 (approximately the 9:50–10:07 ET window; the transcript does not state the fill time): long below the relative equal lows ahead of Aug 21's FPFVG; first target the nearby high (4 contracts off just above it); terminus the old high.
- **Timestamps:** [0:11:36](https://youtu.be/MD1Ts09dkYs?t=696) plan: low then Friday's first presented FVG · [0:14:50](https://youtu.be/MD1Ts09dkYs?t=890) why he did not wait · [0:15:38](https://youtu.be/MD1Ts09dkYs?t=938) fill below the low · [0:16:26](https://youtu.be/MD1Ts09dkYs?t=986) first target
- **Nuance / caveats:** He did not draw the midpoint line live ("my experience says I can eyeball it").

title: NQ Trade Review & Deep Dive Into Price Delivery
head: Wick consequent encroachment and "upper half of the wick supports price"  (aliases: wick CE, mile marker, bodies stay in the upper half)
body:
- **Kind:** rule / refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - When price is above a wick and the market is bullish, the upper half of the wick should support price: the bodies should stay in that upper half. He highlights that upper half in blue.
  - Bullish: bodies in the upper half and not touching CE, even if wicks touch or come within one tick. Bearish mirror: in a bearish market the lower half of a key wick or array should cap price; bodies cannot get to or above CE.
  - On a candle that opened right below the middle of the upper half he was nervous, but trusted that a probe lower would be a wick and "not likely to touch the inversion fair value".
  - A candle that opened and wicked into the upper half and then responded immediately to the upside, coming within one tick of his stop, meant "we're done", the wick now acts as a barrier.
  - He copies the same measurement down onto another candle's open (anchoring the half-wick measure at that candle's open down to 523.75 captioned) to show the logic repeats at each scale; price respected the upper half of each ("same thing here"). He then expects a big up-close candle, "a strong large green close".

  - "Event horizon" (as he used it here): the midpoint between the high of the iFVG and the middle of the wick; no bodies should be put down there if longs are on side.
- **How to use:** continually measure wicks; use their CE as a checkpoint rather than a hard stop; if the CE is not violated by a body the long is still "on side".
- **Example in this video:** the 10:07 ET candle opened, wicked down to NQ 29,502.00 (his stop was at 29,501.75, one tick away), then rallied.

title: NQ Trade Review & Deep Dive Into Price Delivery
head: Pyramiding rule: add only at or below equilibrium (longs), at or above (shorts)  (aliases: scaling in, equilibrium rule)
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - "I teach my pyramiding needs to be if I'm long it needs to be at consequent encroachment or equilibrium of the range that you're trading in or lower. If I'm shorting I need to be shorting at equilibrium or higher."
  - After price breaches equilibrium, the halfway point of whatever run you expect to reach the target, you are "not permitted" to add or pyramid: "just a rule of thumb and it serves me well".
  - The range widens every time price takes stops: after the stops are taken, the range becomes the new low to the new high/target. Equilibrium is measured from the entry area's low to where you think the move completes (terminus), not just to the existing high.
  - Example: his second entry (four contracts) was above equilibrium of the range between the original low and old high (blue line 29,514.50), so by a strict reading it did not fit. But he had already planned a target above that high, and re-measured the range from the low to his actual intended target (eyeballed higher); the blue line then moved higher and the entry fit. He answers the "you're form fitting" accusation by saying he has taught this behind a paywall and the live commentary shows he thought it on the fly.
- **How to use:** before adding, state the range (low to terminus), mark 50%, and ask whether the add is on the cheap side of it.
- **Example in this video:** 6 contracts long first, then +4 pyramided in discount (total 10); 4 taken off just above the first high; the remaining 6 meant for terminus.
- **Timestamps:** [0:22:01](https://youtu.be/MD1Ts09dkYs?t=1321) rule stated · [0:22:48](https://youtu.be/MD1Ts09dkYs?t=1368) range widens after stops · [0:23:39](https://youtu.be/MD1Ts09dkYs?t=1419) equilibrium 29,514.50 · [0:30:58](https://youtu.be/MD1Ts09dkYs?t=1858) re-measuring to the target · [0:41:40](https://youtu.be/MD1Ts09dkYs?t=2500) contract counts

body:
