- **What ICT says:**
  - Plan: 6 contracts long, add 4 at discount (10 total); 4 off at the first high (limit one tick below the high); of the 6 left, take 5 off at the next high (the high of the green imbalance) and leave one as a runner for the old high. The original terminus was the first high; it was moved higher as price showed strength.
  - Price reached very near the target, then came back and stopped him out.
  - Hindsight: the stop should have been at the open of the candle (the last two up-close candles act as an order block) rather than below it. "I don't want to be holding a stop below change in state of delivery." Price using the green inefficiency as a draw should not overcome that candle's open; the two candles' range becomes an order block and the CE of the green inefficiency protects price from going higher.
  - Price then returned to the same gap: "how's this support and resistance?", unfinished business above.
  - "Cork" observation: a flat block of price slightly sloping up (opposite of a bull flag, which slopes down) is like a champagne cork; pressure builds, then it pops higher ("a very slow bleed before it got to it").
  - Leave the gap partly unfilled: he wants the upper half of the inefficiency to stay open on the way to target. When price is near equilibrium or the high end of the run and close to the target, gaps rarely fill before it reaches the target because it is "in a hurry to get to the liquidity".
  - If stopped out, he says he would have re-entered immediately with the full position and a stop below.

head: Macro Time Entry (9:50–10:10 AM ET)
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:** The window between 9:50 and 10:10 AM ET (last 10 minutes of the 9 AM hour + first 10 minutes of the 10 AM hour) is a macro time boundary. During volatile weeks (Jackson Hole, FOMC), major institutional order clustering occurs at this boundary. Entering trades at this window increases conviction and probability of success because algorithmic order flow is scheduled and forced.
- **How to identify:** Mark 9:50 and 10:10 AM on 1-minute chart; observe price action at these times; identify when lows/highs are being taken out at this boundary.
- **How to use:** Anticipate large moves around macro windows. If you're already positioned before the macro window, expect acceleration into and through the window. Use this window for pyramiding (adding to position).
- **Example in this video:** Entry was executed in the middle of the 9:50–10:10 macro window; subsequent pyramiding added during this same window.
- **Timestamps:** [0:00:01](https://youtu.be/SUcRywSry5U?t=1) "middle of the macro 950 1010," [0:16:20](https://youtu.be/SUcRywSry5U?t=980) "waited for the... macro... 9:50 to 10:10."
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Macro window execution increases volatility and stop-run risk; expect whipsaws.

title: NQ Trading Seek & Destroy Profile Jackson Hole Symposium Day 1
head: Three-PD-Array Defensive Framework
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:** When entering a trade, identify three independent PD arrays that support/defend the position:
  1. **Primary level** — Direct entry reference (inversion FVG high/low, order block boundary, etc.)
  2. **Secondary level** — Wick consequent encroachment (midpoint of prior wick; next friction level)
  3. **Tertiary level** — Volume imbalance or order block low (additional support if primary breaks)
  These three levels form a "stack" of defense. Stop loss is placed just below the tertiary level. If price violates all three, the trade thesis is negated.
- **How to identify:** Identify the entry level; then scan for the next two support levels downward (or upward for shorts).
- **How to use:** Place stops below the tertiary level (the lowest defense). As price moves in your favor and confirms the trend, raise stops to protect profits.
- **Example in this video:** Three PD arrays stacked: (1) inversion FVG low, (2) wick consequent encroachment, (3) volume imbalance high. Stop was placed below all three.
- **Timestamps:** [0:04:03](https://youtu.be/SUcRywSry5U?t=243) "three levels being like my three PD arrays that supports the trade," [0:07:25](https://youtu.be/SUcRywSry5U?t=445) "several wicks and an order block down close candle supporting my trade."
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** All three must be identified before entry; don't add them after the fact.

title: NQ Trading Seek & Destroy Profile Jackson Hole Symposium Day 1
head: Inversion Fair Value Gap (Multiple Uses)
body:
- **Kind:** entry model (advanced)
- **What ICT says:** On volatile days (seek-and-destroy), multiple inversion FVGs may form as price oscillates. Each oscillation creates an inversion FVG zone where the previous wick becomes the reversal target. ICT may enter multiple contracts into different inversion FVG zones on the same day, pyramiding the position as each zone confirms.
- **How to identify:** After price makes a run up and wicks, the wick becomes an inversion FVG target for the next downside run. When price dips back into that zone, it's an entry point for the next leg up.
- **How to use:** Identify inversion FVG zones at different price levels; enter partial position into each zone as confirmed. This is pyramiding into range-bound volatility.
- **Example in this video:** Multiple inversion FVGs were identified and used; ICT entered, took partials at targets, and re-entered into new inversion FVG zones on subsequent pullbacks.
- **Timestamps:** [0:01:39](https://youtu.be/SUcRywSry5U?t=99) "wick... premium wick that's just above me," [0:03:15](https://youtu.be/SUcRywSry5U?t=195) "I want to see it now stay either in the upper half."
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Requires active monitoring; set limit orders for pyramiding; do not chase.

title: NQ Trading Seek & Destroy Profile Jackson Hole Symposium Day 1
head: Wick Consequent Encroachment (Dynamic Stop Level)
body:
- **Kind:** refinement
- **What ICT says:** The midpoint of any wick acts as a dynamic support/resistance level. As the trade progresses and new wicks form, their midpoints become the next friction levels. When raising stops, move them to just below the midpoint of the wick that supports the current position. This ensures maximum profit protection without giving up gains.
- **How to identify:** After each candlestick, note the wick high and low; calculate midpoint; mark it on chart.
- **How to use:** Use wick CE as stops and as retracement targets. Raise stop to wick CE when position is confirmed and moves in your favor.
- **Example in this video:** As the long position moved higher and new wicks formed, ICT raised the stop to just below the consequent encroachment of the most recent supporting wick.
- **Timestamps:** [0:02:27](https://youtu.be/SUcRywSry5U?t=147) "showing basically the wick. That's good encouragement," [0:06:33](https://youtu.be/SUcRywSry5U?t=393) "Just the low of the wick that I measured consequent encroachment."
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Dynamic; must update as new wicks form.

title: NQ Trading Seek & Destroy Profile Jackson Hole Symposium Day 1
head: SIBI (Sell-Side Imbalance, Buy-Side Inefficiency)
body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:** A candlestick with a down-close (close below open) creates a "sell-side imbalance" — the gap between open and close. This indicates selling pressure. However, the wick below that close (the "buy-side inefficiency") represents price that the market didn't stay at; it's an inefficiency that price may fill on subsequent bounces. Multiple SIBIs on a seek-and-destroy day represent successive "tests" of support.
- **How to identify:** Identify down-close candles; mark the open-to-close gap (the imbalance); note the wick low below (the inefficiency).
- **How to use:** For longs: SIBI zones become targets for upside runs. When price pulls back into a SIBI from above, it bounces upward (testing that inefficiency from below). For pyramid entries, target the upper part of the SIBI zone for limit orders.
- **Example in this video:** Multiple SIBIs were identified; price was expected to bounce and fill the upper portions of these zones.
- **Timestamps:** [0:02:27](https://youtu.be/SUcRywSry5U?t=147) "volume imbalance," [0:09:02](https://youtu.be/SUcRywSry5U?t=542) "another sibi," [0:04:54](https://youtu.be/SUcRywSry5U?t=294) "I want to see it now stay... in the upper half."
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Imbalance is the gap; inefficiency is the wick. Don't confuse the two.

title: NQ Trading Seek & Destroy Profile Jackson Hole Symposium Day 1
head: Institutional Order Flow Entry Drill
body:
- **Kind:** refinement
- **What ICT says:** When a volume imbalance or SIBI zone is only partially filled (price dips into lower portion but doesn't fill the entire gap), this indicates institutional buying at discount — they're accumulating without fully committing. This "partly unfilled" condition is bullish and signals continuation upward is likely.
- **How to identify:** Mark a SIBI or volume imbalance; observe price movement: if it dips into lower portion but bounces before filling upper portion, it's an institutional entry drill.
- **How to use:** When you see this pattern, expect strong upside continuation. It's a green light to hold position or pyramid.
- **Example in this video:** "Institutional order flow entry drill" was called out multiple times as price kept partly-unfilled gaps and bounced higher.
- **Timestamps:** [0:15:29](https://youtu.be/SUcRywSry5U?t=929) "institutional order flow entry drill," [0:25:33](https://youtu.be/SUcRywSry5U?t=1533) "You just want to give an opportunity for institutional order flow entry drill."
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Opposite: fully-filled gap = weakness.

title: NQ Trading Seek & Destroy Profile Jackson Hole Symposium Day 1
head: Buy-Side Imbalance, Sell-Side Efficiency
body:
- **Kind:** definition (inverse of SIBI)
- **What ICT says:** An up-close candlestick (close above open) creates a "buy-side imbalance" — gap between open and close. The wick above that close (the "sell-side efficiency") represents price that the market didn't sustain; it's inefficiency that may be filled on subsequent pullbacks. Identifying where buy-side imbalances exist helps predict pullback targets.
- **How to identify:** Mark up-close candles; note the open-to-close gap (imbalance); note the wick high above (efficiency).
- **How to use:** For longs: these areas are where you expect minimal pullback (they're resistant to filling due to sell-side efficiency). For shorts: they're targets to test and fill.
- **Example in this video:** Buy-side imbalances from prior days (August 4th NQ) were referenced as structural support; failing to reach these levels was bullish.
- **Timestamps:** [0:22:10](https://youtu.be/SUcRywSry5U?t=1330) "August 4th, 2026 NQ buy side imbalance sell side inefficiency," [0:24:24](https://youtu.be/SUcRywSry5U?t=1464) "buy side imbalance sell side efficiency."
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Opposite of SIBI; bullish vs. bearish implication.

title: NQ Trading Seek & Destroy Profile Jackson Hole Symposium Day 1
head: Cork Pattern (Consolidation Before Breakout)
body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:** Before breaking through to a new high, price often consolidates into a tight, seemingly odd-shaped price block — the "cork pattern." This is not a classic bull flag or bear flag; it's a sloppy, tight block of price action that resists moving higher (or lower) for a few candles. Once it "pops the cork" (breaks out of the consolidation), it runs quickly to the next target. This pattern is characteristic of seek-and-destroy days.
- **How to identify:** Look for a tight, rectangular-ish block of price action just below (for longs) or above (for shorts) a key target level.
- **How to use:** Patience is critical. When you see a cork pattern forming, know that breakout is coming. Don't exit the trade out of impatience. The consolidation is setup for the next big move.
- **Example in this video:** Cork pattern formed around the intraday high target; ICT identified it and advised patience: "Like a champagne bottle being popped."
- **Timestamps:** [0:19:49](https://youtu.be/SUcRywSry5U?t=1189) "This looks like it's starting to cork," [0:20:36](https://youtu.be/SUcRywSry5U?t=1236) "weird little block of price action," [0:23:01](https://youtu.be/SUcRywSry5U?t=1381) "cork... sloppy little block."
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Requires patience and conviction in the setup; many traders exit prematurely.

title: NQ Trading Seek & Destroy Profile Jackson Hole Symposium Day 1
head: Discount Sensitivity Zone
body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:** The upper half of a wick (or the zone between the wick low and the wick midpoint) is the "discount sensitivity" area. When price trades in this zone on a pullback, it's still in a discount area. Trading in the discount zone (rather than chasing higher) is lower-risk. Expect price to bounce from this zone.
- **How to identify:** Identify a wick; divide into two halves (lower = deep discount, upper = shallow discount/sensitivity).
- **How to use:** For pullback entries, buy the upper half of the discount zone (discount sensitivity area), not the lower half (deep discount where reversals are uncertain).
- **Example in this video:** The upper half of prior wicks was referenced as the ideal zone for maintaining bullish position without over-risking.
- **Timestamps:** [0:03:15](https://youtu.be/SUcRywSry5U?t=195) "use the high of it for discount sensitivity," [0:11:25](https://youtu.be/SUcRywSry5U?t=685) "the discount array... upper half of the wick."
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Context-dependent; in strong uptrends, discount sensitivity area is preferred for entries.

title: NQ Trading Seek & Destroy Profile Jackson Hole Symposium Day 1
head: Limit Orders for Pyramiding
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:** Rather than manually chasing price higher for pyramid entries, use limit orders placed at anticipated resistance/target levels. When price reaches the limit order price, the order automatically fills, adding to the position without requiring manual intervention or emotional decision-making. This is especially valuable on volatile days where multiple pyramids are planned.
- **How to identify:** Identify the next target level (top of next inversion FVG, relative equal high, etc.); place a limit order slightly below that level to increase fill probability.
- **How to use:** Pre-place limit orders before entering the trade; let the market fill them as price runs. Reduces need to stare at the screen for every pyramid add.
- **Example in this video:** Multiple limit orders were placed for pyramid contracts; ICT watched them execute rather than manually chasing.
- **Timestamps:** [0:08:14](https://youtu.be/SUcRywSry5U?t=494) "I'll use a limit order here," [0:13:04](https://youtu.be/SUcRywSry5U?t=784) "put a limit order in there for contracts."
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Risk of limit orders not filling if price gaps over them; must balance fill probability with target precision.

title: NQ High Of Day Short Review
head: First Presented Fair Value Gap (aliases: first presented fair gap, first fair gap, FPFVG)
body:
- **Kind:** definition + rule + example
- **What ICT says:** The earliest fair value gap that can form in a session—occurs at 9:31 ET on NQ (the second 1m candle). It's identifiable before the day even begins by looking at the previous Friday's first presented gap. Must track both Monday and Friday first presented gaps from the last two weeks. These gaps are "Easter eggs" embedded in markets and repeat with high probability; they often signal the daily high or low.
- **How to identify:** Look at open and close of 9:31 candlestick; if no volume imbalance in upper half, examine lower half. The gap is the space between the high of one candle and the low of the next (or vice versa).
- **How to use:** Use these gaps as reference levels for predicting where price will trade intraday. Watch whether bodies close above/below consequent encroachment (midpoint) to determine bullish/bearish bias. If bodies fail to touch the upper half and stay in lower half, that's bearish. Use the gap to identify session reversals or continuation points.
- **Example in this video:** NQ, Friday Aug 21, 9:31 ET: first presented gap is 426.00 (open/close both 426.00, so use wick). Projected forward to Tuesday Aug 23. Twice during the morning (8:18 ET and again ~9:00 ET), price rallied into this gap's upper half but bodies couldn't touch consequent encroachment—bearish signal. Later in the session, when price trades into the upper half again, it fails to close there, confirming the gap as weak resistance.
- **Timestamps:** [0:13:38](https://youtu.be/P8Pn8DHFSW8?t=818) — identifying Friday's first gap; [0:16:03](https://youtu.be/P8Pn8DHFSW8?t=963) — projecting it to today; [0:28:15](https://youtu.be/P8Pn8DHFSW8?t=1695) — bodies respecting consequent encroachment
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** ICT claims this is original methodology not taught by Wyckoff, Elliott Wave, or other price action traders. The logic applies to stocks, forex, bonds, commodities (he's used it across all instruments). Keep only the last two weeks' Friday and Monday first gaps on charts—don't clutter; use separate workspaces for PD array tracking.

title: NQ High Of Day Short Review
head: Opening Range Gap (aliases: RTH opening range gap, ORG)
body:
- **Kind:** definition + rule + example
- **What ICT says:** Gap between the previous day's 4:14 PM ET close (end of RTH) and the 9:30 ET open of the next day. Premium gap = opens higher; discount gap = opens lower. Divide the gap into octants and consequent encroachment (midpoint). 70% probability of trading to the midpoint (consequent encroachment) within first 30 minutes (by 10:00 ET).
- **How to identify:** Find the close price of previous RTH day and the open at 9:30 ET next day. Measure the difference. Use fib from high to low of gap; mark octants (upper quadrant, upper percentile, consequent encroachment, lower percentile, lower quadrant).
- **How to use:** In a premium gap (opens higher), expect price to retrace to at least the gap midpoint as low-hanging fruit. Don't demand full gap closure. For intraday: take first partial at the low formed before the gap, then manage for midgap. Entry signals: watch how bodies behave relative to octants.
- **Example in this video:** NQ Aug 23, opens at 9:30 ET at higher level than Aug 22 close (premium gap). Consequent encroachment (gap midpoint) = yesterday's 4:14 PM close. Price is expected to trade down to this level by 10:00 ET. ICT shorts into the gap's octants; targets the midpoint; later pushes for new day opening gap.
- **Timestamps:** [0:37:50](https://youtu.be/P8Pn8DHFSW8?t=2270) — defining ORG; [0:41:02](https://youtu.be/P8Pn8DHFSW8?t=2462) — 70% rule and octants; [0:50:47](https://youtu.be/P8Pn8DHFSW8?t=3047) — naked chart with fib on gap
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Don't demand full gap closure; that's greedy. Two partials (one at prior day's low, one at gap midpoint) are often sufficient for a profitable session.

title: NQ High Of Day Short Review
head: New Week Opening Gap (aliases: NWOG, new week gap)
body:
- **Kind:** definition + rule
- **What ICT says:** Difference between Friday's 4:14 PM ET close (end of RTH) and Sunday 6 PM ET open (start of new week in electronic markets). Project this gap across entire week. Keep last five weeks on chart but only mark gaps relevant to current price action.
- **How to identify:** Track Friday close to Sunday 6 PM open difference.
- **How to use:** Price often respects new week opening gap in early morning rally/decline. If price runs above it early, it signals strong directional bias. Mark it as a level not to be taken for granted.

title: NQ High Of Day Short Review

title: NQ High Of Day Short Review
head: Consequent Encroachment (aliases: CE, consequent encouragement, 0.5 level)
body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:** The midpoint (50% Fibonacci) of a PD array (fair value gap, opening range gap, wick). Bodies stopping below CE while wicks can exceed it indicate bearish pressure. Bodies in upper half of PDA = bullish; lower half = bearish. It's the "threshold" between bullish and bearish order flow.
- **How to identify:** Apply Fibonacci from high to low (or low to high) of the imbalance; 0.5 level = CE. Visual: draw horizontal line at midpoint.
- **How to use:** Order flow filter. If bodies can't reach CE, that's rejection of that zone. Watch where closes land relative to CE to confirm direction.
- **Example in this video:** Multiple instances where bodies stop short of consequent encroachment of Friday's first gap, signaling bearish bias. At [0:32:12](https://youtu.be/P8Pn8DHFSW8?t=1932): wick goes above, but body closes way underneath—bearish.

title: NQ High Of Day Short Review
head: Relative Equal Highs (aliases: REH, relative equal lows)
body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:** When price makes two (or more) highs at approximately the same level. This level represents buy-side liquidity above, which traders will target. If price pokes above and rejects, that's a short entry (turtle soup, false breakout).
- **How to identify:** Look for two highs within same session separated by at least one candlestick. Mark them on chart.
- **How to use:** Likely to trade up into REH; watch for wick or body rejection above. Short-entry zone if bodies fail to close above REH.
- **Example in this video:** Two highs in early morning (before 8:18 ET) at approximately same level. Buy side liquidity sits above. When price trades above late morning at ~10:20 ET, it pokes the REH level but doesn't close above it—short signal.
- **Timestamps:** [0:23:23](https://youtu.be/P8Pn8DHFSW8?t=1403) — identifying REH
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Don't expect it to be blown out without first showing rejection.

title: NQ High Of Day Short Review
head: Order Flow and Body Placement (aliases: bullish/bearish order flow)
body:
- **Kind:** rule + example
- **What ICT says:** Where the body closes within a candle is the truth. Don't use complex volume profile or value area—just look at open, high, low, close. If body is in upper half of PDA and candle closes there, it's bullish. If body is in lower half or middle, it's bearish. The wick can go anywhere, but body placement is the real order flow signal.
- **How to identify:** Draw horizontal line at midpoint of PDA; observe where each candle's body (not wick) closes.
- **How to use:** Confirm direction bias. Entry/exit filter.
- **Example in this video:** [0:32:01](https://youtu.be/P8Pn8DHFSW8?t=1921) — multiple candles trade into Friday's FVG upper half but bodies fail to close there, staying in lower half = bearish.

title: NQ High Of Day Short Review
head: Wick Behavior and Imbalance Measurement
body:

- **What ICT says:** Wicks can be treated as gaps/imbalances just like bodies. Measure wick from body low to wick high as an imbalance, apply Fibonacci, and find consequent encroachment. Wicks are allowed to exceed PDAs, so when a wick penetrates above a gap and the body closes below, that's a strong bearish signal.
- **How to identify:** Identify the wick; measure from body close (or low) to wick extreme; grade the 0.5 level.
- **How to use:** Stop placements, target zones. If price climbs via wick alone but body rejects, short it.
- **Example in this video:** Early morning wick at ~6:00 AM ET penetrates Friday's 9:31 FVG, but body closes below it—bearish setup confirmed. Later shorts placed in premium of wicks, betting on body rejection.

title: NQ High Of Day Short Review
head: Inversion Fair Value Gap (aliases: iFVG, reversal FVG)
body:
- **Kind:** definition + rule
- **What ICT says:** When a gap that was bullish (buy-side efficiency) gets traded into from above, it becomes a bearish inversion gap on the way down. First utilization = buy-side efficiency; second = inversion. The bodies behavior inside the iFVG (upper/lower half) still applies.
- **How to identify:** Track when a prior bull gap becomes a reversal point. Watch for close below the wick of that gap.
- **How to use:** Confirm continuation lower. If bodies stay in upper half, iFVG is weak; if bodies are in lower half and close below wick, iFVG is strong and price will continue lower.
- **Example in this video:** Friday's first FVG transitions from buy-side (first utilization) to iFVG (second utilization) when price trades into it from the short side. The structure repeats on smaller ranges throughout the day.
- **Timestamps:** [0:49:11](https://youtu.be/P8Pn8DHFSW8?t=2951) — iFVG recognition; [0:53:59](https://youtu.be/P8Pn8DHFSW8?t=3239) — iFVG behavior and continuation
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** A "failed" FVG is valuable as an iFVG; don't see it as a loss. ICT says this gives him "an out" for every scenario, which critics mock, but he argues it's the reality of how markets work.

title: NQ High Of Day Short Review
head: Session Phases and Consolidation/Expansion (aliases: four-phase market, consolidation vs expansion)
body:

- **What ICT says:** If London (overnight) trended up, the next session (7–9 AM pre-market, 9:30+ RTH) will likely consolidate or reverse—rarely do three straight sessions trend the same direction. After consolidation, expect expansion. Consolidation looks like a tight range; expansion looks like a breakout move.
- **How to identify:** Compare overnight range size to pre-market range to early RTH move.
- **How to use:** Bias for consolidation after overnight trend; bias for expansion after consolidation.

title: NQ High Of Day Short Review
head: Identifying Daily High/Low via Fibonacci Measurements
body:
- **Kind:** example + technique
- **What ICT says:** Anchor a Fibonacci to the low of a swing (using bodies, not wicks), then look at the negative 0.5 level. When price comes down from a wick and the body aligns with that negative 0.5 level, that's often the day's high (or low if measuring upward). It's a precise geometric signal.
- **How to identify:** (1) Identify swing low (body close), (2) Apply Fibonacci from that low upward, (3) Watch for price reaching negative 0.5 on the wick and aligning on body at that level on the next pullback.
- **How to use:** Confirm that a high/low is in place. Short into highs with confidence once this alignment appears. Enter short with first add when wick confirms, add second position if bodies align.
- **Example in this video:** NQ swing low around 29,316 (Aug 23 AM). Fibonacci up from there shows negative 0.5 at ~29,413. Wick runs to 29,414.75 (exact!), bodies pull back to align with that level—daily high confirmed. ICT shorts from there.

title: PreMarketSession NQ Consolidation August 25, 2026
head: Inversion Fair Value Gap and Utilization Shift
body:
- **Kind:** refinement + example
- **What ICT says:** A fair value gap has multiple utilizations. First utilization = original function (bearish FVG = down-close, bullish = up-close). When price closes above/outside a bearish FVG, it becomes an inversion FVG on the way back up. When price then closes back below it, it returns to its first (bearish) utilization. Each closure changes the gap's "character"; the shift is confirmed by body placement and close location.
- **How to identify:** (1) Mark the FVG, (2) note the close of the candle that created it, (3) watch if price closes outside (above/below) it—that's the shift to inversion, (4) once price closes back inside it from the inversion direction, it reclaims original utilization.
- **How to use:** Entry zones. On the shift to inversion, do not short immediately. On the return to first utilization (close outside it again), that's the true breakout and short entry. Wait for body placement confirmation (lower half) before committing.
- **Example in this video:** NQ pre-market trades down through a FVG (bearish, first utilization). Price bounces back up into it—this is now the inversion FVG phase. ICT doesn't short here. When price closes back below the FVG, it returns to original (bearish) character. Now short is valid with bodies showing lower half.
- **Timestamps:** [0:09:19](https://youtu.be/ieJSy4YsVgk?t=559) — explaining utilization concept; [0:14:41](https://youtu.be/ieJSy4YsVgk?t=881) — visual diagram of shift; [0:15:30](https://youtu.be/ieJSy4YsVgk?t=930) — drawing utilization layers
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** The shift is mechanical but requires patience. New traders want to short on inversion phase, but that's premature. Wait for the close-back-through and body placement confirmation.

head: Obsidian PD Array (aliases: Obsidian high/low, two-opposing-wicks midpoint)
body:
- **Kind:** new coinage + example
- **What ICT says:** When two wicks point in opposite directions, find the midpoint (consequent encroachment) of each wick. That level is the "Obsidian" and has strong support/resistance. Price tends to find levels there and use them as mini swing points within a range. Specific to consolidation periods.
- **How to identify:** Look for two wicks (one up, one down) in a consolidation range; measure each wick's midpoint (0.5 Fib level); if they align or are very close, you have Obsidian. Draw horizontal line(s) at these levels.
- **How to use:** Intraday range trading target. If shorting into a consolidation, aim for Obsidian to take a partial or place a stop. Price respects Obsidian more reliably in choppy ranges than in trends.
- **Example in this video:** NQ pre-market 7–9 AM consolidation: two opposing wicks, their midpoints form Obsidian levels. ICT watches price bounce between Obsidian high and a lower level. When price closes below Obsidian and stops holding, it signals willingness to drop further.

title: PreMarketSession NQ Consolidation August 25, 2026
head: Consolidation vs. Trending Sessions and Session Phases
body:
- **Kind:** rule + example
- **What ICT says:** After London trends (2–5 AM ET), the 7–9 AM pre-market will likely consolidate (boxy, choppy, rangy), not trend straight. Once 9:30 RTH opens, trending can resume. Each session type requires different tactics: consolidation = take partials quick, tight stops, nimble exits; trending = hold longer, let winners run, wider stops.
- **How to identify:** (1) Look at the previous session (London) for trend direction, (2) the 7–9 AM high/low forms a range, (3) price bounces within that range instead of breaking out, (4) rarely exceeds the prior high/low without quick rejection.
- **How to use:** Plan exits before entering. In consolidation, scale out 25–50% at minor levels (Obsidian, octants); don't wait for the full move. In trending, only take first partial, hold runner(s).
- **Example in this video:** London trended up overnight. 7–9 AM (pre-market) traded in a range, bouncing between highs and Obsidian. ICT planned to take partials here, noted his regret at not taking one at the first Obsidian touch. No trending until 9:30.
- **Timestamps:** [0:02:47](https://youtu.be/ieJSy4YsVgk?t=167) — session phases; [0:20:39](https://youtu.be/ieJSy4YsVgk?t=1239) — consolidation vs. trend explanation; [0:29:43](https://youtu.be/ieJSy4YsVgk?t=1783) — trading consolidation requires different approach; [0:36:45](https://youtu.be/ieJSy4YsVgk?t=2205) — importance of session type awareness
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Consolidation is not a failure; it's predictable and tradeable if you adjust your tactics. Missing partials in consolidation is one of ICT's stated weaknesses.

title: PreMarketSession NQ Consolidation August 25, 2026
head: Partial Taking Strategy in Consolidation
body:
- **Kind:** rule + example
- **What ICT says:** In a consolidation, don't hold the full position to the ultimate target. Take 25–75% at minor levels (Obsidian, consequent encroachment of key wicks, octants), lock in some profit, then let smaller position run if it does. ICT regrets not taking a partial at his first identified level; this costs him swing-to-swing scalps. By taking partials, you convert risk-free or near-risk-free situations.
- **How to identify:** Mark the minor levels (Obsidian, wick CE, quadrants) before trade; plan exits at each. Execute them on close confirmation.
- **How to use:** (1) Enter full position, (2) first target = take 50%, (3) second target = take 25% or half of remaining, (4) last 25% = runner or hold per plan. Adjust position size accordingly.
- **Example in this video:** ICT enters short 6 contracts into NWOG. First planned target = Obsidian low. Second = sell-side level lower. Meant to take 4 contracts off at Obsidian but didn't (regret noted). Later takes 6 contracts off entirely instead of scaling, then re-enters with 4. Says he should have split positions: 2–2–2 (three separate exits) instead of 6 then 4.
- **Timestamps:** [0:16:17](https://youtu.be/ieJSy4YsVgk?t=977) — mentions partials and missing opportunity; [0:24:12](https://youtu.be/ieJSy4YsVgk?t=1452) — planning multiple exits; [0:30:29](https://youtu.be/ieJSy4YsVgk?t=1829) — teaching about ranges and partial discipline
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Partial taking is harder in real-time than on replays; timing and emotional discipline required. ICT openly admits struggle with this.

title: PreMarketSession NQ Consolidation August 25, 2026
head: Wick Behavior and Rejection Signals in Consolidation
body:
- **Kind:** rule + example
- **What ICT says:** In consolidation, watch the wicks as they form. If a wick points up but the body stays in lower half and closes below the wick's midpoint (CE of the wick), that's rejection of the upside and a signal to continue lower. Conversely, if a wick points down but body closes in upper half, it's rejection of downside. The body's half-placement is the order flow truth; the wick is bait/test.
- **How to identify:** Watch each candle: wick direction, body close location (upper/lower half of prior PDA or range midpoint). Non-alignment = rejection.
- **How to use:** Confirmation for staying in trade or adding. If you're short and see upwick + lower-half body, hold/add. If upwick + upper-half body, consider exit.
- **Example in this video:** Multiple candles form in pre-market range; upwicks followed by bodies in lower half = continuation of short. When a body finally shows up in upper half of a wick, ICT considers taking a partial or tightening stop.
- **Timestamps:** [0:06:45](https://youtu.be/ieJSy4YsVgk?t=405) — wick behavior; [0:12:41](https://youtu.be/ieJSy4YsVgk?t=761) — body placement rules; [0:19:52](https://youtu.be/ieJSy4YsVgk?t=1192) — watching for upper-half body as warning
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Mohawk (wick touch + quick close back down) is permissible but weakest form of order flow.

body:

  - The new week opening gap (Friday close to Sunday 6:00 pm ET open) is plotted and used as a reaction level: price sold off from it, cleared sell-side, and pulled right back up into it, around the BISI's quadrant level, a confluence with the daily array. "We need to use the new week opening gap."

title: Monday Review On NQ & PreMarket Session Rules Revisited
head: The 7:00–9:00 am ET consolidation rule (pre-market)  (aliases: "seven to nine", pre-market range, 7-9 rule)
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - Mark 7:00 am ET and examine 7:00–9:00: whether price consolidates or trends over that window "tells you how the morning session's going to move". He says nobody else teaches this and it is "the rules".
  - If the window consolidates, expect big one-directional movement at 9:30 ET; the direction comes from the higher-timeframe narrative (here the daily BISI and the seasonal tendency toward lower prices, which he had told followers on Saturday's space).
  - Distinguish a pop from a trend: in the example price ran up for about 40 minutes at the start of the window only to take the buy side out ("just running liquidity, that's not a trend"), then dropped back inside the low-high range and gyrated around its middle: "not being allowed to protract. So, it's consolidating."
  - Read the bodies, not the wicks: smooth = where the bodies are; jagged = where the wicks are; "the wick is where the damage is allowed to be done". The range's liquidity is at the extreme of the bodies. Expect price to approach 9:30, clear the bodies on the high side (buy-side liquidity of the opening minutes) and "flutter and run above" in the first minutes of the opening range.
  - Once price is above the CE of a prior wick, that wick is no longer a factor; the normal bearish rule (stay in the lower half of the wick) does not apply when you expect the bodies' buy side to be cleared first.
- **How to identify:** (1) mark 7:00; (2) grade the 7:00–9:00 range; (3) is it consolidating around its middle (no protraction) or a trend; (4) locate the extreme of the bodies as the liquidity.
- **How to use:** consolidation in the 7–9 range + a daily bias → plan for a one-directional move at 9:30 and look to enter on the setup that follows (here a short after clearing the buy side).
- **Example in this video:** Monday Aug 24, 7:00–9:00 NQ: a ~40 minute run up took the buy side, then a drop back inside and a rotation around the midpoint; 9:30 then produced a very fast fall out of the open (he missed it).
- **Timestamps:** [0:06:31](https://youtu.be/grcLMbjs-zs?t=391) 7:00 marked · [0:07:22](https://youtu.be/grcLMbjs-zs?t=442) pop vs trend, consolidation · [0:08:10](https://youtu.be/grcLMbjs-zs?t=490) bodies not wicks · [0:17:51](https://youtu.be/grcLMbjs-zs?t=1071) "consolidating between 7 and 9, that's the rules" · [0:21:50](https://youtu.be/grcLMbjs-zs?t=1310) nobody else teaches it
- **Nuance / caveats:** Title says "revisited" (earlier teaching exists; this clip adds the bodies-not-wicks reading and the "pop is liquidity, not trend" distinction). Time zone is ET (7:00–9:00 am). Compare the overnight-trend/consolidation reasoning in [[L26-018]].

  - "While the market is not allowed to go lower": price tried to sell off using the SIBI as a bearish FVG, took out the swing low and bodies, then came back above it. Because price closed back above the bearish gap it became a bullish inversion FVG.
  - He notes the run lower counts as a run below even though the wick was not taken out: "the wick is allowed to do the damage"; the volume you need is "all in the candlestick".
  - After the iFVG, price rallied toward the high of the SIBI/its low draw ("look for it to trade up into this high because we have the low of this SIBI right here").
  - Subsequent path: consolidates, trades back down to quadrant 0.75, accumulates, rallies to the next octant, consolidates, trades into the order block, rallies to the low of the SIBI, then into a small gap; later hits the upper quadrant of the daily BISI and sells off sharply.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 1m, Monday Aug 24 ~10:00-10:30 ET: SIBI first presented FVG → short attempt fails → closes back above (iFVG) → rally to the SIBI low and nearby gaps.

title: Friday Review On NQ & PreMarket Session Rules Revisited
head: 7:00–9:00 am ET dealing range: trending vs consolidating predicts the AM session  (aliases: 7-9 rule, pre-market dealing range)
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - Look at the range between 7:00 am and 9:00 am ET (a "small little two-hour window"); the highs and lows of that window are the bookends. When a report is due at 8:30, use 7:00 to 8:30 instead of 9:00 (he mentioned this for a CPI or PPI day).
  - Determine how price books: trending ("allowed to protract", moving) versus consolidating (a block, a swatch of price that cannot even get to the CE of an earlier wick with bodies).
  - If 7–9 is a trend, the AM session is "a block, up and down, up and down" (choppy, harder to trade for an average student; he can trade it but it is not for those who do not understand this algorithmic phenomenon).
  - If 7–9 is consolidation, the AM session after 9:00/9:30 should trend. Friday: "Consolidation between 7:00 and 9:00 on Friday tells us what is likely to occur in the AM session... We're going to get trending environments."
  - General statement of the logic: "If the previous session is in consolidation, the next session's going to move. The next session after that expected to be in consolidation, but be prepared in the event that it is trending in the 24-hour cycle." The algorithm compresses into holding patterns, lulls traders into thinking nothing is happening, then makes a big move.
  - Grade the 7–9 range: draw the high-to-low fib; keep the 50% (equilibrium) line a different color; above it is premium, at or below is discount (his words: "anything at that price or higher... premium. Anything less than this level or at that level is considered discount").
  - The levels carry forward across sessions: "my levels don't have an expiration date"; Thursday's 7–9 levels were still in use on Friday. Looking back "the last three sessions" supplies all the information needed; you "don't even need a daily chart".
  - Source claim: no Wyckoff book teaches looking at the 7–9 range to predict how the AM session trades; he repeats that the premium/discount concept is also not in Wyckoff.
- **How to identify:** mark the high and low of 7–9 (e.g., Thursday: high at the 7:00 candle, low at 8:36 am); ask if bodies rotate in a tight block (consolidation, exact equal highs) or progress (trend).
- **How to use:** consolidation → expect trending AM session; trend → expect block/chop AM. Direction of the trend comes from higher-timeframe narrative and where the bodies fail (see below).
- **Example in this video:** Thursday Aug 27 7–9: clear trend; high at 7:00, low at 8:36; AM session was chopping ("block", seek and destroy; see [[L26-021]]). Friday Aug 28 7–9: a block whose two highs were the same price, 29,539, with bodies unable to touch the CE of Thursday's range wick; AM session then trended down.
- **Timestamps:** [0:00:51](https://youtu.be/4KW2acdPi-M?t=51) no Wyckoff source · [0:01:39](https://youtu.be/4KW2acdPi-M?t=99) rules and window, 8:30 caveat · [0:03:15](https://youtu.be/4KW2acdPi-M?t=195) Thursday is a trend · [0:04:03](https://youtu.be/4KW2acdPi-M?t=243) trend means AM session is a block · [0:11:56](https://youtu.be/4KW2acdPi-M?t=716) Friday is a block · [0:12:48](https://youtu.be/4KW2acdPi-M?t=768) previous session consolidation → next moves · [0:14:23](https://youtu.be/4KW2acdPi-M?t=863) consolidation 7–9 → trend after 9
- **Nuance / caveats:** Extends the Monday review in [[L26-026]] (bodies not wicks; pop vs trend). The "8:30 report" exception is new here. On Thursday the low printed at 8:36, after 8:30, so he evidently still used the full window that day (caption does not say why).

title: NQ Consolidation Day Algorithmic Rules In Action
head: 7:00–9:00 am ET rule: trending 7–9 means a consolidating AM session  (aliases: 7–9 rule, pre-market session rule)
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - Make sure charts are on New York (Eastern) time. Mark 7:00 am and 9:00 am with vertical lines; take the highest high and lowest low between them.
  - "The algorithm will absolutely go into a consolidation during the AM session if 7 to 9 is trending." The AM session here is 9:30–11:30; it will likely go sideways, frustrate and chop traders; inexperienced traders complain.
  - "If you're going to be trading morning session, you remove 75% of the adversity if you understand this simple principle."
  - The probability of a hard market (consolidation) increases further if price trades to a key level during 7–9. Here the daily key level was the August 6 low (29,241.25); 7–9 hit 29,240.00 ("modestly below it, but it still got there"), met a daily objective while trending, and no later candle in the window went lower ("it stopped right there on the lowest candle").
  - These lessons are found in the "long dry portions" of his lectures: take notes of rules, caveats and "quirky little things" that tell you when to dismiss something.
- **How to identify:** 7–9 high and low; is price progressing in one direction (trend) or rotating around the middle (consolidation); did it tag a key HTF level.
- **How to use:** trending 7–9 + key-level tag → plan for a sideways AM; trade smaller or wait for traps; do not demand a trend.
- **Example in this video:** NQ Sept, 7–9 low 29,240.00 at the Aug 6 daily low.
- **Timestamps:** [0:02:23](https://youtu.be/0olLwAiLa3o?t=143) 7:00–9:00 NY time, charts on NY time · [0:03:58](https://youtu.be/0olLwAiLa3o?t=238) the rule · [0:04:46](https://youtu.be/0olLwAiLa3o?t=286) AM session 9:30–11:30 will chop · [0:05:36](https://youtu.be/0olLwAiLa3o?t=336) 75% of adversity, key-level tag · [0:06:23](https://youtu.be/0olLwAiLa3o?t=383) met daily objective
- **Nuance / caveats:** The "75%" figure is his estimate of how much adversity is removed. Same rule as [[L26-026]] and [[L26-027]].

head: 7–9 range equilibrium and octant sensitivity (bodies cannot touch the 0.625 octant in premium)  (aliases: premium sensitivity, discount sensitivity)
body:
- **Kind:** rule / example
- **What ICT says:**
  - After the 7–9 window closes, the equilibrium of the 7–9 range (the 50% line) tells you where premium is: price above it is "absolutely in a premium".
  - Price rallied to the 0.625 octant (caption "625 octant") of the 7–9 range, but the bodies could not touch or lay down on it while above in premium: "the algorithm can't hide it; it's simply going to be visible in the price delivery." Market then "breaks down aggressively".
  - Premium sensitivity = the lower half of a PD array when bearish (price should be capped/supported below it); when bullish, the upper half is the discount sensitivity. Wicks are allowed to do the damage; the bodies say "absolutely not, can't go up here".
  - Later a SIBI on the intraday chart: price rallied into the gap, threw a wick up, and left bodies in the lower half: "exactly what you want to see with real order flow, algorithmic order flow."
- **Timestamps:** [0:06:23](https://youtu.be/0olLwAiLa3o?t=383) equilibrium of the 7–9 range · [0:07:11](https://youtu.be/0olLwAiLa3o?t=431) bodies don't touch the 0.625 octant · [0:12:00](https://youtu.be/0olLwAiLa3o?t=720) wick up, bodies in lower half · [0:12:47](https://youtu.be/0olLwAiLa3o?t=767) premium sensitivity vs discount sensitivity
- **Nuance / caveats:** The octant is "625" in captions; I read it as 0.625 (one octant above midpoint on the premium side, if measured from the low).

title: NQ Consolidation Day Algorithmic Rules In Action
head: Waiting for traps on a consolidation day; unfinished business at a shallow low  (aliases: soft bias, traps)
body:
- **Kind:** rule / example
- **What ICT says:**
  - The run down to the Aug 6 low (29,241.25) was so shallow that it is a reasonable draw to be revisited: it may have "unfinished business, wanting to go a little bit deeper". But "even though the market's likely to consolidate, we wait for traps."
  - What a trap looks like here: an inefficiency above (a SIBI), the market rallies into premium to take highs (relative equal highs) and run buy stops/shorts' stops, drawing breakout buyers in (their stops sit right below the low), then breaks lower.
  - He holds a "soft bias" for lower prices because of the unfinished business below, while expecting consolidation; he would prefer the Aug 6 low be taken "more convincingly" but says "today's just not a day that you want to be pushing it".
  - Mechanics of the day: after the 9:30 open, price rallied to premium, gave indication that order flow was not continuing higher, broke lower, and consolidated around the 9:30 opening price.

title: ICT Obsidian Teaching
head: Obsidian (two opposing wicks, second wick higher for shorts)  (aliases: Obsidian model/PD array)
body:
- **Kind:** entry model / new coinage (first teaching; he promises more details later)
- **What ICT says:**
  - "Obsidian is two opposing wicks within a narrative", and the second wick has to be higher than the first one when you are bearish. You split both wicks in half (CE of each); price action will "do these types of things" between the two CE levels.
  - You look for such wicks when you expect price to eventually turn lower: a candle with a wick above it and a candle with a wick below it, grading both and extending the midpoints to the right. The opposing wick that forms later must be above the first.
  - Sequence in the example: price trades lower and closes below the structure; on the first run back up into the zone price is not willing to put a body in the upper half of it; the focus zone is between this candle's CE and the other candle's CE.
  - He has already shorted higher but wants to build the short every time price enters the zone, targeting low-hanging fruit.
  - A SIBI/gap that sits between the wick low and wick high can be used as the entry reference ("I see a gap, so I'm putting something in there because I'm pretty confident that we're not going up here"). When the second wick forms higher, "that confirms to me that now I have obsidian".
  - Anytime price keeps tapping inside the zone it is "building a false consolidation" that bull-flag traders will buy, and it will deny them. Bodies later respect the wick's CE.
  - Requirement: you have to be right on the direction/narrative, on side; "otherwise this isn't going to work in your hands".
- **How to identify:** (1) bearish narrative from the daily chart; (2) two opposing wicks (an upper wick and a lower wick) with the later one higher; (3) mark CE of each and extend right; (4) price closes below, then retraces into the zone without bodies above its upper CE.
- **How to use:** short and add inside the zone; first target the low-hanging fruit projection (30,137.50 in the example); add more if price reaches the upper quadrant of the 7–9 dealing range; partial at lows and the first relative equal lows; lower stop as price drops. Entries were by market orders.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 1m, a Monday: after a Judas-style run up that swept the Friday morning buy-side pool, two opposing wicks formed (wick high above, wick low below, the second higher), a FVG sat between them anchored to the 7–9 range CE; he shorted inside, price dropped below a BISI whose close (253.75) validated an iFVG one tick under the gap high (254.00; leading digits not clear in the captions), bodies could not touch it on retests, then partials at the lows, relative equal lows and the NWOG upper quadrant; the final order rested just above 30,137.50.
- **Timestamps:** [0:23:39](https://youtu.be/EC0UuarROyo?t=1419) wick above and wick below, graded · [0:24:28](https://youtu.be/EC0UuarROyo?t=1468) zone between the two CEs · [0:26:58](https://youtu.be/EC0UuarROyo?t=1618) "Obsidian is two wicks opposing, the second higher than the first" · [0:33:27](https://youtu.be/EC0UuarROyo?t=2007) closing definition
- **Nuance / caveats:** Which wick forms first (up- vs down-wick) is not explicit in the captions; the rule he states is "second wick higher than the first" for bearish. A bullish mirror is implied, not taught. He explicitly says the details come in a later video.

title: ICT Obsidian Teaching
head: Take one PD array at a time ("marrying the vein"); daily premium PD arrays that built the bearish narrative  (aliases: narrative, daily PD arrays)
body:
- **Kind:** rule / process
- **What ICT says:**
  - Last week he gave two specific daily premium PD arrays: relative equal highs (which price cleared) and a wick (premium array). Take one array at a time: it's easy to say "we're going to all-time highs"; but price has to "prove itself" at the next array first. "Marrying the vein" (gold-miner expression): don't assume the mother lode because you found a few flakes.
  - Wick rule for the daily wick: if bullish (heading for the high, relative equal highs, maybe all-time highs) price must be able to post bodies above its midpoint; if it cannot, "that's a problem". Bearish: bodies stay in the lower half. For PDAs below market: the upper half should show discount sensitivity, with no willingness to put bodies in the lower half. "Nobody else has that."
  - A SIBI he drew is not a supply/demand zone: those become stale and want fresh zones; he deals with no expiration dates ("only the futures contract expires").
  - The relation of the three nested arrays (wick high lower than the SIBI candle's low; gap high above the wick but below the candle's high) is "what I talked about last week".
  - Warning to beginners: don't build the idea from will, desire or the thrill/anxiety of demo, funded challenges or live money; "the experience you're going by" is emotion.
- **Timestamps:** [0:00:47](https://youtu.be/EC0UuarROyo?t=47) marrying the vein · [0:01:37](https://youtu.be/EC0UuarROyo?t=97) wick body rules · [0:03:16](https://youtu.be/EC0UuarROyo?t=196) not supply and demand · [0:04:07](https://youtu.be/EC0UuarROyo?t=247) one PDA at a time, emotions · [0:04:55](https://youtu.be/EC0UuarROyo?t=295) no expiration dates

head: 7:00–9:00 am rule, graded and projected forward; Judas swing after 9:30  (aliases: 7–9 rule, Judas swing, protraction)
body:
- **Kind:** rule / example
- **What ICT says:**
  - Carry the weekend trader round-up's logic into Monday: if 7:00–9:00 is trending, expect initial consolidation/rangebound action in the morning ("Did we not get that? Sure it did."). Grade the 7–9 range high-to-low with quadrants and octants; the 50% is equilibrium; carry the levels forward.
  - Forget the daily wicks; the real story is between the 7:00 and 9:00 bookends.
  - After 9:30 the ideal is a Judas swing, "some measure of protraction higher" where smart money draws the crowd to chase longs: price goes above half of the range (premium) and sweeps a buy-side pool, in this case Friday's morning session high. If a leg out of 7–9 reaches the upper quadrant of the dealing range he would have added more; it did not.
  - He explains why he even cares about old highs: electronic trading hours (overnight Globex/London/Asia) trading needs to be booked as real delivery in RTH, so levels seen overnight may need redelivery in RTH; "we're going to need to see this level be traded to if we're opening up down here at 9:30."
  - Early in the morning price hit the NWOG several times (bearish, a weak showing) and rallied to clear the buy side.
- **Example in this video:** Monday: 7:00 high and 9:00 low graded; price traded down to the NWOG, started protraction higher after 9:00, high at 9:32 (not special, just the high after 9:00), swept Friday's morning high and the SIBI high on the daily, then collapsed.
- **Timestamps:** [0:10:47](https://youtu.be/EC0UuarROyo?t=647) 7:00–9:00 as dealing range · [0:11:36](https://youtu.be/EC0UuarROyo?t=696) trending 7–9 means rangebound morning · [0:16:28](https://youtu.be/EC0UuarROyo?t=988) Judas swing, premium sweep · [0:17:14](https://youtu.be/EC0UuarROyo?t=1034) ETH vs RTH redelivery · [0:22:53](https://youtu.be/EC0UuarROyo?t=1373) upper quadrant would have meant adding
