title: Trade Management & Removing The Need To Be Right
head: Trade management: fund the trade, partial early, trail the rest  (aliases: "trade management 101", "pay myself a hassle/harassment fee", "take the risk out of the trade")
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - The target (here NWOG high, 30,169.75) is only the best-case scenario. If you have no way of getting paid before price reaches the terminus (the last bit of what you expect to see), it is very hard to be profitable early in a career.
  - Once price has moved in your favor, take a partial so the position is "funded" and the trade cannot become a net loser in theory. The exception he gives is a gap against you that stops the rest out above entry.
  - Once a portion of the trade is locked in as profit, do not let the remaining unrealized profit erode. His analogy: you would not work Monday to Wednesday and then do Thursday and Friday for free.
  - Each time he pays himself he also tightens the stop on the remainder (the "hassle fee"). The stop goes to just above a structural level (a candle high plus 1 tick, then the wick's CE, then a candle high that has already "done its job").
  - Partials always add to the positive column of equity, so nobody can argue against them. He calls "no partials, that's stupid" the view of someone who is not consistently profitable.
  - Even if the last contracts get stopped out and price then runs to target, the trade was still profitable. A stop-out on the final piece is "a good stop out" if it is above a level that would invalidate the idea.
- **How to identify:** the situation is a trade in profit that is approaching a big magnet level (NWOG), or price action that is no longer supporting the idea (heavy retracement, "not organic" spikes).
- **How to use:**
  - Take one contract off when price runs into discount and shows "too much discount sensitivity", to fund the position (about 0:15:32).
  - Use a buy stop above a recent high (30,213) as the trailing exit for one contract. If it fills, that contract is a partial, and the remaining contracts keep their own wider stop.
  - Set a resting buy limit (30,179.75) just above the target as the second exit. Whichever of the two fills first, cancel the other. This is a manual one-cancels-the-other, because fluctuations could fill both and remove the chance of reaching the 30,169.75 terminus.
  - When one contract remains, move the stop in steps (see timestamps).
- **Example in this video:** short on NQ-type price (instrument not stated) from near the 8:30 ET Monday open. Stop initially just above the CE of a SIBI. About 3 contracts total (inferred): one peeled off for funding, one exited by trailing buy stop (he says this "secured $215 more"), one remaining. Final contract stop moved in several steps: high + 1 tick (about 0:31:04), then to the CE of a wick (about 0:49:53), then above a candle high at about 30,196.25 that had already spent two wicks above the BISI (about 0:52:39).
- **Timestamps:**
  - [0:14:42](https://youtu.be/F8s_vfK9HaM?t=882) — limit order to peel one off, placed just above the CE of last Thursday's dealing range
  - [0:25:19](https://youtu.be/F8s_vfK9HaM?t=1519) — buy-stop trailing idea
  - [0:26:07](https://youtu.be/F8s_vfK9HaM?t=1567) — whichever fills first, cancel the other
  - [0:28:40](https://youtu.be/F8s_vfK9HaM?t=1720) — why risk locked-in profit
  - [0:52:39](https://youtu.be/F8s_vfK9HaM?t=3159) — final stop placement logic
- **Nuance / caveats:** he says he would ideally have been in with more size (6 contracts at entry, 4 at the entry drill, 2 added, 3 held at the end) and would have had most of the position off inside the inversion FVG while carrying 3 to the end (about 0:39:13). He says the 60/40 odds shifted against him during the trade (see Process section).

title: Trade Management & Removing The Need To Be Right
head: Right is not required for profitability  (aliases: "removing the need to be right", "correct is not the game")
body:
- **Kind:** rule / mindset
- **What ICT says:**
  - Profitability means getting in while price moves in one direction and finding ways to get out in that direction, without needing the exact terminus you called.
  - Critics focus on "he said it would go there and it didn't" and ignore the entry logic, wick support and partials.
  - A trade can be "fruitful" even if the target is never reached. Seeing price reach the target proves you were right, but it is not what pays you.
  - Every trade is not guaranteed, and you should not demand that price reaches your target.
- **How to use:** build the exit plan so that profit is banked before the last leg, which is the purpose of the partials above.
- **Timestamps:** [0:35:07](https://youtu.be/F8s_vfK9HaM?t=2107), [0:37:33](https://youtu.be/F8s_vfK9HaM?t=2253), [0:41:27](https://youtu.be/F8s_vfK9HaM?t=2487)
- **Nuance / caveats:** he says nobody else teaches "all or nothing is wrong"; he positions partials as a core of his method.

title: Trade Management & Removing The Need To Be Right
head: Inversion Fair Value Gap (iFVG) as a premium array  (aliases ICT uses: "inversion", "first utilization", "give up the ghost")
body:
- **Kind:** refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - The reference gap is a BISI (caption: "buy side of balance, sell side efficiency") that was acting as a bullish PD array. For a short he wants it to fail as support.
  - The wanted behavior: price goes through the gap, or goes through and then comes back up, and respects it from below as a premium array that supports continuation lower. "First utilization" means the first reaction is as buy-side delivery; he does not want price to use it that way. He wants to see it be used as an inversion.
  - Validation is on closing bodies: price must close below the gap (below the candle's high / the gap's boundary), not merely wick through. Wicking down through it without leaving a body below it keeps it "still potentially in play", but not yet validated.
  - If bodies stay out of the upper half of the gap, that is good; any body in the upper half is a warning.
  - He says the gap need not spend any time there. He only does not want it used as first-utilization support.
- **How to identify:** a BISI that price trades down through, followed by a retest from below that is rejected, with bodies closing below its low. He also watches the CE and the opening level of the same candle ("the opening of that same candle, same value").
- **How to use:** short on the retest of the inverted gap. The stop sits just above the candle high that has already rejected twice (see trade management).
- **Example in this video:** the BISI is at 30,196.25 and above, in a retracement area. He wants a close below 30,196.25 (the candle's high / the next candle's open) to confirm the roll-over toward the NWOG. A small orange inversion zone at about 30,188–30,184 (caption garbled) is where he wishes he had taken most of the position off.
- **Timestamps:** [0:06:58](https://youtu.be/F8s_vfK9HaM?t=418) — first description of the BISI-to-inversion idea; [0:23:45](https://youtu.be/F8s_vfK9HaM?t=1425) — "if market is bullish we should see willingness to go higher; I want it used as inversion"; [0:49:06](https://youtu.be/F8s_vfK9HaM?t=2946) — wick through it but no body below, still in play
- **Nuance / caveats:** he notes that to a new trader a BISI looks like an obvious long, but "not necessarily": you have to know the narrative and whether he is even positioned that way (about 0:36:46). Critics who see an FVG that fails and say "ICT's concept doesn't work" ignore the context.

title: Trade Management & Removing The Need To Be Right
head: Bodies and closes versus opens and wicks  (aliases: "stronger on the close, not the open")
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - A move is stronger when a candle closes beyond a level than when it merely opens beyond it. "The open is just not as reliable for continuation."
  - For continuation lower he wanted a body to close below the midpoint (CE) of the gap or candle. A close below that is "usually indicative of a pretty high probability continuation".
  - A close below the body CE and below the midpoint of an earlier gap makes it highly likely price reaches lower at least to the relative equal lows.
  - Wicks are used for precision, e.g. he measures from the wick low to the CE of that wick and says anywhere in this zone you can add.
  - He draws a midpoint line on the volume imbalances and grades price: "as long as it keeps the bodies in the lower half, I'm okay with that."
- **Timestamps:** [0:02:56](https://youtu.be/F8s_vfK9HaM?t=176), [0:16:20](https://youtu.be/F8s_vfK9HaM?t=980), [0:22:08](https://youtu.be/F8s_vfK9HaM?t=1328)

title: Trade Management & Removing The Need To Be Right
head: Relative equal lows as the first target of the move  (aliases: "taking out these lows")
body:
- **Kind:** example only
- **What ICT says:** after a close below the SIBI's body CE and the midpoint of the gap, likelihood is high that price reaches lower, at least taking out the relative equal lows he has marked. How price behaves when it takes those lows is what he then grades. A body closing below the lower wick area is the signal to follow through and to pull the stop down inside the wick-low-to-wick-CE zone.
- **Timestamps:** [0:02:56](https://youtu.be/F8s_vfK9HaM?t=176), [0:04:34](https://youtu.be/F8s_vfK9HaM?t=274)

title: Trade Management & Removing The Need To Be Right
head: Volume imbalance and SIBI used for precision entry, stop and management  (aliases: "cibby" = SIBI in the captions; "institutional order entry drill" — caption unclear whether "drill" or "draw")
body:
- **Kind:** refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - Stop for the initial short goes just above the consequent encroachment (CE) of the SIBI; bodies should stay under it. He says he could make the stop a lot larger, but this "accomplishes the method".
  - A small volume imbalance near the entry candle should act as a premium array.
  - "Institutional order entry drill" (caption unclear): the entry point is one tick above the high of the candle to the left of a gap or volume imbalance, with the stop just above. In this video he cites a candle high at 30,251. He claims nobody else teaches the logic of precise entry, stop placement and stop management around imbalances.
  - He later added into the wick: his fill sat in the lower half of a wick, so the wick (and candle of entry) was treated as a premium array.
  - He calls a stack of "two volume imbalance" inside a SIBI a "suspension block" (caption: likely "suspension block", definition not given beyond that).
- **How to use:** the entry is a limit at or just above the volume imbalance or CE; stops above CE / candle highs; adding is done inside the wick portions (wick low to wick CE).
- **Timestamps:** [0:00:20](https://youtu.be/F8s_vfK9HaM?t=20), [0:09:45](https://youtu.be/F8s_vfK9HaM?t=585), [0:45:49](https://youtu.be/F8s_vfK9HaM?t=2749)
- **Nuance / caveats:** he says he would have gone short on the candlestick at the open but could not because his recording software was rendering the earlier video.

title: Trade Management & Removing The Need To Be Right
head: New Week Opening Gap (NWOG) as a draw and Monday framework  (aliases ICT uses: "Sunday's opening", "terminus draw", "black hole")
body:
- **Kind:** entry model / rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - NWOG is a "big black hole" that can pull price toward it, but price need not reach it. So know where you can get out before the terminus.
  - Monday framework for experienced traders: if price opens and rallies away from the NWOG, and never trades back to it during Sunday evening (Asia) or London, and there is no runaway price action higher or lower, then on Monday it is "very easy" to aim for a run to the NWOG. He calls it a "no-brainer type thing".
  - In this trade the target was the high of the NWOG (30,169.75) and he had also posted that idea publicly before the trade.
- **How to identify:** NWOG not yet traded back to in Sunday evening / Asia / London, price displaced away from it, no runaway trend.
- **How to use:** short or long toward the gap (direction opposite the move away), take partials before the gap, and treat the gap high / low as the terminus.
- **Timestamps:** [0:18:50](https://youtu.be/F8s_vfK9HaM?t=1130), [0:19:38](https://youtu.be/F8s_vfK9HaM?t=1178), [0:20:27](https://youtu.be/F8s_vfK9HaM?t=1227)

title: Trade Management & Removing The Need To Be Right
head: 8:30 ET as algorithmic expansion timing  (aliases: "8:30 time", "algorithmic expansion")
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:** the 8:30 a.m. ET time is when the algorithm can expand whether or not there is news. On this day there was a low-impact "Empire something" report (likely the Empire State manufacturing survey; caption unclear). He treats it as a timing aspect only: look for the volume imbalance to act as a premium array into the 8:30 expansion.
- **Timestamps:** [0:01:08](https://youtu.be/F8s_vfK9HaM?t=68)

title: Trade Management & Removing The Need To Be Right
head: Dealing range, CE, and octants of a prior 7:00–10:00 p.m. ET window  (aliases: "Asian range", "dealing range", ".875 octant")
body:
- **Kind:** refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - His partial limit is placed just above the CE (50%) of last Thursday's dealing range, which he defines as 7:00–10:00 p.m. ET. He clarifies this is not the forex-style Asian range. It is the window when the best trading can be done, 7:00 to 10:00 p.m. ET.
  - He expects price to be drawn to half of that range.
  - He also grades levels off the same range in octants, mentioning a ".875" octant, and says he wants to see what price does there. It is a premium level for a short (about 0:29:28; caption reads "875").
  - Midpoint equals the boundary between premium and discount. For a short he wants bodies in the lower (discount) half of the imbalance and wick, and he is cautious when price trades "inside a two premium array".
- **Timestamps:** [0:14:42](https://youtu.be/F8s_vfK9HaM?t=882), [0:29:28](https://youtu.be/F8s_vfK9HaM?t=1768), [0:48:16](https://youtu.be/F8s_vfK9HaM?t=2896)
- **Nuance / caveats:** the 7–10 p.m. ET window referred to as "Asian" is a point to cross-check against other lectures. It differs from the 8 p.m.–midnight ET Asian killzone more commonly quoted.

title: Trade Management & Removing The Need To Be Right
head: Posted levels create liquidity (influence)  (aliases ICT uses: "pool of liquidity to be sacrificed")
body:
- **Kind:** new coinage / commentary
- **What ICT says:** ICT claims that because so many people watch the levels he posts, those levels become a large pool of liquidity that others can run. People who act on his levels and lose faith in him are the ones being targeted. He compares it to seeing a wallet across the street on the way to a destination: price may take the easy liquidity first and then continue. He says this is "not ego, just market dynamics". He sees "not organic" price action around his levels.
- **How to use:** for the student, the point is to expect that a widely shared level may be run first. That is why stops and partial management matter, and why you should have your own analysis.
- **Timestamps:** [0:31:53](https://youtu.be/F8s_vfK9HaM?t=1913), [0:33:30](https://youtu.be/F8s_vfK9HaM?t=2010), [0:34:20](https://youtu.be/F8s_vfK9HaM?t=2060)
- **Nuance / caveats:** this is opinion; treat it as context, not a testable rule.

title: The Week In The Life Cycle Of Price
head: Continuous contract analysis (versus front-month NQ, and CFD equivalents)
body:
- **Kind:** rule / process
- **What ICT says:**
  - His analysis always begins on a continuous contract chart (he actually starts on a monthly chart). It gives a field of reference for key highs, lows, inefficiencies and arrays that may not exist in the front-month chart because of the rollover.
  - He then checks whether the daily front-month contract (here the September NQ contract) agrees with the levels derived from the continuous chart.
  - Far-dated contracts (e.g. March 2027, December) have no influence on the composite continuous chart.
  - CFD traders (or anyone who cannot trade US futures) should do the same: use the continuous contract for the high/low context and then match the closest correlated highs/lows on their weekly chart (US100 for NQ, US500 for S&P).
  - He says everything he shows works in forex, gold, commodities and bonds. He focuses on one market so he can teach economically.
- **How to identify / use:** (1) weekly continuous chart, (2) mark the previous month's high/low and previous week's high/low, (3) check them on the front-month contract, (4) go to daily, then 15-minute.
- **Example in this video:** the weekly continuous NASDAQ composite chart with July's monthly high and low marked, then the same levels on the September NQ contract.
- **Timestamps:** [0:01:55](https://youtu.be/dmHSwlmS9iY?t=115) — continuous contract vs. front month; [0:04:27](https://youtu.be/dmHSwlmS9iY?t=267) — CFD traders; [0:11:41](https://youtu.be/dmHSwlmS9iY?t=701) — same levels on the September contract
- **Nuance / caveats:** he refers viewers to earlier 2026 lectures where he covers things only visible on a continuous chart.

title: The Week In The Life Cycle Of Price
head: Weekly bias: proximity to previous week/month high vs. low  (aliases: "path of least resistance", "draw on liquidity")
body:
- **Kind:** rule / entry model (bias method)
- **What ICT says:**
  - After the weekly close, ask where price opens relative to the previous week's high/previous month's high and previous week's low/previous month's low. Price is more likely to go to the nearer, easier side. He opens the week "right here", far closer to the previous week and previous month highs than the lows, so those highs are the likely draw. This is "the path of least resistance".
  - He adds the primary trend: he sees a primary bullish market ("propped up"), so he takes the bullish order flow at face value until it is proven otherwise.
  - Even if the market later crashes, he says he does not know what it will do. He waits to see where it opens on Sunday, lets Sunday trade, and watches the opening range on Monday.
  - A modest range (previous week high/low) is a big deal when you do it every week, he says in answer to people calling it small.
  - His weekend routine: right after the Friday close he does the analysis on a notepad (sometimes waits until the family is asleep, or does it early Saturday morning) and shares what is on that pad.
- **How to identify:** open (Sunday/Monday) is much closer to one of the previous-week or previous-month extremes, with the primary trend pointing the same way.
- **How to use:** set the weekly draw on the nearer liquidity pool, look for PD arrays that support it (below), and expect him to be indifferent to the far side.
- **Example in this video:** the week of 10–14 Aug 2026 in NQ: open was near the previous week's high and previous month's (July) high; the draw on liquidity was higher.
- **Timestamps:** [0:07:41](https://youtu.be/dmHSwlmS9iY?t=461) — "where is it likelier to go if we open here"; [0:08:27](https://youtu.be/dmHSwlmS9iY?t=507) — path of least resistance; [0:12:27](https://youtu.be/dmHSwlmS9iY?t=747)
- **Nuance / caveats:** he insists he does not predict the exact number; he names the level he is interested in.

title: The Week In The Life Cycle Of Price
head: Liquidity hierarchy: which highs/lows matter  (aliases: static vs dynamic ranges, session highs/lows, equilibrium)
body:
- **Kind:** definition / rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - Pools to track: Asian session high/low, London session high/low, NY AM session high/low, the 2-hour NY lunch window high/low (he cites a 2-hour window), previous day's high/low, the last three days' high/low (this one is a dynamic range that continuously changes), previous week's high/low, previous month's high/low.
  - Static levels are session-oriented highs/lows plus previous day/week/month. The last-three-day range is dynamic.
  - Always note the midpoint (equilibrium) of each range.
  - The higher the time frame of the level, the more likely price will draw to it, because a daily-level old high carries a lot of institutional sponsorship between price and that level ("rocket fuel").
  - He checks his notes, e.g. "previous Monday's Asian session buy side liquidity pool", to make sure he has the right level.
  - Using a 15-minute chart for the week: he calls the 15-minute a "bellwether" time frame; it shows the whole week and every session level.
- **Example in this video:** the 29,984 level (relative equal highs) was Monday's London session buy-side liquidity; Monday's NY AM session buy-side liquidity and Tuesday's AM session buy-side liquidity were other pools he named for the Wednesday–Thursday run.
- **Timestamps:** [0:26:57](https://youtu.be/dmHSwlmS9iY?t=1617), [0:28:35](https://youtu.be/dmHSwlmS9iY?t=1715), [0:31:50](https://youtu.be/dmHSwlmS9iY?t=1910), [0:32:38](https://youtu.be/dmHSwlmS9iY?t=1958)
- **Nuance / caveats:** he says there is a private-mentorship set of lectures (months 6–12) that map algorithmic moves. He asks viewers to make their own notes. In the transcript he mixes up one level and corrects it (see Process section).

title: The Week In The Life Cycle Of Price
head: Relative equal highs/lows: when to expect they will be taken or ignored  (aliases: "guarded buy side", "chaff")
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - Relative equal highs/lows are not automatically targets and not automatically shorts. He says many students short into relative equal highs and get run.
  - Early in the week, he named the relative equal highs at 29,984 (Monday London buy-side) as his interest and the relative equal lows below as a possible sweep, with nothing lower named. Price swept the lows while remaining bullish and without reaching the daily BISI. He treated that as strong bullish order flow.
  - On the Friday: with relative equal highs just above, he wants evidence they will be guarded. He uses the macro 9:50–10:10 and the first-hour dealing range / close of the opening range (30 minutes long) to decide. If buy-side is being "guarded" during the macro, you will not get your best fill; price might still take those highs, sweep, then go lower.
  - He prefers not to take on losses and wait for a clean read rather than "live through the losses".
- **How to use:** don't short into relative equal highs until bodies show failure (see Rejection Block and iFVG below), and don't "get precise" early. If you are not sure the pool is guarded, wait one more candle.
- **Timestamps:** [0:29:23](https://youtu.be/dmHSwlmS9iY?t=1763), [1:04:37](https://youtu.be/dmHSwlmS9iY?t=3877), [1:05:24](https://youtu.be/dmHSwlmS9iY?t=3924), [1:13:26](https://youtu.be/dmHSwlmS9iY?t=4406)
- **Nuance / caveats:** the later section (1:19:01) says the relative equal highs "are not going to get taken out if the things I explained here are true", i.e. inversion FVG plus rejection block plus bodies below.

title: The Week In The Life Cycle Of Price
head: Reading a daily BISI for bullish order flow (upper half, CE, "glad-handing")  (aliases: "bullish order flow", "unfinished business")
body:
- **Kind:** refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - In a bullish market, smart money wants to buy in the upper half of a BISI (from the candle low of the upper side down to the CE/midpoint). Runs that start in the upper half and run higher confirm bullish order flow.
  - "Glad-handing" (his word for pairing of orders so that business can be booked at that price): if price cannot even trade down to the CE of the gap, that is very bullish, "especially" when no bodies were buried below the CE. A bullish market should leave inefficiencies open, so there is no unfinished business below.
  - He says the evidence is only in the open, high, low and close of the candles. You do not need level 2, depth of market, DOM or footprint (if they agree, fine).
  - Last week's retracement did not touch the CE of the daily BISI. On Tuesday of the current week price again failed to trade to the BISI's high (the low of the candle that forms the gap). He counted these as two confirmations that bullish order flow remained intact.
- **How to identify:** a daily BISI where later retracements stop above the CE and bodies stay out of the lower half.
- **How to use:** treat repeated failure to reach the CE as continuation fuel; keep the bullish draw.
- **Example in this video:** daily NQ BISI formed the week before; the retracement low during the week stopped short of the gap's CE; price then rallied via a bullish breaker toward 29,984 and beyond.
- **Timestamps:** [0:19:43](https://youtu.be/dmHSwlmS9iY?t=1183), [0:20:32](https://youtu.be/dmHSwlmS9iY?t=1232), [0:21:19](https://youtu.be/dmHSwlmS9iY?t=1279), [0:22:56](https://youtu.be/dmHSwlmS9iY?t=1376), [0:30:12](https://youtu.be/dmHSwlmS9iY?t=1812)
- **Nuance / caveats:** he says he was the first to teach the idea that a bullish market should leave inefficiencies open; the "bodies are the real volume" idea appears again at 1:19:01.

title: The Week In The Life Cycle Of Price
head: Premium wick / wick CE (grading wicks like gaps)
body:
- **Kind:** refinement
- **What ICT says:** a wick above where price is currently trading and above the prior close is a premium array and "treated just like a gap". Grade the wick with its consequent encroachment: price trades up to the wick, and if bodies stay below the CE of the wick, it is respected. If the market is below it (e.g. Wednesday's trading and close below the wick), a rally into it is into a premium array. He lists it among the candidates after taking previous week's high: the smoothness of price (a "too smooth" run) is something the market dislikes, and it makes it jagged, so a run goes through candles ("cut through the chaff") before it reaches the next high.
- **How to use (Friday example):** after the short entry, he watches a wick; if bearish there should be "no bodies buried in the upper half of that wick". Price spread its wings twice but closed below, treating the wick as a premium array. Stop sits at its CE.
- **Timestamps:** [0:14:50](https://youtu.be/dmHSwlmS9iY?t=890), [0:16:29](https://youtu.be/dmHSwlmS9iY?t=989), [1:15:02](https://youtu.be/dmHSwlmS9iY?t=4502), [1:15:48](https://youtu.be/dmHSwlmS9iY?t=4548)

title: The Week In The Life Cycle Of Price
head: Rejection block  (aliases: "candle's close that can't be exceeded")
body:
- **Kind:** definition / refinement
- **What ICT says:** a rejection block here is a prior high zone where price goes up to the candle and cannot lay a body (close) above it. On the daily chart on Monday price opened below a candle's close that acted as a rejection block, which created an area saying price was not willing to go above it. He taught the PD arrays in his month 4 mentorship content. If price fails to close above it that is a "check in the box" for failure, then the question is whether price comes back and overlaps the BISI, turning it into an inversion FVG.
- **Example in this video:** Monday opened below the close of the earlier candle; Thursday (large range, PPI day) had not yet closed above the rejection block when he made his call. On Friday, the intraday rejection block is next to the relative equal highs and a BISI below it.
- **Timestamps:** [0:22:08](https://youtu.be/dmHSwlmS9iY?t=1328), [1:09:30](https://youtu.be/dmHSwlmS9iY?t=4170)
- **Nuance / caveats:** captions are loose here ("candlestick's close" vs "highs up close"); take it as the rejection block marked by a candle's high area that bodies cannot close above (caption unclear).

title: The Week In The Life Cycle Of Price
head: Inversion Fair Value Gap (iFVG) after a rejection block
body:
- **Kind:** refinement / entry model
- **What ICT says:**
  - On Friday, after failing at the rejection block, price traded above a BISI (overlapping it). He wants the market to come back and respect it as an inversion: a candle that opens, trades up, cannot touch the high of the gap, and closes lower and outside of it is "bearish" in his order-flow reading.
  - He waited for a second test. "Because I'm up against relative equal highs, I just want to have a little bit more behind me." The next candle traded up to it, gave up the ghost, and came down. Then he was comfortable.
  - Bodies are "the real volume", so he does not need the wick to take the high. The wick is simply a gap/inefficiency being delivered to.
  - If an inversion FVG takes out (closes through) a rejection block, then the relative equal highs above are unlikely to be taken.
- **How to use:** the confirmation is a close below the inversion gap, then a retest that fails.
- **Timestamps:** [1:10:17](https://youtu.be/dmHSwlmS9iY?t=4217), [1:13:26](https://youtu.be/dmHSwlmS9iY?t=4406), [1:19:01](https://youtu.be/dmHSwlmS9iY?t=4741), [1:19:48](https://youtu.be/dmHSwlmS9iY?t=4788)

title: The Week In The Life Cycle Of Price
head: Silver Bullet-style short with suspension block and wick CE (Friday live example)  (aliases: "Model 2022", "suspension block", "change in state of delivery = order block theory")
body:
- **Kind:** entry model (worked example)
- **What ICT says:**
  - Sequence on Friday 14 Aug: 9:30 opening price; price rallies and forms a high in the first 30 minutes; it pulls back to the 9:30 open and closes below it (bodies below the opening price, "lower high, lower high"). He notes a high-then-low sequence where a low is taken, and says "Model 2022".
  - He calls it silver bullet time and says this is "the classic ICT silver bullet", responding to claims that it stopped working.
  - Entry zone: a small FVG that he labels a suspension block, plus the longest wick to the left. He wants to trade as close as possible to about half of that wick (its CE), even if he does not get the gap itself. The stop must go at least to the CE of the wick / gap above.
  - Because the stop requirement was fairly large, he used only 2 contracts. He says normally he uses larger entries.
  - Result: price rolled over; a body sat at the CE of the bearish suspension block; the low from the open was taken, then dropped. The next candle created a wick with its CE respected; no bodies above the CE; price ultimately hit the low formed at about 20% of the weekly range (TGIF).
  - A second reading of CISD: he says the "change in the state of delivery ... is my order block theory". A trade from an order block / CISD one minute after the macro is fine (see Macro concept). It could also be pyramided.
- **How to use:** entry at the CE of the suspension block/wick, stop above its CE, 2 contracts, exit just before the TGIF target (half of 20–30% = 25%). Executions were 2 in, 2 out.
- **Example in this video:** NQ, 1-minute, Friday 14 Aug 2026: 9:30 open, rally during the opening range to the relative equal highs/week high zone, rejection block failure, BISI turned inversion, short around 10:10–10:15 ET (inferred: "one minute after the macro" ending 10:10), out near the 25% retracement level of the weekly range.
- **Timestamps:** [1:10:17](https://youtu.be/dmHSwlmS9iY?t=4217) — "now it's also silver bullet time"; [1:14:15](https://youtu.be/dmHSwlmS9iY?t=4455) — 2 contracts, bearish suspension block body at CE; [1:22:14](https://youtu.be/dmHSwlmS9iY?t=4934) — proof of fills posted on X; [1:24:38](https://youtu.be/dmHSwlmS9iY?t=5078) — order block / CISD entry outside the macro
- **Nuance / caveats:** exact entry and exit prices were not given in the captions. He says he forgot to toggle the trade-arrows display on the chart. The "suspension block" caption is likely correct, but its definition is only implied (a small FVG treated as a block).

title: The Week In The Life Cycle Of Price
head: TGIF — Friday retracement of 20–30% of the weekly range  (aliases ICT uses: "thank God it's Friday", "extraction point")
body:
- **Kind:** rule / entry model (Friday profile)
- **What ICT says:**
  - In bullish weeks, the market usually trades off its high during the week and settles around 20–30% of the weekly range (measured down from the week's high). In bearish weeks the reverse. Price "comes off its extreme" on Fridays.
  - Use the 15-minute chart as the bellwether chart for TGIF reference points; no need to go higher.
  - He halves the 20–30% zone by using the 0.25 level of a Fibonacci (quadrants and octants applied to the week's range). He is personally interested in about 25%.
  - 40% is possible but extreme; given recent volatility, if it does 40% it will probably go deeper, and he does not hold for it. 20% is reasonable and tradable, 30% possible.
  - He also stresses the idea of an extraction point: the "theatre of war" runs from Sunday 6:00 p.m. ET to Friday 5:00 p.m. ET and you need to know where smart money exits. The Friday low-hanging-fruit objective is the TGIF zone, not the previous month's high (the previous month's high merely lines up with it; it is not support/resistance).
  - On the Friday, the week's high had already been taken at 9:00 a.m. ET (the high of the week), then price broke down.
- **How to use:** after a bullish week extends to a new high on Friday morning, expect a retrace; plan partial exits at several levels (see Targets). Do not need to enter at the exact weekly high; avoid being precise at first and take the "big piece of meat in the middle".
- **Example in this video:** NQ weekly range (week high labeled '948', digits unclear in the captions, to the week's low below the relative equal lows swept earlier). Price took the high at about 9:00 a.m. ET Friday, rallied/consolidated, then retraced to the 20% level and then toward 25–30%, which also lined up with the previous month's high and previous week's high.

Reason: it is the end of the big impactful news (PPI), near the last day, and price had not closed above the rejection block.

  - He dates the profile teaching to the 2017 mentorship (he hedges: month 7, perhaps month 6; also says "short-term trading model" material) and states this is not "market profile".
- **How to identify:** weekly narrative (bullish/bearish), a calendar of high-impact news by day, and the PD arrays on daily.

Per his Power of 3 concept, the range high/low are formed between 9:30 and 10:00. During the macro, price may run the highs and sweep, then go lower. If buy-side is being guarded in the macro, you will not get the best fill; wait. Answering "do you only trade inside the macro?": no. When the macro is delivering in close proximity to a PD array you can trade inside it; he entered one minute after, and an order block / CISD entry outside the macro is fine.

A bullish array is the opposite: price drops into the upper half and eats it. Use as the practical test for which half to expect orders in. He applies the same rule to a BISI (upper half = buyers) and to a premium wick (price should not bury bodies in the upper half of the wick when bearish).

title: The Week In The Life Cycle Of Price
head: Model selection by market condition; avoiding problem areas
body:
- **Kind:** rule / mindset
- **What ICT says:** not every model works every day because conditions must be ripe. Reversal models are not what he reaches for in a continuation environment (though he may use one on a lower time frame, e.g. 15-minute/5-minute/15-second chart, when bullish and waiting for a reversal at a low). He matches a model to market conditions based on the weekly profile, like a dentist choosing an instrument. Do not trade if you do not know how your model will form today; backtest until you can see it happening in the future. His goal is not to "live through the losses": he doesn't teach "lose 60% and still win". Instead he identified what lost him real money and built logic that tells you what the chart shows before that trap.

title: PPI Market Review August 13, 2026
head: Order Block and State of Delivery Change
body:
- **Kind:** definition + example
- **What ICT says:** An order block is a PD array (usually on a higher timeframe like daily) where institutional order flow clustered. When price trades into that block from above (after rejection), it's a Change in State of Delivery (CISD). That entry point is where big money commits to a reversal. Watch for bodies in specific halves and wick behavior to confirm the reversal is underway.
- **How to identify:** (1) Find a fair value gap or imbalance on the daily, (2) price rejects it initially, (3) price comes back and trades INTO it, (4) watch bodies stay in lower half (if bouncing upward) or upper half (if continuing downward) as confirmation. (5) Once bodies show "clean" placement away from the gap's midpoint, that's the CISD.
- **How to use:** Entry point. Go long/short into the order block with tight stops at the far end of the gap. Add on confirmation (bodies doing the right thing). Trail stops above/below minor swings as price moves in your favor.
- **Example in this video:** NQ daily has a buy-side imbalance / sell-side inefficiency (FVG). Price trades into it at 8:30 ET on the PPI print. The gap is from [top of FVG range] down to [bottom]. Once price enters and stays below the midpoint, bodies remain in lower half → long entry confirmed. Rallies from there to Wednesday's high.
- **Timestamps:** [0:05:37](https://youtu.be/RVHX56v-gUo?t=337) — defining the order block and CISD; [0:06:27](https://youtu.be/RVHX56v-gUo?t=387) — entry and stop placement
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** The order block is typically a much larger, more stable level than intraday ranges. Trading into it after a failed rejection is high-probability.

title: PPI Market Review August 13, 2026
head: Buy-Side Imbalance / Sell-Side Inefficiency (BSI/SSI) Fair Value Gap
body:
- **Kind:** definition + example
- **What ICT says:** A gap where there's no volume (unfilled space) in one direction. On a daily chart, if there's a bullish move (up-close) followed by a gap up at the open, the gap is a buy-side imbalance (buyers moved price higher); if price then rejects this gap on a down-close, that gap becomes a sell-side inefficiency (sellers dominated that session). These are key institutional entry/exit zones.
- **How to identify:** Look for gaps on the daily after strong directional closes. The gap direction and the follow-up close tell you which side (buy/sell) is in control.
- **How to use:** Entry on pullback into the gap. If bullish, enter long on any probe into the gap's lower half. If bearish, enter short on any test of the upper half.
- **Example in this video:** NQ daily has a gap from Friday → Monday. Sellers rejected it (down close). That makes it a buy-side imbalance (Friday's move) with sell-side inefficiency (Monday's rejection). When price trades back down into it mid-day on PPI, it's the entry for a long.
- **Timestamps:** [0:04:50](https://youtu.be/RVHX56v-gUo?t=290); [0:05:37](https://youtu.be/RVHX56v-gUo?t=337) — defining the gap structure
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Imbalances and inefficiencies are flip sides of the same gap; the functional role depends on context (what happens after the gap).

title: PPI Market Review August 13, 2026
head: Wick Consequent Encroachment as Daily Projection
body:
- **Kind:** example + technique
- **What ICT says:** A wick on a daily can be measured via Fibonacci to find its midpoint (CE). This midpoint often aligns with intraday support/resistance levels or prior highs/lows. It's a geometric projection that price respects with precision. Can be used to set stops or confirm reversals.
- **How to identify:** (1) Identify a significant wick on the daily, (2) Apply Fibonacci from body close to wick extreme, (3) Mark the 0.5 level (CE). (4) Watch if that level aligns with prior swing highs/lows or daily highs from earlier weeks.
- **How to use:** Stop-loss placement. Confirmation level. If price touches wick's CE and bounces, it's rejection; if it closes through, it's a reversal signal.
- **Example in this video:** Large wick on daily; its CE aligns directly on top of Wednesday's daily high. When price pulls back intraday, it stops at that CE level, confirming the bounce. ICT uses this as a stopping point for covering shorts.
- **Timestamps:** [0:06:27](https://youtu.be/RVHX56v-gUo?t=387) — showing wick measurement; [0:08:03](https://youtu.be/RVHX56v-gUo?t=483) — Wednesday's high = wick's CE; [0:08:54](https://youtu.be/RVHX56v-gUo?t=534) — stop placement
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** This alignment is often "brilliant" (ICT's word) because it's precise; not random, but mechanistic—the algorithm respects geometric levels.

title: PPI Market Review August 13, 2026
head: Relative Equal Highs as Resistance in Daily Context
body:
- **Kind:** definition + example
- **What ICT says:** When the daily chart shows two or more highs at approximately the same level, that's a relative equal high. It's a zone where momentum historically failed, so price must "bust through" it with significant follow-through to make a new high. If price just pokes above and closes back down, it's a false breakout. Clearing it cleanly (with wicks/bodies above and no rejection) suggests continuation higher.
- **How to identify:** Zoom out to daily chart; mark the last two swing highs. Are they within ~50–100 points? If yes, that's a REH zone.
- **How to use:** Resistance. On a break above, add longs or short-cover confirmation. On a rejection, short into the level. If body closes above and away, it's bullish breakout signal.
- **Example in this video:** NQ daily shows relative equal highs at 30,094. Price needs to break above this to reach Wednesday's high (30,600 area). Once it clears 30,094 cleanly, the path to Wednesday's high opens up. ICT calls 30,600 and 30,975 as additional targets after breaking REH.
- **Timestamps:** [0:07:14](https://youtu.be/RVHX56v-gUo?t=434) — wick measurement; [0:09:42](https://youtu.be/RVHX56v-gUo?t=582) — identifying REH on daily; [0:10:29](https://youtu.be/RVHX56v-gUo?t=629) — projecting targets past REH
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** REH is most powerful on daily; less so on lower timeframes. Once cleared, don't expect price to come back into it easily.

title: PPI Market Review August 13, 2026
head: Event-Driven Price Action (News Events and Trend Reversals)
body:
- **Kind:** observation + example
- **What ICT says:** Major economic prints (CPI, PPI, NFP) cause sudden moves that can flip intraday bias. Before the event, price consolidates or exhibits uncertain behavior. At the event release, momentum shifts instantly. The direction is often predictable if you've marked key daily levels beforehand (highs, gaps, octants). Events don't create opportunity randomly—they allow the algorithm to execute pre-planned reversals at key times/prices.
- **How to identify:** (1) Know the economic calendar, (2) Mark daily support/resistance well before the event, (3) Watch how price approaches the event time (calm vs. nervous candles), (4) At the release, expect a directional break from consolidation.
- **How to use:** Plan entries/exits before the event. Don't fade the initial move; ride it into your pre-marked targets. Take partials at milestones (prior highs, FVG midpoints, relative equal highs). Trail the runner if bullish bias is confirmed.
- **Example in this video:** CPI yesterday (Aug 12) and PPI today (Aug 13 at 8:30 ET). Before PPI, NQ was consolidating and failing downside (ICT's initial short bias). At 8:30, the PPI beat bullish sent price higher into pre-marked targets (Wednesday's high, REH, old highs). ICT flipped from short to long and rode the move with partials.
- **Timestamps:** [0:00:49](https://youtu.be/RVHX56v-gUo?t=49) — pre-event consolidation; [0:04:03](https://youtu.be/RVHX56v-gUo?t=243) — the 8:30 move; [0:05:37](https://youtu.be/RVHX56v-gUo?t=337) — flipping to long
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Events are catalysts but not the cause of moves; the levels and order flow were already set. Events just trigger the execution.

title: PPI Market Review August 13, 2026
head: Pseudo-Diagonal Trend Line Monitoring
body:
- **Kind:** observation
- **What ICT says:** In consolidation or before directional breaks, price sometimes traces a subtle diagonal (not a strong trend, but a lean). ICT watches for these "pseudo" trend lines and bets against them—they often mark the breakout point. He doesn't emphasize trend lines heavily (as he dislikes them), but he enjoys "seeing them victimized" (broken).
- **How to identify:** Draw a line through two or more candle bodies that lean up or down; watch if price breaks cleanly above/below.
- **How to use:** Breakout confirmation. If price breaks above the pseudo-line with a clean body, expect continuation. This supplements other signals (FVGs, REH, etc.).
- **Example in this video:** Before PPI, NQ showed a pseudo-diagonal structure consolidating downward. The midpoint of that diagonal was a reference. At 8:30, price broke above and never came back—diagonal was "victimized" (broken).
- **Timestamps:** [0:02:27](https://youtu.be/RVHX56v-gUo?t=147) — pseudo-diagonal mentioned; [0:04:03](https://youtu.be/RVHX56v-gUo?t=243) — breakout

title: PPI Market Review August 13, 2026
head: Event Horizon (Fibonacci 50% of a Multi-Day Range)
body:
- **Kind:** definition + example
- **What ICT says:** Measure from one daily high to another (e.g., Tuesday's high to Monday's high), find the midpoint (50% Fibonacci level), and project it forward. That level often acts as a ceiling on strong bullish days or a floor on bearish days. It's a psychological equilibrium point where momentum often fades briefly before continuing.
- **How to identify:** Select two daily highs/lows separated by a few days. Apply Fibonacci; the 0.5 level = event horizon.
- **How to use:** Partial-taking target. Resistance on intraday rallies. If price blows through it cleanly, expect continued momentum. If it stalls there, it might retrace.
- **Example in this video:** Tuesday's high to Monday's high, 50% = event horizon. Price reaches it intraday, hesitates, then blows through on continued strength. ICT calls this out as a reference level.
- **Timestamps:** [0:08:03](https://youtu.be/RVHX56v-gUo?t=483) — measuring event horizon; [0:08:54](https://youtu.be/RVHX56v-gUo?t=534) — price action at/through it
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Works better on intraday charts after a strong directional break. Less reliable on choppy days.

title: PPI Market Review August 13, 2026
head: Trade Management: Flipping from Short to Long
body:
- **Kind:** example only
- **What ICT says:** (Demonstrated) If a short stops working (price refuses to go lower, shows bullish candles in lower half of a bearish FVG), don't hold the loss. Close it early, reassess, and if bullish signals emerge, flip to long. Use the same daily levels for the long that you were using as targets for the short (they work both ways). Scale into the long with tight stops, add on confirmations, and trail partials as price moves higher.
- **Example in this video:** ICT shorts looking for downside into an FVG midpoint. Price "showed an unwillingness" and displayed bullish wicks/bodies. He "collapsed the position, went long" into the same FVG from the bottom side. Took partials at Wednesday's high, took another at relative equal high breakout, trailed the runner to the final stop at 30,120.
- **Timestamps:** [0:04:50](https://youtu.be/RVHX56v-gUo?t=290) — flip decision; [0:05:37](https://youtu.be/RVHX56v-gUo?t=337) — entry as long; [0:08:03](https://youtu.be/RVHX56v-gUo?t=483)–[0:08:54](https://youtu.be/RVHX56v-gUo?t=534) — partials and trail
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** The flip is based on live order flow reading, not emotion. Once you see the unwillingness to continue your original direction, act quickly.

He prefers to define where the high and low of the week can complete, then use the freed time for other things instead of worrying about extra moves.

title: Whats So Smart About My Concepts?
head: Know the draw first (first thing ICT teaches)
body:
- **Kind:** rule / mindset
- **What ICT says:** the very first thing he teaches is to know where the market is likely to go (the draw on liquidity). If you do not understand that, "everything you do afterwards is going to be incorrect". The dealing range and its octants/quadrants then tell you where PD arrays should form and, if they form at graded levels, they are perceived as higher probability or "validated". That does not remove the need to know the draw.
- **How to use:** pick the prominent price leg (high to low or low to high) as the dealing range, apply octant and quadrant levels, and see whether the PD array sits on a graded level.
- **Example in this video:** the swing from the high down to the low that stands out as a prominent leg, graded with octants and quadrants; he projects those levels through price on the 1-minute chart.

title: Whats So Smart About My Concepts?
head: Trading a high-impact 8:30 release: do not trade the first candles  (aliases: CPI/PPI 8:30 candle, "two-stage delivery")
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - You cannot participate in the 8:30 candle on CPI/PPI. Anyone showing a fill on that candle was on a demo account; limit orders are not respected and slippage is severe ("literally impossible" to get a good fill).
  - Wait one or two candles (8:30, 8:31) and start looking around 8:32–8:33 for what the news volatility left behind.
  - CPI can deliver in two stages (like FOMC rate announcements): either a one-sided run, or one swing which then reverses and returns to the initial higher low. People who chase the first dump place protective buy stops just above, and that is where price goes.
  - Since a Monday London session relative equal high pool sat only a little above, a run above the initial 8:30 high was likely; it makes little sense to take out only the nearby high on a data release when a bigger pool is close.
- **How to identify:** news candle first, then raid of the sell-side (or buy-side) opposite the run, then a gap or imbalance formed in the aftermath.
- **How to use:** wait 2–3 minutes, then enter on the imbalance left behind (see next concept).
- **Example in this video:** on CPI morning price rallied on the 8:30 candle up toward a level, came back down through the New Week Opening Gap, raided sell-side resting below, then printed a BISI on the 15-second chart that he bought. Later the rally took out 29,984 with ease.
- **Timestamps:** [0:03:56](https://youtu.be/La2fTewydjw?t=236), [0:04:44](https://youtu.be/La2fTewydjw?t=284), [0:09:32](https://youtu.be/La2fTewydjw?t=572), [0:10:19](https://youtu.be/La2fTewydjw?t=619)

head: Long entry inside a BISI after the sell-side raid (15-second chart)  (aliases: "smart money inversion", "institutional order flow entry drill")
body:
- **Kind:** entry model (worked example)
- **What ICT says:**
  - After the 8:30 rally and the pull back through the NWOG, price went into a discount array (you could not buy it live). Once the candle closed and sell-side below was taken, he looked for the BISI that formed: "the damage was the sell-side raid, this was the get".
  - Execution: he bought inside that buy-side imbalance / sell-side inefficiency, adding "three and three more" (two clips of 3 contracts). He stresses the BISI was not touched at the CE by the wick, which is "what makes it smart" because it tells you order flow is bullish.
  - He took heat: price moved against him about 9 points (the caption reads "824", unclear) after the CPI release. Then price traded above the NWOG, dipped a bit, and ripped higher.
  - After the rip, the candle low to the next candle high became an inversion FVG; if price retraced into the upper half of it, he would add because the high that ran away is the target.
  - He would have liked price to retrace into his entry area as an "institutional order flow entry drill" (caption unclear) but it did not; "it's fine, I'm positioned".
  - The run slowly ground higher and ended with a head-fake before breaking out above 29,984.
- **How to identify:** a BISI that forms right after the raid of resting sell-side and after the first minutes of news volatility.
- **How to use:** buy inside the imbalance (with adds), stop below the raid, target the higher liquidity (Monday London high 29,984 and above).
- **Example in this video:** NQ 15-second, CPI morning; entry inside a BISI after sell-side raid; target 29,984 relative equal highs which were tweeted since Monday.
- **Timestamps:** [0:05:36](https://youtu.be/La2fTewydjw?t=336), [0:07:59](https://youtu.be/La2fTewydjw?t=479), [0:08:46](https://youtu.be/La2fTewydjw?t=526), [0:11:54](https://youtu.be/La2fTewydjw?t=714)
- **Nuance / caveats:** he says he did not get the high candle on the later move and describes his top execution as wanting "the fill so I can rub the nose in it". Exact prices of entry/exit are not stated except 29,984.

title: Whats So Smart About My Concepts?
head: Bearish breaker: two consecutive down-close candles as an order block, and mean threshold  (aliases: "breaker", "mean threshold (MT)", "VIP seating")
body:
- **Kind:** definition / entry model
- **What ICT says:**
  - After the head fake above 29,984, price dropped, failed to touch the NWOG, filled an inefficiency and formed a bearish breaker. The structure was high, low, high: the lowest part between two highs, with the second being the higher high. Two down-close candles in a row are taken together as the order block ("you have to take both of those together").
  - It is an inversion because the block was first used as a bullish order block to run the liquidity above (29,984 was the target; he says nothing above that was ever targeted this week).
  - Breakers are basically a run on liquidity. It is validated when price then trades below the block's low (displacement through it; the SIBI created is the big sell-side imbalance).
  - The best seat ("VIP seating") is at the midpoint: for an order block / breaker it is the mean threshold; for gaps and wicks it is the consequent encroachment. Entry is in the lower half for a bearish breaker.
  - Stop: the high of the candle that created the SIBI through the low (the candle that validates the breaker). If that stop is too big, "you might have to trade with lower leverage".
  - Retail's "break and retest" short at the low of the candle gives you unnecessary heat; he prefers letting price dig into the range. Support/resistance retests can work if you understand liquidity first.
- **How to identify:** price runs buy-side liquidity (29,984), reverses, and trades below the lows of the last up-move's two consecutive down-close candles.
- **How to use:** short at the mean threshold or deeper (graded levels below), stop at the high of the displacement candle, target the new week opening gap low / relative equal lows.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 15-second after CPI: two consecutive down-close candles inside the run up to 29,984, then price broke below; he shorted into the breaker's lower half; price dove to the relative equal lows and back into the NWOG. A bearish-breaker rejection was also pyramided (see next).

head: Grading levels inside a PD array: five specific limit-order levels  (aliases: octants and quadrants, percentile high/low)

The numeric values are my reading of "quadrants and octants" on a 0–1 scale; he did not recite them in this video. "Any one of these levels you could use as a limit order." The midpoint is the best seating; lower levels are for scaling. Anything above the midpoint is a bonus. He rejects "zones" and the shotgun approach.
- **How to use:** place limits at these levels (or get close), stop at the displacement candle high, treat deeper levels as the better entry and use lower leverage if the stop is wide.

title: ES Day Trade Review With 1min & 15Sec Timeframe
head: Swing Trader's Model and Fulcrum Point
body:
- **Kind:** definition + example
- **What ICT says:** A fulcrum is a swing high (short-term high) where if you measure the distance from the low before it up to the high, that same distance (measured down from the high) often projects where price will swing to on the downside. This is based on swing trading principles and represents a natural balance/measurement in market structure. Use it to estimate targets before entering a short.
- **How to identify:** (1) Identify a swing low, (2) measure the vertical distance to the swing high (fulcrum), (3) from the fulcrum, measure the same distance downward. That projection is the expected low.
- **How to use:** Target planning. Don't use it as the *only* target, but combine it with relative equal lows, liquidity zones, and order blocks for confirmation. Entry can come from a retracement into the high after it forms.
- **Example in this video:** ES has a swing low, a swing high (fulcrum), measured distance = X. Projected downside = same distance X below the high. The actual relative equal lows happen to be near that projection. ICT uses this to justify the trade and set a reasonable target.
- **Timestamps:** [0:04:46](https://youtu.be/KEqzv2yOAf0?t=286) — explaining fulcrum measurement; [0:05:36](https://youtu.be/KEqzv2yOAf0?t=336) — applying to ES trade
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Fulcrum is not a hard rule; it's a *reasonable* estimate. Always combine with other levels (FVGs, relative equal lows, liquidity).

title: ES Day Trade Review With 1min & 15Sec Timeframe
head: Relative Equal Lows and Entry Patience
body:
- **Kind:** definition + rule + example
- **What ICT says:** When a market makes two or more lows at the same (or very close) price level, that's a relative equal low. It represents sell-side liquidity below the market, which will be targeted on any decline. More importantly, the sell-side liquidity pool *resting just below the RELs* is the true target; you don't need to hit the exact low—just get close enough to run the liquidity.
- **How to identify:** Look at prior swings (same-day or previous days); mark any two lows at approximately same level.
- **How to use:** Short target. Place limit orders just above the REL (to avoid hitting the exact low and getting stopped out). If you hit the REL midpoint, that's success.
- **Example in this video:** ES shows "perfect" relative equal lows from Friday's London session. ICT places limit orders just *above* that level to capture the sell-side liquidity just below it, exiting before the market reaches the absolute low.
- **Timestamps:** [0:00:47](https://youtu.be/KEqzv2yOAf0?t=47) — identifying RELs; [0:01:34](https://youtu.be/KEqzv2yOAf0?t=94) — entry/exit planning; [0:03:57](https://youtu.be/KEqzv2yOAf0?t=237) — actual fill at planned level
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Don't be greedy and wait for the exact low; capture the liquidity pool just above it.

head: Suspension Block
body:
- **Kind:** definition + observation
- **What ICT says:** Below a relative equal low, there's often a "suspension block"—a zone where selling pressure eases temporarily, creating a small rebound before potentially continuing lower. ICT identifies this but intentionally avoids trading into it, preferring to exit earlier at the liquidity above it.
- **How to identify:** Below a REL, look for a small consolidation or bounce zone before the next potential drop.
- **How to use:** Stop-loss or no-trade zone. If shorting, don't expect to go much beyond the REL into the suspension block; that's a danger zone where you might get run and stopped out.
- **Example in this video:** ES REL has a suspension block just below. ICT avoids planning any trade target there; exits above REL to stay clear of it.
- **Timestamps:** [0:00:47](https://youtu.be/KEqzv2yOAf0?t=47) — identifying suspension block; [0:01:34](https://youtu.be/KEqzv2yOAf0?t=94) — avoiding it

head: ES vs. NQ vs. YM Market Comparison
body:
- **Kind:** observation + market microstructure
- **What ICT says:** ES (S&P 500) is the "gentleman's market"—pristine, professional traders, refined order flow, bodies stop at exact price levels repeatedly, very precise. NQ (Nasdaq) is "wild" and more exaggerated—moves are bigger, order flow is noisier, harder to get exact precision. YM (Dow) is the "lot lizard"—even wilder. ICT prefers NQ for trading *because* of the exaggerated moves and volatility, which help him find cracks in correlation and bigger profits. But ES is *easier* for new traders because it's cleaner and more predictable.
- **How to identify:** Trade all three and observe the precision of body placement, the size of moves, and the frequency of rejections.
- **How to use:** Market selection. If you want clean, predictable price action, trade ES. If you want bigger moves and exaggerated volatility, trade NQ. YM is slower and harder to scalp.
- **Example in this video:** Shows multiple ES candles where the body close equals the open of the next candle to the tick—7,754.50 appears multiple times as exact fills. "You don't see that in NQ," ICT notes. ES is more professional, slower, but more precise.

title: ES Day Trade Review With 1min & 15Sec Timeframe
head: Inversion Fair Value Gap (iFVG) on Lower Timeframes
body:
- **Kind:** definition + example
- **What ICT says:** (Refresher) A gap that was originally bearish (sell-side driven) becomes an inversion when price trades above it. On a short, as price rallies into a bearish gap, that gap becomes a resistance zone (iFVG) where bodies will fail to close above the gap's midpoint or fail to touch it at all. Watch for bodies respecting the gap midpoint to the tick.
- **How to identify:** Track where bodies align relative to the gap's midpoint (using Fib 0.5).
- **How to use:** Stop-loss or partial-taking level. If bodies stop at the iFVG midpoint, that's a partial-taking zone. If price closes above the iFVG, the gap has lost its character.
- **Example in this video:** ES trades down through a bearish FVG, then rallies back up. That FVG becomes an iFVG (inversion). Bodies rally into it but can't close above the midpoint—exact precision at 7,754.50 multiple times. This signals the short is still valid; exit partial here, continue short lower.
- **Timestamps:** [0:08:03](https://youtu.be/KEqzv2yOAf0?t=483) — identifying iFVG; [0:08:50](https://youtu.ye/KEqzv2yOAf0?t=530) — bodies respecting to the tick
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** The precision shown in ES (exact 7,754.50 multiple times) is rare but possible on cleaner markets.

head: Macro Time Windows
body:

You don't need to know *why* it happens; just note that it does and use it as confirmation for your setup.

- **How to use:** Confirmation bias. If a setup aligns with a macro time window, it's more likely to work. If price breaks a key level just as a macro starts, expect a strong run.

head: Buy-Side Imbalance / Sell-Side Inefficiency on Intraday Pullbacks
body:
- **Kind:** rule + example
- **What ICT says:** (Refresher) When price trades down through a bearish gap and later rallies back up, that gap becomes a premium (iFVG). When price is rallied up inside this premium gap, it's inside a buy-side imbalance (from the earlier downside move). Eventually, price will resume lower to work its way below the sell-side liquidity pool. The gap serves as a reference for multiple round-trips.
- **How to identify:** Track the gap structure (upper half = buy-side imbalance zone during rallies; lower half = sell-side inefficiency zone when trending down).
- **How to use:** Entry zones for re-shorts, partial targets, and confidence levels.
- **Example in this video:** ES gap with buy-side imbalance zone. Price rallies into this zone multiple times; each time, ICT sees it as an opportunity to take a partial or add to short.

head: 15-Second vs. 1-Minute Timeframe Coordination
body:

- **What ICT says:** A 15-second chart shows the same price movement as a 1-minute chart; it's just more granular. The levels that work on 1-minute also work on 15-second, but 15-second gives more candles and more entry opportunities within each 1-minute candle. You can use 15-second to fine-tune entries/exits, but the overall structure (FVGs, RELs, support/resistance) is the same.
- **How to identify:** Compare the two charts; note that key levels (midpoints, highs/lows) align on both.
- **How to use:** Entry refinement. Use 1-minute for overall direction and targets; use 15-second to optimize entry/exit timing within that 1-minute move.

title: AM Session Review & Course Correction
head: Relative Equal Highs and Lows as Liquidity Pools
body:
- **Kind:** definition + rule + example
- **What ICT says:** (Refresher) When two or more highs (or lows) form at the same level, that's a relative equal high/low. Each represents a pool of liquidity (buy-side above a high, sell-side below a low). The market will target these liquidity pools. If it initially fails to reach them, that failure is itself a signal—it means that direction isn't being favored; look for a reversal instead.
- **How to identify:** Mark all swing highs/lows from the current session and prior days; identify any at approximately the same price level.
- **How to use:** Bias and target planning. If trying to go long, expect it to reach the relative equal high. If it fails before getting there, flip the bias to short and target the relative equal lows. Conversely for shorts.
- **Example in this video:** NQ opens up; ICT expects it to run to relative equal highs. Price immediately sends it lower instead (failure of his bias). He pivots: now expects a run to relative equal lows, which it hits by midday. Multiple REL zones are marked: confirms the eventual target.

- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** If initial move fails before hitting a level, don't force it—wait for the market to deliver the alternate setup.

title: AM Session Review & Course Correction
head: Retracement Measurement via Wick Fibonacci
body:
- **Kind:** technique + example
- **What ICT says:** When price makes a high and then retraces lower, measure the wick from the high down to the low of that retracement leg. Apply Fibonacci from high to low of the wick. The 0.618 (golden ratio) level often projects how far the next leg can travel downward. It's a "secret sauce" for predicting downside targets before price gets there.
- **How to identify:** (1) Identify a high and low of a retracement, (2) Apply Fibonacci from high to low (wick range), (3) Extend downward using the ratio.
- **How to use:** Downside projection. Know how far you expect price to go lower before placing shorts or sizing your position.
- **Example in this video:** NQ high to retracement low = X points. Applied 0.618 ratio projects downside target. "Boom, there you go," ICT says—price hits that projected level with precision. Even the bodies (which tend to be stronger than wicks) respect it; wicks exceed it but bodies stop short.
- **Timestamps:** [0:01:43](https://youtu.be/0Bu4g-2aMA4?t=103) — demonstrating retracement measurement and projection
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** The bodies/wicks distinction is key—wicks can exceed the projection, but the "real" order flow (bodies) respects it.

title: AM Session Review & Course Correction
head: Gray Pole (Wick Pattern Signal)
body:
- **Kind:** new coinage + observation
- **What ICT says:** When you have consecutive wicks in a specific pattern (usually two or more wicks measured and graded by Fibonacci), their converging midpoints (0.5 levels) can form what ICT calls a "gray pole." This is a zone where price might gap or move quickly because liquidity is concentrated but "unnoticed" by retail traders who use other methods. It's a hidden liquidity cluster.
- **How to identify:** (1) Identify two or more significant wicks, (2) Apply Fibonacci to each wick (high to low), (3) Mark the 0.5 levels (CE of each wick), (4) If they align or are very close, you have a gray pole.
- **How to use:** Breakout/gap prediction. When price reaches a gray pole, expect a directional break through it (either up or down, depending on context). Use it as a stop-loss target or profit-taking level.
- **Example in this video:** NQ shows two wicks graded separately. Their 0.5 levels align, forming a "gray pole." ICT shows it as a "beautiful gray pole." When price approaches it, it breaks decisively (gaps through). This is the moment ICT enters heavily ("I was in there accumulating and building position").
- **Timestamps:** [0:05:47](https://youtu.ye/0Bu4g-2aMA4?t=347) — identifying and explaining gray pole; [0:06:36](https://youtu.ye/0Bu4g-2aMA4?t=396) — price action at the gray pole
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** This is ICT's coinage; highly specific to his framework. Requires practice to spot.

title: AM Session Review & Course Correction
head: Change in State of Delivery (CISD) via Opening Price Selection
body:
- **Kind:** rule + example
- **What ICT says:** When identifying a key level or reversal, sometimes the opening price of a candle is more significant than its close because that opening matches or aligns with prior significant levels (e.g., relative equal lows, liquidity pools). Using the opening of a down-close candle instead of another consecutive up-close shows that the down-close is where "true" delivery changed. It's a technical choice, not arbitrary.
- **How to identify:** (1) Look at the opening of recent candles, (2) Compare them to prior support/resistance, (3) If an opening aligns with a significant level, it's a CISD candidate.
- **How to use:** Confirmation and entry point selection. If you're building a position, using the opening of a candle that changed direction (vs. the close) can be more precise.
- **Example in this video:** ICT selects a down-close candle's opening (not the close) as the CISD because that opening aligns with the relative equal lows he identified. This is why he picks *that* candle instead of consecutive up-closes. It shows where state of delivery truly changed.
- **Timestamps:** [0:02:32](https://youtu.ye/0Bu4g-2aMA4?t=152) — explaining candle selection for CISD
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Not all down-closes are equally valid; pick the one whose opening aligns with key levels.

title: How To Frame Sessions In High Resistance Liquiidity Run Conditions
head: High Resistance Liquidity Run conditions: framing the week by the economic calendar  (aliases ICT uses: "range-bound", "held during regular trading hours")
body:
- **Kind:** rule / context filter
- **What ICT says:**
  - Check the economic calendar for the week. CPI is Wednesday and PPI Thursday (both high-impact "red folder"); Friday's items (consumer sentiment and one more) are medium impact.
  - Because the big volatility injections are on Wednesday and Thursday, there is no reason to expect wildly trending, extrapolated moves on Monday and Tuesday. Volatility is being "held" for the numbers. The one-sided price delivery is more likely on the news days.
  - Caveat: electronic trading hours (London session and the pre-market leading to the 9:30 opening bell) tend to trend in such weeks. Regular trading hours then tend to range, i.e. high-resistance liquidity run conditions.
  - Do not assume you cannot trade it, and one session of the day (AM or PM) may be permitted to trend briefly. Anticipating it helps you avoid forcing trades.
  - When taking trades "look for the best-case scenario, but don't demand it."
- **How to identify:** a week where the heavy news is Wednesday/Thursday and Monday/Tuesday have no equivalent catalysts.
- **How to use:** lower expectations for runaway RTH moves on Monday and Tuesday; use ETH (London / pre-market) for the trend leg; take smaller, faster targets in RTH and don't force breakouts or trending models.
- **Example in this video:** Monday: price consolidated overnight around the midnight open, made relative equal highs in London, drifted lower into the pre-market (the trend leg), and then spent RTH in a range.
- **Timestamps:** [0:01:35](https://youtu.be/C7CwjBOtHwM?t=95), [0:02:21](https://youtu.be/C7CwjBOtHwM?t=141), [0:03:10](https://youtu.be/C7CwjBOtHwM?t=190), [0:04:44](https://youtu.be/C7CwjBOtHwM?t=284)
- **Nuance / caveats:** this extends the "High/low resistance liquidity run" idea to a weekly framing driven by news placement. He says new traders get hurt when they try to force a breakout or trending model on such days.

title: How To Frame Sessions In High Resistance Liquiidity Run Conditions
head: Prior Friday's final-hour RTH dealing range as Monday reference
body:
- **Kind:** refinement
- **What ICT says:** he takes the final hour of regular trading hours on Friday (the low and high of that hour; the lowest low is around 4:00 p.m. ET "or thereabouts") as a dealing range. He draws the fib from the low up to the high; a candle laid right on the 0.75 level of that range was a suspension block (caption), so that level mattered. These two reference points (the last-hour low and high) serve as liquidity targets and as grading levels for where turning points may form on Monday. A "key discount array from last Friday" is what price eventually reached in the PM session.
- **How to use:** include Friday's final-hour range on the chart on Monday; treat its low as sell-side liquidity and its graded levels as places to expect reaction.
- **Example in this video:** Monday morning price made a low in the session from a "green box" graded from Friday, and later sold into Friday's final-hour low during the afternoon.

head: Grading a dealing range with fib levels and carrying it forward  (aliases: quadrants, octants, "gradient levels")
body:

- **What ICT says:** measure highest high to lowest low of the defined window, anchor the fib on the low (for an up leg) and the high; quadrant and octant levels then tell you where a PD array should form. If a BISI/FVG touches one of these levels it is "valid", and the range can be carried forward through the entire first hour of trading. A PD array on a graded level is a higher-probability one.
- **How to identify:** the array's boundary or candle touches the same graded levels as the range (e.g. "touching this level and this level").
- **How to use:** carry the graded range into the first hour; use the validated array as the setup (see next concept).

Monday: a high formed, price traded down to make the lowest low since 7:00, then traded back up to almost 3/4 (if not 80%) of the 7:00–7:30 range. He graded the levels from that swing's low to high.

head: BISI that validates and inverts (iFVG) on graded levels, with midnight open and a macro
body:
- **Kind:** entry model (worked example)
- **What ICT says:**
  - A BISI sitting on the graded levels is "valid". Price opened, traded up into it, hit the upper quadrant level, and closed there. The next candle was anticipated to be lower. A candle low / opening price / volume imbalance that is bullish but then gets traded below and validated by closing lower becomes an inversion FVG, "because it's on this level and this level".
  - Price then sold off into the NWOG, rallied back to Monday's midnight opening price and the inversion FVG again during a macro, "the last minute of the macro from 7:50 to 8:10", and then sold off hard, blowing through sell-side and moving to the final-hour RTH low from Friday.
  - Midnight opening price: price gravitates back to it. He says you must have it toggled and annotated on your chart in any market. Monday's midnight open was 29,878.25.
- **How to use:** short the retest of the inversion FVG into the midnight open / macro; target the NWOG and the session low liquidity.
- **Example in this video:** NQ, Monday 10 Aug 2026 (inferred), 1-minute-ish: relative equal highs form in London; midnight open 29,878.25; pre-market sell-off; BISI at graded levels inverts; price pulls up to midnight open plus the inversion FVG in the last minute of the 7:50–8:10 macro; then sells off to Friday's final-hour low.
- **Timestamps:** [0:07:57](https://youtu.be/C7CwjBOtHwM?t=477), [0:08:48](https://youtu.be/C7CwjBOtHwM?t=528)

title: Navigating High Resistance Liquidity Run Conditions
head: Inversion FVG qualification and long entries on its high  (aliases: "kiss" the high, "qualified two times")
body:
- **Kind:** entry model
- **What ICT says:**
  - The setup begins with a bearish FVG that price closes above, which turns it into an inversion FVG when the market is bullish. He wants it "qualified" before using it for entries. Qualification here was twice: a close above it, then price trades back down through it, and a candle that opens, trades down, comes back up and closes around the high of the gap. That is a second qualification and confirmation. Only after those does he anticipate using it for entries.
  - Entries are made inside the gap, not just at the close: the first buy is at the low end of the iFVG, and he adds each time price comes back and "kisses" the high of the inversion FVG. He adds on the upper quadrant and at the deep end of the gap.
  - Price did not even reach the CE of the inversion FVG (the caption puts the CE at 29,796.25; unclear whether this is the CE or the low of the pullback), which he treats as strength.
  - His average across the adds ended up essentially at the high of the inversion FVG.
- **How to identify:** bearish FVG closed above (iFVG), then a second test that holds on a closing basis; the 9:30 open was in close proximity to its high.
- **How to use:** buy at the iFVG low end, add at its high and on retests; stop under its low.
- **Example in this video:** NQ, Monday morning pre-market through 9:30 ET: price opened close to the high of the iFVG, dipped lower and trapped breakout shorts at the low (smart money buys those sell stops), then rallied back above it. The first long was 4 contracts, stop at the candle low (plus or minus a tick or two), planning to add 2 more when price came back to the high of the gap. Later total sizing is stated as 12 contracts (see below).
- **Timestamps:** [0:00:03](https://youtu.be/O217xQsEUgI?t=3) — first entry, 4 contracts; [0:00:50](https://youtu.be/O217xQsEUgI?t=50) — add 2 at the iFVG high; [0:11:20](https://youtu.be/O217xQsEUgI?t=680) — how the iFVG formed and was qualified; [0:12:07](https://youtu.be/O217xQsEUgI?t=727) — two qualifications
- **Nuance / caveats:** he calls the morning "a little disorganized" because of CPI/PPI later in the week, so the plan stays conservative.

title: Navigating High Resistance Liquidity Run Conditions
head: Stop management in steps (cut risk, cover costs)
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - Initial stop: the candle's low minus a tick or two.
  - After adding, the stop moves to just below the midpoint of the iFVG.
  - Once the average entry sits at the iFVG high, raise the stop to the low of the iFVG minus a tick, "reduced some of the risk".
  - When a candle closes above a key level (a wick's high, the iFVG), roll the stop to cover costs (breakeven). He does this again after a close above the earlier area.
  - After a partial, increase "paycheck" by lifting the stop to just below a wick high.
  - Final structure: the stop on the remaining position sits just below a wick, since a close below it leaves the swing low as the last defense.
- **How to use:** each step is tied to a price structure (candle low, iFVG midpoint, iFVG low, wick low), not to a fixed number of ticks.
- **Timestamps:** [0:00:50](https://youtu.be/O217xQsEUgI?t=50), [0:02:26](https://youtu.be/O217xQsEUgI?t=146), [0:05:42](https://youtu.be/O217xQsEUgI?t=342), [0:16:08](https://youtu.be/O217xQsEUgI?t=968), [0:19:18](https://youtu.be/O217xQsEUgI?t=1158)
