head: Grading a wick: no bodies buried below its CE  (aliases: "wick consequent encroachment", "PD array number two")
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - When long, grade a wick below price by its CE. He does not want bodies buried south of the CE. A body can dip, but then the next candle must show immediate willingness to go higher, preferably a close above.
  - Entry orders can sit at the wick's CE; a lower wick may be "flirted with", but if you are on side price should not take out that low.
  - A body closing above the CE of a wick is bullish. A close above the open of the candle that made the wick is "extremely positive" (here about 29,873.75, which he rounds to 874).
  - He calls this wick "PD array number two". If price closes below it, the last defense is the swing low, which is why the stop sits just under the wick.
  - A close below a small bullish FVG but above in the upper half of the wick is a mixed signal; "we are balancing several things".
- **How to use:** use the wick CE as the line in the sand for stop and for add decisions; watch the next one or two candles.
- **Timestamps:** [0:01:37](https://youtu.be/O217xQsEUgI?t=97), [0:03:18](https://youtu.be/O217xQsEUgI?t=198), [0:04:54](https://youtu.be/O217xQsEUgI?t=294), [0:19:18](https://youtu.be/O217xQsEUgI?t=1158), [0:20:07](https://youtu.be/O217xQsEUgI?t=1207)

head: Bullish FVG should be left partly open (breakaway / measuring gap)
body:
- **Kind:** refinement (restates earlier teaching)
- **What ICT says:** in a bullish run, a BISI (and a volume imbalance inside it) that price does not fully fill is "one of the strongest signatures" that price still wants to go higher. The ideal is that price leaves a portion open or does not trade into it at all; then it acts like a breakaway or measuring gap anchored to the start of the run. If price fills it completely it is not necessarily bad when still low in the run, but it makes it harder for price to prove it wants to keep going. Tether yourself to the idea that order flow is bullish and look for high-probability entries.
- **Example in this video:** a small BISI left a portion open on the run to the midnight open; later a BISI with a volume imbalance at its high was being tested, and he wanted a close above half of its wick (the CE).
- **Timestamps:** [0:09:43](https://youtu.be/O217xQsEUgI?t=583), [0:13:42](https://youtu.be/O217xQsEUgI?t=822), [0:14:28](https://youtu.be/O217xQsEUgI?t=868), [0:17:44](https://youtu.be/O217xQsEUgI?t=1064)

head: Pre-Market Range Definition Before High-Impact News
body:
- **Kind:** rule + example
- **What ICT says:** Before a major economic release (NFP at 8:30 ET, CPI, PPI, FOMC, etc.), you must establish the pre-release range (7:00–8:30 AM). Identify the highest high and lowest low during that 90-minute window. This range is the "dealing range" where price was willing to trade before the news. Once the news hits, price will typically break out of that range, so knowing the range boundaries allows you to anticipate the direction and magnitude of the move.
- **How to identify:** Chart the 1-minute from 7:00 to 8:30 ET; mark the highest candle high and lowest candle low.
- **How to use:** Breakout direction. If price breaks above the range, expect continuation higher. If below, continuation lower. Use range boundaries as support/resistance even after the news.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 7:00–8:30 pre-market range = [high, low]. High-impact NFP at 8:30 ET. Price subsequently breaks well above that range, rallying toward the 29,780 level ICT called for. The range high becomes a support zone on any pullback.
- **Timestamps:** [0:01:36](https://youtu.be/hIusATccCcM?t=96) — defining importance of pre-NFP range; [0:02:24](https://youtu.ye/hIusATccCcM?t=144) — measuring high/low of the range; [0:03:12](https://youtu.ye/hIusATccCcM?t=192) — anticipating breakout direction
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Do not trade the range itself expecting containment once NFP is released; the range breaks almost every time.

head: Buy-Side Imbalance / Sell-Side Inefficiency (BSI/SSI)
body:
- **Kind:** definition + rule + example
- **What ICT says:** (Refresher, but contextualized) When price trades down from a high into a low, there's an unfilled space (gap) if the move is fast. That gap is a buy-side imbalance (buyers moved price higher) + sell-side inefficiency (gap was not filled at every price level). Later, price will be drawn to fill some of this gap or use it as a support zone. Multiple BSI/SSI structures can appear in the pre-market range, each representing potential entry zones for a post-news move.
- **How to identify:** Look for gaps or unfilled spaces in the 7:00–8:30 pre-market range.
- **How to use:** Entry zones. When price trades into a BSI/SSI after the news, it's a valid long or short setup depending on direction.
- **Example in this video:** NQ pre-market shows multiple BSI/SSI gaps. Once NFP is released and price rallies, it trades back down into these BSI zones, offering pullback entry opportunities for longs.
- **Timestamps:** [0:03:59](https://youtu.ye/hIusATccCcM?t=239) — describing BSI/SSI in pre-market context; [0:04:47](https://youtu.ye/hIusATccCcM?t=287) — trading into BSI after NFP
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** BSI/SSI become more significant in event-driven contexts because price needs to know where to retrace during consolidations within the larger trend.

title: Case Study With NonFarm Payroll & NQ Futures \ August 07, 2026
head: Balanced Price Range (BPR)
body:
- **Kind:** definition + example
- **What ICT says:** A balanced price range is when two PD arrays (a buy-side imbalance + a sell-side imbalance, or vice versa) share the same high-low span. The highest high of both and the lowest low of both define a larger BPR. When price trades into a BPR, it's a zone of equilibrium where both sides of the order book are balanced; price tends to respect these levels repeatedly.
- **How to identify:** (1) Find a BSI (gap up, unfilled below), (2) Find an SSI (gap down, unfilled above), (3) If they span the same range, they're balanced. Mark the combined high/low.
- **How to use:** Support/resistance and turning points. Price respects BPR boundaries; use them for stops, partials, and bias confirmation.
- **Example in this video:** Two gaps (one up, one down) share the same high-low range. That combined range is the BPR. Price hits this BPR multiple times during the post-NFP consolidation, using it as a pivot zone. When bodies fail to breach BPR, a reversal is likely.
- **Timestamps:** [0:06:21](https://youtu.ye/hIusATccCcM?t=381) — defining BPR; [0:10:21](https://youtu.ye/hIusATccCcM?t=621) — BPR as support in the trade
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** BPR is more complex than a single level but very reliable once identified.

head: Octants and Standard Deviations
body:
- **Kind:** definition + rule
- **What ICT says:** Divide the pre-NFP range into 8 equal parts (octants: upper quadrant, upper percentile, upper octant, midpoint/CE, lower octant, lower percentile, lower quadrant, below). Standard deviations of the range (±2.0 SD, ±1.0 SD, etc.) can align with these octants. When price reaches +2.0 or beyond, it's extended; expect potential reversal at macro times.
- **How to identify:** (1) Measure the range high/low, (2) Divide by 8 or apply SD formula, (3) Mark each octant.
- **How to use:** Reversal confirmation. If price reaches upper octant during a macro time, expect pullback. Octants also qualify PD arrays; if a gap sits at an octant, it's more significant.
- **Example in this video:** Pre-NFP range octants are marked. After NFP, price rallies beyond +2.0 SD during the macro window (8:50–9:10), confirming a turning point. Bodies fail to close above the +2.0 SD octant, signaling weakness.
- **Timestamps:** [0:08:42](https://youtu.ye/hIusATccCcM?t=522) — calculating standard deviations of the range; [0:09:33](https://youtu.ye/hIusATccCcM?t=573) — showing +2.0 SD reaching during macro; [0:10:21](https://youtu.ye/hIusATccCcM?t=621) — octants and PD array qualification
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Standard deviations require precise calculation; an off-by-one error invalidates the levels.

title: Case Study With NonFarm Payroll & NQ Futures \ August 07, 2026
head: Macro Time Window and Two-Stage Delivery
body:
- **Kind:** rule + example
- **What ICT says:** Major economic events (NFP, FOMC, CPI) follow a two-stage delivery pattern: (1) initial reaction rally (or selloff) in one direction, often reaching extended levels (SD ±2.0+), (2) pullback and reversal, wiping out weak stops from the initial move. The macro time window (typically 8:50–9:10 AM for NFP) is when the turn is most likely. Stops from the initial move get run during the second stage.
- **How to identify:** Watch the initial 5–15 minute move post-event; if it extends into macro time (8:50–9:10), expect reversal in that window.
- **How to use:** Profit-taking and reversal entry. Take partials off at the turning point (macro time). Place reverse orders (shorts if initially long) just inside the previous support/resistance, anticipating the second-stage pullback.
- **Example in this video:** NFP at 8:30 ET. Rally from 8:30 to 8:50 (initial move). At 8:50 (start of macro window), ICT tweeted to take longs off. The market then dipped, hit the BPR, stopped out longs with tight stops, then resumed higher (two stages).
- **Timestamps:** [0:05:35](https://youtu.ye/hIusATccCcM?t=335) — warning to take profits at macro time; [0:06:21](https://youtu.ye/hIusATccCcM?t=381) — second-stage pullback confirming the pattern; [0:10:21](https://youtu.ye/hIusATccCcM?t=621) — completing the two-stage narrative
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Two-stage delivery is a pattern, not a guarantee; occasionally, one-stage rallies occur without pullback. Always have a stop.

title: Case Study With NonFarm Payroll & NQ Futures \ August 07, 2026
head: Institutional Order Flow Entry Drill (IOFED)
body:
- **Kind:** observation + technique
- **What ICT says:** When a PD array (gap, order block, etc.) is "qualified" by sitting at a key octant or standard deviation, price trades into it as the institution are entering orders at that level. This is called an order flow entry drill: the market sweeps into a gap/level, and institutions add to their positions, creating a bounce or reversal. Watching for these drills helps time scalp entries.
- **How to identify:** (1) Mark key gaps/order blocks on your chart, (2) Note which octant they're at, (3) Watch if price trades into that gap on a pullback—that's the IOFED.
- **Example in this video:** Multiple PD arrays in the NQ trade are "qualified because [they sit at an octant]." When price trades into these qualified arrays, ICT knows it's an IOFED and manages the trade accordingly.
- **Timestamps:** [0:11:10](https://youtu.ye/hIusATccCcM?t=670) — describing IOFED; [0:11:56](https://youtu.ye/hIusATccCcM?t=716) — price trades into qualified PDA, executes IOFED
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Not all IOFEDs work; sometimes price breaks through the drill. Have a stop in case.

title: Case Study With NonFarm Payroll & NQ Futures \ August 07, 2026
head: Partial Taking Strategy at Fibonacci 0.5
body:
- **Kind:** rule + example
- **What ICT says:** In an event-driven trade like NFP, don't hold the full position to the ultimate target. Take the first partial at the 0.5 Fibonacci midpoint between entry and a known target/resistance. This locks in a "halfway" profit and reduces risk on the runner.
- **How to identify:** Mark entry and a nearby resistance/target; measure 0.5 between them.
- **How to use:** Partial exit. At 0.5, close 25–50% of the position. Leave the rest to run.
- **Example in this video:** Long entry near the 29,780 level (after initial drop into the BSI zones). 0.5 Fibonacci midpoint between 29,780 entry and the pre-NFP range high = X price. ICT takes one contract off at X. The other contract continues to the macro high before being stopped out or exited.
- **Timestamps:** [0:07:55](https://youtu.ye/hIusATccCcM?t=475) — calculating 0.5 and exiting partial; [0:08:42](https://youtu.ye/hIusATccCcM?t=522) — confirming exit near midpoint
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** The exact 0.5 is an ideal; a few ticks off is acceptable.

head: Pre-NFP Risk Warning and Trading Suitability
body:
- **Kind:** warning + rule
- **What ICT says:** New traders should NOT trade Thursday–Friday (last two days of week 1 of the month) because of high impact news and volatility. NFP Friday is especially challenging. Only experienced traders should participate. Even experienced traders must adjust position sizing and stop placements for event risk.
- **How to identify:** Mark first week of each month (especially Thursday–Friday) as high-danger trading days on your calendar.
- **How to use:** Risk management. Either avoid these days entirely or use micro contracts and tight stops only.
- **Example in this video:** ICT emphasizes upfront: "never really try to participate on Thursday and Friday" for new traders. He then shows his demo trade (not real money) to show how to manage it *if* you must trade NFP. This is honest warning.

title: ICT Price Action Chronicles - The Science Of Anticipation In Price Action
head: Anticipation framework: daily PD array into a 7:00–9:00 ET one-minute entry  (aliases: "science of anticipation", "anticipate, not react", "hunting")
body:
- **Kind:** entry model / process
- **What ICT says:**
  - Profit needs movement; it is "literally impossible" to profit without motion in price. So spend time finding places where price is likely, on a consistent basis, to provide a tradable run, then take measured risk there.
  - A key level on the daily chart gives "a large degree of probability" that price will produce a tradable run. That is odds in your favour, not a guarantee of profit.
  - Anticipate, then verify with footholds: (1) know where the run should start (inception), (2) know what level each stage should respect, (3) watch for continued feedback that the run is sustainable. You are "hunting", not waiting for the deer to start running before you chase it.
  - The one-minute chart gives no room to "fluff" it: you must know exactly what price should do, should not do, and what is permissible. This gets easier as you learn to recognise repeatable volatility and price runs.
  - Time focus he reiterates: 7:00 to 9:00 ET, applying the daily PD-array logic. Here, price traded down into daily discount arrays at 7:00, did so aggressively, rallied, consolidated, folded, then held the upper half of the imbalance.
  - He plans a separate (pre-recorded, YouTube-hosted) talk on "generic price structure that yields continuous opportunities": his claim is that his full teaching compendium already contains enough framework to find a setup every day.
- **How to identify:** daily chart shows a sharp one-way run into a daily PD array (here an inversion FVG) that is also an old high/wick area; that arrival happens during the 7:00–9:00 ET window; price on the 1m chart then shows a reactive gap/imbalance to enter at.
- **How to use:** mark the daily levels first, delineate the 7:00 to 9:00 window, drop to 1m, enter at a refined level inside the daily array (see next concepts), manage with the partial/stop-roll rules below.
- **Example in this video:** daily: four straight up days off FOMC, one pullback day, today opens softer. ICT expects price not to settle on a down close and to try higher (a rally this hard normally takes a break). Price drops sharply into the daily inversion FVG (which also contains an old high and a daily volume imbalance). On the 1m chart in the 7:00–9:00 window he goes long at the consequent encroachment of a gap (see below), targets the relative equal highs above, scales out, trails the stop and finally closes the session note with price holding the upper half of the imbalance below a failed push.
- **Timestamps:** [0:00:00](https://youtu.be/tByaPnk3fc4?t=0) daily context after FOMC rally · [0:04:13](https://youtu.be/tByaPnk3fc4?t=253) drops to 1m, 7:00–9:00 window, goes long · [0:27:15](https://youtu.be/tByaPnk3fc4?t=1635) "we need movement", anticipate not react · [0:48:12](https://youtu.be/tByaPnk3fc4?t=2892) recap of why 7:00–9:00 ET
- **Nuance / caveats:** he shows entries live "not from the charts" afterwards; he admits he got distracted (fed pets, fed deer) and that he mentioned the entry before showing the fill. He also says he had pyramid ideas lower in the same area but did not execute them.

title: ICT Price Action Chronicles - The Science Of Anticipation In Price Action
head: Inversion FVG on the daily chart as a support level  (aliases: daily iFVG, "reversion fair value gap" in captions)
body:
- **Kind:** example only (applies known concept)
- **What ICT says:**
  - Price dropped fast into a daily inversion fair value gap and was supported. The speed of the drop ("in a hurry to get here") is part of why a pop was reasonable to anticipate.
  - The 50% (consequent encroachment) of a daily wick he had tweeted about equals the high of that inversion FVG, so two reference points coincide.
  - He tweets a level only when he also sees something technically align with it.
  - The daily wick is a level he wants price to overcome (get above and hold above) "until we get through" NFP week.
- **How to use:** the iFVG is the daily-timeframe reason; the 1m refinement (CE of a gap, suspension block) is the execution.
- **Example in this video:** price at/near an old daily high and wick; relative equal highs sit just above; after the sharp one-candle decline price comes back and runs over the whole decline.
- **Timestamps:** [0:02:29](https://youtu.be/tByaPnk3fc4?t=149) the daily wick he wants overcome · [0:05:01](https://youtu.be/tByaPnk3fc4?t=301) entry at CE after the daily iFVG is hit

title: ICT Price Action Chronicles - The Science Of Anticipation In Price Action
head: Volume imbalance and the "daily inefficiency range"  (aliases: VI)
body:
- **Kind:** example only
- **What ICT says:**
  - On the daily chart there is a volume imbalance up to yesterday's low, which he calls the range for daily inefficiency; another area shows no volume imbalance.
  - On the 1m chart price "traded down into" a volume imbalance and reacted from it with extreme precision: the open of one candle was 29,390.75 and the low of the other candle was 90.75, meaning price touched the exact edge, and he calls this "perfect".
  - A volume imbalance can sit outside an inversion FVG and that is permissible.
  - On a drop, "walking back to the left" from the lowest candle, the last inefficiency of the run (here a volume imbalance that had already been used, no true gap) is the area where he would have entered and pyramided.
- **How to identify:** two consecutive candles whose bodies do not overlap or connect, even though wicks do (from his wording about "bodies don't connect or overlap").
- **Timestamps:** [0:01:36](https://youtu.be/tByaPnk3fc4?t=96) daily volume imbalance · [0:28:51](https://youtu.be/tByaPnk3fc4?t=1731) exact 29,390.75 reaction · [0:24:48](https://youtu.be/tByaPnk3fc4?t=1488) last inefficiency of the run
- **Nuance / caveats:** he dismisses order flow, level 2 and bubble charts as unnecessary for this precision.

title: ICT Price Action Chronicles - The Science Of Anticipation In Price Action
head: Suspension block  (aliases: none stated)
body:
- **Kind:** new coinage / definition
- **What ICT says:** when there is a volume imbalance at the high of an inefficiency and another at the low of that same inefficiency (bodies on both ends do not connect or overlap), that structure is a suspension block. You carry that information forward as a level.
- **How to identify:** inefficiency (gap) with a volume imbalance at its top edge and one at its bottom edge.
- **How to use:** he likes it as a place to go long; he entered at the midpoint of the gap inside the structure.
- **Example in this video:** 1m chart near the daily iFVG: a small volume imbalance where bodies do not connect, then a section where two candles' bodies do not connect or overlap, bracketing the inefficiency; he buys at its CE.
- **Timestamps:** [0:04:13](https://youtu.be/tByaPnk3fc4?t=253) "A suspension block. I like that." · [0:26:26](https://youtu.be/tByaPnk3fc4?t=1586) definition
- **Nuance / caveats:** first time seen in these notes as a named structure; the caption wording is somewhat loose, so treat the exact definition as "VI at the high and low of an inefficiency".

title: ICT Price Action Chronicles - The Science Of Anticipation In Price Action
head: Entry at the consequent encroachment of a gap, with stop under the key level
body:
- **Kind:** entry model / rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - He enters "exactly at the consequent encroachment" (50%) of the 1m gap right after the daily inversion FVG tag.
  - The stop loss for a trade like this has to start "right at that level and under": at or just below the level (the 50% of the wick/top of the iFVG) that must hold for the idea to be valid.
  - Later stop logic: stop sits below the midpoint of the wick; if price is bullish it need not trade below that area; worst case it wicks to it.
  - He placed a limit order to sell one contract just above entry as a first partial.
- **How to use:** entry at CE, stop below the key level, first partial quickly, then trail (see trade management).
- **Timestamps:** [0:05:01](https://youtu.be/tByaPnk3fc4?t=301) entering exactly at CE · [0:06:44](https://youtu.be/tByaPnk3fc4?t=404) stop must be at/under that level · [0:33:43](https://youtu.be/tByaPnk3fc4?t=2023) stop below midpoint of the wick
- **Nuance / caveats:** he forgot to set the stop at first while talking; he says not to copy that habit.

title: ICT Price Action Chronicles - The Science Of Anticipation In Price Action
head: Midpoint "threshold" test: bodies above 50% of the decline
body:
- **Kind:** rule / refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - There was a big vertical decline in one candle. Take the high of that inefficiency to the volume-imbalance low; the midpoint of that range is a threshold ("think of it like a ladder", not depth of market).
  - Price must show willingness to get above the midpoint and start laying bodies above it. Only after a candle closes above halfway does he roll the stop up to just below the lows of the decline.
  - Ideal sequence: overlap all of the decline, rip above, stay above, and then the next order of business is the order flow around the relative equal highs.
  - You can add all the grading levels (fib/his usual levels) on top if you want to be a "purist"; he shows his fib settings on request. The caption does not say which exact levels.
- **How to identify:** closes (bodies) above the 50% of the one-candle decline; no bodies below it later.
- **How to use:** a close above 50% = permission to trail the stop; bodies below the wick's CE later is why price got "heavy and weighty".
- **Example in this video:** after entry price pops, closes above the line, he rolls the stop up under the decline's lows, then rolls it again to cover commissions.
- **Timestamps:** [0:07:34](https://youtu.be/tByaPnk3fc4?t=454) the ladder/threshold idea · [0:09:14](https://youtu.be/tByaPnk3fc4?t=554) close above halfway then roll stop · [0:21:36](https://youtu.be/tByaPnk3fc4?t=1296) none of the bodies close below the half
- **Nuance / caveats:** none stated beyond "willingness" language (price must keep showing it).

title: ICT Price Action Chronicles - The Science Of Anticipation In Price Action
head: Upper half of a BISI as the strongest support; small portion left open  (aliases: "buy side imbalance sell side inefficiency", upper portion of the gap)
body:
- **Kind:** refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - If price trades back into a BISI that is acting as support, the upper half is where the strongest buying for an entry comes from.
  - You want a small portion of the gap to remain open: a small portion of a gap staying open means the market is unwilling to go lower; if it is unwilling to go lower while you expect higher prices, that is by definition strong.
  - He says nobody else taught it this way and that this is his own idea, not supply/demand boxes.
  - If-then clause he gave live: ideally the wick supports price. If price goes below it, it should stay in the upper half of the gap. If price shows discount sensitivity (below) there and does not want to go lower, the idea stays valid; if it closes below the low (on a closing basis), this is the last line of defence for bullishness.
- **How to use:** stack the three PD arrays he lists as the "support zone" for a long: (1) the old high, (2) the upper portion of the BISI, (3) the wick/its CE. Third and lowest of the three is the upper portion of the BISI (as captioned).
- **Example in this video:** after the first push, price came back toward the area, closed outside the gap, then held the upper half; later he notes "now we're supporting the upper half" as a defensive view of market structure.
- **Timestamps:** [0:34:31](https://youtu.be/tByaPnk3fc4?t=2071) three PD arrays, upper portion of the BISI · [0:35:17](https://youtu.be/tByaPnk3fc4?t=2117) small portion open = unwilling to go lower · [0:32:55](https://youtu.be/tByaPnk3fc4?t=1975) the if/then clause
- **Nuance / caveats:** he attributes the claim to himself; whether others teach it is irrelevant to the lesson.

title: ICT Price Action Chronicles - The Science Of Anticipation In Price Action
head: Discount sensitivity
body:
- **Kind:** new coinage / refinement
- **What ICT says:** he draws a box from the midpoint of an inefficiency up to its high and calls the behaviour inside it "discount sensitivity". If price comes down into that zone it must react to the upside and not be inclined to keep going all the way down. "Worst case" it wicks to the stop-area but he prefers it does not.
- **How to use:** a way to judge strength on a pullback: reactive bounce from the upper half of the box means the long is still intact; if it fails to react, the idea weakens.
- **Timestamps:** [0:33:43](https://youtu.be/tByaPnk3fc4?t=2023) · [0:40:08](https://youtu.be/tByaPnk3fc4?t=2408) repeated for the next inefficiency
- **Nuance / caveats:** term appears here as a descriptive coinage; no numeric criteria.

The first objective is a run into the relative equal high; price showed "a lot of energy" after the equal highs formed, which he liked for the NFP week.

head: Rejection block (definition)
body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:** the rejection block is the highest up-close price in a swing high. In this trade price ran to the rejection block and then gave up; he had already taken a partial at that high.
- **Example in this video:** after the trade went up, price went exactly to the rejection block (near his second partial area) then weakened; bodies printed below the wick's consequent encroachment, which made price "heavy and weighty".

title: ICT Price Action Chronicles - The Science Of Anticipation In Price Action
head: Trade management: partials, stop-rolling and never loosening a stop  (aliases: "give yourself the cookie")
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - Roll the stop as price proves itself (after the close above halfway; later "just to cover commissions"; later to lock in profit). Once you move a stop into profit, commit to it: never move it back down (long) or back up (short).
  - He takes partial profits at obvious liquidity (one contract at the first limit, "tuck two off of three" at the high where price had stretched like "taffy": it can give up at any time).
  - Reason to take a partial when anxious or inexperienced: it rewards you for what you have done and removes the need to be right. "Give yourself the cookie."
  - Stopped out after moving into profit = you get paid; it is not being victimised.
  - He says market "victim" thinking comes from moving the stop back and failing to take profit at a higher price.
- **How to use:** (1) partial at the first liquidity objective; (2) stop to cost/commission after price proves itself; (3) leave a small runner; (4) do not widen once raised.
- **Example in this video:** entry at CE; limit sell of 1 contract just above; stop rolled twice; two of three contracts off at the high; leftover with a stop under the midpoint of the wick.
- **Timestamps:** [0:10:02](https://youtu.be/tByaPnk3fc4?t=602) rolling the stop up · [0:36:56](https://youtu.be/tByaPnk3fc4?t=2216) "you don't need to be right" · [0:39:21](https://youtu.be/tByaPnk3fc4?t=2361) two off of three · [0:42:31](https://youtu.be/tByaPnk3fc4?t=2551) do not move the stop back
- **Nuance / caveats:** the caption is a bit unclear on whether his final fill was a stop-out or a close; he calls it "a wonderful experiment" either way.

title: ICT Price Action Chronicles - The Science Of Anticipation In Price Action
head: NFP week rules and fundamentals view
body:
- **Kind:** rule / opinion
- **What ICT says:**
  - For brand-new traders in NFP week, the cleanest price action is Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday up to about 11:00 ET. Admitting you are new is maturity, not weakness. Don't try to take every possible move.
  - NFP (first Friday of the month, 8:30 ET) is mostly an "invitation to a day of anticipation" with large timed volatility; he believes the data is untrustworthy and it is "one of the largest reports misinterpreted by traders". He never cared about the figures.
  - He sees real fundamental supply/demand in agricultural commodities and livestock (corn, grains, soybeans, wheat, oats, meats), not in bonds, stocks or index futures, where price is driven by "perceived" supply and demand. He calls fundamental analysis of indexes pseudoscience.
- **Timestamps:** [0:02:29](https://youtu.be/tByaPnk3fc4?t=149) beginner rule · [0:14:16](https://youtu.be/tByaPnk3fc4?t=856) NFP unpredictability · [0:15:06](https://youtu.be/tByaPnk3fc4?t=906) commodities vs indexes
- **Nuance / caveats:** consistent with his earlier beginner NFP-week guidance (Thursday/Friday avoid). The rest of this section is opinion plus personal stories and politics, not trading mechanics.

title: Part 2 High Precision Secrets To Intraday Price Action
head: RTH opening range gap (ORG): definition, grading and the 70% / 10:00 statistic  (aliases: opening range gap, "regular trading hours opening range gap", half gap)
body:
- **Kind:** definition / rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - The ORG runs from the 9:30 ET opening price to the previous session's regular-trading-hours final print/settlement at 4:14 pm ET. On this day: high = 9:30 open at 28,576.75, low = Thursday's 4:14 pm print at 28,324.75 (a gap up).
  - Add the levels in the data window to confirm both prices are exact (he toggles RTH and then back to electronic hours to read the prices).
  - Grade the gap: high, upper octant, upper quadrant, consequent encroachment (CE, the half gap), lower quadrant/octant, low. Above the CE is premium, below is discount.
  - Half gap (CE) "70% of the time" gets traded to by 10:00 am ET. Here it traded to the CE at 9:43.
  - The time dimension: 9:30 open is the "tethered" level, so horizontal levels are price relative to time. He also draws a first-hour dealing range (9:30–10:30 high and low) as a second time-based range.
- **How to identify:** gap between prior RTH close (4:14 final print) and 9:30 open; confirm with RTH/ETH toggle.
- **How to use:** the graded levels tell you where PD arrays should form and which levels they should react from; then check where the bodies (not wicks) are relative to those levels.
- **Example in this video:** NQ-like prices, Friday: price returns to the 9:30 open, trades below and up again, falls short of it, then opens lower and trades right into it; a gap in premium acts as a breakaway; it trades down through the CE at 9:43 and fills the gap to the low at 28,324.75, closes beyond it after hours.
- **Timestamps:** [0:09:39](https://youtu.be/BD7kqmgdBU8?t=579) setting the 9:30 high and the RTH low · [0:11:12](https://youtu.be/BD7kqmgdBU8?t=672) CE and the 70% by 10:00 statistic · [0:12:01](https://youtu.be/BD7kqmgdBU8?t=721) first-hour dealing range
- **Nuance / caveats:** he has used two "last price" references over the years: the high of the 4:00 candle (if it is higher than the close) from his 1990s S&P days, and the 4:14 final print; see the shortcut model below.

title: Part 2 High Precision Secrets To Intraday Price Action
head: Octants and quadrants: grading a range and reading body location
body:
- **Kind:** rule / refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - Take the highest of a set of levels to the lowest and measure it, then grade it. Upper octant, upper quadrant, CE, lower quadrant, lower octant are the grading levels.
  - What matters is where the bodies end up, not wicks: if price wicks through a level but the body comes back and closes inside, the range is respected.
  - Example logic: bodies trade down through the upper octant and the upper quadrant but fail to touch the next octant, then are rejected back up = bullish, especially if no body can return to the range that was used to project the daily low.
  - "Where are the bodies?" is his repeated question: bodies below the upper quadrant of the ORG = bearish context.
  - This measurement work is "very specific" to him: "an absolution, not a guesstimate". Don't be put off by the number of measurements: practise on old days.
- **How to use:** a candle touching two graded PD arrays at once (an old gap and the upper octant) is a significant reaction point.
- **Timestamps:** [0:03:59](https://youtu.be/BD7kqmgdBU8?t=239) measure highest to lowest · [0:05:43](https://youtu.be/BD7kqmgdBU8?t=343) body location, bullish or bearish · [0:15:32](https://youtu.be/BD7kqmgdBU8?t=932) upper octant touching two PD arrays
- **Nuance / caveats:** octant (1/8) vs quadrant (1/4) wording is his; the exact percentage is not spoken (assumed 12.5% and 25%).

title: Part 2 High Precision Secrets To Intraday Price Action
head: Breakaway gap in the premium half of the ORG
body:
- **Kind:** new coinage / refinement
- **What ICT says:** if a gap forms after leaving a consolidation (one or two candles working inside a range between two PD arrays) and then price displaces lower, and that gap sits above the CE of the opening range gap (premium), you want it to act as a breakaway gap: price should not trade back up into it.
- **How to identify:** consolidation between two PD arrays, displacement away, gap formed above the ORG CE (for shorts).
- **How to use:** a candle laying on the CE with a bearish close and no return into the gap confirms the move; bodies stay below.
- **Example in this video:** gap at the upper quadrant of the ORG forms after a two-candle consolidation between two PD arrays, then displacement lower.
- **Timestamps:** [0:16:20](https://youtu.be/BD7kqmgdBU8?t=980) breakaway gap defined
- **Nuance / caveats:** "breakaway gap" is his label here; not a canonical earlier term in our list.

title: Part 2 High Precision Secrets To Intraday Price Action
head: First utilization of a gap: BISI/SIBI delivery and inversion
body:
- **Kind:** rule / refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - The first utilization of a BISI is buy-side delivery: if price is above it and trades down into it, it should send price higher. The first utilization of an old gap that is a SIBI is sell-side delivery: when bearish, it is a premium PD array to send price lower.
  - If, after the first utilization, price trades through the BISI and the market is now bearish, the BISI acts as an inversion fair value gap (iFVG): "see how the logic is very simple".
  - Price wicking into the gap, leaving no candle bodies in it, and coming back down = bearish.
  - Rule on the PM short: the gap that matters is the one prior to relative equal highs being taken out. After the equal highs are taken, price breaks lower and that gap becomes a bearish iFVG; internet teachers say "go long when it comes back into the fair value gap" but he is interested in it for a different reason (as a bearish iFVG).
  - To measure the iFVG, include the candle that carries the volume imbalance and anchor to the wick low.
- **How to identify:** a gap with a VI; price returns, wicks in, bodies do not close in it.
- **How to use:** short the iFVG after the equal highs are taken, with price closing below the midpoint.
- **Example in this video:** Friday morning: a BISI formed at about 9:01 (caption unclear), first-utilized as buy-side delivery, then price trades below it and it becomes an iFVG; objective tweeted at 28,400. In the PM: BISI prior to the relative equal highs being taken, price rallies out to the highs, bodies stop below the upper quadrant of the ORG, then big displacement lower closing below the midpoint.
- **Timestamps:** [0:17:07](https://youtu.be/BD7kqmgdBU8?t=1027) first utilization = buy-side delivery · [0:17:54](https://youtu.be/BD7kqmgdBU8?t=1074) becomes an iFVG · [0:22:46](https://youtu.be/BD7kqmgdBU8?t=1366) PM gap prior to the equal highs
- **Nuance / caveats:** he claims other "smart money" teachers do not know the "real" fair value gaps; the transferable point is the sequence of context (equal highs taken, then the prior gap inverts).

title: Part 2 High Precision Secrets To Intraday Price Action
head: Immediate rebalance
body:
- **Kind:** definition (as taught here, caption unclear)
- **What ICT says:** after a candle closes, the very next candle can come right back to it and rebalance it immediately. If the following candle did not touch the first candle's low, it would have to be the very immediate next candle for this to count. Here both candles do it, and neither puts a body above the midpoint of the inversion FVG.

head: Fulcrum point (door and hinge)  (aliases: fulcrum, "climax reversal high")
body:
- **Kind:** new coinage / projection
- **What ICT says:** when there is a climax reversal high (the zenith turning point), drag the fib from that high to the low where the rally started. That low is a fulcrum point, like a hinge: imagine the rally is a door; if the door swung round past the hinge, it would swing equally far below it. So the price target below equals the size of the rally, projected from the hinge. On this day that level was close to where the market had a turning point, which "gives a rich tapestry" to anticipate a significant run the other way, or at least a settled day. The low of the day formed around these levels.
- **How to use:** a measured-move/symmetry projection to confirm a reversal objective alongside ORG levels.
- **Example in this video:** Friday: rally off a low to a climax high; fib dragged from high to the hinge low; the projected equal-distance level sat close to where price eventually made the day's low.
- **Timestamps:** [0:26:47](https://youtu.be/BD7kqmgdBU8?t=1607) fulcrum explained

title: Part 2 High Precision Secrets To Intraday Price Action
head: Gap-based shortcut model: short the 9:30 retest with a tiny gap entry  (aliases: "low-hanging fruit", easy objective)
body:
- **Kind:** entry model
- **What ICT says:**
  - Do not try to predict the high or short the exact high. Use the gap: the 9:30 open versus where it settled the previous day at 4:14 pm ET (the last print).
  - If you are more comfortable, look at whether the close created a short-term high in close proximity (e.g. the high of the 4:00 candle). If the 4:00 candle's high is above the 4:14 close it gives a nearer gap-fill target; two reference points (4:00 candle high, 4:14 final print) plus the 9:30 open.
  - Low-hanging fruit: the easiest objective is the nearer, higher level; the next one is the "classic" half gap of the 4:14 gap. Both were hit within the same one-minute candle here.
  - Entry: price trades back into the range, retests the 9:30 opening price, and a small FVG forms there. The entry is inside that FVG. "Efficient entry": there is a small volume imbalance between bodies at the gap's high; the candle's wick high has no VI (its close was lower than the open); you start shorting at the wick as soon as the midpoint of that wick is breached ("above midpoint of this wick", upper quadrant), one contract.
  - The full sell-side-imbalance/buy-side-inefficiency range is measured from the VI high down to the wick high; entry starts at the upper quadrant.
  - Second order: wait to see if price gets between the two wicks; as soon as price gets above 9:30 open, try to nail another around the 9:30 level (may or may not fill).
  - Pyramiding: if it keeps going higher and enters the lower portion of the wick, at the wick low and just above, add more. Some prop firms do not allow adding to a losing position; if so, don't trade this way. ICT says he has never traded in a prop firm.
  - Stop: just above the CE of the wick (above the upper-quadrant entry region). On a high-volatility day that stop is wide; "that's why you should be trading micros."
  - Stop trail: once price leaves the area and takes out the low of that candle's body on a closing basis, tighten stop to the CE of the FVG, then to just above the high, where it stays until the target (half gap) is reached.
- **How to identify:** gap up (9:30 open above prior 4:14 print), market is bearish, price returns to the 9:30 open, small FVG with a wick high, a body-based VI.
- **How to use:** targets in order: half gap, then the 4:00-candle-high level / full gap, then extensions (see scale-out).
- **Example in this video:** Friday: after trading back into the range, retest of the 9:30 open forms a small gap; short at its upper part, price drops into the half gap and the full gap near the same minute.
- **Timestamps:** [0:34:44](https://youtu.be/BD7kqmgdBU8?t=2084) "shortcut version" · [0:37:03](https://youtu.be/BD7kqmgdBU8?t=2223) two reference points · [0:37:50](https://youtu.be/BD7kqmgdBU8?t=2270) the short at the 9:30 retest · [0:39:24](https://youtu.be/BD7kqmgdBU8?t=2364) entry at upper quadrant, stop above wick CE · [0:42:38](https://youtu.be/BD7kqmgdBU8?t=2558) stop trail
- **Nuance / caveats:** this was walked as hypothetical ("I'll toss in a single contract right there"); "may or may not have been filled". The phrase "SIBI/BISI" for the wick range is ICT's; captions garble which is which.

title: Part 2 High Precision Secrets To Intraday Price Action
head: Scale-out ladder for a gap short  (aliases: low-threshold trading, "give yourself the cookie")
body:
- **Kind:** rule / trade management
- **What ICT says:**
  - New traders should trade a low threshold: easy targets, short time in the trade. Holding longer is built by practice, like the gym.
  - Always expect full gap closure, but take something out along the way: partial at the first target; at standard CE of the ORG you are done with 75-80% of the position off.
  - Graduating: wait for full gap closure and close the rest, or take a partial at full gap closure plus a little for spread (example he gives: don't try to catch 28,367 exactly, aim for about 28,370), and leave one runner to see if the gap overlaps and price continues lower.
  - Extension ladder: something off at half gap; the bulk off at full gap closure; then a partial at -0.2 (price could pierce the gap low and rip up); a partial at -0.5; and leave something to reach one standard deviation (-1.0). Beyond that "who cares".
  - Roll the stop to cover costs once the first partials are in; at full gap closure keep three micro contracts for the extensions.
  - These levels are action points: "do something with it", take it off or roll the stop right above and be willing to be stopped. If price then closes back between those levels the stop will likely be hit, and you risk the final partial you could have taken at the level; that cost is part of trading.
- **How to use:** one practical stretch rule: if you are a 100-point trader aiming at 250–500 point runs, take most off at 100 and leave a runner with no concern for what it does. Even if it comes back and you made nothing extra it is progress: you widened your comfort zone.
- **Timestamps:** [0:43:27](https://youtu.be/BD7kqmgdBU8?t=2607) low threshold · [0:45:03](https://youtu.be/BD7kqmgdBU8?t=2703) 75–80% off at CE · [0:47:25](https://youtu.be/BD7kqmgdBU8?t=2845) bulk at full gap closure · [0:48:11](https://youtu.be/BD7kqmgdBU8?t=2891) -0.2, -0.5, -1.0 · [0:49:48](https://youtu.be/BD7kqmgdBU8?t=2988) consequences of holding the last piece
- **Nuance / caveats:** "28,367" vs ORG low "28,324.75": the 28,367 figure is probably the nearer gap-fill level of the shortcut (caption unclear), so do not treat it as the ORG low.

head: Time-based range: the 7:00–9:00 ET pre-session as the "data window" for the day  (aliases: pre-session, "the 2-hour window", "the multiplication table")
body:
- **Kind:** rule / definition (core method)
- **What ICT says:**
  - A time-based range has a specific start and end (like a session or RTH), so it is finite and specific, unlike an arbitrary range. An old high or low that is not inside such a range is not important (that is why he ignored a higher high on this chart).
  - If an algorithm exists it must collect data from a defined range with a beginning and an end. The 9:30 ET RTH open begins a new session, so pay attention to the 2 hours before it: 7:00 to 9:00 ET. He has taught this for decades.
  - You could build a whole career on that 2-hour window and nothing else (no 9:30 open, no PM, no London or Asia); some days the window is advantageous to participate in, other days it tells you the morning will be eventful.
  - The highest high and lowest low in 7:00–9:00 are final once 9:00 passes (he shows a red line at 9:00 to rebut the comments that he "didn't know the low was there yet").
  - Also usable as "key information that warrants more attention to specific price levels when time agrees with it".
  - If you dislike the algorithm idea, treat the range as "where the buying and selling pressure ends and starts". He says "buying and selling pressure is a myth" but it is not necessary to agree.
  - A mid-day window such as 12:45–1:15 pm is poor input: aside from a macro period there is nothing salient about it. Quality of the information source matters more than quantity: two hours of data is enough.
- **How to identify:** shade 7:00 to 9:00 ET; mark its highest high and lowest low.
- **How to use:** anchor a fib to the low and drag to the high (or reverse), then use the levels (below) after 9:00 for projections and PD-array tethering.
- **Example in this video:** Friday July 31, 2026: price drifted lower through the 7–9 session; its high is slightly lower than a prior high, creating relative equal highs; expectation was a run up to buy side and a minor sell-side sweep before the range closes.
- **Timestamps:** [0:02:23](https://youtu.be/DRTvbkKmuAw?t=143) time-based ranges explained · [0:03:10](https://youtu.be/DRTvbkKmuAw?t=190) algorithm collects data from a defined range, 7:00–9:00 · [0:10:18](https://youtu.be/DRTvbkKmuAw?t=618) "you didn't know that low" rebuttal · [0:52:38](https://youtu.be/DRTvbkKmuAw?t=3158) quality of the data window
- **Nuance / caveats:** consistent with earlier "7:00–9:00" focus teaching (also in L26-040); here it is formalised as the source range for fib projections.

He says it is no coincidence that the run starts one minute after the 9:00 close of the time-based range.
  - The rally makes another BISI that is also a suspension block; he wants to see it act as a breakaway gap: rip higher and take out the short-term high, which it does.
  - Volume-imbalance inclusion rule: whenever a gap has a volume imbalance, include the VI candle; the gap is tethered to it. Example: a candle's close at 28,508.50 and the next open at 28,509.00 (two ticks higher) = VI, so include that candle in the gap. "Very simple rule."
  - Price then trades down into that gap, hits it and rallies; he calls this "anticipating, not reacting".

body:
- **Kind:** example only (with rules)
- **What ICT says:**
  - An inefficiency formed by a down-close candle at the midpoint of the 7–9 range was originally sell-side delivery; if price goes above it and closes north of its high, it becomes an inversion FVG and supports price.
  - Example numbers: the open of one candle was 28,530.00 and the low of the other was 28,529.00, so price tapped into the iFVG by one point on a wick, then rallied.
  - Bullish order-flow conditions when price is above a SIBI/iFVG: bodies should stay out of the lower half; price only trades to the upper quadrant of the gap, cannot even touch the CE, and leaves the body outside; another return falls just short of the CE and rallies.
  - When a gap is first utilised as sell-side delivery, a bearish market would use it to go down; here price falls short at the CE and the next candle opens back down into the lower area, showing the failure of the sell-side use and bullish intent.
- **How to use:** hold longs while bodies avoid the lower half of the iFVG; the more shallow the retrace (upper quadrant, short of the CE), the stronger.

He draws the cluster as a box and then plays the one-minute chart: price trades down into those levels, wicks through, rallies, makes smooth highs and returns to the same level.

  - Daily highs and lows form inside a cluster of PD arrays, not a single one: blend them.
- **How to identify:** yesterday's range; a daily wick within three days that price is trading down into; price at/through a pre-called sell-side.

title: Market Review NQ July 31, 2026
head: Pre-Market Dealing Range (7:00–9:00 AM) and Time-Price Grids
body:
- **Kind:** advanced technique + rule + example
- **What ICT says:** The pre-market range (7:00–9:00 AM, 2 hours) establishes the high and low from which all octant and projection levels for the day are derived. By measuring the highest high and lowest low during this window, you create a "time-price grid": divide the range into 8 octants (vertical prices), and use time as the horizontal grid (specific times: 7:00, 7:30, 8:00, 8:30, 9:00, and the specific time the low formed). This grid is "the keys to the kingdom"—price action will repeatedly reference these grids, and you can predict moves based on grid intersections.
- **How to identify:** (1) Mark 7:00 AM high and low, (2) mark the specific minute the low formed (e.g., 8:44), (3) divide the range into 8 octants, (4) note key time markers (8:30 = news time, 8:50–9:10 = macro, etc.).
- **How to use:** Level projection and bias confirmation. If price is trading at a specific octant during a specific time window, it's no coincidence—the grid predicted it. Enter/exit trades based on grid intersections.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 7:00 AM high = X, low at 8:44 = Y. Range = Y to X. Divide into octants. Time marks: 7:00, 8:30, 8:44, 8:50–9:10, 9:00. ICT annotates where price should align (e.g., "upper octant at 8:30 time" = specific price). Price hits these intersections repeatedly throughout the morning.
- **Timestamps:** [0:06:22](https://youtu.be/uws9egBxPLI?t=382) — defining pre-market dealing range; [0:12:01](https://youtu.ye/uws9egBxPLI?t=721) — building the time-price grid; [0:12:49](https://youtu.ye/uws9egBxPLI?t=769) — grid intersections and market behavior
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** This is ICT's proprietary grid methodology; he claims it's unique and not found in Wyckoff, Elliott Wave, or other traders' work. Requires practice to master.

title: Market Review NQ July 31, 2026
head: Octant Qualification of PD Arrays
body:
- **Kind:** rule + example
- **What ICT says:** A PD array (gap, order block, SIBI, BISI, etc.) is only valid/relevant if it sits at a specific octant of the pre-market dealing range. If a gap sits at the lower octant, consequent encroachment, or upper quadrant, that's why it matters. If it sits randomly between octants, it has less significance. The octant anchors the gap to the algorithmic grid, proving the market is following the grid, not random price action.
- **How to identify:** (1) Identify the gap, (2) Measure where it sits relative to the octants you've marked, (3) If it aligns with an octant, it's qualified.
- **How to use:** Entry/exit filter. Only trade gaps that are octant-qualified. Ignore gaps that fall between octants.
- **Example in this video:** "This fair value gap is valid because it's right here on the lowest octant of that dealing range." Later: "This SIBI touches the consequent encroachment level"—both are octant-qualified, so both are traded.

title: Market Review NQ July 31, 2026
head: Volume Imbalance Validity Rules
body:
- **Kind:** rule + refinement
- **What ICT says:** When identifying a SIBI or BISI (sell-side imbalance / buy-side imbalance), the candlestick that creates the volume imbalance must be selected carefully. If there's a volume imbalance at the high (one side has no volume), use that candle to anchor the gap. If there's a volume imbalance at the low, use the other candle. This detail matters because it determines whether the gap is valid for entry/exit.
- **How to identify:** Look at consecutive candles; if one has an unfilled space at its high/low, mark that candle as the anchor.
- **How to use:** Gap validity. Only use the "correct" anchoring candle; using the wrong one invalidates the setup.
- **Example in this video:** ICT shows a BISI and notes: "There's no volume imbalance at the low, so we don't need to worry about picking a different candle. This one here, it is." This precise selection makes the gap tradable.
- **Timestamps:** [0:18:24](https://youtu.ye/uws9egBxPLI?t=1104) — detail on anchor candle selection; [0:19:12](https://youtu.ye/uws9egBxPLI?t=1152) — confirming validity
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** This is a technical detail often overlooked; it's the difference between a tradable and non-tradable gap.

title: Market Review NQ July 31, 2026
head: Measuring Gap (0.5 Fibonacci Projection as Daily Target)
body:
- **Kind:** technique + example
- **What ICT says:** When you have a range (pre-market high to low), measure it with Fibonacci. The 0.5 level is the halfway point. If price exceeds the 0.5 level on the way up (or down), it's likely to continue to the opposite extreme (prior high/low or a new high). The 0.5 acts as a measuring gap: once breached, it signals continuation.
- **How to identify:** Apply Fib from pre-market low to high; mark the 0.5 level.
- **How to use:** Continuation confirmation. If price breaks above 0.5 while rallying, it will likely reach or exceed the prior high. Use this to set daily targets.
- **Example in this video:** Pre-market range 0.5 = 28,723 (even). ICT expects price to eventually reach or exceed this level. He uses it as a target for his short: "if it trades up into that, it's likely to keep going higher" (to the prior weekly high). Once price reaches 28,723, he shorts it.
- **Timestamps:** [0:08:46](https://youtu.ye/uws9egBxPLI?t=526) — measuring 0.5 level; [0:09:35](https://youtu.ye/uws9egBxPLI?t=575) — projecting target; [0:20:00](https://youtu.ye/uws9egBxPLI?t=1200) — confirming price reaches 0.5
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** The 0.5 is not a stop—price may exceed it, but it's a key zone.

title: Market Review NQ July 31, 2026
head: Tossing Micro Contracts for Market Intelligence
body:
- **Kind:** technique + risk management
- **What ICT says:** Before committing a full position, "toss in one contract" (or a micro) to get real-time feedback from price action. This contract is a "direct link to order flow"—it tells you if your grid/level thesis is correct. If price does what you expect, add. If not, the micro loss is tuition. This is different from demo trading; a live (micro) position gives immediate feedback.
- **How to identify:** Identify a key level or grid intersection you expect price to test.
- **How to use:** Confirmation. Throw a micro in; watch what price does. If it respects your level, that's confirmation to add. If it breaks through, it's early warning to reconsider.
- **Example in this video:** At 9:35 AM, ICT tosses one contract short into the high. He's not committed to a full position; he's gathering intel. Price immediately dips into his target level (28,723 on the 1-second chart), confirming the grid is working. Then he scales in more.

- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** This technique requires discipline—don't let the micro turn into a full position out of emotion. Use it only for data.

title: Market Review NQ July 31, 2026
head: Counting Bodies, Not Wicks (Order Flow Truth)
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:** When identifying swing highs/lows or confirming direction, count the bodies of consecutive candlesticks, not the wicks. Bodies represent real order flow; wicks are noise/tests. If you count a series of candles with wicks up but bodies in lower half, that's bearish (bodies tell the truth; wicks lie).
- **Example in this video:** "Count the bodies, not the wicks. Every one of these is a swing high." Shows a sequence of candles; the bodies form the swing pattern, not the wicks.

title: ICT Algorithmic Time & Price Grids
head: Open space between two daily suspension blocks (the "white space" narrative)  (aliases: daily BISI suspension blocks, narrative building)
body:
- **Kind:** rule / bias framework
- **What ICT says:**
  - On the daily chart there are two BISIs, a blue one above and a gray one below; both are suspension blocks, and between them is a region where price has not overlapped (the "space between two inefficiencies").
  - When price is in a space between two inefficiencies that have been traded back and forth (here price went down into the lower gray one at FOMC, then came back up all night), it is "real easy to forecast and predict" the next move. Bias that morning: weekly low in, and draw up to the lowest octant of the upper blue BISI.
  - He says to anticipate, not react to price; everyone else says the market is random and you must react.
- **How to identify:** two daily BISIs with a gap between them; the day's open sits inside that space (here in its lower portion, between the low of the upper blue block and the high of the lower gray block).
- **How to use:** the nearer daily PD array is the draw; the lowest octant of the blue block was the call. Daily levels continue to anchor the 1m PD arrays (see below).
- **Example in this video:** that day's session on the 1m chart: 9:30 open above a short-term high, up a little, then a 1-minute drop into relative equal lows, a sell-side run at about 9:33, then reversal and rally to the upper block.
- **Timestamps:** [0:00:00](https://youtu.be/4SJlJdIANCo?t=0) daily chart and weekly-low view · [0:00:47](https://youtu.be/4SJlJdIANCo?t=47) the two suspension blocks and the space between · [0:04:55](https://youtu.be/4SJlJdIANCo?t=295) two inefficiencies make it easy to predict
- **Nuance / caveats:** this is a bias statement posted before the open; he insists it is not hindsight and shows the "not market replay" candle-close countdown.

title: ICT Algorithmic Time & Price Grids
head: 9:30 open narrative: open above a short-term high, run the relative equal lows, buy the reversal  (aliases: stop hunt, trapping buyers, Power of 3 / Judas)
body:
- **Kind:** entry model (worked example)
- **What ICT says:**
  - Opening price at 9:30 was above a short-term high (above the buy-side liquidity) with relative equal lows below. First the buy side is taken above, then price comes back for the relative equal lows. Traders who bought above to catch continuation have stops just under the equal lows, "where the books tell you it's support"; the market dives, knocks them out, then the real direction begins.
  - After taking sell-side (about 9:33), grade the resulting wick (see next concept): price cannot even come down to that wick's midpoint, which signals bullish order flow, then it trades above the previous candle (retail calls that an "engulfing candle"; he does not care because he identified the turn at the wick earlier).
  - He ties this to the origin of his Power of 3 idea: Larry Williams said he wished he knew how people buying near the low of the day got in; ICT took that as a challenge.
- **How to identify:** open above a short-term high; flush through relative equal lows within minutes; wick at the low with no body below the midpoint.
- **How to use:** buy after the sell-side run when bodies hold the upper half of the reversal wick; target is the pre-stated PD array (here the lowest octant of the daily BISI).
- **Timestamps:** [0:03:15](https://youtu.be/4SJlJdIANCo?t=195) opens above the short-term high · [0:04:07](https://youtu.be/4SJlJdIANCo?t=247) drops to relative equal lows, sell side taken at 9:33 · [0:06:32](https://youtu.be/4SJlJdIANCo?t=392) trapped buyers' stops below equal lows · [0:08:07](https://youtu.be/4SJlJdIANCo?t=487) Larry Williams and Power of 3

title: ICT Algorithmic Time & Price Grids
head: Grading a wick: bodies must hold the upper half when bullish
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - Measure a wick with the fib: the high is the candle's close (body top), the low is the wick's extreme. When price is bullish, the upper half of the wick supports the narrative: price can wick down through the midpoint but the body should not breach it, and preferably price does not even touch the midpoint (that is "indicative of bullishness").
  - For a series of wicks, the longest wick sets the tone for where bodies should not trade below; a later wick that goes below an earlier wick's CE and also pierces its low is "the lowest one".
  - A big prominent wick: measure it as soon as the candle closes, wait for price to come back to half, and if bullish the body must not breach it; a small wick through it is permissible.
  - Wick after a large drop: once price trades below the graded wick, any move back up toward it should turn into a wick, not a body (short setup, see iFVG below).
- **How to identify:** fib from body-close extreme to wick extreme; CE at 50%.
- **How to use:** buy when a candle opens and trades down inside the upper half of the graded wick; stop below the consequent encroachment of that wick.
- **Example in this video:** the 9:33 reversal wick at the relative equal lows; later a big wick at about the 10:10 macro; later afternoon wicks used as buys ("you shall not pass" = bodies do not breach the wick CE).
- **Timestamps:** [0:07:20](https://youtu.be/4SJlJdIANCo?t=440) grading the first wick · [0:08:56](https://youtu.be/4SJlJdIANCo?t=536) upper half supports bullishness · [0:21:48](https://youtu.be/4SJlJdIANCo?t=1308) big wick after the macro · [0:25:46](https://youtu.be/4SJlJdIANCo?t=1546) buy setup in the upper half of the wick · [1:03:08](https://youtu.be/4SJlJdIANCo?t=3788) afternoon wick CE
- **Nuance / caveats:** consistent with L26-040 ("upper half holds = strong"); extra here is the explicit stop rule below the wick CE.

title: ICT Algorithmic Time & Price Grids
head: Order block as "opening price to the body"; mean threshold; anchoring to an octant  (aliases: bullish OB, mean threshold)
body:
- **Kind:** definition / refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - The order block here is the body of the candle: the algorithm is "reaching into" the opening price down to the body. He draws it from the open to the body.
  - A valid bullish order block inside a bullish FVG: bodies do not violate the halfway point (mean threshold) of the OB, and the block is anchored to the lower octant of the FVG.
  - A candle laying on an octant counts as an order block ("laying on an octant", wick high and open as the sweet spot in a later example).
  - The opening price of the move is marked as the change in state of delivery (CISD) level (caption: he says "that's the change in state of delivery"; he does not elaborate).
- **How to identify:** up-close candle sitting on an octant/quadrant level, bodies in the area stay out of the lower half.
- **How to use:** buy retraces into it; during the macro "price drifts into the order block and sends it higher" with multiple attempts to accumulate.
- **Example in this video:** after the 9:41 run into the upper BISI, price trades back to a lower-octant bullish FVG, forms an OB, bodies stay in the upper half; later, retracement into the same OB again.
- **Timestamps:** [0:10:32](https://youtu.be/4SJlJdIANCo?t=632) the body is the order block · [0:19:22](https://youtu.be/4SJlJdIANCo?t=1162) valid bullish OB within a bullish FVG, CISD at the opening price · [1:06:24](https://youtu.be/4SJlJdIANCo?t=3984) OB laying on an octant
