title: ICT Algorithmic Time & Price Grids
head: PD array validity test: it must anchor to an octant or quadrant level  (aliases: "anchored", "tethered")
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - "That's how you know an ICT PD array is valid": the PD array must be anchored to one of the octant or quadrant levels of the range you are grading. Just because something looks like a gap or order block does not make it valid.
  - FVG anchoring detail: candle 1, candle 2 (the inefficiency), candle 3, and the gap is the area between 1 and 3. The gap is valid because candle number 2 touches an octant, or touches a higher low of an inefficiency or whatever range you are measuring and grading.
  - A small volume imbalance BISI in the form of a suspension block is valid because it touches the lower octant.
  - Homework: grade all turns, order blocks, breakers, FVGs and iFVGs this way. Adding market profile, footprint or other overlays dilutes what he teaches ("the algorithm has no respect for all that stuff").
- **How to use:** a daily chart mapped with key PD arrays gives the octants/quadrants; the 1m PD arrays that sit on them are the ones to trade.
- **Timestamps:** [0:16:07](https://youtu.be/4SJlJdIANCo?t=967) homework: grade everything · [0:48:08](https://youtu.be/4SJlJdIANCo?t=2888) candle 2 anchoring rule · [0:48:55](https://youtu.be/4SJlJdIANCo?t=2935) suspension block anchored to the lower octant
- **Nuance / caveats:** parallels the "tethering rule" in L26-042 (PD arrays must touch a graded level of the time-based range). Here the graded range is a daily BISI/suspension block.

title: ICT Algorithmic Time & Price Grids
head: Low resistance liquidity run conditions vs "efficient buy program"  (aliases: LRLR conditions)
body:
- **Kind:** refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - Low resistance liquidity run conditions: when price opens inside open space between two daily inefficiencies it can run quickly with big candles and speed; here it screamed up 10 one-minute candles in a row from 9:41 (about 200 handles in 10 minutes). The narrative (open space) predicts both that it should go up and how it should behave on the way.
  - The overnight move was a different thing: a slow, systematic grind with very short candle ranges building higher and higher ("buy program"), "death by a thousand cuts" for shorts. He labels that efficient price delivery, not an LRLR, and not something to short.
  - The daily suspension block was "controlling" the efficiency of the overnight grind; once the 9:30 open gets outside that control, the run is the LRLR kind.
- **How to identify:** big-bodied candles moving through nothing vs small candle ranges ratcheting.
- **How to use:** do not fade either; use pullbacks into PD arrays inside the run.
- **Timestamps:** [0:14:32](https://youtu.be/4SJlJdIANCo?t=872) low-resistance conditions · [0:15:19](https://youtu.be/4SJlJdIANCo?t=919) buy program overnight · [0:18:31](https://youtu.be/4SJlJdIANCo?t=1111) 9:41 ten-candle run, ~200 handles
- **Nuance / caveats:** the transcripts are slightly inconsistent on which phase he calls "efficient"; the contrast (slow ratchet vs big-candle run) is clear.

title: ICT Algorithmic Time & Price Grids
head: Algorithmic time and price grid  (aliases: "time & price grid", multiplication-table analogy)
body:
- **Kind:** new coinage / entry framework
- **What ICT says:**
  - Horizontal axis of the grid = price levels from grading a range: octants and quadrants of a gap or inefficiency (examples he names: an opening range gap, new week opening gap, new day opening gap, a daily BISI/suspension block). You must know what you are measuring and grading.
  - Vertical axis = time: the start of a macro (e.g., xx:50) and the top of the hour, ending at the macro close (e.g., xx:10). He draws these grid cells (the "multiplication table") and carries them forward to the next macro.
  - Two primary functions: (1) a specific level based on an octant/quadrant; (2) a time window. Every time price gets to an octant or quadrant level, look for a PD array to form; where level meets macro time, turning points are expected.
  - The low of the move formed at the close of the macro; he argues that is not random.
  - He states you can strip any hour down to time and price this way ("I can trade every hour").
  - You still need a bias first: know whether you expect a draw above the high or a retracement to the low (here the low of the daily suspension block), then look for things to time it on the grid.
  - You do not need to trade only inside macro windows; the macro shows when time influences price (a short just ahead of a macro is fine).
- **How to identify:** a graded range, its octant/quadrant lines extended right, plus vertical lines at macro start/end.
- **How to use:** (1) set bias from the daily range, (2) pick the octant/quadrant where you expect the reaction, (3) wait for PD array (FVG, iFVG, OB) on it, (4) trade inside or just before the macro, stops from the array.
- **Example in this video:** 9:50–10:10 macro: lowest candle at 10:10, order block and BISI both anchored to the lowest octant. The "short fractal of the grid": market leaves the macro at 10:10, trades back into the lower-octant BISI and OB. Later the 10:50–11:10 grid: his last candle at 11:10, the macro close, is where the iFVG-led sell-off runs out.
- **Timestamps:** [0:27:25](https://youtu.be/4SJlJdIANCo?t=1645) the 10:50 grid drawn · [0:28:13](https://youtu.be/4SJlJdIANCo?t=1693) horizontal vs vertical axis · [0:29:04](https://youtu.be/4SJlJdIANCo?t=1744) two primary functions · [0:29:57](https://youtu.be/4SJlJdIANCo?t=1797) lowest candle at the macro close · [0:31:31](https://youtu.be/4SJlJdIANCo?t=1891) know your bias, then time it · [0:42:38](https://youtu.be/4SJlJdIANCo?t=2558) 11:10 close of the macro
- **Nuance / caveats:** presented as the unifying framework of earlier macro and PD-array teaching. He quotes the macro windows as 9:50–10:10 and 10:50–11:10; the standard macro-minute pattern (xx:50–xx:10) is implied, no new numbers.

title: ICT Algorithmic Time & Price Grids
head: Inversion FVG: failure of a BISI turns it into a bearish iFVG; short rules  (aliases: first utilization = buy-side delivery)
body:
- **Kind:** entry model
- **What ICT says:**
  - A BISI's first utilization is buy-side delivery; in a bullish market it supports price. If price trades down through it and closes outside it (a breakdown close), that validates it as an inversion FVG: bearish.
  - Once a bearish iFVG: bodies need to stay out of the upper half; wicks into it are fine; if price wicks into it you can short it just ahead of the macro (here ahead of the 10:50 macro).
  - If price cannot trade to the next octant or the midpoint of the whole blue area, expect failure; retail sees a bull flag, ICT sees the failure to reach CE with a macro approaching.
  - Below the iFVG, a second iFVG short: price trades down, closes below it, opens and trades up into it; short. Confidence from grading the wick below: once price is beneath it, rallies need to be wicks not bodies.
  - After an iFVG forms, the target was the low of the daily suspension block; price went "right down to the low".
  - Mirror for a bullish iFVG (afternoon): body stays in the lower half of an iFVG when bullish; wicks can go to and past its high but bodies are not allowed in the upper half. Bodies that violate that mean the story is not intact.
  - Blending: a former bearish FVG that price crosses over becomes an iFVG that changes its first utilization to supportive; combined with a bullish FVG, both anchored to the lower quadrant of the daily blue suspension block, price stops dead and rallies.
- **How to use:** short the retest into the iFVG ahead of the macro; stop above the iFVG/wick (not specified numerically); cover at the daily block's low.
- **Timestamps:** [0:34:45](https://youtu.be/4SJlJdIANCo?t=2085) breakdown close validates the iFVG · [0:35:31](https://youtu.be/4SJlJdIANCo?t=2131) upper half rule, short before the macro · [0:36:20](https://youtu.be/4SJlJdIANCo?t=2180) short at the iFVG after the new macro · [0:40:17](https://youtu.be/4SJlJdIANCo?t=2417) second short, graded wick · [0:55:13](https://youtu.be/4SJlJdIANCo?t=3313) bullish iFVG lower-half rule · [1:00:01](https://youtu.be/4SJlJdIANCo?t=3601) FVG + iFVG blended
- **Nuance / caveats:** the "bodies stay in the half" criterion flips depending on direction; he does not state how many bodies are tolerated.

title: ICT Algorithmic Time & Price Grids
head: Institutional order flow entry drill and "intraday pinball"
body:
- **Kind:** entry model (named by example)
- **What ICT says:** after price rallies off a key level (the low of the daily suspension block), it creates a fair value gap; trading down into that gap is the institutional order flow entry drill. The FVG is valid because it is anchored to the lowest line of the daily block. The afternoon is a repeating "pinball": FVG, then order block, then iFVG, then back, each time touching the same lower-octant/quadrant levels, with bodies holding the upper half.
- **Timestamps:** [0:45:47](https://youtu.be/4SJlJdIANCo?t=2747) · [0:56:00](https://youtu.be/4SJlJdIANCo?t=3360) pinball · [0:58:23](https://youtu.be/4SJlJdIANCo?t=3503) bodies don't breach CE of the BISI = bullish
- **Nuance / caveats:** the name "institutional order flow entry drill" is an earlier ICT term; not redefined here.

title: ICT Algorithmic Time & Price Grids
head: Learning path: one PD array first, then all of them
body:
- **Kind:** rule / process
- **What ICT says:** learn with a single PD array as your entry model, then take time learning the rest; do not take advice from anyone (even someone claiming to be his student) who says to skip the others. At the top tier you know all the public PD arrays and where they sit in price, which gives extra criteria for why price should or should not do something. Backtest and look at hindsight data until you can recognise things; then tape-read live and anticipate "not even taking a trade, not even demo". This conditions you to anticipate rather than react.
- **Timestamps:** [0:12:10](https://youtu.be/4SJlJdIANCo?t=730) backtest, then watch live without trading · [0:46:34](https://youtu.be/4SJlJdIANCo?t=2794) one PD array as the model
- **Nuance / caveats:** matches his advice in L26-019 (observe and journal before risking money).

title: Predicting Session Low & High With Executions
head: Suspension block (daily PD array with volume imbalance at both ends)  (aliases ICT uses: bullish discount array, "lower BISI / sell-side inefficiency" (caption garbled), bullish order block)
body:
- **Kind:** new coinage (caption partly unclear) / example only
- **What ICT says:**
  - A down-close daily candle that has a gap to its left was already used earlier in the week to set up a bullish order block; price opening below / changing state of delivery on the daily chart means it will not simply reach the zone and stop - it digs underneath it a little first.
  - He calls the structure a "suspension block": a volume imbalance at the top end and a volume imbalance at the low end, with its midpoint being the consequent encroachment (CE) of the inefficiency.
  - It is a bullish discount array in a deep discount relative to where price had been higher up.
  - When price trades below the CE, expect "a bounce ... some kind of a pop ... some kind of a reaction" because it is a daily-chart array.
  - Even if price keeps rolling lower, it is "still worthwhile to hunt something" in that vicinity, especially if time of day agrees.
- **How to identify:** daily down-close candle with gap to its left (used as bullish OB), imbalances at both the top and low end of the candle body/range area; shade the full range and mark the midpoint (CE).
- **How to use:** treat the price zone at/below the CE as an area to hunt long entries on the lower timeframe (1m), not to buy blindly on the daily; confluence with time of day (the 9:30 open) is what he wants.
- **Example in this video:** daily NQ(?) chart; the key level mentioned is about 27,665.5 "or less". Price opens the 9:30 session and trades down into the shaded gray range, below the CE, and further below the low of the suspension block.
- **Timestamps:** [0:00:00](https://youtu.be/J9G1j3-e1GU?t=0) — daily chart, OB with gap to the left; [0:00:46](https://youtu.be/J9G1j3-e1GU?t=46) — suspension block defined, CE reaction expected; [0:01:37](https://youtu.be/J9G1j3-e1GU?t=97) — 27,665.5 or lower is worth hunting
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** "Suspension block" is not a term in the canonical list; treat as a new coinage. Captions render the gap type garbled ("lower by side balance sell side inefficiency" = BISI, a bullish gap, I believe). He had flagged before the week started that price would go up (to a high) and then come down to this area.

title: Predicting Session Low & High With Executions
head: Octants / quadrants of the daily array for depth of discount  (aliases ICT uses: octant, lower quadrant, deep discount)
body:
- **Kind:** refinement / example only
- **What ICT says:** He measures the daily suspension block in finer slices than halves: the CE is the 50%, the lower quadrant and a lower octant sit beneath it. Price then trades to "a lower octant than the low of the daily suspension block", i.e. below the whole array. He likes this ("one, two, three"): market probes in steps, "getting people to chase it, go lower."
- **How to use:** the deeper below the CE / the array low that price trades, the deeper the discount for longs; he is hunting the lowest zone, not the first touch.
- **Example in this video:** 1m chart: price touches the CE of the daily array, continues into the lower quadrant, then to a lower octant beneath the array's low.
- **Timestamps:** [0:02:26](https://youtu.be/J9G1j3-e1GU?t=146) — octant and lower quadrant at the daily CE; [0:03:15](https://youtu.be/J9G1j3-e1GU?t=195) — "one, two, three" probing
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Octant levels are only named, no percentages given.

title: Predicting Session Low & High With Executions
head: Market Maker Buy Model (intraday, from the 9:30 open)  (aliases ICT uses: market maker buy model, smart money reversal, first-stage accumulation, second-stage reaccumulation)
body:
- **Kind:** entry model (example)
- **What ICT says:**
  - Right from the gate at 9:30, price makes a tiny move up leaving relative equal highs, then drops. When it drops like that, "what do you think it's forming?" - a Market Maker Buy Model.
  - The drop goes into the daily PD array (CE and below) and leaves a minor buy-side liquidity pool above plus the engineered sell-side liquidity below.
  - Two things then happen: (1) price accumulates all the engineered SSL; (2) a wick is laid down.
  - After the low, he describes the delivery as "smart money reversal, low risk buy, first stage accumulation, second stage reaccumulation" running all the way to the target.
- **How to identify:** 9:30 open -> small up-move with relative equal highs -> sell-off into a daily bullish PD array (below CE, even below the array) leaving SSL -> wick -> reversal.
- **How to use:** the buy is taken at the low around the wick (see next concept); target is a pre-planned RTH-session objective (prior-day 9:30 open here).
- **Example in this video:** 1m, 9:30 open of the video's day: tiny rally holding equal highs, sell-off into the lower octant of the daily suspension block, wick, then rally in stages to yesterday's 9:30 open.
- **Timestamps:** [0:02:26](https://youtu.be/J9G1j3-e1GU?t=146) — "It's a market maker buy model"; [0:04:02](https://youtu.be/J9G1j3-e1GU?t=242) — smart money reversal, accumulation / reaccumulation to the terminus
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** He says seeing price print retail "continuation patterns like a bear flag" on the way down is extra odds for the reversal (see below). He also calls the MMBM something he teaches "as price action" - no time-window or rule given for how long stage one lasts.

title: Predicting Session Low & High With Executions
head: Entry at the midpoint of the wick (and aggressive entry below it)  (aliases ICT uses: "perfect entry", aggressive entry)
body:
- **Kind:** rule / refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - After the low is formed and a wick is laid down, he wants to get in "around that wick."
  - He tried to time the entry as price dipped below the midpoint of that wick: "anything below that or at that level is perfect entry."
  - He also placed an extra aggressive entry below the wick to make sure he had a position in addition to the main one; total position was three contracts, built up there.
- **How to identify:** the wick left by the sell-off into the engineered SSL; draw its midline.
- **How to use:** buy at or below the wick's midpoint; add an aggressive entry lower; only three contracts were on (he intended to build more but was interrupted).
- **Example in this video:** 1m: the entry fill is shown below the wick; ICT notes "it's probably random" that the print landed exactly there, but that was the plan.
- **Timestamps:** [0:03:15](https://youtu.be/J9G1j3-e1GU?t=195) — wants in at the wick; [0:05:35](https://youtu.be/J9G1j3-e1GU?t=335) — midline of the wick = perfect entry; [0:07:16](https://youtu.be/J9G1j3-e1GU?t=436) — executions drawn below the wick, 3 contracts
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Stop-loss location is not stated in this video.

title: Predicting Session Low & High With Executions
head: Retail continuation patterns (bear flag) as a trap that adds odds  (aliases ICT uses: "bubble gum I chew up")
body:
- **Kind:** refinement
- **What ICT says:** when price prints what retail sees as a bear flag (a bearish continuation pattern) in the area where he wants to buy, that "goes further in the odds of probability" for the reversal because it draws in sellers (stops/entries) that smart money feeds on.
- **How to use:** read an obvious retail bearish pattern into an array/liquidity area as confirmation of engineered sell-side liquidity rather than a reason to short.
- **Timestamps:** [0:03:15](https://youtu.be/J9G1j3-e1GU?t=195) — bear-flag comment
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** One-sentence aside only; no quantification.

title: Predicting Session Low & High With Executions
head: Inversion FVG with "Mohawk" wick; bodies must not close outside the gap  (aliases ICT uses: inversion fair value gap, mohawk)
body:
- **Kind:** refinement / new coinage ("mohawk", caption could be unclear)
- **What ICT says:**
  - After the market rallied above a bearish gap and came back down, a wick went through the gap, and this inverted the gap (iFVG used as support).
  - He pre-annotated the chart ("I want to show you without having to talk") with what would happen at that iFVG.
  - A small wick in the iFVG he calls a "mohawk": "look where the bodies are - the bodies can't even lay down outside of this inversion fair value gap. That's bullish."
  - Because bodies hold inside / above the iFVG, he stays with the idea that price goes higher.
- **How to identify:** a bearish FVG that has been traded through to the upside and is then revisited from above; candle bodies stay within or above the gap while only wicks poke the boundary.
- **How to use:** confirmation that the long remains valid and to hold toward the next objective.
- **Example in this video:** 1m: price rallies from the low, trades up through a bearish FVG, comes back down, wicks through it ("mohawk"), bodies stay above; then the next leg higher.
- **Timestamps:** [0:08:04](https://youtu.be/J9G1j3-e1GU?t=484) — iFVG, mohawk, bodies stay inside
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Same body-vs-wick logic as the SIBI/iFVG behaviour taught in other 2026 lectures (e.g. bodies must keep closing the right way).

title: Predicting Session Low & High With Executions
head: Target = prior day's 9:30 RTH opening price; terminus of the RTH session  (aliases ICT uses: terminus for the trade, 9:30 opening price for regular trading hours)
body:
- **Kind:** rule / example
- **What ICT says:**
  - His objective for the regular-trading-hours session was yesterday's 9:30 RTH opening price; he calls it his "terminus."
  - He moved the target on the chart from the prior-day 9:30 price to the next partial; the partials: first partial just under a minor buy-side level (smooth edges in the move), second partial next, final contract at the 9:30 price.
  - The 9:30 price then got hit, and that level ended up being the high of the regular trading hours session.
  - Underlying objectives in the same area: old areas of a prior sell-off over a premium array, bearish fair value gaps (used like bearish order blocks) in the original consolidation; price draws toward the original consolidation and to the level just above it.
- **How to use:** pre-define the session objective from the previous day's RTH open (and nearby bearish FVG/old consolidation) and scale out toward it; partial at each liquidity pool or minor BSL.
- **Example in this video:** NQ(?) 1m: long from the lower-octant wick; first partial at a minor BSL "right underneath my cursor"; second at a minor buy-side above; remaining contracts targeted at yesterday's 9:30 price - he left before the final part and screenshotted that the level got hit and was the RTH high.
- **Timestamps:** [0:07:16](https://youtu.be/J9G1j3-e1GU?t=436) — where he was aiming; [0:08:53](https://youtu.be/J9G1j3-e1GU?t=533) — partials; [0:09:41](https://youtu.be/J9G1j3-e1GU?t=581) — 9:30 price hit = RTH high
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** He frames this as "man buying the low and knowing exactly where the high's going to be," and says he does this on weekly ranges, daily charts, session highs and lows too. Reference to "something a little bit different over here" is left unexplained.

title: Chain Of Custody Of Price With RTH ORG
head: Chain of custody of price  (aliases ICT uses: chain of custody for price, key PD array to key PD array, autonomous delivery)
body:
- **Kind:** new coinage / definition
- **What ICT says:**
  - The question: how does price move from one key PD array to the next, and what makes a PD array key or high probability?
  - The answer must not rely on "archaic mythology" such as retail support/resistance or supply and demand; it should be "so visual and mathematic." Markets are algorithmic: delivery is autonomous, no one is babysitting it; when it suits them they disrupt it briefly and it returns to autonomous delivery.
  - He says you may keep your own religion about buying/selling pressure, but this is what he means by chain of custody.
  - Operationally (as shown): price is handed from one graded level/PD array to the next - the range gap gives the draw, the graded octant/quadrant levels give the anchor points, and PD arrays that sit on those levels carry price from stop to stop.
- **How to identify:** a sequence of PD arrays each connected to a gradient level of the same range, all consistent with the draw on liquidity.
- **How to use:** build the day's path as a chain: a draw (e.g. full RTH gap closure), graded levels inside it, and the FVGs/iFVGs/breakaway gaps that touch those levels.
- **Example in this video:** Monday's RTH ORG (see below): first presented FVG -> iFVG at upper octant -> gap at the CE -> gap on lower quadrant -> imbalance on the gap low (Friday's last print), each a link in the chain.
- **Timestamps:** [0:00:00](https://youtu.be/V5crdCw0AsY?t=0) — the question; [0:00:47](https://youtu.be/V5crdCw0AsY?t=47) — "visual and mathematic", algorithmic autonomous delivery
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** He does not give a formal checklist titled "chain of custody"; the rules below are my compilation of what he demonstrates (the term is first defined here by use). Part of a multi-video thread (he refers to previous videos and an X post from the day before).

title: Chain Of Custody Of Price With RTH ORG
head: Suspension block (bullish BISI with volume imbalance at both ends), and checking FVGs for a volume imbalance  (aliases ICT uses: buy-side imbalance sell-side inefficiency "BISI", suspension block, volume imbalance)
body:
- **Kind:** definition / refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - The daily chart pattern from the previous video: a bullish BISI that is a "suspension block" because there is a volume imbalance at the top end and the low end ("very, very small, but it's there"). He had removed the small dark-purple volume-imbalance shading earlier so the whole block could be seen.
  - Correction: in the previous video he was fatigued and could not see why a level was not "green"; he suspected the fib was anchored wrong and now says to anchor the fib on the higher price of the candle's open (per the captions the candle's open is about 28,020 with body edges near 28,009.25 and 28,007.75; numbers caption-unclear), because that is the price it reaches down for.
  - On the 1-minute RTH chart he tests individual gaps the same way: compare candle open/close values; if the gap's candle edges do not overlap, there is a volume imbalance. One SIBI had none ("not a suspension block"); another had a small one (close 5xx04.5 vs open 5xx04.25, caption-unclear digits) and he calls that the high-probability gap.
- **How to identify:** (1) an FVG/BISI/SIBI; (2) check the open/close relationship of the adjacent candles for a volume imbalance at the top end and at the low end; if both ends have one it is a suspension block.
- **How to use:** a suspension block (or an FVG with volume imbalance) is the higher-probability version of the gap, to be combined with the graded levels below.
- **Example in this video:** daily NQ(?) chart: the blue shaded block is a bullish BISI with octants/quadrants; on the 1m chart a SIBI at ~28,5xx fails the test (no volume imbalance), a later one passes.
- **Timestamps:** [0:01:34](https://youtu.be/V5crdCw0AsY?t=94) — suspension block explained and fib correction; [0:10:26](https://youtu.be/V5crdCw0AsY?t=626) — this SIBI is not a suspension block; [0:11:14](https://youtu.be/V5crdCw0AsY?t=674) — this one has a volume imbalance
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Price digits in the captions are unreliable for this passage. Compare with L26-045 where the same term was introduced.

title: Chain Of Custody Of Price With RTH ORG
head: Grading inefficiencies (octants, quadrants, CE as gradient levels)  (aliases ICT uses: graded out, gradient levels, octant and quadrant levels, grade it)
body:
- **Kind:** rule / refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - "All inefficiencies need to be graded." If you are trading inside a daily or weekly inefficiency it is "very, very important" to consider these levels.
  - Graded set: high, low, octants, quadrants, midpoint (CE).
  - When time and price agree at these levels - and bias plus draw on liquidity agree - then any FVG, order block, breaker, volume imbalance, wick, consequent encroachment, i.e. any ICT PD array forming around those levels carries high probability.
  - He took the gradient levels off the chart in the video to reduce confusion; the details of where "those key PD arrays overlapped with these levels" are in his earlier video.
- **How to identify:** draw a fib/grid over the full inefficiency (e.g. the daily suspension block or the RTH ORG) and mark octants (eighths) and quadrants (quarters) plus the 50%.
- **How to use:** (1) establish bias and draw on liquidity; (2) grade the relevant range; (3) look for PD arrays whose key candle touches graded levels; (4) take those that agree with time of day.
- **Example in this video:** the blue daily block ("octants, quadrants, high and low, BISI/SIBI in the form of a suspension block"), then the RTH ORG graded in the same way.
- **Timestamps:** [0:02:25](https://youtu.be/V5crdCw0AsY?t=145) — graded blue area; [0:03:13](https://youtu.be/V5crdCw0AsY?t=193) — "all inefficiencies need to be graded", PDA + time + bias
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** No exact octant percentages given in this video (octant = eighth, quadrant = quarter; assumed from standard usage).

title: Chain Of Custody Of Price With RTH ORG
head: RTH Opening Range Gap (RTH ORG)  (aliases ICT uses: regular trading hours opening range gap, opening range gap, Monday's RTH opening range gap)
body:
- **Kind:** definition / rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - The RTH ORG for a given day is bounded by two prices: the 9:30 opening price of regular trading hours (the open of the 9:30 candle) and the last print of the prior RTH session (Friday's last print at 4:14 p.m. ET for Monday's gap; the candle's close is used - he dropped the fib on the higher value, the close at 28,291.25 vs open 28,290.75, per captions).
  - "Those are the only two reference points you really need" when looking at regular trading hours; the CME website offers other data, "it's not a big deal."
  - On Monday the high of the gap was the 9:30 opening price and the low was Friday's last print; the blue box's low is "all the way down there."
  - If price gaps up and you are bearish, full gap closure is the draw.
  - Some students argued about using 4:14; he insists the 9:30 open to the final printed RTH price is correct.
- **How to identify:** switch to the RTH (regular hours) chart; mark the 9:30 candle open and the prior session's last print (4:14 p.m. ET candle close); box between them.
- **How to use:** (1) the box edges and midpoint define a dealing range; (2) grade it into octants/quadrants; (3) trade PD arrays that form on those levels in the direction of the draw (full gap closure).
- **Example in this video:** Monday RTH: last print Friday 4:14 p.m. ET about 28,291; Monday 9:30 open higher (about 28,5xx; implied by 9:3x prices near 28,521-28,536). Bearish bias; draw = fill of the entire gap down to Friday's last print.
- **Timestamps:** [0:04:01](https://youtu.be/V5crdCw0AsY?t=241) — RTH ORG introduced for Monday; [0:04:52](https://youtu.be/V5crdCw0AsY?t=292) — only two reference points (9:30 open and last RTH print); [0:06:28](https://youtu.be/V5crdCw0AsY?t=388) — high = 9:30 open, low = Friday 4:14 last print
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** He mentions that the RTH ORG is separate from the daily suspension block (previous video's levels): you can use it alone and don't need to confer with the daily BISI to find the draw. Instrument not named (NQ implied).

title: Chain Of Custody Of Price With RTH ORG
head: Choosing high-probability FVGs inside a graded range: candle two touches the graded level  (aliases ICT uses: first presented fair value gap, candlestick number two, key PD arrays on octant and quadrant levels)
body:
- **Kind:** rule / refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - In a three-candle FVG, "candlestick number two" - the candle that creates the inefficiency - must be connected to an octant/gradient level of a range that is your analysis leading to a draw on liquidity. That is what makes the gap valid.
  - A middle candle touching two levels (here upper quadrant and lower octant) signals significant contraction in the trend direction ("fall out of bed") if bias is bearish.
  - The first presented FVG (here at the 9:3x candles): a BISI with a volume imbalance; using it as a short requires waiting for price to trade down through it and close below (inversion), then selling at that point ("there's your short if you're using the octant").
  - Illustrated with the question-bait "which gaps do you use? These never work when I try them" -> "because you don't know what you're doing": use graded levels only.
- **How to identify:** (1) range with a known draw; (2) graded levels; (3) three-candle gap where the middle candle overlaps at least one graded level, ideally two; (4) volume imbalance present.
- **How to use:** short in a bearish draw once price closes below the BISI (iFVG) or retraces to a SIBI at a graded level; expect strong delivery if two levels are touched.
- **Example in this video:** RTH ORG: BISI at 9:35 / first presented gap; then a SIBI whose middle candle touches the upper quadrant and a lower octant: he expected a quick fall but price retraced more than he thought and needed more participation lower.
- **Timestamps:** [0:07:17](https://youtu.be/V5crdCw0AsY?t=437) — first presented BISI at 9:35; [0:08:50](https://youtu.be/V5crdCw0AsY?t=530) — candle two must connect to a gradient level; [0:11:14](https://youtu.be/V5crdCw0AsY?t=674) — touches two levels -> significant contraction
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Candle times are caption-garbled (9:32 "CB", 9:35). The retracement above his expectation shows touching two levels is a probability tilt, not a guarantee.

title: Chain Of Custody Of Price With RTH ORG
head: Inversion FVG at an octant (reverse the logic of the first utilization)  (aliases ICT uses: iFVG, inversion fair value gap)
body:
- **Kind:** entry model / example
- **What ICT says:**
  - An FVG's first utilization is in the direction of the delivery that created it (a BISI is made by an up-close/buy-side delivery). When bearish, if price trades down below it (closing through), it can become an inversion FVG and be used with reversed logic (as bearish resistance).
  - When annotating he draws it as reversed to remind students that the logic of first use is inverted.
  - Example: the iFVG formed from the 9:3x BISI; price traded right up into the upper octant of the gap and then "falls out of bed".
- **How to use:** short on the retrace into the iFVG at an octant level in a bearish range-gap draw.
- **Example in this video:** RTH ORG: BISI at ~28,536.5-28,536.75 (caption values); price closes below it; retraces up to the upper octant; then drops sharply.
- **Timestamps:** [0:09:37](https://youtu.be/V5crdCw0AsY?t=577) — iFVG logic reversed; [0:10:26](https://youtu.be/V5crdCw0AsY?t=626) — trades to the upper octant and falls
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Consistent with other iFVG notes; the new bit is tying the iFVG to octant levels of the RTH ORG.

title: Chain Of Custody Of Price With RTH ORG
head: Breakaway gap at the CE of the RTH ORG  (aliases ICT uses: breakaway gap, gap at the midpoint, unrealized dealing range)
body:
- **Kind:** definition / example
- **What ICT says:**
  - A gap that forms exactly at the midpoint (CE) of your range-gap analysis, in the direction of the draw (down), signals a likely continuation toward the unrealized end of the dealing range.
  - It is a breakaway gap if price does not trade back into it or overlap and close it; "Would you want to see it traded back into ... No."
  - A second SIBI forms on the lower quadrant, price trades up into it, then breaks lower; another inefficiency lies right on the low of the range gap (Friday's settlement/last print), validating the SIBI.
- **How to identify:** gap formed at the 50% of the RTH ORG during a one-directional run; subsequent candles never trade back to its far boundary.
- **How to use:** if price stays away from the breakaway gap, hold toward the unrealized range end (full gap closure).
- **Example in this video:** RTH ORG Monday: gap touching the CE of the box; price never returns, trades to the lower-quadrant SIBI, then to the gap low where another gap forms; that SIBI goes to its CE and "stops dead in its tracks" with bodies staying below.
- **Timestamps:** [0:12:01](https://youtu.be/V5crdCw0AsY?t=721) — gap at CE = breakaway gap; [0:12:48](https://youtu.be/V5crdCw0AsY?t=768) — lower-quadrant gap, lower gap on Friday's last print; [0:13:35](https://youtu.be/V5crdCw0AsY?t=815) — SIBI to CE, bodies stay below
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** "Settlement price for previous Friday at 4:14 pm ET" is how he words the low of the RTH ORG here.

title: Chain Of Custody Of Price With RTH ORG
head: Layering the daily bias and daily inefficiency with the RTH ORG  (aliases ICT uses: "ring in" the daily levels, what takes precedence)
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - Answer to "what takes precedence": the RTH ORG framework alone is sufficient when the draw is full gap closure; you "don't need to confer with the daily BISI/suspension block."
  - When price starts doing things beyond the scope of the opening range gap, then bring in the daily bias levels and the daily balance-outside-of-efficiency (blue block) from earlier videos.
  - "The more things that agree on one side of the market, the less likely it is to go the other direction" - that is how he defines high probability.
- **Timestamps:** [0:04:01](https://youtu.be/V5crdCw0AsY?t=241) — precedence question; [0:13:35](https://youtu.be/V5crdCw0AsY?t=815) — ring in the daily levels; high probability = more agreement
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Re-affirms confluence, but with a clear hierarchy: RTH ORG first, daily second when price leaves the ORG's scope.

title: Chain Of Custody Of Price With Daily Inefficiencies
head: Daily inefficiency (May 5, 2026 BISI) graded into octants/quadrants as the chain of custody  (aliases ICT uses: gradient levels, octant and quadrant levels, daily buy-side imbalance sell-side inefficiency, suspension block, volume imbalance upper/lower)
body:
- **Kind:** rule / example
- **What ICT says:**
  - The daily chart's bullish BISI from May 5, 2026 has a small volume imbalance at its upper end and one at its lower end (the two ends of the suspension block). The upper one is where price drove up to at the start of the session; the lower one is where price traded to on Friday (CE of that block was traded to on Friday, then price opened Monday and traded up into the upper volume imbalance).
  - He had told a student (on the Sunday X Space, "trader roundup") that "price would likely draw up into that volume imbalance and then sell off", without giving full analysis for the week.
  - The gradient levels are anchored to the daily timeframe: measure from the high of the May 5th inefficiency (top of the upper volume imbalance) to its low (the low = a candle open/close near 28,000.25 per captions) and project; levels: high of the volume imbalance, upper octant, upper quadrant, next octant, CE, octant below CE, lower quadrant, lower octant, low of the May 5th inefficiency.
  - The upper volume-imbalance also coincides with Friday's new day opening gap (NDOG), a confluence.
  - He had a fib mis-anchoring problem on screen (it showed 28,000.75 which shouldn't have been shown) and says "good enough for government work."
- **How to identify:** daily BISI/suspension block with volume imbalances at top and bottom; fib anchored high to low; mark octants, quadrants, CE; overlay NDOG/NWOG if they coincide.
- **How to use:** (1) trade the daily levels down to the 1-minute chart and look for SIBIs/FVGs whose bodies lie on graded levels; (2) take partials at the graded levels; (3) treat the levels like SSL.
- **Example in this video:** Monday (day of the review), NQ(?) 1m: overnight price hits Friday's NDOG; at the open price trades up into the upper volume imbalance of the May 5, 2026 daily BISI; ICT shorts there; price then breaks down through upper octant, upper quadrant, lower octant just above the CE, CE, octant below CE, lower quadrant and finally the daily block's low, with intermittent bounces.
- **Timestamps:** [0:00:50](https://youtu.be/XKjdVwBUs2E?t=50) — price to draw up into the volume imbalance then sell off; [0:01:39](https://youtu.be/XKjdVwBUs2E?t=99) — daily anchor, agreement with Friday NDOG; [0:07:29](https://youtu.be/XKjdVwBUs2E?t=449) — fib from May 5 high to low projected forward, the level list
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Price digits in the captions are unreliable. This is the same daily block as in L26-045/047 ("suspension block").

title: Chain Of Custody Of Price With Daily Inefficiencies
head: Short entries on SIBI/FVG whose body sits on an octant level; bodies staying outside the upper half  (aliases ICT uses: cibby/sibby = SIBI, "keeping the body outside", fair value gap in the upper quadrant)
body:
- **Kind:** entry model / refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - He found an FVG at the upper quadrant of the May 5 BISI: price traded up into it, then broke lower.
  - The next SIBI formed with its body laying right on the lower octant just above the CE; price traded up to it again, giving a "really nice shorting opportunity."
  - The key tell: bodies stay outside the upper half of that SIBI; all bodies stay outside; "that's an indication it's likely to go down a lot." Then price breaks aggressively lower.
  - He wanted to get short with a limit order near the open, was afraid it wouldn't fill, so entered anyway to manage around it; he got stopped out ("as you saw me get stopped out in the black"), re-entered at the upper volume imbalance high, took a partial, got stopped again on the rally and shorted again.
  - He expected the upper volume imbalance to get "really really heavy" (a clean sell-off) but price returned to trade in it more than once.
- **How to identify:** a SIBI (bearish gap) whose body is on a graded level; later candles rally into it but do not close in its upper half.
- **How to use:** short on the retrace into the SIBI at the octant level; stop above the array; expect a sharp decline if bodies stay outside the upper half.
- **Example in this video:** 1m, morning: FVG in the upper quadrant of the daily block - price trades up into it then breaks lower; SIBI at the octant above the CE - price trades up, bodies stay below its midpoint, breaks lower; price continues down to the octant below the CE.
- **Timestamps:** [0:08:18](https://youtu.be/XKjdVwBUs2E?t=498) — limit order, stop-outs, re-entries; [0:09:56](https://youtu.be/XKjdVwBUs2E?t=596) — FVG in upper quadrant; [0:10:45](https://youtu.be/XKjdVwBUs2E?t=645) — SIBI body on the octant, bodies outside the upper half
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Shows his stop-outs honestly; he also remarks that the market ran up and hit the stop right after he displayed his short and stop on the stream ("I knew they'd run up and hit it").

title: Chain Of Custody Of Price With Daily Inefficiencies
head: Partial profits at gradient levels ("run down equity")  (aliases ICT uses: chasing new equity, trim, partials near gradient levels)
body:
- **Kind:** rule (trade management)
- **What ICT says:**
  - As price approaches the lower graded levels he teaches students to "run down equity": take partials at each key level, "chasing new equity" each time the market gives an opportunity; the key levels being lowest octant, lowest quadrant, octant below the CE, and the CE.
  - Treat each graded level just like sell-side liquidity: once price gets to it or below it, take a partial, or take it as price gets close.
  - It is fine to peel off something and let the low be traded below and then taken out, closing the remainder.
  - He notes entries/partials in this session were all close to gradient levels.
  - Heavy morning: it could easily come back and trade against him, so trimming is wise.
  - "You're never going to get all of it ... be content with just being good enough."
- **How to use:** scale out at graded levels, take the last portion on a sweep of the low, don't wait for the full range.
- **Example in this video:** short from the upper imbalance; partials near the octant below the CE, the CE, the lower octant and the block's low; stop on the remaining position hit once; new entries marked in the lower half; final fill near the low, price goes a bit lower afterwards.
- **Timestamps:** [0:11:34](https://youtu.be/XKjdVwBUs2E?t=694) — run down equity; [0:12:22](https://youtu.be/XKjdVwBUs2E?t=742) — partials near gradient levels; [0:13:13](https://youtu.be/XKjdVwBUs2E?t=793) — be content, never get all of it
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** "Run down equity" is his phrase (captions render it as "run down equity"); keeps the idea of banking at levels ahead of the target.

title: ICT Chain Of Custody Of Price
head: Chain of custody of price  (aliases ICT uses: chain of custody and control of price, one PD array to the next, algorithm "source code")
body:
- **Kind:** new coinage / definition (framing concept for the whole lecture)
- **What ICT says:**
  - We study "the chain of custody from one PD array to the next," not buying/selling pressure, not how many orders or volume increases/decreases at a price. "None of that means anything."
  - It is the same mechanism inside any defined dealing range, whether already delivered or not yet delivered.
  - It is "my algorithm doing exactly how it's coded to do. Every little fluctuation has a purpose." If markets were not algorithmic, these things would not keep repeating.
  - It tells you "how one PD array, one specific candlestick, and how it's formed at what time and price" makes price not move higher ("you shall not pass") or go past.
  - Differences from retail S/R: grading a specific inefficiency "removes all the ambiguity of which high, which low would I use"; 50 traders drawing trend lines in a room will not agree; his rectangles look similar but "the logic is unique to me only."
  - He claims no one else teaches the specific logic: bodies not allowed in the upper half of a bearish PD array, CE/octant validation, unrealized/implied dealing range anchoring.
- **How to identify:** a sequence of dated PD arrays (daily wick CE, daily SIBI, volume imbalance, RTH ORG CE levels, first presented FVG) with each next level predicted before price gets there.
- **How to use:** (1) establish bias/draw on liquidity; (2) pre-draw the levels you will watch (written on a notepad / annotated before the move); (3) validate each PD array by graded-level contact and body behavior; (4) trade from the validated array toward the next level.
- **Example in this video:** The week's chain: premium array (last Thursday's daily SIBI, pink) -> up into it -> sell off to the higher volume imbalance of the daily suspension block (purple, the draw) -> next: CE of the suspension block. Intraday Thursday chain: SIBI high -> octants -> measuring gap at 50% -> iFVG -> 28,701.
- **Timestamps:** [0:55:11](https://youtu.be/dYQSUCSbYn8?t=3311) — studying chain of custody, not buying/selling pressure; [0:57:32](https://youtu.be/dYQSUCSbYn8?t=3452) — "no, you shall not pass" explanation; [0:37:44](https://youtu.be/dYQSUCSbYn8?t=2264) — "chain of custody and control of price"
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Builds on L26-047/048; he says this is advanced and requires awareness of his PD arrays. He plans more videos because it is "a very dense subject."

title: ICT Chain Of Custody Of Price
head: Daily wick CE ("discount wick") and body-through rule  (aliases ICT uses: lowest stretched-out wick, consequent encroachment of a wick, discount wick, premium sensitivity)
body:
- **Kind:** rule / refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - On the daily chart there are two discount wicks (a higher and a lower one), the lowest stretched candlestick wick in the move. Price must trade down below the wick's midpoint (CE) and close below to confirm; trading through the CE on its own "may or may not go lower"; he wants a body through relative equal lows, not just a wick ("insignificant ... with just the wick").
  - Friday's delivery gave a pronounced body run below the relative equal lows.
  - For a bearish stance: the premium (upper) half of a wick is the "premium sensitivity" side - bodies should stay heavy in the lower half; if price goes into the upper half it must show strong rejection.
  - He had called "we're going lower" on Wednesday night's and Thursday's commentary.
  - Rule of halves: if bullish, a revisited inefficiency/wick holds the upper half (price trades down to at least half); if bearish, price goes down to at least half and lower.
- **How to identify:** locate the lowest, most stretched wick on the daily chart; mark its midpoint; note the later candle that closes below it with a body.
- **How to use:** once price closes below the wick CE with a body, expect further lower prices toward the next PD array below (volume imbalance, suspension block CE); re-test of the CE from below should fail.
- **Example in this video:** NQ daily: price trades down through the CE of the daily wick and closes below on Friday; next the market opens, trades up into a daily fair value gap and trades lower; then trades into the higher discount-wick CE; target then the daily volume imbalance.
- **Timestamps:** [0:04:19](https://youtu.be/dYQSUCSbYn8?t=259) — wick CE, close below; [0:05:53](https://youtu.be/dYQSUCSbYn8?t=353) — wick-only run insufficient, want bodies; [0:07:30](https://youtu.be/dYQSUCSbYn8?t=450) — premium sensitivity of wick upper half
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Which two wicks he picks: "the lowest stretched out candlestick wick in all of this price action" - others are not used because they do not touch the same graded line (see "first utilization" below).

title: ICT Chain Of Custody Of Price
head: Suspension block, volume imbalance as draw, premium array down to discount array  (aliases ICT uses: SIBI/BISI suspension block, higher volume imbalance, purple box, pink box)
body:
- **Kind:** refinement / example
- **What ICT says:**
  - The daily buy-side imbalance sell-side inefficiency (BISI) that is a "suspension block" has a volume imbalance on its high end and one on its low end; the purple volume imbalance was the draw on liquidity last week and this week; the pink box on the lower-timeframe charts is last Thursday's daily SIBI (a premium array).
  - "Think of it like this: premium array down to discount array." If price goes below the volume imbalance, it gravitates to the CE (halfway) of the suspension block; the CE is the next target.
  - Deep discount: below last Friday's low and below the relative equal lows with bodies.
- **How to use:** draw on liquidity = the next array down; target the CE of the suspension block if the volume imbalance is breached.
- **Example in this video:** NQ Thursday: price rallies up into the pink daily SIBI (premium) and the premium side is rejected; it sells to the purple volume imbalance (~28,891.25 minor buy-side noted there), turns there at least twice; later closes into the next imbalance region; ICT notes it did not take the whole suspension block in one candle.
- **Timestamps:** [0:08:18](https://youtu.be/dYQSUCSbYn8?t=498) — volume imbalance as DOL, suspension block above; [0:09:06](https://youtu.be/dYQSUCSbYn8?t=546) — premium to discount; [0:09:53](https://youtu.be/dYQSUCSbYn8?t=593) — suspension block with volume imbalances high and low
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Critics say FVGs are just single prints or low-volume nodes; he asks why price turned right at the first level and did not fall through all of the inefficiency: "No, it's algorithmic" ([0:21:00](https://youtu.be/dYQSUCSbYn8?t=1260)).

title: ICT Chain Of Custody Of Price
head: Daily collection of RTH ORG CE and first presented FVG across the week  (aliases ICT uses: first instance fair value gap, collecting consequent encroachment levels, extend to the right)
body:
- **Kind:** rule (process) / example
- **What ICT says:**
  - "This is what you're supposed to be doing each day": collect data. When there is a large RTH opening range gap, annotate it and extend its midpoint (CE) forward. The gap runs from 9:30 ET opening price to the prior day's settlement/last print; extend each day's CE into the following days.
  - Monday's first presented fair value gap is "crucial information": carry it through the whole week (set the box to extend right); price uses it later in the week; "coloring outside the lines is okay."
  - Also carry the CE of the two daily discount wicks and the graded levels of last Thursday's daily SIBI onto the 1-minute chart.
  - He shows each day's RTH ORG: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday (measured close to open, CE), Thursday, Friday; price repeatedly reacts at these CEs; once price trades through one, that CE acts as a premium array.
  - Advice: print the slides to avoid rewinding; as he reveals more data each day, add it.
  - Convergence: on Thursday the CE levels of Monday, Tuesday and Thursday sat in close proximity, giving a cluster; the highest and lowest of the cluster define a range; above the cluster the market is more likely to sell off, below it to rally. With a bearish bias, anything above Thursday/Tuesday/Monday first-instance FVG and the upper half of the higher discount wick is "a premium market."
- **How to identify:** RTH ORG per day = 9:30 open vs prior settlement; use the CE; first FVG after 9:30 on Monday.
- **How to use:** build a map of CEs; when several cluster, treat as one decision zone; with a bearish bias, sell rallies into the cluster/premium.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 1m, Monday-Thursday: price works around Monday's RTH ORG CE, drops from Monday's first presented FVG to the lower discount-wick CE, retests, rallies to the pink SIBI, etc.; Thursday gaps open lower with CE overlap Monday/Tuesday/Thursday.
- **Timestamps:** [0:09:53](https://youtu.be/dYQSUCSbYn8?t=593) — collecting data, RTH ORG CE; [0:11:29](https://youtu.be/dYQSUCSbYn8?t=689) — Monday's first presented FVG carried all week; [0:17:47](https://youtu.be/dYQSUCSbYn8?t=1067) — Monday/Tuesday/Thursday CEs converge; [0:18:37](https://youtu.be/dYQSUCSbYn8?t=1117) — range from highest to lowest CE, above = sell, below = rally
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Relates to NWOG/NDOG thinking, but the new emphasis is the RTH ORG CE as the daily-collected reference level.

title: ICT Chain Of Custody Of Price
head: Grading a daily SIBI (CE, octants, quadrants) as "real natural support and resistance"  (aliases ICT uses: grade, gradient levels, upper quadrant, lowest octant)
body:

Price on the 1-minute chart uses each of these in turn (e.g. price sits between 29,330 and 29,310 in the premium of the SIBI (caption digits), then displaces lower in the PM session and trades just outside the SIBI's low). Grading "removes the doubt" about which levels to use for support/resistance.

title: ICT Chain Of Custody Of Price
head: Implied (unrealized) dealing range anchored on the body-high, not the wick  (aliases ICT uses: unrealized dealing range, implied dealing range, inception of the price run, finite level)
body:
- **Kind:** rule / refinement (the key lesson)
- **What ICT says:**
  - Thursday's range: anchor at the high of a SIBI candle (the body high of the down-close candle) and measure down to Monday's relative equal lows (= Tuesday's electronic-trading-hours sell-side liquidity) at 28,701. The draw is that finite level.
  - Why not the wick high: "the wick is a gap that's allowed to do the damage"; "the bodies tell you the real narrative"; anchoring to the candle body high defines "a range that has yet to be delivered."
  - If you do this anchoring wrong, "everything I'm about to outline will not work for you" - he predicts viewers will anchor to wrong points over the weekend and say it doesn't work.
  - When ranges are unrealized you are only looking at a target/draw; knowing where the price run begins ("the inception of the price run") must be learned from backtesting and collecting information.
  - Known from the moment the SIBI-forming candles close and the next opens: the draw is Monday's relative equal lows and the anchor is the SIBI candle's high.
  - Then "you have to go to a very specific PD array where it makes sense on a higher time frame": the CE of the daily wick (pink line).
- **How to identify:** (1) find a SIBI/down-close candle at the start of the run from a premium PD array; (2) anchor on its body high; (3) anchor the other end at the finite old low/high (relative equal lows) that is the draw; (4) grade the range into octants/quadrants/CE.
- **How to use:** short only from PD arrays that touch the graded levels of this range; targets: the draw (28,701), partials at graded levels; expect no retracement beyond the 50% once below it.
- **Example in this video:** NQ Thursday: premium wick at the CE of the daily wick; SIBI body anchored from its high down to 28,701 (the Monday relative equal lows); gradient levels listed: high, then next lines down to the draw. The SIBI laid on the upper octant; the SIBI's lower boundary (high of the third candle) was 28,941 even "to the tick."
- **Timestamps:** [0:27:18](https://youtu.be/dYQSUCSbYn8?t=1638) — anchor the body high not wick; [0:28:08](https://youtu.be/dYQSUCSbYn8?t=1688) — implied dealing range, inception from backtesting; [0:31:18](https://youtu.be/dYQSUCSbYn8?t=1878) — no projection off a wick; most important part; [0:34:29](https://youtu.be/dYQSUCSbYn8?t=2069) — SIBI on upper octant, you know the draw
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Contradicts anchoring from wick extremes (e.g. earlier events that used full wick range); here bodies define volume of the move.

title: ICT Chain Of Custody Of Price
head: "No bodies in the upper half" rule (premium sensitivity) for bearish PD arrays; wick that fails to reach CE is bearish  (aliases ICT uses: premium sensitivity, body in the upper half, keeps the body outside)
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - If bearish and price trades back up into a SIBI/bearish order block/fair value gap, it must not leave a body in the upper half of that PD array. Bodies stay below/outside: "bodes well for holding."
  - If the wick cannot even touch the CE of an inefficiency, "that's bearish... it can't even deliver a midpoint."
  - The same logic applies on every PD array in the sequence, and he says it applies to wicks (candle with a wick sitting on a gradient level: bodies not allowed in its upper half, from close to midpoint).
  - "I deny it going above" - the wick is respected: he asks why a given wick is used and not another: because it touches a graded level; the first wick utilizing that level counts; later wicks that do not touch the line are only "candles with wicks."
  - Premium/discount lens: when bearish and in a premium array, any market structure shift lower after being in premium should see lower prices delivered.
- **How to identify:** SIBI/bearish OB/FVG sitting on an octant/quadrant; check subsequent candles' bodies relative to the upper half or the gap's CE.
- **How to use:** sell the retrace into such an array (or add/pyramid) while bodies remain out of the upper half; failing to reach the CE is bearish confirmation; patience ("submit yourself to time"); if nervous take one partial off.
- **Example in this video:** Thursday: the first SIBI on the upper octant; the following candle opens, trades up and falls short without touching the OB; price breaks lower; a wick laying on Monday's RTH ORG CE holds with no bodies in its upper half; a later SIBI at the .375 level has a wick that cannot touch its CE.

  - Price breaks lower after trading up into the bearish OB.
- **How to identify:** up-close candle whose range touches the upper quadrant of the implied dealing range; next candle trades down through its open.
- **How to use:** short on retraces into the OB, add on further retraces; hold toward the draw.

head: Premium Array Failure as Bearish Signal
body:

It shows the market has no interest in supporting the bullish bias. A premium array that can't even be traded to is a red flag to flip to short.
- **How to identify:** (1) Identify a bullish gap or up-close PDA, (2) Watch if price tests it, (3) If price breaks away before touching the midpoint, that's failure, (4) If it never even comes back to touch it again, that's extreme failure.
- **How to use:** Reversal entry. When a premium array fails this way, it's a high-probability short setup.
- **Example in this video:** A bullish fair value gap is visible on the chart. ICT expects it to be traded to on any bounce (bullish expectation). Price barely probes the top of the gap but never trades into the midpoint. Instead, it rolls over and breaks below. This failure signals that the bullish scenario is dead; flip to short.

head: Breaker Block (Specific Candlestick Pattern)
body:
- **Kind:** definition + refinement
- **What ICT says:** A breaker block is formed by three consecutive candlesticks: (1) a high, (2) a lower low, (3) a higher high than (1), but (3) closes as a down-close with the lowest close of the three. The breaker block is formed by this bottom candlestick. When used correctly (anchored to the lowest close), it represents rejection of the bullish phase. It can be misidentified if you use two consecutive candles instead of all three + the correct anchor.
- **How to identify:** (1) Find a swing high, (2) followed by a lower low, (3) followed by a recovery high, (4) note the candle with the "lowest close" among the pattern, (5) use that candle's low as the breaker anchor.
- **How to use:** Stop-loss placement or resistance. If shorting from above a breaker block, the block's high is initial resistance; if price closes below the block's true low (the lowest-close candle's low), that's strong bearish confirmation.
- **Example in this video:** Pattern: high (candlestick 1) → lower low (candlestick 2) → higher high (candlestick 3, but closes down). The breaker is identified by the lowest close. If you use the wrong candles, you'll misidentify the breaker level, which is why ICT emphasizes the correct selection.
- **Timestamps:** [0:11:18](https://youtu.ye/2H_qpeIp2rY?t=678) — identifying the breaker block pattern; [0:12:06](https://youtu.ye/2H_qpeIp2rY?t=726) — explaining correct vs. incorrect interpretation
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Breaker blocks require precise candlestick selection; getting it wrong ruins the level.

A gap's first utilization tells you its original intended function. If the market is bearish, you apply the inversion aspect, not the first utilization.

head: High Resistance Liquidity Run Conditions (HRLRC)
body:
- **Kind:** observation + market condition
- **What ICT says:** When the market opens significantly higher (large premium gap) and price is trapped between multiple buy-side liquidity pools (relative equal highs above), it's in a "high resistance liquidity run condition." In this condition, upside continuation is difficult; sellers are defending at multiple levels. Shorts are less attractive because there's little room to run downward. When price gets stuck oscillating between the opening price and these buy-side pools, it's best to step aside and wait for clarity.
- **How to identify:** (1) Large premium gap at open, (2) Multiple relative equal highs above current price, (3) Price oscillating up/down without breaking cleanly in either direction, (4) Bodies struggling to move in any direction (whippy candles).
- **How to use:** Risk management. Recognize the condition and avoid trading it. Profits will be small if you catch any move; risk is high because price will whipsaw. Best to wait for the condition to resolve.
- **Example in this video:** NQ opens ~450 handles premium. Multiple REH zones above. All day, price bounces between the opening price and these REH zones without committing. Trading in this condition yields small profits and frequent stops.
- **Timestamps:** [0:00:00](https://youtu.be/e6XwTK4hVqI?t=0) — noting large premium gap; [0:07:11](https://youtu.ye/e6XwTK4hVqI?t=431) — difficulty navigating; [0:11:57](https://youtu.ye/e6XwTK4hVqI?t=717) — "very difficult time to do anything of significance"
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** HRLRC is not a reversal signal; it's a "wait and see" condition. Many traders force trades here and lose money.

head: Participation Discipline: When NOT to Trade
body:
- **Kind:** rule + philosophy
- **What ICT says:** In choppy, HRLRC conditions with small ranges and multiple false breakouts, it's better to NOT participate. Close the charts, step away, let the condition resolve. The few handles you might capture aren't worth the stress and whipsaws. This is a key risk-management principle: knowing when to sit out is as important as knowing when to enter.
- **Example in this video:** ICT trades in and out multiple times, each with small profits or stops. By mid-day, he decides to close the charts and spend time with family. He explicitly says this type of choppy action isn't worth participating in.
- **Timestamps:** [0:11:57](https://youtu.ye/e6XwTK4hVqI?t=717) — "Leave it alone"; [0:12:43](https://youtu.ye/e6XwTK4hVqI?t=763) — "Wait-and-see"
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** This is advice many traders ignore. FOMO drives them to trade choppy conditions and lose money.

head: High Resistance Liquidity Run Conditions
body:
- **Kind:** definition · rule
- **What ICT says:** A market state where price shares a large amount of price action in a relatively few number of candles—compressed, violent back-and-forth movement where bodies keep returning to the same range, rejecting breaks lower (or higher), then suddenly accelerating once it escapes. Opposed to low resistance runs where price stretches out taffy-like with one or two candles covering large ranges. These conditions are intentionally engineered; they punish traders already in positions and wipe out those trying to enter. "They're coming for everybody. They'll move the price lower because everybody knows the gap is likely to get filled. Everyone that's trying to go short, they're ripping back against them." Occurs when markets want to stop out multiple traders before delivering to an obvious level.
- **How to identify:** (1) Visual: many candlesticks sharing the same price range; bodies repeatedly rejecting at the same level; wicks extending beyond bodies but bodies staying in a narrow band. (2) Behavioral: price goes down, comes right back up, goes down again, repeats. (3) Context: opening range gap present; obvious daily/4H/1H draw on liquidity below; economic calendar or session-specific timing.
- **How to use:** Do NOT participate with live funds. Instead: tape read it, paper trade it, or demo trade it. When not in these conditions, price is obvious and fast—that's when to engage. Sit aside when you identify them. If already in a trade, keep size very small (ICT reduced from standard 6-4-10 contracts to 3 contracts), use tight stops, be prepared to exit quickly, and manage psychology impeccably. Multiple exits in tiers; take partial profits at obvious levels; don't try to capture the full move.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 1-minute, July 21, 9:30–11:00 ET RTH. Price opens with a huge premium gap (up), goes down to take out relative equal lows from 0:02:02 area. Then: 9:30 area, price runs up to 60-minute buy-side balance sell sign efficiency around 0:02:55, ICT shorts 1 contract. Gets stopped out around 0:08:45, immediately re-enters. Gets stopped out again around 0:23:40. Enters again, takes partials at intermediate levels (relative equal lows) around 0:33:18 and 0:49:02. The entire 0:22:06–0:51:25 span is high resistance: bodies keep rejecting below the relative equal lows, wicks extend lower but bodies stay upper-half of ranges. Only at 0:48:14 onwards does price finally break below and accelerate down.
- **Timestamps:** 
  - [0:22:06](https://youtu.be/tp0qkiWCctw?t=1326) — First identification: "lots of price action shared in a few number of candlesticks. That is high resistance liquidity run conditions. Very very manipulated."
  - [0:26:05](https://youtu.be/tp0qkiWCctw?t=1565) — Why traders fail: "The average new trader doesn't have the capacity to manage throughout all these wild retracements. They end up closing it or bringing their stop loss lower too fast."
  - [0:28:30](https://youtu.be/tp0qkiWCctw?t=1710) — Body placement tells the narrative: "They're keeping bodies right at and above that low. If they can bury bodies below that low you're looking for to break through, that's confirmation. A retracement or reversal is signified by something like [keeping bodies above]."
  - [0:50:36](https://youtu.be/tp0qkiWCctw?t=3036) — Teaching refusal: "Don't try to trade in it with live funds. Tape read it, paper trade it, demo trade it. When it's not doing these things and moving in low resistance condition, that's when you want to engage because it's obvious."
- **Nuance / caveats:** ICT emphasizes these are *teaching/training days*, not money days. The lesson is: high resistance ≠ rejection of the original thesis; it's a sign the move *will* happen but traders will be punished first. Conviction + impeccable risk management can allow you to stay in (as ICT does), but most students cannot handle the psychology. The danger: inexperienced traders either close too early (missing the move) or average down (increasing losses). The protection: obvious daily/4H liquidity targets (gap midpoint, relative equal lows) + only trade when those are present + always use stops.

head: Opening Range Gap & Gap Midpoint (Half-Gap)
body:
- **Kind:** rule · entry model
- **What ICT says:** At market open (9:30 ET for NQ), price often gaps up or down. This gap is the area between the previous close and the new opening candle's low (if gapped up) or high (if gapped down). The midpoint of this gap is a powerful magnet; price often retraces into it as a secondary objective after the first target (relative equal lows or structural lows). "Find the mid-gap. There's your target. Aim for that. You might miss it, but it gives you a simple framework to start with."
- **How to identify:** On the 1-minute open candle (9:30), mark the high (if gap up) or low (if gap down). Draw a horizontal line at the midpoint. In this video, ICT marks the half-gap multiple times around 0:13:23–0:21:18 and later around 0:49:02.
- **How to use:** Use as a secondary target after taking partials at the first objective (relative equal lows or sell-side liquidity). Helps with position management: take one partial here, hold for further range. Provides psychological anchor—a hard level to aim for rather than "as low as possible."
- **Example in this video:** Opening gap: 9:30 open at ~18480 (approx), previous settlement lower; huge premium gap marked around 0:02:02. Half-gap calculated and marked as a secondary objective around 0:13:23. Reached and confirmed around 0:49:02 and 0:51:25.
- **Timestamps:** 
  - [0:02:02](https://youtu.be/tp0qkiWCctw?t=122) — "So there's a relative equal lows... enormous gap. It's a premium gap."
  - [0:13:23](https://youtu.be/tp0qkiWCctw?t=803) — Marking half-gap: "I'm going to remove all risk here... take one off underneath those relative equal lows... if it takes that out and fills me... then I'm going to bring the stop down."
  - [0:49:02](https://youtu.be/tp0qkiWCctw?t=2942) — Half-gap finally hit: "Half gap down here is what we're looking at."

head: Relative Equal Highs & Lows (Old Highs/Lows)
body:
- **Kind:** rule · liquidity target
- **What ICT says:** A previous swing high or low from an earlier session that is retested at roughly the same price level. When price approaches these levels in a new session, they act as draw-on liquidity points (magnets) because market makers know traders want to break/clear those levels. Price often reverses near them after a retest, or uses them as "trap" zones where stops are run.
- **How to identify:** Chart previous 1-3 sessions' highs and lows; when price returns to those zones, note them as zones of interest.
- **How to use:** Use as bias confirmers: if price reaches and respects (reverses off) relative equal low, it's bearish; if price reaches and reverses off relative equal high, it's bullish. Use as stop-placement guides (put stops slightly above relative equal highs if shorting). Use as entry or exit targets.
- **Example in this video:** Relative equal lows marked around 0:02:02 and repeatedly referenced. Price reaches and respects them around 0:22:06–0:33:18, then revisits them around 0:49:02. ICT places orders to exit at these levels.
- **Timestamps:**
  - [0:02:02](https://youtu.be/tp0qkiWCctw?t=122) — Marking the target lows.
  - [0:15:03](https://youtu.be/tp0qkiWCctw?t=903) — "I'll take one off underneath those relative equal lows we were aiming at earlier."

head: Sell-Side Liquidity (SSL)
body:
- **Kind:** definition · liquidity concept
- **What ICT says:** Resting sell orders (limit orders waiting to be filled at higher prices) left behind when price falls sharply. Traders who longed near lows and want to exit at breakeven or profit place sell orders; when price returns up into that zone, those orders get hit. For a short trader, this is a drag on momentum upward—the zone resists upward movement.
- **How to identify:** Look at the 4H or 1H chart: find a recent sharp fall. The zone where the rise stopped (relative low before that fall) often contains SSL. Visually: bodies above a level but no bodies below (suggesting sellers waiting above, not below).
- **How to use:** As a short trader, use SSL zones as profit-taking zones or as "drag" zones where upward momentum stalls. Use as a pullback magnet if price is falling through SSL—price will pull back into it before resuming down.
- **Example in this video:** Around 0:04:40, ICT notes "sell side there" and uses it as a target for the short.
- **Timestamps:**
  - [0:04:40](https://youtu.be/tp0qkiWCctw?t=280) — "Next point of interest is this sell side here."

head: Fair Value Gap (FVG) / Inversion FVG / SIBI
body:
- **Kind:** definition · PD array · price delivery method
- **What ICT says:** An inversion FVG is an inefficiency (void) left on the chart when price gaps up on a single candle, leaving a gap in price (no candle body in that range). Later, price retraces into that void to "fill" it. In this video, ICT references these as "inversion fair value" and uses them as retracement magnets. BISI (buy-side inefficiency) and SIBI (sell-side inefficiency) are the terms for the upper and lower sides of these gaps.
- **How to identify:** Look for a single candle that opens above the prior close with space between (a gap). Highlight that gap zone. Price will eventually retrace into it.
- **How to use:** Use as a magnet for retracements. If shorting, expect price to bounce into an inversion FVG before resuming down. Use as a "re-entry zone" if stopped out.
- **Example in this video:** Marked around 0:07:09, 0:15:49, 0:32:25. ICT draws them with dashed lines and annotates them as defensive levels or retracement zones.
- **Timestamps:**
  - [0:07:09](https://youtu.be/tp0qkiWCctw?t=429) — "This is an inversion fair value gap."
  - [0:15:49](https://youtu.be/tp0qkiWCctw?t=949) — Managing retracements: "Keep bodies out of the upper half. Touching that is okay. I don't want to see it leave a body up there."

head: Consequent Encroachment (CE) / Midwick Level
body:
- **Kind:** definition · price level · entry/stop guide
- **What ICT says:** When a candle closes with a long wick (upper or lower), the midpoint of that wick is a "consequent encroachment" level. It represents the point where the body rejected that extreme move. Price often retraces back to that midwick level after moving beyond it. Can be used as a stop-placement guide or as a retracement magnet.
- **How to identify:** Identify a candle with a long wick. Calculate the midpoint between the body close and the wick tip. Mark that level.
- **How to use:** Place stops slightly beyond this level (to allow for one more spike but to exit before a full reversal). Use as a "last line of defense" for a trade.
- **Example in this video:** References around 0:07:09, 0:15:49, 0:62 (end of transcript).
- **Timestamps:**
  - [0:07:09](https://youtu.be/tp0qkiWCctw?t=429) — "This longer wick, I'm watching that, it's consequent encroachment or midwick level right there."

head: Body Placement as Market Bias Indicator
body:
- **Kind:** rule · market structure
- **What ICT says:** Where the candle body (open to close) closes relative to a price level tells you the intent. If bodies keep closing above a level, it's bullish; if bodies keep closing below, it's bearish. Wicks that extend below a level but bodies that stay above = likely reversal / retracement coming. Bodies buried below a level = confirmation to break lower.
- **How to identify:** Look at the last 3–5 candles at a key level (relative equal low, FVG, etc.). Are bodies above or below? Are wicks alone touching the level?
- **How to use:** Use as a refusal/confirmation filter: refusal to stay below (bodies above despite wicks below) = likely to retrace or reverse. Confirmation to continue (bodies below) = likely to break further.
- **Example in this video:** Central theme from 0:22:06 onwards. ICT repeatedly emphasizes: "Keep bodies out of the upper half," "Whenever you're watching a liquidity pool right below an old low and you want to keep going lower, you don't want to see this type of event [bodies above]. You want to see them laying bodies underneath."
- **Timestamps:**
  - [0:22:53](https://youtu.be/tp0qkiWCctw?t=1373) — "Whenever you're watching a liquidity pool right below an old low and you want to keep going lower, you don't really want to see this type of event. You want to see them laying bodies underneath."

head: Judas Swing (False Breakout / Swing Trap)
body:
- **Kind:** definition · price pattern
- **What ICT says:** A sharp, directional move at the open (often on high volume or a gap) that goes one way (e.g., up), reaches a short-term high, then reverses sharply in the opposite direction. Named after Judas's betrayal—the move "tricks" traders into thinking the direction is set when it's actually engineered to trap them. "Right off of a Judas swing which is one directional rate at the 9:30 opening regular trading hours."
- **How to identify:** Look for a directional move at the open (9:30 ET for NQ) that creates a short-term high/low without consolidation; follows that with a sharp reversal (typically a candle or two) that breaks back down.
- **How to use:** When you see a Judas swing, expect a reversal shortly after. Use it as a sell signal if it's an upward Judas (short the breakout). Anticipate that stops above the short-term high will be run before the main down move; place your stop just above the short-term high or use a wider stop to account for this.
- **Example in this video:** NQ opens at 9:30 with a gap up (premium gap from Friday's close). Price runs straight up in one shot to a short-term high without consolidation. This is the Judas swing. Reverses sharply on the very next candle. ICT shorted this move.
- **Timestamps:**
  - [0:09:51](https://youtu.be/2L88yH3LKcs?t=591) — "That's a Judas swing. It took out buy side. We gapped higher."
  - [0:13:57](https://youtu.be/2L88yH3LKcs?t=837) — "We went above a short-term high right off of a Judas swing which is one directional rate at the 9:30 opening."
