head: Engineered Liquidity & Buy-Side / Sell-Side Distribution
body:
- **Kind:** definition · market structure
- **What ICT says:** Market makers create the appearance of strength (or weakness) by distributing (or accumulating) positions at key levels. On a Judas swing (false breakout up), market makers will allow price to rip higher to reach old resistance levels, sell heavily into the move to retail traders who see "confirmation," then dump it lower. This is called "engineering buy-side liquidity"—creating the appearance of buying pressure to trap buyers. "Smart money can go long here, sell, and sell more to the engineered liquidity that it forms." Bodies stay out of key levels; wicks may touch, but bodies won't, signifying that the move is engineered redistribution, not organic buying.
- **How to identify:** (1) Price reaches an old high or resistance level (relative equal high, previous swing high, etc.). (2) Bodies cannot touch or cannot stay above a key level (like consequent encroachment), but wicks do. (3) Price fails to go higher despite reaching an old level. (4) The failure is followed by a sharp reversal.
- **How to use:** When you see engineered liquidity signatures (bodies avoiding a level, wicks touching but bodies above), expect a reversal. Sell into the engineered move (short at the engineered buy-side; long at engineered sell-side). This is a higher-probability trade because you're front-running the reversal.
- **Example in this video:** 9:30 opening: price runs up in Judas swing, wicks reach up to touch upper levels (consequent encroachment between the hourly low and high, octant levels), but bodies cannot touch them. This signals engineered buy-side distribution. ICT shorted this.
- **Timestamps:**
  - [0:12:17](https://youtu.be/2L88yH3LKcs?t=737) — "Bodies can't touch consequent encouragement breaks lower then it runs through these highs. This is engineered buy liquidity."
  - [0:17:57](https://youtu.be/2L88yH3LKcs?t=1077) — "Bodies are not touching consequent encouragement. The wick can, but the wicks are allowed to do damage. The narrative and volume is really shown in the bodies."

head: Octant / Quadrant (Half-Level / 25/75 Splits)
body:
- **Kind:** definition · price level
- **What ICT says:** When measuring a range, divide it into four equal parts (quarters). The octant or quadrant levels are the 25% and 75% lines within that range. For a range with a low of X and high of Y, the octants are X + (Y−X)×0.25 and X + (Y−X)×0.75. "This is an octant... the uh 375 level." Used to identify price levels where order flow is likely to stall. (Note: "octant" here seems to refer to quarterly divisions, not the traditional 8-part octant.)
- **How to identify:** Mark a key range (e.g., the low and high of a swing, or the gap range). Divide that into quarters. The lines at 25% and 75% are octant levels.
- **How to use:** Use as secondary support/resistance. Bodies avoiding octant levels indicate engineered moves; bodies respecting octants indicate organic moves.
- **Example in this video:** The range between the hourly low and the 1H buy-side balance sell-side efficiency high has octant levels. Price fails to touch or sustain above these octants around 0:14:45, 0:22:43, 0:28:30.
- **Timestamps:**
  - [0:14:45](https://youtu.be/2L88yH3LKcs?t=885) — "Rallies up the bodies can't even touch the upper octant at 875... and then the high here can't even touch the upper quadrant."
  - [0:22:43](https://youtu.be/2L88yH3LKcs?t=1363) — "Using an octant which is the uh 375 level in agreement with an order block."

head: Breaker Block (Shift of Market Structure)
body:
- **Kind:** definition · price pattern · market structure
- **What ICT says:** A three-candle pattern: higher high, lower low, then higher high again. Once this pattern completes, the previous "lower low" is no longer a support; it's been "broken." The pattern signals a shift in market structure and confirms that buyers have taken control and are now in command. "High, low, higher high. This is your breaker."
- **How to identify:** Look for three candlesticks: (1) higher high, (2) lower low, (3) higher high again. When confirmed, the pattern shifts bias to bullish.
- **How to use:** Once a breaker is formed, do not place shorts below the lower low. If price does pull back below the lower low after a breaker, it's a "failure" and signals a reversal back down (not a breakout continuation). Use the breaker as a bias confirmation—if it forms without bodies going below it, it's a bullish breaker.
- **Example in this video:** Marked around 0:20:22. Breaker forms on intraday chart; price goes higher high, then down to lower low, then higher high again. No bodies trade below the lower low of the breaker, confirming its validity.
- **Timestamps:**
  - [0:20:22](https://youtu.be/2L88yH3LKcs?t=1222) — "There was a breaker here. High, low, higher high. This is your breaker... If it's a good, valid breaker, you wouldn't want to see the bodies trade up outside of it."

head: Event Horizon / Midpoint Between PD Arrays
body:
- **Kind:** definition · price level
- **What ICT says:** The midpoint between two key price delivery arrays (FVGs, order blocks, highs, lows, etc.). This is a zone where price often stalls or reverses because it's the geometric center of a range. "Event horizon. It's a midpoint between two key PD arrays."
- **How to identify:** Identify two key levels (e.g., a swing high and swing low, or two gaps). Calculate the midpoint between them. That's the event horizon.
- **How to use:** Use as a secondary target or stall zone. Expect bodies to struggle to cross through event horizons without a reversal or consolidation.
- **Example in this video:** Event horizon mentioned around 0:14:45 between the hourly efficiency and the opening range gap.
- **Timestamps:**

head: Short-Term High/Low
body:
- **Kind:** definition · price level
- **What ICT says:** The highest or lowest price reached within the most recent few candles (e.g., the last 5 candles on the 1-minute chart). Used to identify potential reversal zones or confirmation of trend changes. "We create a short-term high and give me evidence around consequent encouragement."
- **How to identify:** On the 1m or 5m chart, mark the high/low of the last 3–5 candles.
- **How to use:** Use as a confirmation level. If price is reverting below a short-term high and showing bodies rejecting above it, that's bearish. Use as a stop-placement guide.

head: Full Gap Closure
body:
- **Kind:** definition · price target
- **What ICT says:** When price has opened with a gap (e.g., gap up from previous close), a "full gap closure" occurs when price retraces all the way back down to fill that entire gap, reaching the previous session's close or the low of the gap range. Distinguished from "half-gap" (midpoint of gap) or "consequent encroachment of the gap" (midpoint of gap).
- **How to identify:** Mark the opening gap (high and low of the gap range between sessions). A full closure means price reaches the low of that gap.
- **How to use:** Use as a longer-term target when in a downtrend. If you shorted a gap-up move, a full gap closure is a viable final target.
- **Example in this video:** Mentioned as a potential target around 0:27:29 if price continues lower.
- **Timestamps:**

title: NQ Futures Trade Review - July 20, 2026
head: Public Stop Loss Sharing & Market Manipulation
body:
- **Kind:** rule · risk disclosure
- **What ICT says:** When ICT publicly shares his stop loss on social media or in a live stream, the market immediately gravitates to it and runs it. This proves (to him) that markets are not random buying/selling but are algorithmically manipulated. "If I have a stop-loss at a particular price level and I have 2 million plus people following me, at least 10% of you are contemplating doing something similar... They will muscle it up there and just there it is by any means necessary." If 10% of 2 million followers try to copy, that's 200,000 contracts on the same stop—enough to move the market. Market makers see this and deliberately run the stop to liquidate all of them.
- **How to use:** Do NOT publicly share your exact stop loss if you have a large following. If you must share it, expect it to be run. Place your actual stop tighter than you publicly state (or use a different stop in the actual trade). Understand that the market will hunt stops when they're known.
- **Example in this video:** ICT mentions a stop loss around 0:30:40, and price goes straight to it. He later shares the impact of publicizing his levels: "They came up for my stop loss first and then went down to it."

title: Futures General Commentary - July 20, 2026
head: Seasonal Tendencies (July to October Energy Rally)
body:
- **Kind:** rule · macro context · cyclical pattern
- **What ICT says:** Every year, starting the first week of July and running through October, crude oil and energy commodity prices tend to rally. This is because large industrial companies (heating oil suppliers, natural gas distributors) must stock up on supplies *before* the cold winter months arrive. They buy at lower "summer" prices and accumulate inventory so they can meet customer demand in winter. "Large companies have to buy that stuff before the cold months get here... they're buying it at technically what it's considered the lower prices." Seasonal tendencies work because they reflect real supply/demand fundamentals in commodities (unlike stocks/futures, which are purely "hot potato" games where traders just chase higher prices). However, event-driven markets (wars, geopolitical tension, sanctions) can override seasonal patterns. (0:06:45–0:24:19)
- **How to identify:** Look at 5–10 years of historical crude oil (or energy) charts. Mark each occurrence of the first week of July. Observe whether a rally occurs into October. Calculate win-rate: how many years does the pattern hold?
- **How to use:** Use seasonal tendencies as a *bias tool*, not a guaranteed trade setup. If the seasonal tendency suggests prices should go up, and price is showing weakness instead, that weakness is bearish (prices should be going up and aren't, so when they eventually do, it'll likely be sharp). If seasonal tendencies align with technical levels (e.g., a daily open or structural low), confidence increases. Example: "If I'm watching crude and the first week of July should seasonally rally into October, and price is instead declining, that's very strong bearish indication—prices should be going up." (0:13:14)
- **Example in this video:** 
  - 2024 example (0:12:25): First week of July through October, rally occurred on schedule.
  - 2023 example (0:14:00): First week of July, then rally into end of September/early October.
  - 2020 example (0:17:09): First week of July, drop into August, then rally into October (deferred, but pattern held).
  - 2020 (COVID crash example, 0:17:56): Crude went negative (below $0/barrel). This broke the seasonal pattern entirely and caused destabilization for several years. Eventually recovered to $100+ range, but the shock disrupted the pattern temporarily.
  - Current year (implicit): First week of July 2026 into mid-session showed a drop despite seasonal expectation; attributed to absence of geopolitical conflict. (0:12:25)
- **Timestamps:**
  - [0:10:48](https://youtu.be/xbtW_0ipuos?t=648) — "Seasonal supply and demand factor. Commodities have real supply and demand factors. Stocks and futures, there's really no supply and demand factor."
  - [0:11:37](https://youtu.be/xbtW_0ipuos?t=697) — "First week of July, all of the large companies that provide your fuel... have to have their supply to meet demand. So they build up their stockpile."
  - [0:13:14](https://youtu.be/xbtW_0ipuos?t=794) — "If you can't see the price run higher when it should be seasonally going higher, it's very strong indication we're likely to keep going lower."

title: Futures General Commentary - July 20, 2026
head: Event-Driven Markets Override Seasonal Tendencies
body:
- **Kind:** rule · macro context
- **What ICT says:** Geopolitical events (wars, sanctions, military conflict, supply disruptions) can completely override seasonal patterns. In 2024–2026, crude oil experienced supply disruptions and geopolitical tensions, which caused the seasonal pattern to break. "If things start to heat up... if they drop a tactical nuke... this is going straight up above $200 a barrel." (0:08:24) The 2020 COVID crash (crude went negative) is the extreme example of event-driven market disruption. (0:17:56)
- **How to use:** When trading commodities with seasonal bias, monitor geopolitical news. If major events occur (wars, sanctions, supply disruptions), expect the seasonal pattern to break or reverse. Use this as a filter: "Is the seasonal tendency holding? If not, why not?" If the "why" is a major event, the event take precedence over seasonal bias.
- **Example in this video:** 
  - 2024–2026: Military tensions and geopolitical conflict between Middle East powers. These events caused crude to rally when it might have otherwise drifted lower per seasonal tendency alone. "We have a wartime scenario and we have the two major straits in that area... it's going to cause prices to go up." (0:19:33)
  - If Iran or its allies use a "tactical nuke," crude would spike above $200/barrel regardless of seasonal tendency. (0:08:24)
- **Timestamps:**
  - [0:08:24](https://youtu.be/xbtW_0ipuos?t=504) — "If they drop a tactical nuke... this is going straight up above $200 a barrel."
  - [0:12:25](https://youtu.be/xbtW_0ipuos?t=745) — "We weren't at war then... but then we went into that scenario this year and then rallied up."
  - [0:19:33](https://youtu.be/xbtW_0ipuos?t=1173) — "We have a wartime scenario... it's going to cause prices to go up."

title: Futures General Commentary - July 20, 2026
head: Fair Value Gap as Retracement & Recovery Tool
body:
- **Kind:** definition · PD array · retracement magnet
- **What ICT says:** When an FVG is created (price gaps up on a candle, leaving an inefficiency), price typically retraces back into it. This is passive tool use: you identify FVGs and expect price to return to them during consolidations or retracements. "Whatever fair value gap that lays in the week... we can use that and interpret that as a potential bullish inversion fair gap to make a much more meaningful run above here." (0:04:16)
- **How to identify:** Mark FVGs on the daily, 4H, and 1H charts; note them as potential retracement magnets.
- **How to use:** In bullish scenarios, use FVGs below price as "buy the dip" zones. In bearish scenarios, use FVGs above price as "sell the rally" zones. Inversion FVGs (created on bullish gaps up) become targets for bullish reversals—price retraces into them, uses them as springboards for further upside.
- **Example in this video:** Crude oil daily chart, around 0:06:45. An FVG is created; price trades into it, bounces, then uses the FVG as a floor for further rallies.
- **Timestamps:**
  - [0:04:16](https://youtu.be/xbtW_0ipuos?t=256) — "Whatever fair value gap that lays in the week... we can use that as a potential bullish inversion fair gap."

title: NQ Futures Weekly Range Market Wizardry
head: Weekly Suspension Block (Volume Imbalance)
body:
- **Kind:** definition · price delivery array · range framework
- **What ICT says:** A bullish or bearish fair value gap on the weekly chart, typically created at the open of a new week. It's a "suspension block" because it has volume imbalances (inefficiencies) at both the high and low of its range, creating a "trapped" zone. During the week, price will trade up and down within this zone, eventually breaking out to the downside (if bearish) or upside (if bullish). In this week's example: the weekly suspension block was bullish at the open; price was inside it early week; by week's end, price breaks below it to fulfill the bearish weekly draw. "This suspension block... when we start the week... we're inside the middle of this inefficiency... specifically a suspension block because a volume imbalance at the high and a volume imbalance at the low." (0:04:03)
- **How to identify:** On the weekly chart, mark the opening candle (Sunday–Monday open). Look for an incomplete price delivery (body does not touch high or low, or a gap). This is the suspension block. Mark its high, low, and midpoint.
- **How to use:** Use the suspension block as a weekly framework: (1) Identify the block early Monday; (2) Forecast where weekly price will go (usually the opposite direction of the open); (3) Use daily chart levels (relative equal lows, FVGs) to confirm intra-week targets. (4) On Friday, use TGIF to pinpoint the weekly close.
- **Example in this video:** Weekly chart, July 15–19 (Monday–Friday). Suspension block marked at the open; identified as bullish initially but the block indicated a break below for the week. Lower volume imbalance at the bottom of the block was the draw-on-liquidity target (weekly relative equal lows at 28,512). Price broke out Friday, hitting that target precisely. (0:04:03–0:08:13)
- **Timestamps:**
  - [0:04:03](https://youtu.be/NPU4gsM9jqA?t=243) — "This suspension block... when we start the week, we're inside the middle of this inefficiency."
  - [0:06:35](https://youtu.be/NPU4gsM9jqA?t=395) — "If price is bearish this is going to act like an inversion fair value gap."
  - [0:08:13](https://youtu.be/NPU4gsM9jqA?t=493) — "We'd like to see it gravitate get below that. If it does, we'll likely see continuation."

title: NQ Futures Weekly Range Market Wizardry
head: New Week Opening Gap (NWOG) / Premium & Discount
body:
- **Kind:** definition · gap · liquidity reference
- **What ICT says:** When a new week starts (Sunday 6 PM ET or Monday pre-market), the settlement price from Friday may differ from the opening price of the week. This creates a gap. If the gap is "premium" (above Friday's close), price will likely retrace back down into that gap mid-week. If "discount" (below Friday's close), price will likely rally back up into it. The gap defines the weekly trading range boundaries. "So, if price is bearish and we went lower, we're trading back up in, it's reasonable. It's reasonable for price to trade up into that on Friday of last week and then open on Monday or Sunday or whatever you want to look at it lower than where we closed on Friday. So, we have a new week opening gap." (0:05:43)
- **How to identify:** On the daily chart, mark the Friday RTH close. Mark the Monday/Sunday opening price. If opening > close, gap is premium. If opening < close, gap is discount.
- **How to use:** Premium gaps typically act as resistance (inversion FVG); price will retrace into them mid-week. Discount gaps act as support; price will rally into them. Use the gap as a weekly target or waypoint.
- **Example in this video:** Monday opens in premium relative to Friday's close, indicating a weekly bearish bias (down move expected). (0:05:43–0:07:25)
- **Timestamps:**
  - [0:05:43](https://youtu.be/NPU4gsM9jqA?t=343) — "So we have a new week opening gap."
  - [0:06:35](https://youtu.be/NPU4gsM9jqA?t=395) — "If we're bearish this is going to act like an inversion fair value gap."

title: NQ Futures Weekly Range Market Wizardry
head: TGIF (Thank God It's Friday) — Friday's 20–30% Retracement
body:
- **Kind:** rule · weekly close pattern · target model
- **What ICT says:** On Friday, price will retrace 20–30% of the entire weekly range (measured from the high that forms during the week down to the low that forms during the week). This creates a predictable close zone on Friday afternoon. You can use this to forecast Friday's close in advance. "If we measure the high of the week that formed on Wednesday down to Friday's low, once it pierced this and worked its way back above that low, how far can it retrace? 20 to the 30% of the weekly range. 20% levels here. 30% is here." (0:18:37)
- **How to identify:** (1) On Friday, identify the weekly high (typically formed mid-week). (2) Identify the weekly low (typically hit by Friday or late Thursday). (3) Calculate 20% and 30% of that range above the low. (4) Watch for price to close in that 20–30% zone.
- **How to use:** Use TGIF as your Friday target close forecast. Once price hits the weekly low (draw on liquidity), expect it to retrace into the 20–30% zone and close there. This is one of the highest-probability price actions in the week. Avoid trading below this zone on Friday unless new weekly range-extending moves are happening.
- **Example in this video:** Weekly high on Wednesday, weekly low hit Friday morning. 20% and 30% retracement levels calculated. Friday close landed precisely in the 20–30% zone (0:18:37–0:19:24, 0:37:53–0:38:41).
- **Timestamps:**
  - [0:18:37](https://youtu.be/NPU4gsM9jqA?t=1117) — "20 to the 30% of the weekly range. 20% levels here. 30% is here. Look where we closed for the week. Right in there."
  - [0:19:24](https://youtu.be/NPU4gsM9jqA?t=1164) — "You're forecasting where the close of the week is going to be."

head: Low Resistance Liquidity Run Conditions (Easy Days)
body:
- **Kind:** definition · market state · trading environment
- **What ICT says:** Days after major economic news (CPI, PPI, FOMC) has passed, typically Thursday and Friday. Price stretches out in low resistance, meaning fast, directional candles with large ranges that cover significant distance. These are "easy money" days for traders who understand the direction. "Trading will get really nice after the PM session on Wednesday. So, what does that mean? Well, overnight Wednesday into Thursday, it'll be easy trading Thursday session, Friday session." (0:15:23) On these days, position size can be larger, stops tighter, and executions more straightforward.
- **How to use:** On low-resistance days, trust your daily/4H direction bias and trade with confidence. Take larger position size. Expect straight runs without much retracement. On Friday (assuming weekly low is already hit), trade longs into the TGIF retracement zone.
- **Example in this video:** Thursday and Friday (0:15:23–0:16:12). Both showed low resistance—fast expansions lower to the weekly target, then retracements up into TGIF zone.

title: NQ Futures Weekly Range Market Wizardry
head: High Resistance Liquidity Run Conditions (Hard Days)
body:
- **Kind:** definition · market state · trading environment
- **What ICT says:** Days when major economic news (CPI, PPI) is released, typically Monday–Wednesday. These days have choppy, back-and-forth price action with lots of small candles in tight ranges (high resistance). Don't expect easy trades; expect to be stopped out multiple times or forced to sit out. "I told him, I said, you know, Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday is going to be a little bit more difficult for someone that's brand new." (0:10:37) Accept that new traders will struggle on these days and it's normal.
- **How to use:** On high-resistance days, keep size smaller. Accept wider stops. Don't fight the noise. Many professional traders sit out these days entirely. If trading, use only the highest-probability setups (clear daily bias + clear draw on liquidity).
- **Example in this video:** Monday–Wednesday in this week had CPI and PPI; price whipsawed. (0:10:37–0:11:24)

title: NQ Futures Weekly Range Market Wizardry
head: Pre-Market Session (7:00–9:00 AM ET) Liquidity Runs
body:
- **Kind:** rule · session-specific behavior
- **What ICT says:** The pre-market session (7:00–9:00 AM ET, one hour before regular trading opens at 9:30 ET) is a crucial liquidity-running window. Price will often run overnight highs and lows, taking out relative equal highs/lows from the previous day or previous session(s). This creates fast, directional momentum that carries into 9:30 open. "Relative equal highs and lows... they're going to run them. Even though price existed there and booked overnight, regular trading hours are going to run up there and run down below them relatively sharply." (0:26:36) On Friday especially, the pre-market session is the "rocket fuel" that allows price to reach the weekly low target before the day is over.
- **How to identify:** Mark overnight highs and lows (electronic trading hours 6 PM–9:30 AM). Also mark previous day's relative equal highs/lows. At 7:00 AM, watch for fast runs into these levels.
- **How to use:** Trade into these levels in pre-market. Use them as entries if they align with your daily bias. On Friday, expect the pre-market session to deliver the final push to the weekly low. (0:29:02–0:31:25)
- **Example in this video:** Friday, 7:00 AM start to 9:00 AM close. Price runs down, hits the weekly relative equal low at 28,512, briefly rallies into the 9:30 open (Judas swing), then dumps lower. (0:29:02–0:33:02)
- **Timestamps:**

The term "Jesus" suggests redemption or rescue—price "saves itself" by reversing sharply up before dumping down again. (This appears to be a less-commonly-taught term or a playful name ICT uses.)

title: NQ Futures Weekly Range Market Wizardry
head: Electronic Trading Hours vs. Regular Trading Hours (Jigsaw Puzzle Concept)
body:
- **Kind:** rule · session architecture · market structure
- **What ICT says:** Regular trading hours (9:30 AM–4:00 PM ET for NQ) have gaps in price action created by time gaps (4:00 PM Friday to 6:00 PM Sunday open, Sunday 6 PM to Monday 9:30 AM, etc.). Electronic trading hours (6:00 PM–9:30 AM, GlobeEx for NASDAQ) fill in these gaps with price action. The intraday chart is like a jigsaw puzzle: regular trading hours create pieces, electronic trading hours fill in the missing pieces. Understanding both is necessary to see the complete price structure. "It's like a jigsaw puzzle... You have some parts, some pieces... There are pieces missing in here... That's where Electronic Trading Hours fills in those jigsaw puzzle pieces." (0:24:13)
- **How to use:** When analyzing a daily or weekly chart, mentally reconstruct the overnight/electronic trading hours price action by looking at gaps and where price resukes after gaps. This tells you where the real draw-on-liquidity points are and explains intraday price behavior.
- **Example in this video:** 7:00 AM (start of GlobeEx session) to 9:30 AM (RTH open) shows the missing puzzle piece—the pre-market session that delivers the momentum into the 9:30 open. (0:24:13–0:26:36)
- **Timestamps:**
  - [0:24:13](https://youtu.be/NPU4gsM9jqA?t=1453) — "It's like a jigsaw puzzle... There are pieces missing in here... That's where Electronic Trading Hours fills in those jigsaw puzzle pieces."
  - [0:25:49](https://youtu.be/NPU4gsM9jqA?t=1549) — "Many times electronic trading hours goes into these gaps before regular trading hours does."

title: NQ Futures Weekly Range Market Wizardry
head: Time as the Most Important Factor
body:
- **Kind:** rule · context
- **What ICT says:** On the last day of the week (Friday), time becomes the dominant constraint. Price must hit its targets within the trading session before the 5:00 PM close. This means price cannot afford to waste time consolidating or retracing; it must use every minute to reach its targets. Session opens (especially pre-market 7:00 AM) become critical as "rocket fuel" to reach these targets before time runs out. "It only has Friday because when we close at 5:00 Eastern time, it's then you go into the weekend." (0:35:27) You can use this to rule out unlikely price moves on Friday—if a move would require too much time, it's not going to happen.
- **How to use:** On Friday, ask: "What can price accomplish between now and 5:00 PM?" Use this to filter out trades that would require more time than available. Example: on Friday afternoon, don't expect price to make multiple round-trips; expect straight runs to targets only.
- **Example in this video:** Friday morning to close. Price had to hit 28,512 and retrace into TGIF before 5:00 PM close. The pre-market 7:00 AM start was critical to allow enough time for the full week's delivery before close. (0:29:02–0:38:41)
- **Timestamps:**
  - [0:35:27](https://youtu.be/NPU4gsM9jqA?t=2127) — "It only has Friday because when we close at 5:00 Eastern time, it's then you go into the weekend."
  - [0:35:45](https://youtu.be/NPU4gsM9jqA?t=2145) — "Time is the most important factor."

head: Market Maker Sell Model (MMSM)
body:
- **Kind:** definition · model · distribution pattern
- **What ICT says:** A pattern of price rallying (smart money reversing and going long), distributing (selling to retail buyers), then reversing down. Opposite of the market maker buy model. Marked by (1) rally, (2) consolidation/distribution at higher levels, (3) reversal down. "This is my money reversal, low-risk cell, first stage distribution, second stage distribution, biggest part of the run rate to weekly target." (0:23:25) Identified using body placement, order flow, and levels.
- **How to use:** When you identify the MMSM pattern forming on intraday charts, prepare to short after distribution phase completes. Use the distribution zone as a resistance level; shorts placed above it will reverse down into lower targets.
- **Example in this video:** Intraday chart, 5-minute timeframe. Price rallies and distributes into the sell-side zone, then reverses lower. (0:23:25)

title: Midnight ET Principles In Relationship To PreMArket Session
head: Midnight open as fulcrum / bookend of the daily range expansion  (aliases ICT uses: midnight Eastern open, New York local midnight, fulcrum point, Power of Three)
body:
- **Kind:** definition / rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - Midnight ET (New York local) is one of the several openings he teaches.
  - The midnight open price "can act as a fulcrum point," a bookend or beginning of the daily range expansion.
  - Bearish template (normal Power of Three): open at midnight, go above the midnight open, then drop lower and go lower for the day, closing somewhere off the low.
  - In this day's example: after the midnight open, price traded through Frankfurt and London forming relative equal highs; the drop did not reach the daily objective until after 7:00.
- **How to identify:** mark the 00:00 ET open on the chart; watch whether price runs above it (bearish) before the main delivery.
- **How to use:** use the midnight open as the reference for expected daily direction and as a possible upper target on a retracement - but see the next concept: a retracement to it is not necessary.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 5m (for the panoramic view), Friday: midnight open at the start; relative equal highs formed in the Frankfurt/London window; the highs created are "significantly lower than the opening price."

title: Midnight ET Principles In Relationship To PreMArket Session
head: High-timeframe draw on liquidity: daily relative equal lows with a high-probability move  (aliases ICT uses: unrealized objective, daily relative equal low, hard high time frame draw)
body:

head: After London relative equal lows and a 7:00 retake: don't expect a return to the midnight open; target the relative equal highs  (aliases ICT uses: short-covering rally, "clean up the relative equal highs")
body:

- **How to identify:** London relative equal lows -> sweep right before/at 7:00 -> reversal.
- **How to use:** after the sweep and reversal, target the relative equal highs (not the midnight open); bank partial profits; consider being done for the day.

head: First Utilization of a PD Array
body:
- **Kind:** definition · price delivery concept
- **What ICT says:** When a price delivery array (FVG, suspension block, order block, etc.) first forms, it has a "first utilization"—an initial purpose or bias. For example, a suspension block created during a bullish move has an initial bullish utilization; if price comes down into it and the bodies cannot touch the upper quadrant, it shows the block's bullish purpose is being rejected and may now act bearish (inversion). Once price closes and clearly goes through/below it, the first utilization is confirmed, and the array gets recalibrated. "First utilization is when a PD array forms... That validates this as a bearish breaker." (0:21:33)
- **How to identify:** Identify when an array forms and its initial direction bias. Then watch for the first major move through/away from it. If bodies and closes confirm that move, first utilization is validated.
- **How to use:** Use first utilization to set initial bias. But if the array is invalidated (price goes the opposite direction), recalibrate it—it now has a new utilization. Example: a bullish suspension block that gets pierced below becomes a bearish inversion.
- **Example in this video:** The daily suspension block formed bullishly on Wednesday. By Friday, it's being traded into and below, invalidating its bullish first utilization and confirming a bearish recalibration. (0:04:01–0:08:13, 0:21:33)
- **Timestamps:**
  - [0:21:33](https://youtu.be/Dj0663u7VRc?t=1293) — "First utilization is when a PD array forms... That validates this as a bearish breaker."

head: Quadrant & Octant Levels (Detailed)
body:
- **Kind:** definition · price level · order flow tool
- **What ICT says:** When dividing an inefficiency or range into four equal quarters, the dividing lines are quadrants. More specifically, the upper and lower quartile lines are "quadrants"; the 25% and 75% lines are "octants." ICT uses these extensively on daily charts as reference points for entries and exits. For example, "the lower quadrant of the daily suspension block" is the 25% line above the block's low. Price will often stall or reverse at these lines because they divide the inefficiency zone. "That octant this quadrant. Okay? That's what's being carried over into the daily chart." (0:14:28–0:15:18)
- **How to identify:** Mark the high and low of an inefficiency. Divide into quarters. The 25% line above the low = lower quadrant; the 75% line above the low = upper quadrant.
- **How to use:** Use quadrant lines as refinement entry points. For a short, enter at or just below the lower quadrant if it aligns with daily bias. Use upper quadrant as a resistance level; if price wicks into it but bodies can't touch it, that's bearish (rejection).
- **Example in this video:** Daily suspension block marked with quadrant lines. The 9:30 opening candle reaches exactly the lower quadrant of the block and is shorted there. Multiple intraday moves refine around these quadrant/octant levels. (0:04:01–0:15:18, 0:24:13–0:25:31)
- **Timestamps:**
  - [0:10:29](https://youtu.be/Dj0663u7VRc?t=629) — "We have that line right there... We have the low of that inefficiency on the daily chart. Then we have an octant and then we have the lower quadrant."

head: Hangman PD Array (New Trading Pattern)
body:
- **Kind:** definition · price pattern · PD array
- **What ICT says:** A specific candlestick pattern where the body closes above (or near) a key level (like consequent encroachment), but the wick extends below that level and then rejects back up, leaving a small body and longer wick. Named after the hangman's noose—traders going long get trapped as the wick pulls their stops, then the market reverses and leaves them "hanging." The pattern signals likely downward continuation. "That's the hangman. Anyone that was going long here, they get stung right there. So, they're getting dropped and the noose is around their neck, and then you're gone." (0:27:09–0:28:45)
- **How to identify:** Look for a candle where: (1) Body closes above a key level (e.g., consequent encroachment), (2) Wick extends well below that level, (3) The wick is notably longer than the body, (4) The next candle confirms by breaking lower again.
- **How to use:** When you see a hangman pattern, expect continuation downward after the wick rejects. Do not go long into the body close; instead, prepare for shorts below the wick low. Use it as a confirmation pattern.
- **Example in this video:** Marked around 0:27:09–0:28:45. Body closes near consequent encroachment level, wick extends below, then rejection and downside follow. This pattern appears at the convergence of the 1-hour FVG boundary.
- **Timestamps:**
  - [0:27:09](https://youtu.be/Dj0663u7VRc?t=1629) — "So, this is a hangman. I know these crazy names, right? A hangman is where... they're getting hung."
  - [0:27:56](https://youtu.be/Dj0663u7VRc?t=1676) — "The bodies are just above consequent encouragement, which would indicate what? Continuation is likely, but then we move back down outside of it."

head: Lunch Macro (11:30 AM Pullback)
body:

- **How to identify:** Mark the 10:00 AM low on the 1-minute or 5-minute chart. Around 11:30 AM, watch for a retracement/pull back into that level or near it.

- **Example in this video:** Trade moves lower, then around 11:30 AM retraces back into the 10:00 low. Price pulls back into that level at the lunch macro time. (0:17:39, 0:25:31–0:26:19, 0:30:18–0:31:05)

head: Time Distortion
body:
- **Kind:** definition · candlestick characteristic
- **What ICT says:** A period where multiple candles form within a tight range, not covering much price distance. Called "time distortion" because time passes but price doesn't move much. Typically occurs near support/resistance levels or before directional breaks. "Spent a little bit of time in here. This is time distortion." (0:20:45, 0:30:18)
- **How to identify:** Look for a series of small-range candles that don't advance the price much despite forming multiple candles.
- **How to use:** When you see time distortion, expect a breakout soon. Don't expect more movement until the breakout occurs. Use the distortion period to tighten stops or take partials if you're already in a trade.
- **Example in this video:** Marked around 0:20:45 and again around 0:30:18.
- **Timestamps:**

head: Invalidation & Recalibration of Inefficiencies
body:
- **Kind:** rule · price behavior
- **What ICT says:** When a PD array (FVG, suspension block, etc.) is initially bullish but price closes and trades below it, the array is "invalidated" as bullish and must be recalibrated—it now acts as a bearish inversion. Recalibration requires a clear close below the array. "How do you get back in sync with it? Well, you got to give it a chance to take out buy side here. And then once we close below it again, that resets first utilization... That resets first utilization." (0:21:33–0:22:20)
- **How to use:** When an array you thought was bullish gets invalidated, flip your bias. Don't try to fight it; accept the recalibration and trade the new bias. Recalibration gives you a second chance at the trade in the opposite direction.
- **Example in this video:** Daily suspension block is initially bullish (created Wednesday). By Friday, it's being broken below, which recalibrates it from bullish to bearish. Once confirmed, it becomes a bearish inversion FVG. (0:21:33–0:22:20)

head: Parameter-Based Entries (Dual Scenario Setup)
body:
- **Kind:** rule · entry model · risk management
- **What ICT says:** When an economic news event (CPI, PPI, NFP) is about to occur, you don't know which direction the market will move. Rather than guessing, set up two possible parameter zones and wait for price to tell you which one is active. Example: "Either drops down here to go up to new week opening gap, and that's the run for CPI, or it goes up there to drop back down into here." (0:11:19–0:12:07) Whichever zone price enters first becomes the active direction for the trade.
- **How to identify:** On the daily/hourly chart, identify the key PD arrays and supports/resistances surrounding the current price. Mark the two most likely paths price could take after the news. Set one parameter above, one below.
- **How to use:** Do not trade before the news based on guesses. Wait for the 8:30 release. Watch which zone price enters. Once it's clear, build a position in that direction. Use the other zone as your invalidation level.
- **Example in this video:** Tuesday, 8:30 AM PPI release. ICT sets up two parameters: either price drops into a lower FVG zone or rallies into the new week opening gap. Price initially runs up (new week opening gap chosen), so ICT shorts on the way down from there. (0:01:49–0:04:16, 0:11:19–0:12:07)

head: Staging (Creating Short-Term Highs to Take Buy Stops)
body:
- **Kind:** definition · order flow concept · market structure
- **What ICT says:** Market makers create successive short-term highs on the way up, each higher than the previous. These are "stages" that trigger buy-stop orders (traders who want to short wait above each high and place buy stops there to enter long positions, assuming a breakout). Smart money sells into each successive buy-stop zone, taking them out, then the market reverses. "This is staging. Meaning that they'll run it up, create a short-term high, and then that liquidity gets taken, and it becomes counterparty for shorts." (0:04:48) Each short-term high becomes a potential reversal point.
- **How to identify:** On intraday charts, look for a series of ascending candles where each new candle high is slightly above the previous. Each peak represents a stage where buy-stops are clustered.
- **How to use:** When you see staging, do not go long into the new highs. Instead, prepare to short. Buy-stops will be taken out by smart money selling, triggering the reversal. Use the highest stage reached as a resistance level and a short entry (on the reversal below it).
- **Example in this video:** Tuesday morning: price rallies with successive higher highs creating stages. Traders place buy-stops above each high. Smart money accumulates shorts, then reverses price down below all the stages. (0:04:48–0:05:51)
- **Timestamps:**
  - [0:04:48](https://youtu.be/LBrsLPKXZ2E?t=288) — "This is staging. They'll run it up, create a short-term high, and then that liquidity gets taken, and it becomes counterparty for shorts."
  - [0:05:51](https://youtu.be/LBrsLPKXZ2E?t=351) — "With the expectation that the market's not going to breach the halfway point... they're accumulating short positions."

head: Building Positions in Lower Half of Range (Bearish Bias)
body:
- **Kind:** rule · position management
- **What ICT says:** When you're bearish and shorting, build your position in the lower half of a key range (e.g., below the midpoint/consequent encroachment of a PD array). This placement protects you from bodies breaking into the upper half (which would signal bullish reversal). "I want to be selling short in the lower half of this cuz it's going to protect and deny any trespass with the bodies in the upper half." (0:13:46) Bodies in the lower half confirm continuation downward.
- **How to use:** Identify the midpoint/consequent encroachment of your target range. Place your shorts below that line and add to them as price stays below. If price creeps above, take profits and re-evaluate.
- **Example in this video:** New week opening gap range from ~29,570 to lower level. Midpoint around 29,570. ICT builds shorts between the lower quadrant and upper octant of this range, staying well below midpoint. (0:13:46–0:14:32)

head: Taking Partials for Psychology / "Paying the Trader"
body:
- **Kind:** rule · position management · psychology
- **What ICT says:** When you feel concern creeping in during a trade—worry that it might reverse—take off a small partial (1–2 contracts out of many). This gives you a "reward" (realized profit), eases psychological burden, and lets you hold the remaining contracts without fear. "Just take one of your contracts off. If you feel weird about something... Soon as you start feeling that, the only remedy is either completely bail or take something off... That little tiny little cookie, that reward." (0:18:31) ICT calls this "paying the trader"—giving yourself small wins to stay in the trade.
- **How to use:** When doubt creeps in, don't close the entire trade. Take off 1–3 contracts (depending on size). Lock in some profit. This psychological relief allows you to stay with the main move and capture larger gains.
- **Example in this video:** Multiple times during the day, ICT takes partials to satisfy doubts, then continues holding remaining contracts. (0:18:31, referenced multiple times from 0:17:44–0:19:18)

body:

Price will use this first instance as a target/magnet, and if it fails to respect it (closes outside of it), it becomes the first confirmation that price is going further in that direction. "First instance of fair value gap from Tuesday and it's the suspension block... we had a close outside of it right there... there's no gap prior to this one forming." (0:02:23–0:03:10)
- **How to identify:** Identify the most recent inefficiency on the chart. This is your "first instance." Mark it prominently.
- **How to use:** Use the first instance as your initial target. If price respects it (body stays inside), it's neutral. If price closes outside of it decisively, it's confirmation that price will continue past it.
- **Example in this video:** Tuesday's suspension block is the first instance. On Monday, price trades back into it and closes inside it, confirming continued downward direction. (0:02:23–0:03:10, 0:08:47)

head: Close Outside of a PD Array as Confirmation
body:
- **Kind:** rule · order flow signal
- **What ICT says:** A candlestick body that closes outside (below for bearish, above for bullish) a PD array is a confirmation signal. Wicks alone don't count. The body must close fully beyond the array boundary for confirmation. "Make it a little bit bigger. See that candlestick closed below first instance of fair value gap. Okay, there's no gap prior to this one forming." (0:02:23–0:03:10) This is one of the most important order flow signals.
- **How to identify:** Mark the boundary of a key PD array. Observe the candlestick body (not the wick). If the body closes completely outside the boundary, it's confirmation.
- **How to use:** Once the body closes outside, assume the direction and trade with conviction in that direction. Don't wait for more confirmation; the close-outside is your signal.
- **Example in this video:** Bodies close below key FVGs, confirming downward continuation; later, bodies close above other FVGs, confirming bullish reclamation. (0:02:23–0:12:02)

title: Post CPI NQ Futures Commentary \ Monday Analysis Delivered - 07/15/2026
head: Chain of Custody (Price Moving from One PD Array to the Next)
body:
- **Kind:** rule · price delivery concept
- **What ICT says:** In a directional run, price moves from one PD array (inefficiency) to the next. Each array is a waypoint. As long as each array fails to reverse price (i.e., no close-outside in the opposite direction), price continues to the next array. This is the "chain"—a linked series of targets. "When we were dropping down we were using it for the purpose of the chain of custody where price moves lower from one PD array to the next and every PD array that would fail and indicate an opposite direction in price... lower prices are in order." (0:05:33)
- **How to identify:** Mark all key inefficiencies (FVGs, order blocks, suspension blocks) in your analysis. These are the links in the chain.
- **How to use:** Use the chain as a roadmap. Trade from one target to the next. If price respects the array (close inside), continue to the next target. If price closes outside (opposite direction), the chain is broken and you must recalibrate.
- **Example in this video:** Tuesday's inefficiencies link to Monday's targets link to additional targets. Price runs through each in sequence. (0:05:33–0:06:22)
- **Timestamps:**
  - [0:05:33](https://youtu.be/IF7dEkgWoO0?t=333) — "Chain of custody where price moves lower from one PD array to the next."

title: Post CPI NQ Futures Commentary \ Monday Analysis Delivered - 07/15/2026
head: Bullish Reclaimed Fair Value Gap (Reconfirmation of First Utilization)
body:
- **Kind:** definition · price delivery concept
- **What ICT says:** When a bullish (or bearish) fair value gap is initially invalidated (price closes the opposite way), then later closes back in the original direction, the original bias is "reclaimed" or "reconfirmed." The array is now a "bullish reclaimed FVG" and goes back to its first utilization. "It's now become a bullish reclaimed fair value gap. And it's picked up its first utilization there and we'll change this to dark green." (0:08:47)
- **How to identify:** (1) Identify an array with a bullish first utilization. (2) Price closes bearish (below it), invalidating it. (3) Price later rallies and closes bullish (above it) again, reclaiming it. That reclamation is the signal.
- **How to use:** Once an array is reclaimed, resume trading it in its original direction. It's now a higher-probability setup because it's been tested and confirmed twice.
- **Example in this video:** The suspension block was initially bullish, got invalidated (close below), then was reclaimed (close above) confirming it goes back to being bullish. (0:08:47–0:09:38)
- **Timestamps:**
  - [0:08:47](https://youtu.be/IF7dEkgWoO0?t=527) — "It's now become a bullish reclaimed fair value gap... picked up its first utilization there."

head: Institutional Order Flow Entry Drill
body:
- **Kind:** definition · entry pattern
- **What ICT says:** A partial entry into a PD array, typically around the consequent encroachment level or before it, that shows smart money accumulating into a level. When this happens without touching consequent encroachment, it signals that smart money is entering early (before the full move) and expecting significant continuation. "Institutional order flow entry drill. A partial entry into... not even consequent encroachment." (0:08:47–0:09:38)
- **How to identify:** Look for a price level where a candle begins to bounce/enter an FVG but doesn't go all the way into it. This is a partial entry zone—a hint that smart money is entering.
- **How to use:** When you see an institutional order flow entry drill, expect price to soon accelerate to the full inefficiency (consequent encroachment or beyond). Use it as confirmation to add to positions.
- **Example in this video:** Marked around 0:08:47–0:09:38 where price enters a range but doesn't reach the full level.
- **Timestamps:**

body:

- **What ICT says:** Buy-side imbalance (unfilled buy orders) and sell-side inefficiency (the opposite; zone where buyers were swept/stopped) form together as a single composite array. When price moves past one, traders in that direction get invalidated. "We have buy side and balance sell side inefficiency after creating a close above that wick." (0:04:45) The terminology is sometimes used interchangeably with FVG but refers to the specific order flow structure.
- **How to use:** Treat as a composite PD array. The wick high or low of this structure is the key level to respect.

head: Sniper Mentality (Waiting vs. Chasing)
body:
- **Kind:** rule · psychology · execution approach
- **What ICT says:** Don't chase price or actively pursue it. Instead, set up your entry zone (your "hide"), wait for price to "walk right into your crosshairs," and then execute. This is the opposite of chasing. "We're sitting still. We're trying to get to a vantage point where we can see the mark walk right into our crosshairs and we're not chasing it. We're not pursuing it... we're not reacting. We're anticipating." (0:16:02)
- **How to use:** Before each session, identify your target entry zones based on your model. Don't enter until price reaches those zones. If price runs past them without touching, let it go—don't chase. Wait for the next setup.
- **Example in this video:** ICT had setup zones marked in advance; price eventually walked into them. He didn't adjust or chase; he waited. (0:16:02)
- **Timestamps:**

You're depending on me to point to the next thing versus how about you go through your charts and you come to a expectation using your model." head: Toothpick Support (Weak Support)
body:
- **Kind:** analogy · technical observation
- **What ICT says:** When a large amount of price action is supported by a single thin wick or small candlestick body, that support is weak—like a building held up by a toothpick. This is a warning that price may reverse or fall through. "See all this? We have sell side resting right below here, and we have this single toothpick one little chopstick holding up all this price action." (0:13:36) It's unstable.
- **How to identify:** Look for a large range of price bars above a very thin/small body or wick. That's the toothpick.
- **How to use:** Recognize toothpick support as fragile. When you see it, be prepared for a sudden breakdown or reversal. Don't go long into toothpick-supported moves; instead, short below them.
- **Example in this video:** Marked around 0:13:36. Large block of price action supported by one thin structure.
- **Timestamps:**
  - [0:13:36](https://youtu.be/IF7dEkgWoO0?t=816) — "This single toothpick one little chopstick holding up all this price action."

head: Fed-speaker days: wait for 10:00 and expect wicky "Fed-related delivery"  (aliases ICT uses: Fed-related delivery, time distortion, "tomfoolery")
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - He does not trade until 10:00 because the Fed chair speaks at 10:00 ("give it a little bit of time; work out time distortion"); everything before that is "just to hurt people that think they know what they're doing" (back-and-forth stop runs).
  - After CPI (data that morning/day before) price had gone into the half gap (CE) of the RTH opening range gap as he indicated it would on CPI/PPI.
  - During Fed commentary expect "wild little wick-type moves"; conditions to adhere to depend on the state of the market; today is "Fed-related delivery" and tomorrow too.
  - "Don't strangle your position; give it a chance to cook and let it prove to you one way or the other."
  - Be okay with being stopped out prematurely, or stopped out and then price moves your way; "that is characteristic of the environment."
- **How to use:** for a short at 10:00: stop just above the high, target the liquidity below; give the trade room; don't sit with larger risk than necessary; accept stop-outs.
- **Example in this video:** July 14, 2026, 10:00 ET: short after the Fed chair starts talking; stop just above the high; lots of liquidity below the 8:30 lows.
- **Timestamps:** [0:00:00](https://youtu.be/fFi2QEApVGM?t=0) — going short at 10:00 because of the Fed; [0:00:47](https://youtu.be/fFi2QEApVGM?t=47) — why wait until 10:00; [0:12:12](https://youtu.be/fFi2QEApVGM?t=732) — Fed-related delivery, be cautious, don't strangle; [0:13:00](https://youtu.be/fFi2QEApVGM?t=780) — normal to feel resistance
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Complements L26-002's guidance to avoid NFP/CPI/PPI ahead of the release; this day he trades after 10:00, not before.

body:

He wants to add three more contracts inside it ("tap it one more time"). He then adds back inside both the wick and the lower quadrant of the bearish iFVG. After the low is taken he does not want price to return to the iFVG; if it does, the short is in jeopardy. He later notes the gap must not become an inversion against him (a bullish iFVG snapping into his stop).
- **How to use:** short on taps into the iFVG; add inside the iFVG and its lower quadrant; stop above the gap/high; manage as below.

head: Single-candle run below the 8:30 low  (aliases ICT uses: one single delivery, "40 seconds to do this", liquidity below the 8:30 lows)
body:
- **Kind:** rule / refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - He wants price to run below the 8:30 low in one fast candle: "just one single delivery ... not multiple candles. Multiple candles doesn't bode well for a run all the way down" to the target; a single candle through the low bodes well.
  - He counts down the candle ("we have 40 seconds ... 25 seconds") on the 1-minute candle; by the time he spoke, the candle touched the low but did not get below it.
  - The low of that candle was 652.5 vs the 8:30 low at 651 even (1.5 handles below; digits partial in captions); his limit order was slightly too soft.
  - If price walks through the low it should accelerate toward the event horizon; he does not want it to go back above the low once taken.
- **How to identify:** 1m candle trading below the 8:30 low with a large body that closes below.
- **How to use:** if the single-candle run does not occur (price stalls below/at the low), reduce risk, take a partial, expect a possible return.
- **Example in this video:** ~10:03: price reaches but does not clear the 8:30 low in the first attempt; later it takes the low then reluctantly stalls ("big beefy candle shoot lower; that's what we're looking for").
- **Timestamps:** [0:04:02](https://youtu.be/fFi2QEApVGM?t=242) — single run, not multiple candles; [0:04:49](https://youtu.be/fFi2QEApVGM?t=289) — candle low vs 8:30 low, two pools; [0:09:48](https://youtu.be/fFi2QEApVGM?t=588) — big candle needed
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** A fairly new qualitative "speed of delivery" rule; no hard number beyond the one-candle idea. It did not fully deliver, and he explains why he took partials.

head: Event horizon between two old lows  (aliases ICT uses: event horizon, consequent encroachment between an old low and an old low)

- **What ICT says:** There are two pools of liquidity below: the annotated one and another further down. The midpoint between two old lows is the event horizon (ballparked, "don't be so precise"). He wants a walk through the low and acceleration to the event horizon; if price closes below it, that would indicate a run toward the "545s" (price level, caption partial). First partial: one contract at event horizon; the rest left on the book as limit orders; once at event horizon the stop moves to just below the low of the inversion FVG that sits over the suspension block.
- **How to use:** event horizon = partial target; closing below = run to the next major pool.
- **Example in this video:** targets: 8:30 lows then event horizon, then ~545 area.

title: Trading Complex Opening Ranges With Fed Impact 07/14/2026
head: Stop management in a news/Fed environment: risk-free first, stop above swing high, never "strangle"  (aliases ICT uses: take the risk out, free look, lower the stop, stop just above the high)
body:
- **Kind:** rule (trade management)
- **What ICT says:**
  - Initial stop just above the high of the entry area.
  - After price breaks the low, he lowers the stop to "take the risk out of the trade," but not too low.
  - He did not want to bring the stop to just below the low of the inversion FVG until price got below the low with a body, because the Fed could create a quick jump and wick; a stop at that level "becomes a mechanism for me to worry. I don't want to worry."
  - There was a nice swing high just above where shorts have stops; they could wick it once more while bodies stay below the CE of the wick and still deliver lower prices.
  - "If I'm stopped out, I'm okay. I had a free look." Maximum risk after reducing: a small locked-in amount (he cites dollar figures, caption-garbled).
  - With only one contract left he moves the stop at selected levels; wants a close below the (wick) gap before dropping the stop to just above it; "give it room" so as not to be stopped prematurely.
  - After the partial, stops moved down to a candle level to avoid retracement.
- **How to use:** (1) enter with stop above high; (2) after a partial and after the low is taken, reduce risk; (3) only lower the stop below the iFVG low after a body closes below the low; (4) give room in Fed windows.
- **Example in this video:** short; first partial below the old low; second at event horizon region; stop moved; final stop-out at a small profit/flat.
- **Timestamps:** [0:02:26](https://youtu.be/fFi2QEApVGM?t=146) — takes the risk out; [0:10:37](https://youtu.be/fFi2QEApVGM?t=637) — doesn't lower the stop below the iFVG yet; [0:11:25](https://youtu.be/fFi2QEApVGM?t=685) — swing high, free look; [0:17:05](https://youtu.be/fFi2QEApVGM?t=1025) — close below the gap first, give it room
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** He emphasizes not putting the stop where it causes worry; a mental-comfort rule as much as a technical one.

  - "Making what was made here is sufficient enough. This down here is just a bonus."
  - Lesson on being nimble: an aggressive trader who saw the early wicks (a warning sign of adverse delivery) can close the position early rather than wait for the stop; it depends on experience.

title: Part 2 \ How To Probe Low Probability RTH Opening Ranges 07/14/2026
head: Probing a low-probability RTH opening range: how far can it go?  (aliases ICT uses: probing the low probability opening range, how far can it drop)
body:
- **Kind:** rule / new framing
- **What ICT says:**
  - The prior day's RTH opening range (Monday's) was a low-probability one. His question was "how far can it go [down]?" - so he looked for the limit of the probe, not the gap's upper volume bound.
  - A viewer pointed to a volume imbalance at the top of the daily candle (close 9:31.25-ish vs open 37.75, caption values); he replies price was already below it, so "it's not warranted to concern ourselves with the upper volume bounds"; only the lower volume imbalance mattered for how far it could go.
  - Monday's open: price opened at 9:30, went up and hit the lowest octant of the opening range gap and "that was it"; it went lower.
  - He says viewers who did not listen to yesterday's lecture assumed he mis-annotated.
- **How to identify:** an RTH opening range gap where price opens and fails (rejects) at a low-octant level, signalling that the range will not be traded fully; then identify the lower key level (daily volume imbalance, low end).
- **How to use:** define the probe limit using the higher-timeframe key level (here the low end of a daily volume imbalance); then use lower-timeframe lows near it to anchor entries; if the probe low gets taken, expect a rally back toward the opening range gap CE and beyond.
- **Example in this video:** NQ Monday 7/13: 9:30 open, price rallies to the lowest octant of Monday's RTH opening range gap and fails; sells to the lower volume imbalance on the RTH session; electronic hours (after 4:15 p.m. ET) take it lower, take out a low, then MSS.
- **Timestamps:** [0:00:51](https://youtu.be/bz4QNPcpmWE?t=51) — how far can it go, probing the low-probability opening range; [0:01:43](https://youtu.be/bz4QNPcpmWE?t=103) — upper volume bound not pertinent; [0:11:18](https://youtu.be/bz4QNPcpmWE?t=678) — Monday's open hit the lowest octant and failed
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** The term "low probability opening range" is not defined with numbers; it appears to mean an opening range whose gap is unlikely to be filled / traded early (my reading). Linked to Part 1 (L26-062 trade on the same day).

head: Choose the first low dropping from 9:30 that sits inside a higher-time-frame key level  (aliases ICT uses: higher low for the day or session, relative equal lows inside the daily volume imbalance, key level agreement)

- **How to use:** anchor longs near that low; stop beyond it; the target is the retracement into the opening range gap (CE and upper half) and the NWOG.
- **Example in this video:** NQ Monday: RTH low (relative equal lows) inside the daily volume imbalance low end; ETH re-sweep just below it; reversal.

title: Part 2 \ How To Probe Low Probability RTH Opening Ranges 07/14/2026
head: Overnight sequence to the London buy: breaker + FVG "unicorn"  (aliases ICT uses: breaker, unicorn, order block, change in the state of delivery, midnight candle)
body:
- **Kind:** entry model / example
- **What ICT says:**
  - After the Asia peak price sold off again, through the volume imbalance (yellow), swept the low, then rallied back through that volume imbalance; the midnight candle and its open are marked.
  - London: price trades lower into a breaker (a low, a high, a lower low = the breaker pattern: "no volume profile, no footprint required") that also has a fair value gap at the same location, which he calls a "unicorn... super strong."
  - He also describes an earlier retracement into an order block with the change in the state of delivery at the open (draws it); price rallies away, comes back into the breaker; creates another small FVG; expects higher prices; relative equal highs above.
  - A scalper could take the first high and be content; otherwise look higher in the direction discussed the day before.
- **How to identify:** low -> high -> lower low sequence forming a breaker; an FVG overlapping at the same price = unicorn.
- **How to use:** buy the retracement into the breaker/FVG after the sweep; target relative equal highs, then the opening range gap.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 1m, London session on 7/14: sweep of the overnight low, rally, retrace into an order block, drop to a breaker with an FVG at the same location, rally away, small FVG, relative equal highs.

  - A six-to-seven-week big daily range; price dropped between two daily wicks; a volume imbalance sits at the low. He shades the area gray "because I don't want to imply a direction yet."
  - Always grade a wick: put a fib on it and show the 50% (CE). Last Friday's discount wick CE could act simply as a premium array; a close above it on the daily would warrant likely higher prices; the next level is the CE of the other wick.
  - The suspension block below has not fully closed in; wicks are enough "to build an initial idea."
  - Daily volume imbalance down there is what he wants to act like a breakaway gap: if price is not interested in returning to it, the sell-side liquidity there was enough to send price higher.
- **How to identify:** two daily wicks; the volume imbalance/space between their lows; the CE of each wick.
- **How to use:** premium/discount read from the wick CE; look for longs if price is in discount and holds above; use the volume imbalance as the limit of how far a probe can go.
- **Example in this video:** NQ daily: drop between two wicks and into discount; volume imbalance at the low; Friday's wick CE as premium array.

title: How To Probe Low Probability RTH Opening Ranges 07/13/2026
head: Preparing the RTH opening range gap CE before 9:30 (manual fib)  (aliases ICT uses: RTH ORG, half gap, mid gap, regular trading hours opening range gap CE)
body:
- **Kind:** rule (process) / how-to
- **What ICT says:**
  - With a large gap between Friday's settlement (RTH close, about 30,048.5 per captions) and the pending Monday open, prepare before the bell: put the fib on the exact Friday settlement level, drop it down toward the 9:32/9:33 mark on the time axis (not at 9:30, so you can see the candle open), enable "show all levels," make the CE line black and thick.
  - When the 9:30 opening price prints, drag the fib's other anchor to it; the 50% is the "RTH ORG CE" (label it so you do not lose sight of it).
  - Prefer drawing manually to scripts: scripts can only crunch the data they're given, the platform's data sometimes looks wrong, and doing it by hand keeps you involved ("as the author, if it doesn't jive with me, I won't use it").
  - A huge gap tends to attract an attempt to fill; he thinks the market is predisposed to draw toward the purple Friday-settlement line and toward buy-side near the 30,048.5 level, though it doesn't need to get there.
  - He estimates about 70% likelihood that price rallies to the CE of the RTH ORG around 10:00 ("that's usually the statistics"; caption unclear).
- **How to identify:** RTH ORG = prior-day RTH settlement (last print) to the 9:30 open; CE = 50%.
- **How to use:** CE as the first target for the gap draw, expect to approach it by about 10:00; a probe long uses the stop under the CE of the wick, etc.
- **Example in this video:** Monday 7/13: Friday settlement ~30,048.5; Monday's open lower (opening price implied about 29,714.5 given the 7/14 CE of ~29,881.5, my arithmetic from L26-063); RTH ORG CE annotated.
- **Timestamps:** [0:10:33](https://youtu.be/rtIcbG6twrI?t=633) — Friday settlement colored purple; [0:12:09](https://youtu.be/rtIcbG6twrI?t=729) — how I prepare: fib on the level; [0:13:46](https://youtu.be/rtIcbG6twrI?t=826) — CE of RTH ORG labeled; [0:14:37](https://youtu.be/rtIcbG6twrI?t=877) — drag to the opening price, manual preference; [0:17:02](https://youtu.be/rtIcbG6twrI?t=1022) — 70% likely to go up by 10:00
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** The 70% figure is his stated approximate statistic (caption unclear whether it refers to price reaching the CE). Consistent with L26-047 about RTH ORG definitions.

head: Probe trade: one contract, bullish order block, and what failure means  (aliases ICT uses: head fake, probe, paper cut, failure to launch, scratch)
body:
- **Kind:** example / entry model (exploratory)
- **What ICT says:**
  - He only wants "more information from the opening range, first 30 minutes" before committing; with a one-contract paper account ("for compliance reasons") he explores.
  - Trade 1 (long probe): after taking a short-term low he trades into a bullish order block (a down-close candle) with change in state of delivery; he enters long; plan: as long as the close stays above the halfway point (CE) of the wick, he's fine; stop just below that CE and below the low, no partials possible with one contract. A head fake (a 9:30 opening pop then drop) occurs; the long fails.
  - Trade 2 (short): he sells short at the CE of a wick (near a lower low that only had a small shallow wick through it) with a stop just above; the plan: sell-side liquidity is the draw; after taking it, reverse and go long to recover the loss; he wants bodies to stay below half of the wick.
  - Price came right to the event horizon but his limit order did not fill ("classic"); stop moved to break-even; price then dove aggressively; he describes it as "two executions, one scratch, minor little thing, then came back for a run - pretty positive outcome."
  - A body below the level is "much more significant than just doing wicks": he wants the body, not the wick, through the low.
  - Failure of one side tells him what to look for on the opposite side - but "that doesn't mean if you take a loss going long, it's always a sell short."
- **How to use:** take small, defined probes at levels with clear invalidation (stop under the CE/low), and read the failure for information; do not force.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 1m 9:30-10:10 on 7/13/2026: long at a bullish OB after a short-term low is taken; head-fake opening; stopped; short at the CE of a wick with the stop above; draw = sell-side liquidity/lower low; scratch near break-even; price rallies, then reverses.
- **Timestamps:** [0:16:14](https://youtu.be/rtIcbG6twrI?t=974) — bullish OB, CISD, head fake; [0:17:51](https://youtu.be/rtIcbG6twrI?t=1071) — stay in upper half of the wick, one contract; [0:20:18](https://youtu.be/rtIcbG6twrI?t=1218) — short at CE of the wick, draw = sell side; [0:28:13](https://youtu.be/rtIcbG6twrI?t=1693) — body vs wick; [0:41:02](https://youtu.be/rtIcbG6twrI?t=2462) — "two executions, one scratch"
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Paper trading, one contract. He does not give exact entry/exit prices in the captions.

title: How To Probe Low Probability RTH Opening Ranges 07/13/2026
head: Candle-count rule inside an inefficiency (1-2 healthy, 3-5 failure)  (aliases ICT uses: crowded house, block party, a market in a hurry, no more than five candles)
body:
- **Kind:** rule (new/most-emphasized teaching of the video)
- **What ICT says:**
  - "The only time I'm counting candles is when inside inefficiencies." A market that wants to go somewhere does not spend time inside a gap: it enters with one candle, doesn't leave a body there, and doesn't close the gap or even reach half of its range (CE).
  - Ideal: price displaces within the next candle or two. "Inefficiencies, you want to have one, two at most. Three, the probability starts to shift lower. If you're booking three to five candles inside that inefficiency, you don't want to see that." A "crowded house inside of an inefficiency" is not wanted.
  - "No more than five candles" - at the fifth candle "this is the last ditch. It's got to do it now or it's failing."
  - Example: a bearish gap after the drop: candle one went in, then the second; he says it must displace aggressively lower on this or the next candle or "we go to a different neighborhood" (higher). Spending way too many candles inside = a signal; he contrasts this with retail "support turned resistance."
  - He denies counting candles for the 13th/17th/21st candle type of retail counts.
- **How to identify:** when price retraces into a gap/inefficiency, count candles that trade inside it.
- **How to use:** if bearish, require displacement lower within one or two candles of entering the bearish gap; at three the probability shifts against you; five = failed; use the failure to flip to the opposite expectation (here, back up to the old low).
- **Example in this video:** NQ 1m after the morning drop: price retraces into a bearish fair value gap and spends five candles in it, fails to displace, and goes back above; it rallies to the old low.
- **Timestamps:** [0:41:53](https://youtu.be/rtIcbG6twrI?t=2513) — one candle, then the next; no crowded house; 1-2 at most; [0:42:40](https://youtu.be/rtIcbG6twrI?t=2560) — market in a hurry doesn't linger; [0:43:27](https://youtu.be/rtIcbG6twrI?t=2607) — counting candles only inside inefficiencies, no more than five; [0:44:14](https://youtu.be/rtIcbG6twrI?t=2654) — last ditch
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** New explicit candle-count thresholds (1-2 good, 3 weaker, 5 max). Related to earlier "how far into the gap" CE rules.

title: How To Probe Low Probability RTH Opening Ranges 07/13/2026
head: Do not sell short in an extreme discount; PD failing = information  (aliases ICT uses: sell in premium buy in discount, premium sensitivity, no premium sensitivity)
body:
- **Kind:** rule (reaffirmed core principle)
- **What ICT says:**
  - Selling at the low of the day's range (from RTH high to RTH low = extreme discount) "goes against what I taught in the very first month" of his 2016 private mentorship; "you want to buy in a discount."
  - Because the bearish gap failed to offer premium sensitivity (price showed it was unwilling to go higher but then went higher) and spent too many candles there, it was a failing array; recognizing when a PD array is not confirming is "not failure in the sense that they've changed the algorithm" - it is information.
  - When the sell setup fails, price is likely to draw back up to the old low (buy stops); this wiped out shorts who trailed stops; it then tests whether the lower area works as a discount array to go higher or "wilts through it" and the gap acts as bearish again, sending price to event horizon and then relative equal lows.
  - Advice: listen to the first four videos of the 2016 mentorship; more valuable than any new tool.
- **How to use:** don't sell inside a discount just because a bearish FVG formed; require premium sensitivity; if it fails, expect a return to the old low.
- **Example in this video:** NQ Monday 10:00-10:10: bearish FVG formed after a big drop into a discount; fails after 5 candles; price returns to the old low (range from RTH high down to the lows, "one low, two low, three low," then a full rally back).
- **Timestamps:** [0:44:14](https://youtu.be/rtIcbG6twrI?t=2654) — selling at the low goes against month one of 2016 mentorship; [0:45:01](https://youtu.be/rtIcbG6twrI?t=2701) — don't sell in a discount, premium sensitivity failure; [0:46:39](https://youtu.be/rtIcbG6twrI?t=2799) — PDAs not confirming is not failure; [0:49:03](https://youtu.be/rtIcbG6twrI?t=2943) — price draws back up to the old low
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Contrast with L26-062, where a short at 10:00 worked from premium (above the 8:30 low) not from a discount.

title: How To Probe Low Probability RTH Opening Ranges 07/13/2026
head: Liquidity void in RTH; RTH has more weight than ETH  (aliases ICT uses: liquidity void, vacuum of price, regular trading hours vs electronic trading hours)
body:
- **Kind:** rule / definition
- **What ICT says:**
  - On the RTH-only chart, a stretch between one candle's low and another's high with no prints in regular trading hours is a "liquidity void," even if electronic hours traded through it; RTH "has to balance out" ETH "to be an efficiently delivered price."
  - Mismatches create imbalances seen in only one session, but RTH carries more weight because RTH tends to overlap and redeliver to levels ETH has already seen overnight; ETH has been trading since 6:00 p.m. Sunday ET, so those levels haven't been done yet in RTH; hence it is more interesting to see price go up into the gap with no RTH prints.
  - It could drop and never visit, but "more times than not" it adheres to this logic.
- **How to identify:** switch to the RTH chart; look for a price range between candles with no prints in RTH; compare with ETH.
- **How to use:** treat RTH voids as draws/targets (here the opening gap above); weight them over ETH-only inefficiencies.
- **Example in this video:** NQ Monday: RTH gap from Friday's settlement (~30,048.5) down to the open (~29,714.5, implied); price heads up into it later in the day/week.
- **Timestamps:** [0:35:25](https://youtu.be/rtIcbG6twrI?t=2125) — liquidity void with no RTH prints; [0:36:13](https://youtu.be/rtIcbG6twrI?t=2173) — RTH weighted over ETH; [0:37:00](https://youtu.be/rtIcbG6twrI?t=2220) — more times than not
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Links to RTH ORG theory (L26-047) and to "liquidity voids" in the canonical list.
