title: Market Review & NQ Futures Trade Recap 07/08/2026
head: Order Block (aliases: OB, bearish order block, bullish order block)
body:
- **Kind:** definition + rule + entry model
- **What ICT says:** The open of the bearish order block is the last up-close candle among consecutive larger candles. Until price closes below it, changes in state of delivery don't apply. Only when price breaches below it does the level become salient and pertinent to price action decision-making. Specifically mentioned: 29,282.50 level on daily NQ chart on 07/08.
- **How to identify:** Scan left for the largest consecutive up-close candles (last one is the OB); mark the open of that final candle.
- **How to use:** Once breached with a close below, the order block validates directional continuation. When trading near it on lower timeframes (1m), wicking up into it while inside other confluences (macro, breaker) suggests rejection and further downside.
- **Example in this video:** NQ daily, 29,282.50 level (bearish order block open). Price tested it on 1m timeframe at ~10:05 ET while inside the breaker formation; wicked up into it and then fell through, continuing the sell-model decline to 29,250 area.
- **Timestamps:** [0:00:50](https://youtu.be/JmAJfuSkY1g?t=50) (OB defined) · [0:05:42](https://youtu.be/JmAJfuSkY1g?t=342) (daily 29,282.50 level) · [0:13:36](https://youtu.be/JmAJfuSkY1g?t=816) (daily OB being wicked up to on 1m) · [0:18:27](https://youtu.be/JmAJfuSkY1g?t=1107) (confluence: bearish OB + macro + breaker).
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Opening of the candle is irrelevant unless price gets below it. The order block is the *last* up-close candle if it's the largest; consecutive candle size is the deciding factor.

title: Market Review & NQ Futures Trade Recap 07/08/2026
head: Consequent Encroachment (aliases: CE, wick grading)
body:
- **Kind:** refinement + rule
- **What ICT says:** When price leaves a wick, that wick—specifically its extension into the next level—must be "graded" or considered. If price closes below the consequent encroachment (the wick's deep point), it signals continuation. If it doesn't close below, price may retrace, consolidate, or reverse. This applies to daily wicks on lower timeframes (1m) and to inefficiency wicks.
- **How to identify:** Look at the wick on any candle; draw a line at the wick's lowest point (for bearish setups, the wick extends down).
- **How to use:** Use as a rejection filter: if price wicks up into consequent encroachment but fails to close above it (or vice versa for bullish CEs), expect reversal or consolidation. For entries, position stops just outside the CE to avoid wick whipsaws.
- **Example in this video:** NDOG consequent encroachment (the wick extension of the new day opening gap); price fails to leave a body at or above it multiple times, signaling no bullish intent. Also: inversion FVG wick CE at ~29,270; price wicks up but body stays in lower octants, indicating weakness and bearish pressure continuing.
- **Timestamps:** [0:01:40](https://youtu.be/JmAJfuSkY1g?t=100) (wick grading concept) · [0:08:50](https://youtu.be/JmAJfuSkY1g?t=530) (NDOG CE definition) · [0:09:37](https://youtu.be/JmAJfuSkY1g?t=577) (bearish action when failing to leave body above NDOG CE) · [0:15:11](https://youtu.be/JmAJfuSkY1g?t=911) (inversion FVG CE: wick can't touch it).
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Consequent encroachment of a wick is not support/resistance; it's an inefficiency marker. If not breached, it's weakness, not strength.

title: Market Review & NQ Futures Trade Recap 07/08/2026
head: Market Maker Sell Model (aliases: MMSM, sell model)
body:
- **Kind:** entry model + rule
- **What ICT says:** Original consolidation → leaves consolidation → comes back to test consolidation → first stage reaccumulation → second stage reaccumulation → smart money reversal → low-risk sell → first stage distribution → second stage distribution → drop below original consolidation to take lows. When bullish, the model will NOT take out the original consolidation; it will stop in deep discount but outside the sell-side liquidity.
- **How to identify:** Scan for consolidation (ranging price); identify the break and rejection back into it; count two reaccumulation stages, then reversal candle, then two distribution stages.
- **How to use:** The second stage distribution is the largest, easiest, longest-magnitude move. Enter near reversal with targets at sell-side liquidity or relative equal lows below consolidation. Stop above the breaker (high-low-higher high structure).
- **Example in this video:** NQ 1m on 07/08, 9:30 ET open started a MMSM. Original consolidation near NDOG; price rallied into NDOG, failed to break above NDOG CE, retraced, then executed second stage distribution to take lows at ~29,250 and relative equal lows lower.
- **Timestamps:** [0:03:17](https://youtu.be/JmAJfuSkY1g?t=197) (MMSM structure) · [0:18:27](https://youtu.be/JmAJfuSkY1g?t=1107) (MMSM in action: second stage distribution) · [0:20:51](https://youtu.be/JmAJfuSkY1g?t=1251) (MMSM variation: when bullish, doesn't take original consolidation).
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** When bullish, MMSM stops in deep discount, not at original consolidation. Must confirm with other confluences before entry.

title: Market Review & NQ Futures Trade Recap 07/08/2026
head: Fair Value Gap (FVG) and Inversion FVG (aliases: iFVG, bullish/bearish inefficiency)
body:
- **Kind:** definition + rule + entry model
- **What ICT says:** A fair value gap is a sell-side or buy-side inefficiency—the difference between the close of one candle and the open of a later candle, leaving imbalanced price. An inversion FVG is one where the body stays on one side (bullish or bearish). Volume imbalance: one tick difference in open/close (e.g., open 252.75, close 252.50 = 1-tick imbalance). When price trades into an FVG unwilling to lay a body on the opposite side of consequent encroachment, it's weak; when it closes below/above, it's strong directional continuation.
- **How to identify:** Look for gaps in price action; mark the high of the lower candle to the low of the higher candle (sell-side) or vice versa (buy-side).
- **How to use:** Entries can target FVG retracements. Exits can be placed at FVG bodies. If price enters an FVG and fails to commit (body on wrong side), expect reversal.
- **Example in this video:** Bearish inversion iFVG after the 10:00 ET rally into NDOG; price enters it unwilling to close above consequent encroachment, signaling bearish continuation. Second example: bullish iFVG on the 29,250 retest; price enters and commits with body above, launching the next rally phase.
- **Timestamps:** [0:10:24](https://youtu.be/JmAJfuSkY1g?t=624) (FVG/iFVG definition: 1-tick imbalance) · [0:11:13](https://youtu.be/JmAJfuSkY1g?t=673) (inversion iFVG: unwilling to commit) · [0:12:00](https://youtu.be/JmAJfuSkY1g?t=720) (inversion iFVG now being respected, role reversal).
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Inversion FVG role-play: if it doesn't propel price in one direction (e.g., up), it may reverse and pull down.

title: Market Review & NQ Futures Trade Recap 07/08/2026
head: Bearish Breaker (aliases: breaker, high-low-higher high)
body:
- **Kind:** definition + rule
- **What ICT says:** A bearish breaker is a short-term high, a low below it, and a higher high (but lower than the original short-term high). Must use the body that reaches lowest, not wicks. Breaker placement is critical for stop loss above it and for confluence with other sell signals.
- **How to identify:** Scan for a small swing high; then lower low; then test back up but not above the first high. Mark the body of the candle making the highest of that higher high.
- **How to use:** Place sell stops just above the breaker body (not the wick). Enter shorts into the breaker if macro, OB, or FVG confluences support it. Breaker failure (close above) = trend reversal.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 1m, ~10:05–10:12 ET, a bearish breaker formed (short-term high, low, higher high below it). Sell entry was placed at this breaker with stops above the breaker body. Breaker wicked up to daily OB and failed, confirming the short.
- **Timestamps:** [0:12:46](https://youtu.be/JmAJfuSkY1g?t=766) (breaker definition: short-term high, low, higher high) · [0:24:01](https://youtu.be/JmAJfuSkY1g?t=1441) (entry off breaker, finessing stop placement).
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Don't use wicks for breaker identification; use bodies only. Breaker is a 1m-level structure; it must align with higher-timeframe confluences.

title: Market Review & NQ Futures Trade Recap 07/08/2026
head: New Day Opening Gap (aliases: NDOG, opening gap)
body:
- **Kind:** definition + rule
- **What ICT says:** The difference between settlement price (RTH close at 4:59 ET previous day) and RTH open at 9:30 ET next day (actually 6:00 PM ET previous day to 9:30 ET next day in NQ's continuous session). NDOG has consequent encroachment (the wick extension). If price fails to leave a body at or above NDOG CE, that's bearish. If it does and closes above, that's bullish.
- **How to identify:** Mark previous day's RTH close and current day's 6:00 PM open (electronic open); also mark 9:30 RTH open. NDOG CE is the wick into one of these.
- **How to use:** NDOG acts as a bearish or bullish bias filter. Failed body above NDOG CE = no bullish intent. Successful close above = bullish intent. Also used as PD array discount or premium source for targets.
- **Example in this video:** NQ on 07/08, NDOG was set from 07/07 4:59 ET close to 07/08 6:00 PM ET open. Price rallied into NDOG at 9:30 open but failed to leave a body above NDOG CE, signaling bearish.
- **Timestamps:** [0:07:14](https://youtu.be/JmAJfuSkY1g?t=434) (NDOG defined) · [0:08:50](https://youtu.be/JmAJfuSkY1g?t=530) (NDOG CE: doesn't leave body above = bearish) · [0:09:37](https://youtu.be/JmAJfuSkY1g?t=577) (part of MMSM, NDOG failure = selloff).
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** NDOG is a higher-timeframe filter; failure on 1m doesn't mean rejection of entire NDOG; must watch for closes and body placement.

title: Market Review & NQ Futures Trade Recap 07/08/2026
head: Opening Range Gap (aliases: ORG, RTH opening range gap)
body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:** The difference between RTH open at 9:30 ET and RTH close at 4:59 ET the same day. This is a daily structure. 70% likelihood of trading to the 50% midpoint (consequent encroachment) within 9:30-10:00 ET.
- **How to identify:** Mark 9:30 open and 4:59 close on daily; plot Fibonacci levels; focus on 50% midpoint.
- **How to use:** Targets, support in deep discounts, entry confirmation when price holds or rejects at ORG levels.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 07/08, ORG from 9:30 open. Price ran into new day opening gap at 10:00, failed, then dropped. Later, rallied back and used ORG 50% as support.
- **Timestamps:** [0:16:02](https://youtu.be/JmAJfuSkY1g?t=962) (ORG definition, contrasted with NDOG) · [0:16:53](https://youtu.be/JmAJfuSkY1g?t=1013) (ORG 50% = 70% likelihood by 10:00 ET).
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** NDOG is part of ORG; ORG is the 9:30–4:59 structure.

title: Market Review & NQ Futures Trade Recap 07/08/2026
head: Macro (aliases: macros, algorithmic time window, 10:50–11:10, Silver Bullet)
body:
- **Kind:** rule + timing
- **What ICT says:** Macros are algorithmic time windows when institutional order flow has a higher likelihood of executing. 10:50–11:10 ET is cited in this video as a macro. It's a known timing confluence that can validate a turn (especially at second stage distribution).
- **How to identify:** Memorize key macros: 10:50–11:10 ET (often cited for NY AM); also 8:30 ET, 2:00 PM ET, and others.
- **How to use:** Use as a confluence filter; if you're near a turn and macro is active, higher conviction. Do NOT trade macro alone.
- **Example in this video:** At 10:50 ET, price was inside bearish breaker, MMSM, NDOG rejection, and daily OB—all validated by the 10:50–11:10 macro turn; selloff accelerated.

title: Market Review & NQ Futures Trade Recap 07/08/2026
head: Volume Imbalance and Inefficiency
body:
- **Kind:** refinement
- **What ICT says:** A 1-tick difference between candle open and close (e.g., open 252.75, close 252.50) is a micro-volume imbalance and therefore an inefficiency (fair value gap). These micro-imbalances are part of the larger PD array framework.
- **How to identify:** Compare open and close of individual candles; 1-tick (or small) difference = imbalance.
- **How to use:** These micro-imbalances can act as rejections; price unwilling to fully commit above or below them may reverse or consolidate.
- **Example in this video:** Within the bearish iFVG at 10:00, price open 252.75, close 252.50 = 1-tick imbalance, part of the inefficiency definition.
- **Timestamps:** [0:10:24](https://youtu.be/JmAJfuSkY1g?t=624) (1-tick imbalance in FVG).
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Micro-imbalances are beneath most retail awareness; ICT emphasizes they're real inefficiencies.

title: One Shot - One Kill Trade Setup Review
head: Discount Daily Wick (aliases: daily wick, discount wick)
body:
- **Kind:** definition + rule
- **What ICT says:** A wick on the daily chart extending below the body, indicating price exploration to a lower level. This wick's low and its consequent encroachment (the deep point) form the "discount" region. When lower timeframes pull back into this discount wick area, smart money likely to accumulate short positions there or ride the momentum into it.
- **How to identify:** Look at the daily chart; find a candle with a significant wick below the body (usually a reversal or consolidation day).
- **How to use:** Use the discount wick low and its consequent encroachment as target zones for lower-timeframe shorts. If price on a 15m or 1m chart gravitates into the discount wick CE, it signals institutional participation. This is also known as a "draw to liquidity."
- **Example in this video:** Daily Nasdaq discount wick low ~29,021 area, CE at 29,221.75. Price rallied on 1m/15m, then pulled down into this discount wick, targeting it as the delivery zone and delivering exactly to that level before sharply reversing higher.
- **Timestamps:** [0:00:53](https://youtu.be/zq4hz_XiTRE?t=53) (discount wick intro) · [0:02:28](https://youtu.be/zq4hz_XiTRE?t=148) (discount wick boundary: 29,021, CE 29,221.75) · [0:08:05](https://youtu.be/zq4hz_XiTRE?t=485) (discount wick acts as low hanging fruit objective) · [0:20:02](https://youtu.be/zq4hz_XiTRE?t=1202) (price delivered down to discount wick).
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** The discount wick acts as a strong institutional target; once swept, expect mean reversion and sharp reversal higher.

title: One Shot - One Kill Trade Setup Review
head: 15-Minute Timeframe as Bellwether Chart (aliases: 15m, bellwether)
body:
- **Kind:** rule + refinement
- **What ICT says:** The 15-minute timeframe is a "really strong go-to" for intraday and short-term trading. It is a bellwether chart—strong, reliable enough to frame all day trading and scalping. It's versatile: you can use it standalone for day-trade setups, OR you can use it to confirm daily bias. It bridges the gap between daily context and 1-minute scalps. Unlike the 1-minute (which is noisy), the 15-minute shows clean, actionable price structures.
- **How to identify:** Pull up the 15m chart alongside your daily; note how 15m moves are cleaner and easier to define structures on.
- **How to use:** If you can't structure a daily thesis, don't trade intraday—your 15m scalps will be guesses. Build your daily case first, then use 15m to refine entry timing and stop placement. The 15m can also be a standalone timeframe if your daily is unclear.
- **Example in this video:** The entire review is grounded in daily discount wick theory; the 15m chart showed clean relative equal highs/lows, SIBI levels, and gaps that confirmed the daily thesis. Price action was much crisper on 15m than 1m.
- **Timestamps:** [0:00:53](https://youtu.be/zq4hz_XiTRE?t=53) (15m as bellwether) · [0:04:03](https://youtu.be/zq4hz_XiTRE?t=243) (15m as frame for all day trading and scalping).
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Using 15m doesn't mean ignoring daily; it means daily is foundation, 15m is execution timeframe.

title: One Shot - One Kill Trade Setup Review
head: Buy-Side Liquidity and Sell-Side Liquidity (aliases: BSL, SSL, old high, old low, relative equal liquidity pools)
body:
- **Kind:** definition + rule
- **What ICT says:** Buy-side liquidity is resting above a recent high (where buy orders sit unfilled during rallies; smart money looks to take them out with a spike, then reverse lower). Sell-side liquidity is below a recent low (where sell orders sit; smart money spikes lower to take them, then reverses higher). These are the pools of resting orders that institutional order flow "takes out" or sweeps. When you see a spike to a level and then a reversal, that level was likely liquidity being targeted.
- **How to identify:** Mark recent swing highs and lows on your 15m or daily; label them as BSL and SSL respectively.
- **How to use:** Use them as targets. When you're short, your target is often an SSL (take out the sell-side, then reverse). When you're long, target BSL. Smart money adds to positions when these are being swept. When all BSL is taken and price reverses down, expect a continuation of the downtrend.
- **Example in this video:** Monday's relative equal highs contained buy-side liquidity; price spiked to take it, and Michael announced beforehand he expected this. After BSL was taken, price rolled over and delivered down into discount wick.
- **Timestamps:** [0:04:03](https://youtu.be/zq4hz_XiTRE?t=243) (BSL resting above old high) · [0:05:40](https://youtu.be/zq4hz_XiTRE?t=340) (BSL taken, then expected to work toward SSL) · [0:10:26](https://youtu.be/zq4hz_XiTRE?t=626) (smart money accumulates shorts when BSL taken, SSL defined).
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Once BSL/SSL is taken, the direction flips; don't expect another reversal back to it in that move.

title: One Shot - One Kill Trade Setup Review
head: Relative Equal Highs / Relative Equal Lows (aliases: REH, REL, equal levels, relative equal liquidity)
body:
- **Kind:** definition + rule
- **What ICT says:** Relative equal highs are two or more swing highs at approximately the same price level. Same for lows. These represent a "pool of liquidity"—likely where many stop losses or limit orders cluster. When price approaches a REH/REL, it often pauses, reverses, or sweeps through. These are NOT support/resistance; they're institutional reference points.
- **How to identify:** Scan backward for the last 5–20 candles on your 15m or 1m; find two or more local highs or lows within 5–10 ticks of each other.
- **How to use:** Use as targets on reversals. If you're short and price is near a REL, that's a likely target (where the sweep finishes before a reversal up). If long, REH is your target.
- **Example in this video:** Monday lunch macro setup formed relative equal highs; smart money hammered them (took BSL), then reversed down. Later, new RELs formed below the old swing low, and price targeted those as well.
- **Timestamps:** [0:07:15](https://youtu.be/zq4hz_XiTRE?t=435) (REL as target: relative equal lows) · [0:12:01](https://youtu.be/zq4hz_XiTRE?t=721) (REH during lunch macro) · [0:13:37](https://youtu.be/zq4hz_XiTRE?t=817) (REL based on old pool of liquidity, algorithm likely to draw down into it).
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** RELs can be formed on new data (e.g., a current low at same level as an older low), creating a fresh institutional reference point.

title: One Shot - One Kill Trade Setup Review
head: Inversion Fair Value Gap (aliases: iFVG, inversion inefficiency, bullish/bearish inversion)
body:
- **Kind:** definition + rule
- **What ICT says:** An inversion FVG is a gap where price enters but does not commit (i.e., the bodies stay on one side and wicks fail to reach the other side). Example: price gaps up, but all bodies trade in the lower half of the gap, showing no real upside commitment—bearish inversion. It's expected to reverse and use the gap as a target on the reversal. Inversion FVGs act as "first presented" gaps on subsequent moves.
- **How to identify:** Look for a gap (open to close imbalance); then watch if price's bodies respect one side. If bodies stay in lower half and wicks don't reach upper half, it's a bearish inversion FVG.
- **How to use:** Inversion FVGs are reversal filters. If you're short and price approaches a bearish inversion iFVG, it's likely to reverse back down (use it as a target below). On the reversal lower, the same iFVG may act as first presented FVG and offer targets on the new direction.
- **Example in this video:** An inversion FVG formed on Monday opening range; bodies stayed in lower octants, wicks couldn't touch upper half—bearish sign. On subsequent moves down, this same gap was used as a bounce/target.
- **Timestamps:** [0:08:05](https://youtu.be/zq4hz_XiTRE?t=485) (inversion FVG acts as target) · [0:14:26](https://youtu.be/zq4hz_XiTRE?t=866) (first presented FVG is an inversion, treated as such on next move) · [0:18:24](https://youtu.be/zq4hz_XiTRE?t=1104) (correct perspective on iFVG: all volume in lower half, no real upside reach).
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Inversion FVGs change their role; if initially bearish (bodies in lower half), on the next move they often become bullish (liquidity target on the bounce).

title: One Shot - One Kill Trade Setup Review
head: Model 2022 / ICT Optimal Trade Entry (OTE) (aliases: OTE, swing low model, oldest model)
body:
- **Kind:** entry model
- **What ICT says:** A simple structure: find a swing low, watch for price to trade through it (break), then immediately come back up testing that same level as support. This "test back" is the OTE—the optimal trade entry. Enter longs at or just above the swing low on this retest. Stop below the swing low. Targets are usually defined by higher-level inefficiencies or old highs.
- **How to identify:** Identify a swing low on your timeframe; wait for price to break below it; then wait for price to rally back and test it.
- **How to use:** Enter long on the retest (or on the candle break back above). Risk is below the swing low. This is ICT's oldest, simplest model—rock-solid and repeatable on any timeframe.
- **Example in this video:** A swing low was broken on Monday; price came back to test it. This was identified as the OTE setup, and Michael noted low-hanging fruit targets at the first gap level above and then higher inefficiencies.
- **Timestamps:** [0:10:26](https://youtu.be/zq4hz_XiTRE?t=626) (Model 2022 / OTE structure) · [0:11:13](https://youtu.be/zq4hz_XiTRE?t=673) (OTE low-hanging fruit objectives defined).
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** This model is timeless; it works because institutional traders use swing lows as reference points and test them for liquidity.

title: One Shot - One Kill Trade Setup Review
head: Lunch Macro (aliases: lunch period, 11:30 ET – 1:30 PM ET, 11:50 to 12:10 macro)
body:
- **Kind:** timing rule
- **What ICT says:** The lunch period is 11:30 AM to 1:30 PM ET. Within this, a setup usually forms between 11:30–12:30 (first hour). Then, a macro algorithmic window at 11:50–12:10 AM is when the algorithm "spools" and begins moving the market. The 10:00 low (from a prior swing) is a key liquidity reference during this macro.
- **How to identify:** Mark 11:30–1:30 PM on your chart; look for structures forming in the first hour and confirming between 11:50–12:10.
- **How to use:** If a setup is forming during lunch, wait for the 11:50–12:10 algorithm window to trigger. If it doesn't deliver during the second hour (12:10–1:30), hold for entry into the PM session.
- **Example in this video:** Monday's lunch setup formed relative equal highs; at 11:50–12:10, the algorithm took buy-side liquidity and then reversed. The 10:00 low from earlier was used as a target.
- **Timestamps:** [0:12:01](https://youtu.be/zq4hz_XiTRE?t=721) (lunch macro 11:30 to 1:30 PM, setup in first hour) · [0:12:01](https://youtu.be/zq4hz_XiTRE?t=721) (11:50 to 12:10 macro when algorithm spools).
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** If the algorithm doesn't confirm during the second hour, it may re-run in the PM session; don't force it in the first hour.

title: One Shot - One Kill Trade Setup Review
head: SIBI (aliases: single imbalance, SIBI price level)
body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:** SIBI refers to a single imbalance level on a lower timeframe (often 15m or 1m). It's a candle with a small gap between open and close (or a wick), creating a micro-inefficiency. Mentioned in context: price "utilized" the SIBI, then used it again, indicating it's a liquidity reference point for smart money to target.
- **How to identify:** Look for 15m candles with very small bodies or wicks; these are SIBIs.
- **How to use:** SIBIs can act as entry points for smart money; if a SIBI is broken, expect a retest or a continuation through it. They're also stop-loss reference points.
- **Example in this video:** Michael noted SIBIs on the 15m chart (visible on his slides but not detailed in transcript); price used them as entry/exit points.

- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** SIBI is a lower-timeframe detail; don't use it in isolation; always confirm with daily bias.

title: One Shot - One Kill Trade Setup Review
head: Suspension Block (aliases: suspension, suspension candle)
body:
- **Kind:** definition + rule
- **What ICT says:** A suspension block is a candle with volume imbalance at both high and low—neither side commits. It signals neither bulls nor bears are in control; the next candle often delivers direction decisively. Michael notes it as "bearish" in context when it appears near resistance and precedes a breakdown.
- **How to identify:** Look for a candle with a small body and wicks at both ends (near equal high and low wicks).
- **How to use:** Suspension blocks are pause signals; they precede directional delivery. If you're near a level and see a suspension, prepare for a breakout (direction TBD until confirmed).
- **Example in this video:** A suspension block formed on Tuesday morning near the overnight high; this was bearish because it was at resistance, and the market subsequently broke lower.
- **Timestamps:** [0:15:16](https://youtu.be/zq4hz_XiTRE?t=916) (suspension block, volume imbalance at high and low, bearish context).
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Suspension blocks are neutral by themselves; context (location on chart, higher-timeframe bias) determines bullish or bearish significance.

title: One Shot - One Kill Trade Setup Review
head: One Shot One Kill Model (aliases: OSOK, short-term trading swing, 2–5 day trade)
body:
- **Kind:** trading model + psychology
- **What ICT says:** A one-shot-one-kill trade is a single, high-conviction entry with a defined, achievable target, executed with the expectation of being closed by the end of a few days (2–5 days max). Once the target is hit, you're done trading for that swing. Don't hold over weekends due to gap risk. Don't look for the next trade immediately; be content with the win. This is a discipline/psychology lesson as much as a technical one.
- **How to identify:** You execute one trade per multi-day swing, with clear entry, stop, and target. That's it.
- **How to use:** Use daily bias (order blocks, discount wicks, macros) to identify the ONE setup to trade. Enter, manage stops, hit target, exit. Don't override discipline by chasing the market for more; that's when traders get wrecked (especially with high volatility).
- **Example in this video:** Monday–Tuesday setup delivered "several hundred handles" in a clean move from setup to target. Michael took it and was done; he's not looking for more trading this week.
- **Timestamps:** [0:06:28](https://youtu.be/zq4hz_XiTRE?t=388) (OSOK explained: given all analysis upfront, now execute one trade) · [0:24:46](https://youtu.be/zq4hz_XiTRE?t=1486) (OSOK model: two to five day trade, out by end of week).
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** OSOK is not greedy trading; it's high-quality, highly-confluenced trades with defined exits. One big move beats chasing ten small scalps.

title: Analysis Delivering On NQ
head: Buy-Side Imbalance / Sell-Side Efficiency (aliases: inefficiency, BSL/SSL imbalance)
body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:** When there's buy-side imbalance (more buyer interest at a level, creating a gap) paired with sell-side efficiency (willingness to sell at higher prices), this creates an inefficiency—a fair value gap. These imbalances are exploited by smart money for directional moves.
- **How to identify:** Look for a gap between candle close and next candle open; one side (buy or sell) is committed; the other (efficiency) shows price unwillingness to commit.
- **How to use:** These imbalances are targets for the opposite direction. Buy-side imbalance with sell-side efficiency = price likely to reverse down into the imbalance.
- **Example in this video:** 15m NQ chart had identified buy-side imbalance and sell-side efficiency pair, shaded as an inefficiency. Michael expected price to trade down and into it, and it delivered precisely.
- **Timestamps:** [0:00:00](https://youtu.be/N3qz13Hl-gg?t=0) (buy-side imbalance, sell-side efficiency defined) · [0:12:07](https://youtu.be/N3qz13Hl-gg?t=727) (sell-side liquidity pool: result of BSL/SSL imbalance).
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Efficiency is not rejection; it's unwillingness to commit at higher/lower prices, creating a direction bias.

title: Analysis Delivering On NQ
head: Low-Hanging Fruit Objective vs. Best-Case Scenario (aliases: LHF, aggressive target, conservative target)
body:
- **Kind:** risk management + position management rule
- **What ICT says:** When you identify a trading setup, define two targets: LHF objective is the reasonable, highly-probable target (where most of the move should complete). Best-case scenario is the aggressive target (lower for shorts, higher for longs) that only happens if momentum continues. Rule: take 80% of your position (bulk) off at LHF. Hold 1–2 contracts as runners to see if you can reach the best case. If LHF happens and best case doesn't, you're still profitable; if best case hits, the runners are extra profit.
- **How to identify:** Calculate LHF as the first major inefficiency or liquidity pool below (for shorts) or above (for longs). Best case = the deepest inefficiency or furthest liquidity target.
- **How to use:** Size your position knowing you'll sell bulk at LHF. Enter, ride to LHF, take profits, hold runners. Don't be greedy; if LHF doesn't hit, you exit; if LHF hits and best case fails, you're satisfied.
- **Example in this video:** Michael identified LHF objective as the minor sell-side liquidity pool. Best case was to continue into the major sell-side efficiency/inefficiency below. He took bulk at LHF and ran rest for best case.
- **Timestamps:** [0:00:49](https://youtu.be/N3qz13Hl-gg?t=49) (LHF objective vs. best case) · [0:01:37](https://youtu.be/N3qz13Hl-gg?t=97) (take bulk at LHF, runners for best case).
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Psychology: unless you have bulk off at LHF, the best-case target will torture you; take profits.

title: Analysis Delivering On NQ
head: Draw on That Low / Draw to Liquidity (aliases: draw, target, confluence draw)
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:** When price is moving toward a lower timeframe structure (like a 1m inefficiency) that is nested within a higher timeframe (15m) draw, smart money is "drawing" price toward that liquidity or inefficiency. The institutional algorithm pulls price toward these nested draws. If price "wilts" (weakens) into a draw, it's confirming continuation; if it bounces before reaching the draw, the move is questioned.
- **How to identify:** Identify inefficiencies on both 15m and 1m; note when a lower-timeframe inefficiency sits within a higher-timeframe target. That's a draw.
- **How to use:** Use draws as confirmation. If price is moving toward a draw and still showing strength (wicking around efficiently, bodies committed), it's likely to reach it. If weakening before reaching, question the move.
- **Example in this video:** Michael identified a 15m draw (sell-side inefficiency) and a nested 1m inefficiency within it. Price was drawing toward both; the move was so clean it "wilted" exactly into the target inefficiency.
- **Timestamps:** [0:00:49](https://youtu.be/N3qz13Hl-gg?t=49) (draw = target below) · [0:07:07](https://youtu.be/N3qz13Hl-gg?t=427) (any movement lower should find momentum build up to get down into that inefficiency) · [0:12:07](https://youtu.be/N3qz13Hl-gg?t=727) (draw on that low).
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Draws aren't random; they're institutional algos targeting nested inefficiencies. Precision comes from nesting timeframes.

title: Analysis Delivering On NQ
head: Dealing Range (aliases: range, trading range, overall dealing range)
body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:** A dealing range is a consolidated area or high-to-low range within which price is consolidating. Smaller portions can be identified within larger dealing ranges. These define the boundaries for bounces and reversals.
- **How to identify:** Look at 15m or daily chart; identify a zone where price has been consolidating (high and low clearly defined).
- **How to use:** Use dealing range boundaries as reversal zones; if price is at the low of a range, expect a bounce or continuation lower depending on bias; at the high, expect reversal or continuation higher.
- **Example in this video:** Michael identified a "smaller portion of that overall dealing range identified yesterday," zooming into a subset of the larger 15m range for 1m intraday trading.
- **Timestamps:** [0:02:24](https://youtu.be/N3qz13Hl-gg?t=144) (smaller portion of that overall dealing range).
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Dealing ranges nest; a large daily range contains multiple 15m ranges, each containing multiple 1m ranges.

title: Analysis Delivering On NQ
head: First Presented Fair Value Gap (aliases: FPFVG, first presented inefficiency)
body:
- **Kind:** definition + rule
- **What ICT says:** The first presented FVG is the gap that appears when price first breaks into a new area or direction. On subsequent bounces, this same gap may act as a target or rejection level. If it was an inversion FVG (bodies on one side, wicks on other), on the next move it might reverse its role and become a bullish target.
- **How to identify:** Mark the first inefficiency that forms after a break of structure; note its high and low.
- **How to use:** On retracements or reversals, the first presented FVG from an earlier move can act as a bounce or stopping point. Watch to see if it acts as an inversion (bodies respect one side).
- **Example in this video:** Michael identified a first presented FVG and noted it could be used as a target in the afternoon session if price reverses higher. He color-coded it "neutral" (gray) to avoid directional bias.
- **Timestamps:** [0:07:07](https://youtu.be/N3qz13Hl-gg?t=427) (first presented FVG as target) · [0:11:19](https://youtu.be/N3qz13Hl-gg?t=679) (first presented fair value gap to watch in PM session).
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** FVGs can change roles; tracking the "first presented" one helps you identify direction changes on re-entries.

title: Analysis Delivering On NQ
head: Event Horizon (aliases: midpoint, 50% level, halfway point)
body:
- **Kind:** measurement tool
- **What ICT says:** Event Horizon is the midpoint between two price levels (e.g., high and low of an inefficiency, or two historical swing extremes). Price often pauses or reverses at this midpoint. It's a powerful confluence when combined with other factors.
- **How to identify:** Find two price levels (a low and a high, or two equal lows); mark the price midpoint between them.
- **How to use:** Use as a pause/reversal zone. If price is moving toward a low and hits Event Horizon on the way, expect a bounce or consolidation. Also use as a partial profit target.
- **Example in this video:** Michael noted they were "at event horizon between the low of this to the high of that inefficiency." Price was pausing there before continuing lower.
- **Timestamps:** [0:07:56](https://youtu.be/N3qz13Hl-gg?t=476) (at event horizon, expecting further movement lower after close below).
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Event Horizon is a technical level, not an order-flow level; it's useful for timing entries/exits within a larger move.

title: Analysis Delivering On NQ
head: Suspension Block (aliases: suspension candle, volume imbalance at high and low)
body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:** A suspension block is a candle with small body and wicks at both high and low (minimal directional commitment). It shows neither bulls nor bears are in control momentarily; the next candle often delivers direction decisively. Michael notes suspension blocks as confirmations of what will happen next (if the next candle is strong down, the suspension preceded a downmove).
- **How to identify:** Look for a candle with nearly equal upper and lower wicks, small or small body.
- **How to use:** Suspension blocks are setup confirmations, not entry signals. Wait for the next candle after suspension for direction; that candle's strength or weakness confirms the next leg.
- **Example in this video:** Michael noted "that's a suspension block" when price showed balanced wicks at both ends. The next candle then broke lower decisively, confirming the downmove.
- **Timestamps:** [0:05:19](https://youtu.be/N3qz13Hl-gg?t=319) (suspension block noted).
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Suspension blocks are pause signals; they're not entries themselves; they're confirmations of what comes next.

title: Analysis Delivering On NQ
head: Volume Imbalance (aliases: imbalance, micro-inefficiency, gap between open and close)
body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:** A volume imbalance is when a candle's open is significantly different from its close (more than a tick or two), creating a gap or space. This is part of an inefficiency. If a candle has a 6 and a half close and a 6 and three-quarters open, that's a volume imbalance; use the wick to the next candle's open instead of the close.
- **How to identify:** Compare a candle's open and close; if more than 1–2 ticks apart, it's a volume imbalance.
- **How to use:** For gap construction, use wick-to-next-open rather than close-to-next-open when a volume imbalance is present. It refines your FVG definitions.
- **Example in this video:** Michael checked the close (6.5) vs. the open (6.75) of a candle, found it was a volume imbalance (0.25 difference), so he used the wick to the next candle's open for FVG construction.
- **Timestamps:** [0:11:19](https://youtu.be/N3qz13Hl-gg?t=679) (close 6.5, open 6.75; "that is not a volume imbalance" — it's too large, so use wick).
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Volume imbalances appear as gaps visually; they're key to precise FVG definition.

title: Post US Holiday Monday Followup
head: US Holiday Effect on Market Participation (aliases: low participation days, holiday Mondays, no-touch days)
body:
- **Kind:** rule + risk management
- **What ICT says:** When a US bank holiday falls on Saturday or Sunday, the following Monday (the actual observed holiday) is a "no-touch" day. Money stays on the sidelines; participation is predictably low. Low participation = wider bid-ask, less sustained price runs, more chop, and lower-probability setups. If you're starting the week with no established bias (price in middle of range), conviction is hard to come by. Never participate in these days; tape-read, demo-trade, or step away entirely. Missing a move on a low-probability day is better than taking a loss.
- **How to identify:** Check the US holiday calendar; if a major bank holiday (one that would close banks on weekdays) occurs on Saturday or Sunday, mark Monday as a no-trade day.
- **How to use:** Skip live trading on these days. If you feel the urge to trade, step away from the charts. Go do something physical. The discipline of NOT trading is as important as the discipline of trading well. Demo trading or tape reading is OK to learn structure, but not real money.
- **Example in this video:** July 7, 2026 (day after July 4 holiday, which fell on Saturday). Michael warned on X ahead of time not to trade. He tested it anyway to show how probabilities are stacked against you on these days, and the precision was off—he got stopped out on a trade.
- **Timestamps:** [0:01:39](https://youtu.be/2bke4YH6ZuE?t=99) (trading around holidays; low participation) · [0:04:56](https://youtu.be/2bke4YH6ZuE?t=296) (US bank holidays that fall on weekends: Monday is no-touch) · [0:05:46](https://youtu.be/2bke4YH6ZuE?t=346) (Michael warned on X; he was right about low participation).
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** This is a probability rule, not a hard rule (edges can happen anytime); but compliance saves capital and reduces drawdown variance.

title: Post US Holiday Monday Followup
head: Lay of the Land (aliases: LOL, scanning, reading the range)
body:
- **Kind:** process / scanning method
- **What ICT says:** Before the market opens, scan the daily/15m chart and identify: the high and low of the range you're expecting, the key inefficiencies (major buy-side and sell-side liquidity), and minor imbalances. This "lay of the land" is your thesis—what price levels will be in play today. Draw the dealing range high/low, then mark the extreme inefficiencies within that range (one at the low, one at the high). Mark minor buy-side and minor sell-side within that range. This is your map. Don't overcomplicate it; if there are more than 4–5 zones, simplify.
- **How to identify:** Open your daily or 15m chart; identify the recent swing high and low; mark inefficiencies (gaps, FVGs, order blocks) within that range.
- **How to use:** Use LOL as your bias for the day. If price opens at the midpoint (equilibrium), you have no edge; wait for price to show directional intent before committing capital. If price opens near the high, expect a draw to the low (and watch the minor zones on the way). LOL also sets your targets and stop zones.
- **Example in this video:** July 7 LOL was a 15m range from high to low, with two extreme inefficiencies (one at each end of range) and two minor zones inside. Michael used this map to know where to expect bounces and reversals.
- **Timestamps:** [0:00:00](https://youtu.be/2bke4YH6ZuE?t=0) (LOL: 15m inefficiencies shown) · [0:03:18](https://youtu.be/2bke4YH6ZuE?t=198) (LOL on 15m and scaling to 1m) · [0:14:36](https://youtu.be/2bke4YH6ZuE?t=876) (LOL: range high, range low, 50% Fibonacci midpoint; opened at equilibrium = no edge) · [0:15:23](https://youtu.be/2bke4YH6ZuE?t=923) (LOL: dealing range high/low, minor buy-side, minor sell-side).
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** If you open at 50% midpoint with no directional bias, admit there's no edge and wait for price to move 1–2% away from center before committing.

title: Post US Holiday Monday Followup
head: Quadrant and Octant Levels (aliases: price quadrants, octants, 25% and 12.5% levels)
body:
- **Kind:** measurement tool
- **What ICT says:** Divide a range into quadrants (25% increments) and octants (12.5% increments) using Fibonacci levels or price divisions. These levels are where smart money expects reversals and pauses. When price reaches a lower quadrant but fails to reach the octant above it, that's a directional signal. Michael marks quadrants and octants on the daily/15m chart to know where expected pauses or rejection zones are.
- **How to identify:** Draw Fibonacci or divide the high-to-low range into 4 (quadrants) or 8 (octants); mark each level.
- **How to use:** Quadrant/octant levels are interim targets. If price is moving down and fails to reach a lower octant from a higher quadrant, it's weak; expect reversal. Use them as intermediate stops or partial-profit zones.
- **Example in this video:** On the 15m chart, Michael marked quadrants; price traded to the lower quadrant but failed to reach the octant above it, signaling bearish bias (no commitment to higher octants).
- **Timestamps:** [0:00:49](https://youtu.be/2bke4YH6ZuE?t=49) (lower quadrant reached; failed to reach octant above).
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Quadrants/octants are mathematical subdivisions; they're not price-action-specific but serve as algorithmic reference points.

title: Post US Holiday Monday Followup
head: Volume Imbalance and First Presented Fair Value Gap (aliases: FPFVG, first imbalance gap, open-close gap)
body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:** Volume imbalance is when a candle's open-to-close gap is significant (more than a tick or two). This creates an inefficiency—a fair value gap. The first presented FVG is the first gap that forms when price enters a new move. Mark the high of the lower candle and the low of the next candle (if gap exists); that's your FVG. On subsequent retracements, this same FVG may act as support or resistance.
- **How to identify:** Scan for gaps between candle closes and next candle opens; mark the open-close difference as an imbalance.
- **How to use:** FVGs are targets for reversals and bounces. Track the first presented FVG from a move; on subsequent pulls, price often tests it or uses it as a reversal zone.
- **Example in this video:** First potential FVG formed between two 1m candlesticks at the open; this was the volume imbalance between their close and next open. Later in the session, price retested this FVG and acted as an inversion FVG (weak retest = reversal).
- **Timestamps:** [0:08:55](https://youtu.be/2bke4YH6ZuE?t=535) (first potential FVG: volume imbalance between close and next open) · [0:10:34](https://youtu.be/2bke4YH6ZuE?t=634) (first position FVG retraced; bodies at consequent encroachment) · [0:11:23](https://youtu.be/2bke4YH6ZuE?t=683) (first presented FVG as target on pullback).
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** First presented FVGs change role based on direction; track them for multiple sessions as they become targets on reversals.

title: Post US Holiday Monday Followup
head: Draw on Liquidity (aliases: draw, liquidity draw, institutional target)
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:** When price action points toward a specific inefficiency or liquidity pool, smart money is "drawing" price toward it. This is the institutional algorithm doing its work. If price is moving toward a draw and showing no weakness, expect it to complete the draw. If it's weakening before reaching, the draw is questioned. A draw is characterized by sustained directional movement with clean structure (no choppy wicks or reversals).
- **How to identify:** Identify an inefficiency that price is moving toward; watch for commitment (bodies aligned, wicks controlled). If commitment is strong, you're watching a draw.
- **How to use:** Don't fight a draw; if price is drawing to a level, position trades in that direction. Use stops above (for shorts) or below (for longs) the structure showing the draw. Draws often complete cleanly.
- **Example in this video:** Michael was watching for a potential draw on liquidity lower in the evening/early Asian session after the Monday close. If price could "gravitate down towards that" and set up structure implying a continued draw, he'd engage.
- **Timestamps:** [0:08:08](https://youtu.be/2bke4YH6ZuE?t=488) (potential draw on liquidity lower) · [0:08:55](https://youtu.be/2bke4YH6ZuE?t=535) (using event horizon and draw logic).
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Draws are directional; they're institutional moves, not retail chop. Recognize the difference between chop (rangebound wicks) and draws (committed bodies).

title: Post US Holiday Monday Followup
head: If-Then Statement Approach (aliases: conditional analysis, probability framing)
body:
- **Kind:** process / psychology
- **What ICT says:** Instead of making absolute predictions ("price will go down to X"), frame analysis as if-then statements ("If price takes out the buy-side here AND closes below CE, THEN I'm looking for a draw to the sell-side"). This removes ego and adaptation; you're not defending a prediction; you're watching to see if conditions are met. If conditions aren't met, you pivot to the next if-then without losing conviction. This is the opposite of confirmation bias.
- **How to identify:** Write your analysis as conditional statements: "If this happens, then I'm looking for this."
- **How to use:** Use if-then to stay flexible. If price does A, you expect B; if price does C instead, you're looking for D. Both are prepared responses; no surprises, no ego injury.
- **Example in this video:** Michael stated: "If we roll over and take out that low and accelerate and get below here on a sustained run, THEN I'd like to see it make an attempt to get down to this inefficiency." This is if-then thinking. If price doesn't take out the low, the condition isn't met; he has another if-then ready.
- **Timestamps:** [0:17:01](https://youtu.be/2bke4YH6ZuE?t=1021) (if then statement: "If it rolls through these lows, then I'd like to see it attempt here") · [0:17:48](https://youtu.be/2bke4YH6ZuE?t=1068) (if market proves it wants to do specific things, then I align my thinking).
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** If-then removes the emotional burden of being "right"; you're just responding to market conditions.

title: Post US Holiday Monday Followup
head: Dealing Range High and Low (aliases: daily range, range bounds)
body:
- **Kind:** measurement / bias framework
- **What ICT says:** The high and low of the expected trading range for a day (or timeframe). Mark these clearly on your chart. Everything between them is fair game; nothing outside is part of today's range (until proven otherwise). Inefficiencies within the range are the targets; inefficiencies at the range edges are extremes.
- **How to identify:** Identify the swing high and swing low you expect for the day/week; mark them prominently.
- **How to use:** Use dealing range bounds as reference points for targets and stops. If price breaks outside the range, a new range is forming. If it stays within, use internal inefficiencies for trades.
- **Example in this video:** Michael marked dealing range high and low on the 15m chart; all subsequent moves were analyzed within that context. Minor inefficiencies within the range were targets; extremes at the edges were long-term goals.
- **Timestamps:** [0:16:13](https://youtu.be/2bke4YH6ZuE?t=973) (dealing range high and dealing range low, with minor buy and sell inside).
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Ranges shift as price breaks bounds; be ready to update your dealing range if structure breaks.

title: Post US Holiday Monday Followup
head: Minor Buy-Side and Minor Sell-Side Liquidity (aliases: minor buy-side, minor sell-side, internal liquidity pools)
body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:** Within a dealing range, there are inefficiencies at the edges (extreme/major) and inefficiencies inside the range (minor). Minor buy-side liquidity is an imbalance where buyers are resting in the middle of a range (not at the top). Minor sell-side is the same but for sellers. These are "secondary" liquidity pools that may be swept en route to the major (extreme) pools.
- **How to identify:** Identify the dealing range high and low; scan inside for smaller gaps or imbalances; those are minor zones.
- **How to use:** Use minor liquidity pools as intermediate targets. If you're short and moving lower, expect price to touch the minor sell-side on the way down to the extreme sell-side. These are bounce points or partial-profit zones.
- **Example in this video:** Michael identified minor buy-side and minor sell-side within the 15m dealing range; price took out the minor buy-side in the morning, then failed to push higher and eventually worked toward the minor sell-side and extreme sell-side lower.
- **Timestamps:** [0:16:13](https://youtu.be/2bke4YH6ZuE?t=973) (minor buy side and minor sell side inside the dealing range).
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Minor zones are secondary targets; don't mistake them for major support/resistance.

title: Weekend US Holiday Volume Protocol
head: Holiday volume protocol (Monday after a weekend US holiday)  (aliases ICT uses: holiday volume, trashy conditions, failures to launch, false signals)
body:
- **Kind:** rule (day-type filter)
- **What ICT says:**
  - The holiday fell on Saturday; "usually Mondays after that, it's very, very trashy. It means you're going to have a whole lot of false signals."
  - "I've lost more money trading after holidays like this than in any other thing. Always holiday volume."
  - Price is "lethargic," gives "failures to launch," is "ugly price action"; "technicals don't give you that real pristine precision."
  - Why: volume will be light - people are away (summer months, hungover, vacation); participation is thin so "there's no need for them to make the ranges big" and they "don't need to have the market to be that precise." He says "he [the algorithm/market maker] won't be able to engineer participation because there's a vacuum of interest."
  - It "slaps in the face the buying and selling pressure myth": a big range wouldn't be justified without participation.
  - Response: "knowing these things going in helps you preserve capital... not go on tilt... Enough is not trading at all on a day like today. That's the right answer."
  - He had posted on X before the open that people shouldn't trade live funds and to be careful, "these days can be rather fickle."
  - Contrast with low-resistance liquidity-run days where "price moves around really freely" and technicals are clean.
  - Rebuttal to foreign traders ("why does a US holiday matter?"): it's participation, not nationality.
- **How to identify:** the first trading day after a US market holiday (weekend or Friday/Monday holiday), summer especially; look for price repeatedly failing at levels, jagged moves on the upside, price stuck in the middle of a range.
- **How to use:** do not trade live money; if you trade, expect failures, use tiny size and fast protection of stops; watch rather than engage. Seek low-resistance days instead.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 15m/1m, morning: price middles in a 15-minute range, sharp upside jaggedness, failure to launch both ways; the 10:00 news only moves price a little.
- **Timestamps:** [0:00:47](https://youtu.be/cDjxtT4-O-Q?t=47) — holiday on Saturday, Mondays after are trashy, false signals; [0:05:55](https://youtu.be/cDjxtT4-O-Q?t=355) — "lost more money after holidays"; [0:21:04](https://youtu.be/cDjxtT4-O-Q?t=1264) — fickle, lethargic, failures to launch; [0:26:37](https://youtu.be/cDjxtT4-O-Q?t=1597) — participation explanation; [0:27:24](https://youtu.be/cDjxtT4-O-Q?t=1644) — enough is not trading at all
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Related to L26-064's Monday guidance (avoid unless NFP week) and the holiday-protocol theme in this series. The explanation overtly rejects "buying and selling pressure" logic.

title: Weekend US Holiday Volume Protocol
head: First presented FVG as inversion FVG; stop above the candle that went through it  (aliases ICT uses: first presented fair value gap, inversion fair value gap, consequent encroachment)
body:
- **Kind:** entry model
- **What ICT says:** The first presented FVG of the session (formed in the first 30 minutes) "is going to act as an inversion FVG" given what price has done; he watches the candlestick's halfway (CE) and, once the candle closes, uses the high of the candle that went completely through the iFVG as his risk; he wants price to take the sell side below today's intraday low. A small gap sits inside the iFVG; needs "a heaviness campaign to lower"; any more consolidation sends price up to the high. Stop is placed above that candle's high and later lowered to a nearby candle's high.
- **How to use:** short from the CE of the iFVG with the stop above the high of the candle that traded through; require heaviness quickly; otherwise get out.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 1m, ~9:55-10:05: short at the CE of the first presented FVG after the first 30 minutes; target intraday low sell-side; stop above the high of the candle that went through the gap.
- **Timestamps:** [0:03:12](https://youtu.be/cDjxtT4-O-Q?t=192) — first presented FVG acts as iFVG; [0:04:17](https://youtu.be/cDjxtT4-O-Q?t=257) — risk is the high of the candle that traded through; [0:06:51](https://youtu.be/cDjxtT4-O-Q?t=411) — needs to get heavy on this or the next candle

title: Weekend US Holiday Volume Protocol
head: SIBI that fails to close below its CE is not bearish: close the short and reverse long  (aliases ICT uses: initial utilization, standard bullish fair value gap, reclaimed, volume imbalance)
body:
- **Kind:** entry model / rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - The sell-side imbalance buy-side inefficiency (with a volume imbalance) is usually bearish, "but look what it did: it failed to take out that low. It failed to trade and close below its consequent encroachment." He measures with a fib: price did not close below the halfway point, "indicating this is not going to be bearish."
  - So he bailed on the short ("protected the stop loss that would clearly have gotten a larger stop out"), "saved the stop loss, reversed," and treated the area as the initial utilization of a standard bullish FVG that was reclaimed after going below.
  - The long: stop one tick below the open of the key candle; target = event horizon between the 15-minute FVG's CE and the old high (the midpoint of those two reference points).
  - Rule for the retest: the long FVG/iFVG may be traded down into on a wick only, not leaving a body; if it wicks and the next candle opens above the range up to the candle's high, it should draw higher; stay in the upper half of the gap.
  - Partial plan: peel one off at the CE-ish level, another halfway between levels, run the balance.
- **How to identify:** a bearish gap (SIBI) that does not close below its own midpoint, and failed to take out the low.
- **How to use:** exit shorts; flip long into the next bullish FVG, stay long while price stays in the upper half; stop one tick under the open of the key candle.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 1m ~10:05-10:15: short from the iFVG CE; the SIBI fails to close below its CE; he closes (loss ~$1,800 per his words), reverses long; price makes a wick into the bullish FVG and closes above; first target hit, second partial.
- **Timestamps:** [0:11:42](https://youtu.be/cDjxtT4-O-Q?t=702) — closes the trade, reverses; [0:13:25](https://youtu.be/cDjxtT4-O-Q?t=805) — SIBI fails to close below its CE; [0:14:12](https://youtu.be/cDjxtT4-O-Q?t=852) — fib shows no close below the halfway point; [0:14:59](https://youtu.be/cDjxtT4-O-Q?t=899) — wick only, partial plan
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** An explicit instance of "a gap that fails to reach/close beyond its CE flips the bias," as with the earlier iFVG CE failure notes (L26-002).

title: Weekend US Holiday Volume Protocol

body:

  - Target for the long: the halfway between the CE of a 15-minute FVG he had shown on the 15m time frame and an old high. He drew it by hand; price struggled there ("see how reluctant it is to continue").

title: Weekend US Holiday Volume Protocol
head: Management: limited room, lingering above a level, take two off, stop under wick low, final contract on the stop  (aliases ICT uses: peel risk off, runner, strangle with the stop loss)
body:
- **Kind:** rule (trade management)
- **What ICT says:**
  - After taking the long: if price spends 1, 2, then a third minute just above the high without running ("three times we have spent 1 minute here, 2 minutes, more than a third minute above this high"), it needs to "find legs"; he takes two contracts off and rolls the stop under the wick low.
  - One contract remains (a runner); with one contract he can't scale so he manages with the stop and lets it be the "best case scenario exit"; rolls the stop below the wick as price gets above.
  - "If I'm stopped out, it's fine. The loss I had on the initial position is completely mitigated already." He cites an initial loss of about $1,800, then +$220, then another +$1,000 (caption figures).
  - Warning signs: too much wanting to fold and roll over above a high.
- **How to use:** protect the remaining position by rolling stops under the latest wick low; take partials when price stalls; the final contract managed by the stop.
- **Timestamps:** [0:15:45](https://youtu.be/cDjxtT4-O-Q?t=945) — peel some risk off; [0:17:41](https://youtu.be/cDjxtT4-O-Q?t=1061) — three minutes above the high, take two off; [0:19:30](https://youtu.be/cDjxtT4-O-Q?t=1170) — last contract on the stop; [0:24:12](https://youtu.be/cDjxtT4-O-Q?t=1452) — loss mitigated, P&L recap
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Same family as L26-062 (don't strangle, but here he strangles with the stop out of necessity).

title: Missed Entry How To Navigate The Same Trade Idea
head: Limit order just above the CE; "let it come to you"  (aliases ICT uses: sell limit above consequent encroachment, don't chase, needless drawdown)
body:
- **Kind:** rule (execution)
- **What ICT says:**
  - He plans to sell short with a limit just above the consequent encroachment of the fair value gap; stop above the gap's volume imbalance.
  - "Let it come to you. Don't chase it." It is real important not to think you must have the fill, "even if you know it's likely to go down and take out that low." If you sell lower down and it retraces, that is "needless drawdown. You don't have to endure that."
  - He also rejects the use of market replay in demonstrations.
- **How to use:** place the limit at the level (just above the CE for a short), stop beyond the volume imbalance, wait; never chase price lower.
- **Example in this video:** NQ-like 1m chart (prices near 30,1xx / 29,9xx; caption digits partial): short limit just above the FVG CE; price pops into it and then comes up to the wick that prints to a candle's open; the limit is just short of a fill.
- **Timestamps:** [0:00:00](https://youtu.be/EZB4vBUFdHw?t=0) — plan: sell on limit just above CE, stop above the volume imbalance; [0:00:48](https://youtu.be/EZB4vBUFdHw?t=48) — don't chase, needless drawdown; [0:02:28](https://youtu.be/EZB4vBUFdHw?t=148) — price pops up toward the level
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Same concept as "limit orders" in earlier teaching; here the lesson is the cost of missing.

title: Missed Entry How To Navigate The Same Trade Idea
head: Perfect analysis yields missed trades; fallback entry in the lower half of the order block  (aliases ICT uses: missed entry, "perfection will yield missed trades", premium sensitivity, immediate rebalance)
body:
- **Kind:** rule / entry refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - His limit at the level did not fill: the candle's low was 120.5 and the high 122.5 (partial digits), so price went into the gap and two handles beyond but missed his price. "Sometimes perfection and being so precise is a curse." He asks nobody to feel bad: "It is what it is."
  - "When your analysis is perfect, your executions could not execute. So perfection will yield missed trades. That's the oxymoron." You demand the best-case scenario and the spread/fills do not always afford it.
  - Fallback: sell inside the lower half of the (bearish) order block on a confirmed change in the state of delivery - the "premium sensitivity" portion of that candle. "Notice my entries in the lower half of the order block on this fill." Required signs: change in state of delivery occurs; "no immediate rebalance" (price does not immediately fill/retrace the gap after displacement = strength).
  - A close below the wick's CE is "confirmation that follow-through is likely"; he measures it with a fib; it needed to happen on that candle.
  - He has "something to work with": with a rejection block he reduces his stop risk.
- **How to identify:** (1) a defined limit price; (2) a candle that comes within a few handles but doesn't fill; (3) a bearish OB that confirms with CISD.
- **How to use:** if the limit misses by a small distance and the OB confirms, enter in its lower half (below its CE); tighten the stop using the rejection block; targets: relatively equal lows (best case), then nearer lows.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 1m: limit fails by ~2 handles; CISD at the OB; he sells in the lower half; price delivers hard ("institutional delivery, hammered it"), then retraces back to the OB.
- **Timestamps:** [0:03:18](https://youtu.be/EZB4vBUFdHw?t=198) — "perfection is a curse"; limit short of fill; CISD, short if it touches; [0:04:09](https://youtu.be/EZB4vBUFdHw?t=249) — went two handles beyond; use a rejection block to reduce stop risk; [0:05:54](https://youtu.be/EZB4vBUFdHw?t=354) — entries in the lower half of the OB; close below the wick CE = follow-through; [0:16:26](https://youtu.be/EZB4vBUFdHw?t=986) — perfection yields missed trades
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** The caption conflates "discount sensitivity" and "premium sensitivity"; he means the premium (sell) side sensitivity of the bearish OB, i.e., the lower half entry still being valid because price stays below the OB's midpoint.

title: Missed Entry How To Navigate The Same Trade Idea
head: Bearish order block retest = smart money accumulating more shorts  (aliases ICT uses: order block to sell side, implemented order block)
body:
- **Kind:** refinement
- **What ICT says:** "Whenever there's an order block being implemented and it starts to sell off, and then it goes right back to it again, it's allowing smart money to accumulate more shorts" (bearish OB). So the return to the OB is another opportunity to add short; price then takes out the low, accelerates below it, and continues lower. The model: "order block to sell side," not requiring a precise re-use of the block.
- **How to use:** add shorts on the first pullback into the OB while bodies hold below its midpoint; stop just above the OB/high.
- **Timestamps:** [0:05:54](https://youtu.be/EZB4vBUFdHw?t=354) — order block to sell side as a model; [0:06:40](https://youtu.be/EZB4vBUFdHw?t=400) — return to the OB lets smart money accumulate more shorts; [0:07:29](https://youtu.be/EZB4vBUFdHw?t=449) — stop lowered just above the high
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Same pyramiding idea as L26-049 ("add on retraces into a validated OB").

title: Missed Entry How To Navigate The Same Trade Idea
head: Partials to relatively equal lows and event horizon; scaling out contracts  (aliases ICT uses: best-case scenario, event horizon, runner)
body:
- **Kind:** management / example
- **What ICT says:**
  - Best-case target: the relatively equal lows; then this low and that low as intermediate targets; if the low is taken he'll "limit out" three contracts.
  - First partial: three contracts off, "leave six contracts for a runner." He holds risk "at 1920" (caption; probably dollars) until the first partial.

  - He ends the trade "content": "Too much of a retracement on my part for the trade I was in."
- **How to use:** stagger partials: first three off at the first target, then singles into event horizon, runner for the relatively equal lows; lower the stop progressively.

title: Missed Entry How To Navigate The Same Trade Idea

body:

- **What ICT says:**
  - He labels the day a Market Maker Sell Model: the 9:30 run up was Judas, the drop followed, and he used "the second stage redistribution." Sequence he lists: smart money reversal (low-risk short), first-stage distribution, second-stage redistribution; you look for key highs to get short "on the right side of the curve" (the sell side of the curve from the highest point down).

  - A tight block of bodies (a "big square area") would be disrupted, cleared through, then used; equilibrium of the block drops down, a gap forms.

He won't be able to stay with it to the relatively equal lows "and that's okay... if I take it all, it's just greedy."
