title: Futures Market Review \ Lecture On Shadows Validating PD Arrays
head: Shadow (PD array shadow)  (aliases ICT uses: "shadow", "bleeding over of two imbalances", "salmon area")
body:
- **Kind:** new coinage
- **What ICT says:**
  - When one PD array overlaps another imbalance, the overlap is a PD array in its own right; he calls it a "shadow" because it casts a shadow over another imbalance.
  - On the daily NQ chart the bearish daily FVG is shaded pink and the daily suspension block is shaded orange; where they overlap the colour is salmon. That salmon overlap is the shadow, and it can be "graded" (measured with quadrant/octant/fib levels) just like any other range.
  - Other approaches (supply/demand, volume profile, footprint) would not look at that overlap or grade it this way.
  - Once such a range exists, you can measure any PD array that forms against it, but the new PD array "has to be touching" it: the high, the low, or anywhere in between. Touching = anchored.
- **How to identify:** an overlap between two higher-timeframe PD arrays (here: daily bearish FVG and daily suspension block); the shaded overlap region is the shadow. The suspension block's high/low sit at its edges.
- **How to use:** project quadrants/octants (and even 16ths) across the shadow; look for lower-timeframe FVGs, volume imbalances or wicks that touch those levels; trade them with the wick-CE and CE rules below. He says he plots the fib levels on it ("don't tell anybody what they are") but does not state exact fib percentages in this video.
- **Example in this video:** Wednesday session (today): price sells off at 9:30 inside the upper octant of the daily suspension block / daily bearish FVG, then later in the day a bullish FVG forms at the low of the overlap (the shadow) — wick/body prices around 146.50 (full price likely 30,146.50; caption unclear). He calls this FVG "anchored to the low of that shadow", then price trades lower and the next FVG he finds sits exactly on an octant level; he says that is what makes it valid.
- **Timestamps:** [0:34:32](https://youtu.be/pq9WuZ9q4Bg?t=2072) — FVG forms at the low of the overlap of pink bearish FVG and the suspension block; [0:36:12](https://youtu.be/pq9WuZ9q4Bg?t=2172) — he names it a "shadow"; [0:36:59](https://youtu.be/pq9WuZ9q4Bg?t=2219) — the upper quadrant of the range, and "it has to be touching"; [0:39:30](https://youtu.be/pq9WuZ9q4Bg?t=2370) — next FVG is on an octant = valid.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** The title promise ("shadows validating PD arrays") is exactly this: a smaller PD array is validated by being anchored to a level of the shadow's range. How the suspension block itself is constructed is only partly explained here (see next concept).

title: Futures Market Review \ Lecture On Shadows Validating PD Arrays
head: Daily suspension block with quadrants / octants (and 16ths)  (aliases: "daily suspension block", "octant levels", "upper octant", "lower quadrant")
body:
- **Kind:** definition (partial) / refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - The daily chart has a "suspension block" PD array (orange). He subdivides its range into quadrants (quarters) and octants (eighths), and uses those levels as reaction points for intraday entries (Monday short at the "lower quadrant", Tuesday long off the "high of the suspension block", Wednesday selloff in the "upper octant").
  - Partial explanation of the build here: the suspension block's edge exists because one daily candle's high is lower than the next candle's body, so the two overlap; that overlap with the daily bearish FVG creates the colour change. The clean definition is in the next video (L26-072, [0:47:07](https://youtu.be/rbNhlJSXDaA?t=2827)): a single candle suspended between two volume imbalances (one at its low, one at its high), treated as an inversion FVG.
  - He suggests going finer: split the space between an octant and a quadrant in half (16ths). He admits he doesn't do it publicly ("too good") but says everyone should start doing it.
- **How to identify:** the suspension block's high and low; then draw quarters and eighths between them.
- **How to use:** these levels are where lower-timeframe FVGs, order blocks and wicks are anchored. Premium levels (upper octants/quadrants) are used for shorts at macro time; discount levels / the block's high on a dip are used for longs depending on narrative.
- **Example in this video:** Monday: short at the lower quadrant of the daily suspension block, at the session high around the 9:50–10:10 macro. Tuesday 9:30–10:10: opening trades down into the high of the daily suspension block, wick is graded, price rips higher.
- **Timestamps:** [0:00:01](https://youtu.be/pq9WuZ9q4Bg?t=1) — short at daily suspension block octant levels; [0:08:30](https://youtu.be/pq9WuZ9q4Bg?t=510) — orange block, lower quadrant, another octant; [0:14:57](https://youtu.be/pq9WuZ9q4Bg?t=897) — Tuesday: high of the suspension block + macro start; [0:40:18](https://youtu.be/pq9WuZ9q4Bg?t=2418) — 16s comment ([0:39:30](https://youtu.be/pq9WuZ9q4Bg?t=2370) leads in).
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** "Daily suspension block" and its octant grid are 2026-era vocabulary; treat as a dealing-range grid applied to a specific daily PD array, not to the whole dealing range.

title: Futures Market Review \ Lecture On Shadows Validating PD Arrays
head: Fair value gap validation: first presented, or anchored  (aliases: "first presented fair value gap", "anchored FVG")
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - An FVG is valid in one of two ways: (1) it is the first-presented FVG (the first one that forms after the relevant move/open), or (2) if it is not first-presented, it is always anchored to an octant or quadrant level. "Period."
  - Volume profile / low-volume-node logic is explicitly rejected as the way to find "real" FVGs ("wrong, wrong, wrong"); sometimes they agree, but "that is not the logic".
  - On Tuesday, the first FVG after the 9:30 open (about 9:35) was acceptable as first-presented, but he preferred the later one because the run out of it was more prominent.
- **How to identify:** (a) first FVG after the opening/impulse, or (b) FVG whose high, low or interior touches an octant/quadrant (or shadow) level of the higher-timeframe range.
- **How to use:** after validation, wait for price to retrace into the FVG; strength = no trade into the lower half (for longs) and no bodies in the lower half; then enter using the wick/CE entry mechanism below.
- **Example in this video:** Tuesday 9:35 first presented FVG after the open; Wednesday 9:30 selloff clears an area, creates "first presented fair value gap", rallies; price cannot reach the FVG's CE, then a wick forms and also does not touch its own CE.
- **Timestamps:** [0:12:37](https://youtu.be/pq9WuZ9q4Bg?t=757) — Tuesday first-presented FVG at 9:35; [0:26:26](https://youtu.be/pq9WuZ9q4Bg?t=1586) — Wednesday first presented FVG, "very strong entry mechanism"; [0:35:23](https://youtu.be/pq9WuZ9q4Bg?t=2123) — the validation rule stated.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** contradicts the many retail "validate FVG with volume profile" methods. Does not discard FVGs that are neither first-presented nor anchored; they simply aren't treated as valid.

title: Futures Market Review \ Lecture On Shadows Validating PD Arrays
head: Wick consequent-encroachment grading  (aliases: "grade that wick", "premium sensitivity", "discount sensitivity")
body:
- **Kind:** rule / refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - When you anticipate a run off an order block/PD array and that candle prints a wick, measure the wick's consequent encroachment (its 50%). The wick then behaves with "discount sensitivity" for longs (and "premium sensitivity" for shorts).
  - Long case: price may touch the CE of the wick, but must not put a body below it. A body below the wick's CE invalidates the short-term bullishness. If price cannot even touch the CE, that validates the bullishness even more strongly.
  - Short case (mirror): bodies must stay below the CE of the wick above; "I don't want to see the body above that consequent encroachment level — that's the whole point of plotting that." On higher timeframes, a daily wick's CE needs a close beyond it to open the target (Monday recap: a daily wick CE needed a close below it to target the sell side; price did not close below, so no continuation).
  - Wicks are allowed to poke through; it is the bodies that matter. He admits you cannot know in real time if the wick will hold; "trust your analysis" and use a stop.
  - EURUSD example (end of video): he marked a wick CE the previous session and wanted no bodies above its half; bodies stayed below it and price dived. For a continuation lower, price would need to close beyond another wick's CE below.
- **How to identify:** pick the wick created by the candle/order block you are trading; draw its midpoint; track bodies, not wicks.
- **How to use:** a clean wick-CE test is the entry qualifier; stop goes at the wick extreme (see entry mechanism below).
- **Example in this video:** Tuesday PM (2:06 p.m. ET low): after sell side is raided at 2:06, the candle's wick is graded and price never gets a body below the CE; next candle open trades below the order block's opening price and he says "just go in there and take a long." Wednesday morning: a wick forms after the FVG, drawn down to the wick low; it does not touch CE, "perfect... strong qualification that it's going to go higher."
- **Timestamps:** [0:02:34](https://youtu.be/pq9WuZ9q4Bg?t=154) — short side: want the body to stay below the wick's CE; [0:20:41](https://youtu.be/pq9WuZ9q4Bg?t=1241) — long side: touch allowed, body below invalidates; [0:11:50](https://youtu.be/pq9WuZ9q4Bg?t=710) — "premium sensitivity" + allow wicks to wick; [0:44:22](https://youtu.be/pq9WuZ9q4Bg?t=2662) — EURUSD application.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** in the EURUSD/NQ "no man's land" case two opposing wick-CE conditions held at once (price trapped between two CE levels), which he treats as a reason not to trade (see Process).

title: Futures Market Review \ Lecture On Shadows Validating PD Arrays
head: Order block as Change in State of Delivery (opening-price entry)  (aliases: "order block change in the state of delivery", "OB = CISD")
body:
- **Kind:** entry model / refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - An order block is not a "demand zone"; it is one specific price: the opening price of a candle. The change in state of delivery is validated when price trades above (for bullish) that opening price; it does not need to close above it.
  - Context for a bullish one: price is running from a discount to a premium / into a higher-timeframe PD array; price opens, trades down, shows willingness to go higher, and as soon as it trades above the candle's open it validates.
  - Then, when price trades back down into it (back below the open), you can long; if you lack conviction, wait for the candle close down to the wick CE. Anywhere between the open and the wick CE is a valid long.
  - Smooth lows being taken (sell side purged) is why a close above isn't needed.
- **How to identify:** pick the down-close candle at the low whose opening price is later traded above; measure its wick CE.
- **How to use:** entry between the open and the CE of the wick; stop at the wick low; target the nearby buy side (he runs to "buy side right there").
- **Example in this video:**
  - Tuesday ~9:49 ET: a candle opens at 30,226.00. Price had hit the high of the daily suspension block (higher-timeframe PDA), opened and traded down, then trades above that opening price. The retrace low is around 30,224 (caption "224 12"; unclear). Price then runs aggressively through the highs and buy side and rises to the high of the daily bearish FVG (pink).
  - Tuesday PM: an order block opens at 30,519.75; the low of the candle trades to 30,519.00 (three ticks below the open) to "trade into" the CISD, then price runs. Sell-side raid and low at 2:06 p.m. ET, then trades above the opening price, validates, comes back into it on a later candle for the long entry.
- **Timestamps:** [0:15:46](https://youtu.be/pq9WuZ9q4Bg?t=946) — 9:49 candle open 30,226; [0:16:35](https://youtu.be/pq9WuZ9q4Bg?t=995) — "that's not a demand zone... a very specific price"; [0:19:52](https://youtu.be/pq9WuZ9q4Bg?t=1192) — 30,519.75 open, three-tick poke; [0:21:32](https://youtu.be/pq9WuZ9q4Bg?t=1292) — 2:06 pm low and validation.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** "Does not need to close above" is the key difference from the stricter CISD/close-based definitions. This is order block theory expressed through CISD and opening price rather than a zone drawn from the body.

  - Target: the buy side immediately above.
  - He stresses he's showing the logic, not telling people where to buy in live conditions, and claims this is entire-model teaching (entry, targets, stops) that critics say he withholds.

- **How to use:** see above; stops are the wick low; targets are BSL/SSL beyond.
- **Example in this video:** Wednesday: first presented FVG forms after the sell-off; price cannot reach FVG CE; wick below does not touch wick CE; long from the open of the candle down to wick CE with stop at wick low; price rises and tags buy side "right above here" and then dips back into the suspension block before trading significantly higher outside the bearish daily FVG (a market structure shift).

  - Tick-level precision example: one candle's open is 173.75 and another candle's high is also 173.75 = a perfect volume imbalance; and a wick low at 175.00 vs high 175.50, with a close at 175.25 shows how price works inside a volume imbalance to the tick.
  - He says order flow, volume profile, Elliott Wave, Wyckoff and Gann don't give this level of precision.
  - He double-checks (admits he misread) whether a volume imbalance exists on one FVG: the candle close and open both at 146.50; using the wick low down to the wick high as the FVG instead.
- **How to identify:** gap between bodies of consecutive candles where the wicks overlap.
- **How to use:** include in the FVG range when measuring CE; levels used as exact reaction prices.
- **Example in this video:** NQ Wednesday PM: candle with low 30,175.00 vs candle high 30,175.50, close 175.25, open 173.75 vs high 173.75 (caption partially unclear).

head: RTH opening range gap (historical origin and use)  (aliases: "premium gap opening", "regular trading hours opening range gap")
body:

- **What ICT says:** If the market opens above the prior day's close, that is a premium gap (an RTH opening range gap higher). He says this is not part of the current model but influenced him as a technician.

head: Enigma FVG projection: low-hanging-fruit objective and extreme (1.25 projection)  (aliases: "projections and protractions", "unrealized dealing range projection")
body:
- **Kind:** new coinage / entry-target model (target measurement)
- **What ICT says:**
  - There are two distinct ways he teaches targets: the low-hanging-fruit objective and the extreme. The "story is clearest" in between the two, which is why the consequent encroachment / mean threshold of that band matters.
  - Evolution of FVG teaching: first wicks only (classic FVG, candle 1 high to candle 3 low), then the volume imbalance was added (use the candle's close rather than the wick high), giving two measurements of one inefficiency. The two measurements are then projected into the future to find very specific price points in an unrealized dealing range.
  - Steps on the DXY daily (as best reconstructed from the captions and on-screen pointing, anchors partly unclear):
    1. Find the displacement: candle 1 closes at about 100.997; candle 2 opens higher (over 101.005) leaving a volume imbalance (gap between the two bodies) and an opening range gap; candle 2 trades down slightly (small manipulation wick), then rallies. This is "part of the power of three" for that day, carried into the next day.
    2. Low-hanging fruit: draw a fib from the open of candle 2 (the low of its body; the point where the displacement begins) up to the low of the later candle that "showed its willingness to go higher" (discount sensitivity on that low). The 50% of that range is just the CE and "is not the focus". Add the 1.25 level (125%) and project it forward. That gave 101.795.
    3. Extreme: because the volume imbalance sits lower, re-anchor the same fib to candle 1's close ("the body tells the story, the wicks do the damage") instead of candle 2's open. The 1.25 level then gave 101.805.
    4. Fib the band between the two projected levels (101.795 down to 101.805, drawn as a blue line). Its CE is 101.80.
  - Result: the Wednesday high printed at 101.80, equal to the CE of the two projected levels, and price then retraced into the close of that day. He claims this was called live, not replayed or "form fitted", on the recording before it happened.
- **How to identify:** a displacement candle whose open is above (or below) the prior close (volume imbalance + opening range gap) and a following candle whose low (for bullish) marks the first test; price still has an untouched dealing range above.
- **How to use:** targets = low-hanging fruit (shallow anchor) and extreme (deep anchor); expect a reversal/retracement in the band around their midpoint; take profits there (he told viewers to close shorts in EURUSD and GBPUSD while DXY was at this band, and to close the bullish DXY idea).
- **Example in this video:** DXY daily, June 7 analysis said price would use a bullish inversion FVG, take the minor buy side, close above the CE of the range between two liquidity pools, and then draw to an old high. The final terminus he posted was 101.977; the Enigma projection said take profits at 101.795–101.805 on Wednesday. DXY topped at 101.80, then retraced.
- **Timestamps:** [0:11:25](https://youtu.be/rbNhlJSXDaA?t=685) — volume imbalance example (100.997 close, open above 101.005); [0:12:15](https://youtu.be/rbNhlJSXDaA?t=735) — FVG including the volume imbalance = two measurements; [0:19:41](https://youtu.be/rbNhlJSXDaA?t=1181) — fib from the open; [0:21:17](https://youtu.be/rbNhlJSXDaA?t=1277) — 1.25 level = 101.795, low-hanging fruit; [0:22:04](https://youtu.be/rbNhlJSXDaA?t=1324) — extreme = 101.805; [0:24:34](https://youtu.be/rbNhlJSXDaA?t=1474) — high = 101.80 = CE of the two.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** the anchor wording is ambiguous in the captions; "1.25" is stated as a level on the fib ("what's the 25?") with no further justification. He says this is optional ("you don't need this"). The 1.25 projection of a measured range is reminiscent of a standard-deviation-style extension but he doesn't call it that here.

head: Unrealized (implied) dealing range  (aliases: "implied dealing range", "unrealized dealing range")
body:
- **Kind:** definition / new coinage
- **What ICT says:** A dealing range whose far end has not yet traded. Example: start where the displacement candle opened for the day and go up to the high that price has formed so far; because price has taken out the previous day's high, an extension to the next draw is an "all but guarantee". It is "unrealized" because price has not traded there yet, so you have an opinion that price will go there but must submit to time.
- **How to identify:** a candle opens above the prior close, trades down, then rallies; the area above the day's current high is the unrealized portion; the range from the candle's open to that high is the dealing range for projection.
- **How to use:** feeds the Enigma FVG projection (above).
- **Timestamps:** [0:16:21](https://youtu.be/rbNhlJSXDaA?t=981) — definition; [0:18:02](https://youtu.be/rbNhlJSXDaA?t=1082) — start where the candle opened to the high.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** he first says "unrealized dealing range", then "implied dealing range" — same thing.

head: Volume imbalance and the two FVG measurements  (aliases: "volume imbalance", "classic FVG", "FVG including volume imbalance")
body:
- **Kind:** definition / refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - Volume imbalance = the gap between consecutive candle bodies (e.g. candle 1 close 100.997 and candle 2 open above 101.005 = volume imbalance 100.997 to ~101.005) even though wicks overlap.
  - When he first taught FVGs (the "classic" version), he used wicks only; the volume imbalance was added later as a "graduated revelation" so as not to overload students. Now the FVG can include the volume imbalance (disregard the short-term wick high and go down to the close of candle 1).
  - Toggling "adjust for contract rollover" (the tab at the bottom of the chart) shows where the volume imbalances are; later he adds that it also reveals SMT divergence (see below).
- **How to identify:** body-to-body gap between consecutive candles.
- **How to use:** two measurements = shallow (open of candle 2) and deep (close of candle 1) for projections.

head: Volume imbalance converting into FVG, BPR and inversion FVG  (aliases: "changes its characteristic", "inversion fair value gap", "balanced price range")
body:
- **Kind:** definition / refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - A volume imbalance created by down delivery (sell-side delivery, not liquidity) is first measured as a volume imbalance. When price later trades up through it, then back down and leaves the range, it becomes a balanced price range, and is used through the lens of a bearish FVG. If price then trades above it, it is used as an inversion FVG (support). He had labelled this on the June 7 DXY chart.
  - Example on DXY after June 7: a beautiful run off the iFVG; buy side delivered; the old high behind did not even need to be traded.
  - ES example (opposite direction): a volume imbalance began as a bullish PDA (bodies of the two candles do not touch), delivered by buy-side delivery; price traded down through it, another higher/lower round, and left it again, so it becomes a BPR; but with the inversion character it is now bearish and is expected to act as resistance. Warning in advance: this is more complicated and more likely to fail.
- **How to use:** treat inversion as resistance/support after body-close violation; wait for the retrace.

head: Wick CE grading: discount wick vs premium wick; wicks take precedence  (aliases: "wicks take precedence", "premium wick", "discount wick")
body:
- **Kind:** rule / refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - Whether a wick is a "discount wick" or "premium wick" depends where market price is in relation to it: the same wick is discount when price is above it and premium when price is below it. "You have to know where at market price you are in relationship to the PD array or the wick."
  - A wick takes precedence over the body-based order block "just like a gap", because a wick is a balanced price range (price went from the candle's close to the low and all the way back to the same price: traded both directions).
  - ES example: an enormous wick beside the largest down-close candle; it needs a close below the CE of that wick before a run lower becomes high probability; until then it isn't. NQ: price opened, traded up, could not reach CE, dumped lower and cleared lows into the upper quadrant of a wick; he wants a close below that level.
  - EURUSD example: price traded up and just fell short of the wick's CE, hit the "375" octant level, repelled, and closed below the low he had given on June 7.
- **How to use:** a close beyond the CE of the wick is the trigger for continuation; otherwise treat the move as not yet validated.

head: Event horizon (50% of a range between two lows / old high and target)  (aliases ICT uses: "event horizon", "consequent encroachment of the range", "halfway point")
body:
- **Kind:** definition / rule / refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - Anchor a fib on a low and drag to the next low (or from an old high to the target), delete all levels in the settings, and keep only the 0.5 level. That halfway point is the event horizon.
  - It is a "very strong candidate" for price to reach; price may simply touch it and turn around. He uses it to build structure for predetermined partials and to weigh the magnitude and velocity of a price run.
  - A close beyond it (below, in a short) increases confidence that the low/target behind it will be taken out. If it fails to close beyond, treat it as a possible bounce or reversal.
  - Event horizons can be nested: draw one from the first low and another from the second; treat the zone between the two levels as an inefficiency/gap ("good enough for government work"). A close below both raises the confidence that both lows will be taken out.
  - At the event horizon, "it's an event on the horizon you must make a decision about": where to move the stop, and whether to take a partial. He says you should take partials ("pay the trader"); don't demand target-or-nothing, because nothing is easy to hit.
  - Halfway is "always a really good rule of thumb."
- **How to identify:** two reference points (lows/highs/old high and target); midpoint between them.
- **How to use:** use as first target and partial level; adjust stop when reached; read closes beyond it as confirmation; grade the range with octants/quadrants if desired (below).
- **Example in this video:**
  - GBPUSD (short): objective reached; lowest of two relative equal lows is the next level; he says not to demand a target below it and to take something off at that low or at the CE of its wick.
  - NQ long (Monday): old short-term high anchored at roughly 30,869.75 to the target (minor buy side/ATH area) at 30,975.50; midpoint is the event horizon at about 30,922.75 (he had it on 30,923 by eye; "the actual tick is 922.75"). Price reached it, and then could not trade to the 30,975.50 minor buy side before breaking lower.
- **Timestamps:** [0:05:42](https://youtu.be/hxdAOfcp6gE?t=342) — he is asked about "my event horizon concept"; [0:07:16](https://youtu.be/hxdAOfcp6gE?t=436) — only the 0.5 level, "very strong candidate"; [0:08:05](https://youtu.be/hxdAOfcp6gE?t=485) — nested event horizons; [0:27:26](https://youtu.be/hxdAOfcp6gE?t=1646) — NQ midpoint 30,922.75; [0:28:16](https://youtu.be/hxdAOfcp6gE?t=1696) — decision point, partials, "pay the trader".
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** In L26-072 he used the same word for the CE of a range between two liquidity pools with a "close above it" confidence rule. Here it is also a partial/stop checkpoint. Same math (0.5), more management.

head: Sell-stop entry when the anticipated draw fails to trade  (aliases: "sell stop as an entry mechanism")
body:
- **Kind:** entry model
- **What ICT says:**
  - If you anticipate price going to a level (all-time high, or a weekly high) and it fails to get there, a sell stop works as an entry: if already long, trail the stop to just below the low to lock profit; if flat, place a sell stop just below the low, so when it breaks the low you are not stopped out of a long but are put net short.
  - Measure from the high (lower than the event horizon), use the event horizon level, and after the break you want to see price become "very, very aggressive".
  - Anywhere in the range where price breaks below that low is a valid short on the sell stop.
  - It doesn't have to be the all-time high; weekly highs work the same way.
- **How to identify:** a stated target level (here 30,975.50 minor buy side / ATH) not traded to; a small low beneath the event horizon.
- **How to use:** sell stop just under that low; stop above the high; first target the lower liquidity.
- **Example in this video:** NQ: price jumped up to the event horizon (~30,922.75) but failed to reach 30,975.50; the little low beneath was broken; price ran lower aggressively.
- **Timestamps:** [0:40:58](https://youtu.be/hxdAOfcp6gE?t=2458); [0:41:45](https://youtu.be/hxdAOfcp6gE?t=2505); [0:42:34](https://youtu.be/hxdAOfcp6gE?t=2554).

head: Previous day's range retracement rule  (aliases: "how much of the previous day's range", "lower half of the previous day's range")
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - Look at previous day's high/low/range and grade the sensitivity around it: how much of the previous day's range is price retracing? When the market is bearish, it should retrace only into the lower half of the previous day's range. If it does retrace up to the half, expect an afternoon or late-session continuation or the next day; you may have to cut a losing day-trade and look for the downside to resume.
  - Example (EURUSD): price retraced into the lower half and sold off; on another day it did not even reach the half, which tells him "algorithmically" the market is bearish; on a day that opened where it closed he used the wick instead.
  - He taught this in his paid mentorships (2016–2021) and says it underlies many of his executions.
- **How to identify:** plot a fib on the previous day's high to low; mark 50%.
- **How to use:** retrace into the lower half = bearish continuation expected; a trade into the half = caution/resumption later.
- **Timestamps:** [1:05:27](https://youtu.be/hxdAOfcp6gE?t=3927); [1:06:16](https://youtu.be/hxdAOfcp6gE?t=3976); [1:07:50](https://youtu.be/hxdAOfcp6gE?t=4070).
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** he states only the bearish case; the bullish mirror (retrace only into the upper half) is implied, not stated.

head: Draw on liquidity as expectation, not a requirement  (aliases: "drawing liquidity", "reasonable expectation")
body:
- **Kind:** rule / psychology
- **What ICT says:** Draw on liquidity is the premise that builds the idea before the trade; price does not have to reach it. "If you're going to be long, you have to know where it's going to reach to." Without that you are trading blind, which is gambling. If you are new and lack conviction, taking a profit before the target is fine; if wrong, a hypothetical trailing stop below the low gets hit and you "accept it, number one" because it is one transaction. He compares these small, partial wins to earning belts in martial arts: they keep a beginner motivated and teachable.
- **Example in this video:** DXY run into 101.977 target; price near the target by this date.

head: Inversion Fair Value Gap (iFVG), bullish — used as discount support  (aliases: "inversion fair value gap", "reclaim")
body:
- **Kind:** rule / refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - A bearish FVG that price trades above (and "reclaims as bullish") becomes a bullish inversion FVG. "If it can trade above it, we should see that as an inversion of fair value gap, a bullish fair value gap."
  - Once inverted it should be used as a discount-sensitive area: price trades into it, runs up, clears the high. He will enter long inside that gap on the retest.
  - Colour convention (his own chart habit): the gap is shown green once it has turned bullish, so he can see "what it was originally and then when it changes its characteristic". He admits this is a mental aid and he "might be incorrect in this assumption".
  - Invalidation: the stop goes just under the inversion FVG after the entry works ("raise the stop up just underneath this inversion fair value gap now, 'cause if it goes there, I don't want to be a part of this anymore").
  - He says he will "see it reclaim as bullish" — the reclaim is the thing he waits for before treating it as bullish.
- **How to identify:** bearish FVG (SIBI) on the chart; price closes/trades back above it; flip it to a bullish iFVG (BISI-like behaviour) and treat as support.
- **How to use:** buy a retest into the inverted gap; initial stop below the low of the area with "a little bit of a cushion"; once price moves up and clears the high, trail the stop to just below the iFVG; targets are event horizon, then the 1-hour minor buy-side liquidity.
- **Example in this video:** the bearish FVG that he first shorted into gets reclaimed; he buys inside the newly bullish (green) gap, stop under the low with cushion; after the first partial the stop moves to just under the inversion gap.
- **Timestamps:** [0:03:32](https://youtu.be/k2QLuxMIZio?t=212) — bearish gap → bullish iFVG explanation and colour scheme; [0:05:11](https://youtu.be/k2QLuxMIZio?t=311) — stop raised under the iFVG.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** consistent with the standard iFVG teaching; the novel bit is pairing it with "event horizon" as the first target and the opening-range context.

Price reached event horizon (wicks above, bodies not yet on it) but the orders ended up closed out through his own TP-drag error rather than the planned partial structure.

head: Consequent Encroachment of an old 1-hour imbalance: wick yes, body no  (aliases ICT uses: "old 1-hour buy side imbalance sell side inefficiency", "halfway point", "consequent encroachment")
body:
- **Kind:** rule / refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - He identifies an "old 1-hour buy-side imbalance, sell-side inefficiency" (a 1-hour BISI) that price has already accumulated inside and ramped away from.
  - If the market is to stay bullish it should stay above the halfway point (consequent encroachment) of that gap. "It can wick down below it. We don't want to see it leave a body down there."
  - A body below the CE "makes it more difficult for the market to continue", at least for the remainder of the opening range.
  - He says there is "no real reason" for price to come back below the inversion FVG or below that area, given the sequence so far.
  - Price then wicks down fully through the area and recovers ("full closure on the wick") and is back in the gap: wick tap OK.
- **How to identify:** locate the halfway point of the 1-hour gap; watch whether candle bodies close below it versus only wicks.
- **How to use:** as a hold/fail test for the long: wicks through CE tolerated; bodies below CE = lose conviction. Also small 1-minute gaps stacked above ("a small little gap here, then this one here") can be used as stepping stones.
- **Example in this video:** after price pushes to event horizon, it drops back; the wick goes all the way down and fills the area, but no body closes below the CE, so the structure still holds; he is neutral at the moment because price is mid-area.
- **Timestamps:** [0:08:19](https://youtu.be/k2QLuxMIZio?t=499) — no reason to return below the inversion FVG; old 1-hour BISI; [0:09:07](https://youtu.be/k2QLuxMIZio?t=547) — CE: wick allowed, body not.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** same "bodies vs wicks at CE" logic as in the Reaper FVG video (L26-077): the CE is a boundary respected by candle bodies, not necessarily wicks.

title: Futures Market Commentary \ June 18, 2026
head: Volume Imbalance and Sell-Side Imbalance / Buy-Side Inefficiency (aliases: SIBI, sell-side imbalance buy-side inefficiency, volume gap)
body:
- **Kind:** definition + identification tool
- **What ICT says:** When a candle opens significantly lower (or higher) than the previous candle's close, that gap is a volume imbalance—an inefficiency. If a candle opens below the prior close and shows sell-side imbalance (sellers willing at lower prices) paired with buy-side inefficiency (no buyers at those lower prices), it creates a gap. This inefficiency is a target for reversal or draw.
- **How to identify:** Look at the prior candle's close and the current candle's open; if they don't align, there's a volume imbalance. Use the "toggle" feature (zoom in/out) to see gaps more clearly.
- **How to use:** These gaps act as targets. If price opens down into a sell-side imbalance / buy-side inefficiency, expect price to eventually fill or bounce from it. Use it as a reversal zone or draw target.
- **Example in this video:** NQ had a volume imbalance at the open; this was noted as sell-side imbalance with buy-side inefficiency. Market later returned to fill/test this gap.
- **Timestamps:** [0:00:48](https://youtu.be/bUN_f8U_1Eg?t=48) (volume imbalance defined; candlestick high and body) · [0:01:37](https://youtu.be/bUN_f8U_1Eg?t=97) (sell-side imbalance, buy-side inefficiency with volume imbalance) · [0:10:20](https://youtu.be/bUN_f8U_1Eg?t=620) (toggle on/off to see volume imbalances).
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Use toggle (zoom in/out) to make gaps visible; they're institutional reference points.

title: Futures Market Commentary \ June 18, 2026
head: Inversion Fair Value Gap (aliases: iFVG, bullish/bearish inversion, bodies respect one side)
body:
- **Kind:** definition + order flow rule
- **What ICT says:** An inversion FVG is a gap where bodies trade on one side and wicks reach the other, but bodies never commit to the wick's side. Example: gap up, bodies in lower half, wicks touch upper half but no body reaches it = bearish inversion FVG. It's expected to reverse. Key: watch where bodies trade vs. where wicks reach.
- **How to identify:** Mark a gap; then observe: do bodies commit to one side while wicks reach the opposite? If bodies never reach consequent encroachment on the wick's side, it's an inversion.
- **How to use:** Inversion FVGs are rejection signals. If price failed to commit beyond CE, expect reversal. Use them as bounce targets and as confirmation of directional bias on retracements.
- **Example in this video:** Dollar rallied into an inversion FVG; bodies stayed in lower half, wicks reached high but no body commitment. This was bearish, and price later reversed.
- **Timestamps:** [0:02:24](https://youtu.be/bUN_f8U_1Eg?t=144) (rally through CE of inversion FVG, kind of inversion FVG) · [0:05:36](https://youtu.be/bUN_f8U_1Eg?t=336) (bodies using inefficiency, but bodies never came back to CE; bearish).
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** The key is body commitment; wicks are noise; bodies are order flow.

title: Futures Market Commentary \ June 18, 2026
head: Algorithmic Price Delivery vs. Buying/Selling Pressure (aliases: algorithmic execution, price delivery, order flow)
body:
- **Kind:** conceptual framework
- **What ICT says:** Retail traders think "buying pressure = price up, selling pressure = price down." This is backwards. The market is zero-sum: for every buyer, there's a seller. What matters is WHERE the algorithm places price—whether it's sweeping liquidity (stops, limit orders) or drawing into inefficiencies. The algorithm is not creating supply/demand; it's routing price to specific institutional liquidity zones. Recognize this and read price action accordingly.
- **How to identify:** Instead of asking "is there buying or selling pressure?", ask "where is the algorithm routing price?" Use order flow rules (body placement, CE commits, displacement) to read intent.
- **How to use:** Use algorithmic framework for prediction. If bodies show weakness at a level, expect continuation down (algorithmic delivery lower). If bodies are strong and reach CE, expect continuation up.
- **Example in this video:** Crude oil: when price failed to get bodies above CE on an up move, Michael noted "Algorithmically, this is weak" = expect reversal down. Later, price delivered down as the algorithm routed to lower inefficiencies.
- **Timestamps:** [0:02:31](https://youtu.be/bUN_f8U_1Eg?t=151) (net sum zero game; it's not buying/selling pressure, it's the algorithm moving price to higher prices) · [0:05:36](https://youtu.be/bUN_f8U_1Eg?t=336) (bodies never reached CE; is that bullish or bearish based on Michael's order flow rules? Bearish—algorithmic) · [0:11:07](https://youtu.be/bUN_f8U_1Eg?t=667) (failed to get CE with a body; is that bullish or bearish based on algorithmic order flow? Bearish).
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Flip the narrative: it's not supply/demand; it's institutional routing of price to liquidity.

title: Futures Market Commentary \ June 18, 2026
head: Draw on Liquidity (aliases: draw, short-term draw, best-case target, near-term draw)
body:
- **Kind:** rule + targeting
- **What ICT says:** A draw is when price moves toward an identified inefficiency or liquidity pool with institutional conviction (sustained move, clean structure). Michael identifies two draws per setup: near-term draw (lower-probability, closer target) and best-case scenario (higher-probability if momentum continues, further away). Use these to define targets and partial profit zones.
- **How to identify:** Identify inefficiencies at multiple levels; the nearest one is near-term draw; the furthest is best case.
- **How to use:** Set targets at draws. If price is moving toward a draw and showing strength, expect it to reach the draw. Use near-term as first target; best case as runner target.
- **Example in this video:** Euro Dollar: near-term draw was a minor sell-side liquidity pool; best-case scenario was a deeper inefficiency. Michael would take partial at near-term, hold runner to best case.
- **Timestamps:** [0:03:13](https://youtu.be/bUN_f8U_1Eg?t=193) (best-case scenario short-term, near-term draw; minor sell-side liquidity pool) · [0:06:24](https://youtu.be/bUN_f8U_1Eg?t=384) (draw down here; idea to share, not hard and fast).
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Draws don't always complete in the timeframe you expect; they may take days or require additional structure to materialize.

title: Futures Market Commentary \ June 18, 2026
head: Minor Sell-Side Liquidity Pool (aliases: minor SSL, secondary target)
body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:** Within a daily range or between major inefficiencies, there may be a smaller pool of sell-side liquidity (resting sell orders at an intermediate level). This is a minor target—a bounce point or partial profit zone, not the ultimate target. Use it as a first-take profit zone; then run the rest toward best-case (the major inefficiency).
- **How to identify:** Scan the daily chart between the opening range and a lower major inefficiency; if there's a swing high or clustering of small inefficiencies, that's a minor SSL.
- **How to use:** Treat minor SSL as your first target for shorts. Take bulk of position here; hold runners for best case. If minor SSL is taken out, expect a continuation to major inefficiency.
- **Example in this video:** Euro Dollar had a minor sell-side liquidity pool at an intermediate level; Michael noted "That would be enough for me if I was a bearish forex trader" to take considerable profit there.
- **Timestamps:** [0:04:02](https://youtu.be/bUN_f8U_1Eg?t=242) (minor sell-side liquidity pool; take considerable profit there).
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Minor zones are stepping stones; they're not final targets, just profitable exit points.

title: Futures Market Commentary \ June 18, 2026
head: Displacement (aliases: strong move, aggressive break, breakout)
body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:** A displacement is a strong, directional move that breaks through structure with conviction. When bodies are committed and showing aggression (not wicking back into inefficiencies), you have a displacement. Displacements predict continuation; the direction of the displacement tells you where price will go next.
- **How to identify:** Look for candles with minimal wicks and bodies committed to one direction; that's a displacement.
- **How to use:** When you see a displacement, expect the direction to continue. Displacements often precede the largest moves.
- **Example in this video:** Crude oil had "a strong displacement below these relative equal lows"—bodies broke below and continued; no reversal; this signaled lower prices ahead.
- **Timestamps:** [0:06:24](https://youtu.be/bUN_f8U_1Eg?t=384) (strong displacement below relative equal lows).
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Displacements are conviction moves; they're high-probability continuations of the direction.

title: Futures Market Commentary \ June 18, 2026
head: Event Horizon (aliases: midpoint, old low to next target)
body:
- **Kind:** measurement tool
- **What ICT says:** Event Horizon is the midpoint between two price levels. When used in daily analysis, it's often the midpoint between an old low and the next target/inefficiency below. This midpoint is a pause zone or bounce point; price often pauses here before continuing to the next target.
- **How to identify:** Find an old low and a target below it; calculate the midpoint price.
- **How to use:** Use as an intermediate pause/bounce zone. If you're short and price is at Event Horizon, expect a pause or bounce before continuation to the next target.
- **Example in this video:** Bitcoin: Michael used old low to next target; Event Horizon is the midpoint between them.
- **Timestamps:** [0:19:50](https://youtu.be/bUN_f8U_1Eg?t=1190) (event horizon concept: old low down to next target or pool of liquidity).
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Event Horizon is a technical level, less critical than institutional liquidity levels.

title: Futures Market Commentary \ June 18, 2026
head: Judas Swing (aliases: sucker run, trap rally, news-driven spike)
body:
- **Kind:** definition + psychology
- **What ICT says:** A Judas swing is a rally or spike in price that lures retail traders to buy ("come here, Judas!") before the market reverses sharply. Often triggered by news or a brief algorithmic spike. The move is designed to trap long positions. Recognize it and fade it (go short into the spike).
- **How to identify:** Watch for spikes higher that fail to stay above previous highs; bodies don't reach upper inefficiencies; gaps higher on open but then reverse lower.
- **How to use:** Fade Judas swings. When you see a news-driven spike or a brief rally that fails to sustain, short into it with conviction. These often deliver large moves down.
- **Example in this video:** Crude oil: Trump announced military action; oil gapped higher (Judas swing to trap bulls). Michael tweeted "Fade the Cheeto"—fade the Judas swing. Price indeed reversed lower and delivered a $20,000 per contract move down.
- **Timestamps:** [0:11:53](https://youtu.be/bUN_f8U_1Eg?t=713) (Trump announcement; market tried to go higher; Michael faded it; strong sell-off) · [0:12:41](https://youtu.be/bUN_f8U_1Eg?t=761) (last-ditch attempt to get people thinking it's going up; they're trying to trap traders).
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Judas swings are often news-driven; the underlying order flow is bearish despite the spike.

title: Futures Market Commentary \ June 18, 2026
head: Intermarket Relationships (aliases: inverse correlation, Dollar vs. Commodities)
body:
- **Kind:** macro context
- **What ICT says:** Different markets move in opposite directions based on macro conditions. Example: US Dollar Index often moves inverse to commodities (oil, bitcoin). When Dollar rallies, commodities weaken (and vice versa). Use intermarket relationships to confirm directional bias and to avoid trading against correlated moves.
- **How to identify:** Track DXY (Dollar Index), EUR/USD, GBP/USD, Crude Oil, Bitcoin simultaneously. Note which pairs are correlated or inverse.
- **How to use:** If you're bullish on DXY, expect commodities down. If you're short crude oil, expect DXY strong. Use this as a bias confirmation.
- **Example in this video:** Michael noted that Euro Dollar was in a retracement to the daily bullish inversion FVG (bearish euro = bullish dollar). Pound Dollar was also weakening (dollar strong). Crude Oil was plunging (dollar strong = commodity weak). All moves were consistent with a bullish dollar bias that Michael predicted on June 7.
- **Timestamps:** [0:03:13](https://youtu.be/bUN_f8U_1Eg?t=193) (Euro Dollar retracement as dollar rallies) · [0:08:08](https://youtu.be/bUN_f8U_1Eg?t=488) (Pound Dollar weak; order flow bearish) · [0:12:41](https://youtu.be/bUN_f8U_1Eg?t=761) (Crude oil down as dollar rallies; inverse relationship).
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Macro relationships are general rules; geopolitical events can override them temporarily, but order flow eventually reasserts the correlation.

title: Futures Market Commentary \ June 18, 2026
head: Relative Equal Lows (aliases: REL, equal lows, old low reference)
body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:** Two or more swing lows at approximately the same price level. These are institutional reference points—clusters of stop losses and limit orders. When price breaks below RELs, it signals weakness; the sweep is a "liquidity grab" before continuation.
- **How to identify:** Scan recent price action (5–20 candles back on daily); find two or more lows within a few ticks of each other.
- **How to use:** RELs are targets for shorts. When you're short and price approaches a REL, expect a test or sweep. Use as a partial-profit zone or a confirmation of directional continuation.
- **Example in this video:** Crude Oil had relative equal lows; price broke below them with a displacement, signaling institutional participation and lower targets ahead.
- **Timestamps:** [0:06:24](https://youtu.be/bUN_f8U_1Eg?t=384) (strong displacement below relative equal lows).
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** RELs are liquidity clusters; sweeps through them often accelerate the move.

title: Futures Market Commentary \ June 18, 2026
head: Futures Contract Months (aliases: contract symbols, H, M, U, Z)
body:
- **Kind:** reference information
- **What ICT says:** Index futures have four main contract months: March (H), June (M), September (U), December (Z). Always note which contract you're analyzing; the continuous contract (rolling between months) can show different behavior than individual month contracts. For NQ in mid-June, June contract (M) is expiring soon; September (U) becomes the primary contract.
- **How to identify:** Check the futures ticker; note the symbol (ZNU for Sept NQ, ZNM for June NQ, etc.).
- **How to use:** Use the continuous contract for long-term bias; use individual months when near expiration to avoid roll gaps. Michael checks if the June (M) contract made a higher high vs. the September (U) contract to assess continuity of rallies.
- **Example in this video:** NQ June (M) contract vs. September (U) contract; Michael noted that neither made higher highs compared to the recent low, so the continuous contract showed the rally potential.
- **Timestamps:** [0:16:38](https://youtu.be/bUN_f8U_1Eg?t=998) (NQ front month contract September, symbol U) · [0:16:38](https://youtu.be/bUN_f8U_1Eg?t=998) (contract symbols: H=March, M=June, U=September, Z=December) · [0:17:26](https://youtu.be/bUN_f8U_1Eg?t=1046) (June contract not higher high; September contract not higher high; continuous shows rally potential).
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Always check both the month and the continuous contract; don't rely on one without the other.

title: Futures Commentary \ June 09, 2026
head: Inversion Fair Value Gap (iFVG) Validation Across Timeframes (aliases: multi-timeframe confirmation, context-based iFVG)
body:
- **Kind:** rule + validation method
- **What ICT says:** Don't call something an iFVG without context and multi-timeframe confirmation. An iFVG is only valid if: (1) price trades through it with a close outside it, (2) on the retrace into it, bodies fail to reach consequent encroachment, (3) the next candle gives immediate feedback (direction confirmed). To remove ambiguity, watch the hourly chart for first utilization (breakout of the FVG), then drop to 1m to watch for iFVG validation (bodies reject CE). Only then is it a confirmed iFVG.
- **How to identify:** On hourly: identify where price first breaks the gap (this is "first utilization"). On 1m: watch next retracement; bodies must fail to reach CE. Multiple closes and body rejections = true iFVG.
- **How to use:** Once iFVG is validated across timeframes, trade it with high conviction. Expect sharp reversals from validated iFVGs.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 1-minute iFVG was validated when price traded above it, failed to leave a body above, and closed below it. Hourly chart showed first utilization (break above the gap). This multi-timeframe context gave high conviction for the short.
- **Timestamps:** [0:12:22](https://youtu.be/18vX-vv2bsg?t=742) (lower quadrant, iFVG, wanting to see it act as inversion fair value gap on 1m) · [0:13:12](https://youtu.be/18vX-vv2bsg?t=792) (context required; you're guessing if you don't have this; remove all ambiguity) · [0:14:01](https://youtu.be/18vX-vv2bsg?t=841) (open, trade up, fail to leave body, close down = validates iFVG).
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Context is everything; a price structure looks like an iFVG until bodies prove otherwise.

title: Futures Commentary \ June 09, 2026
head: New Day Opening Gap (NDOG) / New Week Opening Gap (NWOG) (aliases: opening gap, weekly gap, settlement gap)
body:
- **Kind:** definition + targeting tool
- **What ICT says:** NDOG is the gap between RTH close (4:59 ET previous day) and RTH open (9:30 ET next day). NWOG is the gap between week close and week open. Michael uses these as reference levels and as targets for reversals. When price approaches these gaps, it often acts as inversion FVGs (weak commitment).
- **How to identify:** Mark the settlement price (4:59 ET close) and the next day's RTH open (9:30 ET); the gap between them is NDOG. Mark Friday close and Monday open for NWOG.
- **How to use:** Use NDOG/NWOG as targets and bounce zones. On the 5m or 1m chart, use the gradient to show the NDOG levels.
- **Example in this video:** Crude oil: Michael graded the new week opening gap (settlement price to next week open). On the 5-minute chart, price utilized the gap and launched lower; it was a target zone.
- **Timestamps:** [0:03:19](https://youtu.be/18vX-vv2bsg?t=199) (new week opening gap: high and last week settlement price) · [0:04:08](https://youtu.be/18vX-vv2bsg?t=248) (shows how NWOG is graded on 5m chart; used as launching price level).
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** NDOG/NWOG act as institutional reference points; use them as targets or bounce zones, not as hard support/resistance.

title: Futures Commentary \ June 09, 2026
head: Breaker with Nested Fair Value Gaps (iFVG nested in breaker) (aliases: Reaper, nested pattern)
body:
- **Kind:** pattern + high-probability setup
- **What ICT says:** When you have a breaker (short-term high, low, higher high but lower than original) AND you nest an iFVG (buy-side imbalance sell-side efficiency) inside it, AND you have a second iFVG opposing the first, you have a variant of the Reaper pattern. This is extremely high-probability. Michael notes: "When you have that and it's part of a breaker, that is a variant of a reaper."
- **How to identify:** Find a breaker structure; identify two nested iFVGs within it (one bearish, one bullish, opposing each other).
- **How to use:** When you spot this, expect sharp moves through both iFVGs in sequence. First iFVG acts as a bounce zone; second iFVG is the target. Use both for entries and targets.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 1m chart had a breaker with nested iFVGs; Michael shorted the first iFVG retrace, then expected price to drop to the second iFVG (which it did).
- **Timestamps:** [0:17:17](https://youtu.be/18vX-vv2bsg?t=1037) (when you have two nested fair value gaps that's part of a breaker; that is a variant of a reaper).
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Reaper is one of Michael's named patterns; the nested structure makes it extremely high-probability.

title: Futures Commentary \ June 09, 2026
head: Buy-Side Bounce / Sell-Side Efficiency (aliases: bearish inefficiency, bull imbalance structure)
body:
- **Kind:** definition + direction indicator
- **What ICT says:** When you see a buy-side bounce with sell-side efficiency (buyers can bounce price up, but sellers show efficiency/willingness at higher prices), it's bearish. This inefficiency acts as an iFVG when price comes back to it. The presence of this structure signals weakness despite the bounce.
- **How to identify:** Look for a bounce higher (buy-side bounce) that fails to sustain; sellers show no commitment at higher levels (sell-side efficiency). Mark it as an inefficiency.
- **How to use:** Treat buy-side bounce/sell-side efficiency structures as reversal zones. When price retraces into them, expect bearish continuation.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 1m: "We have this sell-side bounce buy-side efficiency which is bearish. We want to see price utilize that."
- **Timestamps:** [0:16:28](https://youtu.be/18vX-vv2bsg?t=988) (sell-side bounce buy-side efficiency, which is bearish).
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** The language can be confusing; focus on the outcome: is price showing willingness above, or is it weak? That's the signal.

title: Futures Commentary \ June 09, 2026
head: First Utilization / First Presentation of Fair Value Gap (aliases: first break, initial FVG use)
body:
- **Kind:** pattern + timing indicator
- **What ICT says:** The first utilization is when price first trades through/beyond a fair value gap after it forms. This is often on a higher timeframe (hourly or daily). Once first utilization happens, watch the lower timeframes for the iFVG behavior on the retracement. First utilization confirms the FVG is real institutional reference.
- **How to identify:** On hourly/daily, mark where price first breaks above or below the FVG (this is first utilization). Then drop to lower timeframes to watch the retracement.
- **How to use:** First utilization is confirmation that the FVG is on the institutional radar. After first utilization, the retrace into the FVG will likely show iFVG behavior.
- **Example in this video:** NQ hourly: price first utilized (broke above) the FVG. Then on 1m, the retrace showed bodies failing to reach CE = validated iFVG.
- **Timestamps:** [0:11:26](https://youtu.be/18vX-vv2bsg?t=686) (lower quadrant hourly positive bounce sell-side efficiency; turn inversion fair gap).
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** First utilization is the "green light" for trading the iFVG on lower timeframes.

title: Futures Commentary \ June 09, 2026
head: Volume Bounce and Volume Imbalance (aliases: volume gap, micro-imbalance)
body:
- **Kind:** definition + identification
- **What ICT says:** A volume bounce is when a candle's open is higher than the previous candle's close (or vice versa), creating a small gap/imbalance. This micro-inefficiency shows up in structure. Example: close 905, next open 905.5 = 0.5 point imbalance. These tiny gaps are where smart money enters and exits.
- **How to identify:** Compare candle closes and next candle opens; any difference is a volume bounce/imbalance.
- **How to use:** Use volume bounces as entry points. When you see a clear volume bounce, the next candle's direction often confirms the trend.
- **Example in this video:** NQ hourly: close 905, next open 905.5 (volume bounce). This was part of the hourly iFVG structure Michael was watching.
- **Timestamps:** [0:11:26](https://youtu.be/18vX-vv2bsg?t=686) (close 905.5, next candle open.5; there's a volume bounce).
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Volume bounces are microscopic; they're easy to miss if you don't zoom in.

title: Futures Commentary \ June 09, 2026
head: Nested Inefficiencies on Multiple Timeframes (aliases: nested FVGs, multi-timeframe structure)
body:
- **Kind:** setup structure + high-probability pattern
- **What ICT says:** When an inefficiency on the daily/hourly level contains smaller inefficiencies on the 15m/1m level, you have nested structures. The outer inefficiency is the major target; the inner ones are bounce zones. Michael uses nested structures to define precise entries and exits. Example: daily iFVG contains an hourly iFVG, which contains 1m iFVGs.
- **How to identify:** Zoom from daily to 1m; identify inefficiencies at each timeframe; note how they nest.
- **How to use:** Use the outermost (daily) inefficiency as the long-term target. Use inner (hourly/1m) inefficiencies for entries and partial exits. This gives you precision and confirmation.
- **Example in this video:** NQ had a daily inefficiency; within it, an hourly iFVG; within that, 1m iFVGs. Michael used each layer to refine entry and management.
- **Timestamps:** [0:16:28](https://youtu.be/18vX-vv2bsg?t=988) (two nested fair value gaps; when you have that and it's part of a breaker, that is a variant of a reaper).
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Nested structures are the holy grail of trading; they offer precision and high probability.

title: Futures Commentary \ June 09, 2026
head: Quadrants (aliases: 25% levels, quadrant breakdown)
body:
- **Kind:** measurement tool
- **What ICT says:** Divide a range into four equal parts (quadrants = 25% each). Price often pauses or reverses at quadrant boundaries. When price reaches the lower quadrant of an inefficiency and shows weakness there, expect reversal or consolidation.
- **How to identify:** Mark the high and low of an inefficiency or range; divide into 4 parts; note each quadrant.
- **How to use:** Use quadrant levels as interim targets and reversal zones. If price reaches the lower quadrant and shows iFVG behavior, don't expect it to go further.
- **Example in this video:** NQ hourly had a lower quadrant mark; Michael was watching to see if price reached it with weakness = confirmation of bearish bias.
- **Timestamps:** [0:12:22](https://youtu.be/18vX-vv2bsg?t=742) (lower quadrant hourly positive bounce; sell-side efficiency turn inversion fair value gap).
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Quadrants are mathematical subdivisions; they align with algorithmic price levels.

title: Futures Commentary \ June 09, 2026
head: Risk Management in High Volatility (aliases: position sizing, small risk big play, pack small play big)
body:
- **Kind:** risk management principle
- **What ICT says:** In high-volatility environments (like June 2026 markets), traditional position sizing is dangerous. Instead, "pack small, play big": use very tight stops (small risk per trade), but let winners run with patience. This way, even if you're wrong, the loss is small; when you're right, the gain is huge because you're not exiting early. Example: Happy Meal worth of drawdown ($7 range) vs. thousands of handles of profit.
- **How to identify:** Calculate your account size and maximum loss tolerance; size positions so your stop-loss risk is 0.5–1% of account.
- **How to use:** On high-volatility days, use stops 3–5 ticks away (vs. 10 ticks normally). Hold winners longer because they're likely to run 50–100+ ticks.
- **Example in this video:** Michael took a short with tight stop (near entry), but let it run for 1600+ handles. If he'd been oversized, the tight stop would have been hit multiple times; instead, he stayed in and captured the move.
- **Timestamps:** [0:14:06](https://youtu.be/18vX-vv2bsg?t=846) (fill at one tick below; couple bucks drawdown, like a Happy Meal's worth) · [0:21:20](https://youtu.be/18vX-vv2bsg?t=1280) (pack small, play big: keep risk small, let trades run, exercise patience).
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** In normal markets, you can take on 2–3% risk; in volatility >1000 handles/day, cut that to 0.5% or less.

title: ICT Reaper FVG - Long NQ Terminus Daily V.I. \ June 08, 2026
head: Reaper FVG  (aliases ICT uses: "Reaper FVG" in the title; in the talk he describes the nested "inversion fair value gap + bullish fair value gap" at a sell-side low)
body:
- **Kind:** entry model (named in the title; not defined in the words of this transcript)
- **What ICT says:** the title pairs "Reaper FVG" with "Long NQ Terminus Daily V.I.". In the commentary he stacks two qualifying PD arrays at a low: a small bullish fair value gap and a bullish inversion fair value gap in the same area ("nested areas of two qualified areas for discount sensitivity"), and he expects "a very strong reaction" with price popping up out of them.
- **How to identify (as shown):**
  - Price trades down into relative equal lows / a minor sell-side low and takes those sell stops.
  - At that low there is a small bullish FVG and a bullish iFVG (a former bearish gap that price has traded back above).
  - Entry is taken into this nested area ("let's go 20 contracts into that").
- **How to use:** see Entry/stop/targets sections below.
- **Example in this video:** NQ, Monday 8 June 2026 morning, market replay. Price dips into relative equal lows, takes the sell stops, and reacts off a nested iFVG + bullish FVG; ICT buys 20 contracts there.
- **Timestamps:** [0:00:00](https://youtu.be/kzeFqGK9gCQ?t=0) — "I'm buying these sell stops, all these are relatively equal lows"; [0:02:27](https://youtu.be/kzeFqGK9gCQ?t=147) — minor sell-side left, small bullish FVG plus bullish iFVG; [0:03:15](https://youtu.be/kzeFqGK9gCQ?t=195) — "very strong reaction", enters 20 contracts.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** the formal definition of "Reaper" is not in this transcript; treat the above as the observed pattern only. Reconcile with other Reaper videos in the series.

title: ICT Reaper FVG - Long NQ Terminus Daily V.I. \ June 08, 2026
head: Daily Volume Imbalance as the target ("Terminus Daily V.I.")  (aliases: "daily volume imbalance", "orange box/area", "Terminus" (named model, caption))
body:
- **Kind:** rule (draw on liquidity / target) / example only
- **What ICT says:**
  - He had posted analysis the night before that price would likely trade up into the daily volume imbalance created by Friday's big sell-off ("trading back up into Friday's big sell-off... I told you it would be reasonable to see that").
  - He only needs a small amount of that: "just a little bit inside" the daily volume imbalance (the lower part), and that "pads me out for any potential short".
  - Price must get up into that orange area before any meaningful short could be considered, and even then "it doesn't necessarily mean I'm going to get short today".
  - The consequent encroachment of the daily volume imbalance measured to its low is "29 560 ish" (caption unclear; likely NQ ~29,560) and is a secondary reach; the final target zone he names is "555 560 in that vicinity".
  - He does not want price to come back down immediately to fill the volume imbalance; that would be "a little less bullish" — rushing back to an inefficiency shows weakness.
- **How to identify:** mark the daily volume imbalance (gap between candle bodies on the daily chart left by a big down day). The target is its low, then its CE.
- **How to use:** buy relative equal lows below price when a higher-timeframe imbalance above is the draw; target the low of the daily VI first (partials), and keep a runner for its deeper part; once it's reached, the short-side thesis becomes eligible.
- **Example in this video:** the volume imbalance sits in the daily chart under Friday's sell-off candle; NQ trades up and touches the low of the daily volume imbalance at ~9:05 into the video (as "we wanted to see"), ICT sells partial contracts there and above.
- **Timestamps:** [0:00:51](https://youtu.be/kzeFqGK9gCQ?t=51) — daily chart tour, the draw up into Friday's sell-off; [0:08:09](https://youtu.be/kzeFqGK9gCQ?t=489) — measuring CE of the imbalance, "29 560 ish"; [0:09:05](https://youtu.be/kzeFqGK9gCQ?t=545) — price has touched the low of the daily volume imbalance.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** the caption says "daily volume balance" in places (caption unclear); it is the daily volume imbalance.

title: ICT Reaper FVG - Long NQ Terminus Daily V.I. \ June 08, 2026
head: Inversion FVG + bullish FVG nesting as discount sensitivity  (aliases: "discount sensitivity", "two qualified areas")
body:
- **Kind:** refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - Two qualifying areas stacked — a bullish FVG and a bullish inversion FVG — give "discount sensitivity": price should react from them.
  - After the entry, he does not want price to return and touch the high of the inversion FVG again ("I want to see it run, take out that high, without touching the orange area again" — here the orange area is the zone he is working from; caption mixes the iFVG with the daily VI shade).
  - A "mohawk": a wick that dips a little outside the iFVG and reverses sharply back above the upper half; the body should end inside the iFVG ("look where the body is").
  - The next candle "has to do a lot of work to go higher and not lay a body below the previous candle's wick low" — a body below that wick low is "problematic".
- **How to identify:** small bullish FVG + bullish iFVG at the same low, a sharp rejection wick, bodies inside/above the iFVG.
- **How to use:** hold the long while bodies stay above the previous candle's wick low; a body below it shows the wick's control is lost.
- **Example in this video:** after the entry, a candle wicks slightly outside the iFVG then reverses up outside the upper half; the next candle must run and cannot lay a body below that wick's low.
- **Timestamps:** [0:04:01](https://youtu.be/kzeFqGK9gCQ?t=241) — "mohawk" wick and body inside the iFVG; [0:04:49](https://youtu.be/kzeFqGK9gCQ?t=289) — no body below the previous wick low; [0:15:14](https://youtu.be/kzeFqGK9gCQ?t=914) — "nested areas of two qualified areas for discount sensitivity".
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** reinforces the iFVG as a support PD array; adds the wick-low body rule as a hold condition.

title: ICT Reaper FVG - Long NQ Terminus Daily V.I. \ June 08, 2026
head: Consequent Encroachment of a wick as a barrier / next PD array  (aliases: "consequent encroachment of that wick", "barrier or boundary")
body:
- **Kind:** rule / refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - He places the first stop-trail "just at the consequent encroachment of that wick". Reason: if price is not going for the sell side below, it will go for inefficiencies; if there is no inefficiency below the bullish iFVG he has noted (blue bullish FVG), "then the next PD array is this wick" — i.e. the wick itself is the next PD array and its CE is the boundary.
  - "Consequent encroachment is a barrier or boundary for price action." No gimmicks, no volume or order-count data: it is "very simple, very visual".
  - He wants an energetic run above the CE of that wick into the orange area (the daily VI) for the first payout.
- **How to identify:** take a long rejection wick on the retest candle; its 50% (CE) is the reference level.
- **How to use:** place the initial risk-reduction stop at the CE of the wick; trail the final runners behind it.
- **Example in this video:** after the mohawk, ICT moves the stop to the CE of that wick ("take some of that risk away") and holds the rest for the run into the daily VI.
- **Timestamps:** [0:05:40](https://youtu.be/kzeFqGK9gCQ?t=340) — why the wick CE is chosen; [0:06:30](https://youtu.be/kzeFqGK9gCQ?t=390) — "barrier or boundary for price action".
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** a wick as a PD array in its own right is a notable extension: if there's no FVG below, the wick's CE is the next support.

title: ICT Reaper FVG - Long NQ Terminus Daily V.I. \ June 08, 2026
head: Scaling out a 20-lot with layered limits and stop to the daily VI low
body:
- **Kind:** entry/management model
- **What ICT says:**
  - Entry: 20 contracts into the nested area (accepting a wick slightly outside).
  - First plan: "15 leave five on for a runner" (take 15 off, keep 5), then he layers the exits instead of one price: sells one at the low of the daily VI, drops limit orders above ("stagger one right there"), and keeps four contracts working as "immediate rebounds on this wick".
  - Once price clears that candle's high, he moves the stop to the low of the daily volume imbalance: with a large portion taken above that low, the last two contracts are "locked in" — they can only stop out at the daily VI low, giving "two runners" with no risk of loss.
  - He says it is fine for the final contracts to be forced out at the daily VI low: "no sense of giving back good money".
  - He keeps a limit and a stop on the remaining runner rather than closing it "in case it does run away a little bit higher"; the aim is the "555–560 vicinity" and he'll peel it off there.
  - Frustration beat: price gets close to the limit order and says "not yet" — he keeps limits at target rather than chasing.
- **How to use:** layered limits above the first target; stop trails to the level where the realised partials guarantee profit; leave runners with a defined stop.
- **Example in this video:** 20 NQ contracts; touch of the daily VI low at ~9:05 into the video; scale-outs through 9:54–13:32; stop raised to the daily VI low (orange shaded area); final runner targeted at ~555–560 (caption).
- **Timestamps:** [0:07:18](https://youtu.be/kzeFqGK9gCQ?t=438) — "15 leave five on for a runner"; [0:09:54](https://youtu.be/kzeFqGK9gCQ?t=594) — layering sells; [0:11:51](https://youtu.be/kzeFqGK9gCQ?t=711) — stop to the low of the daily VI locks in the final two contracts; [0:14:20](https://youtu.be/kzeFqGK9gCQ?t=860) — keep limit + stop on the runner.
