head: Twin Candle Highs / Lows as Liquidity Targets
body:
- **Kind:** refinement
- **What ICT says:** When two candlesticks in a row have the same high (or within 1–2 ticks), that is a "twin candle high" and represents a very small, specific liquidity level. These are targets for market makers to run stops and sweep liquidity. Do not mistake these for larger relative equal highs; they are micro-level targets.
- **How to identify:** Look at consecutive candles; if two in a row share the same high/low, mark it as a twin high/low.
- **How to use:** Twin highs are often hit briefly then reversed; use them as quick scale points. On short-term moves (final hour), these are valid targets.
- **Example in this video:** ES. Multiple twin candle highs were hit during the final hour; each was a small liquidity target.
- **Timestamps:** [0:18:55](https://youtu.be/7zlblhLGraA?t=1135) — twin candle highs on 15s chart · [0:19:46](https://youtu.be/7zlblhLGraA?t=1186) — not requiring exact match; relative equal highs suffice
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Do not "demand" exact matching; even relative equal highs within small range are valid.

title: Market Alchemy - Trading ATH \ May 14, 2026
head: Time-first framework (New York local time, 9:30, first hour, 11:30 lunch, 1:30–2:00 PM opening range)  (aliases ICT uses: "it's always time first, then price")
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - Always keep the chart on New York local time. If you are anchored elsewhere you are "off time, late or early", and moves that look like they come from nowhere are just time misreads.
  - Mark 9:30 (the open). The first hour after 9:30 is the first hour's dealing range.
  - 11:30 AM ET starts the New York lunch "without fail" (it can start sooner, he says it "will always start at 11:30"). The New York lunch is a 2-hour period (11:30 to 1:30).
  - 1:30 to 2:00 PM is the opening range of the PM ("4:00 PM") session: all PD arrays in that range are salient for the PM session, the final hour, and the 6:00 PM restart.
  - Price action is read relative to a time grid first; staring at every little candle makes you "lose the forest for the trees", and "the thing that matters most is time".
  - He says algorithmically everything is based on time, then price: "the code, the sequence, the scripting of these markets they follow a sequence."
- **How to identify:** put vertical lines at 9:30, 10:00 (a reference), 11:30, 12:30 (end of the first lunch hour), 1:30 and 2:00 ET.
- **How to use:** use the time lines to decide when to look for a setup (see Lunch Macro) and which swing lows/highs count as targets.
- **Example in this video:** NQ, Thursday 14 May 2026: gaps lower at 9:30, runs up all morning, hits an 8x projection at the start of the lunch window, then reverses down through the lunch macro and finishes by 1:26 PM.
- **Timestamps:** [0:05:06](https://youtu.be/wprXVW1pW9Y?t=306) — 9:30 open and the 11:30 lunch start; [0:09:49](https://youtu.be/wprXVW1pW9Y?t=589) — always set the chart to New York local time; [0:27:09](https://youtu.be/wprXVW1pW9Y?t=1629) — 1:30–2:00 PM opening range.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** he tells viewers to "not call it a lunch hour": it is a 2-hour New York lunch. Two chapters of his volume three cover market-profile-type material that he says you "don't need".

title: Market Alchemy - Trading ATH \ May 14, 2026
head: RTH Opening Range Gap (discount opening range gap) and its retest as discount sensitivity  (aliases: "regular trading hours opening range gap", "discount array", "trampoline")
body:
- **Kind:** definition + rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - The RTH opening range gap is the space between the close of the prior session's last candle (the 4:15 PM ET settle) and today's 9:30 open. A gap lower is a "discount opening range gap": price opened below where it settled the day before, i.e. it is being "offered at a discount".
  - Classic expectation: a premium/discount gap tries to fill; the gap closure happens either way, whether you short it or buy it.
  - But if you trade against the higher-timeframe freight train (here a violent bull run), shorting the fill is not a trade for a new trader.
  - Better use: if price overcomes the gap (a candle goes up through/over it), then the very next candle opens and trades back down to it, and the gap now "acts as a discount array". In a bull market, that first return into the gap is the original first run into the range and should act as discount sensitivity: price uses it like a trampoline, drops in, then runs energetically away.
  - If you miss that move, do not chase candle by candle; anchor with a vertical line at the open so you keep time in view.
- **How to identify:** compare the 4:15 PM ET close of the previous day with the 9:30 open; mark the gap box between them (open as the low, previous close as the high on a gap-down day).
- **How to use:** long on the first retest into the gap after price has overcome it, with the higher-timeframe bias bullish; use the gap's height as the unit of measurement for upward projections (next concept).
- **Example in this video:** NQ opens at 9:30 below the prior close (gap-down). Price immediately overcomes the gap on one candle, the very next candle opens and trades back down into it, and it bounces energetically. ICT also notes he traded the "full mini, not the micro".
- **Timestamps:** [0:01:56](https://youtu.be/wprXVW1pW9Y?t=116) — defines today's RTH opening range gap and expects upside draw; [0:10:35](https://youtu.be/wprXVW1pW9Y?t=635) — discount gap versus 4:15 PM settle; [0:13:45](https://youtu.be/wprXVW1pW9Y?t=825) — retest of the overcome gap acts as a discount array; [0:14:32](https://youtu.be/wprXVW1pW9Y?t=872) — "trampoline".
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** restates and extends his opening-gap teaching: the gap is used (a) as support after being overcome and (b) as a ruler for projections.

title: Market Alchemy - Trading ATH \ May 14, 2026
head: 8:30 micro vs. mini divergence redelivery (news-event stop hunt)  (aliases: "re-deliver", "rerun")
body:
- **Kind:** rule / example only
- **What ICT says:**
  - He posted on X that when a market makes a spike at the 8:30 news event in one contract (micro NQ went down precipitously) but not in the other (mini did not), the market "generally wants to redeliver that": it will go back to repeat that same price run. If the move had been higher, it would repeat that run higher.
  - It does not just overlap the level; it goes through it and operates as a stop hunt.
  - On the day: the micro made a spike low at 8:30; the mini did not. Price later traded lower to take out that low, taking out all the short-term sell-side liquidity, "primed everyone to anticipate it going lower", and then rallied. You can capitalise with either the micro or the mini.
  - He mentions a "bread and butter" setup on a 30-second chart using micros.
- **How to identify:** compare micro and mini NQ around 8:30; a one-sided spike low (or high) in one product that the other lacks marks the level to be revisited.
- **How to use:** expect a revisit and a stop run beyond that spike extreme before the real move; trade the reversal after the sweep.
- **Example in this video:** NQ micro prints a spike low at 8:30; mini does not; at the open price runs lower again, takes the 8:30 low and the short-term sell-side, then extends to the upside through the day.
- **Timestamps:** [0:02:44](https://youtu.be/wprXVW1pW9Y?t=164) — micro vs mini at 8:30 and redelivery; [0:03:30](https://youtu.be/wprXVW1pW9Y?t=210) — "goes through it and operates as a stop hunt"; [0:04:17](https://youtu.be/wprXVW1pW9Y?t=257) — sell-side liquidity taken, then extrapolates to the upside.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** an intermarket-style (instrument-divergence) SMT-like observation inside one index; not a standard named concept, so treat as a coinage-free observation.

title: Market Alchemy - Trading ATH \ May 14, 2026
head: Lunch Macro (11:30 to 1:30 ET): first low to the left of 11:30, setup forms in the first hour  (aliases: "lunch macro", "New York lunch")
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - At 11:30 a 2-hour window begins where "whatever took place in the morning session will roll against that": a retracement back to a low that formed after 10:00 ET.
  - If the morning was one-sided (all buying, here all-time highs), expect the lunch macro to retrace the morning move.
  - Which low: from 11:30 look left toward 10:00 and use the first low you come to (he calls it the best-case lunch macro). Lows right before 10:00 are not used; the proper pick is the first meaningful one after 10:00. Use the very first one when probabilities are against you (deep retracements) or when the market is very strong from the morning.
  - A good lunch-macro low (his pick): relative equal lows that had "a nice run up" first, left the high intact, then a deep retracement, and the biggest run started from there.
  - Timing within the window: the setup optimally forms in the first hour (11:30 to 12:30), especially after one-sided morning price; the delivery can then take place in the second hour.
- **How to identify:** vertical lines at 10:00, 11:30 and 12:30 ET; the first swing low to the left of 11:30 after 10:00; check for relative equal lows.
- **How to use:** in a strong up day, look for the high of the morning to be reached before or at 11:30, expect the retracement in the first hour of the window and the delivery to the low by 1:30.
- **Example in this video:** NQ, 14 May 2026: low at 10:29 AM of 29,595.50 (relative equal lows). The lunch macro delivery came down and took that low at 1:26 PM with a low of 29,595.25, i.e. by one tick, just before 1:30.
- **Timestamps:** [0:16:07](https://youtu.be/wprXVW1pW9Y?t=967) — "That's the lunch macro... going back for a low after 10:00"; [0:19:19](https://youtu.be/wprXVW1pW9Y?t=1159) — use the first low to the left of 11:30; [0:20:53](https://youtu.be/wprXVW1pW9Y?t=1253) — low prices 29,595.50 at 10:29 vs 29,595.25 at 1:26; [0:32:38](https://youtu.be/wprXVW1pW9Y?t=1958) — setup forms in the first hour 11:30–12:30.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** he says he taught this on podcasts and Spaces earlier; here is the extra filter of first-hour formation and "first low after 10:00".

title: Market Alchemy - Trading ATH \ May 14, 2026
head: Opening Range Gap "standard deviations": the gap height as a ruler with a time window (Market Alchemy)  (aliases: "multiplication table", "replications / standard deviations", "projection")
body:
- **Kind:** new coinage / entry-timing model
- **What ICT says:**
  - Draw a Fibonacci tool from the opening price (9:30 open, the low of the gap) to the prior close (top of the gap): that height is "one standard deviation". Project it upward multiple times (1, 2, 3 ... 7, 7.5, 8).
  - Think of a multiplication table: the vertical axis is price multiples, the horizontal axis is time. First go up the vertical axis (count the multiples), then when price enters the time window (here 11:30) look horizontally; the right multiple "unlocks like the tumblers in a lock".
  - He estimates the reachable count with a thumb: he holds his thumb out until it spans the gap height, then steps it up the screen; roughly 6.5 to 7.5 deviations.
  - Testing on the day: 6.5 and 7 were already exceeded before 11:30, so they could not be the turning level. 7.5 (caption: "2.5") was reached just before 11:30 (wonderful but not the turn). 8 deviations is the next level: price turned there at the start of the first hour of the lunch window.
  - Earlier teaching restated: when the market is consolidating, measure the opening range gap at 0.25 and 0.50 (graded levels). Everything is "graded" because the market is algorithmic.
  - An independent projection: the 10:00 to 11:30 run measured with a Fibonacci projection also points to the same vicinity.
  - ICT says this level-by-time technique is "not found anywhere else", and that parts are being held back for his written books but he will teach it on the channel.
- **How to identify:** (1) gap box = 9:30 open to prior 4:15 PM close; (2) project multiples upward; (3) the candidate multiple is the one not yet exceeded before 11:30; (4) watch candle bodies at that multiple inside 11:30–12:30.
- **How to use:** as the profit-taking or reversal-short zone on strong up days: level (multiple) plus time (lunch window) together define the turning point, and a short is taken from there (see Inversion FVG short).
- **Example in this video:** NQ 14 May 2026: gap = open to prior 4:15 close; 8 deviations is where price stalls in the first hour of the lunch window; he calls it "a turning point randomly in the first hour of the 2-hour lunch period" and challenges "talk to me about not picking a daily high".
- **Timestamps:** [0:07:28](https://youtu.be/wprXVW1pW9Y?t=448) — multiplication-table analogy; [0:27:56](https://youtu.be/wprXVW1pW9Y?t=1676) — Fibonacci from the open to the close of the gap; [0:30:16](https://youtu.be/wprXVW1pW9Y?t=1816) — 0.25 and 0.50 grading in consolidations; [0:33:25](https://youtu.be/wprXVW1pW9Y?t=2005) — thumb measurement; [0:35:02](https://youtu.be/wprXVW1pW9Y?t=2102) — test 6.5, 7, 7.5, then 8.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** counts are approximate in the captions (caption unclear around "2.5"/"7.5" and "6.5 to 7.5"). He says you will need to practise daily: it feels cumbersome at first. The Market Alchemy title is not explicitly explained; this section is the main new material.

title: Market Alchemy - Trading ATH \ May 14, 2026
head: Inversion FVG short at the time/price turning point (entry model)  (aliases: "inversion fair value gap", "buy-side imbalance sell-side inefficiency with a volume imbalance")
body:
- **Kind:** entry model
- **What ICT says:**
  - At the 8-deviation level, on the next candle price opened and "didn't go higher than the previous one", only a little wick, then sank. "When it dropped down in there, I already knew we're done" because little time remained before the close of the first lunch hour.
  - Entry structure: a buy-side imbalance sell-side inefficiency (BISI) with a volume imbalance at the top. A candle takes the high and reaches up to the low of that volume imbalance.
  - Why an inversion FVG: the next candle was unwilling to go to the previous candle's high and take it out. That unwillingness plus a drop through = the bullish gap flips into a bearish inversion FVG. "You have to be real quick, Johnny-on-the-spot, or miss it."
  - Fill at the upper portion of the inversion FVG. If the order had not filled there, the next candle's open went right back up to the consequent encroachment of that level, another chance.
  - After the CE tag, nobody wants to buy any higher than that level: "an invitation goes out" for short sellers to run price lower.
  - A second bullish PD array drawn later was run through "as we should have" with a small run up to its high.
- **How to identify:** time (first hour of the lunch window) + price (8x gap-height projection) + a bullish gap that fails to extend and inverts.
- **How to use:** enter short at the upper part of the iFVG (or at the CE retest); stop above (he says the worst that happens is a normal stop-out); first target is the nearest minor sell-side low (first partial), second target event horizon, final target just above/below the relative equal lows (see Event Horizon).
- **Example in this video:** NQ, 14 May 2026 about 11:30–12:00 ET: price reaches the 8x level, one candle fails to exceed the prior high, price drops through the BISI/volume imbalance; short filled at the upper portion of the inversion FVG; the next candle re-tests the CE and the market rolls lower.
- **Timestamps:** [0:37:21](https://youtu.be/wprXVW1pW9Y?t=2241) — new candle fails to go higher, "we're done"; [0:38:56](https://youtu.be/wprXVW1pW9Y?t=2336) — BISI with volume imbalance at the top; [0:40:31](https://youtu.be/wprXVW1pW9Y?t=2431) — fill at the upper portion of the iFVG and why it is an iFVG; [0:41:18](https://youtu.be/wprXVW1pW9Y?t=2478) — CE re-test, buyers disappear.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** he draws the PD arrays only after the market works through them (he keeps the chart naked until then). He notes this is a trade against the higher-timeframe order flow.

body:

It is the second take-profit area when trading against higher-timeframe order flow. Price "took the profit below that", i.e. his exit filled at event horizon.
- **How to identify:** fib between two liquidity points (here two lows); 50% line.
- **How to use:** second scale-out level; the final target is just beyond the relative equal lows.

head: Minor vs. primary sell-side liquidity, and exiting early against the higher-timeframe trend
body:

  - He marks minor sell-side lows as profit targets first and places limit exits slightly above the primary low, because price only took the 10:29 low by one tick at 1:26 PM (29,595.25 vs 29,595.50). An order sitting at or just beneath that low would never have filled ("too shallow"); experience shows exits must be "a tick or two" earlier.
  - Reason: trading against a bull market, if he is wrong "it can violently shift against me", so he takes "easy objectives" ("the cookie", the moral victory) rather than the best-case low.
  - He explains that exits normally have "that little overrun": the market goes a bit further without him; that is not a failure of the analysis.
  - Also keep time in mind: do not spend too much time in the trade as the 1:30 end of the lunch macro approaches.
- **How to use:** short against HTF bias: aim for minor sell-side first, take profit, accept being early.

title: Market Alchemy - Trading ATH \ May 14, 2026
head: Trading at all-time highs: capitulation, one-sidedness, and who should short
body:
- **Kind:** rule / context (higher-timeframe narrative)
- **What ICT says:**
  - The market is in "capitulation": extremely one-sided with no meaningful retracement ("the Fonz jumping the shark", absurd levels). Either it keeps going higher or crashes, but "an intermediate-term high forming is warranted". He compares it to gold and silver, where he told people it would be "uncivilized" not to take profits; both then made deep retracements; indices are next.
  - People are primed to think "the market only goes up" until it violently shifts lower. Do not trade without stop losses.
  - A new trader should not short a bull market: "you should be afraid to take the short because you don't have the experience": study it, paper trade it, tape read it. If you must trade against the freight train you must be highly selective.
  - He is not afraid: the worst case is a normal stop-out; the idea that being stopped at all-time highs hurts more than other shorts is a myth that experience dispels.
  - Without a primary bull trend he would have targeted the relative-equal lows directly; against the trend he must be prudent.
  - After the trade, the market is "in slop": do not trade; let the overnight session pass and look for something in the pre-market session (about 7:00 to 9:00 ET).
- **How to use:** with a strong bull trend, favour longs; if shorting, use time (lunch macro) + price (8x) + iFVG, take profits early; avoid trading mid-range slop.
- **Timestamps:** [0:12:09](https://youtu.be/wprXVW1pW9Y?t=729) — shorting against a bull trend requires selectivity; [0:17:43](https://youtu.be/wprXVW1pW9Y?t=1063) — capitulation; [0:22:27](https://youtu.be/wprXVW1pW9Y?t=1347) — who should short; [0:47:38](https://youtu.be/wprXVW1pW9Y?t=2858) — don't trade the slop, wait for pre-market.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** keeps the same rule as earlier ICT teaching (trade with higher-timeframe order flow) but shows the exception for experienced traders.

title: Turning Loss Into Gain - Market Alchemy
head: 8:30 news run as the mark: fade the news-driven move toward the opposite-side 8:30 liquidity  (aliases ICT uses: "the mark", "8:30 buy side", "economic calendar", "news embargo")
body:
- **Kind:** rule / narrative
- **What ICT says:**
  - The 8:30 news candle was used "to send price lower to build in a bearish narrative"; he is fading that. The high of the 8:30 candle (the buy-side sitting right before the news release) is the target.
  - "You have to identify the economic calendar and the liquidity off of a price run that originates at the 8:30. That's the mark... where the sniper has his crosshairs trained." Everything between is distraction and "wind gusts".
  - Ask "who made money this morning?" (shorts) and "who are they going after?": longs were stopped out, breakout sellers were baited short; he expects both sides to have been delivered before the move up.
  - "I don't have to be leading the pack. I just got to be part of the meal."
  - Why price may be held below: if they take the buy-side above 8:30 they can go short, ride it down and buy back at a low price from sellers, keeping the low intact first.
- **How to identify:** 8:30 (news) candle; a price run that originates from it; the 8:30 high is the resting buy-side pool when the news drove price down.
- **How to use:** go long once the sell-side below has been taken and a bullish PD array holds; target the 8:30 candle high (Terminus), with minor buy-side levels along the way as first partials.
- **Example in this video:** NQ-like chart (levels about 29,2xx–29,3xx). News at 8:30 drove price lower; ICT buys inversion FVGs in the morning chop, targets the minor buy-side highs (the "29,315s" area), then the 8:30 high (around the 29,360 level, caption).
- **Timestamps:** [0:01:43](https://youtu.be/d8du4fMvOQU?t=103) — minor buy-side vs the 8:30 high; [0:02:31](https://youtu.be/d8du4fMvOQU?t=151) — the 8:30 move was implemented to build a bearish narrative; [0:13:08](https://youtu.be/d8du4fMvOQU?t=788) — "the mark"; [1:18:53](https://youtu.be/d8du4fMvOQU?t=4733) — why they may keep lows intact first.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** minor buy-side is called minor "because it's below the low that will be targeted" (i.e. lower than the real draw). The 8:30 buy-side is the final target ("Terminus").

title: Turning Loss Into Gain - Market Alchemy
head: Terminus (the final draw on liquidity) with minor buy-side first partials  (aliases ICT uses: "Terminus", "first partial", "stepping stones")
body:
- **Kind:** definition (as used here) / rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - "The draw overall is here. So, this is Terminus": the overall target (the 8:30 high). Before it there is a logical first objective (a minor buy-side, an old relative-equal-high pool and SIBI) used for the first partial.
  - "I don't care if it goes up to 30,000 today" — the 8:30 high is the terminus; as a developing trader "look for the market to go to specific locations and be content with enough".
  - Knowing the draw on liquidity makes the stepping stones easy to find; it is not support/resistance.
  - After the stop-out he still thinks the 8:30 high will be reached ("daily range"), but he can't stay with the trade.
- **How to identify:** the 8:30 candle's high on a day where news sent price down; minor buy-side = nearer highs ("smooth highs") below it.
- **How to use:** first partial at the minor buy-side (29,315s area), second at event horizon, final at Terminus.
- **Example in this video:** minor buy-side ~29,312–29,315 first partial (filled ~59:32), next objective ~29,360, final = 8:30 high (not reached).

title: Turning Loss Into Gain - Market Alchemy
head: Inversion FVG long: lower-half entry, bodies in the upper half, no bodies in the lower half  (aliases: "reclaimed bullish fair value gap", "SIBI that failed its first utilization")
body:
- **Kind:** entry model / rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - He uses a sell-side imbalance buy-side inefficiency (SIBI) that did not do its job as resistance as an inversion FVG to go long: "I'll buy in the lower half of that. Just wait for the candlestick to put market price inside that."
  - "First presented utilization": a SIBI is first expected to offer bearish prices when price rises into it. If price goes up into it and it does not hold price down ("these two have failed in their initial role of first utilization"), it becomes an inversion FVG that is bullish. "We want this to offer zero resistance."
  - Bodies should stay in the upper half of the iFVG. Once price leaves the gap upward (a wick back in is fine), no candle bodies may be permitted in its lower half "at all". Candle bodies leave and then "bookings" on a closing basis with range expansion above the high confirm.
  - Missed entry: if price is "reluctant" to drop into the entry zone, that is strength (he skips rather than chasing).
  - Stop loss goes below the signal candle's low: "there's no need for it to trade back down there. If it does, I'm wrong."
  - Re-entry after a stop-out: when price takes out that low he looks for a new inversion FVG ("the good long one") with the same idea.
- **How to identify:** SIBI above a low, price trades up into and through it without being rejected; then retests it from above; confirm with bodies holding the upper half.
- **How to use:** buy lower half on retest, stop below the candle low/wick midpoint, partial at first buy-side, trail the stop below the wick CE or the iFVG.
- **Example in this video:** morning chop, first long in the lower half of an iFVG, stop below the signal candle low; stopped out around 14:42 into the video; second long at ~15:34 after a "bear trap" with a stop beneath the CE of a wick.
- **Timestamps:** [0:00:01](https://youtu.be/d8du4fMvOQU?t=1) — "I'm going to use this as inversion to go long"; [0:05:40](https://youtu.be/d8du4fMvOQU?t=340) — no bodies once price leaves; [0:16:22](https://youtu.be/d8du4fMvOQU?t=982) — SIBIs failing first utilization; [0:24:40](https://youtu.be/d8du4fMvOQU?t=1480) — once outside, lower half should see no bodies.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** this is an elaboration of the standard iFVG (first utilization → inverted) with explicit upper/lower-half body rules.

title: Turning Loss Into Gain - Market Alchemy
head: Consequent Encroachment of a wick and the "mohawk" (stop placement)  (aliases: "consequent cushion/coercion" (caption), "midpoint of this wick", "mohawk")
body:
- **Kind:** refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - Stop is placed beneath the midpoint (CE) of the signal wick "allowing for that little Mohawk" (a small poke below the gap then recovery). Then the stop is "brought up just below that low" once price proves itself.
  - A candle that touches the iFVG again is acceptable but "it's better if it didn't"; a mohawk is fine.
  - After a pull-back, bodies should return above the CE of the wick, "at or above, preferably above".
  - Reading: a candle's low "says you can't pass, you can't go below that" — a body below it negates the long.
- **How to use:** stop below the wick CE (or the candle low for the first entry), and move it up to just above the CE of the wick for the balance once partials are done ([1:01:11](https://youtu.be/d8du4fMvOQU?t=3671)).

head: Reading manipulation / chop between two PD arrays ("they're holding it")  (aliases ICT uses: "manual intervention", "porcupine", "Phil" (his joking name for the manipulator), "bear trap", "fake bear flag")
body:
- **Kind:** rule / refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - "Way too many candles" between two PD arrays means price is being held; "this isn't making sense algorithmically". Wicks on both sides ("porcupine needles") signal manual manipulation rather than smooth higher-timeframe (5- or 15-minute) order-flow delivery through PD arrays.
  - A sloppy stretch between two SIBI/BISI zones becomes a balanced price range (wicks both sides).
  - What looks like a bear flag for retail is a trap: "validated that bear flag for retail traders to be short, they're caught offside". He wants the fake bear flag to act as a real bull flag. His criticism is that the classic patterns are "implemented incorrectly" by many.
  - Do not go short here: baiting; strong rejection and abrupt turn expected.
  - If you are less than a year in a live/funded account, hold fewer contracts (e.g. scale off half) because the tug of war shifts your attention from process to whether you'll be stopped.
- **How to use:** stay with the narrative if bodies keep respecting the levels, and size so that being stopped is tolerable.
- **Timestamps:** [0:08:12](https://youtu.be/d8du4fMvOQU?t=492) — "this is all manipulation"; [0:13:08](https://youtu.be/d8du4fMvOQU?t=788) — "between two PD arrays, this doesn't make any sense"; [0:26:17](https://youtu.be/d8du4fMvOQU?t=1577) — wicks like a porcupine = manual; [0:15:34](https://youtu.be/d8du4fMvOQU?t=934) — bear trap.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** "Phil" is his joke name for the manipulator.

head: Speed filter: fewer than seven candles to the target after the confirming close  (aliases ICT uses: "less than seven candlesticks", "range expansion speed")
body:
- **Kind:** refinement (explicitly "not a requirement")
- **What ICT says:**
  - Count: it took seven candles to travel from the earlier low to the current area; after a close above the CE of the wick (candle one) he wants the run to the buy-side to take fewer than seven candles.
  - Reason: run fast so that "those individuals can't pull their orders" and counterparties can hand longs to buyers at higher prices; speed and magnitude indicate liquidity being swept (while he adds that "they don't go for your stop loss, it's just buying and selling pressure").
  - He insists: "ICT counts candles and he only buys at a specific number" is not what he is saying; it is just what he'd like to see here.
  - Failure to meet the speed ("unwilling to do that less than seven candlestick run") is why he brought the stop up and scaled out.
  - One single displacement candle through the candle highs makes it "all but a done deal".
  - Another timing rule: after the "tiny short-term high", he wants price to start moving "inside the next three candles", because three candles would allow a swing low to form; the swing low then formed.
- **How to use:** if price takes longer than expected, reduce risk or exit, do not hold hoping.
- **Timestamps:** [0:36:26](https://youtu.be/d8du4fMvOQU?t=2186) — fewer candles, sharper speed; [0:38:02](https://youtu.be/d8du4fMvOQU?t=2282) — "less than seven candlesticks"; [0:43:56](https://youtu.be/d8du4fMvOQU?t=2636) — candles one, two, three; [0:56:54](https://youtu.be/d8du4fMvOQU?t=3414) — next three candles.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** he warns viewers not to turn it into a rule; treat as a situational quality check.

title: Turning Loss Into Gain - Market Alchemy
head: Position management: layered partials, stop to wick CE, "take a partial on every new high", event horizon  (aliases: "chasing down equity", "event horizon in action", "midpoint between two pools of liquidity")
body:
- **Kind:** entry model / management
- **What ICT says:**
  - Plan stated in advance ("explained ahead of time") so viewers see what and why. The size implied (14 + 10 + 4) is about 28 contracts (inference). Beginners with a funded account should consider something like 24 micros and scale off half.
  - At ~41:20: take 14 contracts off at the buy-side (first partial), the rest at the next level.
  - When price pulled down too far: take 10 off, set a stop such that if the wick low is taken the 10 more come off, and keep four contracts with a stop just below the CE of the iFVG ("not about being perfectly right about everything").
  - Re-checks the orders ("glad I checked that") so he doesn't cancel the wrong ones.
  - Once cleared to the 29,315s area, first partial filled; balance stop moved just above the CE of the wick.
  - "Every time it takes a new high and I'm in a long, as soon as it takes the high out, I'm going to take a partial off there" (taught a couple of years ago); not caring about the full-size final target is for beginners.
  - Event horizon: draw from the relative equal highs to the high of the 8:30 candle (a fib between two pools); the 50% is the midpoint between two pools of liquidity. Place a limit just below it (allow for spread), take a partial there, and raise the stop beneath the consolidation low, because price should not come back through the midpoint of the consolidation after a stop hunt.
  - Two contracts left at event horizon; no desire to hold through lunch. The last point of reference for sell-side liquidity; trading down there would imply a deeper retracement. He took three partials at the high of the session and another extra one.
  - He ended stopped out on the balance but with the day's drawdown mitigated ("20 2850" / "2800 on a mitigated loss" — caption unclear).
  - After a stop-out when price is far along the curve, he would not re-enter or add.
  - Later he tightens the stop above the wick and takes additional contracts off "if it stops me out" so that the exit still pays, and uses positive self-talk instead of "target or bust".
- **How to identify:** decide in advance (a) the first partial level, (b) the event-horizon level, (c) the stop moves tied to specific candle lows/CEs.
- **How to use:** reduce risk at each pool; plan stop moves as functions of structure; avoid babysitting by taking more off when conditions are high resistance.
- **Example in this video:** NQ-like levels; long off the second iFVG, 14 off at the first buy-side, event horizon between the old relative equal highs and the 8:30 candle high; remaining stopped before the 8:30 high.
- **Timestamps:** [0:41:20](https://youtu.be/d8du4fMvOQU?t=2480) — 14 contracts off at the buy side; [0:46:22](https://youtu.be/d8du4fMvOQU?t=2782) — 10 off, four kept; [0:52:57](https://youtu.be/d8du4fMvOQU?t=3177) — full contingency plan explained; [1:03:39](https://youtu.be/d8du4fMvOQU?t=3819) — event horizon drawn; [1:06:48](https://youtu.be/d8du4fMvOQU?t=4008) — partial on every new high; [1:08:22](https://youtu.be/d8du4fMvOQU?t=4102) — two left, don't want the market to roll on him.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** compare with the L26-074 and L26-086 event-horizon definitions: here the fib spans from a relative-equal-high pool to the 8:30 high (two buy-side pools).

title: Turning Loss Into Gain - Market Alchemy
head: High-resistance vs. low-resistance liquidity run conditions
body:
- **Kind:** refinement / context
- **What ICT says:**
  - Beginners want "low resistance liquidity run conditions" ("so easy"); they occur, but days like this (lots of overlap, wicks, many candles) are common: he says "98% of the time" conditions are like this one.
  - In high-resistance conditions the trade needs experience, patience and babysitting: "I try not to participate that much in conditions like this".
  - In low-resistance conditions the stop can be moved aggressively because retracement is not a concern; in high resistance you must be more forgiving with the stop until the first partial is reached.
  - You can make money on good days and give it all back on days like this if you cannot navigate.
- **Timestamps:** [0:51:17](https://youtu.be/d8du4fMvOQU?t=3077) — the 98% statement; [1:00:24](https://youtu.be/d8du4fMvOQU?t=3624) — tradeable but requires babysitting; [1:21:20](https://youtu.be/d8du4fMvOQU?t=4880) — stops more forgiving in high-resistance conditions.

Trade only in the first hour (up to ~10:30 AM ET) or wait until after 4:00 PM ET when the true move begins (at 6:00 PM RTH open). Avoid mid-day trading when money is sitting on sidelines. Be neutral; do not predict the Fed's decision. If you do participate, treat it as observation only (tape reading / demo), not real money.
- **How to identify:** FOMC is announced ahead of time (typically monthly). Pre-announcement price action is jagged, with many reverses; no strong directional move until after the announcement.
- **How to use:** Trade micro-moves and observe only. Use the time to build tape-reading skill, not accumulate risk. If you see a clean setup, take it, but keep size small or trade demo. Post-FOMC (after 4:00 PM) will provide the real trading opportunity; wait for that if unsure.
- **Example in this video:** NQ morning April 29, 2026, FOMC day. Price was choppy, grinding in the opening range gap (ORG) from Friday. Multiple failed attempts to break higher or lower. No strong conviction until post-announcement.

title: ICT 2026 Futures Review & RTH ORG Commentary \ April 29, 2026
head: Regular Trading Hours Opening Range Gap (ORG) and Quadrants / Octants
body:
- **Kind:** definition + use
- **What ICT says:** When US markets open at 9:30 AM ET, price often gaps relative to yesterday's close. This gap is the "opening range gap" (ORG). The gap divides into four quadrants (25% sections). Expect price to eventually fill the gap and test at least the lower quadrant (if gapped down) or upper quadrant (if gapped up). If price gaps down, expect initial trade up to ~25% of the gap (lower quadrant), then expect it to drop further below the gap (gap-and-go).
- **How to identify:** Mark the previous close, mark the open; draw the gap high/low. Divide into four equal segments (quadrants). Identify the octant (1/8) levels within.
- **How to use:** If gap down: expect run to lower quadrant, then run lower (below the gap). If gap up: expect run to upper quadrant, then expect potential reversal or continued run. On FOMC: use the gap as a reference structure; price may oscillate within the gap range, testing quadrants multiple times.
- **Example in this video:** NQ April 29, 2026. Gap down at 9:30 (Friday's close was higher). Price traded up into the lower quadrant (did not reach 25% of gap), then came back down and was testing both lower and upper quadrants as market makers whipsawed retail.
- **Timestamps:** [0:04:38](https://youtu.be/tbEzAhdv_Ak?t=278) — opening range gap explained · [0:06:13](https://youtu.be/tbEzAhdv_Ak?t=373) — octant and quadrant levels identified · [0:17:53](https://youtu.be/tbEzAhdv_Ak?t=1073) — Friday's ORG as reference
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** On FOMC days, the gap may not follow typical rules; be flexible. Upper octant and lower octant are the 1/8 marks; trading within these is precision price action.

title: ICT 2026 Futures Review & RTH ORG Commentary \ April 29, 2026
head: Inversion Fair Value Gap (iFVG) as Resistance / Foothold
body:
- **Kind:** definition + example
- **What ICT says:** When a bullish FVG (gap on an up move, filled as support) is later approached from above, it becomes an inversion FVG (acts as resistance/ceiling). Price will respect the high of that iFVG and the consequent encroachment; bodies cannot penetrate the lower half without signaling weakness. An iFVG can also act as a "foothold" when approached from below (on a recovery), allowing price to spring higher.
- **How to identify:** Mark the original FVG; watch whether price later approaches from above (resistance) or below (foothold). Track whether bodies can touch/cross the consequent encroachment.
- **How to use:** Use iFVG high as a stop-loss level if going short (if it breaks, stop is hit). Use iFVG low as a foothold entry if going long (body touches low, then springs up). If bodies cannot return to CE on rallies, iFVG is being respected as strong resistance (bearish).
- **Example in this video:** NQ morning. A prior bullish FVG became an iFVG that bodies kept respecting on the way down; no bodies returned to touch the CE, indicating weakness and likelihood of continuation lower.
- **Timestamps:** [0:08:38](https://youtu.be/tbEzAhdv_Ak?t=518) — iFVG identified and used · [0:32:50](https://youtu.be/tbEzAhdv_Ak?t=1970) — SIBI (BISI/SIBI) as inversion FVG · [0:42:17](https://youtu.be/tbEzAhdv_Ak?t=2537) — CE behavior and inversion
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** On choppy days, iFVGs may be violated; expect price to test them multiple times before deciding to break them.

title: ICT 2026 Futures Review & RTH ORG Commentary \ April 29, 2026
head: Rock Climber Analogy for Price Action
body:
- **Kind:** new coinage / metaphor
- **What ICT says:** Reading price action is like climbing a rock face. You look ahead and map out where the footholds (price support levels, order blocks, iFVG lows) and handholds (resistance levels, wicks you can "grab" to pull up) are. You do not try to climb the sheer vertical face; you use inefficiencies and structure to guide your path. This analogy teaches you to identify meaningful levels and not force moves where price is not offering purchase.
- **How to identify:** When looking at a chart, ask: "If I were climbing this, where would I place my feet (support) and hands (resistance)?" Order blocks, FVGs, wicks, and relative equal highs/lows are your climbing route.
- **How to use:** Use this mindset when reading tape. Do not demand price go a specific way; observe where it is likely to have "traction" (support for further movement). Identify the next foothold above/below and target it. Once price grabs that foothold (body touches and closes above/below), the next handhold becomes visible, and you can anticipate the next leg of the move.
- **Example in this video:** NQ morning. Price was climbing from the lower quadrant of the ORG; each SIBI, each wick, each order block was a foothold to climb higher toward the relative equal highs above.
- **Timestamps:** [0:30:10](https://youtu.be/tbEzAhdv_Ak?t=1810) — rock climber analogy introduced · [0:37:31](https://youtu.be/tbEzAhdv_Ak?t=2251) — footholds and handholds explained
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** This analogy removes force and desperation; it teaches patience and observation.

title: ICT 2026 Futures Review & RTH ORG Commentary \ April 29, 2026
head: Consequent Encroachment (CE) as Boundary
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:** The CE is the first candle body that enters a PD array (FVG, order block, SIBI). It is a hard boundary. If price cannot bring bodies back to touch the CE on a retracement, it signals strength (bull move) or weakness (bear move, depending on direction). Track whether bodies are respecting or violating the CE.
- **How to identify:** Find the PD array high/low; identify the first body to enter; that extreme is the CE.
- **How to use:** Place stop loss just outside the CE. If CE is breached with the body (not just a wick), structure is broken and re-evaluate. Track CE behavior: repeated failures to return = strong directional move.
- **Example in this video:** NQ. iFVG had a CE; on retracements, bodies could not get back to the CE line, signaling weakness and likelihood of lower prices.
- **Timestamps:** [0:08:38](https://youtu.be/tbEzAhdv_Ak?t=518) — consequent encroachment identified · [0:37:31](https://youtu.be/tbEzAhdv_Ak?t=2251) — CE respecting and strength/weakness signals
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** A wick touching CE and reversing is different from a body closing beyond CE; bodies are the true signal.

head: Tape Reading as Meditative Practice & Confidence Building
body:
- **Kind:** psychology / process
- **What ICT says:** Tape reading (observing candlesticks forming in real-time without trading) is a form of meditation and confidence-building. It conditions the mind to observe without stress, pattern-recognize, and retain information. Do not make it traumatic (force outcomes); make it fun, relaxing, with soothing music. This is how you develop subconscious pattern recognition.
- **How to identify:** When tape reading, observe without trade execution. Ask: "Is price doing what I expected? If not, why not?" Record the observation in a journal.
- **How to use:** Spend 1–2 hours daily doing tape reading without any trades. Learn to recognize PD arrays, order blocks, SIBI patterns, and relative equal highs/lows as they form. Build a model by repetition and observation, not by forcing trades.
- **Example in this video:** FOMC morning was ideal for tape reading; choppy, no clear direction, yet full of learning. ICT tape-read the whole thing, identifying footholds and analyzing why price was stuck (market makers had no reason to push hard pre-announcement).

- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** This is the core teaching; do not skip it. Tape reading is the foundation of pattern recognition and confidence. Avoid getting "sugar rushed" when a trade works; stay calm and humble.

head: CFD vs Futures Equivalence
body:
- **Kind:** refinement
- **What ICT says:** CFD markets (US 100, US 500) are not identical to futures (MNQ, ES, NQ) but they have corresponding structure. Time and price are slightly different (CFD fills may be off by a tick or two), but the logic of price action (FVGs, order blocks, relative equal highs/lows) is identical. If you cannot trade futures (e.g., non-US traders), you can trade CFD equivalents by transposing the levels from the futures chart to the CFD chart using time and price alignment.
- **How to identify:** Pull up both charts (futures and CFD) side-by-side; note when the same candle forms on both; measure levels on the futures chart; transfer those levels to the CFD chart.
- **How to use:** If trading CFDs, use the levels identified on the futures chart as reference. The logic is the same; execution mechanics are the same.
- **Example in this video:** ICT showed MNQ and US 100 side-by-side; price action was nearly identical. The inversion FVG, SIBI, and targets all aligned between the two.

head: Live Data vs Market Replay
body:
- **Kind:** rule / technical
- **What ICT says:** Never use market replay when teaching tape reading or analyzing live execution. Market replay changes the visual display: execution boxes disappear, date/time stamps vanish, the clean border disappears. This makes it harder to verify the time of execution and candle formation. ICT does not use market replay for this reason.
- **How to identify:** In TradingView, market replay mode hides execution details and changes the UI. Live mode keeps all UI elements visible.
- **How to use:** Always use live data. If analyzing a past session, use recorded video of live data, not market replay.
- **Example in this video:** ICT toggled market replay on/off to show the difference; when on, the execution boxes disappeared. This is why he uses live data only.

head: Change in State of Delivery (CISD)
body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:** A change in state of delivery occurs when the nature of price movement shifts. For example, when a larger, protracted candle is followed by a smaller candle, that boundary between them is a CISD. It marks a shift in the rate of delivery or urgency of the move.
- **How to identify:** Look at candle sizes; when a large candle (fast delivery) is followed by a smaller candle (slower delivery), or vice versa, mark that boundary.
- **How to use:** CISD can mark the top of an order block or a transition point. Use it as a reference level for entries / stops.
- **Example in this video:** NQ price action: ICT identified a CISD between a large candle and subsequent smaller ones, marking a potential shift in momentum.

head: ICT Gray Pool (Two-Wick Liquidity Pool)
body:
- **Kind:** new coinage
- **What ICT says:** The ICT gray pool is a liquidity zone formed by measuring the consequent encroachment of two adjacent wicks. You split the area between the two CE levels in half; the midpoint becomes a magnet on price and, when entered from above, acts as "rocket fuel" to send price lower. This is a proprietary technique ICT teaches; it is not published anywhere else.
- **How to identify:** Identify two discount wicks on a down move. Measure the CE of each; the gap between the two CEs is your gray pool. Mark the midpoint.
- **How to use:** Gray pool is used as an entry confirmation / accumulation zone. When price returns to the gray pool from above, expect a sharp drop through it. If price respends time in the pool (too many candles), give it 2–3 more candles to show willingness to move lower; if it doesn't, exit or re-evaluate.
- **Example in this video:** MNQ April 28, 2026. Two wicks (discount wicks) were measured; the CE of each was marked; the midpoint of the gray pool was ~27,205 (approximate). Price traded down into the gray pool, confirming the expected drop lower.

- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Gray pool bodies must stay out of the upper half; if price allows bodies in the upper half, the setup is compromised and re-evaluation is needed.

head: Event Horizon (Gap Between Liquidity Pools)
body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:** Event horizon is the area between two liquidity points (e.g., between a gray pool and a sell-side liquidity pool, or between two relative equal lows). It marks a transition zone. When price pierces through event horizon with conviction, the next liquidity target becomes more likely. It is a measurement tool for partial profit-taking and conviction building.
- **How to identify:** Identify two sequential liquidity points (gray pool low, then the next sell-side pool, or two relative equal lows); the gap between them is the event horizon.
- **How to use:** Use event horizon as a partial-profit-taking zone. When price reaches event horizon, take 20–50% of position. Track whether price moves through event horizon quickly (strong) or slowly (weak). Speed of movement = confidence in the continuation.
- **Example in this video:** MNQ April 28. Event horizon was marked between the gray pool midpoint and the sell-side liquidity pool at ~27,069. Price needed to break through this area with heaviness (stretched out candles, extended bodies). When it did, ICT took 2–3 lots off the 10-lot position.
- **Timestamps:** [0:24:04](https://youtu.be/jz0RbL1oVK8?t=1444) — event horizon identified · [0:27:20](https://youtu.be/jz0RbL1oVK8?t=1640) — speed through event horizon as signal
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Do not demand a measured move through event horizon; speed and heaviness matter more than hitting exact price.

head: Judas Swing
body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:** A Judas swing is when price moves into a bullish order block, briefly reverses (creating a "fake out"), and then continues in the original direction. It "deceives" traders expecting a reversal.
- **How to identify:** Look for a sharp move into an order block, a quick reversal wick, and then a resumption of the original direction.
- **How to use:** Recognize Judas swings as entry confirmation, not as rejection of the setup. When you see a Judas into an order block on the expected direction, it is often a signal to add to the position.
- **Example in this video:** MNQ April 28. Price moved down, briefly "icked" up into the bullish order block on the daily chart (Judas swing), then continued lower (confirming the short thesis).

head: Gray Pool Entry & Time Stop
body:
- **Kind:** rule + execution
- **What ICT says:** When price re-enters a gray pool after the initial move, expect a sharp drop. If price spends too many candles in the gray pool (more than 3–4), use a time stop: give it 2–3 more candles to show willingness to move lower; if it doesn't, exit the position and reassess.
- **How to identify:** Track how many candlesticks are forming inside the gray pool area.
- **How to use:** If 3–4 candles have formed in the gray pool without a strong lower move, manually close the trade or reduce size. This prevents being caught in a potential reversal.
- **Example in this video:** MNQ April 28. Price re-entered the gray pool; after spending several candles there, ICT noted "needs to show willingness to drop" and set a time stop of 2–3 more candles. When the next candle showed heaviness (extended body), the time stop was satisfied.

- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** This is a discretionary risk management technique; it helps avoid being stopped out on artificial bounces.

head: Sell-Side Liquidity Pool (SSLP) / Minor Sell Side
body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:** A sell-side liquidity pool is a zone where sellers' stop-losses are clustered (above a market low). When price approaches this area, market makers will often run those stops briefly before allowing a larger continuation move. A minor sell side is a smaller cluster of liquidity; a major sell side is a larger one. Always identify the CE of the sell-side wick before breaking through.
- **How to identify:** Identify a wick that left behind inefficiency on the way down. The consequent encroachment of that wick marks the minor sell-side level.
- **How to use:** Before breaking below the sell-side level on a close, confirm the order flow by tracking whether bodies are respecting the midpoint. Once bodies close below the minor sell side with heaviness, the move lower is confirmed.
- **Example in this video:** MNQ April 28. A minor sell-side level was at ~27,082 (approximate, from wick CE); price had to close below this with heaviness to confirm the continuation to the relative equal lows.

head: Position Sizing & Partial Profit-Taking
body:
- **Kind:** rule / execution
- **What ICT says:** Enter with a full position (e.g., 10 lots on MNQ). Use event horizon and relative equal lows as partial-profit-taking zones. Take 2–3 lots (20–30%) at event horizon. Let the rest run to the final target (relative equal lows). Once at relative equal lows, close all remaining lots or trail a stop.
- **How to identify:** Pre-plan your targets (gray pool, event horizon, relative equal lows); assign position reduction targets for each.
- **How to use:** Execution: enter 10 lots. At event horizon, close 2–3. At relative equal lows, close the remainder. This locks in profits early while still allowing the best runners to work.
- **Example in this video:** MNQ April 28. ICT entered 10 lots; took 2–3 lots off at event horizon (around 27,069); held 7–8 lots for the final target, closing them at the relative equal lows when price hit the target on X.

head: Consequent Encroachment (CE) as Hard Stop
body:
- **Kind:** rule

head: Three Drives Pattern (Three Indians Pattern)
body:
- **Kind:** definition + example
- **What ICT says:** A classic pattern where price creates three successive highs, each above the prior buy-side liquidity pool. After the third high is made (especially if above prior day's high or a major resistance), the pattern is complete and a breakdown is expected. This is not ICT's invention; it's a well-known pattern documented in "Street Smarts" books (called "three Indians pattern" there, though ICT prefers "three drives"). When price is extremely overbought (no indicator needed), the three drives pattern is a high-confidence short setup.
- **How to identify:** Mark three consecutive higher highs; identify the buy-side liquidity pool that each high exceeds. Count: high 1, high 2, high 3. Once high 3 is confirmed, expect reversal.
- **How to use:** After confirming three drives, short at or near high 3 and target the sell-side liquidity pool(s) below. On all-time highs, add further confirmation by checking daily bias and prior day's high structure.
- **Example in this video:** NQ April 24, 2026. Price had been trending higher, creating multiple highs. Thursday's high (high 2 or 3) was traded above Wednesday's daily high, confirming the three drives pattern. ICT shorted at Thursday's high with target at relative equal lows below, which worked beautifully.
- **Timestamps:** [0:11:12](https://youtu.be/2OVAvl4H3IY?t=672) — three drives pattern defined · [0:12:47](https://youtu.be/2OVAvl4H3IY?t=767) — pattern and smart money behavior · [0:13:36](https://youtu.be/2OVAvl4H3IY?t=816) — confirming three drives and expecting breakdown
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** The pattern works even in isolation, but combining it with previous day's high and relative equal lows increases confidence.

title: ICT 2026 Futures Review \ April 24, 2026
head: Shorting Previous Day's High (Daily High as Resistance)
body:
- **Kind:** rule + refinement
- **What ICT says:** When price trades above the prior day's daily high (especially on consecutive days), it is a prime area to short. The reason: it attracts breakout traders and bull-flag traders expecting continuation; they place buy stops above the daily high. Smart money runs these stops, then drops. This is a structural setup that works across market conditions (bull or bear market); it is not specific to all-time highs. Targeting sell-side liquidity pools below the daily high is the natural target.
- **How to identify:** Pull the prior day's daily high from the chart; watch when price trades above it. If price is above it and showing weakness (bodies not advancing, pullbacks forming), it is ripe for shorting.
- **How to use:** Short entries at or just below the prior day's daily high. Use sell-side liquidity pools below as targets. Confirm entry with PD array structure (fair value gaps, order blocks, relative equal lows that align below the daily high).
- **Example in this video:** NQ April 24. Wednesday's daily high was at a specific level. Price traded above it on Thursday morning, triggering retail breakout buys. ICT shorted at that level and targeted the sell-side pool(s) below (ultimately hitting the relative equal lows near 27,069 / 26,805 range across the week).
- **Timestamps:** [0:06:06](https://youtu.be/2OVAvl4H3IY?t=366) — endless supply of setups from prior day's highs/lows · [0:09:35](https://youtu.be/2OVAvl4H3IY?t=575) — shorting at daily high despite all-time high · [0:14:23](https://youtu.be/2OVAvl4H3IY?t=863) — context as confirmation
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Works in bull, bear, and sideways markets. The key is recognizing retail breakout logic and the structural sell-side pool below.

title: ICT 2026 Futures Review \ April 24, 2026
head: Fair Value Gap (FVG) at 50% Midpoint as Structural Reference
body:
- **Kind:** refinement
- **What ICT says:** When a volume imbalance (fair value gap) forms, its midpoint (50% level) can be used as a reference point during the trade. If price is expected to go lower, and a FVG high is at the midpoint, that midpoint becomes a resistance level. Bodies respecting the lower half of the gap confirm bearish order flow.
- **How to identify:** Mark the FVG high and low; calculate the midpoint (50%). Track whether price respects or violates this midpoint.
- **How to use:** Use the FVG midpoint as a reference for "is the structure holding?" If bodies cannot touch the midpoint on rallies, bearish bias is confirmed. If bodies touch the midpoint but stay in the lower half, the move lower is likely to continue.
- **Example in this video:** NQ April 24. A FVG was marked; its midpoint was used as a reference to confirm that bodies were staying in the lower half, supporting the short thesis.
- **Timestamps:** [0:08:46](https://youtu.be/2OVAvl4H3IY?t=526) — FVG midpoint identified · [0:15:10](https://youtu.be/2OVAvl4H3IY?t=910) — fairness and context of FVG interpretation
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** The midpoint is not a hard stop/target; it is a reference for assessing order flow strength.

title: ICT 2026 Futures Review \ April 24, 2026
head: Inversion Fair Value Gap (iFVG) Confirmation via Body Placement
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:** When a bullish fair value gap is breached and becomes an inversion FVG, bodies must stay in the lower half to confirm bearish intention. Specifically: if a body touches the consequent encroachment (CE) and stays in the lower half, that is textbook confirmation. If a body penetrates the midpoint or upper half, the iFVG is being violated (weakens the bearish case).
- **How to identify:** Mark iFVG; observe the body placement on each candle as price approaches and tests it.
- **How to use:** Only take the short if bodies confirm by staying in the lower half. If a body closes above the midpoint or touches the upper half, re-evaluate or exit the position.
- **Example in this video:** NQ April 24. An iFVG was formed from a bullish FVG; bodies tested it and stayed in the lower half, confirming the breakdown. Bodies later "shared the same space" (consolidated without advancing upper), which ICT interpreted as a signal to take partials.
- **Timestamps:** [0:19:10](https://youtu.be/2OVAvl4H3IY?t=1150) — iFVG confirmation · [0:20:47](https://youtu.be/2OVAvl4H3IY?t=1247) — body placement in lower half
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** A wick into the upper half is acceptable; only bodies violate the structure.

title: ICT 2026 Futures Review \ April 24, 2026
head: Sell-Side Liquidity Pool (SSLP) / Engineering Liquidity
body:
- **Kind:** definition + psychology
- **What ICT says:** When price leaves large wicks (especially down and back up), retail traders using candlestick analysis see those wicks as "bullish accumulation" and protection for their shorts' stop-losses. Smart money capitalizes on this: they use those wicks as areas where they know retail will have stops placed. They then "engineer liquidity" at these levels, raiding them briefly before continuing in the original direction. The wicks are not bullish; they are bait.
- **How to identify:** Look for a down wick with a body that closes well above it (creating a large wick to the downside). Mark that wick; expect price to revisit it and run the stops clustered above the wick.
- **How to use:** The wick area is a sell-side liquidity pool. Use it as a reference: price will likely be attracted to it on retracements. Do not mistake it for support; it is a raid zone. Build your short target accounts for price to attack these wicks and then continue lower.
- **Example in this video:** NQ April 24–Thursday. A sell-side liquidity pool (from wicks) was identified; price returned to it during the short move, briefly rallied into it (causing rallies against the short), then broke lower. ICT uses this knowledge to trail stops and manage partials.
- **Timestamps:** [0:15:59](https://youtu.be/2OVAvl4H3IY?t=959) — engineering liquidity explained · [0:16:46](https://youtu.be/2OVAvl4H3IY?t=1006) — coordinated strike analogy (orcas/killer whales)
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** This requires understanding smart money intent; candlestick theory alone misses it.

title: ICT 2026 Futures Review \ April 24, 2026
head: Body Consolidation ("Sharing the Same Space") as Signal to Take Partials
body:
- **Kind:** refinement / execution
- **What ICT says:** During a downtrend on a short, if candlestick bodies start "sharing the same space" (i.e., the high of one body is near the high of the previous body, no new lows being made), it is a warning signal. It suggests order flow is waning. When this happens, especially as you approach a target, take partials off. This is because the consolidation may precede a reversal; you do not want to be caught holding through a sharp rally.
- **How to identify:** Watch the bodies as price approaches your target. If highs are not advancing lower (bodies are repeating the same high range), mark it.
- **How to use:** Use this as a discretionary trigger to take partial profit. Rule of thumb: as bodies consolidate, take 20-50% off depending on proximity to target. This locks in profit before a potential reversal.
- **Example in this video:** NQ April 24–Thursday. Price was moving lower beautifully, but as it approached the target, bodies started sharing the same space (consolidating horizontally). ICT began taking partials off at each new low, preserving profit while allowing the position to run if it continued.
- **Timestamps:** [0:22:22](https://youtu.be/2OVAvl4H3IY?t=1342) — consolidation and body sharing observed · [0:23:08](https://youtu.be/2OVAvl4H3IY?t=1388) — taking partials during consolidation
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** This is a discretionary tool; it prevents being "greedy" near targets but still allows upside capture.

title: ICT 2026 Futures Review \ April 24, 2026
head: Partial Profit-Taking: "Running Down Equity"
body:
- **Kind:** rule + execution
- **What ICT says:** On short positions approaching targets, take a small partial every time a new lower low is made. This is called "running down equity." For example, if short 10 lots and aiming for a target 100 handles lower, take 1 lot off at new lows, then at the next new low, take another lot. By the time you hit the target, you've taken off 5–6 lots, leaving 4–5 to run. This ensures you lock in profits while still capturing best-case scenarios.
- **How to identify:** Track new lows as price moves lower; each new lower low is an opportunity.
- **How to use:** Mechanical approach: short entry = 10 lots. New low 1: close 1 lot. New low 2: close 1 lot. And so on. At target: close the remainder.
- **Example in this video:** NQ April 24–Thursday. ICT entered the short and took partials at new lower lows; by the time price hit the target level (26,805), most of the position was already closed, and ICT missed the final 100+ handles but was content because profits were locked in before the final leg.
- **Timestamps:** [0:23:08](https://youtu.be/2OVAvl4H3IY?t=1388) — "running down equity" / taking partials
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** There is never an unprofitable partial profit; always take them.

head: Terminus Target / "654 Club"
body:
- **Kind:** definition + execution
- **What ICT says:** A terminus target is the ultimate price level ICT is aiming for on a trade. The "654 Club" is an inside joke referring to the last three digits of MNQ prices (e.g., if aiming for 27,654, it's a "654" target). It is simply shorthand for a specific, pre-planned target. ICT often posts these on X in advance so that followers can verify the call.

- **How to use:** Once posted, it becomes a reference point. The trade is executed toward that level; no adjustments unless structure breaks. Taking partials toward the target is acceptable; holding to the target is the ideal outcome.

head: Opening Range Gap (ORG) Consequent Encroachment as Reference

head: Market Maker Sell Model (MMSM) / Fading ATH
body:
- **Kind:** entry model + example
- **What ICT says:** Identify when smart money (the "fill belly") runs price just short of all-time highs (ATH), fails to break it, then reverses aggressively lower. This setup forms when price rallies into a "suspension block" (tight range at highs) on a bullish close candle, then the body closes inside that block—signaling the run is complete and reversal is coming.
- **How to identify:** Price runs from a breakout point (e.g., Tuesday RTH opening range gap high) all the way up, gets very close to ATH (26,901.75 in this ES example), but fails to take it out on a close. Smart money prints a bullish candle, drawing in late breakout buyers. Then reverses.
- **How to use:** Entry is short after the failed ATH touch. Use a suspension block (the tight range containing the failed run) as a reference zone. Place protective buy limits (partial exit targets) below key resistance (e.g., 26,830, 26,805) to scalp out on the way down. Stop placement sits above the wick of the "premium wick" (the candle that touched consequent encroachment of the high). Scale in on retracements into the SIBI.
- **Example in this video:** ES 1m, April 22, 2026, 8:00–9:30 ET. Price rallied from 26,745 (7:45 ET) to 26,901.75 (just shy of ATH), failed to break it, closed in a tight suspension block. ICT went short off this failure, layered buys at 26,830 (Monday RTH opening range high), 26,805 (sell-side), and lower levels. Took multiple partials as price worked lower, demonstrating when to scale out (when spending "too much time" in a SIBI = loss of directional pressure).
- **Timestamps:**
  - [0:00:01](https://youtu.be/6VaEdP4TYe8?t=1) — Setup overview; suspension block identified
  - [0:05:43](https://youtu.be/6VaEdP4TYe8?t=343) — First partial at suspension block high (1/4 of the zone)
  - [0:28:38](https://youtu.be/6VaEdP4TYe8?t=1718) — Trade turning; two partials taken off
  - [0:46:08](https://youtu.be/6VaEdP4TYe8?t=2768) — Spending "too much time" in SIBI; risk of reversal; remaining contracts held for documentation
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Critical refinement: when price touches your profit target but **doesn't fill your limit order**, don't wait. Manually take a market order and peel it off. This happens when smart money is keeping price just away from your target to trap shorts—a sign they're about to turn. Spending "way too much time" in a SIBI (multiple candles, no acceleration through the zone) is a rejection signal and reason to reduce conviction.

title: ICT 2026 Fading Run To ATH Using MMSM \ Judas Swing \ April 22, 2026
head: Suspension Block
body:
- **Kind:** definition + identification rule
- **What ICT says:** A tight, narrow candle range that forms at a reversal point—typically where price is held from breaking into new territory. It's the zone the market maker "suspends" the move to prevent a break, drawing in late entries before reversing.
- **How to identify:** Look for the bullish close candle that marks the rejection of ATH. The body of that candle and the range it contains is the suspension block. In this example, the ES block is around 26,880–26,901 (the high of day).
- **How to use:** Use it as a reference for partial targets and stop placement. Bodies staying **below** certain zones within it signal you should hold the short; bodies breaking **above** it signal a failed short setup and require immediate exit.
- **Example in this video:** ES, April 22, 2026. The suspension block is the 20–point range where price rejected the ATH; ICT references "the high of that suspension block" as a first partial target.

head: Consequent Encroachment
body:
- **Kind:** rule + entry/exit filter
- **What ICT says:** When a candle wick touches a resistance or fair value gap level but the **body stays below** it, price is showing "consequent encroachment"—respect for the level without a full break. The body **must stay below** the midpoint or low of that wick to keep the trade valid; if the body closes above it, the setup is broken and you exit.
- **How to identify:** After identifying a key wick or FVG high (e.g., premium wick), watch the next candle(s). If the wick touches it but the body stays in the lower half, you have valid encroachment. If the body closes above the midpoint, it's a failure signal.
- **How to use:** On a short setup, keep a mental or charted line at the wick high or midpoint. Any body crossing above it = exit half the position or bail entirely, depending on your stop placement. Use consequent encroachment as a profit target—"take the profit at consequent encroachment of that premium wick."
- **Example in this video:** Multiple examples: the premium wick above the FVG (ICT watches bodies staying below it), the inversion FVG consequent encroachment (bodies must stay **at or below** the line), the Monday RTH opening range gap high (traced as a dotted line; trade accelerates through it = target hit).
- **Timestamps:** [0:12:08](https://youtu.be/6VaEdP4TYe8?t=728), [0:14:10](https://youtu.be/6VaEdP4TYe8?t=850), [0:22:26](https://youtu.be/6VaEdP4TYe8?t=1346)
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** The wick itself is valid only once. If it gets "touched" intracandle and then price pulls back, that first touch is the candle to watch; future candles are "encroaching" on it, not touching it fresh.

title: ICT 2026 Fading Run To ATH Using MMSM \ Judas Swing \ April 22, 2026
head: Inversion Fair Value Gap (iFVG)
body:
- **Kind:** definition + role in trade
- **What ICT says:** After a bearish move (down run), an inversion FVG forms in the gap left behind. If price retraces back into this zone, it's a resistance zone. Price will either respect the consequent encroachment level (low of the wick at the top of the iFVG) and reverse lower again, or it will fully fill the iFVG (indicating loss of bearish control).
- **How to identify:** After a down move, mark the iFVG formed in the gap. It's an imbalance going upward. Consequent encroachment = the wick that just touched the top of that gap.
- **How to use:** On a short trade, expect price to retrace into the iFVG. Use the consequent encroachment (top wick) as a resistance line—bodies must stay in the lower half of the iFVG, or the setup is in trouble. If price rallies back and fills the entire iFVG, it's a sign smart money has lost control and you should exit.
- **Example in this video:** After the down move from 26,830, an iFVG forms. Price retraces into it; ICT watches consequent encroachment at the premium wick. When price spends multiple candles in the iFVG without exiting down, it signals loss of conviction (the "Jaws music" moment).

head: Sell-side Liquidity (SSL) & Buy-side Liquidity (BSL)
body:
- **Kind:** definition + identification
- **What ICT says:** Sell-side liquidity is resting above price where late sellers are holding stops or sell orders. Buy-side liquidity is resting below price where buyers are hiding. Smart money "takes" (sweeps) one side to trigger stops and create panic, then reverses and "leaves" liquidity resting in that zone for the next move.
- **How to identify:** SSL is above the recent high; BSL is below the recent low. Mark them on the chart at round levels or key resistance/support zones. In this trade, SSL sits at 26,830 and 26,805 (marked as "sell side imbalance" after a bearish FVG forms).
- **How to use:** Target the SSL with your profit-taking limit orders. Expect smart money to take one side (BSL first, leaving SSL intact) before reversing. Place partials just at the top of buy-side inefficiency (the zone that absorbed the buy orders when price was higher).
- **Example in this video:** SSL at 26,830 and 26,805 (the high area from Monday RTH open and prior trading). ICT places limit orders to buy partials at these levels, expecting smart money to sweep BSL and leave SSL for the retracement back down.

head: Equal Highs / Relative Equal Lows
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:** When price prints two consecutive lows at or very close to the same level, that's a "relative equal low." This level often becomes a support or exit target (limit order level). It's a sign price is trying to hold support or is vulnerable to a drop through it.
- **How to identify:** Chart tool: mark the lows of the last two candles (or recent lower lows). If they're within a few ticks, you have a relative equal low.
- **How to use:** Place limit orders to exit partials at these levels, as they often get swept. Also use them as a reference for stops—if price trades below the relative equal low convincingly, the setup has failed.
- **Example in this video:** ICT refers to "relatively equal lows" (around 26,804–26,805) as his partial exit zone and as a point where, if price won't go through quickly, he expects reversal (loss of momentum).

title: ICT 2026 Futures Market Review \ April 21, 2026
head: Principle of First Utilization (PFU)
body:
- **Kind:** definition + rule
- **What ICT says:** Every PD array (fair value gap, imbalance/inefficiency, order block, etc.) has an original utilization—the direction it forms and the price movement it facilitates. Once that PD array is traded **through** (i.e., price goes past it in the opposite direction), its characteristic reverses and it becomes an inversion. Once it inverts, it can be used again (in the opposite sense) and often becomes a much more formidable level than it was originally.
- **How to identify:** Step 1: mark the original FVG (e.g., bearish FVG in a down move; this is the original utilization zone). Step 2: if price rallies back up and trades **above** that FVG, it has been "traded through"; now it is inverted. Step 3: when price falls back into the inverted FVG, expect it to repel price (act as resistance), not support.
- **How to use:** Don't blindly trade every FVG. Ask: has this FVG been traded through yet? If yes, it's inverted and acts in the opposite direction. If no, it's still in original utilization. Bodies staying out of the upper half of an inverted FVG (below midpoint) = strong bearish rejection; bodies entering the upper half = loss of rejection / potential for the FVG to be fully filled (bullish).
- **Example in this video:** ES, April 21, 2026. A bearish FVG forms in the down move (original utilization = bearish, acts as supply/resistance from below). Price rallies back and trades above it (through), so it inverts. Now, when price retraces back into it on the way down later, it acts as resistance and repels price away (inversion utilization = bullish delivery into resistance, then reversal). Shown multiple times: the 26,695 level forms a sell-side imbalance / buy-side inefficiency that first acts as resistance (original utilization), then price trades below it, so when price rises back up into it, it acts as inversion (resistance/repulsion).
- **Timestamps:** [0:07:02](https://youtu.be/PCMv3J6_9Lg?t=422), [0:12:36](https://youtu.be/PCMv3J6_9Lg?t=756), [0:18:10](https://youtu.be/PCMv3J6_9Lg?t=1090), [0:26:56](https://youtu.be/PCMv3J6_9Lg?t=1616)
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** The FVG doesn't "fail" when traded through; it **changes characteristic**. A failed setup (bodies entering the upper half of an inverted FVG) is not the same as trading through the FVG in the original direction. The transition from original to inverted is instantaneous and deliberate by smart money; recognize it quickly.

title: ICT 2026 Futures Market Review \ April 21, 2026
head: RTH Opening Range Gap (Regular Trading Hours)
body:
- **Kind:** definition + rule + filters
- **What ICT says:** The gap between the previous day's close (or end of RTH) and the next day's 9:30 ET open. These gaps are pools of liquidity. You only need the **three most recent RTH gaps** to do intraday trading without bias or higher-timeframe bias. Use them hierarchically: today's gap, yesterday's gap, Friday's gap. Mark both the high and low of each gap as price targets.
- **How to identify:** Chart tool: mark the zone between yesterday's close (4:00 PM ET) and today's 9:30 AM ET open. The high of the gap is the "RTH opening range gap high"; the low is the "RTH opening range gap low". Also mark the "consequent encroachment" level—the midpoint or lowest wick touching the gap.
- **How to use:** When targeting a move, use the RTH gaps as sequential targets: first target = today's RTH opening range gap (high or low, depending on direction); if taken, next target = yesterday's RTH opening range gap; if taken, next target = Friday's RTH opening range gap. When price reaches a gap, expect it to stop, pause, or reverse at that level. Mark the gap on a notepad to keep the chart clean. Use the octant or quadrant (dividing the gap into 8 or 4 zones) for finer entry points.
- **Example in this video:** ES, April 21, 2026.
