head: Sell-side vs. Buy-side Imbalance / Inefficiency
body:
- **Kind:** definition + pair of terms
- **What ICT says:** When price makes a down move fast and aggressively, it leaves behind imbalances: (1) **sell-side imbalance** = unmet sell orders above (when price ran down, sellers didn't have a chance to exit); (2) **buy-side inefficiency** = untested buy orders below (buyers weren't active on the way down, their bids were skipped). Together: "sell-side imbalance / buy-side inefficiency" (SIBI). This is a barrier. When price retraces back up, it must respect that barrier or re-engage in the down move.
- **How to identify:** After a down move, mark the zone from the top of the down run back to the bottom. That zone is the SIBI. It's a visual imbalance (wide candles, aggressive drops, no bodies in certain areas).
- **How to use:** SIBI acts as resistance on retrace. Expect price to struggle to break above it on the way back up. If price does break above it with bodies in the upper half, the down move is losing conviction and you should reduce or exit your short. Use the SIBI as a reason for price to reverse lower again (entry for shorts, or hold shorts).
- **Example in this video:** After the rally from 26,695, a SIBI forms. When price retraces back up into it from the lower low, bodies must stay in the lower half of the SIBI to show continued selling pressure. When price breaks above it (bodies in upper half), the setup is weakening. Also, at 26,830, a SIBI / buy-side inefficiency acts as a target on the way down, then when price rallies back into it, it becomes an inversion resistance.

head: Engineering Liquidity
body:
- **Kind:** concept + advanced technique
- **What ICT says:** Smart money deliberately creates patterns that appear to be targeting buy-side or sell-side liquidity, luring retail traders into false breakouts and reversals. "Engineering buy-side liquidity" means leaving relative equal highs (false highs that look like resistance) so that when price rises again, retail traders place buy stops just above them. Smart money then runs price up, takes those stops, and reverses. This is not random; it's deliberate market structure manipulation.
- **How to identify:** Watch for patterns: price makes a high, retreats, makes another high at roughly the same level (relative equal high). This looks like failed breakout resistance. Next, watch if price rallies back up and above those equal highs with bodies in the upper portions of FVGs (usually a bullish sign), but then reverses sharply downward. That's engineered buy-side liquidity (the equal highs were the bait).
- **How to use:** When you see equal highs being formed, don't assume they're traditional resistance. Ask: am I being set up to buy here and get stopped out? Watch the bodies—if they're in the upper half of inversion FVGs on the way up, it's a trap. Respect it and don't go long. Expect a reversal once the equal highs are cleared. Use this as a sign to place short entries instead.
- **Example in this video:** ES, April 21, 2026. Equal highs are engineered at 26,800+, then price rallies back up, takes those highs, but bodies print in the upper half of the inversion FVG with no continuation. This signals engineered buy-side liquidity—the rally is a trap. Price then reverses and sells off aggressively. This is exactly what ICT predicted on the livestream.

- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Engineering liquidity is not the same as simple support/resistance. It's active market making, not passive level holding. Recognize it by the deliberate pattern and the body placement in FVGs—not just the wick behavior. Bodies in upper halves of inversion FVGs + equal highs = trap in progress.

head: Balanced Price Range (BPR)
body:
- **Kind:** definition + defensive structure
- **What ICT says:** A price range that bounces between two levels (high and low) over a period of time. Unlike entry models (which get you into trades), a BPR serves a **defensive** function—it's a barrier that keeps price outside of it, protecting your stop loss (like a "bolo" or fortress wall). If price breaks through the BPR, it signals a significant market structure shift and suggests strong momentum in the opposite direction.
- **How to identify:** Chart tool: mark a high and a low that have been tested multiple times over several candles or hours. Price respects both levels, bouncing between them.
- **How to use:** Use BPR as a mental or charted reference for where your stops should sit (just outside the BPR). If the BPR fails (price breaks through it), don't despair—it's giving you information that smart money has shifted direction. Take the new PD array that's forming in that opposite direction and catch the bigger move ("catch a tiger by the tail").

body:

head: Bodies vs. Wicks (Price Action Filter)
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:** When evaluating whether a level is being respected or broken, focus on the **candle bodies**, not the wicks. A wick can touch resistance and retreat; that's normal. But if the **body** closes above or below a level, it shows intent. In inversion FVGs, bodies must stay below the midpoint to show continued selling pressure; if bodies enter the upper half, the down move is losing conviction. Similarly, "no candlestick bodies in the upper half" of an FVG is a bearish structure.
- **How to identify:** Draw a level (e.g., inversion FVG top). Watch the next few candles. Check: do the bodies stay below the midpoint, or do they cross above? Wicks can go above; bodies must stay below for the setup to remain valid.
- **How to use:** When managing a short position, watch the bodies. If bodies start closing in the upper half of your target zone, reduce conviction. If bodies stay in the lower half, hold and expect acceleration lower. Use this as a filter for partial exits and stop placement.
- **Example in this video:** Multiple instances: "no candlestick bodies in the upper half" of the SIBI / inversion FVG. Also, "bodies being just below the low of today's regular trading hours opening range gap low" indicates that smart money wants to dig lower (bodies respecting a threshold below a zone = bearish intent).

head: Premium vs. Discount Sensitivity
body:
- **Kind:** definition + filter
- **What ICT says:** When a PD array (FVG, imbalance, inefficiency) is in its first utilization (original direction), it shows **premium sensitivity** = bodies allowed only in the lower half (bearish) or upper half (bullish), with wicks allowed to exceed the boundary. When inverted, it flips—discount sensitivity = bodies in the opposite half. This is the key to reading smart money intent: watch bodies, not wicks. A wick touching a level is permissible; a body crossing into the forbidden half signals loss of conviction.
- **How to identify:** 
  - **Premium sensitivity (bearish FVG, first utilization):** Candle bodies stay in lower half of the FVG; wicks can wick into upper half. High bodies above the midpoint = loss of premium.
  - **Discount sensitivity (bullish inversion, second utilization):** Candle bodies stay in upper half; wicks can wick down into lower half. Low bodies below the midpoint = loss of discount.
- **How to use:** When you see bodies violating the expected half, reduce conviction. Use it as a warning signal. If you're short and bodies start printing in the upper half of a bearish FVG, the setup is weakening. If you're long and bodies print in the lower half of a bullish inversion, the setup is weakening.
- **Example in this video:** MNQ 1m, April 21, 2026. Bearish FVG formed; ICT expects bodies in lower half (premium sensitivity). When bodies respect the lower half, the short setup is valid. Later, an inversion FVG forms—ICT looks for bodies in upper half (discount sensitivity). If bodies can't sustain in the upper half, the bullish setup is invalid and price should revert to the bearish FVG's first utilization.
- **Timestamps:** [0:16:17](https://youtu.be/5PpnT-l-zSk?t=977), [0:17:51](https://youtu.be/5PpnT-l-zSk?t=1071), [0:28:07](https://youtu.be/5PpnT-l-zSk?t=1687), [0:39:11](https://youtu.be/5PpnT-l-zSk?t=2351)
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** A wick that touches the boundary is always permissible (called a "mohawk"—a small wick outside the FVG). It doesn't invalidate the FVG. What matters is the body placement on the next candle(s). Bodies in the forbidden half = loss of structure.

head: Low-Probability Conditions & Trading Discipline
body:
- **Kind:** process + psychology
- **What ICT says:** When the economic calendar has major events (Fed speaker, news, data releases), precision drops. The market becomes 50/50 because the data can go either way. In these conditions, the "correct" bias may no longer matter—one piece of news can reverse everything in seconds. Smart trading in low-probability conditions is: (1) identify your model/bias, (2) wait for price action to confirm it, (3) if price doesn't confirm, do nothing and lose zero dollars. Forcing a trade because you're "right" in low-probability conditions is gambler's mentality.
- **How to identify:** Check the economic calendar (Forex Factory). Look for "high impact" events (Fed speakers, major data releases, FOMC decisions). If these are happening, assume low probability until proven otherwise.
- **How to use:** Don't force entries. Wait for your target level to be reached. If it's not reached before the event, accept it and walk away. You're not "wrong"; you're just waiting. "If information presents itself, I'll call candlesticks. If it doesn't, I'm waiting for more information." Doing nothing is a valid trade decision.
- **Example in this video:** April 21, 2026, 10:00 ET Fed chair speaks. ICT was looking for MNQ to drop to Monday's RTH opening range gap low (~26,695). Instead, the Fed caused unpredictable moves. He took a small short position early (when the bias was clear), but reduced conviction as news approached. By 10:00, he was watching, not trading, because "low probability for precision."
- **Timestamps:** [0:03:27](https://youtu.be/5PpnT-l-zSk?t=207), [0:10:40](https://youtu.be/5PpnT-l-zSk?t=640), [0:13:06](https://youtu.be/5PpnT-l-zSk?t=786), [0:20:14](https://youtu.be/5PpnT-l-zSk?t=1214)
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Low probability doesn't mean zero probability. It means you adjust your risk management and accept that your model may not work today. It's not a failure if price doesn't hit your target in low-probability conditions; it's a wise pause.

head: Rock Climber Analogy (Price Structure & Footholds)
body:
- **Kind:** metaphor / analysis framework
- **What ICT says:** Think of price action like a rock face. Your goal (at the top) is a high you want to reach. The current price is where you're standing. Between where you are and the top are footholds (support levels, FVGs, imbalances) you can use to "climb" higher. By identifying these footholds (PD arrays), you can forecast where price "wants" to climb. It's not about predicting the future; it's about seeing the available structure price can use to move higher or lower.
- **How to identify:** Draw a vertical line from the current price up to the resistance/high you want to reach. Identify all the PD arrays between them: FVGs, sell-side imbalance / buy-side inefficiencies, order blocks, equal highs, etc. These are the footholds.
- **How to use:** When price breaks above a resistance and then consolidates, ask: "What's the next foothold?" Use that PD array as your next entry point or partial target. This helps you think of price structure as a series of connected levels, not random noise. On the way down, use the same logic: handholds are support levels you can use to slow a descent.
- **Example in this video:** MNQ is trading near a high at 26,830 (Monday's RTH gap high). To forecast if price can reach a higher high (all-time highs or the inversion FVG above), ICT identifies the footholds: the sell-side imbalance / buy-side inefficiency, the midpoint of the wick (consequent encroachment), the inversion FVG, etc. Each foothold is a test point where price must prove its intention to continue higher.
- **Timestamps:** [0:33:41](https://youtu.be/5PpnT-l-zSk?t=2021), [0:34:28](https://youtu.be/5PpnT-l-zSk?t=2068), [0:35:16](https://youtu.be/5PpnT-l-zSk?t=2116)
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** This analogy works for uptrends. For downtrends, reverse it: the goal is at the bottom, and you're looking for handholds (resistance levels) to slow or stop a fall.

head: Order Block Identification (CISD—Change in State of Delivery)
body:
- **Kind:** rule + advanced entry model
- **What ICT says:** An order block forms when price prints a series of consecutive candles in one direction (e.g., up close candles), then reverses sharply. The last candle in that series—specifically, the opening price of that last candle—becomes the order block (a bearish order block if it's reversing from bullish). However, the rule depends on which candle is "largest" in the series: (1) if the last candle is the **largest**, use its opening; (2) if it's the **smallest**, also use its opening; (3) if they're all **equal**, use the opening of the **first** candle in the series.
- **How to identify:** 
  1. Find a series of up-close candles (or down-close, for bullish order blocks).
  2. Look for the reversal candle (opposite direction).
  3. Measure the body size of the last candle vs. the series average.
  4. Apply the size rule above.
- **How to use:** Plot the order block level on your chart. When price returns to that level later in the day, it acts as an entry point or a support/resistance. Order blocks are areas where smart money aggressively liquidated or established positions, so they're often reversal points.
- **Example in this video:** MNQ charts show multiple candle series; ICT references the rule when analyzing where to enter shorts. The order block opening becomes a reference level for both entries and stop placement.
- **Timestamps:** [0:42:26](https://youtu.be/5PpnT-l-zSk?t=2546), [0:43:15](https://youtu.be/5PpnT-l-zSk?t=2595)
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Don't "write this in your book and sell it on Amazon" — there are many YouTubers misinterpreting this rule. The candle size (largest, smallest, or equal) determines which opening to use. This is a precise rule, not an approximation.

head: Draw on Liquidity (DOL) & Entry Models
body:
- **Kind:** entry signal + process
- **What ICT says:** A "draw on liquidity" occurs when price approaches a known liquidity level (a gap, an old high/low, a pool of buy-side or sell-side orders). Not every draw is an entry. An entry requires **order flow confirmation**—additional price action (a specific candle formation, body placement, wick behavior) that signals smart money is about to move. Just because price reached your target doesn't mean you enter; you wait for the order flow signal. "It's not 'he said that level, so let's go short.' That's not what this is at all."
- **How to identify:** Identify where price is going (RTH gaps, old highs/lows, key wicks). Watch for price to approach that level. When it does, pause and ask: "Do I see order flow confirmation here?" Look for bodies in specific halves of FVGs, bodies respecting key wicks, or small reversal candles. If you don't see that confirmation, don't enter.
- **How to use:** Use draws on liquidity as an **observation** tool. When price hits your target level, annotate it and study what happened. Did bodies respect the level (order flow confirmed)? Or did it blow through? This builds your intuition. Over time, you'll recognize order flow signals instinctively. In real-time trading, use it as a filter: draw on liquidity + order flow confirmation = entry.
- **Example in this video:** ICT drew on liquidity at Monday's RTH opening range gap low (26,695) on April 21. Price approached it. But because the Fed speaker was at 10:00, he didn't force an entry—he waited for order flow confirmation. The market didn't provide clean confirmation due to the news event, so he reduced conviction.

- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Many retail traders watch ICT's livestreams, see a level, and assume it's a "signal" to trade that level. It's not. It's an **observation point**. The entry signal is the order flow. If you're a new trader watching, focus on learning order flow patterns, not just level identification.

head: Emotional Discipline & Journal Methodology
body:
- **Kind:** psychology + long-term skill development
- **What ICT says:** Build your journal to record observations, not complaints. Don't write, "I was wrong, the market didn't do what I expected." Instead, write: "I was looking for price to do X, but price was unwilling. Here's what price did instead." This reframing prevents bitterness and self-criticism from poisoning your development. Many traders destroy their potential by beating themselves up early on; this creates a lifelong pattern of unsatisfactory results (you succeed but never feel good enough). Start fresh: observe neutrally, record facts, stay constructive.
- **How to identify:** After each trading session or study session, review: Did price hit your target? Did your model work? If not, why? Write it down.
- **How to use:** Use your journal as a learning tool, not an emotional release. Build a library of observations so you can later back-test and refine your model. Don't share your trading journal on social media early on—external criticism (from people who don't know your full model) can derail your development. Build in private.
- **Example in this video:** ICT's experience: he made a lot of money early on but beat himself up internally, so the wins never felt good. Now, as a grandfather, he's focused on being present for family rather than obsessing over trading. The lesson: emotional discipline is as important as technical skill.

head: Inversion Fair Value Gap (iFVG) — Revisited with Validation
body:
- **Kind:** rule + validation framework
- **What ICT says:** Not all FVGs that "look" like inversions are valid. An inversion FVG is valid only if it meets specific criteria: (1) The original FVG was used in its first utilization (bodies respected the zone correctly), (2) price traded **through** the original FVG (fully leaving a body outside), and (3) price then retraced **back into** that gap showing the new (inverted) characteristic. If price wicks outside a gap but doesn't leave a body outside, the inversion has not been confirmed yet. This nuance prevents false inversions from being traded.
- **How to identify:** 
  1. Mark the original FVG (with appropriate body placement).
  2. Watch price trade above/below it and leave a body outside.
  3. Watch price retrace back in. 
  4. Only then does it act as inversion with certainty.
- **How to use:** Don't assume every gap that looks inverted is inverted. Wait for the confirmation (body outside, then retrace with new characteristic). This prevents premature entries.
- **Example in this video:** MNQ shows several gaps. Some look like they could invert, but ICT emphasizes: "We did not trade outside of this gap yet. We just wicked outside. A small body, but that's not validating the inversion FVG." The wick alone doesn't confirm; you need a body outside and a retrace with the new characteristic.
- **Timestamps:** [0:32:05](https://youtu.be/5PpnT-l-zSk?t=1925), [0:38:25](https://youtu.be/5PpnT-l-zSk?t=2305)

head: Premium wick / discount wick and its Consequent Encroachment as a PD array  (aliases: "wick CE", "grading the wick")
body:
- **Kind:** definition + rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - Pick the high whose wick is longer than the wicks of the previous candle and of the two subsequent candles; that is why October 30, 2025 was selected.
  - A "premium wick" is a wick at the high of a candle (above the body). A wick below the body is a "discount wick". But relative to price: if market price is below a wick it is a premium wick; if price is above, it is a discount wick. First thing to check: where is market price relative to that specific wick.
  - Grade the wick with a midpoint: "when we're having a midpoint like that, that's consequent encroachment". It matters more because it is part of Friday's daily range and today's, i.e. current price is inside the same area.
  - Treat the wick as a premium gap, "think of this as an inversion fair value gap": price below it coming up into it should not be able to leave a body at or above the CE of that wick; if a body lays at or above it, "I'm probably wrong".
  - Best entry for a short: from the CE down to the low of that wick ("anything inside of that is useful for an entry looking for shorts").
  - First order of business after the first test: price must show no willingness to get up into the CE of the wick, "not even for a wick", because the wick test has already been done; bodies staying low and "blunt-ended" confirm it.
  - He colours the wick/gap with his usual inversion FVG colour so it looks familiar.
- **How to identify:** longest wick vs neighbours; measure its 50%; mark it; watch bodies.
- **How to use:** short between wick CE and the wick low after the first test; stop outside the wick high / CE; targets sell-side below.
- **Example in this video:** MNQ 1-minute, Monday 20 April open: price runs up to the CE of a wick (around the 9:30–10:00 area) and shows no body at/above; ICT shorts the CE-to-close region of that candle ("anything in here is fair game").

- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** the premium/discount wick terminology is explained a little confusingly in the captions; the rule of thumb is "relative to market price".

head: RTH Opening Range Gap at highs: gap high = prior RTH settlement; octants and CE as read of intent  (aliases: "RTH ORG", "discount gap", "lowest octant")
body:
- **Kind:** rule / refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - RTH opening range gap = Friday's settlement (RTH close at 4:14 PM ET candle) versus Monday's 9:30 open. Monday opened lower: a discount gap near all-time highs. The gap high is Friday's settlement; he labels the gap box "RTH ORG" and its midpoint is consequent encroachment.
  - Expectations at ATH when bullish: price can trade above the gap high and then use the gap as a discount PD array ("something to support price"), possibly making a higher ATH; or price can fill to half (CE) and on to full closure.
  - Gap-fill tendency: price tends to go all the way to full closure, but if still bullish "you have to at least yield" to the possibility it trades above the high and uses the gap for support.
  - He was not interested in trading the first run into half gap, being unsure of full closure, and he would not have entered at full closure either: he would wait to see if it uses the high.
  - Reading the morning: a candle went to CE of the gap and closed below the gap's lowest octant (an eighth-division line, caption unclear). Because bodies would not even sit near the lowest octant, let alone above it, he read that as unlikely to run for full closure, and perhaps the extreme high of the gap, so the session high might be in.
  - Same gap logic as in the L26-086 video (RTH opening range gap and its overcome-then-retest behaviour).
- **How to identify:** prior day RTH settlement vs 9:30 open; box; midpoint; octant lines.
- **How to use:** at ATH a discount gap can be bought only if price proves it by exceeding the gap high and holding the gap as support; a sale idea starts when bodies refuse to approach the gap's upper range.
- **Example in this video:** MNQ, Mon 20 April 2026: Friday 4:14 PM settle vs 9:30 open lower; the first candle goes to CE and closes below the lowest octant; ICT interprets as the high of the morning.

head: TGIF: 20–30% retracement of the weekly range  (aliases: "Thank God It's Friday", "20% of the weekly range")
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - On Friday (or as early as Thursday at 1:00 PM ET) if the weekly candle is forming as an up-close/bullish week, look for a retracement from the weekly high of 20% to 30% of the full weekly range, in some instances up to 40%.
  - Method: Fibonacci anchored at the weekly low dragged to the highest high; set the 50 level to 20 (0.2) to show the 20%. Do this intraday on Thursday around 1:00 PM and keep referring back.
  - If it does not form on Friday and a new week starts, still look for it on Monday; if it has not formed by Tuesday, abandon it: price is probably continuing in its longer-term direction.
  - Last week closed up on the high without the TGIF pullback, so the Monday retracement was still a potential.
- **How to identify:** weekly range fib; 20% level.
- **How to use:** as a downside objective/bias anchor for the short (the "two key levels" together with Friday's RTH ORG CE).
- **Example in this video:** MNQ weekly: the 20% level = 26,489.25 (caption: "26,489 quarter"). It was anchored in green on the lower time frames.
- **Timestamps:** [0:11:16](https://youtu.be/r-ztz7kReYc?t=676) — last week closed on the high, no TGIF; [0:12:05](https://youtu.be/r-ztz7kReYc?t=725) — 20–30% (up to 40%) and the fib method; [0:28:56](https://youtu.be/r-ztz7kReYc?t=1736) — Monday allowed, abandon by Tuesday.

body:

- **What ICT says:**
  - He marks the FVG that formed right before the displacement down that takes a short-term low; "I want to see this be treated as first presented fair value gap" (the first one in the leg). He notes the 9:31 candle's gap is not the first-presented one; he promised to explain why (the explanation is not in this transcript).
  - If price lacks conviction at the wick, wait: once the buy-side imbalance sell-side inefficiency breaks down, it becomes a premium FVG / inversion FVG: "use it as a catalyst to get short".
  - Price keeps returning to the low end of the inversion FVG; each time it fails to reach CE (bodies below), he adds ("every time we were working toward the low end of that gap, which is first presented, I felt confident we weren't coming back up").
  - Keep such gaps on the chart: "they don't go stale; they're not supply and demand zones"; extend them into the next session (here Friday's → Monday's).
  - Tiny gaps ("common gap", small separations) are not helpful; the gap needs to be more significant.
  - Small time frame check on a 15-second chart: the first 15-second candle to close below the iFVG low, then a retrace that does not reach CE; "if this can't trade up to the low of that, that's heaviness"; look for minor sell-side first and a more significant sell-side further down.
- **How to identify:** BISI formed in the displacement leg; later broken and inverted; bodies staying in the lower half.
- **How to use:** add on retests into the low end that fail to reach CE; partials at minor sell-side below; do not re-add if close to the exits.
- **Example in this video:** MNQ, 20 April: price takes out a short-term low after displacing lower, the FVG before that displacement becomes the first-presented gap; shorts fill on retests into it; price then dives below the iFVG and the lows, hits minor sell-side, and finally Friday's RTH ORG CE.

title: ICT 2026 Futures Market Review \ April 18, 2026
head: Event Horizon
body:
- **Kind:** definition + calculation
- **What ICT says:** The midpoint between two significant price levels, calculated by (Level A + Level B) ÷ 2. Event horizon is a price magnet—a level where smart money often holds price temporarily before continuing higher or lower. It's not a target; it's an observation point. When price reaches event horizon, pause and ask: does it have support/resistance there? Can it continue? If price moves through event horizon decisively with strong bodies, the move is likely to continue to the next target.
- **How to identify:** Identify two key levels (e.g., Thursday's daily high at 26,563 and all-time high at 26,859). Calculate midpoint: (26,563 + 26,859) ÷ 2 = 26,711. Mark it on the chart.
- **How to use:** Don't trade at event horizon; use it as a reference. When price is below it, event horizon acts like support (price wants to reach it). When price is above it, it acts like resistance (price wants to push past it to the target). If price stalls at event horizon, it may be a sign of weakness or consolidation.
- **Example in this video:** ES, April 18, 2026. Event horizon = 26,711 (between Thursday's 26,563 high and ATH 26,859). Price ran up from the morning low, reached 26,711, and continued higher to 26,859. Event horizon was a way station, not a reversal point.
- **Timestamps:** [0:04:40](https://youtu.be/9nmjg331xGQ?t=280), [0:10:11](https://youtu.be/9nmjg331xGQ?t=611), [0:14:56](https://youtu.be/9nmjg331xGQ?t=896), [0:30:48](https://youtu.be/9nmjg331xGQ?t=1848)
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Event horizon can be calculated from any two levels (daily highs, RTH gaps, key wicks, all-time highs). Use it when you need a midpoint reference. It's different from relative equal highs or balanced price ranges—it's purely mathematical, not based on historical price touching.

title: ICT 2026 Futures Market Review \ April 18, 2026
head: Propulsion Block
body:
- **Kind:** entry model + structure
- **What ICT says:** When two consecutive down-close candles form (e.g., in a bearish move), they can be combined into a single "propulsion block" if certain conditions are met. The block's defining feature: the low body (the lower of the two down closes) must stay above the mean threshold (midpoint) of the higher body. In a bullish reversal (after propulsion), price should not retrace into the mean of the propulsion block. If it does, the setup is compromised.
- **How to identify:** Find two consecutive down-close candles. Mark the high and low of each. Draw a line at the midpoint of the upper candle (the mean threshold). The propulsion block is valid if the lower candle's body doesn't cross below that midpoint.
- **How to use:** After a propulsion block forms, it acts as a **defense**—like a bolo or barrier. On a retracement, price should not trade back into the propulsion block's mean; if it does, you're likely to get stopped out. Use it to place stops just below the mean, not inside the block itself. Alternatively, when price breaks above a propulsion block after a bounce, it's a bullish signal.
- **Example in this video:** ICT shows a propulsion block formed near the morning low; price later bounces off it, confirming its defensive function. The bodies stay above the mean threshold, showing respect for the structure.
- **Timestamps:** [0:15:44](https://youtu.be/9nmjg331xGQ?t=944), [0:17:21](https://youtu.be/9nmjg331xGQ?t=1041)
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** "This might be a little unsettling, but that's OK"—sometimes the wick will touch just below the mean and barely miss the low of the order block. This is a rare but valid exception. The rule is bodies staying above the mean, not wicks.

title: ICT 2026 Futures Market Review \ April 18, 2026
head: Bolo (Defensive PD Array)
body:
- **Kind:** definition + defensive structure
- **What ICT says:** A bolo is a defensive PD array formed by the combination of a **rejection block** (a candle that wicks down and back up, rejecting the lower level) and the **consequent encroachment** of that wick. The zone between these two levels is the "bolo"—a defensive line in the sand. You don't trade inside a bolo; it protects your stop loss. If price touches the bolo on a retrace, you'll get stopped out. The name comes from the weapon: a rope with two weights that entangles the legs of a target. The metaphor is that you're trying to "run away" for higher prices, but if you get tangled in the bolo, you trip and fall.
- **How to identify:** Find a rejection candle (wick down, close up). Mark the low of that wick. Draw consequent encroachment (the midpoint of the wick, or a reference level). The zone between the rejection block opening and the wick's consequent encroachment is the bolo.
- **How to use:** Place your stop just above the bolo. Don't penetrate it. If price touches the bolo, you're being "leg-swept" (stopped out). Use it to place mental stops or actual stops to protect your position. It's purely defensive—you're not trading inside it; you're protecting yourself from being caught there.
- **Example in this video:** After the morning push higher, a rejection candle forms and subsequent retracements show respect for the bolo. ICT acknowledges the bolo and warns: "Don't want to see it touched. Treat it like a land mine."
- **Timestamps:** [0:18:57](https://youtu.be/9nmjg331xGQ?t=1137), [0:19:44](https://youtu.be/9nmjg331xGQ?t=1184), [0:20:31](https://youtu.be/9nmjg331xGQ?t=1231)
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** A bolo is one of several "defensive" PD arrays (alongside balanced price ranges). It's not an entry model; it's a structure you learn to respect and avoid.

title: ICT 2026 Futures Market Review \ April 18, 2026
head: Rejection Block
body:
- **Kind:** candle formation + signal
- **What ICT says:** A candle that wicks down significantly (testing a lower level) but then closes higher (near the open or above), rejecting the lower level. This wick shows an attempt to go lower; the close shows a rejection of that lower level. Rejection blocks often mark the point where smart money stops accepting sellers and starts buying again.
- **How to identify:** Look for a candle with a long lower wick and a close near the open or higher. The contrast between the wick low and the close high is the "rejection" signal.
- **How to use:** When you see a rejection block form, it's a bullish signal—price is rejecting lower levels. Use it as a buy signal or as confirmation that a pullback is done. It's often the candle where you'd start adding to long positions or entering longs.
- **Example in this video:** The early morning candle that wicks down but rejects (closes higher) is marked as a rejection block. This forms the top part of the bolo.
- **Timestamps:** [0:18:57](https://youtu.be/9nmjg331xGQ?t=1137)

title: ICT 2026 Futures Market Review \ April 18, 2026
head: Consequent Encroachment (Wick Midpoint Reference)
body:
- **Kind:** rule + reference level
- **What ICT says:** When a wick extends beyond a support/resistance level, the midpoint of that wick (from the low wick point to the close) becomes "consequent encroachment." This level is a threshold: bodies should not cross it in the opposite direction (if bullish, bodies shouldn't cross below it). If a wick goes down to a low and back up, the midpoint of that wick is a reference line. Futures/scalpers use this as a target level or a rejection point.
- **How to identify:** After a rejection candle (wick down, close up), mark the low of the wick. Mark the close. Calculate the midpoint. That's consequent encroachment.
- **How to use:** Use it as a threshold for body placement. In a bullish setup, bodies should stay above consequent encroachment on any pullbacks. If bodies drop below it, the setup is weakening. In a bearish setup, the opposite: bodies should stay below it. Use it as a reference for partial exits or as a level where you expect price to pause or reverse.
- **Example in this video:** Multiple references to consequent encroachment of key wicks. Bodies must stay above it to show bullish continuation.

head: Stop Hunting & Manual Market Intervention
body:

- **How to use:** Accept that stop hunting happens. Place your stops tactically, not predictably. Don't announce them publicly (or if you do, as ICT does, expect them to be run). Consider using stops that are far from obvious levels, or use position sizing + mental discipline instead of hard stops. Alternatively, understand that a stop run might be a final capitulation that precedes your move higher—it's a feature, not a bug, of the market structure.

head: Inversion Fair Value Gap (AAA Rating / Premium Grade)
body:
- **Kind:** structure + visual confirmation level
- **What ICT says:** Not all inversion FVGs are created equal. A "premium grade" or "AAA" inversion FVG is one where the bodies cannot even touch consequent encroachment (the midpoint/high of the gap) and the bodies don't lay down on top of it at all. This is the strongest signal—the market is showing absolute rejection of anything below the gap, meaning buyers are in complete control and the move is likely to continue without pause.
- **How to identify:** After an inversion FVG forms and price retraces into it, watch the bodies: (1) If they touch or cross the midpoint = normal inversion FVG, (2) If they can't reach the midpoint and stay in the lower half = AAA grade. The AAA signal is the absence of bodies at the midpoint—that's what makes it premium.
- **How to use:** When you see an AAA-grade inversion FVG, it's a strong continuation signal. Add to longs, don't take partials yet, and expect price to run hard. It's the "real one, baby"—ICT's phrase.
- **Example in this video:** The 9:20 fair value gap (inverted) shows an AAA rating: bodies stay well below consequent encroachment, and even the wicks don't touch it. This is a textbook premium-grade inversion FVG, confirming the bullish continuation.

- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Most inversion FVGs will have bodies touch the midpoint at some point—that's normal. AAA-grade gaps where bodies can't even reach the midpoint are rare and represent the strongest bullish continuation signal.

head: Bullish Order Block (CISD—Change in State of Delivery)
body:
- **Kind:** reversal entry model
- **What ICT says:** When a down-close candle prints at a key reversal point (after a series of down closes), it marks the opening price where smart money is now buying. This opening price is a **bullish order block**—the lowest price where buyers are willing to step in. When price retraces back down to that level later, it often acts as support. ICT states: "I'm not selling a bearish down close when I'm looking for 859"—meaning once the order block is identified, the bias has shifted bullish.
- **How to identify:** After a series of down closes, find the last down-close candle that marks the reversal. The opening price of that candle is the bullish order block. Draw a horizontal line at that level.
- **How to use:** Use the bullish order block as a support level for long positions. If price retraces back to it, you can add to longs or expect a bounce. If price closes above the order block, the reversal is confirmed. If price traded below the order block with a body, the reversal may have failed.
- **Example in this video:** The reversal candle from the morning downmove is marked; its opening price becomes the bullish order block for the day's bullish bias.

title: ICT 2026 Futures Market Review \ April 17, 2026
head: RTH Opening Range Gap Exploration & Standard Deviation
body:
- **Kind:** daily structure + extension rule
- **What ICT says:** When the market is in an uptrend (longer-term bias bullish), it can "explore" (temporarily dip) below the RTH opening range gap to a standard deviation level. The standard deviation is calculated from the opening range gap midpoint, extended downward by 0.5 standard deviations. This level is a magnet during the morning session. Once price reaches the -0.5 standard deviation, it often reverses and returns to the opening range gap high or above. This is a structured exploration, not a breakdown.
- **How to identify:** 
  1. Mark RTH opening range gap high and low.
  2. Calculate midpoint (event horizon).
  3. Calculate the range of the gap (high - low).
  4. Extend downward by 0.5 × range to find the standard deviation level (-0.5σ).
  5. Price will often test this level in a bullish day before reversing.
- **How to use:** When price drops below the opening range gap in a bullish market, don't panic. It's an exploration to the standard deviation level. Place limit orders at the -0.5σ level, expecting a bounce. Once price bounces from -0.5σ and returns to the opening range gap high, it's a strong bullish signal (it's confirmed the structure and is now ready to run to the next target).
- **Example in this video:** MNQ, April 17, 2026. RTH opening range gap was high 26,xxx, low Wednesday's 4:14 PM settlement. Price dipped below the gap to approximately -0.5σ, hit, and reversed back up to opening range gap high, then continued higher to 26,711 (event horizon) and eventually 26,859 (all-time high).
- **Timestamps:** [0:18:14](https://youtu.be/X-xYcsOG9Yg?t=1094), [0:19:03](https://youtu.be/X-xYcsOG9Yg?t=1143)
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** The -0.5σ standard deviation is a mapped level before price reaches it (not after). ICT mentions "I mapped this out before we went down there"—meaning he calculated the level in advance and annotated it on the chart.

title: ICT 2026 Futures Market Review \ April 17, 2026
head: Accumulation During Time Distortion
body:
- **Kind:** structure + entry signal
- **What ICT says:** During periods where price gyrates sideways (wicks going up and down, bodies staying within a defined zone), but bodies remain inside a pre-established fair value gap, smart money is **accumulating**—building long positions quietly. The wicks are noise (attempting to shake out weak hands), but the bodies show real order flow. Once accumulation is complete (bodies have been consistently placed in the lower/middle portion of the zone), price then leaves and runs hard in the bullish direction. This is the opposite of distribution.
- **How to identify:** Look for 3–5 candles where wicks wick down (or up, depending on direction) but bodies stay firmly inside a fair value gap or zone. Ask: are the bodies respecting the zone, or are they breaking out? If bodies stay in the zone, it's accumulation.
- **How to use:** When you see accumulation (bodies in zone, wicks noise), don't exit. Hold through the wick noise. Accumulation is a setup signal—once complete, expect an aggressive run in the direction of the zone boundary above. Add to positions rather than reduce.
- **Example in this video:** MNQ shows candles in time distortion where wicks wick down (hurting traders), but bodies stay inside the pre-session FVG. This is accumulation—smart money is building, not shaking out the strong hands (the bodies prove it). Once accumulation ends, price leaves that zone and runs higher.
- **Timestamps:** [0:19:50](https://youtu.be/X-xYcsOG9Yg?t=1190), [0:20:38](https://youtu.be/X-xYcsOG9Yg?t=1238)
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Time distortion is when price moves sideways without clear direction, often seen during lunch (11:00–13:00 ET) or low-volume hours. Bodies staying in a zone during time distortion is more reliable than wicks.

head: Daily High/Low Prediction & Algorithmic Price Delivery
body:
- **Kind:** advanced concept + market structure philosophy
- **What ICT says:** Daily highs and lows aren't randomly determined by supply/demand—they're delivered by algorithms that know where they need to run price to hit liquidity, shake out weak hands, and complete institutional orders. By mapping out the PD arrays (FVGs, RTH gaps, previous wicks, event horizons), you can forecast where the daily high and low will print, often to the tick. This isn't luck or cherry-picking; it's structural. The market is "rigged" in the sense that it's autonomous and algorithmic, not random. No one else in retail trading could make that call and have it hit to the tick.

These are the candidate zones where the daily high or low will be. Ask: which one is most "random" (least obvious) and aligned with the larger bias? That's likely the daily high or low.
- **How to use:** Use it as proof of concept—if your mapped levels hit, you're reading the algorithm correctly. If they don't, recalibrate. Don't force predictions; let the market tell you. Once the daily high is hit, reduce conviction for longs and look for reversals. Once the daily low is hit, flip to bullish bias.
- **Example in this video:** ICT predicted 26,562.75 as the daily high at 11:40 AM. At the time, price was trading around 26,700+. Price later ran down, consolidated, ran back up, and hit 26,562.75 to the tick. No one else in the trading community predicted this level. It was called in real-time during a livestream (documented).

title: ICT 2026 Futures Market Review \ April 17, 2026
head: Algorithmic vs. Dealing Market Structure
body:
- **Kind:** market philosophy + distinction
- **What ICT says:** There's a critical difference between (1) **market makers as dealers** (individuals managing inventory, not driving price) and (2) **the algorithm** (the autonomous system that delivers price). Dealers provide liquidity (they pair buy and sell orders), but they don't "make" price go higher or lower. The algorithm does. Price action is driven by algorithms that know where to go to hit PD arrays, not by the combined sentiment of millions of traders. This is why you can predict highs/lows—you're reading the algorithm's path, not guessing at supply/demand.
- **How to identify:** Look for patterns in where price runs. If price runs in a way that "cleans up" all the buy-side and sell-side liquidity in a predictable manner, it's algorithmic (not random buying/selling). If it runs differently each day, it's more likely driven by external factors (news, sentiment).
- **How to use:** Stop thinking about "supply and demand" or "buying pressure." Instead, think about "where does the algorithm need to go to complete its delivery?" Map the liquidity pools (RTH gaps, previous wicks, FVGs), and the algorithm will likely run price through those zones in a logical order. This mental shift changes your analysis from passive (watching supply/demand) to active (reading the algorithm's path).
- **Example in this video:** ICT argues that bodies respecting the 9:30 opening price on the way up aren't a coincidence—they're the algorithm saying "this is the level; respect it." The algorithm is rigging price, which ICT sees as a good thing: "It should be a good feeling. You should be happy that it is because if it wasn't rigged, nobody would know what the hell was going on. It would be all guesswork."
- **Timestamps:** [0:20:38](https://youtu.be/X-xYcsOG9Yg?t=1238), [0:22:16](https://youtu.be/X-xYcsOG9Yg?t=1336), [0:23:04](https://youtu.be/X-xYcsOG9Yg?t=1384)
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** ICT is not arguing that individual market makers are "bad" or "evil." He's saying the system is autonomous, not manual. Dealers are just liquidity providers, not price drivers.

head: Pre-Session Fair Value Gaps & Their Persistence
body:
- **Kind:** structure + identification
- **What ICT says:** Fair value gaps that form during pre-market hours (before 9:30 ET) often persist throughout the intraday session as reference levels. Price will revisit these gaps multiple times: first as a target (draw on liquidity), then as a zone to trade through (inversion), and finally as a barrier. Once you identify a pre-session FVG, it's a level you can count on to be utilized at least once during the day.
- **How to identify:** Open your chart 30 minutes before the RTH open (9:00 ET). Look for any gaps in price action during electronic trading hours (pre-market). Mark those gaps as pre-session FVGs. They're usually the first levels price will touch after the RTH open.
- **How to use:** Use pre-session FVGs as intermediate targets. When price is moving in the morning, ask: "Will it hit the pre-session FVG?" If yes, that's your first scalp target. If price doesn't hit it, re-evaluate the bias. Pre-session FVGs can also act as resistance (if inverted) or support.
- **Example in this video:** A pre-session FVG formed during ETH; price used it multiple times on the intraday: as a draw, as a retracement zone, and eventually broke through it as the bullish bias continued. Each touch was a reference point.

head: Event Horizon (Intraday Management)
body:
- **Kind:** reference + midpoint calculation
- **What ICT says:** The midpoint between two significant levels (daily high and all-time high, for example) is an intraday management tool. Price often gravitates toward event horizon during the mid-morning or afternoon session. When price is below event horizon, it's attractive for longs (price wants to reach it). When price is above event horizon, it's a consolidation zone (price is between event horizon and the next target). Use it as a reference, not a hard target.
- **How to identify:** Calculate (Level A + Level B) ÷ 2 = event horizon. For April 17, event horizon was (26,563 + 26,859) ÷ 2 = 26,711.
- **How to use:** When trading intraday, know your event horizon. It's a psychological midpoint. Price often runs to it, consolidates, then continues. Use it to scale partials or add to positions depending on where you are relative to it.
- **Example in this video:** Event horizon 26,711 became a visible holding point and reference level during the afternoon session.

title: ICT 2026 Entries & Drills Part 2 \ April 16, 2026
head: RTH Opening Range Gap (ORG) and the 70% CE tendency  (aliases: regular trading hours opening range gap, opening gap, "the 9:30 gap", half gap, CE of the gap)
body:
- **Kind:** rule (reinforcement of a known concept, with new framing for beginners)
- **What ICT says:**
  - The gap is framed only on regular trading hours: the previous day's RTH settlement price (he says "4:14 p.m." ET, the last RTH print/candle) to the 9:30 ET opening price. He insists it is always framed on RTH, not on the 24-hour session.
  - If a gap forms at the 9:30 open, there is about a 70% probability that price makes an attempt to trade back to half the gap (the CE of the gap). It does not have to reach it, and it does not have to reach full closure, though it can.
  - Best-case targets for the drill: the half gap first, then 3/4 gap closure, then full gap closure (the RTH settlement price = "opening range gap low" when the gap is a premium gap).
  - Even after price trades through the gap, "always allow for return back to consequent encroachment of the opening range gap".
  - The 9:30 opening price itself is a level that can be re-traded and revisited at any time ("retested, rebooked, repriced").
- **How to identify:** compare the 9:30 opening price with the previous RTH settlement. Open above settlement = premium gap (bearish bias for the drill). The CE is the midpoint between the two prices.
- **How to use:**
  - Pre-stage the chart before the open: no indicators, just a line pre-drawn at the previous settlement and a second line/tool parked near price. When the 9:30 candle opens, drag the second anchor to the candle's open price and read off the CE so you can state the level immediately (his example CE read as "370 and 3/4").
  - Premium gap = look only for shorts, only for things that will participate in going lower. Use the gap's lower pools of sell-side liquidity as the draw.
  - Before the open, do not treat a pending price as the open price. Wait for the opening bell.
- **Example in this video:** 16 Apr 2026 (Thursday). Roughly ten minutes before the open price is inside a small sloppy range, above the prior RTH settlement, so a premium opening gap is expected. The CE is staged ahead of the bell. At 9:30 the gap opens higher ("premium gap opening's up here"); he wants price to return to the gap, with two sell-side pools below as the draw, the nearer one higher probability. He shorts (demo on TradingView), price trades down to the sell side, then later runs through the gap low area and on to the negative 0.5 projection, before coming back up to the CE of the gap.
- **Timestamps:** [0:05:29](https://youtu.be/eft9_3ekDCY?t=329) 70% probability of trading to CE of the gap, not necessarily full closure · [0:07:23](https://youtu.be/eft9_3ekDCY?t=443) anchoring CE to the 9:30 candle open and tweeting it · [0:13:01](https://youtu.be/eft9_3ekDCY?t=781) "half of the gap ... 70% of the time it makes an attempt to trade to half gap" · [0:55:19](https://youtu.be/eft9_3ekDCY?t=3319) student plan: shorts only in premium gaps in first 30 minutes, aim for half gap, best case 3/4 or full
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** frames the 70% as a statistical tendency to be confirmed by the student over about 20 days of observation, not a guarantee. He says repeatedly it need not close fully. The "4:14 p.m." settlement reference is stated by him; treat the exact timestamp as his convention for the last RTH print.

head: Inversion Fair Value Gap (iFVG) as the entry trigger in the drill  (aliases: inversion fair value gap, "act as inversion", reclaimed bullish FVG)
body:
- **Kind:** entry model (applied example) with refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - A gap formed by an up move can later act as an inversion gap: after price trades up through a bearish FVG it can be used as a bullish FVG; and when price comes back up into a bullish gap and fails, that gap flips to resistance. The wording "this gap here could return back to its original characteristic of bearish fair value gap" shows he sees a gap as able to flip back and forth.
  - Price comes back up to half of the buy-side imbalance (a gap that is also a sell-side inefficiency) and should act as an inversion, then sell off hard below the prior low into the sell side.
  - Wants heavy, aggressive selling below the low, not a "toe beneath the water" touch of the sell-side liquidity.
  - Bear-flag analogy: he would like the pullback into the gap to behave like a bear flag, because there is unfinished business below (sell-side liquidity and the remainder of the ORG).
  - For a Tuesday-evening Asian session short he had liked an iFVG that "respected the lower half" (price should not trade into the upper half of the gap), after multiple attempts higher.
- **How to identify:** a gap price has already traded through; price returns to it and is rejected; the candle bodies close back on the other side. (Details of the exact closing rule are not restated here.)
- **How to use:** short the rejection of the iFVG, stop above the gap/recent high, target the sell-side liquidity, then the lower part of the ORG. He puts the position on first and then shows stop and target, and dislikes drawing a hypothetical risk/reward box instead.
- **Example in this video:** 16 Apr 2026 after the open. Price comes back up into the gap ("we come out, hit that, so far that's positive"), then drops to the sell side but only barely wicks it at first. A possible alternative: price swipes the stop above and still runs lower.

body:

- **What ICT says:**
  - When price is hemming and hawing, a recent high becomes the line in the sand for the bears: if price comes back above it the short idea is in doubt.
  - Bears need price to go to the gap low and through it now; if it takes the low out on a closing basis (not just a wick), the wick below becomes a point of interest and its CE becomes the new line in the sand: bodies must then stay below that midpoint.
  - He wants bodies below the CE of that wick, and a return back to it later is allowed.
  - Stop placement logic: with the stop above the high, "if I were making the market, I'd run that high before I took it lower", so he does not take a short with no clean framework.
- **How to use:** minor buy-side liquidity (the small high) can be taken first; he would rather see price run that high (he calls the spike a "mohawk") and then drop, and short after that.

  - One-to-one makes money only once you are educated in price action; for an uneducated trader it fails, which is why "risk to reward" talk is a misnomer.
  - First four weeks: take many executions and do not fear overtrading. This desensitizes you to each outcome.
  - After that, study winners against losers and look for features that repeat in the winners. These become your own setup checklist.
  - Then spend two to four weeks only taking shorts in premium opening gaps in the first 30 minutes (and presumably the mirror); then learn the projection measurement.

head: Macro Time Windows (9:50–10:10 ET)
body:
- **Kind:** time filter / algorithmic trigger
- **What ICT says:** The period from 9:50 AM to 10:10 AM ET (approximately 20 minutes into the RTH open) is a high-probability algorithmic time window (a "macro"). During this window, smart money is actively executing orders. Setups identified before or during this macro are more likely to trigger. Price action during this window is often more decisive than earlier (9:30–9:50).
- **How to identify:** Mark the time on your chart: 9:50–10:10 ET. Watch price action during this window. If a pattern forms (wick touch, FVG formation, liquidity pool test), it's a macro setup.
- **How to use:** Don't trade before 9:50. Wait for this window. If your setup (turtle soup, FVG entry, etc.) aligns with macro time, conviction is higher. If price doesn't move decisively by 10:10, the setup may have failed.
- **Example in this video:** Asian session had a macro window around the 10:00 hour (9:50–10:10). A turtle soup setup formed during this window, and ICT entered short, targeting sell-side liquidity below. The macro time gave confidence that the order would execute decisively.
- **Timestamps:** [0:00:48](https://youtu.be/3J8drYX2zHM?t=48), [0:05:06](https://youtu.be/3J8drYX2zHM?t=306)
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Macros vary by market and day. The 9:50–10:10 ET macro is typical for US index futures. Other macros occur at noon, 2:00 PM, etc. Learn to identify them through observation.

title: ICT 2026 Asian Session Short Review \ April 14, 2026
head: Turtle Soup Entry Model
body:
- **Kind:** entry setup + liquidity trap
- **What ICT says:** A turtle soup is when price runs above a **two-stage buy-side liquidity pool** (buyers holding stops above two different levels), then reverses sharply into the zone between the two pools, where sell-side liquidity rests. The "soup" is the trap: retail buyers place buy stops above the first pool, smart money runs price up and through those stops, then reverses and trades through the second pool, creating panic selling. Entry is in the zone between the two pools (or just above the upper pool, expecting reversal). Target is the sell-side liquidity below the lower pool.
- **How to identify:** 
  1. Identify two buy-side liquidity pools (two previous highs or resistance levels).
  2. Price runs above the first, then above the second (taking both buy-side pools).
  3. Expect sharp reversal and downside run.
  4. Entry: above the second pool (where reversals form) or in the "soup" zone (between the two pools).
- **How to use:** Turtle soup setups in macro time windows have the highest probability. Short aggressively once both pools are taken and bodies show reversal (up close candles shift to down close). Target the sell-side liquidity below.
- **Example in this video:** Two buy-side pools were identified on the Asian session chart. Price ran above both during the macro window. ICT then entered short, targeting the sell-side liquidity below. The trade worked as expected.
- **Timestamps:** [0:03:26](https://youtu.be/3J8drYX2zHM?t=206)
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Turtle soup is one of the most reliable setups when macro time aligns. However, in very strong bull markets, it may fail—price may run through and keep going. Identify bull market bias first before using turtle soup.

head: Wick as Gap / Fibonacci on Wicks
body:
- **Kind:** analysis tool + reference
- **What ICT says:** A wick that extends beyond a previous level can be treated as a gap for Fibonacci purposes. You can draw a Fibonacci retracement from the wick low to the wick high (or from one major wick to another). Use consequent encroachment (the midpoint of the wick) and the low as your key Fibonacci levels. This creates micro-level targets within the wick zone.
- **How to identify:** Find a large wick that extends beyond a key level (e.g., a wick that drops below an FVG or support). Mark the high and low of the wick. Draw Fib from low to high.
- **How to use:** When price is trading below the wick, place limit orders at the Fib levels (especially 0.5, or midpoint/consequent encroachment, and the low). These act as micro-targets during retracements or consolidations. When price pulls back up and touches the wick, expect resistance at consequent encroachment.
- **Example in this video:** A wick on the daily chart was treated as a gap. ICT drew a Fib on it to find precise entry and exit points during the intraday trade.
- **Timestamps:** [0:02:31](https://youtu.be/3J8drYX2zHM?t=151), [0:03:26](https://youtu.be/3J8drYX2zHM?t=206)

head: Bearish Fair Value Gap (Entry Model)
body:
- **Kind:** entry signal + reversal filter
- **What ICT says:** When price forms an up close candle, it leaves a small gap above it (the space between the close and the next candle's open/high). This is a potential inversion FVG. When price later comes back up and trades into this gap, it's a bearish setup. Entry is when price closes above the gap (confirming the inversion), and target is the sell-side liquidity below.
- **How to identify:** After an up close candle in a down move, mark the gap left above the close. This is the inversion FVG. When price retraces back up and trades into this gap, watch for bodies staying in the lower half. If bodies break above the midpoint, the setup is weak. If bodies stay below, it's strong.
- **How to use:** Short when price trades into the inversion FVG and bodies stay in the lower half. Target the next sell-side liquidity pool below. Use consequent encroachment (midpoint of the gap) as a mental stop—if price breaks above it, exit.
- **Example in this video:** An up close candle left an inversion FVG. Price later came back up into it, and ICT shorted, targeting the sell-side liquidity. The trade worked.
- **Timestamps:** [0:02:31](https://youtu.be/3J8drYX2zHM?t=151), [0:05:06](https://youtu.be/3J8drYX2zHM?t=306)

head: Breakaway Gap
body:
- **Kind:** structure + continuation signal
- **What ICT says:** When price trades through a fair value gap, exits the gap completely, and leaves the upper or lower portion of the gap open (unfilled), it's a breakaway gap. This signals that the move is likely to continue in that direction without immediately retracing back into the gap. Breakaway gaps are bullish or bearish continuation signals depending on direction.
- **How to identify:** Price trades through a gap, leaves a portion unfilled (visually, you see gap space above the candles in a down move, or below in an up move). This unfilled portion is the breakaway gap.
- **How to use:** When a breakaway gap forms, the move is likely to continue. Don't expect price to immediately retrace and fill it. Instead, use the gap as a reference for stops or partial targets. If price does come back and fills the breakaway gap, it's a reversal signal.
- **Example in this video:** After the short entry, price traded down through an FVG and left a portion unfilled (the upper portion). This was a breakaway gap, indicating the down move would continue.
- **Timestamps:** [0:09:10](https://youtu.be/3J8drYX2zHM?t=550)

head: Premium Array (Wick-based Resistance)
body:
- **Kind:** filter / reversal zone identification
- **What ICT says:** A wick that extends into a zone above price, combined with an FVG or gap, creates a "premium array"—a resistance zone where price is unlikely to close above. Even in strong bull markets, premium arrays act as speed bumps. Don't ignore them; instead, use them as shorting opportunities (turtle soup, etc.).
- **How to identify:** Find a wick that extends significantly into a zone above recent price action. This wick + the zone = premium array. Mark it.
- **How to use:** When price approaches a premium array, expect resistance. If it's combined with a turtle soup setup, short it. If price closes above it, the bullish bias is confirmed and the premium array is neutralized.
- **Example in this video:** A premium array was identified on the daily chart wick. This gave ICT confidence that the turtle soup short setup would work, even though the market was bullish overall.
- **Timestamps:** [0:00:48](https://youtu.be/3J8drYX2zHM?t=48), [0:01:41](https://youtu.be/3J8drYX2zHM?t=101)

title: ICT 2026 Asian Session Short Review \ April 14, 2026
head: Two-Stage Liquidity Extraction
body:
- **Kind:** market structure + execution model
- **What ICT says:** Smart money often extracts liquidity in two stages: first, they take out the obvious buy-side pool (the first high that everyone sees), then they take out the second, less-obvious buy-side pool. Only then do they run price lower to the sell-side liquidity. This two-stage extraction is a signature pattern. When you see both stages hit, conviction is very high that the move will continue in the opposite direction.
- **How to identify:** Watch price run higher. First high = first buy-side pool. Price pulls back slightly, then runs higher again. Second high = second buy-side pool. Both are hit. Now expect reversal lower.
- **How to use:** Don't short after the first pool is taken; wait for the second. Once both pools are taken, short aggressively. This reduces false signals and aligns your trade with smart money's order flow.
- **Example in this video:** Two buy-side pools were taken during the macro window. ICT waited for both, then entered short with conviction.
- **Timestamps:** [0:05:06](https://youtu.be/3J8drYX2zHM?t=306)

head: Real Execution Proof (Market Replay vs. Live)
body:
- **Kind:** documentation method + skeptic response
- **What ICT says:** Real executions (shown as green dots on a chart) persist when you toggle between market replay and live data. If a trade was only in market replay (a hypothetical, not real), the green dot execution markers disappear as soon as you switch to live data. This is the proof that a trade happened in real-time, not during a hindsight review. Critics often claim ICT's trades are "cherry-picked" or "market replay hindsight." The green dot persistence proves otherwise.
- **How to identify:** When viewing a chart in TradingView, toggle between "Market Replay" mode and "Live" mode. If executions disappear in live mode, they were market replay only. If they persist, they were real.
- **How to use:** When sharing trades, always toggle between modes to prove they're real. This builds credibility and shuts down "hindsight" critics. ICT does this in his videos to prove he's not editing after the fact.
- **Example in this video:** ICT points out that the green execution dots persist even when he's toggling market replay, proving the trade was real-time, not a post-hoc review.
- **Timestamps:** [0:07:34](https://youtu.be/3J8drYX2zHM?t=454), [0:08:22](https://youtu.be/3J8drYX2zHM?t=502)
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Many retail traders who watch market replay trades (even their own) don't realize they're trading in a "what-if" mode, not recording real executions. Market replay is useful for backtesting, but it's not the same as real execution.

title: ICT 2026 Entries & Drills \ April 15, 2026
head: Drills (practice method for entry models)  (aliases: labs, "little exercises", "leg day", "yellow belt")
body:
- **Kind:** rule / new coinage (a practice protocol, not a trade setup)
- **What ICT says:**
  - Drills are small participations in price action with "no monetary hope of making money and no fear of losing". Paper/demo account only. He explicitly says do NOT copy his drill entries into funded or live accounts; he is "not licensed to give trading advice".
  - Goal: desensitize yourself to entering inside a fair value gap, remove the need to be right, and record a personal baseline (how you felt: scared, nervous, euphoric, frustrated; how price behaved). Being indifferent to the outcome is the target state ("muscle of indifference").
  - Entry model for the drill: wait for the fair value gap to form, enter it, put a stop on, use a "one-for-one model" with one micro (MNQ). Target = a 10-handle minimum, 15 handles maximum run off the FVG. Treated as "low-hanging fruit" on sub-1-minute charts. (Exact stop distance is not stated; "one for one" is later used to mean win/loss symmetry, so read it as roughly 1:1 risk to reward - caption-limited.)
  - Execution chart is 15-second; ranges, liquidity and inefficiencies are all derived from the 1-minute chart.
  - Practice on the hard days, not just clean ones. High-resistance conditions "record things subconsciously" about how price fails to run, which cannot be learned from a book, lecture or mentor.
  - Do drills even when you have no model yet and even when you are already profitable. If you have already made your profit for the day, do not go back to live; go to demo and drill.
  - Minimum 15 minutes per day (analogy: 20 minutes on a treadmill); "leg day" needs to be done only once a week, more is overtraining.
  - Log for every drill: time in trade, drawdown taken, whether a full stop-out still yielded anything first, and how much it yielded. If a trade stops out, note the maximum it yielded before that ("cheerlead yourself in your study journal").
  - Do not read failed drill runs as a failure of you, the model or the concept.
  - Gamify: when the drill target is hit ("your little cookie", "yellow belt") that is your reward; then ask the next-stage question: is price willing to continue/extrapolate beyond the target? That is feedback without risking anything.
  - Series plan: today fair value gaps, tomorrow order blocks, Friday mixed; next drill stream tomorrow 9:25 ET.
- **How to identify:** n/a (a method). The inputs are a visible FVG/iFVG, a draw on liquidity (some old high/low or pool), and a pre-set stop and 10–15 handle target.
- **How to use:** run 2–3 drills per hour for a short session; screenshot and annotate afterwards if you cannot be at the charts; log feelings and outcomes; repeat daily.
- **Example in this video:** about seven drills on MNQ (see the FVG/iFVG, wick-CE and equilibrium-projection entries below). Two or three stopped out or never filled; others yielded 15–22 handles. ICT stresses that "not all of them panned out".
- **Timestamps:** [0:04:20](https://youtu.be/KASpfAd1MnI?t=260) — drill premise, don't copy; [0:17:28](https://youtu.be/KASpfAd1MnI?t=1048) — one micro, 10 min / 15 max handles; [0:28:09](https://youtu.be/KASpfAd1MnI?t=1689) — definition of drills; [1:28:02](https://youtu.be/KASpfAd1MnI?t=5282) — target hit as "your cookie", then test continuation; [1:53:31](https://youtu.be/KASpfAd1MnI?t=6811) — at least 15 minutes a day.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** he says the same logic can be used with other methodologies; the point is the conditioning, not the model.

head: Fair Value Gap entry (drill entry on 15-second chart)  (aliases: "entering into the gap", FVG with CE stop)
body:
- **Kind:** entry model
- **What ICT says:**
  - Enter when price trades back into a fresh FVG that is aligned with the intended run to liquidity. For a bullish FVG: price should trade down into the upper half only, keep the bodies out of the lower half, then rip strongly higher. (He is describing the ideal, not a hard filter on every drill.)
  - Consequent encroachment (midpoint) can be used as the stop ("we'll use consequent encroachment as a stop" on a buy-side FVG entry).
  - After entering, a body/candle that fails to run (stalling, "stutter", small wick above a high then nothing) is a warning; consider partials and a stop move.
  - On a stalled long: "there should be no give back at all"; if a higher high forms and it does not accelerate, take some off.
  - Roll the stop to where a stop-out covers commissions ("painless") once the next candle shows the right behaviour.
  - If nothing qualifies, sit still: "If there's nothing in the chart, don't force it."
- **How to identify:** a 3-candle gap on the 15-second chart that sits inside a 1-minute context with a nearby pool (relative equal highs/lows, old high/low) to run to.
- **How to use:** entry in the gap, stop at CE or beyond the high/low (long: CE or below; short: above the high), target 10–15 handles or the nearest small pool.
- **Example in this video:** MNQ, 15-second, about 9:55–10:00 ET. After price runs the sell side and reclaims above the 9:30 open, ICT enters long in a buy-side FVG with stop at CE; paper-trading platform fails to fill the stop/limit, so he closes the trade manually "for fairness" and notes it would have stopped out ([0:30:32](https://youtu.be/KASpfAd1MnI?t=1832)). Later long at 1:22 into a fresh FVG after a stop hunt of equal lows (see "Equilibrium projection").
- **Timestamps:** [0:36:33](https://youtu.be/KASpfAd1MnI?t=2193) — buy-side FVG entry, CE stop; [0:39:47](https://youtu.be/KASpfAd1MnI?t=2387) — short in an FVG, midpoint noted; [1:44:49](https://youtu.be/KASpfAd1MnI?t=6289) — ideal bullish-FVG behaviour (upper half, bodies out of lower half).
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** in a choppy tape he would rather see it run once inside the gap; "too small" a wick/gap above a high is not enough for him to short.

head: Inversion Fair Value Gap (iFVG) use on the 15-second chart  (aliases: inversion, "reclaimed bearish fair value gap")
body:
- **Kind:** entry model / example
- **What ICT says:**
  - A gap that price closes through and respects from the other side becomes an inversion. For a reclaimed bearish FVG, bodies close above it and later come back and the level holds as support (the 9:30 opening price can confluence with it).
  - Key condition: the bodies stay out of the gap. Wicks into it are acceptable; a wick can touch the 9:30 opening price and the level can still be used.
  - If price comes back through and stops you out, that is just one transaction; the body staying in the upper half after a stop-out can keep the iFVG idea alive ("as long as we don't take out these highs").
  - For shorts: stop above the high; entry once a body trades below the imbalance/the high of the relevant candlestick; target the RTH opening range gap CE.
  - He also uses the volume imbalance as a level that can be wicked to alongside CE; want bodies to stay outside the upper half.
- **How to identify:** a prior FVG that price has closed through, then a retrace into that gap/level with bodies holding on the far side.
- **How to use:** enter on the retrace to the iFVG, stop beyond it (above the high for shorts), target nearby liquidity or the opposite side of a nearby gap (10–15 handles).
- **Example in this video:** MNQ, 15-second, about 9:44–9:50 ET: price runs sell-side, reclaims the 9:30 opening price, a bearish FVG gets reclaimed ("it would look like this when drawn on the chart"), price retraces to that level with the bodies staying out; he treats it as support and price runs up with a small gap and a volume imbalance toward the high ([0:26:17](https://youtu.be/KASpfAd1MnI?t=1577)). A short idea: price breaks below a small imbalance with a body, iFVG for a run back to the RTH ORG CE ([0:33:25](https://youtu.be/KASpfAd1MnI?t=2005)). Later (ES, observation only) price takes sell side, rallies, uses a portion of a gap as an iFVG and runs to the target ([1:50:20](https://youtu.be/KASpfAd1MnI?t=6620)).
- **Timestamps:** [0:21:51](https://youtu.be/KASpfAd1MnI?t=1311) — reclaimed bearish FVG; [0:26:17](https://youtu.be/KASpfAd1MnI?t=1577) — iFVG works; [0:30:32](https://youtu.be/KASpfAd1MnI?t=1832) — iFVG idea after a stop-out; [1:49:34](https://youtu.be/KASpfAd1MnI?t=6574) — ES iFVG run example.

head: Low Resistance vs High Resistance Liquidity Run Conditions  (aliases: "fast and loose", "all lanes open", "barcode / UPC candles", "time distortion")
body:
- **Kind:** definition / filter (the core conceptual lesson of the video)
- **What ICT says:**
  - High resistance (the day of this video, rated 9 out of 10 difficulty): candles keep sharing the previous candle's range, bodies overlap ("fuzzy"), few imbalances are created, price keeps going back and forth inside consolidations, often inside a wick ("time distortion" - wait for it to resolve by leaving the range). He compares the look to a UPC barcode.
  - Low resistance: market is "fast and loose", lots of inefficiencies, open lanes of traffic ("not rush hour"); price runs freely in expansions, gives multiple clean setups per hour, and you do not need to babysit or jam your stop.
  - Why high resistance is dangerous: it can spike through the stacked consolidation in one wick and traverse 50–60 handles to take the liquidity on the other side; also repeated small false runs.
  - Do not trade real money in high resistance conditions; practice in them. Learn to recognize the transition from low-resistance/high-probability to lesser probability.
  - Continuity check: clean price action should show on the 1-minute and on your executable timeframe (e.g. a 15-minute chart with a 1-minute below it). It does not matter that this is a 15-second chart; the cleanliness test applies at every timeframe.
  - Warning signs ("canaries in the coal mine"): a higher high followed immediately by a wilt; a shallow peek above a high then back inside; stutter instead of acceleration; sharing prior range. These force you to babysit positions.
  - If it is "a day where you really would not be wanting to do any live trading with real money," the recommended use is practice. He says he told viewers at the start it would be such a day.
- **How to identify:** look at the last 10–20 candles on your trading timeframe: do bodies overlap with the previous candle? Are there few gaps? Does price keep returning inside a small range? If yes, high resistance.
- **How to use:** skip live trading; use only for demo drills; or demand extra from any setup (see "to it and through it").
- **Example in this video:** MNQ 1-minute after 9:30 ET: candles stack into "all back and forth", no FVGs form since the open for the first ~10 minutes ([0:18:18](https://youtu.be/KASpfAd1MnI?t=1098)); at about 10:30 ET (video 1:07) the 1-minute shows fuzzy overlapping candles under a premium and he refuses to participate in the long ([1:07:14](https://youtu.be/KASpfAd1MnI?t=4034)).
- **Timestamps:** [0:13:01](https://youtu.be/KASpfAd1MnI?t=781) — "high resistance liquidity run conditions" as a practice day; [1:10:29](https://youtu.be/KASpfAd1MnI?t=4229) — fuzzy candles, want a day with inefficiencies; [1:12:04](https://youtu.be/KASpfAd1MnI?t=4324) — barcode candles, 50–60 handle spike risk; [1:32:04](https://youtu.be/KASpfAd1MnI?t=5524) — low resistance has no babysitting; [1:32:53](https://youtu.be/KASpfAd1MnI?t=5573) — "all lanes of traffic open".
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** he ties this concept explicitly to "if you have a way of measuring when the market is difficult vs easy" and says other methodologies never define what makes their model strong or weak except after the fact.
