head: Relative Equal Highs/Lows — "to it and through it"  (aliases: REH/REL, stop hunt, false breakout, turtle soup)
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - When price sits just below relative equal highs and has already run (taken) sell-side/short-term lows, the stops of longs have already been trailed under those lows and "enough damage" is done. A move through the equal highs should then accelerate ("to it and through it").
  - A shallow peek above the equal highs, then back into the range, is a false breakout and more indicative of an intraday reversal or a deeper retracement (bulls chased, "dragged across the coals"). If it then rolls over and takes the low, he is "not interested at all for the rest of the day".
  - After going above, you want to see it expand aggressively, not stall.
  - If a high had buy-side above and gets run, and a lower high etc. all keep running without give-back, longs should be developing without stutter.
- **How to identify:** two or more highs within a tick or two (his words: "look how relatively equal they are"), with sell-side already taken below.
- **How to use:** if long, expect continuation immediately after the high is taken; if it fails (small run then back inside), exit/partial and consider the opposite as a stop-hunt reversal; practice false-breakout (turtle soup) shorts here in demo only.
- **Example in this video:** MNQ, about 10:45 ET: price took a stop hunt of equal lows, rallied via an FVG, sat under REH; he outlines both outcomes; price went through the highs and hit the drill target, then continued ([1:24:51](https://youtu.be/KASpfAd1MnI?t=5091) to [1:28:02](https://youtu.be/KASpfAd1MnI?t=5282)). Earlier ([1:01:14](https://youtu.be/KASpfAd1MnI?t=3674)) price takes a higher high but falls back into the range, which he calls wrong behaviour if bullish and possibly a failure swing.
- **Timestamps:** [1:25:37](https://youtu.be/KASpfAd1MnI?t=5137) — "to it and through it"; [1:26:24](https://youtu.be/KASpfAd1MnI?t=5184) — false breakout for the day; [0:43:41](https://youtu.be/KASpfAd1MnI?t=2621) — how to practice becoming a turtle-soup type trader.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** he says repeatedly "I could have it wrong"; it is a conditional read, not a prediction.

head: Wick midpoint (CE) body-protection rule  (aliases: bodies above wick CE)
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - When price makes a higher high and the prior high was a wick, watch the CE (halfway point) of that wick: price bodies should stay at or above it. Wicks can tap it (preferably not), but a body closing below it is problematic for continuation higher and must be resolved in price action.
  - After a wick pushes down into a CE of a gap, the very next candle should show willingness to reach its own midpoint and close beyond it; otherwise continuation is problematic.
  - Also: when price makes a higher high with a wick and the bodies drop inside the wick range, that's a warning.
- **How to identify:** a wick that made the previous high; mark its 50%.
- **How to use:** hold longs only while bodies stay above the CE; use it as a quick invalidation read and for stop roll/partials.
- **Example in this video:** MNQ 1-minute at ~10:25 ET (he checks the daily and quotes a draw around "349/355/360", captioned shorthand, probably 26,3xx): a higher high above a prior wick high; ICT says bodies must hold above the wick's 50% for continuation; price then stalls and he declines to participate ([1:04:01](https://youtu.be/KASpfAd1MnI?t=3841) to [1:05:38](https://youtu.be/KASpfAd1MnI?t=3938)).
- **Timestamps:** [1:04:47](https://youtu.be/KASpfAd1MnI?t=3887); [0:46:58](https://youtu.be/KASpfAd1MnI?t=2818) — next-candle midpoint rule and break-even-ish stop.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** extends his long-standing CE rule from gaps to wicks.

head: Equilibrium projection of a stop-hunt leg (half-leg target)  (aliases: algorithmic price levels, "new thresholds")
body:
- **Kind:** refinement / rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - After a stop hunt (a leg down that raids equal lows), take the high-to-low range of that leg, mark its equilibrium (50%), then project that same half-range distance above the high of the leg (i.e. high + half the range). If price takes the relative equal highs, it should "at least" reach this level; this is a repeatable target ("by taking half that drop down on that stop hunt, project that higher").
  - It gives algorithmic price levels to reach for; failure to reach it and reversal is weakness and sets the stage for lower prices into about 1:30 PM.
- **How to identify:** a clear leg down that ran sell-side, followed by a rally into REH.
- **How to use:** target for longs after the highs are taken; if price rejects before it, treat as a warning.
- **Example in this video:** MNQ 1-minute, about 10:45 ET: the drop of the lunch-time stop hunt is measured; price trades up to exactly that level ([1:34:28](https://youtu.be/KASpfAd1MnI?t=5668)), "so it was able to overcome it", though ICT notes a low-resistance market would not have had the hiccups on the way.

head: SMT "Sick Sister" (intermarket decoupling)  (aliases: sick sister, decoupling, MES/MYM/MNQ divergence)
body:
- **Kind:** definition / example
- **What ICT says:**
  - Closely correlated markets (ES and Nasdaq) should confirm each other; when one makes a higher high and the other does not, there's a break in correlation. The lagging market is the "sick sister" and the leader "encourages it".
  - It does not need to match the size of the move; a higher high intraday on MES is all that is necessary. When decoupled, he reads it as heavy manipulation.
  - When MES finally makes its higher high and NQ (the leader) then breaks down and uses a 1-minute iFVG, the decoupling goes away for the near term and sell side can be engaged.
  - YM ("MYM") is completely decoupled in the early part.
- **How to identify:** compare MNQ/MES/MYM highs/lows over the same window.
- **How to use:** a decoupled tape plus a premium wick supports false-breakout shorts (small, demo only); when the laggard catches up, expect a retracement.
- **Example in this video:** NQ makes slightly higher highs while ES/YM are lower (~10:05 ET) ([0:41:21](https://youtu.be/KASpfAd1MnI?t=2481)); later MES catches up with its higher high at ~10:20 ET ([0:56:19](https://youtu.be/KASpfAd1MnI?t=3379)); on ES he repeats the same drill pattern ([1:40:02](https://youtu.be/KASpfAd1MnI?t=6002)).
- **Timestamps:** [0:41:21](https://youtu.be/KASpfAd1MnI?t=2481); [0:57:07](https://youtu.be/KASpfAd1MnI?t=3427); [1:40:50](https://youtu.be/KASpfAd1MnI?t=6050) — definition for newcomers.

title: ICT 2026 Futures Review \ April 14, 2026
head: TGIF (Thank God It's Friday) & Weekly Retracement
body:
- **Kind:** time-based pattern / weekly structure
- **What ICT says:** TGIF is a pattern where price retraces 30% of the **weekly range** by Friday. The weekly range is calculated from the weekly low to the weekly high of the past week. After retracing to 30% of that range, price often reverses and runs back to the highs (or higher) by week's end. This is a structural pattern that reflects profit-taking and then resumption of the longer-term trend.
- **How to identify:** 
  1. Calculate last week's range: high - low.
  2. Multiply by 0.30 to get 30% retracement level.
  3. Find the weekly low and add 30% of the range.
  4. On Friday, watch if price approaches this level.
  5. If it does, expect reversal and rally higher.
- **How to use:** On Fridays, if price has retraced to 30% of the weekly range, be ready for a bullish reversal or resumption of the uptrend. Don't short into 30% retracement on a Friday; instead, expect buyers to step in. Use it as a support level or as a confirmation that the weekly trend remains up.
- **Example in this video:** April 14, 2026 (Tuesday). ICT mentions that price traded down into 30% of last week's weekly range and found its footing, confirming the weekly trend is bullish.
- **Timestamps:** [0:01:45](https://youtu.be/DJ67ft6XENo?t=105)
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** TGIF is specifically for Fridays, but the concept of finding support at percentage retracement levels of the weekly range can apply mid-week as well if that level is tested.

title: ICT 2026 Futures Review \ April 14, 2026
head: Lunch Macro (10:30–11:10 ET)
body:
- **Kind:** time window + retracement expectation
- **What ICT says:** The lunch macro is not the traditional lunch time (11:30–13:30 ET). Instead, it's a profit-taking / retracement window that begins around 10:30 ET (when the first full hour of trading, 9:30–10:30, is complete). The micro came from FX trading: between 10:00–11:00 ET is London close time, and the midpoint (10:30) marks the start of profit-taking. During lunch macro, expect price to retrace back into the range established since the 9:30 open. In a bullish market, the retracement is shallow (only to intermediate lows). In a bearish market, it can go much deeper (to the lowest low of the day).
- **How to identify:** Mark 10:30–11:10 ET on your chart. Within this window, price will typically pull back. Identify the range since 9:30 (opening price to the high of the run).
- **How to use:** In a bullish market, short during the lunch macro with tight stops, targeting only intermediate lows within the range. Don't expect a deep reversal. Once the target is hit, immediately take profits and prepare to re-enter longs as price recovers. In a bearish market, shorts can target deeper lows. Time your entry to coincide with the lunch macro window (10:30–11:10).
- **Example in this video:** April 14, 2026. Price rallied from 9:30 until 10:30, then the lunch macro window opened (10:30–11:10). A minor pullback occurred at 10:50, but not significant. The main pullback happened slightly later (around 10:50 onward). ICT waited for the right conditions and entered a short trade targeting the buy-side imbalance / sell-side inefficiency within the range.
- **Timestamps:** [0:04:07](https://youtu.be/DJ67ft6XENo?t=247), [0:05:52](https://youtu.be/DJ67ft6XENo?t=352), [0:08:20](https://youtu.be/DJ67ft6XENo?t=500), [0:14:40](https://youtu.be/DJ67ft6XENo?t=880)
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** The lunch macro CAN start as early as 10:30, but strong markets may not show a significant retracement. Watch for a pullback attempt, but in very bullish markets, it may be shallow or fail entirely. The macro isn't a guarantee; it's a time-based opportunity window.

title: ICT 2026 Futures Review \ April 14, 2026
head: Buy-side Imbalance / Sell-side Inefficiency (BISI)
body:
- **Kind:** PD array + order flow marker
- **What ICT says:** When price makes a significant move in one direction (e.g., bullish push from 9:30–10:30), it leaves behind an imbalance: buy-side imbalance (unmet buyers who tried to enter on the way up but were skipped) and sell-side inefficiency (untested sell orders). When a BISI forms during a bullish run, the buy-side imbalance is in the zone the price covered, and the sell-side inefficiency is below (orders that were never tested during the run). On a retracement, price targeting this BISI is targeting the sell-side inefficiency (the unexploited sellers). This is a high-probability retracement target.
- **How to identify:** After a bullish move, mark the range covered (high to low of the move). Look for tight consolidation or wicks within this range. The BISI is the zone between the high and the consolidation point where sellers are resting (sell-side inefficiency).
- **How to use:** During lunch macro, target the BISI as your first profit-taking level on a retracement. Price will often drop to this zone and bounce back. Once the BISI is "broken" (price closes below the wick low or consequent encroachment), expect the move to continue downside to deeper sell-side pools.
- **Example in this video:** A BISI formed at 26,600+ after the morning run. During the lunch macro, price retraced toward this zone, and ICT shorted into it, targeting the sell-side inefficiency (lower sells) within and below it.
- **Timestamps:** [0:09:55](https://youtu.be/DJ67ft6XENo?t=595), [0:13:04](https://youtu.be/DJ67ft6XENo?t=784), [0:20:11](https://youtu.be/DJ67ft6XENo?t=1211)

title: ICT 2026 Futures Review \ April 14, 2026
head: Dealing Range vs. External Range Liquidity
body:
- **Kind:** liquidity structure + targeting framework
- **What ICT says:** The **dealing range** is the range of price from the high of the current move down to a significant low (e.g., the 10:00 low during the morning session). **External range liquidity** is the sell-side liquidity that sits OUTSIDE and BELOW the dealing range—further lows that were formed earlier (yesterday, earlier this week). When price retraces into the dealing range (say, a lunch macro retracement), targeting the low of the dealing range is one target. Targeting external range liquidity is the more aggressive target, going below the dealing range to unexploited sellers.
- **How to identify:** Draw the dealing range (high to low of current session/move). Mark the external range liquidity (previous session's low, earlier week's low, or other old support).
- **How to use:** In lunch macro shorts, first target the low of the dealing range (smaller profit). If price breaks below that, the next target is external range liquidity (larger move). Use the dealing range low as a first partial, then hold for external range.
- **Example in this video:** The dealing range was from the morning high (26,600+) to the 10:00 low. External range liquidity was older support levels below. ICT targeted both, taking a partial at the dealing range low, then holding for the external range liquidity.

head: Bearish Order Block (Activation & Entry)
body:
- **Kind:** entry model + pyramiding point
- **What ICT says:** When price makes a down-close candle after a series of up closes, the **opening price** of that down-close candle activates as a bearish order block. When price later retraces back up and touches that opening price level, it becomes an **entry or pyramiding point** for shorts. You don't enter at the down-close itself; you wait for the retracement back to the open price, then enter as price fails to hold above it.
- **How to identify:** Find a down-close candle at a reversal point (after up closes). Mark its opening price. Later, when price retraces back up and touches that open price, you have a confirmed entry point for shorts.
- **How to use:** Use the bearish order block open price as a trigger for additional short entries (pyramiding). Once price fails to hold above this level and closes below it again, the order block is validated and the downside move accelerates.
- **Example in this video:** A candle closed down after the morning rally. Its opening price became the bearish order block. When price retraced back up during the lunch macro and touched that open price, ICT used it as a pyramiding entry point for adding to his short position.

head: Premium Sensitivity (Bearish Validation)
body:
- **Kind:** rule + order flow confirmation
- **What ICT says:** When trading into a bearish fair value gap (an inversion FVG where we expect prices to fall), the bodies must stay in the **lower half** of the gap. This is premium sensitivity in a bearish context. If bodies enter the upper half, the setup is weakening. The moment a candle closes with a body in the upper half, cancel the bullish interpretation and expect continued downside. This is the "give up the ghost" moment for bullish reversals.
- **How to identify:** After price trades into an inversion FVG on a retracement, watch the bodies. Stay in lower half = valid short; bodies in upper half = invalid.
- **How to use:** Hold shorts as long as bodies stay in the lower half. The moment a body closes in the upper half, be ready to exit or reduce. Use premium sensitivity (bodies in lower half) as confirmation to add to shorts.
- **Example in this video:** Price retraced into an inversion FVG (bearish setup). Bodies stayed in the lower half, confirming premium sensitivity and validating the short. Price then accelerated lower.

body:

The lower portion of the wick (from wick low to midpoint/consequent correction) becomes the target zone for a retracement. When price trades down and touches the consequent correction of a wick, it's a high-probability support/resistance level.
- **How to identify:** Find a wick that extends significantly (e.g., from a previous high down 50 points). Mark the low and midpoint (consequent correction). This zone (low to midpoint) is the wick-as-gap zone.
- **How to use:** When price dives down and reaches the consequent correction of a wick, expect a pause, reversal, or final target achievement. Use it as a precision exit point or as confirmation that the target has been hit.

head: TGIF (Thank God It's Friday)  (aliases: weekly retracement, Thursday pull-back)
body:
- **Kind:** rule + entry model
- **What ICT says:** Algorithmically, on Thursday around 1 p.m. ET, price tends to retrace 20–30% of the weekly range (sometimes to 40% as extreme outlier). It's tied to the highest value-high reached by 1 p.m. Thursday. If 20–30% retracement doesn't occur by Friday close, watch for it to occur on the following Monday. The retracement is real and measurable via Fibonacci settings (50 level, change to 30 for 30%, or 20 for 20%).
- **How to identify:** Weekly candlestick stretched one direction. Mark the high by Thursday 1 p.m. ET. Measure range. At 20–30% level, look for retracement candle that opens inside the range, trades down (if bullish week), then closes above mid-range but below the high.
- **How to use:** On Thursday approaching 1 p.m. ET, be ready for retracement into that level; this is a normal, repeating signature, not trade entry per se, but a place to understand where price will pull back before continuing higher Friday.
- **Example in this video:** Previous week's range measured; this week (starting Sunday evening opening) had already retracted into the prior week's 30% level on Monday, then never returned—showing TGIF delivered (deferred to Monday instead of Thursday) and then rocketed higher. Continued higher all week toward May Fed target.
- **Timestamps:** [0:16:04](https://youtu.be/G9mVorSyvR0?t=964) TGIF intro on weekly, [0:17:41](https://youtu.be/G9mVorSyvR0?t=1061) 20–30% retracement rule, [0:23:21](https://youtu.be/G9mVorSyvR0?t=1401) TGIF deferred to Monday shown live.
- **Nuance / caveats:** This is algorithmic market structure, not buying/selling pressure; the signature repeats regardless of trader emotion or news; if you don't see it in a week's close, watch the following Monday open.

head: Judas Swing  (aliases: opening drop, opening drawdown)
body:
- **Kind:** definition + rule
- **What ICT says:** On a bullish range (any timeframe), measure the distance from open to the low of that day. Add that same distance to the opening price. That sum is the "smart money accumulation zone" where you can still be a buyer beyond that low without chasing; below that level is chasing. It's the same measurement used in a Judas swing—drop from open, then add that drop to open to get buy-zone.
- **How to identify:** Bullish day candle: opens, immediately trades down, then rallies. Measure open to low. Add that distance to open.
- **How to use:** Entry zone if day is bullish-biased; anything below that zone is overextended/chasing.
- **Example in this video:** Referenced generally for understanding bullish structure; not detailed live example.

head: Fair Value Gap (FVG) / Inversion FVG  (aliases: imbalance, inversion gap, discount/premium gap)
body:
- **Kind:** definition + rule
- **What ICT says:** FVG is an imbalance (price gap unmet by bodies). On micro/30s/15s charts, wicks define discount (sell-side) imbalances; bodies in upper half = bullish. Inversion FVG is when price trades above a gap, leaving the gap below as potential support. When bodies stay out of lower half of a FVG, market remains bullish. Don't need to touch midpoint; if body closes in upper half, that's strength.
- **How to identify:** Candlestick gap (wick-defined). Bodies above = bullish inversion. Wicks that don't touch midpoint = strength.
- **How to use:** On retracement, if price approaches FVG but bodies stay above midpoint, that's continuation signal. If body closes above high of FVG, that's continued bullish. Screenshot the range on 1m, then zoom to 30s or 15s to confirm bodies staying in upper half.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 1m: After drop into discount gap (wick-defined), price rallies, bodies stay above midpoint of gap. Lower-timeframe (30s) retest shows bodies not touching midpoint—very strong, continued up. Equilibrium measured via Fib, price touches it, bounces away = bullish. 15s chart shows same signature repeating.
- **Timestamps:** [0:40:19](https://youtu.be/G9mVorSyvR0?t=2419) inversion and gap anatomy, [0:45:25](https://youtu.be/G9mVorSyvR0?t=2725) bodies closing above midpoint = bullish agreement, [0:46:14](https://youtu.be/G9mVorSyvR0?t=2774) retracing inside FVG shows strength.
- **Nuance / caveats:** Don't confuse wicks (accept them as discount taken) with bodies (which show real institutional flow); "real point of control" is FVG + wicks, not market profile value area.

title: ICT 2026 Futures Opening Range Tape-Reading \ April 14, 2026
head: Consequent Encroachment (CE)  (aliases: CE midpoint, wick midpoint)
body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:** The midpoint of a wick that has been "encroached upon" (price has traded through the gap it represents). Used as a reference level; price behavior around CE midpoint indicates whether buyers or sellers are in control. If price overshoots a wick without touching CE midpoint, that's very strong (no congestion).
- **How to identify:** Wick on chart. Find midpoint visually or via measurement. Note whether price touches it or overshoots it.
- **How to use:** If price drops into a CE zone and bounces away without touching the midpoint, that's institutional rejection (strength). If it trades through midpoint and bodies don't touch, still bullish.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 1m drop: Wick measured for CE midpoint; price drops but doesn't touch CE midpoint of the wick below the recent low, then bounces. That lack of touch = strength. Repeated on 30s chart.
- **Timestamps:** [0:39:27](https://youtu.be/G9mVorSyvR0?t=2367) CE midpoint explanation.
- **Nuance / caveats:** It's a reference, not a hard stop; the instruction is "if it overshoots, still watch for inversion."

title: ICT 2026 Futures Opening Range Tape-Reading \ April 14, 2026
head: Order Flow Reading (Real Institutional Order Flow)  (aliases: candlestick read, body/wick structure, real OOF)
body:
- **Kind:** rule + method
- **What ICT says:** Read price action by candlestick structure alone (open, high, low, close). No indicators, no paid services, no gimmicks needed. Body position (upper half vs lower half of a range) + wick position (overshoot vs touch) tells you where institutions are; bodies closing in upper half of a range = agreement above that level; bodies staying out of lower half of a gap = rejecting that level. This is real order flow, not random buying/selling, and it repeats statistically predictable.
- **How to identify:** Candlestick. Is body in upper or lower half? Does wick touch the gap midpoint? Overshoots?
- **How to use:** Score the market: upper-half body closes = buyers won that price; staying out of lower half = sellers rejected lower level. String these together across 1m, 30s, 15s to confirm bullish or bearish bias.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 1m → 30s → 15s: Each shows bodies closing above halfway of prior gap, wicks not touching previous support midpoints, bodies rallying up and making higher highs with minimal retracement below those bodies. This is institutional bullish order flow confirmed at every timeframe scale.
- **Timestamps:** [0:44:38](https://youtu.be/G9mVorSyvR0?t=2678) bodies need to stay out of lower half rule, [0:45:25](https://youtu.be/G9mVorSyvR0?t=2725) body closes at midpoint = agreement, [0:47:02](https://youtu.be/G9mVorSyvR0?t=2822) wick rejection at gap midpoint = strength.
- **Nuance / caveats:** This is "visually represented" institutional flow, not volume-weighted; don't confuse it with market profile (which groups price by time at level, irrelevant to directional intent).

head: Equilibrium Price  (aliases: midpoint, Fibonacci equilibrium)
body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:** Measure a range (low to high). Use Fibonacci (50 level = 50% = midpoint = equilibrium). Price trading above equilibrium = potential inversion (premium setup); trades back to equilibrium = no directional advantage (break-even area). No cost, no indicator needed.
- **How to identify:** Range marked. Fib applied. 50 level is equilibrium.
- **How to use:** If price is above equilibrium and retraces to it, that's a neutral zone; if it bounces away, it's still bullish. If it closes below equilibrium after being above, that's potential shift.
- **Example in this video:** 1m chart: Range from low to high marked, Fib applied, price trades above, retraces to 50 level (equilibrium), bounces. Repeated on 30s; no advantage at equilibrium, but once above it, strength shows in bodies staying above.
- **Timestamps:** [0:48:38](https://youtu.be/G9mVorSyvR0?t=2918) Fib 50 level as free equilibrium measure.
- **Nuance / caveats:** Market profile value area high/low is not equivalent; equilibrium is geometric midpoint, not time-weighted price consensus.

head: SMT Divergence / Six Sisters  (aliases: cross-market divergence, weak market, strong market)
body:
- **Kind:** rule + context
- **What ICT says:** When NQ, ES, and YM (the three major indices) are not moving in lockstep, you have divergence. The weakest index (making lower lows, lower highs) will have the least retracement and the smoothest move lower (fewest consolidations). The strongest index (making higher highs, higher lows) will have deeper retracements and more time distortion. Use the weak market as short target and the strong market to wait for retracement before shorting (more noise). This is "six sisters"—the behavior of the three averages around each other.
- **How to identify:** Compare the three indices on the same timeframe. Which is making higher highs (strong)? Which is making lower lows (weak)? Which is in between?
- **How to use:** If shorting, short the weak one; take long retracements into shorts on the strong one. If long in a weakening market (ES weak, NQ strong), the weak one (ES) can drag on NQ—use ES weakness as a timing tool to get NQ long when ES bottoms first.
- **Example in this video:** Monday/Tuesday: YM took out low (weaker); NQ made lower low; ES did not take out that low (strongest). This SMT divergence suggests ES can be slow, so use ES levels as delayed-timing confirmation for NQ entries.
- **Timestamps:** [0:30:33](https://youtu.be/G9mVorSyvR0?t=1833) Dow (YM) taking lower low, NQ lower low, ES did not, [0:32:58](https://youtu.be/G9mVorSyvR0?t=1978) six sisters concept explained, [0:34:39](https://youtu.be/G9mVorSyvR0?t=2079) weak market smooth moves, strong market more retracements.
- **Nuance / caveats:** Dow can act independently due to different weighting (30 vs 100 vs 500 stocks); use ES/NQ divergence more than YM/NQ.

head: Opening Range Gap (RTH Opening Range Gap / New Week Opening Gap)  (aliases: NWOG, gap closure)
body:
- **Kind:** definition + entry context
- **What ICT says:** Mark the gap formed at 9:30 ET (RTH open) or at Sunday 6 p.m. ET (electronic/new-week open). The high and low of that gap are reference levels. A "full gap closure" means price trades all the way back through the gap and out the other side (below the low, if it opened with a premium gap above prior close). Consequent encroachment of that gap (the midpoint) is often a first test. Bodies closing above or below that midpoint tell you whether the move is committed.
- **How to identify:** Find the bar at 9:30 or 6 p.m. ET. Mark the high and low. Measure the midpoint. Track whether bodies breach and hold above/below it.
- **How to use:** If looking for bullish, you want to see bodies stay above the gap's midpoint and then full gap closure + continuation above the prior close (RTH close from previous Friday, 4:14 p.m. ET). If full gap closure doesn't happen with strength, that's a warning sign. Gaps can serve as support/resistance for future retracements.

Throughout the morning, price tested the consequent encroachment (gap midpoint), then bodies moved above it. Full gap closure (return to Friday's 4:14 p.m. close level of 18,400+) and continuation above it was the bullish outcome being watched.

head: Consequent Encroachment (CE) / CE Midpoint  (aliases: wick midpoint, inversion wick CE)
body:
- **Kind:** definition + rule
- **What ICT says:** The exact midpoint of a wick (the gap between the body and the extreme of the wick). When bodies trade back to that midpoint and close **at or just above it** (not into the lower half), that shows institutional rejection of the lower price. The CE midpoint is graded as "strong" (body away from midpoint) or "reluctant" (body touching midpoint).
- **How to identify:** Wick visible. Measure/eyeball midpoint. Watch where body closes relative to it on the next candle(s).
- **How to use:** If bodies close above CE, that's strength. If bodies touch CE and struggle away, that's reluctance/warning. On micro-timeframes (30s, 15s), CE rejection (not touching) on repeated tests = very strong bullish setup.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 1m: early candles dropped into a gap with wick. CE midpoint of that wick was referenced. When price came back down to it and the body closed just above CE (not into lower half), that showed "agreement" = continued bullish. When bodies touched CE and bounced without hesitation, that was strength. Repeated on 15s: bodies respecting CE midpoint and bouncing.
- **Timestamps:** [0:01:14](https://youtu.be/Il_DM4T7nzg?t=74) consequent encroachment above upper quad of opening gap. [0:12:13](https://youtu.be/Il_DM4T7nzg?t=733) wick midpoint rule: if bodies stay below it, strong rejection. [0:13:02](https://youtu.be/Il_DM4T7nzg?t=782) watch midpoint for acceleration signal. [0:20:06](https://youtu.be/Il_DM4T7nzg?t=1206) reluctance at CE = warning (any other day it would have already taken sell side).
- **Nuance / caveats:** CE is not a hard support; it's a reference point where you read body behavior. "Reluctance" at CE (not taking out the level when it "should") is the canary—a sign price is planning to go the other way.

title: ICT 2026 Futures Opening Range Tape-Reading \ April 13, 2026
head: Fair Value Gap (FVG) / Inversion FVG / Reclaimed FVG  (aliases: imbalance, inversion, reclaimed bullish/bearish)
body:
- **Kind:** definition + entry model + rule
- **What ICT says:** A FVG is a gap not covered by candlestick bodies. On 1m, 30s, 15s, a FVG below price (sell-side gap) can become an "inversion FVG" when price trades back into it. If bodies subsequently close above the midpoint of that inversion FVG, it "reclaims" as a bullish FVG (buy signal, further upside likely). If bodies close below, it "reclaims" as bearish FVG (sell signal, further downside likely). Entries are taken at the **next FVG after confirmation**, not at the retracement FVG itself.
- **How to identify:** Price gap (wick-defined). Body positions relative to that gap. Subsequent candlestick's body position (upper vs lower half of prior gap).
- **How to use:** When a potential reclaimed bullish FVG forms (bodies above midpoint of inversion gap), screenshot it. Drop to lower timeframe (1m to 30s, 30s to 15s). Wait for the next FVG to form on that lower timeframe. Once bodies confirm they're rejecting the lower half of that new FVG, that's your entry. Target is typically the next minor buy/sell side level. Stop below the low of the entry candle.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 1m dropped into a gap (discount FVG), bodies stayed above midpoint. Price rallied. At the top, a new gap formed (premium FVG, inversion). Bodies closed above that inversion's midpoint = reclaimed bullish. Drop to 15s: bodies confirm they're above lower halves of subsequent gaps = continuation up. Entry at a confirmed new FVG on 15s when it shows no willingness to go lower, then accelerates up. Target the prior short-term high or next minor buy side.
- **Timestamps:** [0:06:13](https://youtu.be/Il_DM4T7nzg?t=373) full gap closure expectation. [0:14:49](https://youtu.be/Il_DM4T7nzg?t=889) inversion FVG becomes reclaimed bullish if closed above. [0:35:26](https://youtu.be/Il_DM4T7nzg?t=2126) bread-and-butter entry: inversion FVG, bodies above midpoint, next FVG entry. [0:48:59](https://youtu.be/Il_DM4T7nzg?t=2939) reclaimed bearish FVG criteria: bodies below midpoint on closing basis. [0:50:44](https://youtu.be/Il_DM4T7nzg?t=3044) 15s chart shows FVG formation in proximity to 1m reference levels.
- **Nuance / caveats:** Entry is **not at the inversion retracement**; it's at the **next new FVG** after the inversion reclaim is confirmed. Many traders enter too early (at the inversion) and get whipsawed.

title: ICT 2026 Futures Opening Range Tape-Reading \ April 13, 2026
head: Stop Hunt  (aliases: stop run, liquidation run)
body:
- **Kind:** rule + market maker behavior
- **What ICT says:** When price rapidly dips below a key support level (where retail traders' stops are placed), takes them out, then immediately reverses back up (often higher than before), that's a stop hunt. Market makers/institutions are "hunting" for retail stop orders. The subsequent reversal (after stops are cleared) shows their real intent is to go the opposite direction. This happens in sync with algorithmic models firing once the algorithmic condition is met.
- **How to identify:** Price drops sharply, wicks below a key low (often below a support zone or FVG), then body closes far above that low on the next candle. The wick is much longer than the body.
- **How to use:** When you see a stop hunt (bodies didn't go lower, just the wick), don't assume the move is over. Expect the opposite direction. Follow the same model, watch for the next FVG on the lower timeframe, and anticipate a run in the opposite direction. Don't be fooled into shorting after the hunt.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 1m: bodies reluctant to go lower, then a sharp wick down (stop hunt likely), followed by a powerful rally. ICT warns: don't assume this is an inversion; watch the bodies stay above subsequent levels (which they did) and re-affirm bullishness. Another run down (potential stop hunt) then reversal and run to higher minor buy side. This is "the same model, just in a different location."
- **Timestamps:** [0:12:13](https://youtu.be/Il_DM4T7nzg?t=733) wick here but body avoiding lower half = stop hunt coming. [0:20:06](https://youtu.be/Il_DM4T7nzg?t=1206) reluctance = warning; price about to reverse (stop hunt). [0:25:44](https://youtu.be/Il_DM4T7nzg?t=1544) engineering sell side liquidity via stops, then running it. [0:26:31](https://youtu.be/Il_DM4T7nzg?t=1591) orders aren't just "stops"—they're also algorithmic triggers for shorts expecting weakness. [0:35:26](https://youtu.be/Il_DM4T7nzg?t=2126) using the prior high after stop hunt dips.
- **Nuance / caveats:** Stop hunts are not "rigged" against you in a moral sense; they're algorithmic efficiency: once the algorithmic condition is met (stop cleared), the dormant model fires up and hunts longs.

title: ICT 2026 Futures Opening Range Tape-Reading \ April 13, 2026
head: One-Sidedness / High-Probability Setup  (aliases: obvious direction, strong setup, conviction)
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:** High-probability setups are "one-sided"—they show obvious, undeniable directional bias. The bodies line up, the wicks reject, the levels cascade in your favor with minimal retracement noise. Low-probability setups feel 50/50; you have to frame logic for both sides. When you see one-sidedness, that's where you should engage. When you see both sides feeling equally likely, sit still.
- **How to identify:** Candlestick patterns: do bodies all close in the upper half? Do wicks all reject the same level? Does price run with minimal pullback? Or do bodies jump around, wicks are long, pullbacks are deep? One-sided looks clean; 50/50 looks messy.
- **How to use:** Only take setups when one-sidedness is clear. If you can't definitively pick a direction in the first few candles, walk away for that move. This is not FOMO; it's discipline. The next one-sided move is 5 minutes away. Wait.
- **Example in this video:** Early Monday: opening was low-probability (event-driven, geopolitical uncertainty, reluctance visible). ICT didn't trade. Then mid-morning: bodies started lining up above CE, wicks rejecting lower halves, no deep pullbacks, cascading higher. That's when the "bread and butter" setup appeared—clean, one-sided, obvious.
- **Timestamps:** [0:10:39](https://youtu.be/Il_DM4T7nzg?t=639) 50/50 interpretations = avoid trading. [0:15:36](https://youtu.be/Il_DM4T7nzg?t=936) sitting still because of low-probability is a permission many traders never get. [0:32:18](https://youtu.be/Il_DM4T7nzg?t=1938) strong rejection, one-directional run = high probability. [0:40:13](https://youtu.be/Il_DM4T7nzg?t=2413) snipers don't react; they anticipate one-sided moves.
- **Nuance / caveats:** "One-sided" doesn't mean straight line; it means the trend is so obvious that wicks/consolidations are minor noise.

title: ICT 2026 Futures Opening Range Tape-Reading \ April 13, 2026
head: Anticipatory Price Reading (Sniper vs. Reactive)  (aliases: prediction, foresight, not reacting)
body:
- **Kind:** skill + mindset
- **What ICT says:** Most traders react: they wait for price to move, then jump in. ICT teaches anticipation: you set your "crosshairs" ahead of where price is going. Like a sniper accounting for wind, distance, target speed—you're shooting ahead, not at the bird. This requires knowing what "should" happen, then watching to see if price does it. When it doesn't (canary dies), you know to expect the opposite.
- **How to identify:** Recognizing patterns before they complete. Expecting a wick rejection before the wick appears. Knowing "if it takes out that low, I'm expecting a run to that target."
- **How to use:** Build a model (FVG sequence, body positions, gap rules). Before price moves, say "if bodies stay above this CE, I expect acceleration to that minor buy side." Watch. If price does what you predicted, confidence rises. If it doesn't (canary warning), expect reversal. This is tape reading in the moment.
- **Example in this video:** ICT saying, "If we get above this level, this won't act as an inversion; it'll act as a bullish FVG" before the body even closed. Then watching price confirm exactly that. Or: "This reluctance tells me they're not done; they're going higher" before the reversal happened. Pre-announcing what should happen, then proving it (or proving it won't).
- **Timestamps:** [0:40:13](https://youtu.be/Il_DM4T7nzg?t=2413) sniper analogy: anticipate, don't react. [0:44:58](https://youtu.be/Il_DM4T7nzg?t=2698) warning signs (canary) when price doesn't do what should happen. [0:52:35](https://youtu.be/Il_DM4T7nzg?t=3155) anticipate before they form; don't wait for chart to show it after the fact.
- **Nuance / caveats:** Anticipation requires you to get wrong sometimes. The skill is improving prediction rate over time (70%+), not achieving 100%.

title: ICT 2026 Futures Opening Range Tape-Reading \ April 13, 2026
head: Reticular Activating System (RAS) / Pattern Recognition  (aliases: seeing repeating signatures, confidence building)
body:
- **Kind:** psychology
- **What ICT says:** When you buy a car, you suddenly see that car everywhere—not because it's more common, but because you're now tuned to notice it (RAS activated). Same with price action: once you activate your RAS for a FVG sequence or body rejection pattern, you start seeing it everywhere, and your confidence grows. You begin to **anticipate** it before it forms.
- **How to identify:** Exposing yourself to price action repeatedly. After 10 times seeing a body close above a CE and then rally, your brain automatically expects the 11th time.
- **How to use:** This is why tape reading (not trading) is valuable: repeated exposure builds RAS. Once RAS is activated, you recognize setups in real time, and entries become obvious (not guessing).
- **Example in this video:** ICT's students who've watched streams develop the ability to spot FVG sequences and body rejections immediately, without thinking. His own prediction of "reluctance here tells me they want higher" happens because his RAS has seen it 1,000 times.
- **Timestamps:** [0:37:49](https://youtu.be/Il_DM4T7nzg?t=2269) car analogy: your eye jumps to it subconsciously; same for patterns in price.
- **Nuance / caveats:** This is not mystical; it's neurobiology. Repeated exposure + conscious study = pattern recognition.

head: Bread and Butter Setup  (aliases: simple entry, foundational setup)
body:
- **Kind:** entry model
- **What ICT says:** A basic, repeatable entry model that doesn't require all the bells and whistles. Simple: inversion FVG (bodies above midpoint), next new FVG forms, bodies reject the lower half of that FVG, take entry at the break of the low (or at the body close above midpoint), target the next minor buy/sell side or prior short-term high. Stop is tight (below entry candle low or at CE midpoint).
- **How to identify:** After an inversion FVG reclaims as bullish, drop to lower timeframe. Wait for the next gap to form. Watch body positions.
- **How to use:** Entry point: when body closes above the gap's midpoint on lower timeframe, you're in. Tight stop (2–5 handles on NQ). Target: nearest minor buy side or prior short-term high.
- **Example in this video:** At [0:35:26](https://youtu.be/Il_DM4T7nzg?t=2126), ICT marks: inversion FVG (bodies above its midpoint) = draw to minor buy side (prior high). Entry at the next FVG's midpoint break. Stop below the prior low. Target: event horizon (split between two prior highs) or next minor buy side.
- **Timestamps:** [0:35:26](https://youtu.be/Il_DM4T7nzg?t=2126) bread and butter: simple, obvious, high probability.
- **Nuance / caveats:** Bread and butter doesn't mean "always works"; it means the logic is clear and repeatable. You'll miss some, and some will stop out, but the win rate is high.

title: ICT 2026 Futures Opening Range Tape-Reading \ April 13, 2026
head: Event Horizon  (aliases: midpoint split, equilibrium target)
body:
- **Kind:** target method
- **What ICT says:** When you have two key levels (e.g., high of inversion FVG and high of new week opening gap), split the difference (midpoint). This is often a reversal zone or partial-profit target. It comes from the idea that "octave" or "gradient" levels have algorithmic significance.
- **How to identify:** Mark two highs or two lows. Measure the midpoint between them. Apply Fib if needed.
- **How to use:** As a partial profit target or a place to watch for reversal/congestion.
- **Example in this video:** High of new week opening gap + inversion FVG high, split in half = event horizon. Price stops there or reverses. Use as a target on bread and butter entries.
- **Timestamps:** [0:35:26](https://youtu.be/Il_DM4T7nzg?t=2126) split difference = event horizon.
- **Nuance / caveats:** Not guaranteed; just probabilistic.

head: Volume Imbalance / Empty Bar  (aliases: gap, imbalance)
body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:** A candlestick (usually on opening) that has no overlap with the prior candlestick's range. This creates a gap. The term "volume imbalance" refers to the fact that no trades occurred at those price levels. It's ripe for a retracement or a run-away in the direction of the gap.
- **How to identify:** Look for candlesticks that don't touch the prior bar's range (gap up or gap down).
- **How to use:** As a reference for measuring FVGs and as a potential retracement target or breakout zone.
- **Example in this video:** Opening candles at 9:30 had volume imbalance from the prior close (no trades at those levels due to overnight gap). Tracked throughout the morning as a retracement target.
- **Timestamps:** [0:08:53](https://youtu.be/Il_DM4T7nzg?t=533) volume imbalance in opening candles.
- **Nuance / caveats:** Volume imbalance alone isn't an entry; it's just a gap to reference.

title: ICT 2026 Futures Opening Range Tape-Reading \ April 13, 2026
head: Rejection Block  (aliases: rejection zone)
body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:** A level where price shows rejection or slowdown; it's a prior high that is being tested but not overcome. It can also be a level identified by FVG structure or consequent encroachment where bodies are rejected.
- **How to identify:** Price runs to a prior high, then reverses or consolidates (bodies fail to go above it).
- **How to use:** As a reversal zone or as a place to take profits. If price takes out a rejection block, that shows strength (no longer rejected).
- **Example in this video:** Various prior highs marked as "rejection blocks"; when price failed to take them out, ICT watched for reversal into minor buy sides.
- **Timestamps:** [0:25:44](https://youtu.be/Il_DM4T7nzg?t=1544) rejection block marked; used for reversal logic.
- **Nuance / caveats:** Not all rejections lead to reversals; sometimes they break through (shows strength).

head: Tape Reading Journal / Notepad Method  (aliases: study journal, anticipation logging)
body:
- **Kind:** process
- **What ICT says:** Use a physical notepad (not on the chart) to log your **real-time anticipations** as price unfolds. Write timestamps, abbreviated terms (FVG, CE, minor buy side, etc.), and your prediction of what should happen next. You're not annotating the chart in real-time; you're jotting notes while watching. After the price run completes, go back to the chart and annotate it with your notes. Then screenshot it. Finally, add to your **study journal** (separate doc) your emotional/psychological state: Did you feel confident? Uncertain? Did you expect it to work?
- **How to identify:** This is a personal practice; no chart tells you how to do it. It's discipline.
- **How to use:** The notepad creates a record of your predictions vs. reality. Over time, you see which predictions you get right and which are wrong. Emotional notes help you understand your psychology during success vs. failure. When you're in drawdown, you go back to your study journal and read how you felt during winning periods to rebuild confidence.
- **Example in this video:** ICT says, "Write down 10:28 on your notepad, anticipated run to buy side, happened." Then after, annotate the chart with that entry point and screenshot. In the study journal: "I felt certain this would work; bodies were clean. No uncertainty." Over months, you'd have dozens of these records, showing patterns in your psychology.
- **Timestamps:** [1:09:42](https://youtu.be/Il_DM4T7nzg?t=4182) notepad method: jot timestamps and expectations in shorthand. [1:11:18](https://youtu.be/Il_DM4T7nzg?t=4278) annotate chart after, screenshot, then journal emotion/psychology. [1:12:51](https://youtu.be/Il_DM4T7nzg?t=4371) study journal: record what you felt, whether confident or uncertain.
- **Nuance / caveats:** This is tape reading, not trading. You risk no capital. The goal is building skill and emotional awareness, not piling up winning trades.

title: ICT 2026 Futures Opening Range Tape-Reading \ April 13, 2026
head: Canary in the Coal Mine (Warning Sign)  (aliases: dying canary, price reluctance)
body:
- **Kind:** rule / psychology
- **What ICT says:** Coal miners used to bring canaries down into mines; if the canary died, oxygen was too low and miners had to evacuate. Same principle in trading: when price does something it "shouldn't" (shows reluctance, doesn't take out a level it should, wicks don't touch a CE it should), that's your canary dying. It's telling you the environment has changed; stop what you're doing and get out of that line of thinking. Expect the opposite direction.
- **How to identify:** Recognize what "should" happen in your model. When price doesn't do it, that's the canary dying.
- **How to use:** When the canary dies (price shows reluctance), pivot your expectation. Don't defend your original thesis; pivot to the opposite side and wait for confirmation of the new thesis.
- **Example in this video:** Early Monday, price showed reluctance to go lower (didn't take out sell side when it "should" have). That was the canary. ICT recognized it and pivoted to expect a run higher (which happened). He didn't get frustrated; he just flipped the switch.
- **Timestamps:** [0:20:06](https://youtu.be/Il_DM4T7nzg?t=1206) reluctance = canary dying = warning. [0:45:46](https://youtu.be/Il_DM4T7nzg?t=2746) canary analogy explained fully.
- **Nuance / caveats:** This requires you to know what "should" happen. If you don't have a model, you can't recognize when it's violated.

title: ICT 2026 Futures Weekend Review \ April 11, 2026
head: Continuous Contract vs. Front Month Contract (aliases: contract rollover adjustment, settlement price toggle)
body:
- **Kind:** refinement
- **What ICT says:** The continuous contract shows price as if contracts roll seamlessly; it smooths gaps that occur at rollover dates. But ICT does not use this toggle to find fair value gaps. He uses it to reveal volume imbalances that exist on one contract but are hidden on the other due to the gap. Both closing prices must agree (e.g., 25,333.00 on both); when they don't match exactly, the toggle is useful. The settlement price toggle also changes what you see; if you have settlement price toggled on/off differently than ICT, you won't see the same suspension blocks or volume imbalances.
- **How to identify:** In TradingView, the continuous contract has a toggle button for rollover adjustment (lower right, gray hue). The front month contract shows only settlement price toggle. Check both; compare the PD arrays across them.
- **How to use:** Start analysis on continuous contract to get historical context unobstructed by rollover gaps. Identify breaker blocks and key levels. Then compare how the same price action uses those levels on the front month. If one contract's suspension block aligns better with bodies closing, use that as your key reference. Document both in your notes as alternates.
- **Example in this video:** MNQ June (front month) vs. MNQ continuous: when toggling the continuous adjustment off/on, a suspension block appears with a volume imbalance that the front month doesn't show cleanly. The consequent encroachment of the continuous is 25,495 (10.5 handles above front month's 25,474.5). This 20-handle spread reveals whether traders on each contract are using the same level.
- **Timestamps:** [0:05:28](https://youtu.be/RY67bW2UhxY?t=328) shows the toggle button; [0:13:20](https://youtu.be/RY67bW2UhxY?t=800) explains why both levels matter; [0:18:03](https://youtu.be/RY67bW2UhxY?t=1083) contrast with spotty price action on front month only.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Some traders have the settlement price toggle on when ICT doesn't; this is why they don't see suspension blocks. If you don't see a volume imbalance or suspension block in your chart, check both toggles. The continuous contract function is NOT for finding new fair value gaps; it is for finding volume imbalances that wouldn't be visible otherwise and for ensuring you have clean historical price data before contract rollovers.

title: ICT 2026 Futures Weekend Review \ April 11, 2026
head: Volume Imbalance (aliases: suspension block, gap between bodies)
body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:** A volume imbalance occurs when candlestick bodies do not connect (there's a gap between one candle's close and the next candle's open) but the wicks overlap or touch. This separation of bodies creates inefficiency that price will later come back to fill. A suspension block has a volume imbalance at high and low; it's bracketed. The gap is only in the bodies, not the wicks.
- **How to identify:** Look for candlesticks where the close of one and open of the next have space between them, but wicks reach into or past each other. Measure: candlestick 1 close to candlestick 2 open = volume imbalance.
- **How to use:** These are targets. If price gaps up above a volume imbalance, that level becomes a pull-back target; if it gaps down, the inefficiency is a recovery target. Use for both entry zones and stop-loss levels.
- **Example in this video:** Daily suspension block on MNQ: a volume imbalance with a low and high; lower quadrant at 25,000 level; trading back down into this imbalance signals discount sensitivity and potential continuation lower.
- **Timestamps:** [0:11:44](https://youtu.be/RY67bW2UhxY?t=704) defines suspension block visually; [0:12:33](https://youtu.be/RY67bW2UhxY?t=753) shows the toggle making it visible/invisible.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** None stated; this is foundational ICT teaching.

title: ICT 2026 Futures Weekend Review \ April 11, 2026
head: Consequent Encroachment (aliases: half gap, 50% level, midpoint of suspension block)
body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:** Consequent encroachment is the halfway point between the high and low of a suspension block (or any inefficiency). It's a key intraday target; 70% of the time, the opening range gap fill reaches at least the consequent encroachment. This makes it your first, easiest draw for the morning session.
- **How to identify:** Suspension block high + low ÷ 2 = consequent encroachment. Mark it on your chart.
- **How to use:** If price opens above the gap midpoint, expect it to trade down to consequent encroachment. If below, expect a run up to it. This gives you a bias for the first 30–60 minutes.
- **Example in this video:** MNQ opening range gap: gap high and low were far apart (huge premium opening); consequent encroachment became the first target. Price respected it, then continued lower.
- **Timestamps:** [0:20:24](https://youtu.be/RY67bW2UhxY?t=1224) defines "half gap"; [0:33:17](https://youtu.be/RY67bW2UhxY?t=1997) states 70% probability.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** This is not a guarantee, but the probability is high enough to base your session bias on it.

title: ICT 2026 Futures Weekend Review \ April 11, 2026
head: Bodies Cannot Touch (Key Levels) — Bearish Signature
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:** When price is bearish (in downtrend, below a key level), the candlestick bodies must stay out of that level. Wicks are allowed to tag it; bodies are not. If the bodies breach or even rest on that level, it signals weakness to the downside is over and bullishness may return. This is algorithmic: smart money executes orders such that bodies honor the level while wicks test it.
- **How to identify:** Track the high and low (or close) of the candlestick body. If it stays below the key level (e.g., lower quadrant of daily suspension block), that's bearish. If a body pierces the level, that's a reversal signal.
- **How to use:** Use this as a filter. While price is below a level with bodies unable to touch it, continue with your downside bias. The moment a body closes above or within that level, prepare for a turn or continuation of the upside.
- **Example in this video:** Daily suspension block lower quadrant at 25,000: bodies repeatedly failed to close above this level during the downtrend, confirming bearishness. When bodies finally touched it during a retracement, that signaled potential bullish shift.
- **Timestamps:** [0:42:58](https://youtu.be/RY67bW2UhxY?t=2578) explains bodies vs. wicks in FVG context; [0:43:47](https://youtu.be/RY67bW2UhxY?t=2627) body placement as bearish/bullish indicator.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** This applies to all key levels (old highs/lows, breaker blocks, PD arrays). It's a universal rule of institutional order flow.

title: ICT 2026 Futures Weekend Review \ April 11, 2026
head: Breaker Block (aliases: structural high/low, swing high/low used as support/resistance)
body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:** A breaker is a swing high followed by a swing low, then a higher high—or the inverse. Price "breaks" the prior swing low/high with authority. The original swing low (or high) then becomes a key support (or resistance). Use it to identify premium/discount zones and anticipate where price will return.
- **How to identify:** Swing low → swing high → higher high (bullish breaker). Swing high → swing low → lower low (bearish breaker). Mark the original swing (the one that got "broken") as your breaker level.
- **How to use:** Target for fills, entry zones, stop-loss placement. If price breaks above a breaker block, expect it to come back and test the breaker itself before continuing.
- **Example in this video:** MNQ intraday: price formed a breaker on the continuous chart; ICT watched it to see how the price action used that level on the front month contract.
- **Timestamps:** [0:04:41](https://youtu.be/RY67bW2UhxY?t=281) introduces breaker concept; [0:07:04](https://youtu.be/RY67bW2UhxY?t=424) explains why breaker is important across contracts.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** None stated in this video.

title: ICT 2026 Futures Weekend Review \ April 11, 2026
head: First Presented Fair Value Gap (aliases: first FVG, first inefficiency, gap before high)
body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:** After price opens and begins to move, the first gap in candlestick bodies that forms is the "first presented" FVG. It shows where the first inefficiency is created. This is crucial because price typically honors this before moving to deeper targets. The wick that creates the gap is the real gap; the visual gap on the chart is secondary.
- **How to identify:** In the first 1–2 minutes post-open, watch for candlesticks with bodies that don't touch. The separation is your first FVG.
- **How to use:** This is a key level for short-term tape reading. If price breaks above it with a bullish wick, expect it to come back and test the bottom of the wick (not the visible gap). If it comes back in on a pullback, the lower half should remain untouched if you're bullish.
- **Example in this video:** MNQ 9:30 candle: the first FVG formed immediately. Bodies stayed out of the lower half even during retracements, confirming bullishness short-term; then price later failed and turned bearish.
- **Timestamps:** [0:37:18](https://youtu.be/RY67bW2UhxY?t=2238) example of first FVG and wick distinction; [0:52:10](https://youtu.be/RY67bW2UhxY?t=3130) shows how bodies use (or don't) the first FVG.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** The wick, not the visual gap, is the true inefficiency. Traders often miss this.

title: ICT 2026 Futures Weekend Review \ April 11, 2026
head: Wicks vs. Bodies Distinction
body:
- **Kind:** refinement
- **What ICT says:** A wick is created when price extends beyond the closing price of the body. The wick represents the rejection of that price. When you see a gap visually, the wick created that gap, not the bodies. If you only look at the visual gap between candlesticks, you miss the real story in the wick rejection. This distinction changes how you read fair value gaps: the wick is what matters for entry and target placement, not the open/close separation.
- **How to identify:** On each candle, the body is open-to-close; the wick extends from high/low beyond the body.
- **How to use:** When analyzing a "gap," look left to the prior candle's wick. If the wick already extends into what would be the gap, that wick rejection is the real PD array, not the gap itself. Place entries and stops accordingly.
- **Example in this video:** MNQ consolidation with no fair value gap: a wick forms; that wick's rejection is the key level, not an open/close gap. Price respects the wick level.
- **Timestamps:** [0:37:18](https://youtu.be/RY67bW2UhxY?t=2238) distinguishes wick gap from open/close gap; [0:42:10](https://youtu.be/RY67bW2UhxY?t=2530) applies to fair value gap mechanics; [0:52:10](https://youtu.be/RY67bW2UhxY?t=3130) shows wick as the real level.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** This is not commonly taught; ICT says no other methodology (Wyckoff, Elliott Wave, supply/demand) teaches this distinction.

head: Opening Range Gap & 70% Rule (aliases: 9:30 gap, regular trading hours opening range gap, RTHORG)

- **Kind:** rule

title: ICT 2026 Futures Weekend Review \ April 11, 2026
head: Low-Hanging Fruit Objectives (aliases: easy targets, conservative drawdowns, measured short runs)
body:
- **Kind:** entry model
- **What ICT says:** Reject the desire to run for large moves (500 handles, 200 handles). Instead, aim for low-hanging fruit: small, repeatable drawdowns of 20–40 handles that happen dozens of times intraday. This build experience, confidence, and capital preservation. Once you have skill, scale up.
- **How to identify:** After identifying a PD array or key level, measure the distance to the next reasonable level (not the ultimate target). This is your low-hanging fruit.
- **How to use:** In live trading, this is your bread-and-butter model. Wait for price to present a PD array, take your small win at the next level, and move on. Repeat multiple times a day.
- **Example in this video:** MNQ: continuous contract offered a 160-handle run to consequent encroachment vs. 400-handle run on front month to a distant target. The 160-handle run is the low-hanging fruit; it's more likely and requires less luck.
- **Timestamps:** [0:24:24](https://youtu.be/RY67bW2UhxY?t=1464) contrasts high expectations with low-hanging fruit; [0:25:15](https://youtu.be/RY67bW2UhxY?t=1515) advises new traders to focus here.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** This is not weakness; it's wisdom. It's how you build a sustainable edge.

head: Event Horizon (aliases: midpoint of a large range, void, ether level)
body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:** When a range (premium to discount, old high to old low, PD array) is very wide, the midpoint often appears to be empty—a void. But price gravitates to it with uncanny precision. This "event horizon" is where the market holds balance; algorithms use it as a target.
- **How to identify:** Measure a large range (e.g., daily suspension block high to low). Find the exact midpoint. Draw it as a reference.
- **How to use:** Use as a pullback target, reversal zone, or continuation staging point. If price overshoots it, expect it to come back.
- **Example in this video:** MNQ daily chart: event horizon level between the low of suspension block and the upper quadrant; price bounced in this area, used it as support, then continued.
- **Timestamps:** [0:06:02](https://youtu.be/RY67bW2UhxY?t=362) introduces event horizon conceptually.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** This level is not marked on the chart; it's pure geometry. Some traders miss it because it "doesn't exist" visually.

title: ICT 2026 Futures Weekend Review \ April 11, 2026
head: Inversion Fair Value Gap (aliases: inversion FVG, inverted inefficiency, gap in wrong direction)
body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:** When price is in a premium (bullish) area but trades down and creates a fair value gap on the downside, that gap is an "inversion." It's bullish by structure (it's an FVG) but appears inverted (gap on wrong side relative to trend). Use inversions to understand directional context: an inversion FVG below a bullish level signals that downside is temporary and the higher trend resumes.
- **How to identify:** In an uptrend (or at a premium level), a candlestick gap forms on the downside. That's an inversion FVG.
- **How to use:** This is a strong continuation setup. When price trades back above an inversion FVG, it confirms bullishness. Sell-side is exhausted; re-test the level and run higher.
- **Example in this video:** MNQ: after a rally, an inversion FVG formed on a pullback. When price traded back above it with conviction, it resumed the uptrend.
- **Timestamps:** [0:06:17](https://youtu.be/RY67bW2UhxY?t=377) mentions Ryan (Dodgy D) and his iFVG focus; [0:39:24](https://youtu.be/RY67bW2UhxY?t=2364) shows inversion FVG usage live.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Inversion FVGs are not on every chart; they're special. Dodgy D built a full strategy around them, which is valid but narrow. ICT uses them as one tool among many.

title: ICT 2026 Futures Weekend Review \ April 11, 2026
head: Octant Levels (aliases: eighths, gradient levels, divisions of suspension block)
body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:** A suspension block (or any large range) can be divided into eighths (octants). Mark the quarters (upper/lower quadrants) and the eighths. These provide micro-targets and precision entries. The lower octant is one-eighth up from the low; the upper octant is one-eighth down from the high.
- **How to identify:** Use Fibonacci tool set to octaves (1/8), or manually divide the range into eight equal parts.
- **How to use:** Pullbacks within these gradient levels help you fine-tune stops and targets. If price pulls back into a lower octant during a downtrend, that's support; if it pulls back into the upper octant during an uptrend, that's resistance.
- **Example in this video:** MNQ daily suspension block: ICT drew octant lines and used them to grade price action through the day.
- **Timestamps:** [0:35:41](https://youtu.be/RY67bW2UhxY?t=2141) shows Fibonacci octane settings; [0:30:00](https://youtu.be/RY67bW2UhxY?t=1800) references octants as gradients for measurement.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** This is precision work; it requires clean, wide ranges to be useful.

head: Decoupling (aliases: lack of agreement, divergence, three averages not in sync)
body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:** Decoupling occurs when NQ (Nasdaq), ES (S&P 500), and YM (Dow) do not move in agreement. One might be up while another consolidates or declines. This breaks the algorithmic precision of price action and makes trading harder and riskier. Probability drops; you lose clean structure.
- **How to identify:** Watch all three in real-time. If NQ rallies but ES stalls and YM drops, you have decoupling. No clean bias; price action is choppy.
- **How to use:** When decoupled, tighten stops, reduce size, or stop trading that session. Wait for agreement to return. Do not try to force trades in decoupled markets.
- **Example in this video:** Friday (Good Friday) CPI miss; NQ tried higher, ES hesitated, YM declined. ICT closed interest and stepped away.
- **Timestamps:** [0:06:26](https://youtu.be/Hiq47zliJ_Y?t=386) watches for decoupling; [0:07:17](https://youtu.be/Hiq47zliJ_Y?t=437) identifies it; [0:22:39](https://youtu.be/Hiq47zliJ_Y?t=1359) explains decoupling effect on precision.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Decoupling often precedes major moves or reversals; it's a warning flag, not a reason to panic, but definitely a reason to reduce risk.

title: ICT 2026 Tape-Reading Opening Range \ April 10, 2026
head: First Presented Fair Value Gap (aliases: first FVG, first inefficiency, first gap post-open)
body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:** The gap visible on the chart (candlestick low to next candlestick high) is not the real gap. Look at the wick to the left of that gap. The wick itself is the real inefficiency. The first presented FVG is the first one that forms after the opening bell, and it's your key reference for the session bias.
- **How to identify:** 1st candle opens at 9:30, 2nd candle opens; look for separation in bodies. The prior wick rejection is the real level.
- **How to use:** If bodies fail to touch inside the first presented FVG, that's bullish continuation. If bodies breach it or lay in the lower half, bearishness resumes.
- **Example in this video:** MNQ: first presented FVG after 9:30 open; bodies stayed above it on retracements, confirming bullish bias short-term; when bodies fell below it, it turned bearish.
- **Timestamps:** [0:12:06](https://youtu.be/Hiq47zliJ_Y?t=726) explains wick vs. visual gap; [0:18:02](https://youtu.be/Hiq47zliJ_Y?t=1082) applies to live price action.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Most traders look at the visual gap and miss the wick. The wick is the true PD array.

title: ICT 2026 Tape-Reading Opening Range \ April 10, 2026
head: Rejection Block (aliases: wicked-high candle, failed-run candle, wick rejection)
body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:** A rejection block forms when a candle wicks up (or down) but closes below (or above) that wick, creating a wick extension that rejects a price level. This is a powerful signal that the level is held; price will not easily penetrate it on the next attempt.
- **How to identify:** Look for a candlestick that extends far with a wick but closes in the body far from the wick extreme. The wick is the rejection block.
- **How to use:** Use as a key level for entries and stops. Price will often respect the wick rejection and reverse. If price gets above this wick rejection, the level is breached and price can continue higher.
- **Example in this video:** MNQ: rejection block forms where price tries higher but closes lower; bodies cannot stay above this wick rejection short-term, confirming bearish tone.
- **Timestamps:** [0:12:54](https://youtu.be/Hiq47zliJ_Y?t=774) shows rejection block formation; [0:15:28](https://youtu.be/Hiq47zliJ_Y?t=928) uses it as a key level.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** None stated; foundational concept.

body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:** An inversion FVG forms when price is bullish but creates a gap on the downside (or vice versa). It's called an "inversion" because the gap is inverted relative to the direction of the trend. When price trades back above an inversion FVG, it signals continuation of the original trend.
- **How to identify:** In an uptrend, a candle gaps down (body separation, wick reaching down). That's an inversion FVG.
- **How to use:** When price trades back above an inversion FVG, expect continuation higher. This is a continuation pattern.
- **Example in this video:** MNQ: inversion FVG formed on a pullback; when price retraced into it and broke above, it was a green light for continuation.
- **Timestamps:** [0:12:54](https://youtu.be/Hiq47zliJ_Y?t=774) shows inversion FVG formation.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Inversions are not as common as regular FVGs; when they form, they are strong signals.

body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:** The midpoint of the opening range gap is the consequent encroachment; price draws to this level in 70% of first-hour trades. This is the lowest-probability miss in ICT's methodology. If you're watching the market at 9:30, the consequent encroachment is your first target to watch.
- **How to identify:** (Settlement price at 4:15 PM + Opening price at 9:30 AM) ÷ 2 = Consequent Encroachment.
- **How to use:** This is your first-hour bias. Premium gap → target consequent encroachment on downside. Discount gap → target upside. Once price reaches it, look for the next level or consider taking profit.

head: Sell-Side Liquidity (aliases: short stops, sell orders waiting, liquidity pool)
body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:** Sell-side liquidity is a cluster of sell orders or old resistance levels where traders have stop losses (shorts). When price reaches sell-side, it runs through it quickly (often called a liquidity sweep or raid). Identify sell-side using old highs, prior swing highs, and FVG boundaries.
- **How to identify:** Look at prior session's highs, swing highs, tops of consolidations. These are sell-side pools. Also, the upper boundary of an FVG is sell-side.
- **How to use:** When price approaches sell-side, expect a potential run through it (liquidity sweep) or a stall/reversal. If you're short and price is approaching sell-side below you, tighten stops.
- **Example in this video:** MNQ: multiple sell-side pools identified at prior highs and FVG boundaries; when price reaches them, it either sweeps through or reverses.
- **Timestamps:** [0:08:07](https://youtu.be/Hiq47zliJ_Y?t=487) identifies sell-side; [0:13:45](https://youtu.be/Hiq47zliJ_Y?t=825) references liquidity sweeps as myth vs. reality.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** "No such thing as liquidity sweeps" is a myth; ICT just proved one live on tape.

head: Buy-Side Liquidity (aliases: buy stops, long stops, liquidity at lows)
body:

- **How to identify:** Look at prior session's lows, swing lows, bottoms of consolidations. These are buy-side pools. Also, the lower boundary of an FVG is buy-side.
- **How to use:** When price approaches buy-side, expect potential interaction (bounce or sweep). If you're long, watch buy-side below as support.
- **Example in this video:** MNQ: buy-side at opening range gap low; price drawn to this level repeatedly.
- **Timestamps:** [0:10:05](https://youtu.be/Hiq47zliJ_Y?t=605) watches for buy-side interaction.

head: SMT Divergence Failure Swing (aliases: SMT, structural shift, Smart Money Trap)
body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:** A failure swing in the Smart Money Technique occurs when price makes a swing high or low but then fails to make a new swing in the expected direction. This divergence is a trap or reversal signal. When the three averages (NQ, ES, YM) create a divergence in their swings, market structure is uncertain and precision drops.
- **How to identify:** Swing high, then lower high (failure). Or swing low, then higher low (failure). Look for it across NQ, ES, YM separately.
- **How to use:** When SMT divergence appears, reduce size and precision. Do not trade with high conviction until agreement returns.
- **Example in this video:** Friday: ES and YM made failure swings (could not follow NQ higher), confirming decoupling.
