title: ICT 2026 EOD Market Review \ March 13, 2026
head: Market Structure Shift (Break of Structure / Displacement)
body:
- **Kind:** definition / rule
- **What ICT says:** When price takes out a prior low (or high) and closes beyond it, market structure has shifted. This is a signal for continuation in the new direction. In the micro-Nasdaq example, ICT identified the shift in market structure and immediately began looking for shorts into a lower target.
- **How to identify:** Price breaks a prior swing low/high and closes beyond it; bodies confirm the move.
- **How to use:** Entry trigger; expect continuation in the direction of the break.
- **Example in this video:** Micro-Nasdaq 1m: Thursday's first-percentage FVG held; price then broke market structure below it, validating short entry.
- **Timestamps:** [0:30:58](https://youtu.be/l7hRTBvK7to?t=1858), [0:36:40](https://youtu.be/l7hRTBvK7to?t=2200)
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** ICT compares it to a "pseudo model 2022" (a Mentorship model named Zircon or similar).

title: ICT 2026 EOD Market Review \ March 13, 2026
head: First Percentage Fair Value Gap (FPFVG)
body:
- **Kind:** entry model / reference level
- **What ICT says:** The first FVG that forms after a key event (e.g., morning opening, post-FOMC). In the micro-Nasdaq example, the FPFVG from Thursday serves as a reference level; price rallies back into it but fails to close above it (bodies reject), validating bearish bias. Later, when price breaks back down, the FPFVG becomes the inversion FVG target.
- **How to identify:** First gap in the morning or after a key event.
- **How to use:** As a reference level; bodies should reject if bearish; once rejected, expect return into it as inversion FVG target.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 1m, Thursday opening: FPFVG formed; used as rally target and reference; on Friday, rejected, then became inversion FVG target on break lower.
- **Timestamps:** [0:30:11](https://youtu.be/l7hRTBvK7to?t=1811), [0:33:26](https://youtu.be/l7hRTBvK7to?t=2006), [0:35:04](https://youtu.be/l7hRTBvK7to?t=2104)
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Used as both a reference level and later as an inversion FVG depending on price action.

title: ICT 2026 EOD Market Review \ March 13, 2026
head: Order Block (At Bottom of Inversion FVG)
body:
- **Kind:** entry model / stop placement
- **What ICT says:** An order block at the bottom of an inversion FVG is a "big brick wall." When price rally attempts to retrace back into the iFVG, the order block acts as a hard stop. ICT placed his stop loss just above an order block in the micro-Nasdaq trade; price came close but held above it. "If you didn't write that down, you missed a beautiful piece of information right there."
- **How to identify:** The low of the inversion FVG formation (the order block level).
- **How to use:** Stop-loss placement; set stops just above the order block when shorting into the inversion FVG.
- **Example in this video:** Micro-Nasdaq trade: order block at the bottom of the iFVG; stop loss set there; price spike up close to it but held.
- **Timestamps:** [0:31:45](https://youtu.be/l7hRTBvK7to?t=1905)
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Serves as both a structural reference and risk management tool.

title: ICT 2026 EOD Market Review \ March 13, 2026
head: Swing High (Three-Candle Pattern)
body:
- **Kind:** entry model
- **What ICT says:** When price shows High-Higher High-Lower High pattern over three consecutive candlesticks, it forms a swing high. This is often followed by immediate displacement lower. In the micro-Nasdaq example, this pattern preceded the sharp drop. "Look at the bodies, not the wicks. See the bodies? High. Higher high. Lower high. There's your swing high. And then displacement lower."
- **How to identify:** Watch three consecutive candlesticks; compare highs; if pattern is H-HH-LH, that's a swing high. Bodies must validate it.
- **How to use:** As a reversal signal; expect lower prices after the third candle closes.
- **Example in this video:** Micro-Nasdaq 1m: multiple swing highs formed before the main dump lower. Price action used this pattern to set up lower moves.
- **Timestamps:** [0:36:40](https://youtu.be/l7hRTBvK7to?t=2200), [0:37:26](https://youtu.be/l7hRTBvK7to?t=2246)
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Focus on bodies, not wicks; wicks can be misleading.

title: ICT 2026 EOD Market Review \ March 13, 2026
head: Discount/Premium Wick
body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:** A discount wick is one that is lower in range than prior wicks; a premium wick is higher. When trading at a lower level relative to a discount wick above, that wick acts as premium (even though it's labeled "discount wick") because the range has changed. ICT teaches grading wicks by drawing fibs and identifying midpoint (consequent encroachment).
- **How to identify:** Grade the wick with fib; note the midpoint and octant/quadrant levels.
- **How to use:** As target levels; if price is below a discount wick, that wick's midpoint can be a target for a bounce.
- **Example in this video:** Crude oil daily: discount wick graded with fib; consequent encroachment is the first target for continuation higher. ES and NQ: similar wick grading to identify midpoint targets.
- **Timestamps:** [0:18:15](https://youtu.be/l7hRTBvK7to?t=1095), [0:23:51](https://youtu.be/l7hRTBvK7to?t=1431), [0:26:13](https://youtu.be/l7hRTBvK7to?t=1573)
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** The label "discount" or "premium" is relative to current price position; always re-evaluate as price moves.

title: ICT 2026 EOD Market Review \ March 13, 2026
head: Suspension Block
body:
- **Kind:** entry model
- **What ICT says:** A candlestick that closes with a small body and a wick extending in the opposite direction of intended move, showing suspension of momentum. In the micro-Nasdaq trade, ICT identified a suspension block-like pattern (small body, wick below) as a signal to add to the short.
- **How to identify:** Small body, wick in opposition, at a key level.
- **Example in this video:** Micro-Nasdaq 1m: suspension block pattern used to add to short position.
- **Timestamps:** [0:33:26](https://youtu.be/l7hRTBvK7to?t=2006)
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Similar to a pin bar; indicates indecision followed by direction.

title: ICT 2026 EOD Market Review \ March 13, 2026
head: Displacement (Sharp Move Lower After Pattern)
body:
- **Kind:** entry model / outcome
- **What ICT says:** After a swing high or suspension block forms, price often experiences "displacement" lower—a sharp, aggressive move. This is the money move. In the micro-Nasdaq example, displacement occurred immediately after the swing high pattern, delivering price down into the target levels.
- **How to identify:** Follows a reversal pattern (swing high, suspension, etc.); bodies accelerate and show strength in one direction.
- **Example in this video:** Micro-Nasdaq: after swing high, immediate displacement lower; sharp drop into multiple targets.
- **Timestamps:** [0:37:26](https://youtu.be/l7hRTBvK7to?t=2246), [0:38:13](https://youtu.be/l7hRTBvK7to?t=2293)
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Displacement is the expected outcome after pattern confirmation; do not over-stay trades that have already displaced significantly.

title: ICT 2026 Market Commentary \ March 13, 2026
head: Order Block (Hierarchical Parent/Child Relationship)
body:
- **Kind:** definition / rule (heavily refined)
- **What ICT says:** An order block is a candlestick formed at a key level (often at the bottom of a fair value gap or at a gradient level). Order blocks have a hierarchy: a parent order block is one that is laying on top of a gradient level (quadrant or octant). A propulsion block is a child order block that trades down into a parent order block; it need not be on a gradient level because it "borrows" the parent's discount sensitivity. "This candlestick right here is part of this overall run to this liquidity... If this wasn't a run just to get here, dropping back down there, that would have been used to go long. This would have been a bullish fair value gap. But because we're part of a bearish narrative, this becomes a mitigation block."
- **How to identify:** Look at where a candlestick is positioned relative to: (1) a gradient level (quadrant or octant), (2) a fair value gap, (3) prior price action. If laying on a gradient level and used for entry, it's an order block. If it's part of a run to liquidity, it can be a mitigation block instead.
- **How to use:** Parent order blocks anchor stop losses and define turning points. Propulsion blocks validate continuation and provide adding-in opportunities. Mitigation blocks define the rejection of a directional move and often precede reversal.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 1m, March 13: opening price at 9:30 becomes an order block (laying on the upper quadrant of RTH opening range gap). Later price uses it as a mitigation block, changing its function based on subsequent order flow. "That candlestick right here that starts these two down close handle. This is the parent order block. Why? Because it's laying over top of... the quadrant level... of the regular trading hours opening range gap."
- **Timestamps:** [0:30:25](https://youtu.be/sPKglrJAVFY?t=1825), [0:31:58](https://youtu.be/sPKglrJAVFY?t=1918), [0:32:45](https://youtu.be/sPKglrJAVFY?t=1965), [0:34:18](https://youtu.be/sPKglrJAVFY?t=2058)
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Order blocks change their state based on order flow context; a down-close candle is NOT automatically a bullish order block. "Just because you see a down close candle doesn't make it a bullish order block." The gradient level anchoring is critical; without it, the level lacks validity.

title: ICT 2026 Market Commentary \ March 13, 2026
head: Propulsion Block
body:
- **Kind:** definition / entry model
- **What ICT says:** A candlestick that trades down into a parent order block (which is laying on a gradient level). In a bullish move, this is a "buy side delivery going to buy side liquidity." It need not be on a gradient level itself because it borrows the parent order block's discount sensitivity. Validates continuation in the intended direction.
- **How to identify:** Look for a candlestick that trades into (not just near) a prior order block; measure if it's a valid entry point based on order flow.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 1m: "This is a valid propulsion block when it's bullish or buy side delivery going to buy side liquidity. This cannot go down to half of this range. It clearly didn't do that. The only thing it did was what? Use the opening. On this candlestick right there which is a change in the state of delivery."
- **Timestamps:** [0:32:45](https://youtu.be/sPKglrJAVFY?t=1965)
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Distinct from parent order block; it's a child that validates the parent's function.

title: ICT 2026 Market Commentary \ March 13, 2026
head: Mitigation Block
body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:** An order block that, due to the bearish order flow context, becomes a rejection point rather than an entry point. Instead of facilitating a bullish move, it gets used and then prices collapse, indicating the market is mitigating the buy-side run. "Since it's a run just for liquidity, this order block can't... be part of a buying scenario. So, what is it going to be? Mitigation block."
- **How to identify:** An order block that is taken out (price runs through it to take buy-side liquidity above), but then price reverses aggressively lower, rejecting the move.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 1m, March 13: the order block at the upper quadrant is mitigated; price runs up to take liquidity, then reverses sharply lower, validating the bearish narrative.
- **Timestamps:** [0:30:25](https://youtu.be/sPKglrJAVFY?t=1825), [0:38:18](https://youtu.be/sPKglrJAVFY?t=2298)
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Function of an order block is determined by subsequent price action, not its formation. Context is king.

title: ICT 2026 Market Commentary \ March 13, 2026
head: Gradient Levels (Octants & Quadrants)
body:
- **Kind:** definition / reference levels
- **What ICT says:** The opening range gap (RTH or new week opening gap) is divided into gradient levels using fibonacci divisions: quadrants (four divisions: 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.0) and octants (eight divisions: 0.125, 0.25, 0.375, 0.50, 0.625, 0.75, 0.875, 1.0). These levels act as anchors for order blocks, propulsion blocks, and all intraday targeting. "Every time it gives me an opportunity to trade at the consequent crush zone just close to it, I'm going to add one more. And I built a position of four micro contracts." All his entries and scalps use these gradient levels as reference points.
- **How to identify:** Calculate the opening range gap (high - low of the gap); divide by 4 (quadrants) or 8 (octants); mark them on the chart.
- **How to use:** As anchors for order block placement, entry points, stop losses, and target levels. ICT's instruction: "Everything has to be anchored to these gradient levels. Otherwise, you're guessing."
- **Example in this video:** NQ 1m, RTH gap at 9:30 has gradient levels marked; every major turning point uses a quadrant or octant level.
- **Timestamps:** [0:24:03](https://youtu.be/sPKglrJAVFY?t=1443), [0:30:25](https://youtu.be/sPKglrJAVFY?t=1825), [0:34:18](https://youtu.be/sPKglrJAVFY?t=2058), [0:43:09](https://youtu.be/sPKglrJAVFY?t=2589)
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Gradient levels are foundational to ICT's 2026 teaching. Without them, levels are "guessing." "A lot of you 20 year olds run around saying... Michael doesn't teach market structure. I don't need to look at any relationship... I just got to read the candlesticks... All I got to do is read the candlesticks just like this."

title: ICT 2026 Market Commentary \ March 13, 2026
head: Buy-Side Inefficiency (BISI) / Sell-Side Inefficiency (SIBI)
body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:** BISI (buy-side inefficiency, sell-side inefficiency) is when there is a separation between a candlestick's close and the next candle's open on the buy side (or sell side), forming a gap. This is different from a volume imbalance. When there's a volume imbalance on one side OR both sides of an inefficiency, you must note it—these are distinct details. "If it would have had a volume imbalance on the high end, that's a suspension block. It's not suspension block. They're all treated the same way. Differences is when there's a inefficiency that has a volume imbalance in one side or both, you have to note it."
- **How to identify:** Look at the close of one candle and the open of the next; if there's a gap (close lower than open, or open higher than close), that's an inefficiency. If the bodies also show a volume imbalance, note both.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 1m: "That candlestick's low. 24,834 quarter. That is a SIBI. I'm sorry, it's a BISI. Buy side and sell side inefficiency."
- **Timestamps:** [0:26:28](https://youtu.be/sPKglrJAVFY?t=1588)
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** BISI/SIBI must be distinguished from volume imbalances; both can be present, or only one.

title: ICT 2026 Market Commentary \ March 13, 2026
head: Volume Imbalance
body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:** A gap between a candlestick's close and the next candle's open, where the bodies themselves show separation (one candle's close does not align with the next candle's open). Distinguished from BISI/SIBI by the fact that it shows a clear body separation. "You're getting more detail, okay? And it's not changing. Nothing's changing about it."
- **Example in this video:** "The close on that candlestick right there? 24,828 half. Okay, or 0.50. The open on this candlestick is 24,828.75. So, it's 1 quarter of a handle higher. That's a volume imbalance."
- **Timestamps:** [0:26:28](https://youtu.be/sPKglrJAVFY?t=1588)
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Details matter; noting volume imbalances makes the difference between profitable and unprofitable trading.

title: ICT 2026 Market Commentary \ March 13, 2026
head: Inversion Fair Value Gap (Revisited in Order Flow Context)
body:
- **Kind:** entry model
- **What ICT says:** When price trades into an FVG area that was originally bullish (would have been bullish if the narrative was bullish), but because the order flow is bearish, it becomes an inversion FVG. The FVG itself doesn't change; the context does. "This gap would have been bullish if order flow was bullish and the narrative was bullish, but we're not. So, this needs to become what? Inversion. So it becomes an inversion fair value gap."
- **How to identify:** Look at a fair value gap; if price is trading up into it but bodies are rejecting and staying below a certain level, and your bias is bearish, it's an iFVG.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 1m: Thursday's first-presented FVG would have been bullish, but because bodies rejected and order flow was bearish, it flipped to an iFVG for the short setup.
- **Timestamps:** [0:35:54](https://youtu.be/sPKglrJAVFY?t=2154)
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Context determines whether an FVG is bullish or inverted; the level itself is objective.

title: ICT 2026 Market Commentary \ March 13, 2026
head: Change of State of Delivery (CISD)
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:** When price action shifts from one delivery context to another (e.g., from seeking buy-side liquidity to seeking sell-side), that's a change of state. It's often marked by an opening price that becomes an order block, shifting the entire narrative. "Change of state of delivery, it opens up here. And trades down right to it by a tick more. Below it and then comes here."
- **Example in this video:** NQ 1m: the 9:30 opening creates a shift from the prior structure.
- **Timestamps:** [0:32:45](https://youtu.be/sPKglrJAVFY?t=1965)
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Often tied to macro time events or structural breaks.

title: ICT 2026 Market Commentary \ March 13, 2026
head: Macro Time
body:
- **Kind:** definition / time-based trigger
- **What ICT says:** Specific times when algorithmic activity spikes (8:00, 9:00, 9:30 ET, etc.). Orders placed at macro times are executed with precision. "It's running to get that liquidity. Going to macro time, the highest candlestick that runs that liquidity out is 4 minutes after 9:00."
- **Example in this video:** 9:00 ET and 9:30 ET macro times on NQ 1m; price runs to liquidity predictably at these times.
- **Timestamps:** [0:35:05](https://youtu.be/sPKglrJAVFY?t=2105), [0:44:42](https://youtu.be/sPKglrJAVFY?t=2682)
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Macro times are algorithmic; understanding them unlocks clarity on order flow.

title: ICT 2026 Market Commentary \ March 13, 2026
head: Consequent Encroachment (Wick Midpoint)
body:
- **Kind:** definition / targeting
- **What ICT says:** The midpoint of a wick measured by fib. Used as a premium/discount reference, a partial exit point, and a rejection level. "Consequent encroachment of this wick. That candlestick closed below it right there."
- **Example in this video:** "Consequent encroachment of this wick. 24,856 .75. I'm selling above it as a premium to that price."
- **Timestamps:** [0:42:19](https://youtu.be/sPKglrJAVFY?t=2539)
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Identical concept to earlier lesson, reinforced here in context of order flow.

title: ICT 2026 Market Commentary \ March 13, 2026
head: Relative Equal Highs/Lows
body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:** Two highs or lows very close to each other, indicating a liquidity pool. When price runs above relative equal highs, buy-side liquidity is created. "This one here is part of this overall run to this liquidity. That opening price."
- **Example in this video:** NQ 1m: "Relative equal highs here. And during the uh the recording, you can watch it on my X feed. This posted yesterday. I highlighted it just like I'm doing right here... they run above it, and I'm shorting it."
- **Timestamps:** [0:35:05](https://youtu.be/sPKglrJAVFY?t=2105), [0:52:18](https://youtu.be/sPKglrJAVFY?t=3138)
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** When shorts into relative equal highs' buy-side liquidity, expect reversal.

title: ICT 2026 New York Lunch Algorithmic Theory \ March 11, 2026
head: NY Lunch Reversal Inefficiency (new PD array, previous day carried forward)  (aliases: "the new PD array", "yesterday's lunch inefficiency"; ICT gives no formal name in this video)
body:
- **Kind:** new coinage / entry model (PD array)
- **What ICT says:**
  - Look at the *previous day's* New York lunch window, a 2-hour window ending 1:30 PM ET. If there is a reversal after liquidity is taken in that window, find the inefficiency (fair value gap) that formed *immediately before the liquidity was taken*, and carry it forward into the next day.
  - If price trades up into it the next day, it can set the tone for a short (if the lunch event was a buy-side raid); reverse for longs.
  - You pick the gap formed right before the liquidity is taken, not the gap one candle earlier. He says it matters because this gap belongs to a complex reversal at a macro time (lunch), a time when reversals take place.
  - Contrast stated by ICT: this is not classic support/resistance. He does not draw a line on the old high; he marks the inefficiency that sets the reversal. "Everything in here sets the stage for revisiting these specific PD arrays."
  - He says he will release two new PD arrays this year and this is one of them. Nobody taught it; he says it came from his own research.
  - Homework: go back through old price action, find the 2-hour lunch periods with a turtle soup short or long, mark the first FVG right before the liquidity is taken, carry it to the next day, and observe whether the next day's high or low forms there ("many times").
- **How to identify:**
  1. Previous-day NY lunch window (he marks it with vertical lines; lunch ends 1:30 PM ET; 1:30–2:00 is the PM opening range).
  2. Liquidity is taken near the end of lunch (example: relative equal highs into 1:31; buy-side raided just ahead of the 1:30 close, "not random").
  3. The candle sequence just before the raid shows a buy-side imbalance / sell-side inefficiency (BISI-type gap with a volume imbalance).
  4. Reversal follows (turtle soup).
- **How to use:**
  - Extend the gap's boundaries to the right into the next session as a rectangle (he drew thin ray lines on his phone and used a rectangle for the recording).
  - Next day, when price trades up into the carried gap (after the 8:30 data, for example) look for shorts; the gap behaves as an inversion FVG (bodies respect it).
  - Other confluences he layered: yesterday's RTH opening range gap (and its CE), first instance of FVG, sell-side liquidity pool at 24,892.50.
- **Example in this video:** MNQ (micro Nasdaq), Tue Mar 10 into Wed Mar 11, 2026.
  - Tue, near the end of lunch: the candle just before the buy-side raid has a close of 25,165.75; the next candle opens 25,166.00 (higher than that close), so a volume imbalance exists and the gap is anchored from 25,165.75 (that candle's close) up to the candle low at 25,177.50 (he says "low here 25,177 and 1/2"). That is the lunch BISI with volume imbalance at its low.
  - Tue PM: after the buy-side raid and 1:30 close of lunch, price retraced lower in the PM session (sell-side liquidity pool + first-instance FVG + the BISI turning into an inversion gap). It dumped through the first-instance FVG, respected CE with bodies, traded down into Tuesday's RTH opening range gap low, reacted, then went up into an inefficiency to close the day.
  - Wed: overnight, then 8:30 CPI ("wonky"); price traded down into old order flow, was back inside Tuesday's RTH opening range gap, then ran up into the carried 25,165.75–25,177.50 level; the bodies stopped at it, price opened just slightly beyond it, then collapsed (he calls it "a complex reversal").
  - Mechanics later in the day: price ran to sell-side at 24,892.50 (two ticks beyond, to 24,892.00), then rallied back in the afternoon; at 1:30 ET it traded into the gap that had become an inversion FVG, then dived to a candle low of 24,873.75 near the event-horizon midpoint (see below).
- **Timestamps:**
  - [0:01:38](https://youtu.be/C90xGr3kW8Y?t=98) — NY lunch = 2-hour window, equal highs into 1:31, PM opening range 1:30–2:00
  - [0:02:28](https://youtu.be/C90xGr3kW8Y?t=148) — buy side taken before 1:30 "is not random"; BISI right before the liquidity
  - [0:09:41](https://youtu.be/C90xGr3kW8Y?t=581) — states the rule: 2-hour lunch window, reversal after liquidity, take the inefficiency right before it, carry it into the next day
  - [0:19:16](https://youtu.be/C90xGr3kW8Y?t=1156) — "you're picking the one that's formed right before the liquidity's taken"
  - [0:27:19](https://youtu.be/C90xGr3kW8Y?t=1639) — homework recap
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Brand-new teaching (2026 release). He says it is part of "algorithmic price delivery", not buying/selling pressure. No stop/target rules are given for the gap itself beyond using the reaction and nearby liquidity.

title: ICT 2026 New York Lunch Algorithmic Theory \ March 11, 2026
head: Volume imbalance inclusion in a BISI (anchoring rule)  (aliases: buy side imbalance sell side inefficiency, volume imbalance at the low)
body:
- **Kind:** refinement
- **What ICT says:** To include a volume imbalance in a bullish gap, the next candle's open must be higher than the previous candle's close. Anchor the gap's bottom to that previous candle's close (not to its body-high or wick). Example: close 25,165.75; next open 25,166.00 or higher qualifies (he states "anything like 25,166 even or higher"). He pulls prices from the candle data window to verify.
- **How to use:** The gap becomes a "buy side imbalance sell side inefficiency with a volume imbalance at the low".
- **Example in this video:** the 25,165.75 close / 25,166.00 open / 25,177.50 low example above.
- **Timestamps:** [0:03:17](https://youtu.be/C90xGr3kW8Y?t=197) — the open-versus-close test; [0:04:05](https://youtu.be/C90xGr3kW8Y?t=245) — "volume imbalance at the low"
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Consistent with his 2026 teaching to include volume imbalances inside the FVG boundary (see also L26-113).

title: ICT 2026 New York Lunch Algorithmic Theory \ March 11, 2026
head: Inversion FVG / reclaimed bullish FVG from a BISI  (aliases: iFVG, inversion fair value gap, reclaimed bullish FVG, nested gaps)
body:
- **Kind:** refinement / example
- **What ICT says:**
  - A BISI such as the lunch gap changes character to an inversion FVG once price trades through and fails; bodies then respect it as resistance, so price trading up to it is a reason to anticipate lower prices.
  - Multiple gaps can nest ("this one here also nests together"), producing a very strong inversion area; this is "why you got that big pop" up into it.
  - On Wednesday morning a short-term high formed at 9:42; the next gap above (BISI) was expected to act as inversion as well. First it offered discount sensitivity (price traded down into the gap and rallied), then came back up to the BISI, which became a reclaimed bullish FVG; price ran above the 9:42 high into his level, which is the turtle soup, then sold off.
  - Time-frame note: his inversion FVG on the lower time frame is anchored to a sub-1-minute model; on the 1-minute you can anchor from one candle's high to the other candle's low and be fine.
- **How to use:** Short on the way down inside the gap, on a down-close candle (see Execution).

title: ICT 2026 Market Commentary \ March 10, 2026
head: Regular Trading Hours Opening Range Gap (RTH ORG)
body:
- **Kind:** rule / definition
- **What ICT says:** RTH ORG is defined by comparing the previous day's settlement price (4:14 p.m. ET) to today's 9:30 a.m. ET opening. If opening is higher = premium gap; if lower = discount gap. Can be divided into quadrants and octants (eighths) to create reference levels. Previous 5 days' RTH ORGs remain relevant reference points even after price has moved away.
- **How to identify:** On daily chart, mark previous day's 4:14 p.m. closing and current day's 9:30 a.m. opening. Draw line between them. When market opens above settlement = premium; below = discount.
- **How to use:** On intraday charts (1-min, 5-min), algorithmic price action will respect these levels, particularly quadrant and octant subdivisions. Bodies of candlesticks should respect these support/resistance levels. If they do, it's algorithmic. Use as bounce/fail references for order flow confirmation.
- **Example in this video:** Thursday's RTH ORG high was used as octant reference on Tuesday intraday. Candlestick bodies stopped precisely on this octant level multiple times. When price refused to go above it after driving up, it indicated algorithmic rejection of further upside.
- **Timestamps:** [0:09:25](https://youtu.be/54kzPj03Rkg?t=565) — explaining settlement price anchors; [0:14:07](https://youtu.be/54kzPj03Rkg?t=847) — showing octant levels in use; [0:15:43](https://youtu.be/54kzPj03Rkg?t=943) — confirming Thursday's gap becomes Tuesday's discount array
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** RTH ORG uses regular trading hours only (9:30–4:14 ET), not electronic hours. Must distinguish between Monday's gap (using Friday settlement) and Tuesday's gap (using Monday settlement). When price trades above an RTH ORG, it becomes a discount array for future references if you're bullish.

title: ICT 2026 Market Commentary \ March 10, 2026
head: Sell Side Imbalance Buy Side Inefficiency (SIBI)
body:
- **Kind:** definition / rule / entry model
- **What ICT says:** SIBI is a gap that appears when a candlestick leaves a gap below it (sell side unfilled). The rule: "If it wants sell side, this SIBI will remain unfilled." If market does not take the sell side (stays above the SIBI wick), that SIBI will completely fill in later when price retraces. If the SIBI does stay partially open, it means sell side will eventually be taken.
- **How to identify:** Find a down close candlestick with a gap below its low; the unfilled portion is the SIBI. The gap is the inefficiency; the body close shows delivery direction.
- **How to use:** Anticipate: if SIBI unfilled → market doesn't take sell side liquidity → SIBI fills in on retrace. If SIBI fills → market is going lower to take sell side. Stop placement: just above SIBI high if you're short expecting sell side. Entry: on the retrace into SIBI if using as reversal signal.
- **Example in this video:** 10:07 candlestick created a SIBI by closing down with a gap below. The gap (inefficiency) was 24,892.50 level. Market action: price later tried to fill it but stopped at consequent encroachment (higher), proving it was NOT going down to take sell side, so SIBI stayed largely unfilled.
- **Timestamps:** [0:03:00](https://youtu.be/54kzPj03Rkg?t=180) — explaining the post about SIBI; [0:04:37](https://youtu.be/54kzPj03Rkg?t=277) — showing the SIBI on chart; [0:06:13](https://youtu.be/54kzPj03Rkg?t=373) — proving it will fill if NOT taking sell side
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** This logic is algorithmic/conditional, not mechanical. Beginners misread it as "the candle will stay open forever." What it means: IF market is bullish AND doesn't take sell side, THEN SIBI will fill. Read the logic, not just the gap. He contrasts this with people who say "ICT was wrong—the candle didn't stay open," but they missed the condition.

title: ICT 2026 Market Commentary \ March 10, 2026
head: Consequent Encroachment (CE)
body:
- **Kind:** definition / refinement
- **What ICT says:** The midpoint (50% level) of a fair value gap or inefficiency. When a candlestick body touches or stops at CE, it shows algorithmic precision and order flow balance. CE acts as a turning point: bodies stopping at CE indicate hesitation, likely reversal.
- **How to identify:** Divide any gap (SIBI, premium FVG, opening range gap) into two halves. The line separating them is CE. Mark it on your chart.
- **How to use:** If price retraces into an inefficiency and stops at CE (not lower), it's a sign the inefficiency will NOT be fully closed; expect bounce. If price closes BELOW CE on a body, the inefficiency is likely to be fully exploited.
- **Example in this video:** Multiple times on Tuesday, price came down into 10:07 SIBI, touched CE (consequent encroachment midpoint), and bounced. This showed bullish control and failure to take sell side.
- **Timestamps:** [0:06:13](https://youtu.be/54kzPj03Rkg?t=373) — "stopped dead in its tracks" at CE; [0:18:09](https://youtu.be/54kzPj03Rkg?t=1089) — teaching bodies vs wicks at CE level
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Wicks are allowed to go through CE; only bodies matter. Wicks are "coloring outside the lines like a child." Bodies tell the truth.

title: ICT 2026 Market Commentary \ March 10, 2026
head: Fair Value Gap (FVG) — First Presented vs Premium/Discount Arrays
body:
- **Kind:** definition / entry model
- **What ICT says:** FVG is created when a candlestick leaves a gap. Premium FVG = gap left above price (when close is above open). Discount FVG = gap left below price (when close is below open). "First presented FVG" is the FIRST FVG that confirms the direction of the move. Must have displacement (candle not trading back into opening range). Displacement = move outside the previous day's or session's range in the direction you're trading.
- **How to identify:** Identify the gap (high of one candlestick to low of next, or vice versa). Confirm displacement has occurred. Only then label it "first presented FVG." Do not form-fit or cherry-pick; only the first one that meets criteria.
- **How to use:** First presented FVG becomes your initial resistance/support. Entries: trade into it expecting reversal OR trade above/below it expecting continuation. Targets: subsequent buy/sell side liquidity pools. Stop loss: outside the FVG opposite your direction.
- **Example in this video:** At 9:44 a.m., after displacement upward, the first presented FVG was identified (with consequent encroachment annotated). It became the initial resistance that price later tested and held, then bounced from.
- **Timestamps:** [0:27:40](https://youtu.be/54kzPj03Rkg?t=1660) — defining first presented FVG vs secondary; [0:28:27](https://youtu.be/54kzPj03Rkg?t=1707) — showing the FVG on Tuesday chart; [0:29:16](https://youtu.be/54kzPj03Rkg?t=1756) — trading into premium FVG
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** He emphasizes NOT calling a FVG "first presented" until displacement is confirmed. Many traders form-fit and call every gap a FVG. His rule: no displacement = wait for more data. Displacement = now it matters.

title: ICT 2026 Market Commentary \ March 10, 2026
head: Inversion Fair Value Gap (iFVG)
body:
- **Kind:** definition / entry model
- **What ICT says:** iFVG is a fair value gap used in REVERSE. A candlestick that hasn't displaced below its opening (if bearish scenario) or above its opening (if bullish) can function as an iFVG. Entry: trade below it (if it's a premium array) and then back UP into it, using the iFVG to confirm bullish order flow inside it.
- **How to identify:** Look for a candlestick whose body never extended into the opposite direction's range. Example: a down-close candlestick (bullish bias) whose body stayed above the midpoint, with upper gap unfilled.
- **How to use:** If using as iFVG, trade back into the upper portion and watch for order flow confirmation. Stop loss below iFVG midpoint (consequent encroachment). Target: buy side liquidity above.
- **Example in this video:** The 8:57 SIBI was analyzed as an iFVG. Price traded down to test it, then bounced and ran higher, using it as a launching pad.
- **Timestamps:** [0:26:52](https://youtu.be/54kzPj03Rkg?t=1612) — introducing iFVG concept
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** iFVG is NOT the same as a regular FVG. It's a candlestick that never violated a certain threshold, allowing it to serve as reversal confirmation.

title: ICT 2026 Market Commentary \ March 10, 2026
head: Order Block (Propulsion Block variant)
body:
- **Kind:** definition / entry model
- **What ICT says:** An order block is a candlestick (or series of candlesticks) that represents institutional accumulation or distribution. When price trades above an order block's opening after it closes below, it's bullish; when price trades below its opening after it closes above, it's bearish. A propulsion block is an order block that "propels" price—the signal to extrapolate.
- **How to identify:** Find a down-close candlestick during a downtrend (represents selling at support). When price later breaks above its open = activation. The prior candlestick(s) backing it up (if also down-close) = the propulsion setup.
- **How to use:** Once the signal candlestick (order block) has its opening breached on an opening or close basis, project upward extrapolation to next liquidity level. This is NOT support/resistance; it's a trigger.
- **Example in this video:** Not deeply explored, but referenced in passing as part of broader price action reading.
- **Timestamps:** [0:30:04](https://youtu.be/54kzPj03Rkg?t=1804) — mentioning "it can wick beyond, but bodies stop at octant"
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Propulsion blocks are a subset of order blocks and imply rapid extrapolation ("like rocket fuel").

title: ICT 2026 Market Commentary \ March 10, 2026
head: Buy-Side Liquidity (BSL) vs Sell-Side Liquidity (SSL)
body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:** Buy-side liquidity = resting above current price (buy orders waiting for a rally to fill). Sell-side = resting below current price (sell orders from shorts wanting to cover). Identifying these pools and whether they'll be taken = the core of his algorithmic trading.
- **How to identify:** Look at the daily high (BSL) and daily low (SSL) of prior days' ranges. Also, intraday, look at incomplete runs or failed breakout levels that leave liquidity hanging.
- **How to use:** If market structure is bullish, you expect price to run to BSL and stop (or wick through and reverse). If bearish, expect SS. Entry: anticipate the liquidity run and size accordingly. Targets: the known liquidity pools.
- **Example in this video:** Intraday highs (25,000 146.75, 25,108 even) = minor buy side. Sell side at 24,892.50.
- **Timestamps:** [0:08:38](https://youtu.be/54kzPj03Rkg?t=518) — listing the levels; [0:11:01](https://youtu.be/54kzPj03Rkg?t=661) — explaining how algorithm uses sell-side info
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Not all highs/lows = major liquidity pools. Know your context and whether a level was "fought over" (many rejections) vs "breezed through."

title: ICT 2026 Market Commentary \ March 10, 2026
head: Displacement
body:
- **Kind:** definition / rule
- **What ICT says:** Displacement is a candlestick or price move that goes AWAY from the previous session's/day's opening range. Bullish displacement = close above the range. Bearish = close below. Displacement confirms direction and is necessary before calling a FVG "first presented."
- **How to identify:** Check if the candlestick closes outside the prior session's open/close range in the direction of your intended trade.
- **How to use:** Only trade setups (FVGs, order blocks) after displacement in your bias direction is confirmed. No displacement = no signal = wait.
- **Example in this video:** Tuesday morning opened down but displaced UP during the day, confirming the bullish bias. This allowed the "first presented FVG" to be called.
- **Timestamps:** [0:27:40](https://youtu.be/54kzPj03Rkg?t=1660) — emphasizing displacement confirmation
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Displacement must be meaningful (a full candlestick or clear move, not a small wick).

title: ICT 2026 Market Commentary \ March 09, 2026
head: SMT Divergence (Smart Money Trend Divergence)
body:
- **Kind:** definition / rule
- **What ICT says:** SMT divergence occurs when correlated indices move in opposite directions at key levels. Example: Nasdaq makes a lower high while S&P makes a higher high at the same time (relative strength divergence). This indicates the weakest index will pull the broader market lower; strong ones hide the distribution happening underneath.
- **How to identify:** On daily line charts (plotting high or low, not close), overlay correlated pairs (NQ vs ES vs YM). Mark significant highs/lows at the same time period. If one can't keep up = divergence. NQ failing to make new highs while ES makes them = bearish for Nasdaq.
- **How to use:** When weakest index (Nasdaq) shows distribution (lower high), expect pullback to be MORE aggressive in that index. Use divergence as bias confirmation. Don't expect normal correlated moves; expect weakness to cascade.
- **Example in this video:** Nasdaq failed to make higher highs in late January while S&P did. This = distribution. Expect Nasdaq to pull down harder than S&P in any selloff. Also, S&P rejected higher highs last night (March 8) while Dow tried.
- **Timestamps:** [0:03:18](https://youtu.be/CodF_0llnuk?t=198) — explaining how to set up the charts; [0:04:06](https://youtu.be/CodF_0llnuk?t=246) — showing the divergence visually; [0:11:05](https://youtu.be/CodF_0llnuk?t=665) — connecting divergence to bearish distribution
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** This is a FORM of relative strength analysis, not a standalone indicator. Use it with PD arrays and order flow, not alone. SMT is a filter, not a signal.

title: ICT 2026 Market Commentary \ March 09, 2026
head: Macro Times (Algorithmic Time Windows)
body:
- **Kind:** rule / definition
- **What ICT says:** Markets move on scheduled algorithmic time windows. Examples: 8:50–10:10 macro (opening algos), 2:50–3:10 macro (lunch end), 3:15–3:45 macro (last hour spool / market on close setup). Last hour has multiple macros: 2:50–3:10, 3:15–3:45, then market on close (MOC) at 3:45–4:00. These are NOT indicators; they're algorithmic activity triggers.
- **How to identify:** Note the times on your charts. Watch for acceleration or volatility spikes at these windows. Compare across days—pattern should repeat.
- **How to use:** Anticipate moves within these windows. Don't fight them; expect liquidity runs during macro times. If a macro is supposed to create a move and nothing happens, market may be in consolidation or manipulation.
- **Example in this video:** Crude oil March delivery: opened at ~10:40 p.m. ET Sunday, ran to near inefficiency high, sold into evening macro (10:20–11:00 p.m.), then ripped down at 3:15 p.m. macro on Monday. Lowest candle at 3:39 p.m., confirming the last-hour macro window.
- **Timestamps:** [0:13:08](https://youtu.be/CodF_0llnuk?t=788) — teaching macro windows in detail; [0:15:34](https://youtu.be/CodF_0llnuk?t=934) — showing 3:15–3:45 macro in crude oil
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** These are general patterns, not absolutes. During high volatility or geopolitical events, they can shift. He uses 50–10 macro (mentioned in Trader Roundup) frequently but rarely details exact times on video. Lunch macro is roughly 11:50–12:10 and 12:50–1:10.

title: ICT 2026 Market Commentary \ March 09, 2026
head: Propulsion Block & Order Block Theory
body:
- **Kind:** definition / entry model / rule
- **What ICT says:** An order block is a candlestick or series representing institutional activity. A propulsion block is the LAST down-close candlestick in a series; when price trades above its open, it "propels" upward (like rocket fuel). Minimum criteria: price never breaches mean threshold (50% of block range) on retrace—if it does, block is invalid. Once breached on opening basis, expect extrapolation.
- **How to identify:** Find a down-close candlestick (or series). Check if it's the "last" (is the next candle up-close or outside the block range?). Measure the range and mark mean threshold.
- **How to use:** Entry: when price breaks above the opening of a propulsion block. Stop loss: just below the block (or mean threshold, depending on risk tolerance). Target: trace to next unmet buy-side liquidity. Expect rapid extrapolation.
- **Example in this video:** ES March 09: series of down-close candles = order blocks. Last one = propulsion block. When price broke above its open, it "shot all the way" up (his words). Two propulsion blocks in series = "double rocket fuel."
- **Timestamps:** [0:27:00](https://youtu.be/CodF_0llnuk?t=1620) — defining propulsion block; [0:27:47](https://youtu.be/CodF_0llnuk?t=1667) — showing the two-candlestick propulsion setup and extrapolation
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** He references "Month 4 content of the 2016 playlist" (his mentorship videos, now free) for deep order block teaching. Emphasizes: mean threshold is MINIMUM; block can fail if breached on close. Common mistake: calling any down-close candle an "order block" without confirming the last-in-series rule and mean threshold hold.

title: ICT 2026 Market Commentary \ March 09, 2026
head: Turtle Soup (Failed Breakout Reversal)
body:
- **Kind:** entry model / example only
- **What ICT says:** Turtle soup = price trades below a recent low (fails to break out) and immediately reverses. Classic manipulation setup: run a low to stop out bears, then reverse. Not a buy signal itself; rather, context for where NOT to be short and WHERE to go long (back above failed low).
- **How to identify:** Recent swing low broken = turtle soup potential. Watch for immediate reversal back above that low.
- **How to use:** Do NOT short below the low when it's being tested (likely to fail). If it fails, trade long above it. Stop loss: below the low just tested. Target: buy-side liquidity or next key level.
- **Example in this video:** ES on March 09: traded below an earlier low (looked like continuation trade), but immediately bounced back up = turtle soup environment. Not shorting opportunity; a long opportunity using the failed break as confirmation.
- **Timestamps:** [0:27:47](https://youtu.be/CodF_0llnuk?t=1667) — "In other words, go below it, outside of it, and trade back up into it" = turtle soup definition
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Common in low-volatility or consolidation ranges where algos shake out weak positions before the real move.

title: ICT 2026 Market Commentary \ March 09, 2026
head: Change in State of Delivery (CISD)
body:
- **Kind:** definition / refinement
- **What ICT says:** CISD is when price action shifts from consolidation/ranging to a trending move, or from up to down. Identified by candlestick pattern: a change in the candlestick's character (from up-close to down-close or vice versa) that signals the end of a prior trend or the start of a new one.
- **How to identify:** Look for a candlestick that closes opposite the prior candlestick's direction. For example: several up-closes, then a down-close with body below previous range = CISD.
- **How to use:** CISD can be an exit trigger (trend ended) or entry confirmation (new trend starting). Once CISD occurs, check if price is respecting new levels; if bodies are above/below previous inefficiencies, use those as targets.
- **Example in this video:** Not deeply explored in this video, but referenced in passing during ES review.
- **Timestamps:** Mentioned but not detailed with specific timestamp.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** CISD is subtle; wicks don't count, only bodies. One down-close doesn't mean the trend reversed forever; wait for confirmation through subsequent candles respecting new structure.

title: ICT 2026 Market Commentary \ March 09, 2026
head: Market Maker Buy/Sell Model (MMBM/MMSM)
body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:** Market makers use a buy model (accumulation at lower prices) and sell model (distribution at higher prices) to drive order flow. When Nasdaq shows unwillingness to make higher highs = market maker is in sell mode (distribution). Understanding the model = understanding what price must do next.
- **How to identify:** Cross-asset divergence (like SMT) + candle rejection patterns = evidence of sell/buy model in play.
- **How to use:** If market maker is selling (shown by distribution/SMT divergence), expect pullback and lower prices. If buying (NQ leading), expect higher prices. Trade WITH the model, not against it.
- **Example in this video:** Nasdaq failing to make new highs while others do = market maker is selling Nasdaq; expect Nasdaq lower.

- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** This is not a mechanical rule; it's an observation of algorithmic behavior. Multiple factors (news, geopolitical events) can override.

head: Inversion Fair Value Gap (iFVG) in Entry Strategy
body:
- **Kind:** entry model / example only
- **What ICT says:** An iFVG is a candlestick (or small range) that hasn't traded into the opposite direction, leaving an inefficiency. Using it as an entry: wait for price to trade INTO the iFVG, then break back OUT, confirming order flow. Entry on the break above/below the iFVG with body confirmation (not just a wick).
- **How to identify:** Candlestick with upper gap unfilled (bullish context). Body stays in upper half. No close below midpoint = iFVG candidate.
- **How to use:** Entry: Buy above the iFVG high once bodies confirm bullish order flow. Stop loss: below the iFVG low (or below the wick, slightly). Trail stop as price runs.
- **Example in this video:** Early morning, a candlestick left an iFVG. Instruction: watch for bodies trading into it; if they do, check if the body closes below the midpoint (invalidates iFVG). In this case, bodies came into the iFVG but stayed in upper half = bullish. Entry signal confirmed. Trade executed at the break above.
- **Timestamps:** [0:00:02](https://youtu.be/clG2IDpEcjE?t=2) — "using this portion as iFVG"; [0:00:51](https://youtu.be/clG2IDpEcjE?t=51) — showing wick structure and what bodies should NOT do (not close below iFVG midpoint); [0:02:34](https://youtu.be/clG2IDpEcjE?t=154) — confirming the level still valid
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** iFVG is NOT automatically a buy signal. It's a FRAMEWORK. Confirmation = bodies respecting the boundary, not closing below midpoint on attempt(s).

head: Stop Loss Placement & Trailing Strategy
body:
- **Kind:** rule / process
- **What ICT says:** Place stop loss (SL) just below the wick of the iFVG. Once price takes out a higher high (confirms bullish), roll the SL up to just below that new high. This "minimizes open risk." He uses the term "rolling the stop" or "trail the stop." Goal: turn a losing trade into a breakeven or small profit within seconds of confirmation.
- **How to identify:** Mark the wick/low of key candlesticks. This is your SL anchor point.
- **How to use:** 1. Entry with SL at iFVG low. 2. Price breaks higher = first target hit, roll SL to breakeven or just below new high. 3. Price breaks another high = roll SL again, now locked in $50 profit (example). 4. Keep rolling until target or stop is hit.
- **Example in this video:** Initial SL just below iFVG. Price breaks high of previous candlestick = roll SL to just below that high, now "risking less than it would cost for pizza delivery." Price continues, roll SL again to now lock in $50. Final exit at intraday high target = $100 (before commissions).

- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Rolling SL is NOT the same as moving stop loss DOWN (which would be bad risk management). Always roll UP (in favor of longs) or DOWN (in favor of shorts). Never against your position.

head: PD Array Settings & Volume Imbalance Sensitivity
body:

title: ICT 2026 Market Commentary \ March 08, 2026
head: Balance Price Range (BPR) & Dealing Range
body:
- **Kind:** definition / rule
- **What ICT says:** A balance price range = an area where price traded UP and then DOWN (or vice versa), showing TWO directional deliveries within the same range. BPR is relevant because it suggests a range may be established; price may trade inside it or use specific levels within it for reversals.
- **How to identify:** Candlestick or range where price traded up (high touched), then closed down (low touched), or vice versa. Two candlesticks showing two directions = balanced.
- **How to use:** In BPR, expect price to use inefficiencies within the range rather than break out. If price breaks out of BPR, it's likely a shift from high-resistance to low-resistance conditions (or vice versa). Use BPR as context for whether to expect range-bound or trend-following behavior.
- **Example in this video:** Crude oil: BPR exists from a prior candle that had both up and down delivery. When price is inside this BPR, he expects it to use the inefficiencies and stay inside. When it breaks BPR on a close, it can open the door to new draws (lower levels).
- **Timestamps:** [0:40:26](https://youtu.be/JIs96_2rfkE?t=2426) — "Balanced price range exists here... we've seen two directions"; [0:41:13](https://youtu.be/JIs96_2rfkE?t=2473) — explaining BPR implications for retracements
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** BPR is a context filter, not a standalone signal. It tells you what kind of price action to EXPECT, not what to trade. If you're bearish and price is inside a BPR, you expect lower prices to come eventually, but they may not come immediately (BPR may be respected first).

title: ICT 2026 Market Commentary \ March 08, 2026
head: Nesting PD Arrays & Multi-Level Inefficiencies
body:
- **Kind:** definition / refinement
- **What ICT says:** When two PD arrays (FVGs) are positioned one inside the other (nested), they create nested inefficiencies. The OUTER array is typically the premium/discount bias; the INNER is a secondary reference. When you have nested arrays, price can utilize either. High-volatility conditions may cause price to wick through outer array into inner array and back (wild swings), so stops must account for this.
- **How to identify:** Mark FVGs on your chart. If one FVG is entirely above/below another FVG of opposite nature (e.g., premium FVG nesting above a discount FVG), you have nesting.
- **How to use:** In nesting zones, expect wider stops and more volatile retracements. Don't assume price will respect just the outer array; be prepared for it to visit the inner array on wicks. Stops must be wide enough to avoid being shaken out on noise. Targets can utilize either level.
- **Example in this video:** Pound dollar (or EURUSD): two PD arrays nested. Upper array = premium (normal FVG). Lower = inversion FVG below. When price retraces, it can touch outer, inner, or bounce between them.
- **Timestamps:** [0:55:33](https://youtu.be/JIs96_2rfkE?t=3333) — explaining nested arrays on EURUSD; [0:56:20](https://youtu.be/JIs96_2rfkE?t=3380) — clarifying why both arrays matter
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Nesting isn't always present. Only relevant when multiple inefficiencies are stacked. When present, it's because the market is showing BOTH bullish and bearish potentials; use it as a warning to use wider stops or wait for directional clarity.

title: ICT 2026 Market Commentary \ March 08, 2026
head: Breakaway Gap (vs Measuring Gap vs Closing Gap)
body:
- **Kind:** definition / rule
- **What ICT says:** Breakaway gap = a gap that remains OPEN (unfilled) and signals the start of a trend or impulsive move. Measuring gap = a gap that forms mid-trend and projects the extent of the remaining move. Closing gap = a gap filled on a subsequent trading period. A breakaway is strong if it STAYS open and price doesn't retrace into it.
- **How to identify:** After a breakout of a level, if a gap is left unfilled and price accelerates away, it's breakaway. If price comes back and fills it, it becomes a closing gap (weak breakout).
- **How to use:** Identify breakaway gaps to confirm strong directional move. Use a filled gap as a failed break. Unfilled gaps = trend strength. Example: short a market expecting sell-off; if price gaps down and doesn't fill the gap, the sell-off is strong. Target = measuring gap (or further inefficiencies).
- **Example in this video:** Crude oil: run from low up to near inefficiency high, then pullback. Small gap left in retrace could act as breakaway gap if price doesn't return to fill it. If it stays open, next run up is likely.
- **Timestamps:** [0:41:13](https://youtu.be/JIs96_2rfkE?t=2473) — "I prefer it doesn't do that because I think this should act as a breakaway gap"; [0:40:26](https://youtu.be/JIs96_2rfkE?t=2426) — discussing next fair value gap as measuring gap
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Breakaway gaps are more meaningful in intraday timeframes; on daily/weekly, gaps are sometimes filled weeks later (less relevant for short-term trades). Context matters: in strong trend, gaps stay open; in reversals, gaps are quickly filled.

title: ICT 2026 Market Commentary \ March 08, 2026
head: Discount Sensitivity vs Premium Sensitivity (Price Action Behavior)
body:
- **Kind:** definition / rule
- **What ICT says:** Discount array = inefficiency below current price (from down-close candle). When price retraces into discount array, "discount sensitivity" means bodies should stay in UPPER half of the inefficiency. If bodies breach lower half, discount is lost. Premium array = inefficiency above price. Premium sensitivity = bodies must stay in LOWER half. Sensitivity = the boundary that bodies must respect to maintain bullish/bearish control.
- **How to identify:** Mark FVG. Identify if it's above (premium) or below (discount) current price. When price retraces, watch if body respects the boundary. Upper half vs lower half = midpoint (CE).
- **How to use:** In discount array, if retracement bodies stay above CE, it's bullish. If they breach below CE on close, discount is lost and bear control is in question. Same logic reversed for premium. Use this to confirm or invalidate your bias.
- **Example in this video:** ES March 09: FVG formed (premium = above price). When price retraced, bodies came DOWN into it but didn't close below CE = bullish, discount sensitivity held. Price then ripped higher.
- **Timestamps:** [0:26:09](https://youtu.be/JIs96_2rfkE?t=1569) — explaining discount sensitivity on S&P; [0:27:47](https://youtu.be/JIs96_2rfkE?t=1667) — "Bullish order flow is going to respect the upper boundaries of a discount array"
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** This is the CORE of reading order flow without looking "inside the candle" at tick data or volume profiles. Bodies + levels = pure order flow.

title: ICT 2026 Market Commentary \ March 08, 2026
head: Relative Equal Highs/Lows & Old Highs/Lows (Liquidity Pools)
body:
- **Kind:** definition / rule
- **What ICT says:** Old highs/lows = liquidity resting at prior significant levels. Relative equal highs = price is making a similar high to a prior high but not higher (resistance). These are pools of buy-side (above, for shorts to cover) or sell-side (below, for longs to cover) liquidity. Algorithm will run these levels to "sweep" trapped traders' stops.
- **How to identify:** Mark on daily/weekly prior significant highs and lows. When price approaches them, mark as potential liquidity pool.
- **How to use:** Anticipate runs to old levels. Use these as target references. Stop placement: beyond old levels (to avoid being swept). If you're short and old high is being run, either exit or expand stop beyond the high (if risk allows).
- **Example in this video:** Dow: old high from prior month is a draw. Nasdaq August lows are a draw for first half of year. Dollar index: old high is a draw if risk-off scenario plays out.
- **Timestamps:** [0:11:05](https://youtu.be/JIs96_2rfkE?t=665) — discussing August lows as draw; [0:21:27](https://youtu.be/JIs96_2rfkE?t=1287) — "these lows here... uh again, this is March contract, so... I like these"; [0:28:35](https://youtu.be/JIs96_2rfkE?t=1715) — marking sell-side and buy-side liquidity
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Not all old levels matter. Significance = how recent, how violently rejected, and how many times price has returned to it. Recent highs/lows within 5–10 days are more relevant than years-old levels.

title: ICT 2026 Market Commentary \ March 08, 2026
head: Contract Rollover: Nearby vs Next Month Inefficiencies
body:
- **Kind:** definition / process
- **What ICT says:** When March contract is about to expire, he examines both March (nearby/front month) and June (next month out) contracts. Inefficiencies that exist in June but NOT in March can be used as hidden targets for March trading. This is because June is thinner (less volume), showing unmet inefficiencies. Those inefficiencies will eventually be filled once June becomes the front month. Use June inefficiencies as target guidance for March trades.
- **How to identify:** Pull up continuous, March, and June contracts side-by-side. Compare for inefficiencies. If June shows a clear gap that March doesn't have, mark it.
- **How to use:** When trading March, use June's inefficiencies as additional target levels. This gives you "hidden" targets that the retail crowd isn't seeing (they only look at front month). Also, it's a way to identify longer-term draws.
- **Example in this video:** Nasdaq March vs June: June shows spotty inefficiencies (less helpful visually), but when comparing to March and continuous, the overall picture becomes clearer. He uses this to confirm bearish draw to August lows.
- **Timestamps:** [0:07:06](https://youtu.be/JIs96_2rfkE?t=426) — explaining March vs June contracts; [0:08:43](https://youtu.be/JIs96_2rfkE?t=523) — using next month inefficiencies as macro targets
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Rollover mechanics: March expires around mid-month (roughly 3rd Friday); traders begin shifting to June as March nears expiration. Volume migrates. Use this to time when hidden inefficiencies become relevant.
