title: ICT Technical Review \ NQ Futures March \ February 03, 2026
head: Suspension Block
body:
- **Kind:** definition · rule
- **What ICT says:** A consolidation pattern with volume bounce at both the high and the low. On the daily chart shown (NQ March 2026), this created a "positive balance outside efficiency" which made it a suspension block. The upper and lower edges are the extremes where volume was transacted; the interior is the range of equilibrium.
- **How to identify:** Two clear volume bounces (one at the top, one at the bottom) with balanced or positive volume profile. Must see volume confirmation at both extremes.
- **How to use:** The midpoint of the suspension block is the fulcrum. If price trades above it and closes above it in the upper half, it becomes bullish. If price whips into the upper half but fails to close above it, that turns the suspension block into a bearish inversion fair value gap (iFVG). Price action inside the range is extremely difficult; traders new to this should wait for cleaner market conditions (post-spring, after early-year manipulation).
- **Example in this video:** NQ March daily chart: suspension block formed with lows around 18,390 area and highs in upper range; the midpoint served as the trigger level. Price went up, only whipped into the upper half with a wick, then reversed—turning bullish into bearish.
- **Timestamps:** [0:00:53](https://youtu.be/486N8ow3U2A?t=53) (suspension block defined) · [0:02:29](https://youtu.be/486N8ow3U2A?t=149) (testing relative equal highs) · [0:06:30](https://youtu.be/486N8ow3U2A?t=390) (suspension block as fulcrum, upper half wick action) · [0:04:04](https://youtu.be/486N8ow3U2A?t=244) (advice to wait until spring if inexperienced in ranges)
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** The suspension block midpoint can act as a reversal trigger *before* price reaches it. Merely touching the upper half without closing above it creates a bearish bias. Not every consolidation with volume at extremes is a suspension block; you need the "positive balance outside efficiency" structure.

title: ICT Technical Review \ NQ Futures March \ February 03, 2026
head: Consequent Encroachment (CE)
body:
- **Kind:** definition · refinement
- **What ICT says:** The midpoint of the suspension block, used as the key trigger or fulcrum level. "As long as we remain below that we were going to be bearish." If unable to trade above it and establish above it, the bias stays bearish.
- **How to identify:** Calculate the midpoint of the suspension block (high + low) / 2. This is the consequent encroachment level.
- **How to use:** Use it as a pivot level: if price closes above it and stays above, switch bias to bullish. If price fails to close above it or only wicks into the upper region, the bearish bias remains. It's a decision point, not an entry point itself.
- **Example in this video:** NQ March: the daily suspension block midpoint was approximately in the zone of the previous day's close. Price rallied up to it on 1-minute chart, hesitated, and reversed—exactly what ICT was watching for to confirm bearish bias continuation.
- **Timestamps:** [0:00:53](https://youtu.be/486N8ow3U2A?t=53) (setup) · [0:04:50](https://youtu.be/486N8ow3U2A?t=290) (trigger point on 1-minute, rally up to CE of daily suspension block) · [0:06:30](https://youtu.be/486N8ow3U2A?t=390) (inversion FVG at the midpoint showing bearish turn)
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** CE is specific to the suspension block's midpoint, not a generic midpoint level. It's a qualifier and confirmation tool, not a selection or timing tool by itself.

title: ICT Technical Review \ NQ Futures March \ February 03, 2026
head: Gradient Levels / Quadrant Levels / Eighths
body:
- **Kind:** refinement · entry model
- **What ICT says:** Fibonacci subdivisions (eighths, sixteenths) applied to create more granular price levels for entries and draws on liquidity. "If you put these levels in there, you'll get levels that would be pertinent for more highly specific quadrant levels or gradient levels." Originally used "gradients" terminology to avoid confusion when discussing quadrants and eighths.
- **How to identify:** Apply Fibonacci tools set to display eighths and sixteenths in addition to the standard quarters (or quadrants). These subdivisions create "gradient" levels within the larger framework.
- **How to use:** Use gradient levels to fine-tune entries and to identify micro draws on liquidity within larger structures. Discount and premium wicks can be graded (subdivided) using these levels to show where specific inefficiencies occur.
- **Example in this video:** NQ daily chart: the discount wick was graded into gradient levels; on the 1-minute, price traded down into these gradient levels, identifying precise support/resistance zones. The "lower of the two" discount wicks' gradient subdivisions acted as an intermediate-term draw on liquidity.
- **Timestamps:** [0:01:41](https://youtu.be/486N8ow3U2A?t=101) (introduction to fib settings for eighths and quadrants) · [0:05:39](https://youtu.be/486N8ow3U2A?t=339) (two wicks graded with gradients, lower wick as DOL)
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Gradient/quadrant/eighths terminology can be confusing; the principle is the same—subdivision of price ranges into smaller imbalances to identify precise liquidity.

title: ICT Technical Review \ NQ Futures March \ February 03, 2026
head: Discount Wick & Premium Wick
body:
- **Kind:** definition · entry model
- **What ICT says:** Wicks are gaps, just like full gaps. They can be graded (subdivided) using fibonacci levels. Discount wicks form when price trades down to a lower level and leaves a gap on the way back up; premium wicks form when price trades up and leaves a gap on the way back down.
- **How to identify:** Look for wicks on daily charts; they appear as small gaps between the close and the next open or between candles. These can be graded and subdivided for precision.
- **How to use:** Graded discount/premium wicks become draws on liquidity. Price will often gravitate back to these levels. On the 1-minute chart, price can then target the gradient levels within those wicks.
- **Example in this video:** NQ daily: there were two discount wicks graded. The lower of the two became the intermediate-term draw. On the 1-minute, price traded down into the gradient levels of this lower discount wick (the red line ~18,225 area) after breaking down.
- **Timestamps:** [0:01:41](https://youtu.be/486N8ow3U2A?t=101) (wicks as gaps, not new concept) · [0:02:29](https://youtu.be/486N8ow3U2A?t=149) (discount wick on daily chart) · [0:05:39](https://youtu.be/486N8ow3U2A?t=339) (two graded discount wicks) · [0:08:55](https://youtu.ie/486N8ow3U2A?t=535) (low of daily discount wick as intermediate-term DOL)
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Not every wick is tradeable; context (daily bias, market structure) matters. The grading (gradient subdivision) is what makes precision entry/exit points.

title: ICT Technical Review \ NQ Futures March \ February 03, 2026
head: New Week Opening Gap (NWOG)
body:
- **Kind:** definition · rule
- **What ICT says:** The gap formed at the opening of the new week (Sunday evening into Monday morning in electronic trading). Treated as a liquidity pool. When price breaks below it and then returns to its halfway point or full range, this becomes a draw on liquidity.
- **How to identify:** Find the Sunday open (first tick of the week) and Monday's first candle; the gap between them is the NWOG. Identify the high and low of this gap, and the midpoint.
- **How to use:** NWOG acts as a liquidity pool. Once broken, traders hunt for equilibrium (halfway point) or full closure. Use it as a target after initial moves away from it. It's a reference structure for intraday traders.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 1-minute chart: market opened (RTH 9:30) above the NWOG, then gravitated down to the gap's low, broke below it, traded to the low, found premium sensitivity, and broke further into the halfway point of the lower discount wick on the daily chart.
- **Timestamps:** [0:04:04](https://youtu.be/486N8ow3U2A?t=244) (trading hours opening range gap, specific to ICT's framework, not a breakout strategy) · [0:08:07](https://youtu.be/486N8ow3U2A?t=487) (NWOG as liquidity reference, "just like a dog whistle") · [0:10:30](https://youtu.be/486N8ow3U2A?t=630) (new week opening gap in the larger price sequence, next area of interest when trading down from higher levels)
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** ICT's NWOG framework is distinct from "opening range breakout" strategies—he's not chasing breakouts. He's identifying NWOG as a liquidity structure to run through or draw back to, depending on larger bias.

title: ICT Technical Review \ NQ Futures March \ February 03, 2026
head: SMT Divergence
body:
- **Kind:** definition · qualifier
- **What ICT says:** A comparison of relative price highs between NQ and ES at the same time of day. If NQ makes new highs but ES does not (or vice versa), there's a divergence. "It is not a selection tool. It is not a timing tool." It's a qualifier—a warning that momentum is not synchronized across the indices.
- **How to identify:** Plot the highs (or cumulative high prices) of both NQ and ES on the same timeframe for the same session. Draw a line showing cumulative highs. If one index rises while the other flatlines or falls, you have divergence.
- **How to use:** Divergence indicates weakness or lack of follow-through. If NQ rallies into inefficiencies and ES diverges, shorts can be taken because the move lacks institutional conviction across the complex.
- **Example in this video:** ES chart shown plotting only the high price (cumulative) against NQ's highs. NQ rallied and made inefficiency highs, but ES failed to keep pace—divergence confirmed weakness. When SMT broke the divergence and moved lower, shorts could be taken as the breakdown accelerated and took out SSL.
- **Timestamps:** [0:07:19](https://youtu.be/486N8ow3U2A?t=439) (SMT divergence setup, comparing NQ highs with ES highs) · [0:08:07](https://youtu.be/486N8ow3U2A?t=487) (divergence breaks aggressively lower, shorts taken)
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** SMT divergence is a confirmation and risk qualifier, not a standalone trade signal. It works best when you already have a bias and are looking for confirmation of reversal.

title: ICT Technical Review \ NQ Futures March \ February 03, 2026
head: Opening Range Gap Theory vs. Opening Range Breakout
body:
- **Kind:** rule · refinement
- **What ICT says:** ICT does NOT use opening range breakout strategy. His approach is specifically about the opening range *gap* structure and drawing on liquidity within it. "I don't use a opening range breakout strategy. You know, that's all chasing price. I'm not interested in that. I want to know what I'm looking for and then key off of a very specific price level and I'm trading against the direction of where the market's going to go."
- **How to identify:** Mark the RTH (regular trading hours) open time (9:30 ET) and the previous day's close or electronic session settlement. The gap and the range created by these constitute the opening range.
- **How to use:** Instead of chasing a breakout above or below, use the opening range's midpoint, edges, and draws on liquidity as targets. If bearish, scale into shorts on rallies into inefficiencies within or near the opening range, not on breakouts.
- **Example in this video:** NQ opened gapped up from the previous close, but instead of chasing the gap higher, ICT showed how to use the gap's internal structure (halfway point, full range) as targets on down moves. The market opened at the gap high, traded to the midpoint, then broke out of the range low—all of this price action was driven by the gap structure, not by breakout chasing.
- **Timestamps:** [0:04:04](https://youtu.be/486N8ow3U2A?t=244) (explicit statement: "my trading hours opening range gap theory, which is not what everybody else talks about... I don't use a opening range breakout strategy")
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** This is a critical distinction. Breakout chasers buy highs and sell lows; ICT traders use the gap structure to predict reversals and trade against the initial direction.

title: ICT Technical Review \ NQ Futures March \ February 03, 2026
head: Tape Reading & Inefficiencies
body:
- **Kind:** rule · entry model
- **What ICT says:** "I want to sell short when the market's going up into some kind of inefficiency, some kind of a premium array or take out an old high." Reading the tape means watching for resistance (old highs, premium zones) being taken out, then shorting as the market pushes into these inefficiencies.
- **How to identify:** Identify old highs, premium areas (previous resistance), and inefficiencies (gaps, imbalances). Watch price rally into these zones.
- **How to use:** On rallies into inefficiencies or old highs, place shorts. Combine this with time-of-day context (pre-market, early RTH) for timing. The tape shows where resistance exists; price moving through it is the trigger.
- **Example in this video:** NQ rallied up to take out the previous Friday's high and old resistance levels on the 1-minute chart—these were inefficiencies. Shorts could be taken as price moved through these zones, with targets below at draws on liquidity.
- **Timestamps:** [0:11:19](https://youtu.be/486N8ow3U2A?t=679) (tape reading definition and entry approach)
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Tape reading requires experience. New traders should practice by observing price action and marking where entries *would have been* before risking real capital.

title: ICT Technical Review \ NQ Futures March \ February 03, 2026
head: Market Difficulty & Volatility During Geopolitical Periods
body:
- **Kind:** psychology · risk management
- **What ICT says:** Early-year trading is extremely difficult due to geopolitical manipulation and metals market volatility. If you're brand new and not experienced in range trading, take 2-3 months off and come back in spring (end of March into April) when price action is cleaner. "The markets are stuck in these large ranges. Unless you know how to trade inside these ranges, it's going to be very problematic for you." Current high volatility means "everyone's methodology" has been questioned; it's not the trader or the method that's failing—it's the environment.
- **How to identify:** Watch for wide ranges, choppy price action, and inability to establish new daily trends. Geopolitical news and metals market moves (FX, commodities) drive this.
- **How to use:** New traders should reduce or pause activity. Experienced traders should reduce position size (micros instead of minis, 1-3 contracts instead of 30) and only take high-confidence setups. Avoid revenge trading and over-sizing.
- **Example in this video:** NQ range-bound action on Feb 3, 2026—a difficult, choppy environment. ICT used this as an opportunity to teach but also warned viewers that this is not the environment to learn trading.
- **Timestamps:** [0:03:17](https://youtu.be/486N8ow3U2A?t=197) (description of difficult environment) · [0:04:04](https://youtu.be/486N8ow3U2A?t=244) (advice to wait until spring) · [0:12:07](https://youtu.be/486N8ow3U2A?t=727) (current volatility affecting all traders, regardless of methodology) · [0:12:55](https://youtu.be/486N8ow3U2A?t=775) (position sizing during high volatility: micros, 1-3 max)
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** This is a key teaching moment: market conditions matter more than method. Adapting position size is not a failure; it's professional risk management.

title: How Do I Engage Markets When I Don't Have An Initial Bias?
head: Engaging the market with no initial bias: wait for the first hour range  (aliases: first hour's range, 9:30-10:30 range, submitting to the opening range)
body:
- **Kind:** entry model / rule
- **What ICT says:** If you don't know which side to focus on and are waiting for more information, submit to the first half hour of the opening range, look for the first FVG, and let the market consume 9:45 or 10:00 news. If you are reluctant to do anything until the first hour trades (also when you "don't trust the direction"), it is usually because the market rips off in one direction. After the first hour (9:30 to 10:30), mark the highest high and lowest low of that range and grade it with a fib: "all of your key PD arrays are going to form in close proximity to one of these gradient levels". The 50% level of that range is the pivot: if bullish, the upper half is sensitive, so focus on it and ignore the lower half; if the market stops you out and goes back below equilibrium into the lower half, look for the lower quadrant or a complete roll-over to the low of the first hour. Also usable when markets run one-sided, when he waits for 9:45/10:00 news, or when he has a hard-line bias.
- **How to identify:** First-hour range = highest high to lowest low between 9:30 and 10:30 ET; 50 percent = equilibrium; gradient levels at the fib quarters/eighths.
- **How to use:** Once the range is set, trade PD arrays that sit on the gradient levels in the half that agrees with your higher-timeframe draw. Here he was bullish because price looked headed for the consequent encroachment of the daily suspension block, so he used the upper half of the first-hour range.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 1m March contract: he highlighted the first-hour high and low, then zoomed into the upper half. Price almost reached the first-hour high, then broke a low and went to the next gradient level; just above that level was a small gap, a swing low sat on the level, and further left an inefficiency, a valid candidate for a high-probability discount BISI. Price traded to its CE with bodies staying in the upper half, rallied, dropped back to touch the gradient level, rallied and eventually took out the buy-side above the relative equal highs.
- **Timestamps:** [0:05:46](https://youtu.be/zyKAPNk_prA?t=346) — what to do when you don't know which side; [0:06:33](https://youtu.be/zyKAPNk_prA?t=393) — mark the 9:30-10:30 high and low, grade it, upper half if bullish; [0:08:11](https://youtu.be/zyKAPNk_prA?t=491) — gradient level, swing low, discount BISI candidate; [0:13:50](https://youtu.be/zyKAPNk_prA?t=830) — why the upper half; lower-half contingency
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** He promises more specifics on the first-hour range later in the year. He admits that anyone can do it in hindsight; the point is the procedure.

title: How Do I Engage Markets When I Don't Have An Initial Bias?
head: Discount BISI at a gradient level, respected in the upper half
body:
- **Kind:** example / entry criteria
- **What ICT says:** A valid discount PD array: a BISI (buyside imbalance sellside inefficiency) sitting on a gradient level, with a swing low on that level. Within the upper half of the high-to-low range, it stays at equilibrium: accumulation, second-stage reaccumulation, then it rips higher attacking the buy-side; the bodies converge around the same level (ignore the wick that was marked as highest high at the time).
- **Example in this video:** 1m March contract. A bullish model: price falls into the discount BISI, the bodies of the following candles bunch together, then price takes the buy-side above the relative equal highs. His long used the original stop below the low and he sat through some heat before price ripped above the bodies and he exited.

head: Inversion FVG + CISD + bearish order block (demo executions)
body:
- **Kind:** entry model (applied example)
- **What ICT says:** Price traded up toward an inversion FVG ("I was watching to see if it was going to use that"); it went below it, producing a change in state of delivery marked by three consecutive up-close candles, which he treats as the bearish order block, and the opening price of that sequence as the entry reference. Price traded up until it hit that level quickly and pulled away; he entered as it pulled away (some slippage), then added three more times, including when price traded back up into it, and exited at the CE of the BISI below, exactly to the tick, with a limit order. If instead price had traded above the order block he would have stopped out, then looked long using the market maker buy model.

body:

If price gets above the half and trades outside it, he anticipates the block acting as an inversion FVG and a challenge to the relative equal highs. title: ICT 2026 Smart Money Concepts Lecture \ January 29, 2026
head: Draw on liquidity first ("where is it going?")  (aliases ICT uses: "where is it drawing to", "the secret ingredient", "reach for", cookie-cutter run)
body:
- **Kind:** rule / philosophy (central lesson of the video)
- **What ICT says:**
  - The first and most important skill is knowing where the market is likely to go next. Until you know that, entries, stop loss and targets are "not even important yet".
  - Knowing the draw lets you frame risk (where your stop goes), which he calls the first real measure of understanding what you are doing.
  - Price is always doing one of two things: running to liquidity or running to an inefficiency, above or below the market. It is not "buying and selling pressure", indicators, or bookmap bubbles. He calls the repeating pieces "signatures", not patterns.
  - If you know the draw correctly you can trade "any old thing" (his "flip a quarter" line) with a realistic stop and still win.
  - Beginners should not try to pick entries at all at first. Only pick the direction/draw; afterwards, in hindsight, look back to see what PD arrays (FVG, breaker, Silver Bullet, market maker model) formed in the delivery.
  - The "cookie cutter" moves he lists, in rising difficulty: (1) run from an inefficiency to a liquidity pool; (2) run from a liquidity pool to an inefficiency; (3) run from one liquidity pool to another, e.g. a false breakout above an old high into a false breakout below an old low (he calls this the highest form of what he teaches, "not all that complex" but needs experience).
- **How to identify:** On the chart ask: where is the nearest premium (or discount) liquidity, and where is the nearest inefficiency? Price in a discount reaches up for the nearest short-term high / minor BSL or an unfilled gap.
- **How to use:**
  - Pick the smallest, easiest objective. Short-term high (minor BSL) is easier to find than an inefficiency because shorts will have trailed their buy-stop protection just above it.
  - Two-stage exit with multiple micros: partial at the minor BSL / short-term high, final exit (his word "terminus") at the low of the inefficiency above.
  - If the expected draw is not clearly there, do nothing; be content with it.
- **Example in this video:** NQ, pre-8:30 to 9:00 ET. Price had sold off overnight leaving lows jagged (no equal lows). A minor BSL sat at the lower of two relative equal highs. Above it was an upper-quadrant inefficiency. After the 8:30 news price ran to the short-term high and then up to the bottom (low) of the inefficiency, then sold hard. He calls that "low-hanging fruit" and says "you could be done".
- **Timestamps:**
  - [0:09:45](https://youtu.be/8wHewi6N6dg?t=585) — first identification of minor BSL above the .375 level and the inefficiency (volume imbalance + SIBI) above it
  - [0:28:25](https://youtu.be/8wHewi6N6dg?t=1705) — "you already remove 90% of the struggle if you can define the range"
  - [0:52:58](https://youtu.be/8wHewi6N6dg?t=3178) — the three cookie-cutter run types
  - [1:39:32](https://youtu.be/8wHewi6N6dg?t=5972) — "if you know where the market's going, you can trade any old thing"
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** He says you do not need price to take the range high or break the range low; the whole point is "disarming" the need to be right about how far it goes. This is the same "first lesson" he claims to have taught on his first live stream after the BabyPips days.

title: ICT 2026 Smart Money Concepts Lecture \ January 29, 2026
head: Dealing range from the pre-session high and low (and use the smaller/lower reference high)  (aliases ICT uses: dealing range, "the canvas", range between two reference points, pre-session range)
body:
- **Kind:** rule / refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - Before 9:30 ET, define the range as the pre-session low and a pre-session high. Everything that matters for the first idea is inside that range. You may never need price to trade above the high or below the low.
  - When there are two candidate highs (here a lower high and a higher relative-equal-high), use the lower/smaller reference as the range high "to make things very simple" and to reduce the need to be right. The lower high is also the more reactionary one (the sell-off from it was more energetic than from the other).
  - Why not assume the higher equal high is the draw: when the two highs sit close together and are obvious, price may bump the lower one, stay inside the range and never clear the higher one. He explicitly says this is what he watches for between 9:30 and 10:00.
  - Using the larger high instead would still have been "fine, not grossly out of spec"; the inefficiency below it was still the focal point.
  - Time scope: for a 9:30 plan he cares about the previous 30 minutes, hour or hour and a half; he says you can do this all day on sub-1-minute charts.
  - Beginner benefit: trading inside a defined range removes the need to know where the next big run is. Big runs "color outside the lines" and a new trader is not equipped to find those yet; aim for "base hits".
- **How to identify:** Pre-9:30 low to pre-9:30 high. Within it, locate where price rejected (bodies and wicks show it has no interest in going lower). Look for relative equal highs/lows (smooth) vs. a jagged run.
- **How to use:**
  - Three quarters of the range (upper quadrant for a rally) is the OTE zone. An inefficiency near that area is a valid target; he says a run to the OTE-area inefficiency is enough and price need not reach the equal highs.
  - Frame stop and target from the range edges; use the range as the canvas for choosing a draw.
- **Example in this video:** NQ pre-session: range low at the pre-8:30 low (sell-side taken, failing to reach a lower eighth), range high at the lower of the two relative-equal highs (a minor BSL). Inefficiency sat roughly at three quarters of the low-to-high range.
- **Timestamps:**
  - [0:12:13](https://youtu.be/8wHewi6N6dg?t=733) — defines the pre-9:30 range to observe
  - [0:19:49](https://youtu.be/8wHewi6N6dg?t=1189) — "inside this low and this high, that is your dealing range"
  - [0:36:19](https://youtu.be/8wHewi6N6dg?t=2179) — use the lower high as the high of the range
  - [0:56:08](https://youtu.be/8wHewi6N6dg?t=3368) — use the smaller reference point; the larger high would still have been fine
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** "Three quarters of that range is optimal trade entry" is his loose phrasing (upper quadrant of the range, he calls it OTE); he says OTE was the flagship thing he taught for years before PD arrays (revealed 2016 behind the paywall, now free).

title: ICT 2026 Smart Money Concepts Lecture \ January 29, 2026
head: Jagged vs smooth levels (relative equal highs/lows as the draw)  (aliases ICT uses: made jagged, smooth levels, relative equal highs, relative equal lows)
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - A side of the market where price keeps making lower low after lower low with no relative equal lows is "jagged". There is nothing smooth below to draw to.
  - After a jagged run, look for where the market left smooth levels (relative equal highs or lows). The market gravitates to the smooth level. He said he has taught this "this year and previous years".
  - A shift in market structure after the jagged drop, keyed off a sell-side-imbalance gap that then inverts, signals the turn toward the smooth level.
- **How to identify:** Count the lows in the leg down: if each is lower and none matches another, it is jagged. The relative equal highs above, where bodies converge (here near the .125 level), are smooth.
- **How to use:** Use the smooth level (or the nearest minor pool before it) as the draw after a jagged run; wait for 8:30 or 9:30 as the starting gun (see time section).
- **Example in this video:** NQ overnight: lows kept dropping with no equal lows (jagged). Relative equal highs sat above with bodies converging on the .125 line from yesterday's RTH opening range gap. He used this as the "I like that as a draw, staying inside the range, needing it not to trade there" idea.
- **Timestamps:**
  - [0:26:05](https://youtu.be/8wHewi6N6dg?t=1565) — "levels that are smooth after levels that have been made jagged"
  - [0:26:52](https://youtu.be/8wHewi6N6dg?t=1612) — explains jagged meaning nothing relatively equal on the way down
  - [0:46:33](https://youtu.be/8wHewi6N6dg?t=2793) — jagged lows vs smooth relative equal highs again
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** none contradicting earlier teaching; this reuses his relative equal highs/lows liquidity concept, framed as "jagged vs smooth".

title: ICT 2026 Smart Money Concepts Lecture \ January 29, 2026
head: Minor buy-side liquidity / where short stops sit (short-term high as the draw)  (aliases ICT uses: minor buy side, short-term high, buy stop above an old high)
body:
- **Kind:** definition / reasoning
- **What ICT says:**
  - A short seller protects the position with a buy stop above a high. After a big energetic sell-off that makes a new lower low, shorts trail their stops down to just above the most recent short-term high; that clustered buy stop is the minor BSL.
  - Traders that kept stops above the relative equal highs (thinking the short-term high was "too close, give it some room") leave the higher pool intact, which is why there are two levels to consider.
  - He says he needs no heat map, book map or "other maps": he knows where liquidity pools because he knows what traders do when they are short.
- **How to identify:** Short-term high just before a sharp sell-off leg (energetic drop from it).
- **How to use:** Treat as an objective for a long from discount; the short-term high is easier to find than an inefficiency (look at how energetic the drop from it was).
- **Example in this video:** NQ: the high at which the sell-off began (lower of the two relative equal highs) = minor BSL; price ran into it after 8:30 and rejected.
- **Timestamps:**
  - [0:45:47](https://youtu.be/8wHewi6N6dg?t=2747) — why a short-term high attracts price (shorts trail buy stops there)
  - [0:46:33](https://youtu.be/8wHewi6N6dg?t=2793) — no heat map needed
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** none.

title: ICT 2026 Smart Money Concepts Lecture \ January 29, 2026
head: Fair Value Gap as a "two SIBIs plus a volume imbalance" array; how to draw it and test it  (aliases ICT uses: SIBI, sell-side imbalance buy-side inefficiency, volume imbalance, inefficiency, PD array, "split")
body:
- **Kind:** refinement / rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - A candlestick low, then a sell-off creating a volume imbalance, then a continuing sell-side imbalance (SIBI), is another PD array: two SIBIs connected by a volume imbalance. He explicitly calls it "another PD array".
  - Draw it from top to bottom to include the volume imbalance ("encapsulate the entire thing") to get the full range and precision. Drawing the two parts separately is "not technically wrong", but you lose the precision of the full range.
  - Split it in half (classic mid-range / consequent encroachment) and watch how price trades into it.
  - Tests when price rallies into an overhead gap (before 9:30): does it treat it defensively (reject at the low, "sensitivity")? Or does it trade into the upper half, go completely through without coming back to the midpoint, and treat it as an inversion (he would change the colour to orange)?
  - Upper-quadrant rule: if the array sits in the OTE/upper quadrant of the range, you need to see price trade into it and then "stay outside the lower half" (bodies); only then expect a run higher. If it only touches the low of the array and sells off, that shows "premium sensitivity" and weakness.
  - Gap respect rule for an overhead gap price has traded down through (post-9:30): wicks to the halfway point are acceptable; bodies in the lower half or below are best; bodies laid in the upper half make it much less likely price reaches for the lower liquidity before a deeper retracement.
- **How to identify:** Candle low, one sell-off candle that leaves a volume imbalance, then another down-closed candle leaving a SIBI; combine them into one box.
- **How to use:** Use as a target (final exit at the low of the array), or as a resistance/support zone watched for how it is treated (respect vs inversion).
- **Example in this video:** NQ after 8:30: price ran up and touched exactly the low of the array and sold off immediately, "giving up the ghost", so the array was not explored. After 9:30, a different overhead gap (the "blue box") was traded down through; he wanted bodies to stay in its lower half.
- **Timestamps:**
  - [0:09:45](https://youtu.be/8wHewi6N6dg?t=585) — two SIBIs with a volume imbalance explained
  - [0:10:33](https://youtu.be/8wHewi6N6dg?t=633) — "you have to encapsulate the entire thing"
  - [0:39:28](https://youtu.be/8wHewi6N6dg?t=2368) — in the upper quadrant it must trade up and stay outside the lower half
  - [1:13:27](https://youtu.be/8wHewi6N6dg?t=4407) — respect rule for the overhead blue box (upper half vs lower half bodies)
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** He reiterates that FVGs and inversions need classification: "how to anticipate inversion fair value gaps, when they should be implemented, when they shouldn't, what would negate it" (1:14:14). The earlier "wick later at top of it clears the candle's high" comment is hard to follow (see next concept).

title: ICT 2026 Smart Money Concepts Lecture \ January 29, 2026
head: Inversion FVG as part of a bullish breaker (A+ pre-news setup) and the FVG-qualification wick comment  (aliases ICT uses: inversion fair value gap, iFVG, breaker, "fulcrum point", discount array)
body:
- **Kind:** example / refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - He labels the pre-8:30 pattern an A+ setup. Ingredients: (1) liquidity left in the market (lows made jagged); (2) price comes down ahead of news and takes that liquidity; (3) it does not reach a lower eighth level (a blue line carried from yesterday's RTH opening range gap) - if it were weak it should have come down to it, but it did not; (4) it rallies back above the lowest portion of a bullish breaker; (5) it comes back down into an inversion FVG that is part of that breaker and holds there; (6) it then rallies to the minor BSL and to the low of the inefficiency above.
  - The lows create the liquidity pool and the "fulcrum point"; drive down, take that liquidity, then the inversion FVG forms.
  - Body behaviour: price may wick through the inversion gap, "not a big deal"; what matters is where bodies stop. Bodies holding there show the market is being held there, not that buyers and sellers changed; "the algorithm is going to keep offering higher prices whether there's buyers or sellers".
  - The iFVG sat "laser at top of an eighth" on the RTH opening range gap lines.
  - Qualification comment (caption confusing, treat with caution): he says the gap area "is not an inefficiency" in the plain sense because a later green candle's wick clears the previous candle's high; if that wick had instead stayed inside the lowest candle's low (26,161.25) he would have treated that area as "a different type of PD array", a discount array, which he declined to teach, adding that he has never taught all of them and never will ("82 of them", and he never promised that).
  - That run from the iFVG to the minor BSL (as a partial) and to the inefficiency's low "is a model in and of itself".
- **How to identify:** Sweep of lows (sell-side taken) into a bullish breaker whose lowest portion is reclaimed; a bearish FVG inside the breaker that price trades up through (inverted) and then retests with bodies holding; also confirm it sits on a reference level (eighth line).
- **How to use:** Buy the retest of the iFVG; first target the short-term high (minor BSL), final target the low of the inefficiency above (two-stage exit). Stop beyond the sweep / below the array (he does not state an exact stop here).
- **Example in this video:** NQ 1m (approx.): low of the lowest down-closed candle 26,161.25; price takes lows pre-8:30 and fails to reach a blue eighth line below; rallies above the bullish breaker low; returns into the iFVG, holds, then runs to the short-term high at 8:30 news and the low of the inefficiency.
- **Timestamps:**
  - [0:21:23](https://youtu.be/8wHewi6N6dg?t=1283) — drops into the inversion FVG; the wick/previous-high detail
  - [0:22:10](https://youtu.be/8wHewi6N6dg?t=1330) — the "different PD array / discount array" aside with 26,161.25
  - [0:22:56](https://youtu.be/8wHewi6N6dg?t=1376) — iFVG is part of the breaker; lows create the liquidity pool
  - [0:24:30](https://youtu.be/8wHewi6N6dg?t=1470) — rallied back above the lowest portion of a bullish breaker ("CB", caption unclear); bodies hold
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** The caption near 0:22 ("not an inefficiency because we have this wick later at top of it...") is genuinely unclear; the take-away is only that a specific wick/candle relationship decided how he classified the area. He does not state the condition cleanly. He also says the price action at the iFVG is not buying/selling pressure but algorithmic delivery.

title: ICT 2026 Smart Money Concepts Lecture \ January 29, 2026
head: Opening range gap eighths carried forward from the previous day (RTH ORG levels)  (aliases ICT uses: eighths, .125, .375, gradient levels, quadrants, "opening range gap on the eighths")
body:
- **Kind:** refinement / reference levels
- **What ICT says:**
  - The horizontal lines on his chart are the eighths (.125 increments) of yesterday's RTH opening range gap (settlement at the prior close to the 9:30 open), still drawn forward after the gap closed. Price continues to react to them, which contradicts the claim "everybody is trading the eighths after the gap closes" (he says they do not, so this is "technical science", not other people's stuff).
  - Overnight they are useful as levels. A rally was rejected exactly at the area just above the .375 level; a sell-off failed to reach a lower eighth; the final sell-off ran through eighth after eighth with one eighth at 26,144.25 and another at 26,122.50 acting as the next targets.
  - Relative equal highs formed with their bodies converging on the .125 level of that gap, which he used to argue the high might be kept intact.
  - "The inability to get to this eighth" above is why the sell-off after the inefficiency was so sharp.
- **How to identify:** From the RTH opening range gap (previous settlement to 9:30 open), divide into eighths; carry those lines to the next sessions.
- **How to use:** Use as magnets/reference levels; failing to reach an eighth before reversing signals strength/weakness; sell-side liquidity rests just below an eighth.
- **Example in this video:** NQ: price dipped at the 9:30 open candle to a low of 26,122.50, "exactly the price level" of an eighth from yesterday's RTH opening range gap.
- **Timestamps:**
  - [0:04:56](https://youtu.be/8wHewi6N6dg?t=296) — explains the lines as the eighths of the RTH opening range gap
  - [0:27:38](https://youtu.be/8wHewi6N6dg?t=1658) — iFVG sits on the eighth; "technical science"
  - [0:39:28](https://youtu.be/8wHewi6N6dg?t=2368) — sell-off through eighths; 26,144.25 down level mentioned shortly after
  - [1:05:27](https://youtu.be/8wHewi6N6dg?t=3927) — 9:30 candle low 26,122.50 equals the eighth
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Which eighths are .125 vs .375 on his chart is not fully clear from the captions (price is quoted at 26,161.25, 26,144.25, 26,122.50). He used a "blue" line for the lower eighth and calls this part of the opening range gap framework.

title: ICT 2026 Smart Money Concepts Lecture \ January 29, 2026
head: Today's RTH opening range gap behaviour (9:30 open, partial fill, abandon rule)  (aliases ICT uses: opening range gap, gap closure, discount gap opening, opening price, "magnet", first presented fair value gap)
body:
- **Kind:** rule / example
- **What ICT says:**
  - The gap is from yesterday's RTH settlement (close of the regular session candle) to today's 9:30 open. Here it was a discount gap opening (open below settlement).
  - Price rallied about three quarters of the way up the gap (he says "almost like a 3/4 of a closure") and was rejected, then ran lower.
  - Rule: once price breaks outside the gap past the opening price and starts to run, respect that it is probably going to leave the open. It does not need 15 or 30 minutes to be clear. After a partial fill and a rip lower, anticipate deeper discounts; look at the old regular trading hours price action for references, not only the electronic trading hours chart.
  - Abandon rule (stated live): if price slices through the lower gap level on a closing basis, abandon the idea of gap closure for the morning session; it "would remain heavy".
  - The opening price is very sensitive, like the midnight New York opening price: "many times a magnet", and it also helps with daily directional bias. At 9:30 he saw the open, a rally above (Judas), a break down that hit the open and then lower.
  - First presented FVG after 9:30: he chose the gap formed when price displaced into the previous-session (RTH) inefficiency over a small earlier gap, because the small one would be viewed as a "breakaway" gap (caption: "order or break away coming gap", unclear) and "doesn't have that much of a range". He expects price to gravitate back to that first-presented FVG eventually before the week closes: they act as magnets "like new week opening gaps, new day opening gaps".
  - If price goes right through the downside with no interest, he would skip the morning and wait until about 1:30 PM, check for smooth sell-side/buy-side left intact and use it for the PM session.
  - In the 1990s he taught students on day 1 to mark settlement, opening price, range, half, three quarters, lower quadrant, and watch whether the gap closes fully; day 2 to ask where it goes next if not; day 3 to add an entry mechanism (an order block, selling short on a stop, buying on a stop).
- **How to identify:** Mark RTH settlement and the 9:30 open; split into quadrants; watch partial fills and where the open is first broken.
- **How to use:** Treat the open as a reference/magnet; abandon a gap-closure idea on a closing-basis slice through the lower level; pick the first presented FVG with the displacement as the later magnet.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 9:30: 9:31 candle bumps the high (clears tweezer highs) and rejects; price returns to the opening price, trades up to it, sells off; opens at a discount, rallies about 3/4 into the gap, then rips lower into deeper discounts, taking liquidity for longs below.

title: ICT 2026 Smart Money Concepts Lecture \ January 29, 2026
head: 8:30 and 9:30 as algorithmic starting guns; trade the news reaction  (aliases ICT uses: 8:30 algorithmic time, 9:30 opening, news driver, signatures, "the race")
body:
- **Kind:** rule / timing
- **What ICT says:**
  - 8:30 ET is always an algorithmic time to expect a measurable price run, whether there is news on the calendar or not (he says you will be surprised how often runs start at 8:30 with no news). 9:30 is the same.
  - Race analogy: everyone lines up at 8:30 and 9:30 and the gun goes off; by 3:00 the race has been run and you see which finishes strongest, followed by a flurry in the last hour (3:00 to 4:00 ET close).
  - He wants beginners to learn when volatility starts, not yet which direction.
  - News is an injection of volatility that forces the market to show its hand: study price around red-folder and medium-impact drivers (even on demo/tape reading). Avoiding news because "I don't like trading around news" removes the best classroom. His poker tell analogy: you see whose stops are being targeted.
  - On the day: 8:30 US unemployment claims (labour costs, trade balance also mentioned).
  - Pre-session: the pre-8:30 shorts (people short from the 7:00 overnight drop) are the ones price is likely to run against at 8:30; same at 9:30.
- **How to identify:** Note the time (8:30, 9:30, 3:00 to 4:00), the pre-session range, and who is positioned.
- **How to use:** Do the exercise every day: build the range, state the draw, wait for 8:30/9:30, and watch the run to liquidity or inefficiency.
- **Example in this video:** 8:30 jobless claims: price took the lows ahead of the release, reversed and ran to the minor BSL / inefficiency; then 9:30 opening candle swept a tweezer high and rejected.
- **Timestamps:**
  - [0:36:19](https://youtu.be/8wHewi6N6dg?t=2179) — jobless claims; study price around news
  - [0:37:54](https://youtu.be/8wHewi6N6dg?t=2274) — "8:30 whether there's news or not is an algorithmic time"
  - [0:48:09](https://youtu.be/8wHewi6N6dg?t=2889) — the race analogy, 8:30/9:30/3:00-4:00

head: Market Maker Sell Model: retracement to 3/4 of the range without returning to the consolidation
body:
- **Kind:** refinement (brief mention)
- **What ICT says:**
  - Reason he talks about three quarters of the range: in the market maker sell model price can go up into three quarters of the range and not come back to the original consolidation. That is what happened here: it failed at that area and never revisited the original consolidation.
  - If you do not know when the market maker buy/sell models complete you will be in a profitable trade, think "it's so easy", and then be reversed.
  - Refers viewers to his mentorship to see this taught.
- **How to identify / use:** Treat the upper quadrant of the retracement as the place the model can be completed; do not require price to return to the consolidation.
- **Example in this video:** NQ: the run into the inefficiency in the upper quadrant failed without returning to the original consolidation; sell-off followed.

head: Seasonal participation: sitting out January, starting the first Tuesday of February  (aliases ICT uses: first month of the year, sentiment build-up)
body:
- **Kind:** rule / personal process (seasonal tendency)
- **What ICT says:**
  - He does not actively trade the first month of the year. He starts the first Tuesday of February (a self-imposed parameter: not a Monday, a Tuesday, in February). He has done this for about three decades.
  - Reason: over the holidays traders build opinions and sentiment; at the start of a new year they have the most energy and are impatient and greedy, putting down heavy bets. Market makers know there is a shift in sentiment and big bets are coming.
  - Observation: January more often fails to deliver efficiently; it is "sloppy, choppy, indecisive, weird, wild opening range gaps" far from the prior settlement. Some Januaries in recent years delivered well, but that has never made him change what he does.
  - This year adds geopolitics, making lower-timeframe precision harder.
- **How to use:** Be a light/no-risk participant in January; observe and study rather than size up.
- **Timestamps:**
  - [1:15:00](https://youtu.be/8wHewi6N6dg?t=4500) — start the first Tuesday of February
  - [1:15:49](https://youtu.be/8wHewi6N6dg?t=4549) — sentiment builds over the holidays
  - [1:16:35](https://youtu.be/8wHewi6N6dg?t=4595) — January tends to fail to deliver efficiently
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Personal rule, not a market law. He says he is not worried about "giving up" January.

title: ICT 2026 Smart Money Concepts Lecture \ January 29, 2026
head: Low-resistance delivery vs "fuzzy" delivery  (aliases ICT uses: low resistance liquidity runs, porous wake, fuzzy, intervention)
body:
- **Kind:** rule / filter
- **What ICT says:**
  - He wants low-resistance liquidity runs where price leaves pools of liquidity and inefficiencies in its wake ("a porous wake").
  - If price spends a lot of time back and forth over previous candles, sharing the same space as previous ranges, he calls that "fuzzy": it is not algorithmic delivery, it is intervention ("them working previous ranges, constantly going after orders"). In that case he will not bet his heaviest hand.
- **How to identify:** Overlapping candle bodies, repeated re-trading of old ranges; no clean inefficiencies left behind.
- **How to use:** Reduce size or stand aside when delivery is fuzzy; save size for clean runs.
- **Timestamps:**
  - [1:17:24](https://youtu.be/8wHewi6N6dg?t=4644) — wants low resistance liquidity runs
  - [1:18:12](https://youtu.be/8wHewi6N6dg?t=4692) — "fuzzy" = shares space with previous ranges = intervention
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Relates to his "high/low resistance liquidity run" teaching; here the emphasis is on porous vs overlapping candles.

head: Three tools: draw on liquidity, frame risk, entry mechanism  (aliases ICT uses: "three paint brushes", Bob Ross)
body:
- **Kind:** philosophy / framework
- **What ICT says:**
  - All you need: (1) the draw on liquidity, (2) the ability to frame risk (where the stop goes), (3) an entry mechanism. Everyone looks at the same chart; what separates profitability is knowing what to do with it.
  - Over time you find the one PD array that is easy for you to recognise (Silver Bullet, order block, breaker, 2022 model, Reaper, etc.). If it is not present, do nothing and be content with that; the model did not tell you to act.
  - Do not abandon the model you were using to chase a new one because it changed; if the one you stopped using delivers, take responsibility.
  - Some students must use a breaker; others the Silver Bullet; do not force yourself into a mold. He can use different PD arrays and models on a 15 or 30 second chart all day without repeating a setup, but students cannot replicate that.
  - Entry mechanism he gave 1990s students: an order block, sell short on a stop (sell weakness), buy on a stop (buy strength).
- **Timestamps:**

title: ICT 2026 Smart Money Concepts Lecture \ January 13, 2026
head: First Presented Fair Value Gap in the pre-market window (7:00 to 9:30 ET): validity rules  (aliases ICT uses: first presented FVG, "common gap", imbalance, displacement)
body:
- **Kind:** rule / refinement (re-statement of his FVG rules, with the "common gap" distinction)
- **What ICT says:**
  - The time window for the first presented FVG in pre-market is 7:00 AM ET (pre-market start) to the 9:30 open, a 2.5 hour window. His interest is "zeroed into a very specific candle, a very specific time of day".
  - A tiny gap that forms in the first minutes after 7:00 (7:00, 7:01, 7:02 candles) is a "common gap" and is not the first presented FVG, because it does not cause displacement. A critic saying "ICT got it wrong because price went to the first gap after 7:00" is looking at a gap he explicitly excluded.
  - The qualifying gap is the one made by a displacement that takes price above a prior high (a candle that displaces above a high, "not engulfing the previous candle"). That displacement is technically a shift in market structure.
  - He states emphatically that an engulfing candle is not a market structure shift.
  - Three-candle construction: candle number one, candle number two (the one that contains the imbalance in the middle), candle number three (closes the pattern). The imbalance is between candle one and candle three.
  - Stop placement: for a bullish FVG the stop goes below the low of candlestick number one; for a bearish FVG the stop goes above the high of candlestick number one.
  - A candle body must stay inside the FVG. A small wick through an inherent small common gap inside the zone is permissible because the real stop (candle one's low) was never in jeopardy.
  - The gap must displace and be significant; "it can't be just a little common gap".
- **How to identify:** After 7:00, wait for the first gap formed by a displacement leg (breaks above a high or below a low); ignore the micro-gaps in the 7:00 to 7:02 candles; mark candle one (low for bullish, high for bearish).
- **How to use:**
  - Use that gap as the point of entry; stop beyond candle one's extreme; plan a partial in advance; if only one contract, plan how and where you will move the stop (see risk section).
  - Entry price within the FVG: he buys the high or upper quadrant of a bullish gap (see "Entry at the FVG high / upper quadrant" below).
- **Example in this video:** NQ, Monday 12 Jan, pre-market (during the previous day's stream). The 7:00 candle (small wick above), then 7:01/7:02 leave a tiny gap that he does not count. Later, a candle displaces above a high; the gap that forms is the first presented FVG. After the 9:30 open, price trades down into this gap and also into the small common gap inside it, but never breaches the low of candle one. Price then rips higher.
- **Timestamps:**
  - [0:16:30](https://youtu.be/Rwao8f6oD0Q?t=990) — why the tiny 7:00 gap is not the first presented FVG (no displacement)
  - [0:18:06](https://youtu.be/Rwao8f6oD0Q?t=1086) — displacement above the high = shift in market structure; engulfing candle is not
  - [0:18:57](https://youtu.be/Rwao8f6oD0Q?t=1137) — candle 1/2/3 and stop at candle one's low
  - [0:19:47](https://youtu.be/Rwao8f6oD0Q?t=1187) — bullish stop below candle one low, bearish above candle one high; the inherent small gap wick is permissible
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** The caption on the exact displacement sentence ("displaces above this high, not engulfing the previous candle") is a little muddled; the clear rules are the stop placement and the "displacement, not engulfing, equals MSS" statement. He says the rules are consistent with what he has taught before.

title: ICT 2026 Smart Money Concepts Lecture \ January 13, 2026
head: Inversion FVG used as a launch pad during a pre-9:30 "holding pattern"  (aliases ICT uses: inversion fair value gap, iFVG, SIBI, foothold, holding pattern)
body:
- **Kind:** rule / example
- **What ICT says:**
  - An inversion FVG (iFVG) is a gap used as the opposite of how it was expected to work when it formed. A SIBI (sell-side imbalance, buy-side inefficiency; a down-close candle gap) is normally something to sell into if you are bearish; if price overtakes it, it becomes a foothold to propel price higher. Critics say "it doesn't work", but that is the inversion.
  - If you expect a Judas swing lower, you look at the bearish FVG, wait for it to be overtaken, and then use it as a foothold to push price higher, which is what happened at the 9:30 break time.
  - He taught the idea about two years earlier in "Kit's ICT Concepts trader roundup" (caption unclear): look at your FVGs and invert them.
  - In the live stream he said not to short the iFVG because the market was in a holding pattern: with the daily draw above (the 26,133.5 daily relative equal highs), price was expected to hold until the 9:30 opening range / 10:00, then run bullish through the trendline liquidity.
  - Price had to come down first to absorb liquidity (stops of those buying the apparent trendline breakout) into the first presented FVG, then it releases.
  - The volume imbalance: the iFVG here was a sell-side imbalance with a volume imbalance at the low of it. He recalls that when he first taught volume imbalances to mentorship students he pointed only to the volume imbalance (not the whole range) to teach gradually, because of leakers; here it is part of the bigger iFVG.
  - Anything that trades up into this iFVG and drops is a short-term fluctuation. It is useful for tape reading, but it looked "muddy and dirty" because it was part of the holding pattern.
- **How to identify:** A bearish FVG overtaken by an up-close that holds above it; the volume imbalance at its low is a precise level; check what time of day (holding pattern until 9:30).
- **How to use:** Do not short a pre-9:30 iFVG when daily bias is up; wait for the 9:30 opening range release and buy the retest of the iFVG low / first presented FVG with the stop below candle one.
- **Example in this video:** NQ Monday 12 Jan: the 9:30 candle opens at the RTH opening range low, trades down to the low of the iFVG (with the volume imbalance), then rips through and higher.
- **Timestamps:**
  - [0:23:49](https://youtu.be/Rwao8f6oD0Q?t=1429) — "would you go short with that? No, we're in a holding pattern"; daily draw 26,133.5
  - [0:28:29](https://youtu.be/Rwao8f6oD0Q?t=1709) — 9:30 candle opens at opening range low and trades to the low of the iFVG
  - [0:30:56](https://youtu.be/Rwao8f6oD0Q?t=1856) — iFVG explained (SIBI overtaken, then used as a foothold)
  - [0:31:44](https://youtu.be/Rwao8f6oD0Q?t=1904) — price and time agree: iFVG at 9:30 sends price higher
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** The "holding pattern until 9:30" idea is a new framing in this video (a pre-9:30 gap is not traded against the daily bias). Specific volume-imbalance remark is partly history/story (leakers).

head: Trendline "phantom": ascending trendline as sell-stop liquidity, not support  (aliases ICT uses: trend line phantom, retail diagonal support fallacy, channel, pitchfork)
body:
- **Kind:** refinement / opinion on retail concepts
- **What ICT says:**
  - An ascending diagonal "support" that retail traders see (as a channel or pitchfork) is a fallacy for him: the stops resting below the trendline and below a specific low are the liquidity price targets.
  - Retail buys the apparent breakout; they are trapped when price first dips to absorb the liquidity into the first presented FVG, then runs.
  - He says he does not normally draw the trendline; he draws it for teaching so students understand the internal dialogue. Also something about looking at three points where the line is trying to gravitate (caption unclear).
  - Price, time and liquidity agree: it is anchored to a time (the first presented FVG, relative to the 7:00 start) and a price/liquidity (the stops below).
  - Homework: re-listen to the live stream to confirm he said the trendline would be the liquidity and that this FVG was the first presented one. Review the next day after sleep, to see what you missed and to solidify the model.
- **How to identify:** Retail-looking diagonal support with obvious stops below a specific low (minor SSL).
- **How to use:** Expect a run down into the trendline liquidity / first presented FVG, then reversal in the direction of the higher-timeframe draw.
- **Example in this video:** NQ Monday 12 Jan pre-9:30: ascending trendline from the Asian session; liquidity resting below one low; price opens and trades down into the first presented FVG and absorbs it, then reverses.
- **Timestamps:**
  - [0:20:37](https://youtu.be/Rwao8f6oD0Q?t=1237) — "trend line phantom", retail diagonal support fallacy
  - [0:22:11](https://youtu.be/Rwao8f6oD0Q?t=1331) — stops below the trendline are what they target
  - [0:23:00](https://youtu.be/Rwao8f6oD0Q?t=1380) — liquidity below the low; market trades down into the first presented FVG
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** The "midpoint of the trend line phantom" and "three points" statements are caption-unclear.

title: ICT 2026 Smart Money Concepts Lecture \ January 13, 2026
head: Daily bias, higher-timeframe draw, and "hold for the close" (Larry Williams)  (aliases ICT uses: higher time frame draw on liquidity, daily candle close, trading with the larger move)
body:
- **Kind:** rule / bias
- **What ICT says:**
  - Frame direction from the higher time frame draw: here the daily relative equal highs around 26,133.5 were the draw (discussed about a week earlier). The best intraday moves are framed by daily bias, even though counter-trend shorts can work briefly.
  - Idea credited to Larry Williams: if you day trade, be on side with where the daily candle is likely to close and hold something into the close. Decide before you sit down whether the daily candle should close up, and look for longs, holding at least part of the position.
  - His own timing version: long at the 9:30 to 10:00 opening range or pre-market from 7:00 onward, then off-board something between 10:00 and 11:00 (profit-taking; London close; entering NY lunch).
  - Trading only on the side of the daily candle's expected extension lets you catch the big running moves; trading every minor fluctuation against that bias (e.g., a short from the Asian session BSL FVG) will not.
  - Time and price meet like a multiplication table (liquidity price on one axis, time on the other): the algorithm finds where time and price meet.
- **How to identify:** Daily chart: nearby old high/low or relative equal highs/lows or imbalance above/below price; recent liquidity events (e.g., sell side just run).
- **How to use:** Trade only in the daily-bias direction, partial off 10:00 to 11:00, hold remainder to the close if running.
- **Example in this video:** Daily bullish toward 26,133.5; Monday's session (12 Jan) went long from the first presented FVG at the 9:30 release.
- **Timestamps:**
  - [0:13:17](https://youtu.be/Rwao8f6oD0Q?t=797) — the question for the day: run to 26,133.5 or use CPI for a sentiment drop first
  - [0:24:35](https://youtu.be/Rwao8f6oD0Q?t=1475) — Larry Williams "hold for the close" idea
  - [0:25:21](https://youtu.be/Rwao8f6oD0Q?t=1521) — off-board something from 10:00 to 11:00
  - [0:26:54](https://youtu.be/Rwao8f6oD0Q?t=1614) — time and price like the multiplication table
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** He explicitly says it will "be in the book" (his three-book set) but is all on YouTube.

title: ICT 2026 Smart Money Concepts Lecture \ January 13, 2026
head: Precision from price and time (not volume): NWOG / previous-settlement level, eighths, minor sell-side liquidity  (aliases ICT uses: new week opening gap, regular trading hours opening range gap high, eighth, old daily high, minor sell side pool)
body:
- **Kind:** example / refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - He had said before the run that price would go to a specific price: the new week opening gap / RTH previous settlement (the "purple line"), and it hit that price (25,933.5) to the tick as the candle high.
  - A minor sell-side pool sat below a low where long stops (protective sell stops) were placed. His stated condition (before the move): do not want to see this low taken before price trades to the NWOG; if it was taken first there would likely be a deeper retracement and he would be done for the morning. In fact price went to the NWOG first and then dropped to take the low (he calls this foresight).
  - After that, price traded down to another reference to the tick: the low of a candle equal to an eighth (quoted as "938 and a quarter", caption leading digits unclear) and then reversed.
  - Earlier reference: an iFVG from 10:40 Friday 9 Jan was extended forward and price reacted at it; it also sits on an eighth.
  - The 7 Jan old daily high was swept (liquidity) and then price broke lower back into the NWOG overnight.
  - He argues that exact price/time knowledge beats volume profile, DOM, iceberg detection or contract counts; volume profile will not show where price will turn. His tooling costs only data fees (about $45 a month at AMP, plus about $7 for TradingView), no "gimmicks".
- **How to identify:** Mark NWOG, RTH previous settlement, eighths of the gap, old daily highs, minor sell-side pools beneath obvious lows.
- **How to use:** Treat NWOG/settlement/eighth levels as targets and reversal levels; state the condition for a failure (low taken before the target reached) in advance.
- **Example in this video:** NQ Monday 12 Jan: price runs to NWOG/previous settlement at 25,933.5 (candle high exactly), then drops to take the minor SSL, then reverses off an eighth (low about 938.25).
- **Timestamps:**
  - [0:32:34](https://youtu.be/Rwao8f6oD0Q?t=1954) — what's more advantageous: exact price/time or counting contracts/volume
  - [0:34:10](https://youtu.be/Rwao8f6oD0Q?t=2050) — NWOG and RTH previous settlement hit at 25,933.5
  - [0:35:02](https://youtu.be/Rwao8f6oD0Q?t=2102) — minor sell-side pool; condition about the low not being taken first
  - [0:37:26](https://youtu.be/Rwao8f6oD0Q?t=2246) — reversal at an eighth, low 938.25 (caption)
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Numbers are as heard from captions: "25,933 half", "938 and a quarter", "80%" (an incomplete statement, caption unclear). The levels do not reconcile cleanly from captions (a later low of 938.25 is quoted above a high of 933.5), so treat numeric details as unreliable and rely on the described behaviour.

title: ICT 2026 Smart Money Concepts Lecture \ January 13, 2026
head: News-day risk: CPI/PPI/FOMC and the 8:30 release  (aliases ICT uses: high-impact news driver, volatility injection, red folder, economic calendar)
body:
- **Kind:** rule / risk
- **What ICT says:**
  - Before CPI, he told over-leveraged or inexperienced traders to close their trades.
  - He is generally wrong more often than right on CPI/PPI direction: the data and interest are used by the market because many people want to trade big volatility. He treats the morning as an "intel session": review, then observe.
  - Question for the day: will price run toward the 26,133.5 daily draw, or use the 8:30 CPI to facilitate sentiment lower first, then use PPI the next day to go toward 26,133.5.
  - Result: one 8:30 candle traversed 104 handles in one minute (starting from a low he gives as "9005", caption unclear); price pierced Monday's RTH high and the 7 Jan high (red line) and moved toward the daily relative equal highs. He says traders short 10-piece lost badly.
  - Calendar for the week as stated: CPI Tuesday 8:30; PPI the next day 8:30; retail sales Wednesday; Thursday Philly Fed, manufacturing index and unemployment claims. FOMC rate announcements matter (not the minutes); they come in the afternoon.
  - Rule of thumb: calendar is published far ahead; he does not trade the morning of CPI or PPI and not the afternoon of the FOMC rate announcement. He would start looking for trades about 9:00 that morning.
  - He will not be in ahead of 8:30 unless it is a higher-timeframe trade carrying unrealized profit that is already protected; he no longer holds trades for days (geopolitics, overnight gap risk): "surgical strikes", get it and go home.
  - A single event like this can leave a lasting scar that makes you fearful of the "report waiting around the corner".
- **How to use:** Know the calendar; flatten or reduce size before the release; wait for the wake before looking at setups.
- **Timestamps:**
  - [0:11:42](https://youtu.be/Rwao8f6oD0Q?t=702) — warning to close trades before 8:30
