title: ICT 2026 Smart Money Concepts Lecture \ January 13, 2026
head: Core tenet checklist: bias to first presented FVG entry  (aliases ICT uses: "central core tenets", multiple choice, kitchen sink approach)
body:
- **Kind:** entry model / process
- **What ICT says:**
  1. Choose a market on a higher-timeframe premise that leads to a specific price level: an old high or old low (single or relative equal highs/lows) or an imbalance above or below price.
  2. Check what recently happened. If there was a stop hunt (raid on sell side), look for a premium array: the first imbalance that price climbs back through inside the range; then decide whether the draw is a single high or relative equal highs. If the buy side was run recently, do the same in reverse. It is multiple choice: one of the three, not all.
  3. Drop to the lower timeframe and wait for the first presented FVG in the time window he specified (he has taught several). It is a finite reference point, not shifting.
  4. The FVG must displace and be significant (not a common gap); enter there, stop from the first candle (candle one).
  5. Pre-plan a partial; if trading one contract, pre-plan where the stop moves, graduating it to protect, and manage until the end.
  - Warnings: do not pile on everything (inversion breaker, 2022 model, COT, seasonals, structure, MMBM/MMSM). That is a "kitchen sink". There is a tool for bias, a tool for timing entry/exit, a tool that confirms or qualifies.
  - But also: it is not a "one candle" premise. A single candle needs supporting actors (market structure, seasonality, range logic); they do not all have to agree. You must know what you are buying, where it is going, where the stop is, how price works inside the range, and whether it is worth holding once it leaves the range.
  - Students may avoid order blocks (too many down-close candles, uncomfortable) and use only the FVG; that is fine. Example: daily looks bullish after sell side ran, relative equal highs above; only take longs at FVGs.
  - It works in every market (gold, indices, crypto per students; he has not used crypto himself).
- **Timestamps:**
  - [1:22:19](https://youtu.be/Rwao8f6oD0Q?t=4939) — higher timeframe premise to a specific level
  - [1:23:08](https://youtu.be/Rwao8f6oD0Q?t=4988) — stop hunt? raid sell side? look for premium array, single vs relative equal high
  - [1:23:56](https://youtu.be/Rwao8f6oD0Q?t=5036) — LTF first presented FVG, displacement, stop at first candle, partials
  - [1:26:18](https://youtu.be/Rwao8f6oD0Q?t=5178) — tools for bias, timing, confirmation; one candle is not enough
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** His position is a balance: do not stack every model, but do not rely on a single candle.

title: ICT 2026 Smart Money Concepts Lecture \ January 13, 2026
head: Entry at the FVG high / upper quadrant (not the CE or lower)  (aliases ICT uses: consequent encroachment, upper quadrant, limit order, stop loss size)
body:
- **Kind:** refinement / rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - On a bullish FVG, buy the high (upper boundary) or the upper quadrant of the gap. Do not try to buy the lowest low of the gap.
  - Price often goes down and touches one tick into the high of the gap and runs away; a resting limit at the CE or lower is the greedy approach (you want a better fill, more contracts, a smaller stop) and misses the trade.
  - Current volatility makes very small stops on every trade hard; tiny stops are possible sometimes but it is a knack/experience matter.
  - Overleveraging to hit a profit goal quickly is the danger.
- **How to identify:** Bullish FVG; the entry at its upper boundary/upper quadrant after the first touch.
- **How to use:** Place the entry at the high of the FVG; stop below candle one's low; size down rather than squeezing the stop.
- **Timestamps:**
  - [1:28:40](https://youtu.be/Rwao8f6oD0Q?t=5320) — buy the FVG high or upper quadrant, not the CE or lower
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Refines the common "limit at the CE" approach. He says "just look at my executions" as evidence.

title: ICT 2026 Smart Money Concepts Lecture \ January 12, 2026
head: Session vs. Kill Zone (Asian / London / NY AM / pre-market)  (aliases ICT uses: "the entirety of the session" vs "ICT kill zone")
body:
- **Kind:** definition / rule (new emphasis; clarifies a common misuse)
- **What ICT says:**
  - A session is the whole stretch of a region's trading; a kill zone is a specific, narrower window inside it. Brokers and others label whole sessions as "ICT kill zones" and that is wrong. "If it was just that easy, I would never have said kill zone."
  - Asian session: starts 7:00 pm ET, closes about 5:00 am ET. Asian KILL ZONE: "7:00 to 9:00" ET, a roughly 2-hour scalping window with usually a first-presented FVG and an old high/low to run for (caption garbled as "7:00 a.m. to 9:00 p.m."; read as 7–9 pm (caption unclear)).
  - London KILL ZONE: 2:00 am–5:00 am ET. Sweet spot is 2:00–4:00 am; it extends to 5:00 because of overlap with Asia's close. He says this is a 3-hour window and the same for forex and index futures.
  - London SESSION runs until about 10:00–11:00 am ET (European close). The London extreme is usually set by 10–11 am, so that is a profit-taking time for London/European traders who traded overnight into NY hours; often a tradeable high or low forms then (not guaranteed).
  - New York session reference range: 9:30 open to 4:00 pm close ET.
  - Pre-market session: 7:00–9:00 am ET. Between London KZ end (5:00) and 7:00 am is "dead time": he does nothing there, avoids it ("keeps you out of the molasses"). He admits he occasionally traded it in forex with strong conviction but tells learners to avoid it.
  - After 4:00 am, London-zone moves are only of interest if they make a parabolic run to a higher-timeframe PD array (e.g., a daily suspension block high in the example).
  - Always set platform time to New York local time.
  - You can do every setup between 7:00 and 9:00 am and never engage the 9:30 open/opening range at all; people avoid the open because they do not know what to look for.
- **How to identify:** vertical lines at session start/close for the "session" box (7 pm–5 am for Asia; 2 am–11 am for London) vs. a separate smaller box for the kill zone (2–5 am London).
- **How to use:** the SESSION range is where you search for liquidity (smooth highs/lows, session high/low). The KILL ZONE is where you expect the setup/entry to form. Do not limit the search for equal highs/lows to the kill zone, because price may already have traded beyond it and used the level.
- **Example in this video:** Mon Jan 12, 2026. Asian session box from Sunday 7 pm to 5 am; London kill-zone box 2–5 am (London low formed 3:43 am, "right before 4:00", reacting off a stale daily-chart volume imbalance/suspension block); London session box to 11 am.
- **Timestamps:** [0:29:00](https://youtu.be/dt9mk4n5g_o?t=1740) — session vs kill zone shown with boxes · [0:31:22](https://youtu.be/dt9mk4n5g_o?t=1882) — London KZ 2–5 am, sweet spot, 10–11 am profit taking · [0:44:49](https://youtu.be/dt9mk4n5g_o?t=2689) — 7–9 am pre-market, never need the 9:30 open · [0:47:13](https://youtu.be/dt9mk4n5g_o?t=2833) — dead time between KZ close and 7:00
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** the Asian KZ stated here (7–9 pm ET, per caption) differs from the commonly circulated 8 pm–midnight ET window (my background knowledge, not in this video). The audio/caption is garbled, so treat the exact hours as (caption unclear). The point of the lecture is the session/KZ distinction, not the exact clock numbers.

title: ICT 2026 Smart Money Concepts Lecture \ January 12, 2026
head: Time-first framing: which look-back range to scan for which trading window
body:
- **Kind:** rule / process
- **What ICT says:**
  - "First time, then price." Frame time first, then within that window look for the price feature (smooth high/low).
  - For pre-market (7–9 am) trading, the reference is the overnight Asian session (7 pm–5 am), plus the London range for 2:00–7:00 am; look for smooth highs/lows inside that window.
  - For PM-session trading (afternoon equities), the first frame of reference is the 2:00 am–11:00 am range (close of Asia to London "lunch"). He says use NQ and ES for the PM session; avoid the Dow ("unruly"); a third index in the caption is unclear.
  - For New York session trading, use the 9:30–4:00 range; an Asian or London trader then uses that information overnight.
  - Rolling it forward: each session uses the previous session's range as its reference window.
  - A beginner needs nothing more than: the price action inside the 7–9 am window plus overnight highs/lows and overnight relative equal highs/lows.
  - Look-back for PD arrays: 20, 40, 60 days. Highest-probability, crispest, most responsive PD arrays are formed within the last 20 TRADING days (not calendar days). Within that, the most salient set for the day is last ~5 trading days (a week).
- **How to identify / procedure (as he walks it):** (1) draw vertical lines for the reference window; (2) find the highest high and lowest low in it (time aspect complete); (3) inside that range, scan for smooth highs/lows, compressing/zooming out the chart; (4) decide which are likely to be run in the next window.
- **How to use:** a hypothetical at 1:30 pm: take the 2 am–11 am range, find the high and low; if the high end has been made already (premium market), look for smooth lows (relative equal lows) inside it as the next liquidity run.
- **Example in this video:** the same procedure applied at 8:25 am Mon Jan 12 to the Asian range; Asian highs identified as the draw before 7:00 am.
- **Timestamps:** [0:36:54](https://youtu.be/dt9mk4n5g_o?t=2214) · [0:40:04](https://youtu.be/dt9mk4n5g_o?t=2404) — PM session frame 2 am–11 am · [0:41:39](https://youtu.be/dt9mk4n5g_o?t=2499) — time first then price · [1:33:46](https://youtu.be/dt9mk4n5g_o?t=5626) — NY session 9:30–4:00 as reference for the next session
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** if you only use kill-zone ranges you may miss that price already took out the level outside the KZ.

title: ICT 2026 Smart Money Concepts Lecture \ January 12, 2026
head: Smooth highs / smooth lows = relative equal highs / lows (engineered liquidity, retail S/R trap)  (aliases: "obvious level", "single high / single low" when only one)
body:
- **Kind:** definition / refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - He looks for "smooth" highs or lows within a time frame: clean, textbook-looking support/resistance (high, high, high) that retail is taught to trust. Smooth areas tend to be made jagged: price runs to the level, trades through it, and the cleanness is destroyed.
  - He does NOT trade at the level when it forms; he looks back across the session for it, because that is the trap. It is "engineered liquidity": price runs to an obvious level on purpose.
  - Retail logic is "diametrically opposed" to his: if a new trader would see it as support/resistance and he sees it as a likely run for liquidity, he puts it at roughly 90% likelihood of being right, and the last 10% is why you use stops.
  - His definition of the relative-equal-high structure: price runs to a level, a later high falls short of it (closest to current price is LOWER than the anchoring one), then the little "red herring" run. The failed second high is the retail "strong resistance" trap.
  - Why the liquidity is bigger there: new shorts entered at the failed high and existing short stops were moved down to that second high, so the pool just below the first high is larger and a stronger draw. This is how "bigger bubbles" are known without BookMap.
  - If there is no smooth high/low inside the range (e.g., a single swing high followed by continuation lower), then the single high/low (e.g., overnight high) is the target.
  - Odds of a run into the level increase "exponentially" if the smooth level sits at or around a quadrant level of the whole range (e.g., lower half of the 7 pm–5 am range).
  - Zoom out/compress ranges so the smooth edges stand out ("nose to the tree" analogy).
- **How to identify:** eye jumps to the level; flat highs/lows in a session; second one slightly under the first (for highs).
- **How to use:** expect a pre-market (7–9 am) run to it; pair with first presented FVG as the entry catalyst; target is run on the stops above/below.
- **Example in this video:** NQ overnight Sun Jan 11–Mon Jan 12: smooth highs formed Sunday around 10:00 pm ET; price then only fell overnight; a later, lower high failed to reach the first = the trap; at 7:00 am price displaced up and ran to them.
- **Timestamps:** [0:25:42](https://youtu.be/dt9mk4n5g_o?t=1542) — smooth highs, engineered liquidity · [0:57:34](https://youtu.be/dt9mk4n5g_o?t=3454) — the lower right high is "the trap" · [1:05:41](https://youtu.be/dt9mk4n5g_o?t=3941) — why the pool is larger · [1:42:54](https://youtu.be/dt9mk4n5g_o?t=6174) — beginner minimum
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** refines earlier "equal highs/lows" teaching: explicitly requires the second extreme not to exceed the anchor (see next concept).

title: ICT 2026 Smart Money Concepts Lecture \ January 12, 2026
head: Relative equal highs/lows — anchor point and wick grading
body:
- **Kind:** refinement / rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - Anchor point = the leftmost swing, the one that starts the definition. For relative equal HIGHS the anchor is the higher of the pair; for relative equal LOWS the anchor is the lower of the pair. The one closest to price must be lower (highs) / higher (lows) than the anchor.
  - If the anchor swing has a wick, you must grade the wick (lower quadrant, consequent encroachment, upper quadrant). Price may only trade into the wick (to its upper quadrant, CE, or lower quadrant) and then reject, instead of taking out the extreme.
  - Not every relative equal high/low is equal in quality.
  - Always (he stresses "never ever not do this") take a partial when running to such a level: he likes a partial anywhere between the wick's lower quadrant and its consequent encroachment, i.e., split it in half. You do not need the high taken out.
  - Stopping short of the wick's CE (not even touching it) signals weakness; expect reversal.
- **How to identify:** a candle with a wick forming the anchor; mark quadrants/CE on the wick.
- **How to use:** target the wick (not necessarily the extreme); partial near lower-quadrant-to-CE area of the wick when running up (mirror for lows); read failure to reach CE as a warning.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 1-minute, after the Asian BSL run (~8:00–9:00 am): two relative equal lows, left one has a wick/shadow; he says if price dives to disrupt it, it might only trade into the wick's lower quadrant or CE and turn.
- **Timestamps:** [1:17:40](https://youtu.be/dt9mk4n5g_o?t=4660) — wick on REL · [1:19:18](https://youtu.be/dt9mk4n5g_o?t=4758) — anchor definition, partial rule · [1:20:05](https://youtu.be/dt9mk4n5g_o?t=4805) — CE as weakness test
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** new refinement; his wording on which quadrant to use for partials on highs is "between the lower quadrant and consequent encroachment" (low side of the wick = the part price meets first when coming from below).

title: ICT 2026 Smart Money Concepts Lecture \ January 12, 2026
head: Asian-session buy-side liquidity (overnight smooth highs) → pre-market run
body:
- **Kind:** entry model / bias framework
- **What ICT says:**
  - Take the whole Asian session (7 pm–5 am ET), find the obvious smooth highs (or lows) inside it; that is the "Asian session buy-side liquidity" and it is the draw for 7:00 am onward. Overnight price only went down, so the smooth highs are left above.
  - The pre-market (7–9 am) job is to run to that overnight liquidity; once it has done that job, price consolidates ("holding pattern").
  - It does not matter what discipline you use (profile, footprint, Elliott, moving average): look at what price did overnight and look for smooth highs/lows in it.
  - He had this highlighted before the stream began as the draw on liquidity.
- **How to use:** expect the 7:00 am displacement toward it, trade the first-presented FVG toward it, partial there.
- **Example in this video:** NQ, Mon Jan 12: Asian BSL = smooth highs from Sunday ~10 pm. 7:00 am: displacement up through a short-term high leaves the first presented FVG (discount relative to the equal highs); price races down into it and rallies to the equal highs; the stream began with price roughly 12–15 handles below the level before it ran up. Price then consolidated 8–9 am.
- **Timestamps:** [0:49:35](https://youtu.be/dt9mk4n5g_o?t=2975) — bread-and-butter pre-market setup · [0:53:40](https://youtu.be/dt9mk4n5g_o?t=3220) — Asian BSL definition · [1:06:29](https://youtu.be/dt9mk4n5g_o?t=3989) — red herring run, pool size
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** after the run, "don't marry the idea": the draw may not be reached until later, which is why he teaches partials, stops and tape reading before demo.

title: ICT 2026 Smart Money Concepts Lecture \ January 12, 2026
head: First presented fair value gap (pre-market 7:00–9:00 and 9:30–10:00) with displacement
body:
- **Kind:** entry model / refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - The "first presented FVG" is the first FVG created by genuine displacement in the window (7:00 am start for pre-market; 9:30–10:00 for the open). It must be displacement: a run through a short-term high or low at the specific time; it also shows direction and magnitude ("tipping my hand").
  - Not the tiny gap between two candles that does not displace; not an engulfing candle; the previous candle's body is irrelevant.
  - Rule of thumb: if the gap is under 10 handles in NQ, "80% likely" it is NOT the first presented FVG; wait for another FVG. This explains why his examples sometimes skip an earlier small gap.
  - It is the real "point of control" (his words, versus volume-profile POC).
  - Old first-presented FVGs (Jan 2, Jan 7) are kept on the chart, graded on eighths/quadrants, and treated as PD arrays; his bearish SIBI example: when bullish, don't short a SIBI but watch whether it acts as an inversion FVG, framing high/upper quadrant/midpoint/lower quadrant/low and checking if price respects it (less likely during consolidation).
- **How to identify:** 7:00 am; run through a short-term high; FVG sized more than ~10 NQ handles; within the framework of the Asian BSL.
- **How to use:** enter in the FVG (discount), target the smooth highs; ICT-style partials.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 1m Jan 12 ~7:00 am (see Asian BSL). Contrast case: if the high had not been run and price instead dropped into the Jan 2 FVG, that drop in the 9:30–10:00 window would be read as a Judas swing and he would look for upside displacement.
- **Timestamps:** [0:48:49](https://youtu.be/dt9mk4n5g_o?t=2929) · [0:51:16](https://youtu.be/dt9mk4n5g_o?t=3076) — why the small gap does not count · [1:07:19](https://youtu.be/dt9mk4n5g_o?t=4039) — 10-handle rule · [1:51:46](https://youtu.be/dt9mk4n5g_o?t=6706) — which candle is the FVG
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** the 10-handle (NQ) rule of thumb is new numeric guidance to me; stated as general, not strict.

head: Time then price: premium market → look for smooth lows next
body:

You do not care which way it goes after the run; you are looking for low-hanging fruit, not trying to ride the entire move or be right.

head: RTH Opening Range Gap (previous settlement → 9:30 open) — procedure and statistics
body:
- **Kind:** entry model / definition
- **What ICT says:**
  - Distinct from the New Day Opening Gap and New Week Opening Gap. RTH opening range gap = difference between previous RTH close/settlement (4:00 pm ET) and the 9:30 am open. Monday's gap = Friday's RTH settlement to Monday 9:30 open.
  - Procedure each morning: switch the chart to Regular Trading Hours (tab at lower right), read the previous close (OHLC at top left), draw a line at it and label it "RTH opening range gap" (high or low unknown until the open), then at 9:30 draw the open price as the other side. Drop a fib across it and grade it on quadrants/eighths: upper quadrant, consequent encroachment, etc.
  - At the open, the market will likely explore into the gap. Stat stated: about 70% of the time the gap's consequent encroachment (CE) is delivered/tagged by 10:00 am; knowing this is a "huge advantage."
  - The gap needs not be fully closed. Three quarters (upper quadrant) is often enough.
  - Vacuum: RTH had no trading between the settlement and the open, so price rushes back into that unpopulated area even though overnight ETH already traded some of it (soda-cap-release analogy).
- **Example in this video:** NQ Jan 12: Friday RTH settlement 25,933.50; Monday 9:30 open 25,746.25, so a discount gap with the settlement line as the gap HIGH. At 9:07 he already draws the 25,933.50 line (well above current price) and labels it ORG high, then adds the low at the 9:30 open. After the open, CE (about 25,839.9) is tagged within roughly a minute and the upper quadrant (25,887) around 9:39 ET (the 3/4 mark), a run of about 150 handles in total; the last quarter up to full closure at 25,933.50 was not needed. Stacked above the open: Asian session high (the range's highest high, run after the open and read as "cleared"), then this week's NWOG low, with Friday's settlement just below it; daily relative equal highs at 26,133.50 are the higher draw. Exact order of the Asian high vs. upper quadrant is read from his walkthrough (caption unclear).
- **Timestamps:** [1:21:42](https://youtu.be/dt9mk4n5g_o?t=4902) — mark previous settlement · [1:25:03](https://youtu.be/dt9mk4n5g_o?t=5103) — what the gap is, fib grading · [1:47:46](https://youtu.be/dt9mk4n5g_o?t=6466) — CE tagged, 70% stat · [1:48:33](https://youtu.be/dt9mk4n5g_o?t=6513) — vacuum / soda analogy
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** CE tag-by-10:00 70% figure restated at [2:09:19](https://youtu.be/dt9mk4n5g_o?t=7759). The 25,746.25 open is read from "746 quarter" in captions and prefixed 25,; the arithmetic of CE/upper quadrant (25,839.88 / 25,886.69) matches the 25,887 he reads out.

title: ICT 2026 Smart Money Concepts Lecture \ January 12, 2026
head: Opening gaps as PD arrays: NWOG / NDOG / RTH ORG — keep them after they fill
body:
- **Kind:** rule / refinement
- **What ICT says:** weekly opening gap, new day opening gap, RTH opening range gap are all different. Industry says a filled gap is "one and done"; he says that is a mistake. Keep them on the chart for at least five days, whether they fill or not; filled or traded-through gaps remain reference points. They matter most within the last 20 trading days.
- **How to use:** stack the levels numerically (highest to lowest with shorthand labels, in his notebook) for the last ~5 trading days: first-presented FVG Jan 7, NWOG this week, RTH ORG, etc. He does not use Friday's or Thursday's opening ranges.

  - Open, high, low, close is everything the market refers to.
  - Market makers need counterparties, so deep pockets wait for participation; with no news (CPI Tue, PPI Wed ahead) they won't run aggressively either way, hence the holding pattern 8–9 am.
  - Floor traders who say stop runs do not happen contradict the largest Nasdaq pit trader (Pax Trader) who described another house trying to run his orders.

title: ICT 2026 Smart Money Concepts In Action \ January 06, 2026
head: Buy-Side Liquidity (BSL) Above Structural Highs
body:
- **Kind:** entry model
- **What ICT says:** "I'm wanting the buy side is resting above the pre-market session highs. And then this high up here, which is overnight relative equal highs." The market is biased to run higher and collect stops/liquidity resting above these structural resistance points.
- **How to identify:** Identify overnight session highs (electronic trading, pre-market). Mark where relative equal highs formed. These become BSL pools above the current price.
- **How to use:** Use these points as targets for long entries. Enter on wicks or pullbacks into demand (discount areas), with the expectation that price will run up to collect these higher BSL pools.
- **Example in this video:** NQ on Jan 6: overnight relative equal highs were marked; ICT wanted to see price rally up to challenge and take out these levels. Entry was taken on a wick down into demand, with BSL above as the target.
- **Timestamps:** [0:03:03](https://youtu.be/Jxl5UJk_ylc?t=183) (identifying BSL above pre-market highs and overnight equal highs)
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** BSL is not the same as a simple "resistance"—it's specifically liquidity pools where stop-losses and limit orders rest, waiting to be hit.

title: ICT 2026 Smart Money Concepts In Action \ January 06, 2026
head: First Presented for Everybody Gap (FPEG)
body:
- **Kind:** definition · reference level
- **What ICT says:** The gap formed from the previous Friday's close into Monday's open. "This orange box up here is first presented for everybody gap from Friday." It's a reference point for assessing whether price is trading in premium or discount to last week.
- **How to identify:** Identify Friday's close and Monday's open; the gap between them is the FPEG.
- **How to use:** Use FPEG as a support/resistance zone and as context for bias. A gap-up entry (trading above FPEG) opens with premium bias. A gap-down open would be discount. Price will often test these extremes before extending.
- **Example in this video:** NQ gapped up from Friday's close on Monday, Jan 6 (first full week of 2026). The FPEG was a reference to understand whether price action was extended or retraceable.
- **Timestamps:** [0:03:03](https://youtu.be/Jxl5UJk_ylc?t=183) (FPEG identified as orange box) · [0:03:50](https://youtu.be/Jxl5UJk_ylc?t=230) (FPEG context in evaluating morning session)
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** FPEG is a structural reference, not a standalone trade signal. Context (bias, volatility, NFP week, etc.) determines how to use it.

title: ICT 2026 Smart Money Concepts In Action \ January 06, 2026
head: Electronic Trading Hours vs. Regular Trading Hours (RTH) Settlement
body:
- **Kind:** definition · reference level
- **What ICT says:** Electronic trading hours (Sunday open through Friday close, continuous) have a settlement price; RTH settlement (9:30 to 4:00 ET) is different. "Regular trading hours settlement is down here... we're showing electronic trading hours." The reference changes depending on which "official" settlement you're watching.
- **How to identify:** Note the settlement price for electronic trading (usually from Friday night's settlement) and RTH settlement (from previous day's close at 4:00 ET). These are marked as distinct levels on the chart.
- **How to use:** Use RTH settlement as a reference for the "official" previous day's close in terms of technical analysis. Electronic settlement is where overnight futures trading cleared. Both matter: RTH for daily technicals, electronic for context on overnight positioning.
- **Example in this video:** NQ's RTH settlement was marked below the current price; ICT noted that if price were to trade down to that level, it would represent a full gap closure and bearish rejection of the initial gap-up.
- **Timestamps:** [0:03:50](https://youtu.be/Jxl5UJk_ylc?t=230) (both settlements marked and explained)
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Many traders miss the distinction; always note which settlement you're referencing for daily bias confirmation.

title: ICT 2026 Smart Money Concepts In Action \ January 06, 2026
head: Premium Gap-Up Entry & The "Non-Participation" Test
body:
- **Kind:** entry model
- **What ICT says:** When a market gaps up (premium opening), ICT tests whether the gap will fill (bearish) or be rejected (bullish). "So, what I'm looking for is it to kind of like shun that, not want to do it at all. And then if it does negate that and not go back down into this orange shaded area, then this was a draw." If price refuses to fill the gap down to the previous RTH settlement, it proves the gap is a legitimate bullish move.
- **How to identify:** Gap up opens. Draw a line at the previous RTH settlement (the fill point). Watch if price wants to test it or rejects it.
- **How to use:** If price shuns the gap-fill and rallies instead, the gap is real; stay long. If price fills the gap and closes below it, the gap was a trap (what's sometimes called "trap and run" or rejection).
- **Example in this video:** NQ gapped up on Jan 6; ICT was watching to see if it would pull down to RTH settlement (blue line) or immediately reject that level and rally. His longs were predicated on price NOT wanting to fill the gap.
- **Timestamps:** [0:04:38](https://youtu.be/Jxl5UJk_ylc?t=278) (setting up the test: "if it's going to go back down here...I think it's going to be bearish")
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** This is a live trading decision point. Many trades fail because price DOES fill the gap; only reject participation when price truly shuns the fill level.

title: ICT 2026 Smart Money Concepts In Action \ January 06, 2026
head: Minor Buy-Side Liquidity Pool (Short-Term High)
body:
- **Kind:** reference level · entry model
- **What ICT says:** A recent short-term high (often just 1-2 bars back) where buy orders may be resting, expecting price to go higher. "There's like a minor short-term high. So, that would be a minor buy side liquidity pool."
- **How to identify:** Mark the previous 2-5 bars' highs; the most recent significant high (relative to the current bar) is a minor BSL.
- **How to use:** Use minor BSL as an initial target for long entries. Once reached, consider taking partial profits or rolling stops above it to let the trade run further. Multiple minor BSL pools at different levels create a ladder of targets.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 1-minute chart: there was a recent high marked as "minor buy side"; ICT wanted to see price tag it on the opening rally, take partial profits there, and then assess whether to roll and run the remaining position higher.
- **Timestamps:** [0:07:02](https://youtu.be/Jxl5UJk_ylc?t=422) (identification of minor BSL) · [0:14:11](https://youtu.be/Jxl5UJk_ylc?t=851) (price tags minor BSL, ICT takes half the position)
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Minor BSL is distinct from major BSL (overnight equal highs, pre-market highs). Use both in a hierarchy: enter at minor BSL, target major BSL above.

title: ICT 2026 Smart Money Concepts In Action \ January 06, 2026
head: Suspension Block (Buy-Side Imbalance, Sell-Side Inefficiency)
body:
- **Kind:** definition · reference level
- **What ICT says:** "This green shaded area here, that is the daily chart's suspension block, which is a buy side imbalance, sell side inefficiency within volume imbalance at the top and the bottom of it." On a bullish day, the suspension block from the daily chart becomes a target the intraday move should take out without resistance. "We want to see it cut right through that like a hot knife through butter."
- **How to identify:** On the daily chart, identify the suspension block (volume at extremes, balanced range). Then drop to intraday (1-min) and see where that daily range sits relative to the intraday price action.
- **How to use:** On long entries, the daily suspension block high is a major target. Price should run through it aggressively if the move is legitimate. Hesitation or wicks into the block signal weakness.
- **Example in this video:** NQ daily suspension block (green shaded area) was above the intraday price action. ICT wanted to see the 1-min rally aggressively break through this green zone without hesitation, proving strong bullish momentum.
- **Timestamps:** [0:10:01](https://youtu.be/Jxl5UJk_ylc?t=601) (identifying the daily suspension block as BSL imbalance / SSL inefficiency) · [0:12:13](https://youtu.be/Jxl5UJk_ylc?t=733) (price moving through the suspension block aggressively)
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** On intraday charts, the daily-level suspension block is a macro target. Failure to break through it aggressively suggests the move is not as strong as it appears and could be a trap.

title: ICT 2026 Smart Money Concepts In Action \ January 06, 2026
head: Bull Flag & Follow-Through Confirmation
body:
- **Kind:** pattern recognition · refinement
- **What ICT says:** "This is one of the times where I'd like to see a potential bull flag be valid and go higher. Not just simply because I have a position on, but I want to see it kind of like shake off any bearishness." A bull flag (brief pullback within a larger uptrend) is valid only if it breaks out above the flag's highs with conviction and follow-through.
- **How to identify:** After an initial rally, a minor pullback within the rally forms a "flag" pattern. For a bull flag to be valid, the next rally must break above the previous highs before the pullback.
- **How to use:** Don't trade the flag itself. Wait for the breakout above the flag and then take action. Assess follow-through: does price continue higher aggressively, or does it stall (indication the flag failed)?
- **Example in this video:** NQ formed a minor pullback/flag structure during the opening rally on Jan 6. ICT was waiting to see if the next rally would break above the prior highs with conviction, proving the bull flag was valid.
- **Timestamps:** [0:07:02](https://youtu.be/Jxl5UJk_ylc?t=422) (bull flag setup and the desire to see follow-through breaking above the high)
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** A bull flag that fails to break above prior highs is a weak setup; walking away is often the correct trade decision. Not all patterns deliver; the smart trader knows when to abandon a setup.

title: ICT 2026 Smart Money Concepts In Action \ January 06, 2026
head: Position Management: Rolling Stops & Taking Partials
body:
- **Kind:** execution · risk management
- **What ICT says:** Entry at a wick or pullback into demand. At the first target (minor BSL), take 50% profits. Roll the stop up to just below the half-way point or the entry-point level. Allow the remaining 50% to run to the next target (major BSL or daily suspension block high).
- **How to identify:** Mark your entry, first target, and secondary target before entering. Plan your partial-profit level (50% at first target is common).
- **How to use:** Mechanical execution: enter signal triggers → place stop at market risk level → if first target hit, immediately close 50%, roll stop up → let remaining 50% run. This locks in profit, removes the risk of giving back gains, and keeps you in the game for the bigger move.
- **Example in this video:** ICT entered long on a wick, set initial stop (to be adjusted). Minor BSL (previous high) was the first target; at that level, he placed a limit order to sell 50%. If filled, he would roll the stop to just below the minor BSL low to protect the remaining half.
- **Timestamps:** [0:13:01](https://youtu.be/Jxl5UJk_ylc?t=781) (stop management one minute before opening bell: "I don't want to roll the stop...I want to see it just rip aggressively higher") · [0:14:11](https://youtu.be/Jxl5UJk_ylc?t=851) (executing the partial profit at minor BSL and rolling the stop) · [0:14:58](https://youtu.be/Jxl5UJk_ylc?t=898) (technical difficulty with TradingView's paper trading fill execution)
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Take partial profits to lock in gains and reduce risk; it's not "leaving money on the table"—it's professional trade management. Many trades fail; securing 50% ensures you're not underwater if price reverses.

title: ICT 2026 Smart Money Concepts In Action \ January 06, 2026
head: Market Timing: Avoiding NFP Week & Geopolitical News
body:
- **Kind:** risk management · psychology
- **What ICT says:** "With the whole thing with Maduro being snatched up every weekend by Trump and then first real full week of trading for 2016... there's just a lot of things making it more complex than it needs to be." Jan 6, 2026 is the first full week of trading, NFP is coming, and there's political news driving volatility. ICT generally waits until the second week of February before putting on positions. "That's the reason why dad waits until the second week of February generally each year before I start putting anything into the marketplace."
- **How to identify:** Note the economic calendar (NFP, CPI, FOMC dates). Note the date of significant geopolitical events. These create uncertainty and wider ranges.
- **How to use:** Plan to reduce or pause trading the first 2-3 weeks of January and during major news weeks. If you do trade, reduce size and only take high-confidence setups.
- **Example in this video:** Jan 6, 2026: first full week of the year, NFP week coming, post-election volatility still present. ICT is trading, but with caution and awareness of the elevated risk environment.

title: ICT 2026 Smart Money Concepts In Action \ January 06, 2026
head: Paper Trading & Execution Issues as Teaching Tools
body:
- **Kind:** execution · caveat
- **What ICT says:** While demonstrating on TradingView's paper trading (demo account), the platform glitches and fails to fill limit orders properly. He acknowledges the teaching limitation: "It should have already filled. It hasn't." He uses this to illustrate that even paper trading platforms can be unreliable, and live traders must be prepared for technical failures.
- **How to identify:** Watch fill confirmations carefully. If a limit order should have filled but doesn't appear, note the discrepancy.
- **How to use:** In live trading (with a real broker), double-check all fills immediately. Don't trust the platform; verify with your broker. Ensure stops and limit orders are active, not invisible.
- **Example in this video:** TradingView showed the half-position sale at minor BSL appearing on the chart (where it should have filled) but not showing the actual filled order confirmation or closing the position in the account. This is a critical lesson: platform bugs cost real money; always verify.

- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Even on the platform he's using to teach, executions can fail. This is why he warns against over-sizing: if you can't exit cleanly, a large position becomes a serious problem.

title: ICT 2026 Smart Money Concepts Lecture \ January 02, 2026
head: FVG on the left side (buy side of the curve) of a swing high — acts as an inversion FVG / premium array  (aliases ICT uses: "inefficiency on the buy side of the curve", "left side of the swing high", "premium fair value gap")
body:
- **Kind:** new coinage / refinement (new PD-array twist; he calls it "two more PD arrays")
- **What ICT says:**
  - When a swing high forms and there is an inefficiency (volume imbalance / FVG) on the LEFT side of it, i.e. on the rising "buy side of the curve" before price rolls over, use that one.
  - Boundaries as he describes them: take the swing-high candle's wick high and the volume imbalance high and call that a fair value gap; the volume imbalance itself is the separation between one candle's body close and the next candle's body open (between the bodies). Exact box edges are not fully clear in the captions.
  - It will act as an inversion fair value gap because it is part of the buy side of the curve before the market rotates lower. It is a premium array.
  - Compare with the usual FVG on the RIGHT side (sell side of the curve) of the swing high, which is what Model 2022 or the turtle-soup false breakout uses. He prefers the left-side one: it is "hyper-sensitive", more precise, because price can wick through the right-side gap.
  - The downside: you may not get filled. A smaller FVG lower down (right side) can be used by price and the market never reaches the left-side one, so your limit/market order never fills. Otherwise being wrong is just being wrong.
  - Not wrong to use the right-side gap (it still worked that day and he says that is fine), but to be a purist in his concepts you must not disregard the volume imbalance.
- **How to identify:** a swing high; look to its left for a gap/volume imbalance on the up-move; mark it from the volume imbalance to the wick high.
- **How to use:** with a bearish daily bias, wait for price to trade up into the left-side FVG (premium); short from it, preferring entries above its consequent encroachment (midpoint).
- **Example in this video:** NQ daily swing high with a left-side FVG; on Fri Jan 2 price opened, rallied hard up into it (premium), failed to quite reach its consequent encroachment, rotated down. On the 1-minute he marked a red box: volume imbalance with candle close at "52.25" and next open at "52.00" (hundreds digit not stated; caption read) and secured entries above its midpoint/CE.
- **Timestamps:** [0:06:23](https://youtu.be/1X0A-Lgf9RY?t=383) — the rule, "for your notes" · [0:08:46](https://youtu.be/1X0A-Lgf9RY?t=526) — volume imbalance vs. wick high · [0:10:23](https://youtu.be/1X0A-Lgf9RY?t=623) — the no-fill downside · [0:30:54](https://youtu.be/1X0A-Lgf9RY?t=1854) — entries above the midpoint
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** extends the FVG teaching with a side-of-the-curve preference. At [0:11:10](https://youtu.be/1X0A-Lgf9RY?t=670) he notes price "failed to get to consequent encroachment", saying that is not strength but an inability to get there.

title: ICT 2026 Smart Money Concepts Lecture \ January 02, 2026
head: Turtle soup false breakout + first presented FVG carried forward (Model 2022 in fractal form)  (aliases: Model 2022, "high, higher high, failure")
body:
- **Kind:** entry model / refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - Sequence: a short-term high, then another short-term high above it (breakout), which rejects and pulls back into the range. This is the turtle-soup false breakout. It need not be a complete reversal; it only needs that characteristic.
  - The FIRST presented fair value gap after that failure is the one to carry forward. This is a fractal of Model 2022: the same pattern amplified to higher timeframes or reduced to lower ones.
  - New this time: in Model 2022 as originally taught you did not keep that FVG; the revelation of the previous night is to keep it and extend it into the future.
  - Short-term high definition applied: a candle high with a lower high on each side (he says people argue it's not a swing high; "they didn't short the high. I did").
  - In this day: the short-term high was pierced and price went into the premium array he was waiting for; then the swing low gets taken out, which sets the stage for Model 2022. He says he uses it every day, multiple times on lower timeframes, and rejects claims the algorithm changed.
  - He criticizes people who want to find it going forward without backtesting.
- **How to identify:** high, higher high, rejection, break of the swing low (MSS), first FVG left behind.
- **How to use:** short from the first presented FVG, when its context is bearish (premium array, daily bias down). He wants to see the FVG offer no resistance (see next entry for this day's version).
- **Example in this video:** NQ, Fri Jan 2: after the 9:30 open price rallied, blew through an old buy-side pool (relative equal highs), made a short-term high at the 9:48 candle (captioned "9:48 p.m."; presumably a.m.), whose neighboring highs were both lower; price tagged the left-side FVG premium array, then broke the swing low, left the first presented FVG, and sold off.
- **Timestamps:** [0:07:10](https://youtu.be/1X0A-Lgf9RY?t=430) · [0:07:58](https://youtu.be/1X0A-Lgf9RY?t=478) — keep and extend the first presented FVG · [0:26:06](https://youtu.be/1X0A-Lgf9RY?t=1566) — 9:48 short-term high · [0:26:54](https://youtu.be/1X0A-Lgf9RY?t=1614) — swing-low break, Model 2022

title: ICT 2026 Smart Money Concepts Lecture \ January 02, 2026
head: The Jan 2 trade walk-through: bias → target → entry → "speed below the low" → management
body:
- **Kind:** example / live trade
- **What ICT says (sequence):**
  - Bias: the night before he said price would drop and he was not interested in going long; he told family/friends that morning he expected a slam down after the run at 9:30. The daily chart view is "destructive mindset": where can they run stops/purge positions, acquire their position, and go the other way (or continuation).
  - Target: half of the RTH opening range gap = 25,567.25 (told to his group before the trade); he wanted price to dig a little through the half-gap. Even though it passed 10:00 am, shorting was still preferred over longing because the big daily suspension block is an elephant in the room.
  - Premium: price opened, rallied into the premium inversion array at the top of the day, taking out multiple stages of buy side (an old relative equal high pool plus the 9:48 short-term high).
  - Entry area: inside the red FVG box, above its midpoint/CE ([0:30:54]); the entry candle sits at the top of the range at that CE level ([0:36:34]).
  - Confirmation: first presented FVG forms on the sell-off (orange box). He wanted the FVG to offer no resistance: "no bodies up there at all", price ripping through its low; he moved a marked line from the FVG to its low to show he wanted that low to give way quickly ("speed under this low").
  - Retest: one candle's wick pokes just above the FVG's midpoint, then price closes below the FVG low; the next candle opens and trades up but stops short, leaving a small space below the orange box's low (an inversion-FVG retest that never arrives). He says a wick into the lower quadrant would have been a beautiful place to add. Failure to retest = heaviness, very bearish.
  - Run: an old low could not even be retested; straight run from entry to half gap; then price ripped through the half-gap, made a short-term low, came back above and swept the consequent encroachment of the opening range gap, then dropped to the lower quadrant of a daily wick (25,267.50).
  - ICT mentions this had "over 200 handles" of washout that day.
- **How to identify/use:** (1) HTF bias from the daily PD array, (2) opening-range-gap half as a target, (3) premium inversion array as the entry zone, (4) first presented FVG after the break, (5) heaviness if retests fail, (6) partial and stop management.
- **Timestamps:** [0:16:50](https://youtu.be/1X0A-Lgf9RY?t=1010) — 1-minute chart, target 25,567.25 · [0:31:42](https://youtu.be/1X0A-Lgf9RY?t=1902) · [0:32:31](https://youtu.be/1X0A-Lgf9RY?t=1951) — "speed" below the FVG low · [0:34:07](https://youtu.be/1X0A-Lgf9RY?t=2047) — failed retest, would have added at lower quadrant · [0:36:34](https://youtu.be/1X0A-Lgf9RY?t=2194) — entry candle at CE

head: Opening range gap half (CE) as the low-hanging-fruit objective
body:
- **Kind:** rule / entry model
- **What ICT says:** the RTH opening range gap's consequent encroachment (half the gap) is the primary objective; focus on half the gap only, do not look for a full close (something to evolve into). Stated again: about 70% of the time price trades back to it by 10:00 am. If the higher-timeframe chart is bearish, it is still viable to go short and aim at half gap after 10:00. He used this to coach his sons, a brother-in-law and best friend (a minimalist morning framework); take partials before the target.
- **Example in this video:** gap from the Friday RTH settle to the 9:30 open measured on the RTH chart with a fib (halves and lower quadrants); half-gap target 25,567.25, price tagged and slightly exceeded it.

title: ICT 2026 Smart Money Concepts Lecture \ January 02, 2026
head: Grading wicks (quadrants on a candle wick) as turning points  (aliases: "quadrants on a wick", mohawk for related wick behavior)
body:
- **Kind:** refinement / new emphasis
- **What ICT says:**
  - Grade a wick exactly like a FVG: upper quadrant, consequent encroachment, lower quadrant (and optionally eighths; "then you get really stupid with the precision"). He says "filling wicks" talk from stages is the same idea.
  - Use the candle range at first, until price trades through that candle's open; then switch to the wick because it extends below the open (caption unclear on which candle).
  - Daily wick of the swing-high candle graded: lower quadrant = 25,267.50 (caption reads "25,000 267 and a half"). The day's low on Jan 2 formed right there, which he says is not random.
  - Price behavior at the level: candle bodies stop just above it; one wick sweeps through a little, one a hair of a tick below; bodies do not close through.
  - He asserts nobody else teaches this, and says this has "always" been how price delivered since electronic markets.
- **How to use:** put the graded levels on higher-timeframe charts in an annotated workspace; look for reversals (including MMBM-type reversals) at the quadrant levels.
- **Example in this video:** after the half-gap run, price made relative equal lows (a low with a higher low to its right) near 25,267.50, swept them, then reversed. After trading above the last down-close candle it formed an order block; retest of its mean threshold; FVG; "smart money reversal", "low-risk buy", "second-stage reaccumulation"; cleared the high. He calls it a market maker buy model off a quadrant level on a daily wick.
- **Timestamps:** [0:11:59](https://youtu.be/1X0A-Lgf9RY?t=719) · [0:12:48](https://youtu.be/1X0A-Lgf9RY?t=768) · [0:45:22](https://youtu.be/1X0A-Lgf9RY?t=2722) — relative equal lows sweep · [0:46:11](https://youtu.be/1X0A-Lgf9RY?t=2771) — bodies stop north of the level · [0:47:01](https://youtu.be/1X0A-Lgf9RY?t=2821) — order block / MMBM · [0:56:33](https://youtu.be/1X0A-Lgf9RY?t=3393)
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** same wick-grading idea as the relative-equal-high wick grading in L26-138 (Jan 12); here it is applied to a daily wick.

head: Daily suspension block (volume imbalance at both ends of a BISI/SIBI range)
body:
- **Kind:** definition / example
- **What ICT says:** a daily buy-side imbalance sell-side inefficiency (BISI) range containing two volume imbalances, one at its high end and one at its low end, is a suspension block. These imbalances are the "true inefficiency". Grade the block: low, lower quadrant, CE/midpoint, upper quadrant, high. Price is likely to work inside it and it acts as the big "elephant in the room" for intraday bias. He told the audience to grade it and keep the levels on an annotated workspace.
- **Example in this video:** green shaded block on the NQ daily; price on Fri Jan 2 traded from the premium (above) down into it, tagging a lower quadrant level (see wick grading).

head: Mohawk (wicks outside, bodies inside a gap)
body:
- **Kind:** example / named behavior
- **What ICT says:** when price wicks above the FVG but candle bodies stay inside it, that is permissible price action; he names it a "mohawk". The wick is the algorithm referring back to the old swing high to collect the last bit of liquidity before moving on, like a market that leaves the range after you place an order. The bodies staying inside the FVG tell him it is respected.

head: Relative equal highs/lows as sweep candidates
body:
- **Kind:** refinement (restates rule)
- **What ICT says:** what makes a pool a good candidate to be run: the right-hand extreme is slightly lower (for highs) / slightly higher (for lows) than the left one. For lows: "a low with a higher low to the right of it" is a high-probability sweep candidate; the market trades down through it. For highs: the equal highs were an old buy pool that price blasted through at the open before going to the premium inefficiency.

title: ICT 2026 Smart Money Concepts Lecture \ January 02, 2026
head: Trade management: partial near target, roll the stop, never let it go stale
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - When you are close to target (10–15 handles) after a straight run and feel the urge to get out ("please just get to my target"), take a partial immediately; it relieves the pressure. A partial is also planned before the target is reached.
  - After the partial move the stop; roll it so the remaining position cannot give back everything.
  - Trail: each time price makes a new swing low (or an elongated candle breaks below), move the stop down, but do not strangle it, give about three handles of room, closer to price.
  - Never let the stop go stale: each new equity high (unrealized), find a way to move the stop closer to the exit. This is mindfulness about money, not paranoia.
  - If you take partials you can be somewhat more liberal about leaving the stop where first adjusted, but if you see overlapping PD arrays, a fast move can erase unrealized profit (stop left at break-even or a little plus).
  - In a "normalized" lower-volatility market you don't need to be this sensitive; in the recent break-neck volatility, do it. For new traders, getting stopped out of winners and making slightly less is a good thing to grow into.
  - Add to a short on a retest of the lower quadrant of the first presented FVG (he would have).
- **Timestamps:** [0:38:57](https://youtu.be/1X0A-Lgf9RY?t=2337) · [0:39:44](https://youtu.be/1X0A-Lgf9RY?t=2384) · [0:40:32](https://youtu.be/1X0A-Lgf9RY?t=2432) · [0:41:20](https://youtu.be/1X0A-Lgf9RY?t=2480) · [0:42:09](https://youtu.be/1X0A-Lgf9RY?t=2529)

head: Order flow / volume vs. forecasting ("yesterday's weather")
body:
- **Kind:** philosophy
- **What ICT says:** order flow, volume profile, number of contracts inside a candle are old data: "yesterday's weather". He is the weatherman forecasting future price from where liquidity and imbalance sit; "real order flow" for him is the open/high/low/close of candles. If order flow, heat maps or BookMap help you see salient pools of liquidity, use them; they can be a "visual crutch", and he would have used BookMap in 1992 if it had existed. Some of his students use them. He also says that if what you do makes consistent money, nobody's opinion should bother you. Precision (turning at the exact quadrant on a wick) is his evidence.

body:
- **Kind:** rule (process)
- **What ICT says:** study old/past data in hindsight as a routine; it builds independence so you don't need his or anyone's videos; hindsight is only criticism if you stop there; he also shows it live. Keep separate workspaces per timeframe with graded levels (NWOG/NDOG, turtle soup highs/lows, first presented FVG, suspension block quadrants) and toggle through them rather than loading everything on one chart; otherwise moves will surprise you. He is only surprised by geopolitical events. Takes about 10 years to get to knowing what you're looking for (his experience).
