head: Pre-conditions for any PM-session trade

title: 2022 ICT Mentorship Episode 39
head: NY lunch hour (bearish): clearing buy stops; smart money "cannibalizing" two order types
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - NY lunch is 12:00–1:00 PM NY time.
  - If bearish, the market clears the stops above the highs formed in, and just before, the lunch hour. At about 1:00 the algorithm reprices and runs those buy stops.
  - Large-range days often have a "busy lunch". In a fast market, lunch can form a significant high or low (as just taught in the previous lecture).
  - Why: the algorithm does not want morning shorts to be profitable, so it knocks them out by flooding the market with buyers at a higher price. Smart money sells to that buying.
  - Those buyers are of two kinds: shorts' buy stops, and breakout traders' buy stops. Both are buy-side liquidity, the counterparty smart money needs for its shorts.
  - Aggressive traders can short during lunch on such a directional day. Under the model's rules, wait until after lunch.
- **Example in this video:** ES 5m. Highs formed in and before lunch were run at about 1:00 PM. Price then broke lower toward 4070, then 4040, then the daily FVG.
- **Timestamps:** [0:16:16](https://youtu.be/yFpHbBnsK_c?t=976) — lunch is 12–1; [0:17:05](https://youtu.be/yFpHbBnsK_c?t=1025) — bearish lunch rule, reprice at 1:00; [0:17:51](https://youtu.be/yFpHbBnsK_c?t=1071) — fast-market lunch; [0:18:38](https://youtu.be/yFpHbBnsK_c?t=1118) — smart money cannibalizing buy stops.

title: 2022 ICT Mentorship Episode 39
head: ICT Bearish Breaker
body:
- **Kind:** definition / rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - A breaker is a pattern where price runs out a pool of liquidity (here buy-side), then reverses and trades back below the short-term low. When price later trades back up to that zone and the narrative is bearish, it is a short.
  - The reference is the down-closed candle: the lowest one before the up-move that cleared the short-term high.
  - You must know what the market is likely reaching for. "If you leave that out it's not a breaker, it's a gamble", aimless speculation.
  - After it repels price, expect acceleration through the sell-side below. Price should not hold the low to go higher.
- **Example in this video:** ES 5m afternoon. The swing low, then a higher high (BSL taken around lunch), then a break back below the swing low. Price returned to the bearish breaker, then fell through 4070 with only a small consolidation and no retracement, down to about 4040 and into the daily FVG.
- **Timestamps:** [0:20:13](https://youtu.be/yFpHbBnsK_c?t=1213) — breaker definition, needs a DOL; [0:21:00](https://youtu.be/yFpHbBnsK_c?t=1260) — down-closed candle; [0:21:48](https://youtu.be/yFpHbBnsK_c?t=1308) — expect acceleration through SSL.

title: 2022 ICT Mentorship Episode 39
head: Algorithmic sell day (no retracement)
body:
- **Kind:** rule / example
- **What ICT says:** On an algorithmic sell day, price accelerates with only small consolidations, no retracement and no return to old lows. "Broken support becomes resistance, forget about it." Retail concepts get little chance. You are either on board beforehand or you watch the ship sail.
- **Timestamps:** [0:22:35](https://youtu.be/yFpHbBnsK_c?t=1355)

title: 2022 ICT Mentorship Episode 39
head: Time and price in algorithmic theory; macro defined; support/resistance as a fallacy
body:
- **Kind:** definition / rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - Price is delivered by an algorithm. "Buying/selling pressure" is an excuse.
  - Algorithmic theory is time and price, and it leans heavily on time: time of day, day of week, week of month, month of year, seasonal influences.
  - "Price levels are useless until time is considered." That is why support/resistance is a fallacy: anyone can find a line that worked in hindsight, but picking the right level live, consistently, does not work.
  - The algorithm "works a specific macro": a short sequence of instructions. Seek a level, move to a premium or discount, move suddenly or consolidate, then wait for another time element in the same day, week, or month.
  - The reverse also holds: "time is of no use unless price is at a key PD array". Blending the two gives the precision.
  - Learning time is where students have the largest growth but also the first adversities.
- **Timestamps:** [0:32:08](https://youtu.be/yFpHbBnsK_c?t=1928) — algorithm, time and price, time-heavy; [0:32:55](https://youtu.be/yFpHbBnsK_c?t=1975) — time factors; price useless without time; [0:34:29](https://youtu.be/yFpHbBnsK_c?t=2069) — macro definition; [0:36:05](https://youtu.be/yFpHbBnsK_c?t=2165) — time useless unless at a PD array.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** He tells his own 1992–94 story: stopped out at "resistance", afraid to re-enter, abandoned a framework that was still valid. Better: keep the framework, admit the entry was wrong, and re-enter with less risk and leverage.

title: 2022 ICT Mentorship Episode 39
head: Daily range as a programmed "game map"; algorithm blind to order volume
body:
- **Kind:** definition (analogy)
- **What ICT says:**
  - The algorithm is not aware of how much volume rests above or below a high or low, and it does not need to be. It just has to take out the short-term high or low.
  - Like Pac-Man's maze or a Fortnite/Call of Duty map, the daily range has programmed boundaries, until manual intervention removes them.
- **Timestamps:** [0:44:11](https://youtu.be/yFpHbBnsK_c?t=2651) — algorithm unaware of volume; [0:45:48](https://youtu.be/yFpHbBnsK_c?t=2748) — daily range limits programmed.

title: 2022 ICT Mentorship Episode 39
head: Manual intervention and the economic calendar
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - Every price move is controlled, engineered, and premeditated, either by the AI/algorithm following its code or by manual intervention.
  - Manual intervention (for example FOMC or rate announcements) sends price abruptly to a level well outside what is reasonable for the short-term perspective.
  - Use the economic calendar. In his son's model, engage on days with medium or high-impact news. On days without news you can practise, but not with your normal risk percentage.
- **Timestamps:** [0:41:44](https://youtu.be/yFpHbBnsK_c?t=2504) — AI vs manual intervention; [0:42:32](https://youtu.be/yFpHbBnsK_c?t=2552) — FOMC, calendar, risk on no-news days.

title: 2022 ICT Mentorship Episode 39
head: "The model I teach my son" (Caleb's 5-point model)  (aliases: one-trick pony model)
body:
- **Kind:** entry model
- **What ICT says:**
  - Built to fit his son's personality (short attention span), with a very low points threshold. Index futures were chosen: no spread issues as in forex, a professional and very liquid market, and systematic price delivery.
  - **Time first.** Set the TradingView clock to New York time. Key windows:
    - 8:30 ET: the news embargo lifts, so it is the first time element.
    - 9:30 ET: equities open.
    - 1:30 PM ET: the PM session, after lunch.
    - 3:00–4:00 PM ET: the "market on close macro", which forms a small setup most days, buy or sell.
  - **Setup (bearish example at 8:30):**
    1. At 8:30 price is above the midnight opening price on a bearish day.
    2. It runs a short-term high (buy stops of 1-minute traders), so it is now at a premium.
    3. It then trades lower through a short-term low, leaving an FVG.
    4. It rallies back up into the FVG. Sell short there, targeting the sell-side pool below (old lows or relative equal lows; here 4101 / the 4100 big figure).
    5. Mirror all of this for buys.
  - **Target:** exactly 5 ES points, then out, even if the framework allows 30. Then watch whether price reaches the liquidity pool. Later, he will take a partial at 5 and hold the rest for the pool.
  - **Why 5 points:** it is easy and is the lowest threshold a setup should yield. Less than that is ultra-short-term scalping where commissions kill you. Even on a choppy day, an experienced trader can reasonably get 5 points once in the AM and once in the PM.
  - The DOL must be clear: buy-side above or sell-side below. This is not trading a level to watch it repel.
- **How to use (daily trade-count rules):**
  - Morning: one trade, at either 8:30 or 9:30. If he gets 5 points at 8:30, he does not trade 9:30. If he misses 8:30, he tries 9:30. A loss at 8:30 may be made back at 9:30.
  - Afternoon (1:30): traded live only if he missed the 9:30 setup or took a morning loss. If the morning was profitable, the afternoon is demo or paper only. Not pushing the edge teaches discipline, not greed.
  - Up to three opportunities a day; he looks for just one to yield 5 points.
- **Example in this video:**
  - **8:30:** ES was above the midnight open, ran a short-term high, traded lower through a short-term low creating an FVG, rallied into it, then sold toward the 4100/4101 SSL.
  - **1:30 PM:** buy stops were taken. Price broke down, returned to the bearish breaker, displaced lower, and broke relative equal lows ("this low, this low and this low"), leaving an imbalance. Price traded back up into it: short for 5 points, then watch for 4070 and the daily FVG.
- **Timestamps:** [0:39:20](https://youtu.be/yFpHbBnsK_c?t=2360) — time first, 8:30 news embargo, NY clock; [0:46:36](https://youtu.be/yFpHbBnsK_c?t=2796) — 8:30 sequence: BSL run, premium, reprice to 4100 SSL; [0:47:23](https://youtu.be/yFpHbBnsK_c?t=2843) — short-term low broken, FVG, sell short, 5 points; [1:06:24](https://youtu.be/yFpHbBnsK_c?t=3984) — AM/PM trade-count rules; [1:10:20](https://youtu.be/yFpHbBnsK_c?t=4220) — 1:30 PM setup; [1:12:44](https://youtu.be/yFpHbBnsK_c?t=4364) — 3–4 PM market-on-close macro.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:**
  - His son reportedly went from an equity low of about $2,810 to about $18,300 in roughly four weeks of live trading (from the first week of May), "about 400%". ICT stresses this came with him co-piloting minute by minute, and that you should not quit your job on it.
  - Earlier he made his son take a trade at every window (8:30, 9:30, PM, sometimes 3–4 PM) as practice.

title: 2022 ICT Mentorship Episode 39
head: 9:30 recap and reading a failing short: multiple SSL levels taken + bearish order block traded through
body:
- **Kind:** rule / example
- **What ICT says:**
  - At 9:30 price first dropped. He tweeted that price would reprice up to 4105, where buy-side liquidity and an FVG sat, and then the real move would come.
  - He shorted 4105 on demo and tweeted "pay the trader" before taking a 2-contract partial below the short-term low. He then moved his stop slightly better than breakeven.
  - Why he knew it was turning: after BSL was taken, price should have been "off to the races". Instead it took sell-side at many levels (old lows, then relative equal lows, then another low, and more) "without moving very much".
  - The last up-close candle (a bearish order block) should have capped price under bearish institutional order flow. It might be touched once more or slightly exceeded, then price should drop aggressively. Price instead traded up into and through it.
  - After taking multiple levels of sell-side and then that candle, the algorithm seeks buy-side.
- **How to use:** When this happens, take a further partial before the stop is reached rather than closing everything in panic. He closed 3 more contracts as price went through the order block. The remaining 3 were stopped out at better than breakeven, so no losing scratch. Pieces taken off can be added back later (pyramiding) if price resumes.
- **Example in this video:** ES 5m at 9:30: short from about 4105, partial below the short-term low, then the bearish order block (up-close candle) failed. Price ran above the high and back above the midnight open, consolidated, then broke down in the afternoon.
- **Timestamps:** [0:58:29](https://youtu.be/yFpHbBnsK_c?t=3509) — 4105 BSL + FVG call; [1:01:40](https://youtu.be/yFpHbBnsK_c?t=3700) — partials and the order block he watched; [1:03:16](https://youtu.be/yFpHbBnsK_c?t=3796) — multiple SSL levels taken without moving much; [1:04:49](https://youtu.be/yFpHbBnsK_c?t=3889) — up-close candle should cap price; through it, the algorithm seeks BSL.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** "You're paying a stop loss to do its job." He does not mind a stop being hit, but takes a portion off ahead of it when price shows failure.

title: 2022 ICT Mentorship Episode 39
head: Backtesting the time windows
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:** He has "laid in your lap" the times these setups form. Go back through the last month, three weeks, two weeks, and one week. Count how many setups at these key times offered 5 points with a liquidity run plus an FVG, then do the math for one mini contract. Backtesting is the only way to kill FOMO from setups that form after you leave the charts.
- **Timestamps:** [0:29:45](https://youtu.be/yFpHbBnsK_c?t=1785) — FOMO and backtesting; [1:13:33](https://youtu.be/yFpHbBnsK_c?t=4413) — count setups at key times.

title: 2022 ICT Mentorship Episode 40
head: Swing high (3-bar definition)
body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:** A swing high is three candles: a high with a lower high on the candle to the left and a lower high on the candle to the right. It is not a Williams fractal and not five candles. "If you're waiting for five candles you missed the boat."
- **How to use:** A daily swing high that forms right after price runs an old high means expect lower the next day.
- **Example in this video:** USDCAD daily. Last week price bumped just above an old short-term high (visible clearly on the 1h), then printed a lower-high candle the next day, forming the swing high. ICT expected lower prices after that.
- **Timestamps:** [0:04:08](https://youtu.be/koN1ge8bewI?t=248) — old high run, 3-candle swing high; [0:04:57](https://youtu.be/koN1ge8bewI?t=297) — not a 5-bar fractal.

title: 2022 ICT Mentorship Episode 40
head: Bullish order block as an impediment to a down move (daily)
body:
- **Kind:** example only / rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - On the way down, a down-closed candle (a bullish order block) on the daily can slow the move. He anchored a dashed line at that candle's opening price.
  - He was not saying price would go into it to go higher. Only that it is the "impediment" to one big down candle clearing the level below.
  - Price dug into about half its body, and the daily candle closed there (21 June 2022).
- **Timestamps:** [0:05:44](https://youtu.be/koN1ge8bewI?t=344) — down-closed candle, half its body; [0:06:32](https://youtu.be/koN1ge8bewI?t=392) — impediment, not a reversal call.

title: 2022 ICT Mentorship Episode 40
head: News-driver manipulation into a premium, then displacement at 8:30 (forex model)
body:
- **Kind:** entry model / example
- **What ICT says:**
  - Ahead of the 8:30 high-impact news, price rallies. "This is all manipulation." It runs into an imbalance and above a short-term high (BSL), building a premium from about 5:00 AM NY.
  - Only high (red) or medium (orange) impact events interest him; he says yellow does not (he seems to call orange "yellow", caption unclear). Calendar source: forexfactory.com.
  - The ICT New York killzone for forex runs 7:00–10:00 AM NY.
  - A small break of a low ("toe in the water") is not enough. Wait for meaningful, energetic displacement through the short-term low. That is the MSS. Here the displacement candle was exactly the 8:30 release.
  - A pre-news FVG short was possible but riskier, because the 8:30 release could spike price up into the area above. The conservative way is to wait for the news, then for the setup. Trusting pre-news continuation "takes a little bit more experience". Practise these on demo in real time instead of forecasting how far the release will push.
  - After the displacement, define risk for a possible return to the higher FVG(s) with the volatility.
- **How to identify:**
  1. Run of the short-term high (BSL) in the killzone.
  2. Energetic displacement through a short-term low at or after the news.
  3. An FVG left behind.
  4. Opposing liquidity (relative equal lows / SSL) below as the target.
- **Example in this video:** USDCAD 15m and 5m, 21 June 2022. From 5 AM NY price built a premium. At about 7:00 AM a short-term high formed, then was run (BSL taken). A first drop was too weak. At 8:30 (core retail sales high-impact, retail sales medium-impact) the displacement candle broke the short-term low, leaving an FVG. Price then delivered into the FVG below (a discount array, past equilibrium of the high–low range) and then into the relative-equal-lows SSL from the morning.
- **Timestamps:** [0:07:19](https://youtu.be/koN1ge8bewI?t=439) — pre-news rally is manipulation into FVG and BSL; [0:08:09](https://youtu.be/koN1ge8bewI?t=489) — high/medium impact only; NY killzone 7–10 AM for forex; [0:08:57](https://youtu.be/koN1ge8bewI?t=537) — meaningful displacement, MSS on the news candle; [0:09:43](https://youtu.be/koN1ge8bewI?t=583) — wait for the news (conservative) vs pre-news entry.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** His tweet at 8:29 AM asked students to note SSL and BSL on the 5m and 15m and "study if it wants to run sell side before buy side or rebounds to a discount".

title: 2022 ICT Mentorship Episode 40
head: Elongated FVG and entering in the premium of the imbalance; stop placement
body:
- **Kind:** refinement / rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - When a sell-side delivery is long, one-sided, and imbalanced, with "not enough buy-side delivery", the algorithm will want to come back up and overlap it. That gives buyers a chance and rebalances the leg.
  - Forex has no central volume measure.
  - Under the model rules, the stop goes above the FVG / the level it could revisit, wherever you enter between the low and that high.
  - To refine the entry, fib the range high to low and sell at or above the 50% (equilibrium), in the premium.
  - About 12 pips of risk is fine because "it's all relative". Forex scales your size to the stop; futures lock you into contract size (or over-leverage).
- **How to use:** Short in the premium of the displacement leg. Stop above the FVG / swing high. First partial at the first discount array, then target SSL.
- **Example in this video:** USDCAD 4m. Entry area about 1.2944–1.2947 (caption "129.44 / 129.47"). Candle bodies respected the premium high of the imbalance. A small false rally took buy-side once more, then the real move ran into the FVG below (partials), then below a low of engineered SSL and into the SSL pool.
- **Timestamps:** [0:12:54](https://youtu.be/koN1ge8bewI?t=774) — 4m chart, elongated imbalance; [0:13:42](https://youtu.be/koN1ge8bewI?t=822) — one-sided delivery must rebalance; stop placement; [0:14:30](https://youtu.be/koN1ge8bewI?t=870) — 12 pips is relative, forex scalable; [0:15:18](https://youtu.be/koN1ge8bewI?t=918) — 50% equilibrium, sell in premium; [0:16:04](https://youtu.be/koN1ge8bewI?t=964) — entry 1.2944–1.2947.

title: 2022 ICT Mentorship Episode 40
head: Partials at the first discount array
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:** Between the high and the low is equilibrium. When short, find a discount array below it (an FVG), take a partial there, and target the sell-side pool. Partials matter because price may come all the way back up and revisit the FVG, and you would lose the chance to bank something at your first discount array.
- **Timestamps:** [0:12:07](https://youtu.be/koN1ge8bewI?t=727) — equilibrium, discount array, partial; [0:12:54](https://youtu.be/koN1ge8bewI?t=774) — why partials.

title: 2022 ICT Mentorship Episode 40
head: London close (10:00–11:00 AM NY): take about 80% off
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - If you are in a directional trade, have about 80% of it off between 10:00 and 11:00 AM NY. That hour usually (not always) creates the opposite end of the daily range. If the session high is in, the low is likely to form 10–11. "That's algorithmic."
  - For CAD on crude oil inventory days, crude news can skew this, so he widens the window to 10:00–noon.
  - He has always taught 10–11 as the "London close profit-taking hour".
- **Example in this video:** USDCAD rolled over during 10–11 after the 8:30 short.
- **Timestamps:** [0:16:50](https://youtu.be/koN1ge8bewI?t=1010) — 10–11 London close, 80% off; [0:17:38](https://youtu.be/koN1ge8bewI?t=1058) — crude oil days, 10–noon.

title: 2022 ICT Mentorship Episode 40
head: Daily bias simplified ("keys to daily bias")
body:
- **Kind:** rule / checklist
- **What ICT says:**
  - Having a bias every day is unrealistic. If he decides a daily bias before the market trades, invariably he will be wrong sometimes. There is no cookie-cutter ABC; the rest is experience.
  - Instead, determine the likely weekly expansion from the weekly chart. Is it gravitating to:
    - an old high to run above it;
    - an old low to run below it;
    - an imbalance above or below to revisit;
    - or is it likely not to move, because this market has no news that week while others do (then expect a lacklustre market)?
  - He is not trying to catch the whole weekly range, buy the weekly low, or predict the weekly close. He only wants the direction of the bulk of the volatility ("volume" in forex means interest, energy, activity). "Who's in the crosshairs?" For example, if longs have been making money, is there a low to run to stop them out?
  - Go top-down: weekly, daily, 4h, 1h, 15m, then 5m. Then scale through 5/4/3/2/1m to whichever shows a clear FVG under the model rules.
  - Focus only on days with high or medium-impact calendar events. Check the calendar ahead (even next month): which day and time.
  - On that news day, in your killzone, in the direction of the expected weekly expansion, look for: a run up into an FVG or above a short-term high (stops), then a breakdown with displacement, then an FVG to short (mirror for longs).
  - If the move happens before the event, it is a missed opportunity. Use another pair.
- **How to use:** This gives a developing student "permission not to know the daily bias outside of these rules". Plan the trade: calendar, time of day, killzone, and the weekly expansion direction.
- **Timestamps:** [0:19:12](https://youtu.be/koN1ge8bewI?t=1152) — daily bias intro; [0:20:47](https://youtu.be/koN1ge8bewI?t=1247) — everyday bias unrealistic; weekly expansion; [0:21:37](https://youtu.be/koN1ge8bewI?t=1297) — weekly targets (old high/low, imbalance, no news); [0:24:47](https://youtu.be/koN1ge8bewI?t=1487) — top-down to 5–1m, high/medium news days only; [0:25:34](https://youtu.be/koN1ge8bewI?t=1534) — news-day setup in killzones.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** He presents this as the simplification of all his earlier daily-bias lessons. "There's nothing else I'm holding back."

title: 2022 ICT Mentorship Episode 40
head: FOMC whipsaw: ignore the two-sided wick range
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:** When price whipsaws both sides (sell-side then buy-side taken), it is usually FOMC or a rate announcement. Ignore those wicks. The "real range" is the body-defined swing; the manipulation is done and "not going to hurt you".
- **Example in this video:** ES hourly. Relative equal lows were taken by a slightly lower low. Then a two-sided FOMC whipsaw, a breakdown, a new low, consolidation (Monday holiday), and a drift higher.
- **Timestamps:** [0:30:24](https://youtu.be/koN1ge8bewI?t=1824) — whipsaw both sides; [0:31:12](https://youtu.be/koN1ge8bewI?t=1872) — ignore wicks, real range.

title: 2022 ICT Mentorship Episode 40
head: Premium FVG as a target (and skipping an FVG that sits on equilibrium)
body:
- **Kind:** rule / example
- **What ICT says:**
  - Take the swing high-to-low range and find equilibrium.
  - He was not interested in an FVG overlapping the 50% level. He wanted an FVG fully in the premium as the draw, as the "first low-hanging fruit", even if the market later goes up to go down.
  - Candle bodies stayed within the FVG in the premium.
  - The hourly FVG's lower and upper levels became the intraday targets.
- **Example in this video:** ES (ESU2022) hourly. The premium FVG above equilibrium was the draw. Price reached the low of the hourly FVG, then the high of it, during the NY AM session.
- **Timestamps:** [0:31:59](https://youtu.be/koN1ge8bewI?t=1919) — skip the FVG overlapping equilibrium; [0:32:46](https://youtu.be/koN1ge8bewI?t=1966) — bodies inside the premium FVG.

title: 2022 ICT Mentorship Episode 40
head: London forms the high or low of day (~70%); consecutive down-closed candles as one order block
body:
- **Kind:** rule / definition
- **What ICT says:**
  - London creates the high or the low of the day "most of the time, 70% of time", if your directional bias is correct.
  - The last three down-closed candles before a rally count as one (consecutive) bullish order block.
- **Example in this video:** ES 15m. From the NY midnight open price went down (not up) into an FVG and the bullish order block of the last three down-closed candles during London. It rallied energetically (a short-term bullish MSS), made a new FVG, ran buy-side, and left relative equal highs ahead of NY. Then it dropped into the FVG and the last down-closed candle (a bullish order block), a buy area ahead of the 9:30 open. ICT trusted the London low as the likely daily low.
- **Timestamps:** [0:33:33](https://youtu.be/koN1ge8bewI?t=2013) — midnight open, consecutive down-closed candles = OB; [0:34:20](https://youtu.be/koN1ge8bewI?t=2060) — London makes the high or low about 70% of the time.

title: 2022 ICT Mentorship Episode 40
head: NY AM session for index futures (8:30–11:00); early setup before 9:30
body:
- **Kind:** rule / entry model
- **What ICT says:**
  - For index futures, the NY AM session runs 8:30–11:00 AM.
  - There is a hierarchy: price trades down into HTF, then lower-TF, then lower-TF down-closed candles (order blocks) and FVGs, all within a bullish bias. FVGs get closed and price goes higher. You need no indicators or moving averages; "the candlestick is telling you everything".
  - When manipulation is already done before 9:30, you do not need to wait for the 9:30 volatility. Price had made a low, then a lower low (SSL taken, a stop run) into an order block, reacted, shifted structure, and closed the only FVG. Then it was not likely to take that low out.
- **How to use:** Buy at the down-closed candle plus FVG in the short-term discount (below 50% of the low-to-high leg). First target is the BSL (relative equal highs) as the first partial. Pyramid as it runs. Then target the hourly FVG low and high.
- **Example in this video:** ES 5m and 3m:
  1. Low, then a lower low into a bullish OB (SSL run).
  2. Rally gives a short-term MSS.
  3. Retrace into the FVG plus last down-closed candle in a discount.
  4. Consolidation at 9:30.
  5. Run to three targets, all hit: BSL relative equal highs, the low of the hourly FVG, and the high of the hourly FVG.
  
  An FVG was overshot slightly ("that's fine").
- **Timestamps:** [0:35:08](https://youtu.be/koN1ge8bewI?t=2108) — 8:30–11 session; hourly FVG levels as targets; [0:35:57](https://youtu.be/koN1ge8bewI?t=2157) — hierarchy of down-closed candles; no indicators; [0:38:20](https://youtu.be/koN1ge8bewI?t=2300) — why the low will not be taken; buy at OB+FVG; [0:39:09](https://youtu.be/koN1ge8bewI?t=2349) — no need to wait for 9:30.

title: 2022 ICT Mentorship Episode 40
head: Intermarket risk-on / risk-off using the pair with the news driver
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - Look at USDCAD's first-named currency (USD). If USDCAD is expected to go down into a discount or run SSL, the dollar is weaker. That is risk-on, so ES, NQ, and foreign currencies rally more easily.
  - Because USDCAD had the high-impact news, he did not need the DXY. He went straight to USDCAD to frame the morning bias for ES.
  - The markets are not "correlated". It is only risk-on vs risk-off.
  - Risk-on: foreign currencies, index futures, and stocks up; dollar down. Risk-off: dollar up, everything else down.
- **Example in this video:** At the 9:30 period, USDCAD traded down into its discount while ES rallied.
- **Timestamps:** [0:40:47](https://youtu.be/koN1ge8bewI?t=2447) — USDCAD bearish means risk-on; [0:41:35](https://youtu.be/koN1ge8bewI?t=2495) — no need for DXY; [0:44:46](https://youtu.be/koN1ge8bewI?t=2686) — risk-on/off definitions.

title: 2022 ICT Mentorship Episode 40
head: SMT for pair selection in forex
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - Pick the market by the economic calendar.
  - If EUR has the high-impact news, compare EURUSD and GBPUSD. If both fell before the release but GBPUSD failed to make a lower low (risk-on), buy GBPUSD, the relative strength leader, even though the news is on EUR, because they move in sympathy.
  - The same applies to AUDUSD vs NZDUSD: buy the one making the higher low when risk-on.
  - On this day he did not check other pairs. He stayed only on USDCAD because the calendar put forex volatility there.
- **Timestamps:** [0:44:46](https://youtu.be/koN1ge8bewI?t=2686) — EURUSD vs GBPUSD; [0:45:35](https://youtu.be/koN1ge8bewI?t=2735) — AUD vs NZD, higher-low currency; [0:46:24](https://youtu.be/koN1ge8bewI?t=2784) — choosing the pair with the calendar and SMT.

title: 2022 ICT Mentorship Episode 40
head: 10-second-chart entry, partials, and holding a runner into the PM session
body:
- **Kind:** example only / rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - He entered the ES long on a 10-second chart. After 9:30 there was consolidation, then a run higher that created an FVG. Price dropped into it and he bought, filled at 3741.75.
  - Take first partials at the logical HTF levels and scale per your plan. Add (pyramid) as price takes out a short-term high.
  - Hold something toward the close, or look for continuation in the afternoon session, 1:30–4:00 PM NY.
- **Timestamps:** [0:43:12](https://youtu.be/koN1ge8bewI?t=2592) — 10s chart, fill 3741.75; [0:43:59](https://youtu.be/koN1ge8bewI?t=2639) — hold a runner for 1:30–4:00 PM.

title: 2022 ICT Mentorship - Episode 41 & Final
head: Failed expectation around a news event: when to walk away
body:
- **Kind:** rule / example
- **What ICT says:**
  - When a high-impact event (here Fed Chair Powell at 10:00) does not pan out as expected, in his experience it is better to step away, close the computer, and come back later. He then looks at the lunch hour and the post-lunch 1:30 window.
  - The NY index AM session (killzone) is 8:30–11:00. He can trade after 11, but he sticks to the rules to show that following them sometimes means missing opportunities, "and it's fine".
  - Being wrong publicly costs nothing when risk is controlled.
- **Example in this video:** ES 1h, 23 June 2022. SSL was taken, then a rally to BSL. His target was 3805, above an old high to the left. If it had hit, he would have watched for a short there. Price went just above a short-term high, "gave up the ghost", and went lower. His long was stopped out at +2 points ("just covering expenses").
- **Timestamps:** [0:01:41](https://youtu.be/2XhDi5GoNUI?t=101) — 3805 target, stopped out +2; [0:03:16](https://youtu.be/2XhDi5GoNUI?t=196) — AM session 8:30–11, sticking to rules; [0:04:50](https://youtu.be/2XhDi5GoNUI?t=290) — walk away after a failed news-driven expectation.

title: 2022 ICT Mentorship - Episode 41 & Final
head: No displacement, no valid FVG
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - After his long was stopped out, price dropped back down but did not take out the short-term low with displacement. So the FVG that formed was "not one that I would have taken". It was not an FVG he would participate in, because there was no meaningful move below that low.
  - Had a candle displaced below the low and then retraced up into the FVG, he "may have" shorted, aimed for that low, and closed it at noon if not reached.
- **Example in this video:** ES 5m and 2m in the morning. He went long from a 2-minute FVG, and the BSL above was taken with a bold bullish candle. Price came back for a complete closure of the FVG, rallied away, then dropped again and stopped him out, because he had rolled his stop up rather than weather a deeper retracement. The subsequent drop lacked displacement through the short-term low, so he stood aside.
- **Timestamps:** [0:09:36](https://youtu.be/2XhDi5GoNUI?t=576) — 2-minute FVG long toward 3805; [0:11:12](https://youtu.be/2XhDi5GoNUI?t=672) — stopped out after rolling stop; complete closure of the FVG; [0:11:59](https://youtu.be/2XhDi5GoNUI?t=719) — FVG without displacement, not taken.

title: 2022 ICT Mentorship - Episode 41 & Final
head: Price overrunning a smaller FVG to reach a larger one
body:
- **Kind:** refinement / example
- **What ICT says:** Price ran over a smaller 15m FVG because a larger one sat beneath it. The top of a candle marked the low end of one gap and also the high end of the other, so price was likely to go over the top of the smaller FVG and run into the larger one.
- **Example in this video:** ES 15m. After running BSL, price drew down, took SSL, and overran the smaller FVG into the larger 15m FVG. Going into the noon lunch hour until 1:00, it made the session low after closing in that FVG.
- **Timestamps:** [0:05:37](https://youtu.be/2XhDi5GoNUI?t=337) — overrunning one FVG into the larger one.

title: 2022 ICT Mentorship - Episode 41 & Final
head: NY lunch: don't initiate into lunch; prefer the lunch stop run; wait for 1:30
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - Once price broke lower going into lunch, he did not want to short, because it might consolidate and "take forever". He does not hold anything new into lunch.
  - He prefers to see a stop run during the lunch hour. Here price ran below the lows into an FVG in a deep discount (of the low–high range) during lunch, and made the session low at about 1:00 when lunch ended.
  - The NY index PM session is 1:30–4:00 PM NY. He likes to wait until 1:30 because the price action is cleaner.
- **Timestamps:** [0:06:23](https://youtu.be/2XhDi5GoNUI?t=383) — 1:30–4:00 PM session; [0:07:10](https://youtu.be/2XhDi5GoNUI?t=430) — no new trades into lunch; prefer the lunch stop run; [0:07:59](https://youtu.be/2XhDi5GoNUI?t=479) — wait until 1:30, cleaner price action.

title: 2022 ICT Mentorship - Episode 41 & Final
head: "Gold standard" ICT pattern: FVG + order block + OTE after an MSS
body:
- **Kind:** entry model
- **What ICT says:** A fair value gap with an order block at optimal trade entry is "the gold standard" and the flagship pattern of the channel. His checklist:
  1. Price traded down into an HTF FVG (15m) and shows willingness to go higher.
  2. A short-term market structure shift.
  3. A gap (FVG).
  4. A down-closed candle (bullish order block) to the left of it.
  5. The retrace into the OB lies at the OTE: the 62–79% retracement (caption says "62 to 70"), below equilibrium of the swing.
- **How to use:** Place a buy limit order. Stop under the swing low. First target is the first "low-hanging fruit": the nearest imbalance or premium level. Further targets are the BSL pools above.
- **Example in this video:** ES 2m and 5m PM session. Price hit the low in the 1:00 hour and rallied, giving a short-term MSS. At about 1:30 it traded back down into the last down-closed candle (OB), inside a 15m FVG (caption says "50 minute"), at OTE. It then ran to the short-term high, then through an FVG and up to 3805. Hypothetical demo entry: limit buy at 3754.75 (he says a quarter point below a candle's low). Stop 3745.75 (the swing low), which is 9 points of risk. First target 3780.25, the high of the imbalance candle in the premium of the high–low range. That is 25.5 points, better than 2.5R.
- **Timestamps:** [0:15:55](https://youtu.be/2XhDi5GoNUI?t=955) — 1:30 MSS, OB, 15m FVG, OTE = gold standard; [0:16:44](https://youtu.be/2XhDi5GoNUI?t=1004) — targets: imbalance, BSL, 3805; [0:18:18](https://youtu.be/2XhDi5GoNUI?t=1098) — checklist, limit 3754.75; [0:19:06](https://youtu.be/2XhDi5GoNUI?t=1146) — stop 3745.75 (9 pts); target 3780.25 (25.5 pts).
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** He traded this PM long live and shows the account briefly (a "1 975" figure; caption unclear).

title: 2022 ICT Mentorship - Episode 41 & Final
head: Position sizing (risk per trade) — worked example
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - Use free lot-size calculators (search for them): enter account size, risk %, and stop size.
  - Worked example:
    1. $10,000 account at 1% risk means $100.
    2. Stop is 9 points, so $100 / 9 is about $11 per point.
    3. One ES mini is $50/point, which is too big, so you cannot trade a mini at 1%.
    4. One micro (MES) is $5/point. $11 / $5 means 2 micros ($10/point).
    5. Actual risk: 9 × $10 = $90, which is under 1%.
    6. Target 25.5 points × $10 = $255. He calls this "basically 2¼%" (the arithmetic gives 2.55%).
  - He does not factor commissions, fees, or spread into the sizing. "Costs are like taxes, you just eat it." Beginners who want to be strict about risk can include them.
- **Timestamps:** [0:20:43](https://youtu.be/2XhDi5GoNUI?t=1243) — lot-size calculators; [0:22:18](https://youtu.be/2XhDi5GoNUI?t=1338) — $10k × 1% = $100, 9-point stop; [0:23:08](https://youtu.be/2XhDi5GoNUI?t=1388) — mini too big, micros; [0:24:46](https://youtu.be/2XhDi5GoNUI?t=1486) — no commissions in math; $90 risk, $255 target.

title: 2022 ICT Mentorship - Episode 41 & Final
head: Compounding and realistic return targets
body:
- **Kind:** rule / numbers
- **What ICT says:**
  - 1% a day, Monday–Friday, over about four weeks compounds to about 22% a month, not 20%.
  - Fund managers consider 12–15% a year stellar and 20%+ a blockbuster year.
  - 1% every single day is unrealistic for a new trader. For a seasoned trader, a 1% average per day is "really easy". It is an average: one 5% trade in a week equals 1% a day for that week.
  - He does not sit at the charts every day for 1%.
  - With 2% risk you can use two orders on the same setup: order 1 at the same limit and stop, targeting 3780.25 (about +2.25%); order 2 targeting the short-term high or 3805.50 (about +4.5% more). That is about 6.75% in one day from one trade idea.
- **Timestamps:** [0:26:21](https://youtu.be/2XhDi5GoNUI?t=1581) — 1% a day compounds to 22% a month; [0:27:55](https://youtu.be/2XhDi5GoNUI?t=1675) — 1% average; one 5% trade a week; [0:28:43](https://youtu.be/2XhDi5GoNUI?t=1723) — two orders for 2% risk, 3805.50 target; [0:29:33](https://youtu.be/2XhDi5GoNUI?t=1773) — about 6.75% in a day.

title: 2022 ICT Mentorship - Episode 41 & Final
head: Funded account challenges
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - If you lack capital, learn the skill set and use funded-account challenges or partners: "it doesn't have to be your money."
  - Their 10%-type targets are achievable if you know what you are doing and can handle drawdown.
  - Once funded, trade soberly: aim for 10–15% a month after the split, then stop. Do not try to get rich quickly.
- **Timestamps:** [0:30:20](https://youtu.be/2XhDi5GoNUI?t=1820) — funded challenges, drawdown; [0:32:42](https://youtu.be/2XhDi5GoNUI?t=1962) — small accounts, other people's money; [0:33:29](https://youtu.be/2XhDi5GoNUI?t=2009) — 10–15% a month after split.

title: 2022 ICT Mentorship - Episode 41 & Final
head: Drawdown control: halve risk after each loss
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - After a loss at 1% risk, the next trade risks 0.5%. Reasons: emotions, revenge, the urge to over-leverage, and impatience (the "loser's cycle, gambler's mentality").
  - You must make back 50% of what you lost before returning to full 1% risk. For example, lose about $100 (with commission), then earn $50 back.
  - If the 0.5% trade also loses, the next is 0.25%, the lowest you go.
  - Three straight losses then total only 1.75% drawdown (1 + 0.5 + 0.25). Compare doubling up: 1% then 2% is already 3%, and spiralling to 3–4% risk, removing or widening stops, leads easily to 10% drawdown and shame.
  - Same logic at 2% risk: after a full 2% loss, the next trade can risk only 1%. For example, 4 micros ($20/point) at 2% become 2 micros at 1% on the same 9-point stop.
  - Stops are not static. This trade needed 9 points, while others may need 5, 10, or 12. Recalculate size each time. Deep drawdown can leave you unable to trade even one micro.
- **Timestamps:** [0:31:07](https://youtu.be/2XhDi5GoNUI?t=1867) — after a loss risk half; [0:31:54](https://youtu.be/2XhDi5GoNUI?t=1914) — make back 50%, then 0.25% floor; [0:34:17](https://youtu.be/2XhDi5GoNUI?t=2057) — 1.75% vs doubling-up spiral; [0:41:25](https://youtu.be/2XhDi5GoNUI?t=2485) — 2% loss means the next is 1% (4 micros to 2).
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Professionals "are not allowed to touch their account when they're highly charged or emotional." Risk management is a psychological game as well as numbers.

title: 2022 ICT Mentorship - Episode 41 & Final
head: Hard stop is mandatory
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - If you do not put in a hard stop, you are not respecting the risk. You are saying "I'll figure out where I'm wrong when it gets there."
  - "I don't really use a hard stop but I know when I want to get out" tells him that trader does not have it together.
  - With this model the stop location is defined, so the hard stop must be placed, period. If it gets hit, it has done you a favor. Then your job is to manage the next trade with less risk to come out of drawdown incrementally.
  - Focus on whether price keeps showing the expected institutional order flow, not on fear of the stop being tripped. "You pay it well" to do its job.
- **Timestamps:** [0:14:21](https://youtu.be/2XhDi5GoNUI?t=861) — stop does its job; watch order flow instead; [0:15:08](https://youtu.be/2XhDi5GoNUI?t=908) — no hard stop means not respecting risk; [0:40:34](https://youtu.be/2XhDi5GoNUI?t=2434) — "I know when I want to get out" criticised; hard stop period.

title: 2022 ICT Mentorship - Episode 41 & Final
head: Systematic stop management (25% at 50% of the target range; breakeven at 75%)
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - Define the expected range from entry to target. Example: 3754.75 to 3780.25, 25.5 points.
  - When price has moved 50% of that range in your favor (about 12.75, rounded to 12.5 points), the stop can be moved up by 25% of the stop-to-entry distance, trimming risk a little. This is not jamming it to breakeven. (Caption is ambiguous between "trim by 25%" and "to 25%"; he describes it as "moving a little bit".)
  - When price has moved 75% of the entry-to-target range, move the stop to breakeven, "period".
  - Meanwhile, judge whether you are still on the right side:
    - Is price still reaching for the objective?
    - Do down-closed candles keep supporting price?
    - Does it run short-term lows (sell stops) and rally with energy?
    - Does it drop into FVGs, re-accumulate, and send another leg higher?
    
    If those hold, together or individually, keep holding for the target.
  - For multiple positions at "competition level leverage" (3%–4.5% risk), use a static partial rule, for example always take something off at +15 or +20 points.
  - These are foundations, not ironclad rules. Adapt them to your personality and model.
- **Timestamps:** [0:45:21](https://youtu.be/2XhDi5GoNUI?t=2721) — stop management: define entry-to-target range; [0:46:10](https://youtu.be/2XhDi5GoNUI?t=2770) — at 50% of range, trim stop 25%; [0:46:57](https://youtu.be/2XhDi5GoNUI?t=2817) — at 75%, breakeven; what to watch; [0:47:46](https://youtu.be/2XhDi5GoNUI?t=2866) — competition leverage 3–4.5%, static partials at 15–20 points.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** He says that in many shown trades he takes partials without rushing his stop up. This rule is meant to build trust in partials and reduce fear of being stopped out.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #1  August 5, 2024
head: Time as the first filter (algorithm runs on New York time)  (aliases: "time is the first hallmark", macro)
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:** Price is not moved by buying and selling pressure. It is "coded" to move based on time. Time is the first hallmark of when and why a market produces displacement, whether that is an impulsive run or a retracement. A move happening at a specific time, or within a 20-minute period, is a macro. Every time he mentions is New York local time; the algorithm runs on NY time "period". Unless a setup is grounded in time first, "if it's not the right time of day it is absolutely not going to work", whoever the trader is.
- **How to identify:** Set a NY world clock on your phone. Do all the study inside the specified windows (see Pre-market range / Bias).
- **How to use:** Look for setups only at the key times. The first line he drew on the chart was chosen because of time first.
- **Example in this video:** NQ, Aug 5 2024. He drew the relative-equal-high line before the session ran and justified the pick with "the algorithm is going to go based on time".
- **Timestamps:** [0:13:38](https://youtu.be/GKeLVR3dPuI?t=818) — price is coded on time, not buy/sell pressure · [0:14:25](https://youtu.be/GKeLVR3dPuI?t=865) — moves within 20 minutes = macro · [1:20:34](https://youtu.be/GKeLVR3dPuI?t=4834) — always NY local time · [1:40:47](https://youtu.be/GKeLVR3dPuI?t=6047) — if it's not the right time of day it won't work
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** He offers his "indicator that beats all others" as just open, high, low, close and the clock. He points at the DOM to show there's no order imbalance (as many sell orders below as above), yet price still marches to the levels. That is his argument against order-flow explanations.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #1  August 5, 2024
head: Pre-market range vs. opening range (30-minute windows)  (aliases: PMR, opening range, "every hourly candle")
body:
- **Kind:** definition (new framing)
- **What ICT says:**
  - The AM session starts at **7:00 ET**, whether you trade Forex or futures.
  - **7:00–7:30 = pre-market range.** **7:30–8:00 = opening range.**
  - 8:00–8:30 is also used as a pre-market-range window. (By the same hourly logic 8:30–9:00 would be its opening range, but that is implied, not stated.)
  - **9:00–9:30 = pre-market range.** **9:30–10:00 = opening range.** The opening range is the first 30 minutes after the NY opening bell.
  - "There is no 15-minute opening range." The opening range is 30 minutes, and that length is algorithmic.
  - He hints that he can trade "every single hourly candle" this way: first half is pre-market range, second half is opening range.
- **How to identify:** A 30-minute box that starts at the top of the hour (7, 8 or 9). Everything to the left of the box is where you look for relative equal highs or lows.
- **How to use:** It is the framework for the bias exercise below. Don't call the pre-market range the opening range.
- **Timestamps:** [1:42:24](https://youtu.be/GKeLVR3dPuI?t=6144) — 7:00 starts the AM session · [1:51:53](https://youtu.be/GKeLVR3dPuI?t=6713) — pre-market range vs. opening range defined; no 15-minute opening range · [1:52:40](https://youtu.be/GKeLVR3dPuI?t=6760) — drawing the 30-minute box
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** This contradicts common "15-minute opening range" teaching.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #1  August 5, 2024
head: Daily bias from smooth relative equal highs/lows (the "secret weapon")  (aliases: smooth vs. jagged, "where it's smooth it's going", contrasting one side of the market against the other)
body:
- **Kind:** entry model / rule (beginner bias framework)
- **What ICT says:**
  - Sit down at a key window: **7:00–7:30, or 8:00–8:30, or 9:00–9:30 ET**. That gives you three opportunities every morning. You don't need the afternoon or London.
  - Look to the left of the window on the **15m, 5m and 1m** charts for **relative equal highs or relative equal lows**. Whichever side has them is your bias, because price will draw to it.
  - **If there are relative equal highs above AND relative equal lows below:** wait for the first one to be disrupted, then work toward the other one. Defer and wait.
  - Each window that passes without the run makes it more likely, not less. Example: the relative equal high formed at 7:00, price didn't go there in 8:00–8:30, so 9:00–9:30 "chances are that's the run".
  - "Key takeaway": the framework starts at 7:00, so look for the relative equal highs to form from 7:00 on, "not before". Relative equal highs/lows from before 7:00 (the London session) may work, but expecting London levels to be run is often wrong, so starting at 7:00 acts as a filter.
  - He calls this a secret weapon he had never given out, even to his private mentorship: "a flamethrower" that "makes every playing field even". The market can't hide it.
- **How to identify:** Smooth means two swing points close together that make a flat, obvious level. Jagged means choppy swings where stops have already been run ("the work has been done").
- **How to use:** Trade toward the smooth side. Use PD arrays (breakers, FVGs, inversion FVGs) as stepping stones toward it. A level or inefficiency visible on all three timeframes is "three timeframes telling you pay attention to me". You don't need to trade every day. Trade when it's obvious, and accept that sometimes you'll miss the move.
- **Example in this video:** NQ, Mon Aug 5 2024. After a multi-thousand-handle selloff there was a big NWOG overhead and the market had dropped early, around 7:00. On the 5m, relative equal highs (each high slightly above the next one to its right) put liquidity at **17,820.75**, and the first line he drew was there. Below, the lows were jagged, so they had already been raided. Price formed a bullish breaker, made a 9:30 Judas-swing drop into it, then ran up through intermediate FVGs and took the 17,820.75 highs.
- **Timestamps:** [1:43:12](https://youtu.be/GKeLVR3dPuI?t=6192) — 7:00–7:30 window, relative equal highs/lows formed prior · [1:47:59](https://youtu.be/GKeLVR3dPuI?t=6479) — "secret weapon": contrast one side of the market against the other · [1:53:31](https://youtu.be/GKeLVR3dPuI?t=6811) — whichever side has equal highs/lows is the bias; if both, wait for the first to break · [2:05:29](https://youtu.be/GKeLVR3dPuI?t=7529) — three windows, likelihood builds; start at 7:00, not before
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:**
  - A higher-timeframe draw is "not necessary". He used only 15/5/1 and time.
  - The level does not have to be hit in that session. That is the risk you take on every trade.
  - Manual intervention (news, geopolitics) can always break it.
  - The wording on the 7:00 window is ambiguous. At 1:43 he says look for relative equal highs/lows "that have happened prior to 7 o'clock". At 2:05 he says start looking for them to form at 7:00, "not before". Most likely the AM framework begins at 7:00 and pre-7:00 (London) levels are the weaker filter (partly caption unclear).
  - He admits relative equal highs/lows aren't new teaching, but says students haven't actually traded this way.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #1  August 5, 2024
head: Relative equal highs/lows: how to tell which ones get swept  (aliases: relative equal highs/lows, "priming", "sympathetic side", failure swing)
body:
- **Kind:** refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - **Highs:** if the swing high on the left is slightly higher than the one on the right, there is a very high probability price will run above them. The lower right-hand high is what "frames these two as relatively equal".
  - **Lows:** the high-probability pair is a low followed by a slightly higher low (the left one is the deeper one).
  - This is the shape of a failure swing, but he is not trading the failure swing. He is identifying what the algorithm refers back to.
  - The algorithm stores these as an array: "this high at this time, and a higher high prior to it, in close proximity". The proximity filter is "not very much" of a price difference, and he won't disclose the exact number.
  - **Priming:** continually creating, inspiring or manipulating the expectations of a large number of participants, so they expect the high to hold or to break.
  - **Sympathetic side:** when price turns down just under the prior high, shorts relax and treat it as resistance. New shorts put their stops just above those highs, and that is the liquidity.
- **How to identify:** Two swing highs or lows close together. For highs, the right one is slightly lower; for lows, the right one is slightly higher. Smooth and flat-looking.
- **How to use:** Mark them as the draw on liquidity. When one is swept, take a screenshot, fade (lighten) it on the chart, and shift focus to the next PD array or target.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 5m: relative equal highs with the left one slightly higher left liquidity at 17,820.75. Smaller relative equal highs formed before 9:30 on top of the bullish breaker and were also swept.
- **Timestamps:** [1:14:55](https://youtu.be/GKeLVR3dPuI?t=4495) — the "secret" to a high-probability relative equal high · [1:15:44](https://youtu.be/GKeLVR3dPuI?t=4544) — priming · [1:17:22](https://youtu.be/GKeLVR3dPuI?t=4642) — the relative-equal-lows version, failure swing · [1:18:12](https://youtu.be/GKeLVR3dPuI?t=4692) — the algorithm references them as an array; filter not disclosed
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** It's high probability, not certain, and it doesn't have to happen in the session you're trading.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #1  August 5, 2024
head: Smooth vs. jagged price (shark / still-water analogy)  (aliases: "still waters invite rocks", "shark with no teeth")
body:
- **Kind:** new coinage (principle)
- **What ICT says:**
  - Smooth relative equal levels are like a shark with no teeth, or still water: they invite disruption.
  - Jagged price is where a shark attack has already happened. You can see the wounds, and the "cannibals" have already eaten. Don't trade into a level where the frenzy has already taken place.
  - The market goes to areas of smoothness to disrupt the orders resting above or below them. This holds on every timeframe, from sub-minute charts up to quarterly.
  - His closing rule: "Where it's smooth it's going; where it's jagged it's going to move away from."
- **How to identify:** Compare the two sides of the current range. Flat, clean highs or lows are smooth. Choppy swings with stop runs are jagged.
- **How to use:** Your target side is the smooth side. A jagged run that then rips the other way tells you buy-side liquidity is next (shorts trapped on a breakout).
- **Example in this video:** NQ: the lows had been disrupted and were jagged after the 7:00 drop and the 9:30 Judas swing. The highs at 17,820.75 were smooth, and price went to them.
- **Timestamps:** [1:09:15](https://youtu.be/GKeLVR3dPuI?t=4155) — the two-sharks analogy · [1:10:05](https://youtu.be/GKeLVR3dPuI?t=4205) — the market goes to smoothness on any timeframe · [1:54:18](https://youtu.be/GKeLVR3dPuI?t=6858) — jagged then ripped higher means look for buy stops · [2:14:17](https://youtu.be/GKeLVR3dPuI?t=8057) — closing rule
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** He ties the jaggedness to "fingerprints" left by consistent winners, using the World Series of Poker final-table players as the comparison.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #1  August 5, 2024
head: Draw on liquidity (DOL)  (aliases: draw, "low-hanging fruit")
body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:** The draw on liquidity is just an initial reasonable assumption about a directional move that could unfold. It is not the be-all, end-all target or the end point of the run. Price can retrace or even make a lower low first, though he says that is highly unlikely. The New Week Opening Gap (Friday settlement to the Sunday 6:00 pm ET open) is a draw on liquidity, but price doesn't need to reach it. For a short-term bias, use the low-hanging-fruit objective, such as nearby relative equal highs.
- **How to use:** It gives you something to focus on, and a way to judge each candle's behavior as it forms against your expectation.
- **Example in this video:** NQ Aug 5: a huge NWOG overhead after a multi-thousand-handle decline. The short-term draw was the relative equal highs instead.
- **Timestamps:** [0:48:19](https://youtu.be/GKeLVR3dPuI?t=2899) — relative equal highs and NWOG as draws · [0:49:08](https://youtu.be/GKeLVR3dPuI?t=2948) — low-hanging fruit for short-term bias · [1:06:50](https://youtu.be/GKeLVR3dPuI?t=4010) — DOL is not the terminus

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #1  August 5, 2024
head: What the algorithm reaches for: old highs/lows and inefficiencies  (aliases: liquidity or inefficiency, 8:30 spooling)
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - Price moves between obvious levels: old highs, old lows and inefficiencies (FVGs). Those are "the only two things you're worried about".
  - At **8:30** the algorithm starts "spooling" for liquidity or inefficiencies. Asked whether it will go for an old high/low or an FVG, he says it goes for both.
  - This happens "every single day" between **8:00 and 8:30**, which he insists on absolutely. That alone, he says, is enough foundation to "make all the money you'd ever want".
  - Beginners aren't trying to predict the day's direction or catch 50-handle runs, only to study and observe.
- **How to use:** Sit down before 8:30, preferably at 8:00. Mark the highs, lows and inefficiencies on the 15m, 5m and 1m.
- **Example in this video:** NQ: just after 8:30 price went below relative equal lows, then traded above the short-term high made at 8:36 and into an FVG.
- **Timestamps:** [0:52:21](https://youtu.be/GKeLVR3dPuI?t=3141) — old highs/lows and inefficiencies only · [0:53:57](https://youtu.be/GKeLVR3dPuI?t=3237) — 8:30 spools for both · [0:57:16](https://youtu.be/GKeLVR3dPuI?t=3436) — 8:00–8:30, write it down · [0:58:54](https://youtu.be/GKeLVR3dPuI?t=3534) — algorithmic characteristic; foundation

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #1  August 5, 2024
head: Displacement
body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:** Displacement is when the market runs against the pre-session, pre-day, pre-trend or price-swing direction. It is a counter move to what has already been in play, and it is aggressive.
- **Example in this video:** NQ after 8:30: price had been dropping, took liquidity below, then moved aggressively above the short-term high.
- **Timestamps:** [0:53:10](https://youtu.be/GKeLVR3dPuI?t=3190) — definition

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #1  August 5, 2024
head: Order block  (aliases: down-close candle)
body:
- **Kind:** example only (with a time condition)
- **What ICT says:** The down-close candle that took the liquidity, followed by displacement, is the bullish order block. What makes this one specific is that it formed after 8:30 (it could also form right at 8:30), when the algorithm begins seeking liquidity or inefficiency.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 1m, around 8:30–8:36: a down-close candle swept the relative equal lows, displacement up broke the short-term high, and price came back down to that down-close candle.
- **Timestamps:** [0:53:10](https://youtu.be/GKeLVR3dPuI?t=3190) — down-close candle = order block, formed post-8:30

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #1  August 5, 2024
head: Fair value gap: SIBI/BISI naming, volume imbalance, CE  (aliases: SIBI, BISI, inefficiency, mid gap, consequent encroachment)
body:
- **Kind:** definition / rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - A fair value gap made by a down-close candle is a **SIBI** (sell-side imbalance, buy-side inefficiency).
  - One made by an up-close candle is a **BISI** (buy-side imbalance, sell-side inefficiency).
  - When a volume imbalance sits next to the gap, include it in the gap. Watch the candle bodies being encapsulated by it.
  - When price is above an FVG, that FVG is a discount array. Price trading down to its mid-gap (CE) and holding is the signal to look for the run.
  - FVGs visible on all three timeframes act as "stepping stones" toward the draw.
- **Example in this video:**
  - NQ 1m after 8:30: it took 6 candles from a volume imbalance to run above the short-term high and into the SIBI above.
  - Later, a wick traded down to the mid-gap of an FVG below price (a discount array), and then the run started.
  - A volume imbalance encapsulated in a gap (caption "SIII", unclear whether SIBI or BISI) saw price run exactly to that gap's high.
- **Timestamps:** [1:01:16](https://youtu.be/GKeLVR3dPuI?t=3676) — 6-candle count, SIBI/BISI definitions · [1:25:28](https://youtu.be/GKeLVR3dPuI?t=5128) — include the volume imbalance; bodies encapsulated · [1:30:21](https://youtu.be/GKeLVR3dPuI?t=5421) — trade into mid gap = discount array CE · [1:39:12](https://youtu.be/GKeLVR3dPuI?t=5952) — three timeframes; stepping stones

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #1  August 5, 2024
head: Breaker block (bullish), and breaker vs. MSS
body:
- **Kind:** definition / example
- **What ICT says:**
  - To know whether you're looking at a breaker or a shift in market structure, you need a higher-timeframe premise and a directional draw (where the market is going).
  - **Bullish breaker:** when price drops through relative equal lows, the whole run of consecutive up-close candles before the drop is technically the breaker. The most sensitive part is the last up-close candle.
  - The candle bodies respect the level even when wicks run through it. Bodies "tell you the narrative".
  - This is not a supply/demand zone. He reads algorithmic candle bodies, not floor-trader perception, and contrasts it with Sam Seiden.
- **How to use:** If the narrative is higher, expect price to come back to the bullish breaker and then reach for the short-term high and inefficiency above.
- **Example in this video:** NQ: relative equal lows were taken, the bodies stopped at the range low of the last up-close candle (wicks went through), and the range high is the bullish breaker. Price later came back down into the breaker (and again at the 9:30 Judas swing), then rallied. He calls one bounce a nice scalp of about 20 handles if read on a 15-second chart (exact prices caption unclear).

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #1  August 5, 2024
head: Inversion fair value gap
body:
- **Kind:** example
- **What ICT says:** Once price trades above a short-term high and its inefficiency, he wants that inefficiency to act as support. That makes it an inversion FVG, and from there price reaches for the next high and inefficiency.
- **Example in this video:** NQ: a gap that was overhead was traded through and became an inversion FVG. It sent price higher, price retraced, and then a second leg ("redistribution") took the smooth highs.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #1  August 5, 2024
head: Balanced price delivery vs. runs with separation
body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:** Back-and-forth price, where each candle overlaps the prior highest high and lowest low, is very balanced delivery, with no liquidity or inefficiency inside it. Runs leave separations (gaps). A spike that stops right at the top of a breaker after a balanced creep is meaningful.
- **Timestamps:** [1:25:28](https://youtu.be/GKeLVR3dPuI?t=5128) — balanced, overlapping delivery · [1:55:05](https://youtu.be/GKeLVR3dPuI?t=6905) — creeping up balanced, spike stops at the top of the breaker

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #1  August 5, 2024
head: Equilibrium measured from the relative equal lows, not the lowest low
body:
- **Kind:** refinement
- **What ICT says:** For the midpoint of the expected leg, draw a fib from slightly above the relative equal highs (the target; no special logic to the exact price) down to the relative equal lows, not the lowest low. The lowest low is the manipulation. The FVG near that equilibrium is the entry area. An FVG slightly above equilibrium is still usable because the relative equal highs haven't been taken yet.
- **Example in this video:** NQ: the fib from just above the 17,820.75 highs to the relative equal lows put the midpoint close to an FVG. He said "watch this fair value gap" in real time, and price took off to the highs.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #1  August 5, 2024
head: Market standard delivery vs. manual intervention
body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:**
  - Normal algorithmic delivery goes up a little and comes back a little.
  - Manual intervention is FOMC, CPI or NFP-type delivery: one direction, no pause. If you're on the wrong side when it hits, "you're dead". It is often untradeable once it starts ("chasing the wind").
  - Manual intervention (and geopolitical shocks) is the one thing that always makes his model wrong, and nobody can predict it. That is the main reason never to over-leverage.
  - Gaps can jump far beyond your stop, which is why brokers make you sign risk disclosures.
- **Timestamps:** [0:54:48](https://youtu.be/GKeLVR3dPuI?t=3288) — standard delivery vs. intervention · [0:55:38](https://youtu.be/GKeLVR3dPuI?t=3338) — untradeable, gambling · [2:07:06](https://youtu.be/GKeLVR3dPuI?t=7626) — intervention always causes losses, so never over-leverage · [0:28:07](https://youtu.be/GKeLVR3dPuI?t=1687) — stops not guaranteed, gap risk

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #1  August 5, 2024
head: Determine your trader type first
body:
- **Kind:** rule (process)
- **What ICT says:** Before learning setups, decide whether you're a trader who trades long-term daily/weekly trend direction only, or one who fades intermediate- or short-term retracements because trend entries keep burning you. He'll teach both: reversal patterns, "real turtle soup", and where price should retrace deeper to set up trend entries. Then plant yourself in that and ignore what others (Caleb, ICT, other students) do. He also gives a personality test: when told "you can't do this", do you agree, or set out to prove them wrong? Being swayed by others' opinions, or taking on criticism aimed at someone else, is a trading barrier. Overconfident "prove them wrong" types overreach, put deadlines on themselves, and collapse at the first adversity.
- **Timestamps:** [0:21:39](https://youtu.be/GKeLVR3dPuI?t=1299) — trend vs. retracement trader · [0:24:05](https://youtu.be/GKeLVR3dPuI?t=1445) — plant yourself, don't copy anyone · [0:32:08](https://youtu.be/GKeLVR3dPuI?t=1928) — the "you can't do it" test · [0:38:38](https://youtu.be/GKeLVR3dPuI?t=2318) — overconfidence and time limits

head: Timeframe universe & chart layout  (aliases: "this solar system of price action", four-quadrant layout)
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - Intraday traders don't need anything above the 15-minute chart: no daily, hourly or 30m. Caleb may not look at, send or ask about any other timeframe until ICT introduces a reason.
  - Layout: upper left = 15m, lower left = 5m, upper right = 1m. If your data allows below 1m, add a 15-second chart. It's not required, but it shows what happens inside 1m candles and "is very forgiving".
  - All charts start "naked" (no annotations).
  - Higher timeframes matter once you're risking money behind a model. The current goal is only learning to read price and getting over the fear of not knowing what comes next.
  - Hardware: a laptop of about 15 inches at minimum. Don't try to learn on a smartphone, even a folding one.
  - All times are New York local time. Everyone worldwide shares the same 7, 8 and 9 o'clock, so the model either works or it doesn't.
- **How to use:** Do your daily observation on these three (or four) charts only.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #2   August 6, 2024
head: 7:00 AM ET start ("punch-in time") & the London-session clarification
body:
- **Kind:** rule / refinement (corrects Lecture #1 wording)
- **What ICT says:**
  - Draw a light vertical line at 7:00 ET. That is the beginner's "punch-in time" and the earliest point you refer to in price.
  - At 7:00 the hunt for relative equal highs and lows **begins**. Beginners must **not** look for relative equal highs or lows that formed before 7:00, even obvious ones right before 7:00 or in London. Ignore them.
  - The apparent contradiction in Lecture #1 ("look before 7" vs "don't look before 7") is explained like this: anything before 7:00 is really London session data and its *profile*. That means: did London make the high or low of the day? Is it consolidation-to-expansion, a trend day, or seek & destroy? (This is not volume Market Profile.) Advanced students who trade London setups, or who use London to anticipate a New York continuation or a New York reversal profile, may use pre-7:00 data. Beginners should not.
  - New York session reversal profile: if London (2:00–5:00 ET) has dropped, a NY reversal profile means price most likely trades back above and overlaps everything that started at 2:00.
- **How to identify:** 7:00 vertical line. Ignore all swing points to its left. Exception: see the London-range rule below.
- **Timestamps:** [0:48:50](https://youtu.be/pkI4AgC4OPI?t=2930) 7:00 line, punch-in time. [0:49:37](https://youtu.be/pkI4AgC4OPI?t=2977) "do not look for relative equal highs or lows prior to 7". [0:51:11](https://youtu.be/pkI4AgC4OPI?t=3071) London 2–5 AM and NY reversal profile. [0:53:37](https://youtu.be/pkI4AgC4OPI?t=3217) advanced vs beginner.
- **Nuance:** Also corrects a Lecture #1 slip: the second stage of the market maker *buy* model is **re-accumulation**. He had called it "redistribution", which belongs to the sell model ([0:06:57](https://youtu.be/pkI4AgC4OPI?t=417)).

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #2   August 6, 2024
head: Hourly hunt for relative equal highs/lows (7:00, 8:00, 9:00)  (aliases: three windows of opportunity)
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - At 7:00, scan the 15m, then the 5m, then the 1m for relative equal highs or relative equal lows that form **after** 7:00.
  - At 8:00 and again at 9:00 you start the whole process over. At 8:00 you may look back before 8:00, but never before 7:00, because you're working inside the morning-session range. Same at 9:00: anything back to 7:00 is fair.
  - Morning session = 7:00–11:00 (technically to noon). ICT likes to be done by 10:15–10:30.
  - **Never annotate or anticipate a pool that hasn't formed.** "Don't predict the setup … wait for the setup." Only take a mental note of a *potential* pair. ICT can anticipate (for example, calling iFVGs before they form), but beginners can't.
  - If relative equal highs and lows are both present (a consolidation), wait for one side to be taken. It usually then attacks the other side.
  - If no obvious pair exists on any of the three timeframes, move to annotating inefficiencies (see the FVG sections).
  - The relative equal high/low is this model's draw on liquidity. Pick the target, then re-measure each hour.
- **How to use:** Get a short-term bias by watching how price attacks or is attracted to a relative equal low or high. Once the bias is set, "stick with it even if it turns against you" during observation.
- **Example in this video:** Aug 6, 2024 (index futures; the instrument isn't named, but he measures in "handles"). On the 15m at 7:00 there's only a single high, so no relative equal highs yet. The two lows visible are before 7:00, so they're ignored. On the 5m, a potential relative equal low pair exists *if* price rallies, but only as a mental note. On the 1m, relative equal highs formed after 7:00 and were then run.
- **Timestamps:** [0:54:24](https://youtu.be/pkI4AgC4OPI?t=3264) 15m scan at 7:00. [0:55:13](https://youtu.be/pkI4AgC4OPI?t=3313) "never lead your expectations with something that has not formed". [1:38:39](https://youtu.be/pkI4AgC4OPI?t=5919) restart at 8:00/9:00, morning session 7–11. [1:56:38](https://youtu.be/pkI4AgC4OPI?t=6998) relative equal highs/lows are the target for this model.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #2   August 6, 2024
head: High-probability relative equal high
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:** A relative equal high is high probability when the right-side high is **slightly lower** than the left one: the market failed to get back to the first high. The algorithm will reprice to it because it "wants to disrupt" that pool. By symmetry, the right-side low would be slightly higher for lows. He only states the highs case explicitly.
- **How to identify:** Two highs at roughly the same level, where the second is a bit lower. It may only look equal when the chart is compressed.
- **Timestamps:** [1:12:51](https://youtu.be/pkI4AgC4OPI?t=4371) "did I teach you yesterday…" (the right one slightly lower). [2:54:59](https://youtu.be/pkI4AgC4OPI?t=10499) restated on the afternoon run to the day's high.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #2   August 6, 2024
head: Smooth vs. jagged (liquidity engagement)
body:
- **Kind:** definition (continued from Lecture #1)
- **What ICT says:** Price delivery has two simple characteristics. When price takes an area that was smooth (resting equal highs or lows) and makes it **jagged**, that was an engagement for liquidity. Expect the opposite direction to follow, especially when other factors (breaker, iFVG) support it. After a run of buy-side liquidity, go back through that price leg for setups.
- **How to identify:** Zoom out or compress the chart. A Larry Williams tip: if you're losing touch, zoom out, go up a timeframe, or look from across the room. Jaggedness that's invisible zoomed in becomes obvious.
- **Example:** Aug 6: relative equal highs after 7:00 were run ("sharp frenzy … blood in the water up here"), so don't trade up into that area and look lower. Later, the lows were made jagged, so look for buy side, a run on the high (the 7:00 high).
- **Timestamps:** [0:58:25](https://youtu.be/pkI4AgC4OPI?t=3505) smooth made jagged = engagement for liquidity. [1:00:50](https://youtu.be/pkI4AgC4OPI?t=3650) "blood in the water". [2:01:25](https://youtu.be/pkI4AgC4OPI?t=7285) zoom out and jagged lows (Larry Williams). [2:02:12](https://youtu.be/pkI4AgC4OPI?t=7332) look for buy side next.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #2   August 6, 2024
head: First 30 minutes after the hour = opposing run (Judas swing / manipulation)
body:
- **Kind:** rule (clarifies Lecture #1)
- **What ICT says:**
  - The first 30 minutes after 7:00, 8:00 and 9:00 is a window where you expect a move **opposite** to your expected draw. The caption reads "pression range", possibly "opposition range" (caption unclear). If there are relative equal highs above, you want the first 30 minutes after the hour to *drop*: an opposing directional run, i.e. a Judas swing or manipulation.
  - "Opposite" means opposite to **your** expectation, not to the crowd's.
  - It doesn't *have* to happen only in the first 30 minutes. If it does, interest in the move is "even more". If it doesn't, wait for more information: there may be a deeper retracement than expected, so wait for the breakdown.
- **How to use:** Then wait for price to return to the extended inefficiencies, "wait for a bus to get there and ride it down", and be content.
- **Timestamps:** [1:32:55](https://youtu.be/pkI4AgC4OPI?t=5575) clarification of "first 30 minutes after 7, 8, 9". [1:33:46](https://youtu.be/pkI4AgC4OPI?t=5626) opposing run = Judas swing. [1:51:52](https://youtu.be/pkI4AgC4OPI?t=6712) restated with relative equal highs, so expect the drop. [1:52:41](https://youtu.be/pkI4AgC4OPI?t=6761) not exclusively in 30 min; deeper retracement possible.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #2   August 6, 2024
head: AM session retrades into the London range
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:** The AM session's first and foremost characteristic is to **retrade back into the London range**. The London range is the highest high and lowest low between 2:00 and 5:00 AM ET. Caleb's charts should show from about 6:00 ET ("a taste of London"). He wants nothing before 7:00 *unless* the morning session trades to the London session low or high.
- **How to use:** For "how far can it go" on the downside, use the range low formed before price crossed 7:00. On Aug 6 the protraction reached down toward the London low.
