  - **Validation:** the block is validated when price trades **above that candle's open** (for a bullish block).
  - **Support:** it needs a supporting PD array: here a fair value gap below ("momentum shifted higher; this should stay open"). "An order block is never an island unto itself" and is not supply and demand.
  - **Body range:** the range is the open of the series down to the close of the lowest down-closed candle. The narrative is in the **bodies**: they stay in the **upper half** (open down to the mean threshold). Wicks are allowed to do the damage (they can spike below, even through the mean threshold) but the wicks never pierce "the body's low" (wording unclear in captions; read as: bodies do not trade through the low of the range). Any pullback into that range should have bodies in the upper half.
  - "You don't have to sweat picking the best entry" if you know the range: any return to the open price and/or into the upper half of the consecutive down-closed candles is the entry.
  - It is the same logic as his entry the previous day (the 6-contract short on NQ in Monday's stream), mirrored.
- **How to identify:** (1) a run of consecutive down-closed candles before the up move; (2) a supporting FVG/PD array below; (3) price displaces above the open of the series; (4) mark the open, the mean threshold and the lowest close.
- **How to use:** extend the open price forward to the right through time (here to the end of the 11:10 macro) and watch how bodies respect it. Enter on a return to the open price or the upper half; protect/validate by the bodies, not wicks.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 1m, Tue 13 Aug 2024. Three consecutive down-closed candles above the FVG (10:47–10:52 ET area). Price traded up out of the gap, then at ~11:10 ET came back down to the open price of the series with no wick below, then delivered higher. Between, the bodies stayed in the upper half of the range, and wicks went deeper.
- **Timestamps:** [2:31:32](https://youtu.be/-WItxLARGpE?t=9092) — three candles are one block · [2:32:21](https://youtu.be/-WItxLARGpE?t=9141) — the open is the change in state of delivery · [2:34:51](https://youtu.be/-WItxLARGpE?t=9291) — wicks vs bodies, upper half · [2:38:03](https://youtu.be/-WItxLARGpE?t=9483) — the 11:10 return to the open "cutting through candles" · [2:52:31](https://youtu.be/-WItxLARGpE?t=10351) — validation: does price trade above the open?
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** this changes the old "last down-close candle" definition. It also ties CISD explicitly to the open of the series. He says the books will cover order blocks in full ("you really won't know everything about [it] until the books come out").

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #7   August 13, 2024
head: At least one of three: short-term low, order block, fair value gap
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - In a macro, price needs a reason to go to liquidity. Check for (1) a short-term low (or high) to be run, (2) an order block, or (3) an FVG/inefficiency. You will have **at least one of the three, usually one, at best two, never all three** at the same price and time.
  - If there is **no gap**, wait for the down-closed candle that forms in the retracement: it has to run away and then come back (the order block logic). In his case there was no short-term low until it formed, but there was a gap.
- **Timestamps:** [2:49:18](https://youtu.be/-WItxLARGpE?t=10158) — "either a gap or an order block or a short-term low" · [2:50:06](https://youtu.be/-WItxLARGpE?t=10206) — never all three
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** only a pointer on what to look for inside a macro. He says paid-mentorship students always asked about this.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #7   August 13, 2024
head: Macros (algorithmic time windows) — 10:50–11:10 ET and every hour  (aliases: macro; the "spool")
body:
- **Kind:** definition / rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - A macro is a **20-minute window every hour: 10 minutes before the top of the hour to 10 minutes after** (e.g. 9:50–10:10, 10:50–11:10, 11:50–12:10). Label it on your chart "10:50 to 11:10 a.m. Eastern Time".
  - Always use **New York time** regardless of where you live. If you do not use an alarm (e.g. 10:45 for the 10:50 macro), draw vertical lines framing each macro (but be careful they do not hide candle colors).
  - Inside the macro the market "spools" (like a fishing line leaving a reel). It will: (a) run to a **short-term low** (SSL / sell stops), (b) run to a **short-term high** (BSL / buy stops), or (c) trade to an **inefficiency** (FVG) to give smart money an entry **just before** it spools to the liquidity.
  - The macro is "like a supercharger" for entries: tighter fills, immediate response (price moving away and never near your stop is how you know you are on side).
  - Not every macro is equally good; he leaves "which one and when" for the book. He also mentions a **midnight–1:00 am** macro and a **final-hour-of-the-day** macro.
  - Entries outside macros are fine ("I'm not saying … ICT only teaches the first 10 minutes before and after the hour"), but you demand more of yourself.
  - **90-minute cycles:** he says "there is no 90-minute cycle" to copy; 90 minutes is just the smallest window you should give yourself, because it guarantees at least one macro.
  - Timing is "the most critical function in price delivery". The macro tells you when to look; the higher-timeframe draw tells you which direction.
- **How to identify:** clock window (ET). Then ask which of the three the market needs: SSL, BSL, or an FVG/OB entry first.
- **How to use:** be positioned in the first 10 minutes (before the hour) for the entry into the inefficiency, then expect the spool in the last half. At 10:52 (mid-macro) he saw the entry FVG, then the run up to the daily imbalance, then at 11:10 a second entry in the order block open.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 1m, Tue 13 Aug.
  - 10:50–11:10 macro: a bullish FVG (breakaway gap) trades down into at 10:52 → rally to the 18951.50 high and the daily volume imbalance. The OB open is revisited at 11:10 and delivers higher.
  - 11:50–12:10 macro: price dug down at about 11:50 into a sell-side run into the daily inefficiency at discount (mid-macro, ~12:00 per his narration), then rallied to a smaller volume imbalance above and the liquidity above the high ("rock-climbing footholds"). The real runs start inside the window; after 10:50–11:10 "look how shitty it gets".
- **Timestamps:** [2:40:28](https://youtu.be/-WItxLARGpE?t=9628) — 10:50–11:10, every 60 minutes · [2:41:16](https://youtu.be/-WItxLARGpE?t=9676) — the three things price does in a macro · [2:59:00](https://youtu.be/-WItxLARGpE?t=10740) — New York time always, alarms or vertical lines · [3:07:03](https://youtu.be/-WItxLARGpE?t=11223) — spooling analogy and the 11:50 run · [3:02:12](https://youtu.be/-WItxLARGpE?t=10932) — 90-minute cycle comment
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** he calls this his "clinic on macros" and says most other macros circulating are not macros. In this stream he says the 10:00 macro begins at 9:50 (10 minutes before the hour); this lecture makes the "every hour, ±10 minutes" statement explicit.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #7   August 13, 2024
head: Daily/weekly reference levels (algorithmic references, not "support and resistance")
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - The levels to have on the chart: **previous day's high and low, the last three days' highs and lows, last week's high and low, and the upper quadrant, midpoint and lower quadrant of that range.** "Those are the reference points the algorithm will always go back to": any market, including forex, bonds, gold, indices. He insists this is not classic support/resistance.
  - Daily-chart inefficiencies (volume imbalances, gaps) are the usual first target above/below.
- **Timestamps:** [2:40:28](https://youtu.be/-WItxLARGpE?t=9628) · [2:42:53](https://youtu.be/-WItxLARGpE?t=9773) — the first daily PD array above is the target
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** consistent with IPDA-style reference teaching, here stated tersely.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #7   August 13, 2024
head: Volume imbalance on the daily chart as a target
body:
- **Kind:** example / refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - The daily chart showed a "little gap" between consecutive daily candle bodies (wicks overlapping): a **volume imbalance**. You need to elongate your price chart vertically to see it. He wanted it highlighted on your chart once price was reaching for it.
  - You cannot call buy-side liquidity on the daily above a rally as "short-term" because you have to go further; the first PD array met on the way up is the volume imbalance, and its **CE** (midpoint) is the practical target.
  - His statements for the end of day: price traded to and through it. Next references: the **mean threshold of the up-closed daily candle** (~19255 as captioned), the **new week opening gap high** (Friday close vs Sunday open, a "huge gap"), and above that the volume imbalance that is the year's highest extreme. He would not expect higher than that.
  - He is in a bullish "election year" narrative ("don't try to fight it"), absent a geopolitical shock (Iran/Israel). Opinion, not rule.
- **Timestamps:** [1:32:29](https://youtu.be/-WItxLARGpE?t=5549) — daily VI shown · [2:42:53](https://youtu.be/-WItxLARGpE?t=9773) — target math (CE ~30 handles) · [3:42:24](https://youtu.be/-WItxLARGpE?t=13344) — mean threshold 19255, NWOG, year-high VI
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** prices are as captioned and cannot be verified.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #7   August 13, 2024
head: Manual intervention (FOMC, 2:00 / 2:30 ET)
body:
- **Kind:** definition / rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - He distinguishes algorithmic delivery from **manual intervention**: abrupt, sudden and forceful, with no chance to get in. "Controlled demolition", not organic buying or selling pressure. If you are on the wrong side you are destroyed.
  - FOMC (2:00 pm statement and 2:30 pm press conference) is the example. "The sooner you accept that the better": wait, then trade after it forms.
- **Timestamps:** [2:47:42](https://youtu.be/-WItxLARGpE?t=10062)
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** matches his news-day avoidance rule; adds the label "manual intervention".

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #7   August 13, 2024
head: Low-resistance entries and targets; minimum range  (aliases: low-hanging fruit; bread-and-butter 10–15 handles)
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - Choose entries and targets with the **lowest resistance**: the easiest, which the spread will not defeat. Do not demand precision.
  - He needs at least **~20 NQ handles** of visible, timeable run: from 20 he can take 10–15. A 10–15 handle "bread and butter" trade is enough. If he cannot see a simple 20-handle run, he does not trade.
  - After a clean win on a hard day, "take it and leave"; do not look back.
- **Timestamps:** [2:20:57](https://youtu.be/-WItxLARGpE?t=8457) · [2:42:53](https://youtu.be/-WItxLARGpE?t=9773) · [3:09:24](https://youtu.be/-WItxLARGpE?t=11364)
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** a restatement of low-hanging-fruit targeting.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #7   August 13, 2024
head: Position scaling, partials and size on passive days
body:
- **Kind:** rule / process
- **What ICT says:**
  - On a passive day with only subtle ideas he uses **one or two contracts**: take a partial on one and let the other run to the objective. No max leverage, no "crazy pyramiding".
  - When he is in a winner and uncomfortable, he starts scaling out right away (e.g. take one contract off and see how he feels; take the next partial as soon as price makes a lower low if short or higher high if long). He wrestles with himself, wants additional entries, and cannot just hold.
  - He says he could make more by moving the stop and checking back at about 3:30 pm ET, but "can't live with myself" in the trade. The lesson is about personality fit, not a recommendation.
  - Any first stop-out on a day he already recognizes as the wrong kind of day is a "multiplier" of pain; he now takes money off early on those days.
- **Timestamps:** [0:40:09](https://youtu.be/-WItxLARGpE?t=2409) · [0:52:14](https://youtu.be/-WItxLARGpE?t=3134) · [1:09:12](https://youtu.be/-WItxLARGpE?t=4152)
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** the pyramiding limits were taught in the 2022/2023 mentorship (he is unsure which).

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #8   August 14, 2024
head: Wick as an inefficiency: measure it and use its consequent encroachment (CE)  (aliases: "wick CE", "midpoint of the wick", "quadrants of the wick", "the tell")
body:
- **Kind:** new coinage / refinement (ICT says mentorship students never got this; he claims nobody else has ever taught it)
- **What ICT says:**
  - Every time there is a wick, especially on a swing high or swing low that matters, measure it and mark its midpoint. Measure from the very highest high / lowest low (the extreme), using the real wick tip, not the body. He keeps candle borders switched on so the wick tips plot accurately (without borders the levels are not technically exact).
  - He treats the wick as a gap even though it printed inside a single candle. Because it is a gap, its midpoint is called consequent encroachment, not mean threshold (mean threshold is an order-block term). How long the candle took to print the wick does not matter, only the visual range from the candle's open to the extreme.
  - Long wicks: get the exact number (he draws a Fibonacci on the candle and uses the 50% level, then deletes the Fib; he scolds students who leave Fibs cluttering the chart). Short wicks: eyeball it.
  - The wick range is inefficient (the 8:30 news candle fell "over 100 handles" and printed back up inside the same one-minute candle). Price tends to return to that wick's CE, as a magnet.
  - A wick above price is a premium array, a wick below price is a discount array. If a wick sits above price and you are bearish, price should trade up into the wick's CE and the bodies should stop at or below it.
  - Wicks have quadrants too: CE (50%) and the lower/upper quadrant. In the first wick example he also points to a "3/4 level" as an entry-pattern / partial / Terminus level (caption unclear: it may just be the wick CE level he had marked). (He insists this is not "quarters theory", which he calls nonsense and asks people to stop asking about.)
  - Works on every time frame, down to sub-1-minute charts. "Price is price"; a 1m candle's open/high/low/close behaves like a daily candle's.
- **How to identify:** a candle with a visible wick at an important swing high/low or a big news candle. Draw from open to extreme, mark 50% and the quadrants.
- **How to use:**
  - Anticipation: after a wick forms, expect price to return to its CE, and to explore its lower quadrant if the bodies fail to hold.
  - Tell: when price returns to the wick, watch the bodies. If bodies do not close above the wick CE (bearish case) and the next candle makes a lower high, that is the algorithm "tipping its hand" and it is an entry (see Order block section for stop placement).
  - Failure: if a PD array (FVG, wick CE) cannot even be retraced to while you are directionally biased, the market is "decidedly weak" in that direction.
  - Confluence stacking: wick CE + FVG CE + 6 PM opening price + prior candle high are layered levels, and the more of them agree the stronger the expectation.
  - Even if no other level existed, a candle that runs up and stops short of the wick CE tells him the next candle will want to trade into that candle's body, which then acts as a bearish order block (trade it before others see it).
- **Example in this video:** NQ 1m, Aug 14, 2024. The 8:30 news candle opened, dropped over 100 handles in seconds and came back to close up in its body (long lower wick). ICT marked the wick's CE and the lower quadrant. Price (after running up into the July 28 NWOG and reversing) traded down to the wick CE, held there with the bodies, and later explored toward the lower quadrant/low. A wick's CE (captioned 19,965, unreliable) coincided "to the tick" with the high of a candle on the 15m chart, which he used as a retracement ceiling. Price pushed into an FVG whose CE it failed to reach (stopped about a tick short), and the bodies did not close above a wick CE, then it dropped.
- **Timestamps:** [0:05:18](https://youtu.be/zU7iAqg4sSA?t=318) — wick midpoint, "FVG that can't trade to its CE" · [0:15:23](https://youtu.be/zU7iAqg4sSA?t=923) — first rule: annotate CE on any swing-high/low wick · [0:22:44](https://youtu.be/zU7iAqg4sSA?t=1364) — confluence of wick CE + FVG + prior high · [0:26:02](https://youtu.be/zU7iAqg4sSA?t=1562) — drawing the 50% level, removing the Fib afterwards · [0:51:08](https://youtu.be/zU7iAqg4sSA?t=3068) — measure every wick from highest high/lowest low, all time frames · [1:16:05](https://youtu.be/zU7iAqg4sSA?t=4565) — why it is CE not mean threshold
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:**
  - ICT says explicitly he has never seen anyone else break a wick into quadrants for reversals, short-term trading or targets, and that he is teaching it live for the first time (0:21:06, 1:46:53). Mentorship students did not get it.
  - He refuses to teach everything about wicks ("90% of the mohawks I can anticipate, I'm not teaching it", 2:03:41).
  - Price can wick through the CE; what matters is where the bodies stop.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #8   August 14, 2024
head: Buy-side delivery vs. sell-side delivery (algorithmic programs) — not buy/sell-side liquidity  (aliases: "sell program / buy program", "buy side of the curve / sell side of the curve")
body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:**
  - Sell-side delivery is the algorithm delivering lower prices ("a sell program"), buy-side delivery is delivering higher prices. It is NOT sell-side liquidity (resting sell stops). Do not think buying/selling pressure; it spools in a direction "for the express purpose of delivering" prices.
  - Sell-side delivery means the market is going lower to reprice inefficiencies (FVGs, wick CEs) and then the liquidity below; it matters not how much buying/selling pressure there is.
  - While in a sell program, retracements are short-lived, controlled, "stunted", never protracted to the upside.
  - He ties this to the Market Maker Buy/Sell Models (2017 mentorship): the "buy side of the curve" is the run up; the "sell side of the curve" is the run down. He says everything he trades is part of an MMSM or MMBM even when he does not name it.
- **How to identify:** which way the algorithm is currently offering prices (a sequence of up-closed displacement and old highs being taken = buy-side delivery). See CISD for the switch.
- **How to use:** in a sell program, look for repricing to inefficiencies: bearish FVGs (sell-side imbalance / buy-side inefficiency), wick CEs, order blocks and breakers on the way down, and go to the sell-side liquidity below.
- **Timestamps:** [0:42:17](https://youtu.be/zU7iAqg4sSA?t=2537) — sell-side delivery is not sell-side liquidity · [1:38:03](https://youtu.be/zU7iAqg4sSA?t=5883) — sell program reprices to inefficiencies · [2:21:17](https://youtu.be/zU7iAqg4sSA?t=8477) — MM buy/sell models, buy side of the curve
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** In his words the algorithm "doesn't care how many people are buying or selling". This is his core argument against order flow / depth-of-market.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #8   August 14, 2024
head: Change in the State of Delivery (CISD) at the opening price of the order block  (aliases: "change in state of delivery", "the opening price", order block validation)
body:
- **Kind:** definition + entry trigger
- **What ICT says:**
  - The order block is not just the last up-closed candle. For a bearish order block, take ALL the consecutive up-closed candles that make up the run into the high (two candles in this example). The opening price of that up-closed series (the open of its first candle) is the change in the state of delivery level.
  - When price trades below that opening price (he does not require a close below), the delivery flips from buy-side to sell-side and the order block is validated. "If it's multiple candles, just find the opening price of the up-close candles."
  - Using only the last up-closed candle is called a trap ("white candle / buy demand" thinking).
  - The wicks that overshoot are "colouring outside the lines", ignore them and focus on bodies. Measure the mean threshold of the bodies of all those candles for the order block's midpoint. Price can poke a little above the OB range and it still counts.
  - He separates it from MSS: trading below the short-term low and closing there gives a shift in market structure, but before that the order block is validated by trading below its open, which is the CISD. He also says he does not need to see a close below the OB's open for the flip (caption somewhat unclear, 1:26:38).
  - Once flipped, every premium array that forms in the new sell program matters (new short-term highs, new bearish up-closed candles, new FVGs).
- **How to identify:** (1) buy-side delivery has been running; (2) liquidity above (highs) is taken, ideally into a known objective; (3) a series of up-closed candles forms the top; (4) price trades through the open of that series.
- **How to use:** after the CISD, expect sell-side delivery. Look for entries on retracements into the new premium arrays (OB, FVG, wick CE), and targets at inefficiencies/discount arrays below, then sell-side liquidity.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 1m, Aug 14, 2024 (after the 9:30 open; exact time not stated). The day before he had pointed to the Jul 28, 2024 NWOG (plus the daily short-term high and daily volume imbalance) as an upside objective. Price created relative equal highs, failed to reach the NWOG on the 8:30 news run, then after the open ran into the NWOG, swept the highs, formed a bearish order block of two up-closed candles (a breaker-type high/low/higher-high structure), then traded below that OB's open. Price then fell to the CE of the 8:30 wick, retraced up into an FVG and stopped about one tick under its midpoint (caption unclear), and kept going down.
- **Timestamps:** [1:18:32](https://youtu.be/zU7iAqg4sSA?t=4712) — CISD explained at the order block · [1:24:16](https://youtu.be/zU7iAqg4sSA?t=5056) — buy-side delivery to sell-side delivery · [1:27:26](https://youtu.be/zU7iAqg4sSA?t=5246) — opening price = CISD, mean threshold · [1:29:53](https://youtu.be/zU7iAqg4sSA?t=5393) — all consecutive up-closed candles form the OB · [2:18:54](https://youtu.be/zU7iAqg4sSA?t=8334) — "just find the opening price"
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:**
  - ICT asks: if you had not been taught NWOG, FVG, breakers and the OB, you would not have anticipated this turn (1:23:29).
  - He frames this as "why it reverses", not a candle pattern to eyeball ("it is an order block, not an engulfing / institutional candle").

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #8   August 14, 2024
head: Order block (bearish) — range, trading it early, and stop placement  (aliases: bearish order block, "mile marker", "exit ramp")
body:
- **Kind:** definition + entry/stop rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - The OB range = the bodies of the consecutive up-closed candles before the sell-side delivery. If an FVG sits inside the OB's range, label and trade the OB's range, not the small FVG (1:56:33).
  - He says the algorithm "gives a mile marker" at the OB: it is where your eye should go if you are not yet in the trade.
  - Early entry: if price runs up and stops short of a wick CE, he says the next candle that opens and trades into the body of that candle can be entered before anyone calls it an order block ("I'm trading inside the candle that will later be obvious in hindsight").
  - Stop: above the order block, AND encapsulating the premium wick above it: the stop goes just above the highest point of the wick + 1 tick. If a spike goes through and wicks up toward half of that wick, or falls short of it, and you are stopped out, he re-enters short there.
  - He warns order blocks are not always protected; price sometimes colours just outside the lines and the narrative still stands.
- **How to identify:** consecutive up-closed candle bodies at the top of a buy-side run that ended with a CISD.
- **How to use:** short on retracement into the OB range (bodies/mean threshold); stop above the OB and its premium wick +1 tick; target the inefficiencies and lows below.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 1m, Aug 14, 2024: price retraced up to a bearish OB (below the NWOG high) after the CISD, with the 8:30 wick CE as the retracement low; stop would be one tick above the premium wick above the OB.
- **Timestamps:** [3:08:42](https://youtu.be/zU7iAqg4sSA?t=11322) — "where does your stop go?" quiz on the bearish OB · [3:11:08](https://youtu.be/zU7iAqg4sSA?t=11468) — stop above the OB's premium wick +1 tick, re-enter if stopped · [2:34:43](https://youtu.be/zU7iAqg4sSA?t=9283) — trading inside the candle before it is "an order block"
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Clarifies the usual "last up-closed candle" teaching: he says to include ALL consecutive up-closed candles and warns that people copy only the last candle.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #8   August 14, 2024
head: Turtle soup — only two forms: reversal (change in direction) and in-trend entry technique  (aliases: "Turtle Soup", "run on liquidity", "stop run")
body:
- **Kind:** definition / new refinement (explicitly distinguished from the Street Smarts pattern)
- **What ICT says:**
  - Turtle soup = a run on liquidity that is not always above an old high or below an old low (he says the name was borrowed because he liked it from Connors/Raschke's Street Smarts, which taught him the stop-run idea; he has used the concept since 1995).
  - There are only two forms: buying below old lows or selling above old highs, either (1) as a reversal that changes the direction of delivery (CISD, sustained for a session/day or longer), or (2) as an entry mechanism inside an existing, still-unfolding sell or buy program.
  - Form 1: take out the buy stops above old highs (bodies as well as wicks), hit an objective (e.g., a NWOG or NDOG as a magnet), then CISD. The order block / breaker is part of that reversal ("breakers tend to be turtle soups in changing directional sustained price runs").
  - Form 2: every time you enter a short in a bearish FVG you are selling above an old high (the candle high marking the FVG's edge); every long in a bullish FVG is buying below an old low. It is not support and resistance but an absence of buyers who ever were afforded the chance above that candle's high.
  - Street Smarts version (for contrast): fade a break of the 20-day high/low (and "plus one" = one more day), with a very short profit objective; he calls it infantile, says he does not trade it, and recalls the turtle-trader style strike rate as under about 38%.
  - Harder variant: selling into a rally, a bold-faced bullish candle above short-term highs into a premium array. Takes much more experience and complementary PD arrays; do not start here.
- **How to identify:** (reversal) high swept + objective reached + CISD; (entry) retracement into an FVG in a program that already started.
- **How to use:** form 1: sell above the highs only after the objective and after delivery flips; form 2: put the limit order at the old high + 1 tick (see FVG entry section).
- **Example in this video:** NQ Aug 14, 2024: running above short-term highs / relative equal highs into the Jul 28 NWOG, then CISD at the OB open (form 1); after that, shorting into the FVG that formed in the sell leg (form 2). He adds that if price had reached the NWOG on the 8:30 first leg, then poked above again at 9:30 and failed, that second poke would have been the turtle soup.
- **Timestamps:** [1:10:28](https://youtu.be/zU7iAqg4sSA?t=4228) — turtle soup is anticipating turning points, not always above old highs · [2:22:04](https://youtu.be/zU7iAqg4sSA?t=8524) — reversal vs. entry mechanism · [2:24:27](https://youtu.be/zU7iAqg4sSA?t=8667) — Street Smarts 20-day version contrasted · [2:46:05](https://youtu.be/zU7iAqg4sSA?t=9965) — trading an FVG = trading a turtle soup · [3:33:27](https://youtu.be/zU7iAqg4sSA?t=12807) — "only two forms of turtle soup"
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Narrows/clarifies earlier use of the term. He calls the Street Smarts version the "wish version"/"street-smarts version" and says Linda Raschke and Larry Connors' book helped only to introduce the idea of stop runs.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #8   August 14, 2024
head: FVG entry model for a short (and the mirror for longs): entry, scale-in, stop, and "permissible" fills  (aliases: "lowest barrier to entry", "lowest threshold of entry", "pyramiding", turtle soup entry)
body:
- **Kind:** entry model
- **What ICT says:**
  - Entry: the lowest barrier to entry is the edge of the FVG closest to current price. For a bearish FVG that is the old candle high at the bottom of the gap (the high of candle 3, inference); put the limit order at that high + 1 tick. On the morning's first retracement price came within a tick of the FVG and turned, so even a limit one tick above the old candle high was not filled (he says so at 2:16:31; the caption at 0:11:16 says "would have been filled" but the context, "punishment for trying to be too perfect", points to not filled). His lesson: demanding perfection costs fills, so have fallback entries (wick CE, next array, price delivery continuum) and know that missing a fill still means you read direction correctly.
  - Long version (mirror): buy the high of the bullish FVG or one tick below its highest part, with the largest portion there. Add at the midpoint (CE), and add again if price leaves and retests the CE. Fills at/below the CE are rare, though they are the best entries when they occur.
  - His own scale (as a sample, not a recommendation for beginners): first 6 contracts at the edge (+1 tick), then 4 more at the midpoint, 10 total. He explicitly says Caleb (the beginner) should not trade 10 contracts and should only watch and observe.
  - Stop: above the 3-candle FVG pattern, specifically too far if price trades above candle 1's high (the first candle of the pattern). Caption unclear on the exact candle; context says the entire FVG plus the premium wick is "too far".
  - Tight stop (advanced): if candle 1 has a wick (a premium array above the gap), take the CE of that wick + 2 ticks as the stop. Reasoning: candle 2 opens and trades down through candle 1's low, so the overlap forms a balanced price range; price should not trade back through the whole range to the top, and if it did it would probably go higher and he would not want to be short anyway. So he can put the stop just above the wick's CE.
  - FVG naming: the inefficiency is always candle 2; a down-closed candle 2 is a sell-side imbalance / buy-side inefficiency (SIBI), an up-closed candle 2 is buy-side imbalance / sell-side inefficiency (BISI).
- **How to identify:** FVG that formed during the sell program (the most important ones) and that converges with arrays from the buy side of the curve (see Inversion).
- **How to use:** limit short at the old high + 1 tick, add at CE, stop at candle-1 high (or wick CE + 2 ticks); scale partials at the PD arrays below; see targets section.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 1m after the CISD: an FVG formed in the drop and was later retraced. First retracement: price stopped about a tick short of the FVG and fell away, so the limit at the edge + 1 tick was not filled (ICT, 2:16:31). Later price did trade up into another FVG that formed in the drop and the bodies stopped there. The tight stop is illustrated with the wick of candle 1.
- **Timestamps:** [0:11:16](https://youtu.be/zU7iAqg4sSA?t=676) — "punishment for trying to be too perfect" · [2:11:46](https://youtu.be/zU7iAqg4sSA?t=7906) — buy at the FVG high, add at CE · [2:50:57](https://youtu.be/zU7iAqg4sSA?t=10257) — 6 then 4 contracts at the edge and midpoint · [3:00:37](https://youtu.be/zU7iAqg4sSA?t=10837) — entry/stop drawn · [3:04:43](https://youtu.be/zU7iAqg4sSA?t=11083) — wick CE + 2 ticks stop
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Contrasts with supply/demand: he wants one exact entry, stop and target price, not a zone. He dismisses zones: he asks which price within a 8-20 handle zone you would use, and what stop.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #8   August 14, 2024
head: How the FVG should behave: upper half stays open, speed and distance
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - If you are short and price retraces into a bearish FVG, it is "permissible" (allowed, does not change direction) for it to fill entirely, but it is better and signals strong weakness if price reaches only the midpoint or less and leaves the upper half open (bullish mirror: lower half). Failing to fill means the market is "weak" and lower targets are coming.
  - Two circumstances make large-range candles: (a) the gap leaves a portion open, then the market must accelerate away; (b) it fills the gap entirely, then it must immediately show speed and distance, large-range candles away from it. Absent that, do not stay.
  - Same logic for arrays above price while you are short and still in a trade: keep some FVGs above the target open, which shows the market can't even retrace up to them and fill them in.
  - After price takes out the low (new range low), take a partial there even for one contract, then watch how price behaves around the order block and range.
- **How to use:** demand an immediate response, once price touches the FVG's low. If it leaves part of the gap open you can anticipate fast speed and big range going lower. Observation drill: do this for months as tape reading, with no demo orders ("start with the price level + 1 tick; if it trades there, hypothetically you are in").
- **Timestamps:** [1:52:31](https://youtu.be/zU7iAqg4sSA?t=6751) — want FVGs above target to stay open when short · [2:51:48](https://youtu.be/zU7iAqg4sSA?t=10308) — "permissible" vs. better if only half filled · [3:02:13](https://youtu.be/zU7iAqg4sSA?t=10933) — demand immediate response, speed and distance · [3:06:20](https://youtu.be/zU7iAqg4sSA?t=11180) — the only two circumstances for large-range candles
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** It is a quality filter (conviction), not a requirement; ICT says it does not make the trade more or less profitable, only gives emotional comfort.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #8   August 14, 2024
head: Balanced Price Range (BPR) as the real range of an FVG and the "Mohawk"  (aliases: "mohawk", "coloring outside the lines")
body:
- **Kind:** new coinage / refinement (ICT says it is the first time he is introducing this PD array)
- **What ICT says:**
  - When one candle's wick overlaps another candle's body (or a candle opens and trades down a little into the previous candle's range) inside a gap, the overlap is a balanced price range, and the BPR is the real range of the inefficiency, which you have to encapsulate rather than just drawing the FVG on the standard three candles. He says this is a PD array students "have never learned before".
  - Example logic: a candle runs up and is all body at the top, the next candle opens and makes a flush tap down, overlapping a little portion with no wick. That overlap is the BPR, not the plain FVG. Price then reacts at that BPR boundary instead of filling the FVG fully ("you will not pass").
  - A "mohawk" is the tiny spike outside a PD array boundary (a candle poking a few ticks beyond a level before turning). He says about 90% of mohawks outside a PD array are predictable but he won't teach that.
  - Do not confuse with volume imbalance: a volume imbalance is a separation between two candle bodies inside an FVG; he notes that is absent here.
- **How to identify:** inside an FVG, look for overlap between one candle's wick/body and the next candle's range.
- **How to use:** draw the BPR as the entry/stop boundary: "we never want to see price go back through the whole BPR to the top".
- **Timestamps:** [2:02:53](https://youtu.be/zU7iAqg4sSA?t=7373) — BPR from the overlap of a wick and a body, "mohawk" · [2:03:41](https://youtu.be/zU7iAqg4sSA?t=7421) — 90% of mohawks predictable; won't teach · [2:30:01](https://youtu.be/zU7iAqg4sSA?t=9001) — BPR introduced as a new PD array
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Differs from the 2022 BPR definition (overlap of a SIBI and a BISI). Here it is the overlap of wick/body of adjacent candles around an FVG. Caption/description is thin and chart-dependent; treat as "(caption unclear)".

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #8   August 14, 2024
head: Inversion logic: arrays used as support on the buy side flip to resistance in the sell program; iFVG caveat  (aliases: inversion, inversion FVG, "reverse its role")
body:
- **Kind:** rule / refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - After the CISD, go back through the whole run from the high to the low and see which arrays acted as discount/support on the way up (gaps, down-closed candles/order blocks, FVGs). They reverse role and become inversion levels: resistance for the retracements in the sell program. "That is how I know which PD array to use as an inversion level."
  - An order block that was used as a buy extends to the right as resistance once price has gone below it. An FVG extended to the right, with its CE marked, is an inversion FVG, and the same logic applies: you want it not to fill entirely (upper half stays open when short).
  - Not every FVG becomes an inversion FVG (a jab at an over-eager young trader who implies he invented the idea).
  - Every new array formed in the sell program is salient, and weight builds when it converges with an array from the buy side of the curve; expect price to stay heavy and ask for speed and distance.
  - This is how he applies the Market Maker Sell/Buy Models: extend arrays back through the range.
- **How to use:** list the buy-side arrays after the CISD, extend them forward, treat them as the first resistance levels, enter shorts there with the standard FVG/OB entry rules.
- **Timestamps:** [1:39:41](https://youtu.be/zU7iAqg4sSA?t=5981) — discount arrays reverse role · [2:04:27](https://youtu.be/zU7iAqg4sSA?t=7467) — not every FVG becomes an iFVG · [2:06:05](https://youtu.be/zU7iAqg4sSA?t=7565) — iFVG shouldn't close in entirely · [2:11:00](https://youtu.be/zU7iAqg4sSA?t=7860) — new arrays converging with the buy side of the curve
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Consistent with his 2023 iFVG teaching; adds the "converge with the buy-side arrays" weighting.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #8   August 14, 2024
head: Price Delivery Continuum Theory  (aliases: price delivery continuum, following the delivery chain, joining a run you missed)
body:
- **Kind:** new coinage (ICT says it is "brand new stuff" and mentorship students did not learn it)
- **What ICT says:**
  - If you place a precise limit order (e.g., at the FVG edge) and price runs away without filling, do not abandon the idea. The delivery is underway and a finite target exists, so keep looking for the next specific price level, a new PD array formed by the unfolding move (a new short-term high, a new up-closed candle/OB, a new FVG), and enter there.
  - He says he developed it because as a young trader he would miss his single setup, get angry and stop looking, though a big move was still available.
  - It requires a finite price (entry, stop, partial, terminus); if he does not know the specific price he does not trade.
- **How to use:** after the initial miss, wait for retracements into the newly-formed arrays; use the lowest-barrier edge entry; keep the same stop logic.
- **Example in this video:** after the missed FVG fill, price came back up into the body of an up-closed candle and traded to the CE of the 8:30 wick without taking out that candle's high, which he says could have been the entry.
- **Timestamps:** [0:45:28](https://youtu.be/zU7iAqg4sSA?t=2728) — missed fills led him to develop it · [0:47:53](https://youtu.be/zU7iAqg4sSA?t=2873) — defined: anticipate a move to a finite target · [1:59:41](https://youtu.be/zU7iAqg4sSA?t=7181) — "do you say forget it? no" (continuing to look)
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Also relates to the IOFED label below. He stresses entries are easy and finite; the hard part is knowing where the market is going.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #8   August 14, 2024
head: Institutional Orderflow Entry Drill (IOFED) — named only  (aliases: "institutional orderflow entry drill")
body:
- **Kind:** example only (name-drop; no step list given)
- **What ICT says:** He quizzes viewers on what to call the retracement of an up-closed candle back into a wick CE in a sell program (the entry if the first FVG was missed). The answer is "institutional orderflow entry drill". Context he gives right after naming it: price is in a sell program; first want a trade into the array, then the next target is the lower quadrant of the wick, with sell-side liquidity below; the up-closed candle's high should not be traded above.
- **Timestamps:** [0:40:40](https://youtu.be/zU7iAqg4sSA?t=2440) — retracement to the wick CE as alternate entry · [0:41:28](https://youtu.be/zU7iAqg4sSA?t=2488) — the name
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Do not rely on this note for the drill's steps; refer to the 2016/2017 mentorship playlists where he teaches it.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #8   August 14, 2024
head: 6 PM opening price, NDOG and NWOG as reference levels  (aliases: new session opening price, new day opening gap, new week opening gap)
body:
- **Kind:** rule / refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - If there is no difference between the 5:00 PM close/settlement and the 6:00 PM first print, there is no gap, so you draw one single line at the 6 PM opening price. Use the 6 PM price (the first print), not the 5 PM. It is a single price level, not a range or inefficiency. It can be swept and revisited, and works like a new day opening gap.
  - If there is a difference, annotate the NDOG (the 5 PM-to-6 PM gap).
  - Baseline for charts: last five weeks of NWOGs and last five days of NDOGs. More if you can keep the chart tidy.
  - Old/filled gaps still act as magnets: a NWOG from Jul 28, 2024 that had been traded through was used as the upside objective on Aug 14 ("filled, cast it out, no, it's one and done: no it's not").
  - Without a gap and without an FVG or wick, price still gravitates back to the 6 PM price as the first real level, ahead of the FVG, which can stay open.
- **How to use:** mark them before the session, use as objectives/retracement targets, and as the first target of a retracement after a CISD.
- **Example in this video:** NQ Aug 14: price went back up to the 6 PM opening line during the retracement, the same area as an FVG and the CE of a wick.
- **Timestamps:** [0:09:27](https://youtu.be/zU7iAqg4sSA?t=567) — 6 PM line, a single level · [1:53:20](https://youtu.be/zU7iAqg4sSA?t=6800) — 6 PM not 5 PM, why · [2:22:51](https://youtu.be/zU7iAqg4sSA?t=8571) — five weeks of NWOG, five days of NDOG
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Nothing contradicts earlier teaching.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #8   August 14, 2024
head: Targets and partials: PD arrays on the way, then the quarter-range projection beyond the low  (aliases: "negative .25", "one quarter of the range projection", rejection block partial, Terminus)
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - Partials/terminus can be taken at any PD array below: a rejection block (a candle's close level below the bodies), the CE of the wick, the lower quadrant, the old low. You do not need to hold for the whole run, and not holding to the lowest low does not mean you are bad at trading.
  - If you want to go for a target below an old low, a "low-hanging fruit" projection: take the range (the wick range, or the range from the high down to the low) and project one quarter of that range below the low (a Fibonacci extension of negative .25). That is a decent ballpark, not the exact low.
  - For tighter precision he points to his standard-deviation lessons in the 2017 mentorship playlists (not recalled exactly).
  - Targets are finite: entries and targets are easy, knowing where price is going is the hard part.
  - Whichever PD array "makes the most sense to you" first is your starting point; do nothing when it is not there until you learn more.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 1m, Aug 14: first target was the CE of the 8:30 wick, then the lower quadrant and the low, using the closing price of the 8:30 candle as a rejection-block partial; the quarter-range projection was drawn from the high-to-low range and wick (about a quarter below the low).
- **Timestamps:** [1:46:04](https://youtu.be/zU7iAqg4sSA?t=6364) — rejection block as partial below the bodies · [2:37:07](https://youtu.be/zU7iAqg4sSA?t=9427) — start with the one PD array that makes sense to you · [2:41:10](https://youtu.be/zU7iAqg4sSA?t=9670) — quarter-range projection (-0.25) · [2:44:30](https://youtu.be/zU7iAqg4sSA?t=9870) — project one quarter of the range below the low
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** He notes price doesn't care about indicators, Fibonacci ratios or moving averages (0:59:15), yet uses a 50% on wicks and a quarter-range extension as a measuring convenience, not as a cause. Treat the extension as a rough target.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #8   August 14, 2024
head: Swing highs/lows ("ring highs/lows") and market structure mapping
body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:** A swing high is a candle high with a lower high immediately to its left and to its right (3-candle). On hand-drawn daily charts in the early days they circled these ("ring highs"), which let him map market structure. If swing highs form lower than a cluster of earlier swing highs, price is likely part of an intermediate-term run.
- **Timestamps:** [0:37:25](https://youtu.be/zU7iAqg4sSA?t=2245) — ring highs/lows, hand-drawn charts · [0:39:02](https://youtu.be/zU7iAqg4sSA?t=2342) — swing high definition and structure
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Standard definition restated, not new.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #8   August 14, 2024
head: News-driver days (8:30 high-impact releases) and manual intervention  (aliases: PPI, CPI, FOMC, NFP)
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - On PPI, CPI, FOMC and NFP days the algorithm is interrupted ("manually intervened"). Price either stops just short of the objective it will reach after the 9:30 open, or overshoots it and keeps going. He admits that on this day he expected a spike to the NWOG at 8:30 and was surprised; it deferred until the opening bell.
  - Do not trade the 8:30 candle: the 1m news candle is full of inefficiencies and is untradeable, and TradingView's paper trading lags too much on it. Do not trade at the time of the release at all. On NFP you can trade the afternoon or 15-30 minutes after the number. Trying to predict the release leads to blown accounts.
  - After the report, study how price comes back to the wick and the liquidity below it. He says when there is a high-impact driver you do not need relative equal highs/lows (garbled caption).
  - If you are bullish before the release and price "grinds higher" after, he would not chase.
- **Timestamps:** [3:12:44](https://youtu.be/zU7iAqg4sSA?t=11564) — expected an 8:30 spike to the NWOG, it deferred · [3:14:19](https://youtu.be/zU7iAqg4sSA?t=11659) — two outcomes (short of target or beyond) · [3:15:06](https://youtu.be/zU7iAqg4sSA?t=11706) — do not trade at the release; NFP afternoon is fine
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Reinforces earlier "do not trade the news" advice.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #8   August 14, 2024
head: Projecting a high with a wick when the objective is deferred (scalping range)  (aliases: "projecting highs with the wicks")
body:
- **Kind:** refinement (partly caption-unclear; ICT explicitly withholds details)
- **What ICT says:**
  - If he believes the market will defer a run to an objective (e.g., relative equal highs or an NWOG) until after 9:30 or 10:00 (then maybe a Silver Bullet), and he is scalping long and short inside the range, he watches the candle that creates the first wick and mirrors the wick logic: he gives price one more chance to reach the objective, and then expects it to fall short of the wick's CE.
  - On a candle that makes an initial wick and then the next candle runs above it, that next candle's high was exactly at the half of a wick "that has yet to form" (captioned 19,149, unreliable), which he shows as proof it is algorithmic.
  - He says he can do this on 1m, hourly, daily and weekly ranges but will not teach all of it.
  - Scalp only when the environment gives two-way opportunities; one-sided, lethargic days he leaves to others.
- **Timestamps:** [3:16:41](https://youtu.be/zU7iAqg4sSA?t=11801) — keeping relative equal highs untouched until the open · [3:19:02](https://youtu.be/zU7iAqg4sSA?t=11942) — range staying intact, deferred runs · [3:19:52](https://youtu.be/zU7iAqg4sSA?t=11992) — high exactly at half of a future wick
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** The mechanics are not fully stated; use with care.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #8   August 14, 2024
head: Time over price: the algorithm trades by time  (aliases: macro, "price refers to time")
body:
- **Kind:** rule / philosophy
- **What ICT says:** Price does not care about indicators, divergence, trend following or ratios; it refers to time. If it is not the right time it will not move, and it oscillates in a predetermined algorithmic range (up to the high of the last range, down to the low, back to the middle) until it is time to spool. Session starts/ends and the macros (20-minute intervals, top of every hour) are the key times. The opening range is 9:30-10:00 ET and he uses it when he has no bias, to see how price treats a jagged vs. smooth area.
- **Timestamps:** [0:59:15](https://youtu.be/zU7iAqg4sSA?t=3555) — price refers to time · [1:00:02](https://youtu.be/zU7iAqg4sSA?t=3602) — fluctuates in a set range, macro at 20-minute intervals · [3:39:01](https://youtu.be/zU7iAqg4sSA?t=13141) — no bias before the open, watch the 9:30-10:00 opening range
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Consistent with Lecture #1.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #9  August 15, 2024
head: Premium vs discount: do not chase a rich opening (rule: "too rich, too expensive")  (aliases ICT uses: "long in the tooth", "stretched out", "street money / dumb money chases")
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:** After a gap-higher open plus an 8:30 impulsive run, price is too expensive to buy in the morning session. He will not buy a breakout above the highs and will not even take a bullish FVG in such conditions because the run is "too long in the tooth" and is more likely to revert to fair value (below: lows, relative equal lows, a gap, a consolidation). If it wants to run without him, it can ("it's a move I'm not a part of"). Retail ("the street", "dumb money") buys momentum and sells weakness, perpetually chasing; a professionally minded speculator buys cheap/discount prices and sells expensive/premium prices. Larger pools of capital will not engage while price rallies off the open; they wait for a return into a pool of liquidity where prices are discounted, which is always below old lows, single or relative equal lows.
- **How to identify:** Large gap between prior RTH settlement and the 9:30 open (he annotated the settlement level and the 9:30 open on the chart), an 8:30 impulsive run, price already pushing multiple highs after the open, a "jagged" (choppy-up) market, and a week-and-a-half of grind higher.
- **How to use:** Write the rule in the journal: nothing forces you to pay too much, and nothing should make you feel you will miss out. Chasing runs "five, six hundred... eight points" is very rare; more likely it is "go up, break out, get people caught long" and then reverse. Sit on hands until a signature forms; take the Silver Bullet at 10:00 instead.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 1m (with 15m top-left and 5m bottom-left), Thursday 8/15/2024. Gap up open; 9:30 open price annotated (digits partly uncaptioned); 8:30 impulse had created the high; price opened, dipped briefly into a small FVG, then ran to the buy-side above the 8:30 high and kept making marginally higher highs ("one more bump above the high") through about 10:00.
- **Timestamps:** [0:12:13](https://youtu.be/pg5XBNkpotM?t=733) won't buy this, too rich · [0:15:26](https://youtu.be/pg5XBNkpotM?t=926) write the rule in your journal, nothing forces you to pay too much · [0:24:26](https://youtu.be/pg5XBNkpotM?t=1466) too long in the tooth, would not take an FVG here to go higher · [0:30:30](https://youtu.be/pg5XBNkpotM?t=1830) larger pools wait for discount below lows
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** He explicitly says it can keep going higher all day and he does not care ("I'm not trying to be part of the move"); he is only interested in setups framed with logic he has seen before. He points back to the previous Tuesday stream (live stream of Tuesday Aug 13, 2024; he says "the 7th", caption unclear) for what he is "willing to endure" and what he will not trade.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #9  August 15, 2024
head: Trapped longs and where their stops sit (run on liquidity logic)  (aliases: "snare", "holding traders in", "jagged")
body:
- **Kind:** definition / rule of thumb
- **What ICT says:** A one-sided run that keeps printing small wick/body pushes through highs is work to (a) hurt anyone who bought a breakout, (b) get more people long or stop out anyone already short, and (c) build net-long positioning that the larger player can later sell into. Longs trail their stops to just below the latest consolidation/gap/low, so that is where the sell-side liquidity is; relative equal lows from the 8:30 consolidation, the gap, and the consolidation itself all hold stops. Shorts' stops sit above the highs; he expects a final overshoot to clear them ("if I was making the market... I would do that too and then sink it after").
- **How to identify:** Price holds above a gap/low, refuses to rally away convincingly, small candles that do not run; a "three drives"-type pattern higher inside liquidity; each new high is only a few ticks to slightly more.
- **How to use:** Expect a retracement to engage the sell-side. Frame, don't force: "we're looking for signatures to support an idea that we're hunting", not "arm wrestling" the market.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 1m: 8:30 run up created a consolidation with relative equal lows; after the 9:30 open price ran to buy-side above 8:30 high and kept pushing; he sees "one, two, three" drives higher into the liquidity and says the longs' stops are right under the gap/consolidation.
- **Timestamps:** [0:11:22](https://youtu.be/pg5XBNkpotM?t=682) everyone long trails stops under here · [0:16:14](https://youtu.be/pg5XBNkpotM?t=974) three drives pattern higher inside liquidity · [0:22:00](https://youtu.be/pg5XBNkpotM?t=1320) the hold-above is potentially a trap · [0:25:15](https://youtu.be/pg5XBNkpotM?t=1515) stops just below the consolidation to protect the move
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** "If it doesn't rally and start running away, it's more likely just a snare." Contrast: if price does rally away immediately, he is not in it either.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #9  August 15, 2024
head: Inversion FVG (iFVG) — conditions for a short idea after a premium run  (aliases: "treat it as an inversion fair value gap")
body:
- **Kind:** entry model (framing) / refinement
- **What ICT says:** His morning plan is a sequence he wants to see happen, not a prediction: price breaks below a particular gap (highlighted yellow, sitting below price from the 8:30 run, which he calls a breakaway gap / "institutional order flow entry drill" after a bull flag), comes back up into it and treats it as an inversion FVG (resistance), then sends price down into the sell-side liquidity and into the next gap below. He also wants price to remain above the recent lows and not trade down into the lower gap before the iFVG forms.
- **How to identify:**
  - Price must first close/trade through the gap to the downside; then retest from below.
  - Spikes/wicks above the gap are permissible, but the candle bodies must stay inside the shaded gap ("any spiking up with a wick but the body staying inside of that shaded area validates this as an inversion fair value gap").
  - The upper half (above the gap's consequent encroachment) should remain open/unfilled; if price completely closes the gap by trading over the top of it, the idea is dead.
- **How to use:** He wants bodies inside, upper portion open, then displacement below the CE of the wick, with larger candles accelerating down. Target: first the 9:30 opening price (fair value), then lows / sell-side liquidity, possibly into the afternoon.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 1m ~10:05–10:25 ET (stream clock 0:42–1:04; he states 9:50 at 0:26 and "10:00 now" at 0:36): while price keeps pressing above, he wants the gap (marked in pink) to be traded into with wicks only, upper half left open; "if it completely rolls over top of that pink area and trades higher, I'm standing still, no bias, no touch, no trade". Then wait for the 11:00–11:30 lunch macro and fade whatever has run.
- **Timestamps:** [0:12:13](https://youtu.be/pg5XBNkpotM?t=733) break below the yellow gap, return as iFVG · [0:43:53](https://youtu.be/pg5XBNkpotM?t=2633) wick above but body inside validates the iFVG · [0:45:31](https://youtu.be/pg5XBNkpotM?t=2731) upper half should stay open for a strong conviction · [1:04:54](https://youtu.be/pg5XBNkpotM?t=3894) quadrants on the gap, upper half open, work done in the lower half
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** This is an unusually explicit statement of the "wick may enter, body must not" tolerance for an iFVG, together with a "upper half must remain open" quadrant condition. The exact identity of the yellow vs pink gaps is hard to follow from audio alone (caption unclear on which gap he points at in places).

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #9  August 15, 2024
head: Gap quadrants / consequent encroachment of a gap or wick  (aliases: "run the quadrants", "midpoint", "consequent encroachment of that wick", "discount wick")
body:
- **Kind:** refinement
- **What ICT says:** For a large gap, draw the fib from the candle low to the candle high and watch the quadrants: the 50% is the consequent encroachment (CE). For a bearish idea he wants price to stay mostly in the lower half or underneath, leaving the upper half open, and then trade below the CE of the "wick" (midpoint of the wick/gap) with large candles. A weekly wick is also treated as a gap: NQ was trading in the CE of the weekly gap/wick (level read as about "44450" in captions; digits unclear), and that level could act as an inversion level only if price goes down through it, comes back up and uses it as support.
- **How to identify:** Mark the candle low and candle high forming the gap/wick; mark the 50%.
- **How to use:** Closing below the CE point would "indicate it's most likely going to roll over and then return back into the opening range". No close below and a push above = no bias.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 1m, around 10:12 ET: price touches the CE of the wick again ("there we go, touch the consequent encroachment") and he repeats that the portion above must stay open.
- **Timestamps:** [0:33:00](https://youtu.be/pg5XBNkpotM?t=1980) weekly wick treated as a gap, CE · [0:46:20](https://youtu.be/pg5XBNkpotM?t=2780) CE of the low, candle's high · [0:47:09](https://youtu.be/pg5XBNkpotM?t=2829) close below this point means roll over · [0:48:56](https://youtu.be/pg5XBNkpotM?t=2936) touch CE again, upper portion stays open
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Treating a weekly wick as a gap is a short mention but fits his "wick = gap, use CE" teaching.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #9  August 15, 2024
head: Exhaustion gap (gap that has been traded up into fully and left behind)
body:
- **Kind:** definition (brief) / new usage
- **What ICT says:** If price trades up into a gap and moves away aggressively without leaving part of it open, that gap is "exhausting" — it has done its job and loses relevance as resistance. For the key gap, he wants it traded into only partially; the upper half open means "really heavy" and he would have strong conviction for a return to the 9:30 opening price.
- **How to identify:** Gap that is completely filled with bodies, not just wicks. He notes a tiny "Mohawk" (a small wick) outside the range is fine as long as bodies stop inside.
- **How to use:** Exhaustion = that gap no longer supports the short idea; look at the next higher inefficiency or stand aside.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 1m ~10:18 ET: "this entire gap closed in here, the bodies are stopping, that one little Mohawk outside... I'm viewing that as an exhaustion; press press press press press, high, trade below the gap I have interest".
- **Timestamps:** [0:43:05](https://youtu.be/pg5XBNkpotM?t=2585) don't want it to trade up to there, exhaustion gap · [0:44:42](https://youtu.be/pg5XBNkpotM?t=2682) one gap exhaustion, other stays open in upper half · [0:54:08](https://youtu.be/pg5XBNkpotM?t=3248) entire gap closed with bodies, viewed as exhaustion
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Audio is ambiguous about which of the two gaps he calls exhaustion at each moment (caption unclear); treat as: gap fully traded through by bodies = exhaustion.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #9  August 15, 2024
head: Opening range, 9:30 opening price as fair value, and the gap-open magnet  (aliases: "opening range gap high", "opening range high", "new day opening gap", "RTH opening gap")
body:
- **Kind:** definition / rule
- **What ICT says:** The opening range is the first 30 minutes, 9:30–10:00 ET (set the chart to New York time so what you learn matches the channel). The 9:30 open price is annotated; on a gap-up open it forms the "opening range gap high" (top edge of the gap between the prior RTH close/settlement and the open) and the opening range high. Many times, even when price runs straight away from the open, it comes back down to touch the opening price, and then either continues higher later or goes lower into the close. "Fair value for the sake of fair value" is that 9:30 open price. A large premium opening does not always mean a complete return to the prior settlement, but watch for signs it will try. He also wants price to be traded back through; touching alone is not enough for him ("I want a little bit more than that").
- **How to identify:** Drop a line at the RTH close (4:00 pm settlement) and at the 9:30 open price (he preps a horizontal line near market before 9:30 and sets it to the actual open once it prints).
- **How to use:** Use the opening price as the first target for a short from a premium; the prior settlement as the deeper magnet; lunch/afternoon as the time for a delayed return if it does not happen before 1:00 pm.
- **Example in this video:** NQ, open at "352" (partial digits; e.g., the opening price line adjusted from "348" to "352" once the open printed); price spent the first hour above it. His expectation for the afternoon: "I believe we're going to see that again today" (return to this gap and the opening price level).
- **Timestamps:** [0:03:46](https://youtu.be/pg5XBNkpotM?t=226) annotating the 9:30 open · [0:04:36](https://youtu.be/pg5XBNkpotM?t=276) opening range is 9:30–10:00, set platform to NY time · [0:34:51](https://youtu.be/pg5XBNkpotM?t=2091) price often comes back to touch the opening range high = opening price · [0:39:31](https://youtu.be/pg5XBNkpotM?t=2371) fair value is the 9:30 opening price · [1:02:30](https://youtu.be/pg5XBNkpotM?t=3750) expect it in the afternoon if not before 1:00
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Calling the 9:30 price the "opening range high" is his usage on a gap-up open day; don't over-generalize to days with no gap.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #9  August 15, 2024
head: Buy-side liquidity run → immediate delivery (example screenshot for the log)  (aliases: "bread and butter set up", "heat on the FVG")
body:
- **Kind:** example only / process
- **What ICT says:** Early in the session a small gap was traded back into (a volume imbalance between two bodies after the 8:30 pop, plus relative equal lows), which then ran quickly to the pool of liquidity above (relative equal highs). He calls this one of the really easy bread-and-butter setups: a pool of liquidity is visible, price reaches into a gap/breaker and runs to it. You don't need the candle to close for the FVG to respond. A "low–high–low" structure there makes the move a breaker/FVG entry. For Caleb's journal screenshot, annotate: how long it took (about 1 minute), how much "heat" was on the FVG (zero drawdown), and the immediate run to liquidity.
- **How to identify:** Relative equal highs/lows visible; small gap or volume imbalance; low-high-low into breaker.
- **How to use:** Mark the entry PD array, log elapsed time and drawdown ("heat") to the target. Annotate as a screenshot, don't trade it unless it is in the model's time window.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 1m, about 9:31–9:35 ET: price dips into a small gap after the open, then runs above the relative equal highs (buy-side) at the 8:30 high; ICT notes this as a first screenshot with 0 heat and ~1 minute duration.
- **Timestamps:** [0:07:03](https://youtu.be/pg5XBNkpotM?t=423) small gap engaged, easy bread-and-butter setup · [0:09:37](https://youtu.be/pg5XBNkpotM?t=577) low-high-low breaker acts as FVG; need not close · [0:10:30](https://youtu.be/pg5XBNkpotM?t=630) annotate time taken and heat on the FVG: zero
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** "Heat" = adverse excursion into/through the entry PD array before the delivery; useful metric when studying setups.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #9  August 15, 2024
head: SMT divergence: Dow is the unreliable leg; prefer ES vs NQ  (aliases: "mixed market", "no participation")
body:
- **Kind:** rule / refinement
- **What ICT says:** At the high, NQ made a higher high while YM (Dow) did not, and ES was lagging (checked at 9:50). ICT does not argue SMT on the Dow alone but notes the Dow is "usually the first indication of things starting to crack"; the Dow tends to be lethargic and then suddenly runs, cancelling an SMT, so he prefers to see divergence on ES or NQ against each other. If ES makes a higher high, market breadth/strength is there and NQ should do the same; if NQ doesn't, he won't chase continuation for the session. Specifically: if ES lags, either NQ stays at its highs and ES catches up (so the NQ high gets taken), or NQ breaks down and ES fails to reach the high, in which case he likes the ES gap below.
- **How to identify:** Compare swing highs across NQ/ES/YM at the same time; he wants ES or NQ to diverge. If all three are not in agreement, it is a "mixed market".
- **How to use:** A single index not confirming = reason not to buy; ES not making a high while NQ does and sells = better short signal. He said if the S&P (ES) had been the one lagging, it would have been "really problematic" to be a buyer.
- **Example in this video:** About 9:50 ET: ES lagging NQ; around 10:02–10:05: NQ higher high vs Dow not confirming = "we could be forming an intermediate-term high for Nasdaq".
- **Timestamps:** [0:26:14](https://youtu.be/pg5XBNkpotM?t=1574) ES lagging NQ, what it implies · [0:37:50](https://youtu.be/pg5XBNkpotM?t=2270) Dow is another reason not to buy · [0:38:39](https://youtu.be/pg5XBNkpotM?t=2319) possible intermediate-term high for NQ · [1:03:18](https://youtu.be/pg5XBNkpotM?t=3798) Dow usually the one that doesn't listen; prefer ES/NQ for SMT
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** He reaffirms he doesn't trade the Dow ("why anybody likes to trade Dow is beyond me, only 30 stocks, so sloppy").

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #9  August 15, 2024
head: Stop run overshoot before the reversal  (aliases: "run the high", "10 to 20 handles", "one more gun")
body:
- **Kind:** rule / refinement
- **What ICT says:** Before the retracement he expects one more run above the high that is large enough to engage stops and trap: not "a tick or two", but "10, 15 handles, maybe 20 handles above it", then peter out, especially when ES is weaker. This gives the "street money" comfort that they were right so they raise stops under the new low (second pool of liquidity) that gets run on the way down.
- **How to identify:** Clean old high/relative equal highs sitting just above; an SMT divergence with ES/YM.
- **How to use:** Don't short the initial poke; wait for the sweep, then the inversion of a gap below/MSS-type confirmation.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 1m about 10:23–10:28 ET: price expected to sweep the high, "it should do it now because we had a gap, it overshot, it should spring up there and clear that high", and does pop on the next candle ("there it is, anyone short here has been canceled out").
- **Timestamps:** [0:58:23](https://youtu.be/pg5XBNkpotM?t=3503) bump the high once more to give comfort · [0:59:10](https://youtu.be/pg5XBNkpotM?t=3550) second pool of liquidity · [1:01:43](https://youtu.be/pg5XBNkpotM?t=3703) 10–20 handles above the high then peter out · [1:04:06](https://youtu.be/pg5XBNkpotM?t=3846) it pops, shorts canceled
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** The handle range is explicitly his rough preference, not a fixed rule.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #9  August 15, 2024
head: Silver Bullet (10:00 hour) and lunch macro as fallback windows  (aliases: "10 o'clock Silver Bullet", "11:00–11:30 lunch macro")
body:
- **Kind:** rule / time
- **What ICT says:** The 10 o'clock Silver Bullet is the main focus for the day; "it's always there, it's never not in the charts". Don't trade the early session (opening range) because it's a time you can get caught offside. If the idea doesn't materialize ("no touch, no trade"), wait until around 11:00–11:30 and fade whatever the market has done until then, using it as a "lunch macro". If the retracement does not happen before 1:00 pm, he expects it in the afternoon.
- **How to identify:** Clock based (10:00–11:00 ET window; lunch macro ~11:00–11:30 ET).
- **How to use:** Stand aside during the first 30 minutes, reassess at 10:00 with the pre-defined levels.
- **Example in this video:** He stays flat all morning; afternoon expectation is a return to the gap and the opening price.
- **Timestamps:** [0:13:01](https://youtu.be/pg5XBNkpotM?t=781) 10 o'clock Silver Bullet is always there · [0:28:03](https://youtu.be/pg5XBNkpotM?t=1683) 10:00 Silver Bullet main focus · [0:47:09](https://youtu.be/pg5XBNkpotM?t=2829) wait until 11:00–11:30, lunch macro, fade the run
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Here the lunch macro is used as an 11:00–11:30 fade window on a trend day, not a time-based entry model.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #9  August 15, 2024
head: Election-year / "built-in buy model" bias note  (aliases: seasonal tendency, "election years")
body:
- **Kind:** context (opinion)
- **What ICT says:** In election years the stock market tends to be pumped to flatter the incumbent; markets are also meant to go up over time, so it is easier to go higher than lower and shorting every wobble gets you chopped up. That is why he adopted models where certain things must trade first (e.g., a sell-side engagement) before he takes a short.
- **How to use:** Don't fade strength without the model's criteria; accept it can keep going.
- **Timestamps:** [0:28:03](https://youtu.be/pg5XBNkpotM?t=1683) election-year pump tendency · [0:28:54](https://youtu.be/pg5XBNkpotM?t=1734) why models require sequence before shorting
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Opinion-level note, no numbers.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #10  August 16, 2024
head: Opening Range (9:30–10:00 ET) and its quadrants  (aliases ICT uses: "OR", "first 30 minutes", "opening range CE")
body:
- **Kind:** definition / refinement
- **What ICT says:** The opening range is the first 30 minutes of trading, 9:30 am to 10:00 am New York time. There is **no 15-minute opening range** (he explicitly rejects that idea as spread by "another YouTuber"). You mark the highest high and lowest low formed 9:30–10:00 and divide the range into quadrants: high, upper quadrant (75%), midpoint = consequent encroachment (CE, 50%), lower quadrant (25%), low; the 9:30 opening price is also a reference level. If price opens and trades up, the high formed by 10:00 relative to the open defines the range; if it trades down, the low formed by 10:00 does. He stresses this is not Quarters Theory, pivots, Wolfe waves, or Elliott wave.
- **How to identify:** Measure on a 1m chart after 10:00 (he draws it as lines, not rectangles, on live streams, because the rectangles "fight" him). He abbreviates in notes, e.g. "8/15 OR CE".
- **How to use:** Yesterday's (and the previous two days') opening range levels are reference points for today's reactions: price returned to Thursday's opening range high/upper quadrant and bounced; the CE and lower quadrant of Thursday's range were not yet "booked" (explored) on Friday, so the CE was the minimum he wanted to see traded to. A level that is confluent with another (e.g., 20% weekly retracement, an opening range gap level two days back) and with a PD array in a macro window is expected to give a strong reaction.
- **Example in this video:** NQ, Fri 8/16/2024. Early in the session (about 9:30–9:35 ET by stream clock), price dropped to a level that was both the 75% (upper quadrant) of Thursday 8/15's 9:30–10:00 range and 20% of the week's range, and rallied from it ("kinging off of it" more than once).
- **Timestamps:** [0:02:06](https://youtu.be/qoNQfVzVXZQ?t=126) upper quadrant of yesterday's OR plus opening range gap high · [0:10:27](https://youtu.be/qoNQfVzVXZQ?t=627) OR defined as first 30 min, quadrants not quarters theory · [0:20:07](https://youtu.be/qoNQfVzVXZQ?t=1207) no 15-minute opening range · [0:49:23](https://youtu.be/qoNQfVzVXZQ?t=2963) confluence of OR/ORG level + PD array + macro time = good reaction
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** In the previous lecture he called the 9:30 open "opening range high" on a gap-up day; here the range proper is high-to-low of 9:30–10:00 and the opening price is its own level. He admits he mislabeled gap vs. range on Thursday's recording and omitted the word "gap", which is why he re-teaches the distinction.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #10  August 16, 2024
head: Opening Range Gap (ORG) vs. New Day Opening Gap (NDOG)  (aliases: "opening range gap high/low", "RTH gap", "new day opening gap")
body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:** The **opening range gap** is the difference between the previous day's regular-session (RTH) settlement price and the first print at 9:30 (first tick). On a gap-down open (his example) the settlement price is the "opening range gap high" and the 9:30 open is the "opening range gap low"; for a gap-up the settlement would be the low edge and the open the high edge (my inference, consistent with lecture 9, where the 9:30 open was the gap high). It is an inefficiency (a gap), whereas the opening range is a travelled distance; "one's an inefficiency as a gap, one's an actual travelling from an opening price at 9:30 to the extreme". The **NDOG** is the separate gap between the 5:00 pm settlement and the 6:00 pm reopening (globex), from yesterday's formation. Quadrants can be run on the ORG too, but only when price is near it.
- **How to identify:** Toggle the platform from electronic trading hours (ETH) to regular trading hours (RTH): in RTH view the gap between the previous RTH settlement (he mentions a 4:15 settlement time, caption slightly unclear) and the 9:30 open is visible; in ETH view it gets filled and disappears, so you must draw the settlement and open levels manually (and the same applies on platforms lacking an RTH toggle).
- **How to use:** Treat gap highs/lows, CE, and the 9:30 open as targets and reaction levels; keep them on a notepad rather than the chart.
- **Example in this video:** Thursday: settlement of Wednesday's session vs. Thursday's 9:30 open. On Friday price traded up into the Thursday ORG area and the NDOG (a wick traveled through the previous settlement; relative equal highs at the open swept to roughly the ORG high). Levels shown on a 1m chart by dropping the RTH view, then back to ETH to show the gap vanishes.
- **Timestamps:** [0:23:24](https://youtu.be/qoNQfVzVXZQ?t=1404) settlement vs yesterday's opening price = ORG · [0:25:38](https://youtu.be/qoNQfVzVXZQ?t=1538) settlement and first print define the gap; chart view change shows it · [0:26:28](https://youtu.be/qoNQfVzVXZQ?t=1588) naming gap high vs gap low · [0:41:19](https://youtu.be/qoNQfVzVXZQ?t=2479) ETH vs RTH, draw levels if unavailable
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** "Opening range gap" in this video is strictly the RTH close-to-9:30-open difference; the earlier uses of "new day opening gap" (6 pm) remain separate. The exact wording of which end is "high" depends on gap direction (he gives the gap-down case).

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #10  August 16, 2024
head: Carry-forward of OR / ORG levels for three days  (aliases: "key levels list", "naked chart with a notepad")
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:** Every opening range and opening range gap, if the levels have not been completely used (explored, tested, traded to, repriced), is carried forward as a look-back reference for **three days**. "Very influential in terms of price delivery"; wonderful setups form around them. He keeps the levels on a notepad (or a screenshot of it on his phone) and trades off a **naked chart**, because lines on the chart pull his eye and bias him; he is deliberately quiet about a few purely personal notes that "aren't make-or-break".
- **How to identify:** Yesterday's and the previous day's: OR high, CE, low, lower/upper quadrant, opening price, ORG/NDOG levels, plus weekly 20%/30% levels.
- **How to use:** Ask which of these levels have been "booked" already; use the unvisited ones as draws. If price rips through all intraday levels, go to the 15m/60m/4H/daily to see what it is reaching for (e.g., an old daily high discussed Tuesday).
- **Example in this video:** Friday: today's price had touched the Thursday OR high and upper quadrant but not the CE or lower quadrant, so he watched for an attempt at the CE.
- **Timestamps:** [0:08:04](https://youtu.be/qoNQfVzVXZQ?t=484) carry forward three days · [0:12:56](https://youtu.be/qoNQfVzVXZQ?t=776) notepad abbreviations · [0:14:33](https://youtu.be/qoNQfVzVXZQ?t=873) why a naked chart · [0:43:41](https://youtu.be/qoNQfVzVXZQ?t=2621) if it rips through all of them, go to a higher timeframe
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** First time he states the "three days" carry rule this explicitly; levels you annotate publicly shouldn't be used as your own stop (see Stops/liquidity below).

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #10  August 16, 2024
head: TGIF — Thursday-1 pm to Friday retracement of the weekly range  (aliases: "20–30% of the weekly range", "TGIF 20%", "weekly Power of 3 done")
body:
- **Kind:** rule / new coinage refinement
- **What ICT says:** On an up week, after the weekly high forms, expect a retracement of **20% to 30% of the total weekly range**.
