title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #18  August 27, 2024
head: Opening Range Gap (RTH ORG) — previous settlement to 9:30 open  (aliases: opening range gap, "settlement gap", discount opening range gap)
body:
- **Kind:** rule / definition
- **What ICT says:**
  - The ORG runs from the previous day's settlement, the last print at 4:14 PM ET, to the 9:30 AM ET opening price. The session ends at 4:15, so there is no 4:15 print. Electronic trading continues until 5:00 PM, pauses for an hour, and resumes at 6:00 PM ET.
  - The "opening range" is 9:30-10:00, a 30-minute interval, not 15 or 5. He calls the other timeframes people teach wrong.
  - First order of business each day is to determine whether there is a gap. A "significant" gap is more than about 20-30 handles on NQ.
  - The midpoint (consequent encroachment, CE) is "our first threshold". Roughly 70% of the time, price trades at least to the CE in the first 30 minutes. He restates this as "you got 70% chance" that at least half the gap is filled. He calls this algorithmic, and the captions once render it as "7%" in error.
  - No bias is needed to study this: no daily bias and no session bias. It is just a way to watch how price is delivered.
  - Plot quadrant levels (25/50/75%) on the gap. Set an alert on the CE so a one-tick cross rings.
- **How to identify:** High = previous settlement (4:14 PM print). Low = 9:30 opening tick (when the open is below settlement, a "discount" ORG). Reverse if the open is above settlement. Extend the lines across the day.
- **How to use:**
  - Pre-plot the settlement line before the open (he did this at ~9:25). Park a second line away from price during electronic hours, then drag it to the 9:30 print when it appears.
  - Watch for the first reach to the lower quadrant, then the CE, then the full closure. The partial-fill sequence is the study.
  - If no FVG has formed yet on the 1m and there is minor sell-side liquidity just under price, he flags a profile to study: drop, clear the sell side, then return up and hit the mid-gap.
  - "Don't use it to pick every entry". Use it to learn what constitutes a valid run from a level.
- **Example in this video:**
  - NQ 1m, Tue 8/27/24. Settlement is quoted as "568 and 3/4" (likely 19568.75, caption unclear). The open was well below it, so the gap is a "very deep discounted" ORG, and the settlement price sat inside the Aug 16 NDOG.
  - Price first dipped to the lower quadrant and could not reach the CE (swept minor sell-side liquidity first).
  - It later ran back up and closed about 3/4 of the gap, "fell short" of full closure. ICT notes this meant the 70% half-fill happened before the 10:00 mark.
  - Afterwards price consolidated near the gap high (the settlement price) and then ran on into the NDOG/NWOG cluster.
- **Timestamps:**
  - [0:02:16](https://youtu.be/yOZHawAE8QI?t=136) — plots settlement and prepares the ORG.
  - [0:07:55](https://youtu.be/yOZHawAE8QI?t=475) — CE of the ORG, 9:30-10:00 is 30 minutes not 15, 70% trade to mid-gap.
  - [0:30:38](https://youtu.be/yOZHawAE8QI?t=1838) — restates: gap over ~30 handles, 70%, half minimum.
  - [0:47:32](https://youtu.be/yOZHawAE8QI?t=2852) — settlement is the 4:14 PM print; session hours.
- **Nuance / caveats:**
  - ICT says "find it in a book, it's not out there".
  - He uses the ORG purely as a draw/target framework, not a trade signal.
  - Extra context: he opens his operating window at 7:00 ET (see Rules).

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #18  August 27, 2024
head: First Fair Value Gap after 9:30 (inside 9:30–10:00)  (aliases: "first presentation", "initial FVG", "the first FVG after 9:30")
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - The first FVG that forms between 9:31 and 10:00 is the one to extend across the entire day. He says he taught this in Twitter Spaces in 2023.
  - "Your FVG can't form on the 9:30 candle," so the window starts with the candle after the open (exact three-candle mechanics are not spelled out; caption unclear).
  - On the 1m chart, study what the market does to this one gap while the ORG is still unfilled. He calls the first interaction the "first presentation".
  - Earlier in the session, a pre-9:30 FVG (outside the opening range) was the only gap in use. He wants to see it traded to once more before the real first-FVG appears.
- **How to identify:** Take the first 1m FVG that completes after the 9:30 candle and before 10:00. Annotate it in grey and extend it forward "in perpetuity throughout the day."
- **How to use:**
  - Price tends to go above it, close above, then return to it on a later candle and reverse "to the tick".
  - Once price has swept sell-side liquidity below (disturbing the water), the next draw is the smooth, unfilled side (short-term buy side, ORG remainder).
  - ICT repeats there should be "no more sellers below that candle's low" only because the code says the level holds. His point is that nothing in buy/sell pressure explains stopping on the tick.
- **Example in this video:**
  - NQ 1m. Price opens, drops below relative equal lows (accumulation of sell stops), then pushes back above the initial FVG and closes above it.
  - A later candle opens above, trades down into the gap and stops exactly at its top. ICT gives the candle low as 19555.25 (caption reads "1955.25"; read as 19555.25).
  - Price then runs to the short-term buy side and on to the ORG gap high.
- **Timestamps:**
  - [0:25:47](https://youtu.be/yOZHawAE8QI?t=1547) — "first presentation… first one inside of 9:30 to 10".
  - [0:37:47](https://youtu.be/yOZHawAE8QI?t=2267) — the 2023 Twitter Spaces rule.
  - [0:59:38](https://youtu.be/yOZHawAE8QI?t=3578) — the stop to the tick at 19555.25.
  - [1:12:34](https://youtu.be/yOZHawAE8QI?t=4354) — recap: "first FVG that forms between 9:31 and 10".
- **Nuance / caveats:** The pre-9:30 FVG (the "A" gap, see iFVG below) and the first-after-9:30 FVG (the "B" gap) are two different gaps in this walkthrough; the captions blur which one he is pointing at on several lines.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #18  August 27, 2024
head: Inversion FVG (iFVG) and "Reclaimed" FVG — role reversal  (aliases: inversion fair value gap, reclaimed bullish FVG, PD array that changes its state)
body:
- **Kind:** refinement / new coinage ("reclaimed")
- **What ICT says:**
  - A PD array is not static. A bullish FVG used as support (price rallies off it from discount) can be traded below, so it becomes an inversion and sends price lower. If price later gets back above it, it reverts: a "reclaimed bullish FVG" that should again act as real support.
  - He says he was not wrong in his earlier lecture; the lesson is how the array is used and whether its mode of delivery changes. "Stop saying all fair value gaps are the same."
  - He colors an inverted gap orange in his charts ("if it's ever a hue, it's orange: its role has reversed").
  - Intraday order: price must first get above the gap's high ("reclaimed"). Typically that is accompanied by a sudden, abrupt market structure shift (he wants them "sudden and abrupt").
  - Climbing metaphor: a PD array above price is first a handhold; after price gets above it, it becomes a foothold.
- **How to identify:** A gap that held price, then price traded/closed through it, and later closed back through it again. Orange = inversion; reclaimed = back to the original role.
- **How to use:**
  - Frame a paper/tape-reading short at the inverted gap's CE-to-low (the candle's high). Partial one tick below the low it makes, then extend.
  - As an inversion short, "the easiest objective" is the next low-hanging low or relative equal lows. Quick method: quadrant the range you are working in and project.
  - When reclaimed: if price opens above and trades back down into it, that is where support should show.
- **Example in this video:**
  - NQ 1m: the first gap (outside 9:30-10:00) acts as discount support, price takes relative equal highs above, then trades below it (inversion).
  - He frames a hypothetical short at 19493 (the high of the candle that forms the gap's low). Price runs the low to 19476.
  - His arithmetic for the target: "one quadrant extension of the range" gives 19460.25, about 30+ handles. How the range is measured is not clear in the captions; it is roughly the 19493–19476 range projected below the low.
  - Later price closes back above the gap: now a reclaimed bullish FVG, and the sell-side raid at the low becomes the springboard.
- **Timestamps:**
  - [0:16:24](https://youtu.be/yOZHawAE8QI?t=984) — "first elements to understanding how FVGs can invert".
  - [0:18:02](https://youtu.be/yOZHawAE8QI?t=1082) — range to 19493/19476, quadrant method.
  - [0:19:38](https://youtu.be/yOZHawAE8QI?t=1178) — partial one tick below, extension to 19460.25.
  - [1:04:25](https://youtu.be/yOZHawAE8QI?t=3865) — "reclaimed bullish fair value gap".
  - [1:10:54](https://youtu.be/yOZHawAE8QI?t=4254) — a PD array can impede, support or reject.
- **Nuance / caveats:** Tolerance for the closing candle's body slightly outside the gap is addressed under "Mohawk / body versus wick" below. He frames this as the first elements; he has not taught everything about the iFVG yet.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #18  August 27, 2024
head: Liquidity accumulation: why smart money drops price below relative equal lows first  (aliases: accumulation, sell-stop accumulation, "time-based delivery")
body:
- **Kind:** definition / explanation
- **What ICT says:**
  - When a large unfilled range (here the ORG) sits above, price often first drops below relative equal lows. Smart money needs a counterparty. It "accumulates" the sell stops/sell orders resting there, which become their buy orders in size.
  - It does not matter whether those sell orders are protective stops on longs or breakout entries. Relative equal lows are the visual shorthand he uses so he does not have to reveal how he distinguishes them.
  - Accumulation means price spending time at a pre-determined liquidity level. Inefficiencies (FVGs) are different: you do not want price meandering inside them (no "bull flags"). Price should trade to them, through them, and use them as a "springboard / rocket fuel".
  - Smart money never buys on an uptick or breakout. It buys on sell-side (momentum-down) delivery at discounted prices. The first down-close candle after a run of up-closes is the first "discounted" delivery. They add as price trades up, but the volume comes from the loading below.
  - The longer price spends below a pool, the larger and more protracted the later run ("it's spending time now because it's going to be a longer protracted run").
  - Delivery speed is in proportion to how close the inefficiency or liquidity is. Once the buying is done, candles expand and the run accelerates toward the full closure.
  - He contrasts this with a prior-day observation where price stabbed down inside a wick's CE and immediately came out: that is not accumulation.
- **How to use:**
  - If price keeps ignoring a PD array in the narrative direction and spends time at a liquidity pool, expect the repricing leg to be fast.
  - If price goes "off script" after a run to a level, do not over-leverage or force a trade; sit still.
- **Example in this video:** NQ: price opens, runs a little above, then drops below relative equal lows (inside the lower ORG half) and sits there, forming the pre-move FVG and ORG remainder above. After the sweep it reprices up to the first FVG and on to the ORG gap high.
- **Timestamps:**
  - [0:46:43](https://youtu.be/yOZHawAE8QI?t=2803) — what benefit for smart money to engage sell stops.
  - [0:57:17](https://youtu.be/yOZHawAE8QI?t=3437) — unfinished business above, accumulation below.
  - [0:58:50](https://youtu.be/yOZHawAE8QI?t=3530) — liquidity vs inefficiency: spend time below liquidity, never inside FVGs.
  - [1:02:50](https://youtu.be/yOZHawAE8QI?t=3770) — smart money never buys breakouts; off-script = sit still.
- **Nuance / caveats:** He says the "delivery to terminus" has already started (caption unclear on exact meaning; "terminus" appears here as the destination of the delivery, likely not the named model).

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #18  August 27, 2024
head: Smart-money counterparty / why "buying and selling pressure" is rejected  (aliases: algorithm, Composite Man, market maker, draw on liquidity)
body:
- **Kind:** rule / philosophy
- **What ICT says:**
  - Price is delivered by an algorithm. Stops "to the tick" at pre-announced levels cannot be explained by random buying and selling pressure. Depth of market is a facade; orders can be pulled or spoofed, so a big book at a price is not a magnet.
  - PD arrays are "arrays" in the programming sense: reference data points the algorithm refers back to, like ingredients in a recipe. The outcome is sometimes over- or under-cooked but still profitable for the market maker.
  - Draw on liquidity analogy: you go to the shoe store because you want shoes; the store is the draw.
  - Smart money does not need much volume at the end of the move because it loaded earlier. Retail can push orders into a single candle that smart money cannot.
  - Market structure is a controlled environment that can be "manipulated and disturbed".
- **Timestamps:**
  - [0:33:48](https://youtu.be/yOZHawAE8QI?t=2028) — start of the "no algorithm" rebuttal.
  - [0:46:43](https://youtu.be/yOZHawAE8QI?t=2803) — draw on liquidity / counterparty.
  - [1:07:40](https://youtu.be/yOZHawAE8QI?t=4060) — depth of market spoofing; not a magnet.
  - [1:14:10](https://youtu.be/yOZHawAE8QI?t=4450) — what an "array" is.
- **Nuance / caveats:** Mostly argument rather than rules. Treat as motivation; the usable rules are in the neighboring concepts.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #18  August 27, 2024
head: Bullish Breaker (as used here) and PD array body-versus-wick rules  (aliases: breaker, "coloring outside the lines")
body:
- **Kind:** refinement / example
- **What ICT says:**
  - After sell-side was engaged and price ran above the short-term high (a market structure shift), an up-close candle with a long discount tail is called the bullish breaker. It "broke the market structure and took anyone that's long out," leaving buy side "neutral" with no held longs above.
  - His breaker candle: it opened, wicked down into the first FVG's top (low 19555.25) and closed up. The wick did the damage; the body is what you reference.
  - Use the upper half of the body for a bullish breaker: between the body's midpoint (the CE) and its high. Do not worry about the wick.
  - Price held in the upper quadrant of the body without ever touching the halfway point, consolidating (accumulating) before expanding.
  - Tolerance: a body should not exceed a PD array's boundary, and if it does, one tick, "no more than two". A wick can go a few ticks outside. On NQ he allows about two ticks; on ES it is tighter, generally one tick.
- **How to use:** Treat the breaker as a brick wall for rejecting lower prices. If bullish, price should not trade into its lower half. Accumulation inside the upper quadrant is the signature.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 1m after the first FVG tap at 19555.25: breaker candle closes up; price ranges inside its upper half, then rallies to the ORG gap high (settlement), sits sideways, then expands into the NDOG/NWOG cluster.
- **Timestamps:**
  - [1:19:04](https://youtu.be/yOZHawAE8QI?t=4744) — "this up close candle here is your bullish breaker".
  - [1:21:28](https://youtu.be/yOZHawAE8QI?t=4888) — wick versus body, tick tolerance (NQ two ticks, ES one).
  - [1:23:52](https://youtu.be/yOZHawAE8QI?t=5032) — use the body's upper half.
  - [1:24:41](https://youtu.be/yOZHawAE8QI?t=5081) — accumulation in the upper quadrant.
- **Nuance / caveats:** This is not the classic definition of a breaker (failed order block that flips). ICT here ties the label to the candle at which structure broke and longs were cleared. The captions are noisy on candle-by-candle identification.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #18  August 27, 2024
head: Upper-half / lower-half rule for PD arrays  (aliases: "rules of engagement with my PD arrays", highest form of order flow around them, premium/discount inside an array)
body:
- **Kind:** rule (he says he was not going to teach it to paid students)
- **What ICT says:**
  - If you are bullish, you do not want the lower half of a PD array to be traded to. If you are bearish, you do not want the upper half to be traded to. The array should show an inability to deliver price in that half.
  - The lower half can be traded into, but then price must respond immediately off the deepest part. If it does not, "chances are you have a dud": cancel the trade, take a scratch or lose only commission.
  - The same applies to inversion FVGs (a bearish inverted gap should not be revisited in its upper half) and to order blocks.
  - His mentorship-era shortcut was just the low of the up-close candle or the opening price; this half-rule is the more refined version.
- **How to use:**
  - Enter in the allowed half (for a short, the lower part of an order block or candle). Place the stop where the invalid half and the supporting reference would both have to fail (see rejection block).
  - Having the other half untouched also lets you pyramid with more confidence.
- **Example in this video:**
  - NQ short: price kept the upper half of the volume imbalance/inversion FVG untraded while wicking into the lower half and CE ("mohawk" above the halfway), which gave him confidence to add.
  - ES short: "I trust we're not going in the upper half of this range".
- **Timestamps:**
  - [1:23:04](https://youtu.be/yOZHawAE8QI?t=4984) — if bullish, lower half should fail.
  - [1:35:08](https://youtu.be/yOZHawAE8QI?t=5708) — respect upper half when bullish; respond at the deepest part or cancel.
  - [2:54:01](https://youtu.be/yOZHawAE8QI?t=10441) — bearish: upper half never redelivered.
  - [3:18:01](https://youtu.be/yOZHawAE8QI?t=11881) — "the highest order of order flow around them".
- **Nuance / caveats:** Refines the simple "enter at the low of the up-close candle" version of an order block entry. He insists this is not supply and demand.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #18  August 27, 2024
head: Mohawk (tolerance beyond a PD array's boundary)  (aliases: coloring outside the lines)
body:
- **Kind:** new coinage / refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - A "mohawk" is a small wick or a body slightly outside a PD array's exact boundary, behavior you as the analyst allow. Annotate it as a mohawk when journaling.
  - A close a tick or two beyond the edge (example: a close just above a volume imbalance high at 19598.25, caption approximate) is permissible and does not change what you expect.
  - When an FVG overlaps a volume imbalance, use the volume imbalance range as the true inefficiency, not just the wick, because two PD arrays agree on the same context.
- **How to use:** Do not abandon a thesis for a one/two-tick mohawk. In journaling, label it so a bold candle poking through does not scare you in real time.
- **Example in this video:** NQ short: a wick poked above the volume imbalance high and the CE of the inefficiency, closes stayed outside the gap, price then dropped.
- **Timestamps:**
  - [2:31:24](https://youtu.be/yOZHawAE8QI?t=9084) — body slightly above the PD high is permissible.
  - [2:33:59](https://youtu.be/yOZHawAE8QI?t=9239) — naming and annotation of the "mohawk".
  - [2:34:49](https://youtu.be/yOZHawAE8QI?t=9289) — volume imbalance as the true inefficiency range.
  - [2:38:49](https://youtu.be/yOZHawAE8QI?t=9529) — mohawk above the CE of the inefficiency.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #18  August 27, 2024
head: Propulsion Block  (aliases: part of the order block family; taught in 2016 core content)
body:
- **Kind:** definition applied / example
- **What ICT says:**
  - A propulsion block is a candle that trades back into a prior order block (an inefficiency-reaching OB) and whose body does not breach, close above or cross the order block's mid-point (mean threshold). He treats that as a tipping of the hand that price should repel away.
  - The propulsion block's entire range is referenced, and he uses its opening price as an entry reference. A later candle that digs into that previous order block adds conviction.
  - He points to the PD array lectures in the 2016 mentorship (his "month four" content) and says the full rules will be in the book trilogy.
- **How to identify:** A candle moving back into a prior OB, with its body holding below (for shorts) the OB's mean threshold, and an immediate move away.
- **How to use:**
  - Short entry near the propulsion block's opening price, then add on the CE of the wick/inefficiency.
  - Required supporting context: the order block must not stand alone (see Order-block caveats).
- **Example in this video:**
  - NQ demo short: order block reaches the high end of the inefficiency; a following candle pushes into it but its body does not cross the OB's half; ICT shorts the propulsion block's open, then adds at the CE of the next wick.
  - ES short: later order block with an indecisive candle that creates a volume imbalance. Every candle that comes back up into the OB fails to reach half.
- **Timestamps:**
  - [2:36:26](https://youtu.be/yOZHawAE8QI?t=9386) — "this candle's body cannot breach half of the order block".
  - [2:39:37](https://youtu.be/yOZHawAE8QI?t=9577) — why it is a propulsion block.
  - [2:54:49](https://youtu.be/yOZHawAE8QI?t=10489) — entries on the propulsion block's open and wick CE.
  - [3:13:57](https://youtu.be/yOZHawAE8QI?t=11637) — ES: did price reach the OB's mean threshold? No, so propulsion.
- **Nuance / caveats:** Captions are rough on exactly which candle is which; core-content definition is not restated in this video.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #18  August 27, 2024
head: Order block caveats and the reclaimed order block
body:
- **Kind:** rule / new coinage ("reclaimed bearish order block")
- **What ICT says:**
  - An order block "is not just an up-closed candle and certainly not just the last up-closed candle before the down move"; it must have other supportive PD arrays around it.
  - An inversion FVG alone is not a trade either unless supported by an OB etc.
  - A "reclaimed bearish order block": price moved away from the OB, then comes back up into it. It needs an immediate response lower. When it did, he took it as a sign of heaviness.
- **Example in this video:** ES 1m: after the propulsion block/volume imbalance, price came back up and dug into the original order block; it dropped again immediately, then retraced into an FVG, displaced, took out the low, matched the high of the inefficiency, and showed no willingness to enter its upper portion.
- **Timestamps:**
  - [2:52:27](https://youtu.be/yOZHawAE8QI?t=10347) — OB needs support from other things.
  - [3:15:36](https://youtu.be/yOZHawAE8QI?t=11736) — reclaimed bearish order block.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #18  August 27, 2024
head: Rejection Block (as a stop-loss reference)
body:
- **Kind:** application / refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - His stop on the NQ short sat above the rejection block: the highest up-close in the swing (high, higher high, lower high) — the closing price of that up-close candle.
  - A rejection block should be traded to one time; if it is good, price does not go back above it. The later run reached exactly 19592.75, the same as the close of the up-close candle, then reversed.
  - Because everything else lined up (propulsion block, inversion, upper half untouched), he was not afraid the stop would be hit: "the CE won't go back to the rejection block".
  - Taught in the 2016 mentorship month-four content.
- **How to use:** Put the stop above the rejection block's level and only after the supporting conditions are present. The stop is logic-based and tight.
- **Example in this video:** NQ short demo: wick up to the CE of the inefficiency; price reverses; rejection block price 19592.75 never traded above. (The transcript also reads "19552.75" once, which is a caption error.)
- **Timestamps:**
  - [2:43:34](https://youtu.be/yOZHawAE8QI?t=9814) — rejection block stop, 592.75 high equals the close.
  - [2:50:01](https://youtu.be/yOZHawAE8QI?t=10201) — "that's algorithmic, why did this candle stop right there?"
  - [2:51:38](https://youtu.be/yOZHawAE8QI?t=10298) — CE not going back to the rejection block, so not worried about the stop.
- **Nuance / caveats:** He says stop placement is learned "every time I lecture"; no fixed-tick rule is given.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #18  August 27, 2024
head: Execution walk-through: NQ short (demo, recorded morning of 8/27) — pyramid, partial, target NDOG
body:
- **Kind:** entry model / example
- **What ICT says:**
  - Trade context: price had traded up into a volume imbalance, dropped, tapped it again, then closed slightly above it (mohawk). The next candle confirmed willingness to go lower. Price broke lower and created an order block, which he used as initial entry. Then, as price wicked up to the CE of the wick/inefficiency, he added ("I'll take that too").
  - Position: 12 contracts total (about 6 + 6 across two entries, 10-12 contracts "is not a lot"). Demo account; recorded over a live feed, not replay.
  - Partial: a limit buy (to cover) at the half of the range to the target, 19574; he would have taken 3 (he also says 5 as an example) off the 12. The mechanics: right-click on the price axis, choose buy at the level, and set the contract count.
  - Target: the old NDOG from Aug 16, 2024 ("low-hanging fruit"). He notes that using only this much would still be a successful trade.
  - After the entry, price slammed up into the CE of the wick, hit it, and the trade ran. He emphasizes the trades are fast ("eager to please").
- **How to use:** Enter at the propulsion block's open, add at the CE of the wick/inefficiency, stop above the rejection block, partial at the midpoint, final target an old NDOG.
- **Timestamps:**
  - [2:30:36](https://youtu.be/yOZHawAE8QI?t=9036) — setup: volume imbalance tapped, then slightly above.
  - [2:37:12](https://youtu.be/yOZHawAE8QI?t=9432) — entries: order block, then CE of the wick.
  - [2:47:31](https://youtu.be/yOZHawAE8QI?t=10051) — partial at half the range, target NDOG Aug 16.
  - [2:55:39](https://youtu.be/yOZHawAE8QI?t=10539) — 3 of 12 contracts off at 19574; limit-order mechanics.
- **Nuance / caveats:** Whether he labelled the first order block correctly is flagged by him ("I falsely called it an order block because I'm talking about it live"). This is a demo; he repeats it is not financial advice and that live results with real money (AMP / TDM Trade) exist on his channel.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #18  August 27, 2024
head: Previous Day High/Low and the 3-day high/low reference list  (aliases: PDH/PDL, "honey pot", old highs/lows, buy-side/sell-side)
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - Keep a written list of the highest high and lowest low of the last three trading days, plus each of those days' own high and low (e.g., on Tuesday: Monday, Friday, Thursday). Sundays do not count; the only thing taken from Sunday is the 6:00 PM ET opening, for the NWOG.
  - Markets will refer back to these. Liquidity sits above old highs (buy stops) and below old lows (sell stops). They act as draws on liquidity "just like a new week opening gap or a new day opening gap".
  - Mark them by hand with a horizontal ray rather than relying on an indicator ("high touch over high tech"). He criticizes dependence on indicators such as LuxAlgo and says some of their smart money plotting is not what he would use.
  - Simple rule: when you sit down to trade and the market is in the lower half of the previous day's range, always look for a return to the previous day's low. The PDH/PDL is "like a honey pot", available every single day.
  - Tendency while approaching the target: speed and distance should increase as price nears the previous day's low. Anyone with a protective stop there can quickly pull it, so price runs to the pool fast, jumping and skipping (visible on 1-second or 5-second charts) before they can. One contract is enough to book the print.
- **How to identify / use:**
  - Opening in the lower half of the prior day's range = bias toward a sweep of PDL (and vice versa for the upper half).
  - After the sweep, look for the reaction: price rallies, takes relative equal highs.
- **Example in this video:**
  - ES 1m, Aug 27: price drops toward Monday Aug 26's low. Short entries at the order block / propulsion block, then at the volume imbalance as price opened and tagged it. The exit filled one tick from the candle low just above Monday's low area, then price spiked below it.
  - After taking Monday's low, price rallied easily above the relative equal highs, which shows the run on liquidity done.
  - He calls these two or three a week "easy ones", fractal to smaller ranges.
- **Timestamps:**
  - [3:08:27](https://youtu.be/yOZHawAE8QI?t=11307) — highest high/lowest low of last 3 days; each day's high/low.
  - [3:10:03](https://youtu.be/yOZHawAE8QI?t=11403) — Sunday: only the 6 PM opening matters.
  - [3:19:35](https://youtu.be/yOZHawAE8QI?t=11975) — previous day's low as a "honey pot"; lower half → look to PDL.
  - [3:24:22](https://youtu.be/yOZHawAE8QI?t=12262) — why the approach to the low is fast.
- **Nuance / caveats:** ES price levels for this trade are not stated in the transcript. He says he does not trade or teach crypto and has no view on it.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #18  August 27, 2024
head: ES short review: sequence of order flow before the previous-day-low run
body:
- **Kind:** example
- **What ICT says (step by step):**
  1. Price is dropping toward Monday's (8/26) low. Every candle returning to the order block fails to take half, so it is a propulsion block.
  2. An indecisive candle (open equals close) builds a volume imbalance; the next candle comes up and fills the void with no bodies ("patchwork", his term for the algorithm filling inefficiencies).
  3. Price displaces lower. It comes back and digs into the original OB (reclaimed bearish OB), responds immediately, retraces into an FVG, hits it, displaces lower, takes out the low, retraces to match the high of the inefficiency with no willingness to enter, and then breaks lower.
  4. He sells in the lower part of the large down-close candle as the next candle opens and digs into it, then adds in the volume imbalance, expecting the upper half never to trade.
  5. The market "rolls over energetically" and runs just below Monday's low; his fill was one tick from the candle's low.
- **How to use:** The "heaviness" signature is repeated refusal to trade the upper half of arrays on the way down. He said the market was "indicating in every shape, facet or form that it's heavy".
- **Timestamps:**
  - [3:13:10](https://youtu.be/yOZHawAE8QI?t=11590) — OB and the mean-threshold test.
  - [3:14:47](https://youtu.be/yOZHawAE8QI?t=11687) — volume imbalance and patchwork.
  - [3:21:12](https://youtu.be/yOZHawAE8QI?t=12072) — entries and the one-tick-from-low fill.
  - [3:27:37](https://youtu.be/yOZHawAE8QI?t=12457) — rally above relative equal highs after taking the low.
- **Nuance / caveats:** He notes he does not use bull flags/trend line breakouts; he fades them.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #18  August 27, 2024
head: New Day / New Week Opening Gap clusters ("black hole") and shelf life  (aliases: NDOG, NWOG, nested opening gaps)
body:
- **Kind:** rule / refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - When NDOGs and NWOGs are nested or clustered, they act like a gravitational pool that keeps drawing price in, trading back and forth to them over several days. He says it is "not one and done".
  - Do not treat them as stale after one visit. "Keep them" and extend them. Do not do the "old pivots (R1, R2) trace it and throw it away" behavior.
  - Beginner scope: for a month or two, only focus on NDOGs within the last 5 days and NWOGs within the last 5 weeks. He says NDOGs older than that can be used, as he addressed in comments, and he used the Aug 16 NDOG as the NQ short target on Aug 27.
  - A single low can be a three-way confluence: the old NDOG low (Aug 23), the lower quadrant of the NWOG of Aug 18, and the CE of a candle's wick. Price stopped to the tick there and ran higher.
  - Backtest note: log how many candles it took to reach the CE of the NWOG and how much drawdown in handles it had before.
- **How to use:** Draw on liquidity, targets, and confluence for reversals ("the algorithm is going to refer to them").
- **Timestamps:**
  - [1:01:14](https://youtu.be/yOZHawAE8QI?t=3674) — "huge black hole" of nested NDOG/NWOG.
  - [1:25:31](https://youtu.be/yOZHawAE8QI?t=5131) — clustering; don't throw them out when traded to.
  - [1:39:59](https://youtu.be/yOZHawAE8QI?t=5999) — Aug 23 NDOG low + Aug 18 NWOG lower quadrant + wick CE.
  - [2:27:26](https://youtu.be/yOZHawAE8QI?t=8846) — 5 days / 5 weeks beginner rule.
- **Nuance / caveats:** The week-opening gap on "the 18th of August" is a Sunday open (i.e. the NWOG of the week beginning Aug 19); the captions give it as stated.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #18  August 27, 2024
head: IPDA data ranges: 20 / 40 / 60 trading-day look-back
body:
- **Kind:** rule / clarification
- **What ICT says:**
  - His own parameter: PD arrays older than 60 trading days are generally not used. It is 60 trading days, not calendar days (he is correcting a commenter).
  - Sensitivity ranking: a 20-day-old PD array is more sensitive than 40-day-old, which is more sensitive than 60-day-old. If you only focus on arrays formed in the last 20 days you work with the most active ones and never need to complicate it.
  - Arrays never hide; they are always on the chart.
- **Timestamps:**
  - [1:26:19](https://youtu.be/yOZHawAE8QI?t=5179) — 60 days is trading days.
  - [1:27:06](https://youtu.be/yOZHawAE8QI?t=5226) — 60 vs 40 vs 20 sensitivity.
- **Nuance / caveats:** "Depending upon how I feel about market structure and where I think the market may go", so it is a judgment boundary, not a hard rule.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #18  August 27, 2024
head: Lunch macro and the daily flow after the open
body:
- **Kind:** rule / time
- **What ICT says:**
  - In a bullish narrative, little consolidations at the levels he teaches, at the times he teaches, are accumulation. After a run, expect a reasonable retracement to a short-term discount, not a reversal.
  - Keep the narrative until about 11:30-12:00, then the "lunch macro", which is technically 11:30 to 1:30 ET. Expect deeper retracement there, and find the first low prior to where price is trading in the range that forms in the lunch hour.
  - 11:30 is also London close; CFD traders on NQ/ES CFDs typically close up then.
  - Afternoon session follows.
- **Timestamps:**
  - [1:30:18](https://youtu.be/yOZHawAE8QI?t=5418) — lunch macro 11:30-1:30.
  - [1:31:08](https://youtu.be/yOZHawAE8QI?t=5468) — London close at 11:30.
- **Nuance / caveats:** Brief aside only. Other lectures probably give a fuller account.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #18  August 27, 2024
head: Journaling, back-testing and positive self-talk  (aliases: reticular activating system, "romancing your future trading self")
body:
- **Kind:** rule / psychology (see also Process section)
- **What ICT says:**
  - Back-testing is hunting a specific "track" (his deer-print analogy): decide what you are hunting (order blocks, FVGs that invert, breakers, institutional order flow entry drills, OTE, the FVG after 10:00 for turtle-soup style (caption unclear)) and mark up every instance.
  - Annotate old charts in the first person as if you expected it: "it excites me to see these opportunities repeating". Log the number of points moved, how many candles to the target/CE, and the drawdown in handles before it worked.
  - Do not use his charts for your journal; model each one on your own charts and study why each reference point mattered.
- **Timestamps:**
  - [1:37:35](https://youtu.be/yOZHawAE8QI?t=5855) — model it on your own charts.
  - [1:48:46](https://youtu.be/yOZHawAE8QI?t=6526) — what are you hunting.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #19  August 28, 2024
head: Previous days' highs and lows as liquidity / algorithmic reference points  (aliases: old highs/lows, last three days' highs and lows, PD array, draw on liquidity)
body:
- **Kind:** rule / definition
- **What ICT says:** Note the high and low of each of the last three days on your chart. Even if a later day has already traded through the stops above/below one, the algorithm still refers back to that same price. The algorithm does not know how many orders are resting there and does not need to; the reference point is defined by time (the daily interval's highest high / lowest low). Large, deep-pocket institutional participants keep buying/selling interest around those levels, and coded logic assumes resting stops (trailing stops of trend followers sit just under higher lows / over lower highs). So price keeps being drawn back to old levels and market participants can trade the fluctuation right after the level is touched. "One and done" is retail logic.
- **How to identify:** Mark the daily high/low of each of the last ~3 sessions as horizontal lines (he marks them on both charts so the same price shows on the 1m and 15s).
- **How to use:** Use them as draws on liquidity (targets) and as catalysts for turtle soup: e.g. a break above a previous high while bearish is a place to look to short, even on a daily chart for a position trader. Same logic works on daily/weekly/monthly charts; you just wait much longer for it to play out. "If you note the previous days highs and lows you're never going to run out of setups."
- **Example in this video:** NQ on Wed Aug 28: the area around Tuesday's (Aug 27) daily low is the focus. Morning: price sells down into and below Tuesday's low, makes an intraday short-term low, retraces, then dives lower again. Afternoon: after the sell-off to a lower low of the day, price is drawn back up toward Tuesday's low again (the "fishing" target at the end).
- **Timestamps:** [0:08:21](https://youtu.be/i3olkndPmEE?t=501) — why old highs/lows still matter; [0:12:19](https://youtu.be/i3olkndPmEE?t=739) — algorithm only needs the time-based reference; [0:13:56](https://youtu.be/i3olkndPmEE?t=836) — use as DOL, turtle soup catalyst, higher-timeframe use.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** The area just above and just below a previous day low is "rich in order flow" and can be "mined" repeatedly, but only if you know what you are looking for ([0:39:55](https://youtu.be/i3olkndPmEE?t=2395)).

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #19  August 28, 2024
head: Taking partials when targeting a previous day's low  (aliases: partial profits, graduated approach to holding runners)
body:
- **Kind:** rule / refinement
- **What ICT says:** When you are inside the range and reaching down for an old daily low (previous day's low), do not take your partial the first time price pierces it. Let it make a short-term low below the old low, retrace, and dive again; take the partial beneath that low. If you take profit just under the old low you may sell yourself short of a large run, because you cannot know how far the first drop goes. It teaches patience and holding.
- **How to identify:** Distinguish the type of low you are holding for: (a) a previous day's low, vs (b) an intraday low (a low formed inside the range between the day's highest high and lowest low). He says he does not like applying the wait-for-the-second-leg method to intraday lows (caption unclear on exact wording).
- **How to use:** A graduated plan for those who cannot yet hold runners: Stage 1 — if price breaks the same-day low, measure the day's high down to that low and project one quarter (one quadrant) extension below the low; getting out around there is a reasonable first partial ([0:26:09](https://youtu.be/i3olkndPmEE?t=1569), [0:31:03](https://youtu.be/i3olkndPmEE?t=1863)). Stage 2 — wait for price to make the short-term low below the target, then use the dynamic trailed partial (next concept). He says it is fine to simply exit below the low while you are learning, then watch whether the run materialises and grow into the trail.
- **Example in this video:** Price runs down through Tuesday's low, pops back above it with a wick, then dives again; the second leg is where the partial belongs. He also notes the "low of the day" keeps being reset: first low, then a lower one, then the current low of day, and attention shifts to each new one.
- **Timestamps:** [0:17:59](https://youtu.be/i3olkndPmEE?t=1079) — don't partial on first pierce; [0:26:09](https://youtu.be/i3olkndPmEE?t=1569) — range + 1 quadrant extension for same-day low; [0:31:03](https://youtu.be/i3olkndPmEE?t=1863) — stage 1 then stage 2.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** He frames this as "a graduate perspective" so students do not force themselves into holding like he does and feel "like a deer in headlights". The one-quadrant extension references earlier teaching (range from high to low, quadrant projections).

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #19  August 28, 2024
head: Dynamic trailed partial (trail stop on part of the position)  (aliases: dynamic trailing stop, trail buy stop on one contract, runner management)
body:
- **Kind:** entry/exit model (trade management) — new emphasis
- **What ICT says:** Instead of a limit exit at a guessed level, let the market decide your partial. Example: short 2 contracts. After price breaks below the target low and builds a short-term low, every down-closed candle that creates an imbalance gets a buy stop for ONE contract placed just above that candle's high; as lower candles print, lower the stop to the previous candle's high. When it triggers you take that partial and keep the other contract (core position) running. It adds no risk, no extra leverage, and no new position; you are only managing a portion of the size.
- **How to identify / conditions:** Use it only on the 1-minute chart — "never never" on sub-one-minute charts, which are spiky/fuzzy with overlapping candles. Start trailing only after price has broken below the target low and is "spooling" (running). Stop goes above the previous 1m candle's high, ultra tight.
- **How to use:** Works for a partial or for the entire position (e.g. two contracts, trail all of it). Alternative of trailing from larger/structural candle highs gives back too much range intraday; he considers it better for swing trades held over a week (reading slightly uncertain from captions). Accept that you will be stopped out very close to the low; do not berate yourself for exits that are "not good enough". Keep trailing the remainder lower after each new lower low; do not be involved in retracements back into the old low. Averaging matters if you pyramided: your average entry moves as you add, and adding too much early can put you below the waterline (unrealised red) for a while.
- **Example in this video:** On the 1m NQ chart, price breaks Tuesday's low, makes a short-term low, retraces, then drops again; trailing the one-contract buy stop above each successive 1m down-candle high gets stopped out only a candle or two off the swing low. He cites a move quoted as "278 and a half" to "302 and 3/4" (digits of the full NQ price are unclear in the caption), implying a large capture compared with exiting beneath the old low.
- **Timestamps:** [0:20:22](https://youtu.be/i3olkndPmEE?t=1222) — mechanism for 1 of 2 contracts; [0:52:03](https://youtu.be/i3olkndPmEE?t=3123) — 1-minute only, never sub-minute; [0:53:39](https://youtu.be/i3olkndPmEE?t=3219) — ultra tight trail, accept being knocked out near the low; [0:56:50](https://youtu.be/i3olkndPmEE?t=3410) — objective, mechanical, "all you're doing is dropping your stop to the previous candle's high".
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Answers repeated viewer questions about how to take partials and hold runs. He also says the same dynamic trail can be used on the whole trade. His recorded trade videos show stops far from entry because he is "not rushing to strangle the position."

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #19  August 28, 2024
head: Intraday highs/lows tracking and post-session review  (aliases: low/high of day, same-day low, daily range expansion)
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:** Keep track of the highest high and lowest low since the 9:30 open. If bearish, note each successive lower high / lower low as it forms; the current low of day is what you watch (older lows stop being the low of the day). It is a dynamic study of whether the daily range keeps expanding or caps. Study your charts after the close (5:00 PM or later) and list everything that was in play and the catalysts.
- **Timestamps:** [0:33:25](https://youtu.be/i3olkndPmEE?t=2005) — intraday highs/lows since 9:30; [0:34:15](https://youtu.be/i3olkndPmEE?t=2055) — low of day shifts; study after 5 PM.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** He ties this to how price "dives" through each successive low once structure has shifted.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #19  August 28, 2024
head: Contract symbols and rollover (NQ futures)  (aliases: contract expiration, quarterly rollover)
body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:** NQ has four delivery months: March (H), June (M), September (U), December (Z). In Aug 2024 you trade the September 2024 contract; next is December 2024 (Z), then March 2025 (H), June 2025 (M), then the cycle repeats (U, Z). Contracts expire the third Friday of the delivery month; you must then trade the next month out. He expects to be trading September until roughly the first two and a half weeks of September, then the December contract.
- **Timestamps:** [0:28:37](https://youtu.be/i3olkndPmEE?t=1717) — current September contract and TradingView symbols; [0:30:16](https://youtu.be/i3olkndPmEE?t=1816) — expiry third Friday.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #19  August 28, 2024
head: Fake bull/bear flag at relative equal highs  (aliases: stop hunt then consolidation; fake bull flag)
body:
- **Kind:** definition / identification
- **What ICT says:** Relative equal highs followed by a retracement/consolidation that holds above them looks like a bull flag/breakout to the unlearned (trend lines, waiting for a breakout "that never comes"). When the market is predisposed lower, that is a fake bull flag: the stop hunt above the highs followed by time spent there, then displacement down. Taught in the 2016/2017 mentorship (fake bull flags and bear flags).
- **How to identify:** A stop run above equal highs, then price lingers (spends time) inside inefficiencies or above the highs instead of leaving fast. Companion rule: you do not want price to stay in an inefficiency; you want it to spend little time and leave; for a bearish premium array you want the upper half not filled, and ideally not even traded to.
- **Example in this video:** NQ morning: highs relatively equal, price bumps them and spends time, then displaces down, entering several models at once.
- **Timestamps:** [0:35:02](https://youtu.be/i3olkndPmEE?t=2102) — fake bull flag logic; [0:36:40](https://youtu.be/i3olkndPmEE?t=2200) — what the unlearned see.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #19  August 28, 2024
head: Stacking models and pyramiding  (aliases: OTE, 2022 Mentorship model, Silver Bullet, institutional order entry drill)
body:
- **Kind:** refinement
- **What ICT says:** In the same morning drop he points out several valid entries: optimal trade entry on the high-to-low swing (his "flagship pattern" for about 10 years), the 2022 model, a Silver Bullet, and an institutional order entry drill ("lowest hanging fruit"). All are profitable and can be used together: enter on a higher one, and if a lower setup appears you can pyramid and build the position bigger. Pyramiding changes your average price (it moves toward where you're aiming), so size additions carefully; heavy early size can produce drawdown below the waterline.
- **Timestamps:** [0:37:27](https://youtu.be/i3olkndPmEE?t=2247) — OTE, 2022 model, Silver Bullet in the same move; [0:55:15](https://youtu.be/i3olkndPmEE?t=3315) — average price and drawdown when pyramiding.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #19  August 28, 2024
head: Heaviness, speed and distance (grading the price swing)  (aliases: heavy vs light price, acceleration into liquidity, midpoint rule)
body:
- **Kind:** rule / confirmation
- **What ICT says:** Grade how price trades once it breaks a low. If it is lethargic, it may reverse; if it becomes quick and heavy, jump to the next pool of liquidity — a lower low should be "not even a speedbump". Heavy (bearish) = a series of candles making lower highs, struggling to make higher candle highs; light price climbs easily toward premium. Before the target low, expect acceleration: the magnitude of the move should increase as price approaches the old low, to "get to it and through it" and drive past it, not stall and consolidate. He annotates "speed and distance" / large down-closed candles in his executions.
- **How to identify / rule of thumb:** Take the range from the high to the low you are targeting; once price trades below the 50% point of that range it should move fast, each candle lower than the previous. He admits there is no fixed number of points (an example was about 25 handles on NQ) — it is relative to the range and a "knack" thing.
- **How to use:** Be patient and hold; long stops sit under the lows and the stubborn ones will be wiped when price accelerates through. Retail often thinks the first drop is the low and will do harmonic/ratio trades there and exit badly.
- **Timestamps:** [0:40:44](https://youtu.be/i3olkndPmEE?t=2444) — grading speed and acceleration into lows; [0:46:23](https://youtu.be/i3olkndPmEE?t=2783) — halfway-point rule; [0:48:03](https://youtu.be/i3olkndPmEE?t=2883) — heavy vs light.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** "We're not trading support and resistance — we're attacking people that use support and resistance for their liquidity." Narrative blends time of day, day of week, week, and monthly chart ([0:49:40](https://youtu.be/i3olkndPmEE?t=2980)).

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #19  August 28, 2024
head: Breakaway gap  (aliases: breakaway FVG)
body:
- **Kind:** definition / refinement
- **What ICT says:** A breakaway gap forms from a consolidation, at the start of the first or second stage of distribution or reaccumulation (market maker sell model: smart money reversal, low-risk sell, area of redistribution). A gap left behind by the run through the first low after a shift in structure that stays open signals that price will go much lower and fast, so "don't be in a rush to get out". It can be closed and price can still drop, but unfilled is better — "a cherry on top", a hallmark, not a requirement.
- **Example in this video:** (1) After the shift in structure, price breaks the post-MSS low and leaves a small gap that remains open; the drop continues lower highs ("heaviness"). (2) The 9:31-10:00 first FVG left open (partly) as the sell-off proceeds. (3) At the 2:50 macro on the 15s chart, an inefficiency formed by a candle's high and a later low acts as a breakaway gap for the rally.
- **Timestamps:** [0:43:58](https://youtu.be/i3olkndPmEE?t=2638) — definition and market maker sell model; [1:15:23](https://youtu.be/i3olkndPmEE?t=4523) — breakaway gap after first-presentation FVG; [1:22:50](https://youtu.be/i3olkndPmEE?t=4970) — 15s version at 2:50.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #19  August 28, 2024
head: Opening range gap (RTH opening gap, ORG)  (aliases: opening range gap, RTH gap, premium/discount gap)
body:
- **Kind:** definition / rule
- **What ICT says:** In regular trading hours view, the ORG is the space between the previous day's RTH settlement (the 4:14/4:15 PM ET close shown on the chart) and the 9:30 AM opening price. If the open is lower than the settle it is a discount gap (he colours it blue; premium gap would be the opposite). He expects price to retrace at least half of the gap within the first 30 minutes of trading, with a roughly 70% chance. Annotate it by drawing a rectangle from the opening price to the settlement price. For a discount gap, the expectation is buy-side delivery (rally) back toward the settle price; minimum 50% in 30 minutes.
- **How to identify:** Toggle RTH on; the 9:30 candle gaps from the prior 4:14 candle. In electronic (24-hour) trading that 9:30 candle has no gap, so the gap does not exist there.
- **How to use:** Treat the ORG's low (the 9:30 opening price) as a magnet/reference. In this video the ORG low coincided with NDOG levels and acted as the target for a sell-off after price ran up to the first FVG.
- **Example in this video:** Wed Aug 28: opens below the 4:14 PM Tuesday settlement (discount gap). Price rallies to take half the gap and the full gap (also overlapping the 6 PM NDOG's two-tick gap), sweeps buy-side, then reverses.
- **Timestamps:** [1:00:07](https://youtu.be/i3olkndPmEE?t=3607) — ORG is not an FVG; [1:06:30](https://youtu.be/i3olkndPmEE?t=3990) — RTH view, 4:14 settle vs 9:30 open; [1:07:21](https://youtu.be/i3olkndPmEE?t=4041) — 70% chance half in 30 minutes.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** He is re-teaching because students rushed. The new day opening gap (6:00 PM ET open vs 5:00 PM close) here was only about two ticks, overlapping half of the ORG.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #19  August 28, 2024
head: First presentation of a fair value gap between 9:30 and 10:00  (aliases: first FVG, first presented FVG, 9:31-10:00 FVG)
body:
- **Kind:** rule / entry model
- **What ICT says:** The 9:30 candle cannot be counted as part of an FVG because it is the opening range gap candle. The earliest a legitimate FVG can form is with the 9:31 candle as the imbalance (middle) candle, confirmed after 9:32. Look for the first FVG formed after 9:30; the 9:30-based gap is not it. Once found, price returning into it and rejecting it (not closing above the upper half of a bearish FVG) is a high-quality entry; place the stop one tick above the high of the wicking candle (high plus one tick). He says if a trade is missed you can short a return into the inversion FVG using the same stop idea.
- **How to identify:** Step through 1m candles from 9:31: a candle that overlaps the previous candle's low (for a bearish FVG) is not a gap; the first true three-candle gap defines it. Count candles carefully (caption unclear on exactly which candle he calls the "third").
- **How to use:** Narrative: liquidity taken (Judas swing), a shift in structure, then a return up into the first FVG; short from there targeting lower levels. Should not close the upper half. Better if the gap left behind by the displacement stays open (breakaway gap).
- **Example in this video:** NQ 1m Aug 28: no FVG until 9:35. At about 9:35 price runs the minor BSL (relative equal highs) in a Judas swing and the first FVG forms on the 9:35 candle. Price breaks down under the 8:15 inversion FVG, then wicks back up into the first-presentation FVG and the bottom of the ORG, closes without taking the upper half, then sells hard to Tuesday's low and below the Aug 16 and Aug 27 NDOGs.
- **Timestamps:** [1:00:54](https://youtu.be/i3olkndPmEE?t=3654) — earliest possible FVG is 9:31; [1:03:20](https://youtu.be/i3olkndPmEE?t=3800) — the day's first FVG forms at 9:35; [1:12:07](https://youtu.be/i3olkndPmEE?t=4327) — check it does not close the upper half; [1:14:34](https://youtu.be/i3olkndPmEE?t=4474) — keep screenshots; first FVG used and hammered.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** He stresses this was in response to many comments and that it is not new. Journaling many examples is the route to seeing it live.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #19  August 28, 2024
head: Inversion fair value gap (iFVG) with minor buy-side liquidity  (aliases: IFVG, inversion FVG, reclaimed FVG (caption unclear))
body:
- **Kind:** example / refinement
- **What ICT says:** Before the open (shared in Tanya Trades' live chat with time stamps), he flagged the 8:15 candle as an inversion FVG and a minor buy-side liquidity pool at the relative equal highs. Price rallied from the iFVG, hit the BSL ("if you had something there and partialed off you have a free look"). Later, when price broke lower beneath the 8:15 iFVG, that gap flips and should be used as resistance; the original bullish FVG reading is "not the right time to take that trade". Not buying it just because it looks like a bullish gap: wait for it to trade below and see whether the first FVG shuts off higher prices.
- **How to use:** Once price trades down through the gap, selling a return into its midpoint/inside it works; stop above its high (plus a tick). He wants it to trade into the iFVG and fail.
- **Timestamps:** [0:58:28](https://youtu.be/i3olkndPmEE?t=3508) — 8:15 iFVG and minor BSL; [1:04:08](https://youtu.be/i3olkndPmEE?t=3848) — not trying to buy it, waiting; [1:09:43](https://youtu.be/i3olkndPmEE?t=4183) — original bullish vs inverted role.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Re-teaching the basic idea of inversion: a gap whose function flips after being traded through.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #19  August 28, 2024
head: 2:50 PM macro and 15-second chart delivery  (aliases: 2:50 algorithm, macro, volume imbalance, CISD, order block mean threshold, institutional order entry drill)
body:
- **Kind:** example / refinement
- **What ICT says:** The 2:50 macro runs until 3:10 PM. At its start price needs to be delivering. On the 15s chart he reads: a down-closed candle's order block (mean threshold is the most sensitive point; price should not trade far below it); a close above the open of a down-closed candle = change in state of delivery (CISD); a volume imbalance on the 15s is all the algorithm needs to begin a rally; delivery cycles through lower timeframes seeking any FVG or volume imbalance. With no FVG and no swing low left (the sell-side stops already taken), price rallies into the nearest inefficiency. Institutional order entry drill: price trades into a gap formed by a candle's high, leaving the maximum range open, then runs — that signals a breakaway gap. At 2:50 on the dot price rallies into the low of an inefficiency, stalls and consolidates (accumulation), rallies to its consequent encroachment, stops just short, retests the volume imbalance, then trades through the high end. A bullish order block: only the wick should enter the upper half; bodies hold. Then price should pierce the volume imbalance on the 1m chart quickly.
- **How to use:** Manage the dealing range properly (the day's high to low); do not just say "it goes to Tuesday's low". Target (Terminus) for the move was Tuesday's low, with an intermediate target as a partial.
- **Example in this video:** NQ afternoon: 15s and 1m show price rallying from the 2:50 candle through successive inefficiencies, respecting the 50% of wicks, order block upper half, to just short of Tuesday's low, which it then tags.
- **Timestamps:** [1:18:47](https://youtu.be/i3olkndPmEE?t=4727) — inside the 2:50 algorithm; [1:21:13](https://youtu.be/i3olkndPmEE?t=4873) — mean threshold / volume imbalance; [1:23:40](https://youtu.be/i3olkndPmEE?t=5020) — institutional order entry drill and ride; [1:26:07](https://youtu.be/i3olkndPmEE?t=5167) — order block upper half and delivery.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** "Terminus" = the target/end of the run (as he uses it). Fishing analogy: casting at the 2:50 candle with the previous day low as the target, line spooling = the run ([1:27:46](https://youtu.be/i3olkndPmEE?t=5266)).

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #20  August 29, 2024
head: Re-entering after being stopped out of a winning trade  (aliases: trail-stop re-entry, getting back in)
body:
- **Kind:** rule / example
- **What ICT says:** If you trail your stop and get stopped out with a profit, the trade idea may still be valid; you can go back in at the next valid PD array. He demonstrates his own trade from the early morning (shown on a live account, replayed with labels).
- **How to use:** In the example he was short from a bearish order block / breaker, added on a wick back up into the area, took a small partial on a sell-side liquidity run, got stopped when he brought the stop down "aggressively", then re-sold a return into the inversion FVG and added more once he knew he was "on side". He says tightening the stop that fast "would never be done" if you understand the market maker sell model: you must let the second stage of redistribution deliver before trailing hard. Later he was stopped out on a trail while away from the screen and price reached Tuesday's low (the draw on liquidity of the MMSM).
- **Example in this video:** Overnight NQ opened Wed 6 PM with a huge gap, rallied to Tuesday's daily low area, formed a consolidation of relative equal lows, rallied, then took out relative equal highs (turtle soup/smart money reversal). He faded that high: the entry was off a bearish order block (a small breaker within a larger one), then later the iFVG. Final target Tuesday's (Aug 27) low.
- **Timestamps:** [0:05:12](https://youtu.be/NMCy1H2_Wr8?t=312) — question of how to re-enter after being stopped out; [0:08:27](https://youtu.be/NMCy1H2_Wr8?t=507) — order block / breaker entry; [0:10:01](https://youtu.be/NMCy1H2_Wr8?t=601) — stop tightened too quickly, MMSM second stage; [0:11:39](https://youtu.be/NMCy1H2_Wr8?t=699) — Tuesday's low reached.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Contrasts with his own tendency; he does it live-account style as a lesson; an explicit re-statement that the MMSM second redistribution stage should not be stopped out of early.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #20  August 29, 2024
head: Bearish order block and CISD as he defines them  (aliases: change in the state of delivery, order block, breaker)
body:
- **Kind:** definition / refinement
- **What ICT says:** A bearish order block is built from a run of consecutive up-closed candles; the change in the state of delivery (CISD) is the opening price of the lowest-opening candle in that run of up-closed candles (when price trades below it). In the example two adjacent candles together form the bearish order block. He says not every up-closed candle is a bearish order block and not every three-candle pattern with a gap-like separation is an FVG — he is correcting people who mis-call these.
- **Example in this video:** The early-morning rally of up-closed candles into the high; he waited for the change in state of delivery (price trading down through the lowest open of the up candles) before selling, and noted a smaller breaker inside the larger one.
- **Timestamps:** [0:08:27](https://youtu.be/NMCy1H2_Wr8?t=507) — definition and mis-calls; [0:11:39](https://youtu.be/NMCy1H2_Wr8?t=699) — "every up-closed candle is not an OB, not every candle separation is an FVG".

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #20  August 29, 2024
head: Grading an inefficiency / price swing (quadrants)  (aliases: quarters theory (he rejects the name), fib quadrants)
body:
- **Kind:** definition / refinement
- **What ICT says:** Do not call it "quarterly/quarters theory"; it is called grading an inefficiency or grading a price swing. Put a fib on the gap/swing and use the quadrants (quarter levels). Taught in the 2017 mentorship core content and subsequent lectures. Applied here to the huge 6 PM gap and the prior afternoon's FVG, whose extension projected the next target.
- **Example in this video:** The 6 PM gap opened Wed evening was graded in quadrants and price rallied to the top of it; the FVG outlined the day before in the afternoon session was extended forward and reached.
- **Timestamps:** [0:06:49](https://youtu.be/NMCy1H2_Wr8?t=409) — name and use.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #20  August 29, 2024
head: Opening range gap (premium gap) and "too expensive" — not chasing  (aliases: ORG, RTH gap, premium gap, don't chase)
body:
- **Kind:** rule / application
- **What ICT says:** NQ opened Thursday with a large gap above the previous settlement (premium opening range gap) and ran straight up for the first minutes without any retracement. When price is "really, really elevated" from the ORG low (the previous settlement), it is expensive: he elects to look for shorts rather than chase longs. The gap can stay open all day, but eventually price tends to trade back to it, giving a better discount. Do not try to catch a run just because it is running ("mass transit": if you miss the bus, wait 20 minutes for the next one, like another macro). If price takes off and you are not already positioned, sit on your hands and let it come back for a low-risk entry (he referenced a Tuesday two weeks earlier).
- **How to use:** Halfway of the ORG is marked as a reference; the ORG low is the prior settle.
- **Example in this video:** NQ Aug 29: opens with a huge premium gap, runs to the Aug 27 NDOG and the Aug 18 NWOG area and through them in about two 1m candles, toward quadruple-high buy-side at 19,694.25. He does not buy; plan is short on the first valid presentation if it breaks down.
- **Timestamps:** [0:18:34](https://youtu.be/NMCy1H2_Wr8?t=1114) — don't chase, let it come back; [0:19:22](https://youtu.be/NMCy1H2_Wr8?t=1162) — bus analogy; [0:29:05](https://youtu.be/NMCy1H2_Wr8?t=1745) — very expensive vs ORG low, ORG may stay open all day.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Continuation of the ORG discussion from lecture 19, now with a premium gap instead of a discount gap.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #20  August 29, 2024
head: First-presentation FVG after the open (continued)  (aliases: first presented FVG, 9:31 FVG)
body:
- **Kind:** refinement / example
- **What ICT says:** No FVG is valid until after the open; the first one can form on the 9:31 candle. The preferred picture for a short here: price runs up into the lower half of the layered premium array (opening gaps) without reaching the midpoint, leaving the upper half untouched, then trades into the first-presented FVG. Once the sell-off works from the lower half, drop to a 15-second chart and use a 15s FVG to ride into the first-presented 1m FVG. If price instead pushes beyond the lower half the setup is less clean.
- **Timestamps:** [0:13:25](https://youtu.be/NMCy1H2_Wr8?t=805) — no first presentation yet; [0:14:31](https://youtu.be/NMCy1H2_Wr8?t=871) — forms on the 9:31 candle; [0:23:33](https://youtu.be/NMCy1H2_Wr8?t=1413) — lower half vs midpoint; [0:28:09](https://youtu.be/NMCy1H2_Wr8?t=1689) — 15s FVG to drop into the first-presented FVG.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** He draws the FVG range for teaching only; in real trading he would just use the lowest low of the range. He also says his TradingView magnet is set to "strong but not strongest" so drawings snap to OHLC.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #20  August 29, 2024
head: Layered NDOG/NWOG levels as a high-resistance liquidity run  (aliases: high resistance liquidity run, spider web, opening gaps layered)
body:
- **Kind:** definition / rule
- **What ICT says:** When many new day and new week opening gaps (here the Aug 27 NDOG, the Aug 23 gap he had called a huge magnet / "black hole", and the Aug 18 NWOG) are stacked around price, a run through them is held back "like a cobweb tangled around its legs". It is not an absence of buying/selling pressure; the algorithm references all those levels and offers back-and-forth price. If price blasts through them in one or two candles it should have no problem reaching the target; if it keeps petering out above them it is a high-resistance run. Traders who do not plot these gaps never notice why. A strong "fly" can still escape the web and run to "the sugar" (the buy-side).
- **How to identify:** Plot NWOG/NDOG levels; look for price stalling and chopping between them instead of expanding.
- **How to use:** If price drives through them fast it implies the buy-side at 19,694 gets targeted and then likely a puke-out and drop into the ORG; if it chops, stay out. Judge strength above the high: does it accelerate through the new week opening gap high and keep a bullish body without wicks retracing?
- **Example in this video:** NQ Aug 29 morning: runs through the gap levels within two candles, gets close to the 19,694 quadruple high and peters out (twice), then hangs around inside the gap cluster for most of the session.
- **Timestamps:** [0:13:25](https://youtu.be/NMCy1H2_Wr8?t=805) — NDOG Aug 27 and NWOG above; [0:30:41](https://youtu.be/NMCy1H2_Wr8?t=1841) — aggressively slicing through them implies a run to buy-side; [1:49:05](https://youtu.be/NMCy1H2_Wr8?t=6545) — high-resistance explanation; [1:52:16](https://youtu.be/NMCy1H2_Wr8?t=6736) — spider web analogy.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** He explains that the paid mentorship streams were built on identifying high- vs low-resistance liquidity run signatures day by day.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #20  August 29, 2024
head: High vs low resistance liquidity runs and when a market is tradable  (aliases: low-resistance conditions, 50/50 market)
body:
- **Kind:** rule / filter
- **What ICT says:** A low-resistance run is easy, one-sided, gives immediate positive feedback; analysis is not conflicted. If the market can be framed both ways, it is 50/50, not high probability, and not worth putting money behind; just study it ("tape it") with no weight on the outcome. If you must be 100% nimble with zero forgiveness for being wrong on either side, that is a high-probability losing day. When references conflict and "it could be this or that," accept it is not time to trade. If the first FVG has not even been traded to and nothing qualifies, close the charts and review that night.
- **How to use:** Frame the scenario in both directions; if both are plausible, skip. Sitting out is a "position that wins every single time" and you never lose money sitting still. If price later does the bullish thing, sitting still was still the right call, not a regret.
- **Example in this video:** NQ stayed below the 19,694 high for most of the session, chopping around the layered gaps: one side said run to 19,694, the other said drop into the first presentation. He wrote it off as 50/50 and said a student following his criteria would be flat.
- **Timestamps:** [0:52:22](https://youtu.be/NMCy1H2_Wr8?t=3142) — framing both directions = low probability; [1:02:52](https://youtu.be/NMCy1H2_Wr8?t=3772) — conflicting references, sit out; [1:05:45](https://youtu.be/NMCy1H2_Wr8?t=3945) — the student would be flat; [1:13:12](https://youtu.be/NMCy1H2_Wr8?t=4392) — sitting still always wins; [1:17:38](https://youtu.be/NMCy1H2_Wr8?t=4658) — high vs low resistance framework.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** This is a restatement of the "high resistance / low resistance liquidity run" ideas from earlier lectures, now applied as a participation filter. He also says rule-less trading is gambling.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #20  August 29, 2024
head: SMT divergence (NQ vs ES)  (aliases: smart money tool/technique, SMT)
body:
- **Kind:** example / refinement
- **What ICT says:** NQ made a higher high that ES did not (ES failed to make the comparable high around the same relative level), so continuation likelihood wanes. It does not mean a top; it only lowers the odds of continuation. If price then technically breaks down you have "the best of the best." He admits he never settled what the T stands for (smart money technique/tool) and uses it interchangeably.
- **Timestamps:** [0:33:57](https://youtu.be/NMCy1H2_Wr8?t=2037) — NQ vs ES highs; [0:34:47](https://youtu.be/NMCy1H2_Wr8?t=2087) — not a top signal alone.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #20  August 29, 2024
head: Trend line phantoms / retail diagonal support  (aliases: connected dots, diagonal trendlines)
body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:** He does not use diagonal trend lines, but looks for places where retail would draw perfect diagonal support under a series of lows, because such lines are fakeable: "trend line phantoms" (2017 core content). Best used when other tools already suggest an easy run lower/higher. Retail looks for connected dots, not inefficiencies or liquidity; banks do not trade connected dots.
- **Example in this video:** The lows of the 1m candles during the morning consolidation formed a clean diagonal; price then broke down through them toward the sell-side and first presentation FVG.
- **Timestamps:** [0:58:36](https://youtu.be/NMCy1H2_Wr8?t=3516) — diagonal support candidate; [0:59:27](https://youtu.be/NMCy1H2_Wr8?t=3567) — phantoms lesson; [1:00:14](https://youtu.be/NMCy1H2_Wr8?t=3614) — gave up the ghost.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #20  August 29, 2024
head: Partials, covering costs and 5:1 gearing  (aliases: first partial, move stop to cover costs, risk to reward 1:5, trade management)
body:
- **Kind:** rule / trade management
- **What ICT says:** Partials are always profit: no partial has ever lost money. Know your first partial before entering. When price has moved halfway to the first partial, move the stop to cover commissions (not just break even, since commission means true break even is above entry) and sit still. Place the first partial at the short-term high that forms at a logical premium level. Because a partial is realised profit, it "scratches the itch" to move a stop prematurely. Aim for roughly 5:1 gearing (risk 1 to make 5): then you can be wrong a lot — at about a 38% win rate (he says he thinks it is 38%) you still make money. Move stops as the position moves your way. Do not overleverage (e.g. 15 contracts on a Topstep-style account is the wrong answer; reduce size so the risk is measured).
- **How to use:** Entry on the first bullish FVG model (devil's advocate long in the video): fill around ...588 (digits prefix unclear), stop under the imbalance (middle) candle's low minus one tick (or first candle's low minus one tick if conservative); he prefers the imbalance candle to keep risk manageable. His arithmetic: entry about 588, stop about 570.5, so risk about 18 handles; with five micro NQ contracts and a first partial 60–100 handles away, that is roughly 5:1. First partial at the high end of the inefficiency above (an FVG formed by a down-closed candle), second partial higher if affordable.
- **Example in this video:** After price dropped into the entry FVG and rallied, the high end of the upper inefficiency (an FVG made by a down-closed candle) was his first partial, because lower levels were too close to partial at and the move could fail; later he watched the consequent encroachment of the premium wick near 19,694.5 (price then traded one tick above it; caption unclear).
- **Timestamps:** [1:20:04](https://youtu.be/NMCy1H2_Wr8?t=4804) — partials are always profit; [1:26:34](https://youtu.be/NMCy1H2_Wr8?t=5194) — first partial at FVG high; [1:39:29](https://youtu.be/NMCy1H2_Wr8?t=5969) — entry/stop math; [1:41:04](https://youtu.be/NMCy1H2_Wr8?t=6064) — 5:1 gearing, win rate; [1:42:42](https://youtu.be/NMCy1H2_Wr8?t=6162) — cover costs after halfway to first partial.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Contradicts the "stop or target" mindset (all-or-nothing). Slippage can still hurt if a big news gap runs over your stop.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #20  August 29, 2024
head: Cutting a fizzling trade in half  (aliases: scale out when trade quality fades)
body:
- **Kind:** rule / psychology
- **What ICT says:** If the technicals that justified the trade fade, take half off immediately if you have a profit (or close the whole position if it is one contract), even if commissions are a "hundred bucks". As a developing trader this reduces anxiety, then tape-read the remainder. You are in control of your actions; nobody sucked you in. If you feel anxious while only tape reading with no trade on, that signals harsh self-criticism.
- **Timestamps:** [1:20:55](https://youtu.be/NMCy1H2_Wr8?t=4855) — trade fizzles, cut in half; [1:21:42](https://youtu.be/NMCy1H2_Wr8?t=4902) — close it if one contract; [1:24:05](https://youtu.be/NMCy1H2_Wr8?t=5045) — anxiety while tape reading.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Lecture #20  August 29, 2024
head: Institutional order entry drill and breakaway gap, restated  (aliases: institutional orderflow entry)
body:
- **Kind:** refinement
- **What ICT says:** In the afternoon-of-this-session example, a gap forms; price trades to the high of one candle and the low of another (into the gap) but leaves it open, "too strong for entry": that is the entry drill, and the unfilled gap is a breakaway gap. For a bullish scenario, the entry is on that candle; a stop beneath the imbalance candle's low. Without the gap closing fully, momentum continues.
- **Timestamps:** [1:09:57](https://youtu.be/NMCy1H2_Wr8?t=4197) — devil's advocate scenario; [1:37:49](https://youtu.be/NMCy1H2_Wr8?t=5869) — gap left open; [1:50:39](https://youtu.be/NMCy1H2_Wr8?t=6639) — inefficiency as institutional order flow.

head: PD arrays all have inversion aspects  (aliases: inversion of PD arrays, 81 PD arrays)
body:
- **Kind:** new coinage / refinement
- **What ICT says:** Each PD array has its own inversion aspect (e.g. a breaker, an inversion FVG); people who say "81 PD arrays but half are just bullish/bearish versions" are wrong: the individual PD arrays themselves invert, so it is "double the 81".
- **Example in this video:** Price traded above a breaker, accumulated at the top of it (a new FVG formed there), and he said that FVG could be treated as a breakaway gap / entry drill setup if bullish.
