title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Tape Reading \ September 25, 2024
head: First presented FVG — exclude the 9:30 candle  (aliases ICT uses: first presented fair value gap, "not on the 9:30 candle", "institutional order flow entry drill")
body:
- **Kind:** rule / refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - The first presented FVG of the day on the 1-minute chart cannot be built with the 9:30 candle ("you can't count this one — that's the 9:30 candle"). Starting with the 9:31 candle you can have the first presented FVG. Today the first one formed on the 9:33 candle (1m).
  - If you are aggressive, comfortable with sub-1-minute charts and have a bias, you can use the first FVG outside the 9:30 one-minute candle on the 15-second chart (the 15s FVG starting from the 9:31 candle).
  - He does not discard an FVG that exists in the 9:30 candle entirely; he simply prefers the first one outside it as the one he uses for setups.
  - Do not confuse yesterday's first presented FVG (gray box carried over) with today's.
  - A gap that does not qualify as "first presented" is still an FVG and must be considered; but the first presented one is the one used for a signal/setup for his son Caleb (who can take the long and later add).
  - He removed his "new day opening gap studies" from the chart because their information was no different from that of the first presented FVG, keeping the chart cleaner.
  - The "institutional order flow entry drill" (written "institutional order entry drill" in captions) is a partial entry into an FVG when there are relative equal highs with buy-side liquidity just above it — "easy gravy train". It never works on market replay in the same way (his remark).
- **How to identify:** 1m chart: no use of 9:30 candle; 9:31 onward; first gap formed after that.
- **How to use:** frame the day's intraday bias and entries (bullish inversion scenario below).
- **Example in this video:** Sept 25: 9:30 candle area had a small gap (the 15s chart showed an FVG within 9:30); the first presented FVG formed on the 9:33 1m candle and overlapped the "new day opening gap" levels.
- **Timestamps:** [0:04:56](https://youtu.be/NDwNIqUkASc?t=296) can't count the 9:30 candle, don't confuse with yesterday's gray box · [0:05:49](https://youtu.be/NDwNIqUkASc?t=349) 15s version for aggressive traders · [0:13:07](https://youtu.be/NDwNIqUkASc?t=787) the 9:30 gap isn't discarded but not used · [0:21:03](https://youtu.be/NDwNIqUkASc?t=1263) removing NDOG studies · [0:27:25](https://youtu.be/NDwNIqUkASc?t=1645) institutional entry drill
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** clarifies the rule from M24-031/032 (9:31 candle or later) — here explicitly "outside of the 9:30 candle".

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Tape Reading \ September 25, 2024
head: First-FVG bullish inversion-FVG setup and its signature  (aliases ICT uses: treat it as inversion, "leaves the lower half untouched", upper quadrant)
body:
- **Kind:** entry model / refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - Bullish plan: let price trade down into the first presented FVG, then rally ABOVE it, then come back down into it; at that point treat the gap as an inversion FVG (support). If price instead breaks below it and fails to hold, the same gap becomes a short-side iFVG for trading lower (he stays with the higher-time-frame long bias).
  - The ideal signature: on the first dive into it as an inversion, price trades down to the lower quadrant but leaves the lowest portion (lower half / lowest part) untouched, and bodies stay in the upper half (from the CE to the top of the gap). He calls this "the signature that the algorithm is absolutely going to send it higher".
  - Do not want price camping inside the inefficiency making many candles. If the market is delivered into an inefficiency, it is only there for a moment (smart money expects the drop to onboard new longs).
  - After going above the first FVG, he wants an energetic move through the midpoint (CE) of the candle's wick and a drive straight toward the target level.
  - He enters by looking for a small 1-minute inefficiency (volume imbalance) near yesterday's first presented FVG when price trades down into it — retail sees such areas as support.
- **How to identify:** first FVG marked; price leaves it, returns, shows lower portion untouched with bodies in upper half.
- **How to use:** long entry from the retest; target relative equal highs / old daily high; scale out early (see terminus).
- **Example in this video:** NQ Sept 25: price traded down into the 9:30 area FVG, worked back up toward the top of the first presented FVG (9:33 candle), rallied above it, then on the retest dove into the lower quadrant, left the lowest portion open and sent price higher; the narrative target was the equal highs (about 20,214.75, caption-derived).
- **Timestamps:** [0:14:27](https://youtu.be/NDwNIqUkASc?t=867) bullish → inversion; bearish alt → below it · [0:19:28](https://youtu.be/NDwNIqUkASc?t=1168) want energy through the wick CE to the target · [0:32:12](https://youtu.be/NDwNIqUkASc?t=1932) process of thinking: trade above it, treat as inversion · [0:46:46](https://youtu.be/NDwNIqUkASc?t=2806) lower portion untouched = signature · [0:47:35](https://youtu.be/NDwNIqUkASc?t=2855) bodies in the upper half
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** relates to M24-031's iFVG. The quoted prices around 0:47:35 are garbled in the caption.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Tape Reading \ September 25, 2024
head: Wick midpoint (CE) at old highs — intel, partials and targets  (aliases ICT uses: mid-wick, premium CE of the wick, scale out early)
body:
- **Kind:** rule / refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - At old highs and turning points, look inside the wicks and go to the midpoint of the wick; you often get intelligence you would not otherwise notice. Price traded right to the CE of a wick at the old highs.
  - For targets: if a buy-side run targets a level (e.g. about 20,214.75) and there is a wick just below it, the wick midpoint is a partial for him — he starts scaling out as price enters the mid-wick, then waits for the rest.
  - When reaching for a premium level above, always exit ahead of it and scale something out early; price can fall short by a little (it did here).
  - Every turning point/consolidation: look for inefficiencies (an FVG or a wick); a long wick gives price a "foothold/handhold" at its midpoint; they are not the strongest.
- **How to identify:** long wick above an old high or below a low; midpoint of the wick.
- **How to use:** partials at wick CE; do not rely on exact fill of target.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 15s/1m: price took the wick CE at the highs and was still short of the 20,214.75 level.
- **Timestamps:** [0:10:27](https://youtu.be/NDwNIqUkASc?t=627) go to the midpoint of wicks at old highs · [0:11:16](https://youtu.be/NDwNIqUkASc?t=676) wick CE as partial · [0:12:12](https://youtu.be/NDwNIqUkASc?t=732) fell short, exit ahead of the premium level · [0:21:52](https://youtu.be/NDwNIqUkASc?t=1312) wicks as foothold
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** expands the "CE of a wick" idea from M24-032.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Tape Reading \ September 25, 2024
head: Hierarchy of PD-array rigidity: volume imbalance < wick < order block  (aliases ICT uses: volume imbalance (weakest), foothold, mean threshold)
body:
- **Kind:** refinement / definition
- **What ICT says:**
  - A volume imbalance (separation between two candle bodies) is the weakest/most flexible PD array — "weakest" in that price moves back and forth through it easily; it can be an entry model but you must be flexible about it. Students often expect them to be rigid and are disappointed.
  - Wick midpoints are footholds (not the strongest).
  - A down-closed candle is a bullish order block; it is best seen with price touching the opening price down to the mean threshold (the middle of the candle), with no body of a later candle trading lower than the mean threshold; ideally price just touches the opening price and then goes higher — "a perfect delivery of a bullish order block".
  - He uses volume imbalances while already in a working trade (confidence to hold, especially a large position), not as a rigid reason to enter.
  - "The wicks do the damage; bodies supporting the volume imbalance is fine."
  - Flexibility is key; characteristics vary by PD array.
- **How to identify:** body-to-body gap = volume imbalance; wick = candle shadow; order block = last down-closed candle before up move.
- **How to use:** adjust stop/expectation by array: tight for OB, flexible for VI.
- **Example in this video:** price traded down into the first FVG's CE, back up, then back down into a volume imbalance with bodies supporting; rallied to the relative equal highs — "that could be your setup".
- **Timestamps:** [0:21:52](https://youtu.be/NDwNIqUkASc?t=1312) volume imbalance is the weakest / most flexible · [0:23:26](https://youtu.be/NDwNIqUkASc?t=1406) bullish OB: open to mean threshold · [0:24:13](https://youtu.be/NDwNIqUkASc?t=1453) don't expect rigidity · [0:24:59](https://youtu.be/NDwNIqUkASc?t=1499) bodies support the VI, wicks do the damage
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** the "mean threshold = middle of candle" is as heard in captions; he gives no further numeric definition here.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Tape Reading \ September 25, 2024
head: Terminus and scaling out  (aliases ICT uses: Terminus, final target, partials, exit strategy)
body:
- **Kind:** new coinage / rule
- **What ICT says:** "Terminus" is where you think price ultimately goes — your final target, where nothing is left on the position, even if partials were taken along the way. Have an exit strategy before the terminus; without one emotions take over and a trade that would have been profitable gets lost. Taking partials as you approach the target is "always sound logic". Any remaining portion should have a stop below the structure (where price shouldn't go unless the idea is wrong).
- **How to use:** set partial exits before reaching the terminus; fully close at the terminus.
- **Example in this video:** terminus for the trade was the relative equal highs at about 20,214.75 (Tuesday noon-hour relative equal highs), not the August 22 high, because he had an appointment and could not guarantee the market would travel that far; if price reaches the Aug 22 high or higher it is a "moral victory" not something to hold for.
- **Timestamps:** [0:29:50](https://youtu.be/NDwNIqUkASc?t=1790) long: start distributing as price engages the Aug 22 high · [0:33:49](https://youtu.be/NDwNIqUkASc?t=2029) exit strategy before the terminus · [0:34:36](https://youtu.be/NDwNIqUkASc?t=2076) terminus for this trade
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** the term appears in the canonical list of ICT's model names; here it is the final-target concept.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Tape Reading \ September 25, 2024
head: Higher-timeframe draw and leverage side  (aliases ICT uses: draw on liquidity, higher-time-frame draw, "by program", not picking the top)
body:
- **Kind:** rule / bias
- **What ICT says:**
  - His interest remains the August 22, 2024 daily high (old daily high with BSL above) and smooth highs / relative equal highs left in place the night before (the "24.75/14.75 level", about 20,214.75, caption unclear). If price goes above the relative equal highs and rejects, that sets the stage for a run into the Aug 22 high; he is "not trying to pick the top in NASDAQ".
  - He cites an election year as a reason the higher-time-frame stays bullish (opinion; he says there is an incentive to keep the stock market looking up).
  - If the higher-time-frame is bullish, sticking to intraday longs is most appropriate; if you use the largest leverage, trade the side of the higher-time-frame draw — it theoretically lowers the chance of an over-leveraged trade on the wrong side (not 100%).
  - The initial run at the open was "not a Judas swing; it's just trying to get somewhere" (the smooth highs).
  - He will be wrong eventually; it is acceptable.
- **How to identify / use:** pick the intraday level as terminus, the higher-timeframe level as the next draw.
- **Example in this video:** Wed Sept 25 small lower gap (<40 handles) that filled; price ran to equal highs, fell back into the first FVG, then rallied again.
- **Timestamps:** [0:03:06](https://youtu.be/NDwNIqUkASc?t=186) small gap <40 handles, election year, HTF interest · [0:09:38](https://youtu.be/NDwNIqUkASc?t=578) relative equal highs, Aug 22 high above · [0:20:15](https://youtu.be/NDwNIqUkASc?t=1215) largest leverage on the HTF side · [0:43:37](https://youtu.be/NDwNIqUkASc?t=2617) not a Judas swing
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** gap size remark (<40 handles "not all that exciting") agrees with M24-032.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Tape Reading \ September 25, 2024
head: Seek and Destroy day  (aliases ICT uses: Seek & Destroy)
body:
- **Kind:** definition
- **What ICT says:** a Seek and Destroy day is one where every high gets taken out and every low gets taken out. The tell is that price spends time inside every inefficiency that forms (consolidating inside gaps instead of leaving them). He says Monday (Sept 23, see M24-033) was like that: unfavorable, so he sat out; he never expected to execute (caption garbled).
- **How to identify:** repeated stay inside each gap; both sides' liquidity swept repeatedly.
- **How to use:** avoid or wait; compare with today where price does not spend time inside the inefficiency and so is tradeable.
- **Timestamps:** [0:37:03](https://youtu.be/NDwNIqUkASc?t=2223) Seek and Destroy day defined and contrasted with Monday
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** ties M24-033's title to this definition (first explicit spoken definition in the notes so far).

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Tape Reading \ September 25, 2024
head: Mid-range / momentum entries are fine — don't need high or low  (aliases ICT uses: setups between the high and the low, Silver Bullet-type setups, momentum trades)
body:
- **Kind:** rule / mindset
- **What ICT says:** he does not need the highest high or lowest low; setups between the extremes are generally Silver Bullet-type setups. He gave Caleb (called "Cameron" once in captions) a framework to get into something already in motion, as long as the bias (draw on liquidity) is right, the move to the next liquidity is likely. Many profitable traders trade only the middle of ranges and momentum; that is the best way to start because it removes the need to be right. You can be wrong and still be profitable. Look for your own segment of price action you trust; forcing a specific pattern makes it hard.
- **How to use:** pick the first FVG / volume imbalance in the middle of the move, aim for the next draw.
- **Timestamps:** [0:15:15](https://youtu.be/NDwNIqUkASc?t=915) in-between setups = Silver Bullet-type · [0:17:38](https://youtu.be/NDwNIqUkASc?t=1058) middle-range momentum trades are fine · [0:25:46](https://youtu.be/NDwNIqUkASc?t=1546) you don't need the low or high of a run
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** answers a student's wish to catch the extremes; he admits his own executions sometimes catch them, but it is not the focus.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ How To Identify High Resistance Liquidity Conditions \ September 27, 2024
head: High Resistance vs Low Resistance Liquidity Run Conditions  (aliases ICT uses: "two types of trading conditions", "high resistance liquidity run days/sessions", "problem market", "lackluster morning")
body:
- **Kind:** definition / rule (a day-classification framework; the core of the video)
- **What ICT says:**
  - There are two trading conditions. **Low resistance:** price goes straight from your entry to the liquidity or inefficiency. Delivery is fast, feedback is immediate, and the day is quick and low-stress. **High resistance:** price struggles to make the easy, fast, straight run to obvious liquidity even though the liquidity is clearly there (here, the relative equal lows). "Resistance" does not mean retail support/resistance. It means resistance to the easy fast run.
  - A high-resistance market teases: it gets close, retraces, consolidates, drops, comes back, and spikes outside inefficiencies. Typically it reaches the liquidity later, after traders have been stopped out or have given up and walked away.
  - Low-resistance days are AI/algorithm-driven, so delivery is "to the tick" and precise around PD arrays. High-resistance days are, in his view, mostly manually intervened: someone is "stirring the pot" with spikes and stop runs, so the precision disappears. Exception: just before a big red-folder event (FOMC, NFP, CPI, PPI) the market marks time sideways. That is not a time to trade either.
  - Losing precision around his PD arrays is not "the algorithm changed" and not "the concept stopped working". It is the sign of manual intervention.
  - High-resistance conditions are not "Seek & Destroy" and not simply "choppy". They just require more time and more experience.
- **How to identify:** (his bullet list at 1:32:19–1:33:05 plus the repeated "one test")
  1. A lackluster opening-range gap: less than 75 handles invites a slow, lethargic morning; under 40 "definitely" means a lackluster morning. A very large gap (he likes about 75 handles or more) is the precursor to a fluid market.
  2. Watch the first 30 minutes (9:30–10:00) to decide which regime you are in.
  3. **The test:** when a fair value gap/inefficiency forms, does price spend a lot of time inside it (multiple candles laid inside, repeated revisits to the same gap or its CE) instead of touching it and repelling quickly? If yes, you are in high-resistance conditions. He says this is all he ever uses to decide, with no hidden PD array.
  4. Price not delivering to the tick on PD arrays; wild spikes beyond inefficiencies; deep retracements; sloppy back-and-forth.
  5. Repeated short-term high runs (buy stops) followed by a sell-off, again and again, when the bias is bearish.
- **How to use:**
  - Recognize it early, ideally before the open from the signatures, and confirm in the first 30 minutes.
  - High resistance: lowest leverage (a micro, or just 1 contract), a wider stop, big partials, or just paper-trade/demo-trade/tape-read. Do not overtrade.
  - Low resistance: push your edge with maximum (not excessive) leverage and take many trades.
  - Classify every day in the journal: "Did the imbalances spend too much time holding price inside them?" Yes means high resistance; no means low resistance.
- **Example in this video:** NQ, Fri 2024-09-27. The opening-range gap was small (a premium gap), so ICT flagged a lackluster morning at 9:30 before anything happened. Price repeatedly rotated inside the first 1-minute FVG and the 15-second FVGs, stabbed up three or four times to run short-term highs, and only later dropped, wicking through the relative equal lows.
- **Timestamps:**
  - [0:49:41](https://youtu.be/nr6CJqNWChw?t=2981) defines high-resistance runs as price resisting the easy fast shot to obvious liquidity.
  - [0:51:17](https://youtu.be/nr6CJqNWChw?t=3077) contrasts low-resistance markets (fast, immediate feedback) and says to dial back leverage when you spot high resistance.
  - [1:32:19](https://youtu.be/nr6CJqNWChw?t=5539) gives the signature list (gap under 75, under 40).
  - [2:08:28](https://youtu.be/nr6CJqNWChw?t=7708) / [2:30:01](https://youtu.be/nr6CJqNWChw?t=9001) give the one-line test and the journal classification.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:**
  - New framework in this series. It also explains why his stop and partial behavior differs from trade to trade.
  - It is distinct from Seek & Destroy (see that concept below).
  - He says this is why you can be right on direction and still get stopped out or scared out before the target is reached.
  - Caption unclear on his remark that the only time such behavior is algorithmic is "time distortion", and that this day was not that.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ How To Identify High Resistance Liquidity Conditions \ September 27, 2024
head: Opening Range Gap (RTH close to 9:30 open) — 70% midpoint fill, quadrants, "no-body zone"  (aliases: opening range gap, ORG, "premium gap", "exhaustion gap")
body:
- **Kind:** definition / rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - The opening range gap is the space between the prior session's regular-trading-hours close/settlement (the 4:14 PM ET RTH close, caption unclear between 4:14 and 4:15) and the 9:30 AM RTH opening price. Use the RTH chart for this. On the ETH (electronic) chart, which runs 6:00 PM–5:00 PM ET (Friday 5 PM close, reopen Sunday 6 PM), it looks different, so make sure you are looking at the right session.
  - The opening range is 9:30–10:00. Algorithms use it as a preliminary range that establishes the first imbalance and the initial highs and lows. You then use that information to build the narrative for how the daily range will unfold.
  - **70%:** about 70% of the time, half of the opening range gap (its consequent encroachment) is traded to in the first 30 minutes. A gap-up opening means the initial bias in the opening range is bearish (he states only the gap-up case; the gap-down mirror is implied, not stated). Sometimes it takes a little longer than 30 minutes.
  - The 9:30 opening price and the prior close are static, non-dynamic reference points. Price can make a higher high in the first few minutes, but the midpoint remains the magnet.
  - Plot the quadrant levels (25/50/75%) on the gap.
  - **"No-body zone" (bearish case):** price may wick into the upper portion of the gap, but ICT does not want candle bodies laid in the upper quadrant, which would make the market more indecisive. Keep bodies out of the upper part and the bearish idea stays intact. Treat the whole gap like a fair value gap: if bearish, any dig back up should stop in the lower half and leave the upper half open. If bullish, leave the lower half open.
  - He also describes a gap-up that sells off, rallies and then folds as something that "could be viewed as an exhaustion gap", where the gap low can then be treated like an FVG.
- **How to identify:** Compare the 9:30 open to the prior RTH close. Mark the gap and the quadrant levels. Note the gap size in handles (see the size thresholds in the High Resistance concept).
- **How to use:**
  - The built-in 70% target gives a high-probability first partial/objective.
  - Gap size sets the regime: large gap (about 75+ handles) leads to a fluid day, small gap (under 75, and especially under 40) leads to a high-resistance day.
  - In his old currency-futures days (British pound, Japanese yen, Canadian dollar) he sold gap-up opens with a roughly 30-handle stop and watched whether the stop or the midpoint was hit first. He said this is an exercise he puts students through (caption somewhat unclear).
- **Example in this video:** NQ 9/27: gap higher open. The gap is shaded and the quadrants drawn. Price tags the gap low and the CE of the first FVG, then wicks into the upper quadrant but the bodies stop at the upper quadrant line, leaving the top slice open. ICT calls that an "algorithmic signature" (the algorithm "not completely closing it in"), which keeps the sell-side draw valid.
- **Timestamps:**
  - [0:05:25](https://youtu.be/nr6CJqNWChw?t=325) defines the opening range gap and the 9:30–10:00 opening range.
  - [0:22:26](https://youtu.be/nr6CJqNWChw?t=1346) gives the no-body zone.
  - [1:21:52](https://youtu.be/nr6CJqNWChw?t=4912) says the 70% midpoint is the static draw.
  - [1:44:30](https://youtu.be/nr6CJqNWChw?t=6270) explains why the left-open upper portion matters.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** The 70% figure is stated as a frequency, not a guarantee. If price had fully closed in and traded outside the upper part of the gap, the bearish idea would be much less likely. This builds on the earlier opening-gap teaching; the new part is using gap size to classify the regime.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ How To Identify High Resistance Liquidity Conditions \ September 27, 2024
head: First Presented FVG (1-minute, 9:31 or later) as the reference point  (aliases: first FVG of the day, "first presented fair value gap", 9:31 FVG)
body:
- **Kind:** rule / refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - On the 1-minute chart, the first FVG that forms at 9:31 or later (through 10:00) is your reference. The FVG that includes the 9:30 candle is not used, because of the volatility and the gap, though he notes it is "still useful" to see. On a 15-second chart a gap that forms inside the 9:30 minute is likewise noted but not used.
  - Everybody should start from the same reference point so he can see how students execute and where they go wrong. After that you can use 15, 30 or 45-second charts.
  - Basic read: the market is bullish when above it and bearish when below it. Allow the first-30-minute volatility to trade above and below it. It matters more when it lines up with a macro window (9:50–10:10).
  - Not "enter on the first FVG": the first FVG alone is not an entry. Wait for the conditions around it (below).
- **How to identify:** First 1-minute FVG after the 9:30 candle. Extend it to the right. A down-close candle that price rallies back into is a potential bearish FVG.
- **How to use:** See the entry model in the next concept. In a bearish read, the stop sits above the whole FVG plus the gap height (see Stops).
- **Example in this video:** The first valid 1-minute FVG formed around 9:34–9:35 (he says "9:35" at one point and "34" at another; caption unclear). It is a bearish FVG on a down-close candle, drawn as a darker box. Price initially traded above it with wicks while bodies stayed inside, then displaced below and later returned to kiss its low.
- **Timestamps:**
  - [0:07:14](https://youtu.be/nr6CJqNWChw?t=434) explains starting at 9:31, not the 9:30 candle.
  - [0:38:34](https://youtu.be/nr6CJqNWChw?t=2314) defines "your one-minute first presented fair value gap".
  - [0:40:11](https://youtu.be/nr6CJqNWChw?t=2411) gives bullish above / bearish below.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** He misspoke "inversion" on this concept on an earlier stream, calling a reclaimed bullish FVG an inversion FVG, and says he will post a short presentation on it that weekend (not covered here). A down-close candle that price rallies into is treated as a bearish FVG, not an inversion FVG, in this video.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ How To Identify High Resistance Liquidity Conditions \ September 27, 2024
head: Entry Model: displacement away from the first FVG, retest, then drop to 15-second FVG  (aliases: "the very first fair value gap on the 15 second chart")
body:
- **Kind:** entry model
- **What ICT says:**
  - Do not short just because price is inside the first FVG. Wait for price to displace below it and leave a candle body away from it. Then watch for price to come back up and touch (trade up into the bottom of) the FVG again; he would expect it to trade lower from there.
  - The most conservative version is to require a body close away from below the low of the 1-minute FVG before doing anything. He wants to see a small imbalance form, with the candle not coming back to it yet, and a "breakaway gap" away from the FVG.
  - After the displacement, switch to the 15-second chart. The very first 15-second FVG that forms and is traded back into becomes the catalyst for the short toward the sell-side.
  - This is building an expectation on one timeframe (1m), then executing on another (15s), based on specific parameters. It is not just "pick the first FVG".
- **How to identify:** (1) bearish context (gap-up open, Friday, relative equal lows below); (2) 1m first FVG; (3) body displacement below it; (4) retest of the FVG low/CE; (5) the first 15s FVG on the move down.
- **How to use:** Short the retest; stop above the first FVG plus its height on high-resistance days; target the CE of the opening range gap (70%), then the 20% and 30% weekly-range levels and the relative equal lows. See Stops and Partials below.
- **Example in this video:** After the first 1m FVG, price displaced below it. ICT said "not yet", wanting the candle to leave that small imbalance open first, then to see displacement. When price came back up, wicked, and kissed the low of the first FVG, "that's your short", and the stop goes above the FVG.
- **Timestamps:**
  - [0:25:38](https://youtu.be/nr6CJqNWChw?t=1538) explains waiting for displacement below and a retest.
  - [0:27:16](https://youtu.be/nr6CJqNWChw?t=1636) explains the 15s FVG as the trigger.
  - [1:46:56](https://youtu.be/nr6CJqNWChw?t=6416) shows price kissing the low of the first FVG as the short.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** He admits that during the live session the market did not give the clean sequence ("it should have dropped here, and it didn't") because it was a high-resistance day.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ How To Identify High Resistance Liquidity Conditions \ September 27, 2024
head: Stop and size on high-resistance days (stop at least 2x the FVG range)  (aliases: wide stop, "stop has to factor the FVG range")
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - On high-resistance days, the stop must factor the entry FVG's range. If you short at the low of a bearish FVG, take the FVG's height and add it above the top of the FVG as well. The stop is at least about 2x the FVG range from entry ("at least two times this range or whatever your favorite gap is").
  - Reason: price can retrace deeply and wick through before still going your way. A wide stop means it takes a real move to stop you, so you can stay in the trade without panic.
  - Because the stop is wide, this likely means a micro-sized position. If you do not want such a wide stop, do not trade that day.
  - Contrast, low-resistance days: stop one tick above the gap's CE (caption somewhat unclear); he says a couple of ticks above the gap is not enough on a high-resistance day.
  - If you have entries early in the day or pre-session, do not rush your stop loss into the range. Let it sit back a while. This is why his own stop management varies between trades (sometimes moved, sometimes left at cost-covering): it depends on which regime he thinks he is in.
- **How to identify:** Regime classification first (above), then size the stop by the width of the reference FVG.
- **How to use:** Entry at the FVG low (short), stop above FVG high plus FVG height, micro size.
- **Example in this video:** The short at the retest of the first 1m FVG, with the stop drawn above the FVG by roughly another gap-height.
- **Timestamps:** [1:46:56](https://youtu.be/nr6CJqNWChw?t=6416), [1:47:45](https://youtu.be/nr6CJqNWChw?t=6465) (the 2x range), [1:29:57](https://youtu.be/nr6CJqNWChw?t=5397) (do not rush the stop).
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** No stated tick or handle count for the stop, only the 2x multiple. This is not a standard ICT stop rule; it applies only to this regime.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ How To Identify High Resistance Liquidity Conditions \ September 27, 2024
head: Partials and position sizing by regime  (aliases: "take a partial every time it takes out a low")
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - He teaches students to take partials on every new low taken (if short), because they cannot yet tell high-resistance from low-resistance days. Even if you take only 1 contract off, it rewards your patience and finding the setup, and it reduces risk.
  - Position-size example: his standard size is 10 NQ contracts. On a day you already know is high-resistance, a student guessed 6–8 contracts off at the first low taken; he said 6 (or 6–7) is good and 8 is high. The remaining 4 sit through the drawdown (price comes back near the entry) and the same process repeats at the next low.
  - Low-resistance days: use maximum (not excessive) leverage and trade many times. High-resistance days: no lots of trades at high leverage ("like running in quicksand").
  - If already in a trade and you recognize price spending a lot of time in or revisiting the gap before moving your way: drop to the lowest leverage immediately. If trading minis, cut to 1 contract; if micros, to 1 micro. That is risk management, not fear. He compares it to keeping a "dummy wallet" for a hold-up.
  - Taking partials below a newly formed low also fits the liquidity logic: longs have sell stops below that low, and price then tends to wick on through the relative equal lows.
- **How to identify:** After the first low is taken below your entry, partial. Evaluate the regime by the FVG-respect test.
- **How to use:** As above.
- **Example in this video:** The demonstrated short: partials come when price trades below the prior low; after the second move, price wicks through the relative equal lows (the original framing target).
- **Timestamps:**
  - [1:49:22](https://youtu.be/nr6CJqNWChw?t=6562) covers partials on every low.
  - [1:50:57](https://youtu.be/nr6CJqNWChw?t=6657) gives the 10-contract exercise and the 6–8 answer.
  - [2:09:16](https://youtu.be/nr6CJqNWChw?t=7756) says to reduce to one contract.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** The 6–7 of 10 figure is a student-answer-plus-ICT-approval, not a formal rule; he said there is no right or wrong answer.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ How To Identify High Resistance Liquidity Conditions \ September 27, 2024
head: TGIF — Friday retracement of 20–30% of the weekly range  (aliases: "Thank God It's Friday", weekly range retracement)
body:
- **Kind:** rule (day-of-week tendency)
- **What ICT says:**
  - After a week that has gone up (a bullish week), he likes to see Friday retrace 20–30% of the weekly range down. After a bearish week he expects a retrace higher. If it does not happen on Friday, he expects a retracement into the prior week's range on Monday.
  - **Measurement:** weekly range = highest high of the week to lowest low of the week. Drop a fib on that range and show the 20% and 30% levels. He changes the 0.25 level to 0.2 (deleting the "5") and toggles 0.3. The levels are measured down from the highest high of the week.
  - Same idea on Mondays is less likely, since it is a new week and the narrative may be different.
  - Use the 20% level as a first partial objective and the 30% level as the next one.
- **How to identify:** A Friday after a week that has traded up (or down) most days, and a clear weekly high/low. Check the levels on the weekly candle and the 1-minute chart so the prices match.
- **How to use:** Combine with a gap-up open (70% midpoint fill) and the first-FVG short. Targets: CE of the opening gap, then the 20% level, then the 30% level.
- **Example in this video:** NQ, Friday of an up week. The 20% level lined up at about 20,421 on both the weekly and the 1-minute chart (caption unclear on the exact figure). Price reached the 30% level inside an FVG, then rolled over again into an inefficiency before breaking down.
- **Timestamps:**
  - [0:10:35](https://youtu.be/nr6CJqNWChw?t=635) introduces the 20–30% weekly range retracement.
  - [1:19:25](https://youtu.be/nr6CJqNWChw?t=4765) shows the weekly-range fib.
  - [1:20:16](https://youtu.be/nr6CJqNWChw?t=4816) gives the fib settings.
  - [1:24:18](https://youtu.be/nr6CJqNWChw?t=5058) says to use the 20% level as a partial.
  - [1:27:32](https://youtu.be/nr6CJqNWChw?t=5252) gives the 30% as the next partial target.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** "Usually" and "like to see": a tendency, not a rule that always works. He frames the opening-gap midpoint plus TGIF as "a sweet spot where you have so many things in your favor".

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ How To Identify High Resistance Liquidity Conditions \ September 27, 2024
head: Narrative (not bias) and stacking factors — time, PD arrays, liquidity  (aliases: narrative, "three factors", macro 9:50–10:10)
body:
- **Kind:** rule / definition
- **What ICT says:**
  - "Narrative is not bias." Bias is bullish or bearish. Narrative also says where price is likely to go and why that is realistic.
  - He wants at least three factors behind a trade or an expectation, and one of the main ones must be time. Setups without time lack institutional sponsorship.
  - **Time:** the first 10 minutes before the top of the hour (9:50–10:00) and 10:00–10:10 form a roughly 20-minute macro window. Algorithms start firing and "spooling" price to run to an inefficiency or to liquidity above an old high / relative equal highs or below an old low / relative equal lows. Spooling is not directional.
  - Questions he asks before the open: Where did we open relative to yesterday's 4:14 PM RTH close? Where is the liquidity? Are there relative equal highs or lows? Is there a large inefficiency above or below? Why should price be interested in going higher or lower?
  - **Direction filter:** if you can justify the trade on both the buy side and the sell side, it is not high probability. Prefer days and times when the evidence leans heavily one way.
  - Other factors stacked: Friday/TGIF, an up week, gap-up open, relative equal lows below, an FVG to sell into.
  - Immediate feedback test: if the idea is right, you should see price quickly doing what you expected. If the things that should keep it from going higher are not showing up, you already have feedback that you are not on side.
  - Monday vs Friday: a retracement idea like this is less likely on a Monday because a new week may have an entirely different narrative.
- **How to identify:** A checklist of time + PD array + liquidity + day/week context.
- **How to use:** Only act when several of these line up; if they do not, sit still.
- **Example in this video:** Narrative for the day: Friday, up week, gap-up (premium) open, relative equal lows below as the draw, inside the macro at 9:57, so look for sells and ignore longs ("I don't care if it went up 100 handles").
- **Timestamps:**
  - [0:13:44](https://youtu.be/nr6CJqNWChw?t=824) gives the "at least three factors, one is time" line.
  - [0:14:32](https://youtu.be/nr6CJqNWChw?t=872) gives the 9:50–10:10 macro description.
  - [0:16:07](https://youtu.be/nr6CJqNWChw?t=967) gives the one-sided versus two-sided test.
  - [0:31:19](https://youtu.be/nr6CJqNWChw?t=1879) gives the narrative-versus-bias line.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** He frames the 9:50–10:10 window as a macro but does not name or number it here beyond those times.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ How To Identify High Resistance Liquidity Conditions \ September 27, 2024
head: Smooth vs jagged — obvious liquidity and retail perception  (aliases: relative equal lows as "support", "smooth lows", "jagged highs")
body:
- **Kind:** definition / refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - Retail sees relative equal lows as support and expects buying there; stops sit just below (sell stops, or "short buy stops"). That makes them a draw.
  - Price action is "smooth" where liquidity remains untaken (here the relative equal lows below) and "jagged" where it has already been run (the upside highs). The market tends to deliver to the smooth side.
  - Retail chart patterns (bull flags, pennants, wedges, descending triangles) are not the cause of price movement. They only "work" if price is already heading to a liquidity pool. If it is smooth above a bull flag and the downside is already made jagged, the flag may deliver, but only because price is running for liquidity.
  - You do not need a bookmap, DOM or ladder. You can see everything on the chart if you know the time, the day, the inefficiencies and the equal highs/lows.
- **How to identify:** Look for untouched equal highs/lows; compare which side of the market is "smooth".
- **How to use:** Frame the draw toward the smooth side; use obvious retail patterns as a clue to where stops will be.
- **Example in this video:** Relative equal lows below were smooth, the top had been made jagged. Later, bull-flag-looking consolidations were the setups for stop runs.
- **Timestamps:** [0:09:00](https://youtu.be/nr6CJqNWChw?t=540), [0:17:41](https://youtu.be/nr6CJqNWChw?t=1061), [0:50:30](https://youtu.be/nr6CJqNWChw?t=3030).
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** The term "smooth/jagged" is used loosely in this video; he does not give a formal definition.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ How To Identify High Resistance Liquidity Conditions \ September 27, 2024
head: Inefficiency-respect test: "stick your toe in the water and run away"  (aliases: accumulation inside FVG, touching a gap multiple times)
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - In a clean market, price enters or touches the FVG (or its CE) and then repels away quickly: "one quick high-five and you're out of there".
  - Accumulation is fine above old highs or below old lows. It is not fine inside inefficiencies. If price shows lots of interest in getting back into the same gap, or keeps laying candles in it, expect it to go through the gap.
  - He compares it to trend lines: the more times a trend line is touched, the weaker it really is, not stronger.
  - Ideal-world bearish sequence: touch the CE, drop immediately, run right through the low, retrace briefly and continue. On a high-resistance day it instead goes back and forth many times.
- **How to identify:** Count visits to the same FVG and the number of candles inside it.
- **How to use:** If the FVG you are trading from is not respected on the first or second touch, reduce risk (1 contract), widen the stop, or step aside.
- **Example in this video:** Price hit the CE of the first FVG repeatedly and kept coming back instead of failing there; the 15-second gaps behaved the same way ("this many times into it here, here, here").
- **Timestamps:** [1:34:43](https://youtu.be/nr6CJqNWChw?t=5683), [1:40:27](https://youtu.be/nr6CJqNWChw?t=6027), [1:41:16](https://youtu.be/nr6CJqNWChw?t=6076).
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** This is the practical form of the high-resistance diagnostic, restated at [2:16:24](https://youtu.be/nr6CJqNWChw?t=8184).

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ How To Identify High Resistance Liquidity Conditions \ September 27, 2024
head: Stop runs on high-resistance days: Judas swing and turtle soup sells  (aliases: Judas, turtle soup, "manual intervention", "stirring the pot")
body:
- **Kind:** example only / refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - On a high-resistance day with a bearish bias, price repeatedly runs short-term highs and equal highs, then sells off. To other traders each run looks like a bull flag or a bullish micro-shift, but it is just a run on the buy stops. Shorts' protective buy stops (and breakout buyers' entries) are tripped, so shorts are stopped out and breakout longs are trapped long.
  - The "algorithmic" version is precise. The "manual" version is characterized by spikes outside inefficiencies and long dwell time at the highs.
  - In his explanation, the dwell time at the highs lets the other side build a position: time & sales shows many contracts trading there, and then price shoots lower. Shorts who held through are stopped or buy back at lower prices, while longs' sell stops below the low give liquidity on the way down. Price then wicks through the relative equal lows.
  - If you are bearish, look for turtle soup sells: small bullish-looking market structure shifts that just take short-term buy stops.
  - Judas swing: the early run into the upper part of the opening range gap (before the drop) is the day's Judas swing even though it did not make a higher high than the opening price.
  - Trailing stops get picked off by these runs: traders who trailed their stops lost the trade and did not get "the ticket ride".
- **How to identify:** A string of failed breakouts above short-term highs followed by sell-offs; relative equal highs forming and being run.
- **How to use:** Allow for them with a wider stop; do not trail stops tightly; use the buy-stop runs themselves as short-entry areas once the run completes.
- **Example in this video:** After the first FVG short, price ran up three or four times (including one clear push above a small inefficiency and a lower high that formed relative equal highs), each time repelling aggressively. The second manual push cleared the buy stops, then price took out the low and went to the target.
- **Timestamps:** [1:46:07](https://youtu.be/nr6CJqNWChw?t=6367) (Judas), [1:54:08](https://youtu.be/nr6CJqNWChw?t=6848) (stops being "onboarded"), [2:02:56](https://youtu.be/nr6CJqNWChw?t=7376) (the relative-equal-high run), [2:14:03](https://youtu.be/nr6CJqNWChw?t=8043) (turtle soup sells).
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Much of this is his interpretation of intent ("they want to build positions on a narrow range"); he acknowledges it sounds like a conspiracy and asks viewers to suspend disbelief for the sake of argument. He says he does not need a bookmap to tell this.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ How To Identify High Resistance Liquidity Conditions \ September 27, 2024
head: High Resistance vs Seek & Destroy
body:
- **Kind:** refinement / caveat
- **What ICT says:** Do not label a high-resistance day "Seek & Destroy". Students (he mentions Tanya) mislabel hard days as S&D to excuse them. You will not get two S&D days in the same week ("never ever happen"), but you can get a potential S&D day and then a high-resistance day. His example of a real S&D: a Monday earlier in the week/series where he kept himself out of trades (caption unclear on which video).
- **How to identify:** A hard day with many FVG revisits and deep retracements is high resistance; do not file it as S&D just because it is hard.
- **Timestamps:** [2:14:50](https://youtu.be/nr6CJqNWChw?t=8090), [2:21:13](https://youtu.be/nr6CJqNWChw?t=8473).
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** This tightens the usage of "Seek & Destroy" from earlier videos in the series; he does not redefine S&D here.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ How To Identify High Resistance Liquidity Conditions \ September 27, 2024
head: The reference points work in markets without gaps (forex)
body:
- **Kind:** refinement
- **What ICT says:** In markets that trade 24 hours without an RTH/ETH gap (e.g. forex), still use the same time reference points: yesterday's 4:14 PM level versus today's 9:30 price. The algorithm refers to those price points by time even if you cannot see a gap on your chart, so you get the same simulation as if there were a gap.
- **Timestamps:** [1:25:10](https://youtu.be/nr6CJqNWChw?t=5110), [1:25:59](https://youtu.be/nr6CJqNWChw?t=5159).
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Stated as a claim; no forex example shown.

head: Live review exercise
body:
- **Kind:** example only
- **What ICT says:** He asks viewers to take the 15-second chart with his markings and find at least two setups, then go back at night and study what price did right before each setup finally worked. He also says to compare every day going forward and note which regime it was.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Premarket Concepts \ September 30, 2024
head: Pre-market / weekly analysis routine (top-down)  (aliases: "soup to nuts breakdown", game plan, bias → narrative → model → time → entry → stop → partial → Terminus)
body:
- **Kind:** rule / process
- **What ICT says:**
  - He looks at the weekly opening gap only (Sunday ~6 PM open vs Friday settlement), then turns the charts off and lets Asia/London print on their own; he comes in the next morning with no preconceived idea. On the weekend (or Friday) he writes scenarios for a higher/lower/no-gap Sunday open.
  - The questions the analysis must answer: what is my bias, what narrative explains why price should do it, which model, what time of day, how do I enter, where is the stop, when is the first partial, when do I move the stop, when am I content at my Terminus, then stop trading for that session/day.
  - He skips the 4-hour chart when he is only session-trading/scalping up to the daily range; he would use the 4H only if swinging the whole weekly range. Flow used here: weekly → daily → 60 min → 15 min → 5 min → 1 min (15-second chart reserved for later in the week).
  - "If it doesn't jump off the chart at you" it is probably being forced; levels should be obvious. On higher timeframes he does not use a fine-tooth comb.
  - Weekly chart must be consulted once at the start of the week so you are not blind to several-hundred-handle runs; a 15-minute-only trader loses that perspective. Once the levels are annotated on the chart you will not forget them, and it becomes easier to trust a drop to them when price is in the area.
  - Annotate every higher-timeframe line (e.g. "Sept 23 weekly low") so the label shows on the price axis when you drop to lower timeframes; unlabeled lines are distractions. Also label each inefficiency with the timeframe it is anchored to.
  - The "boot camp" week is deliberately stripped down: one instrument, one recipe repeated daily; he admits no model is 100% and uncertainty has to be accepted.
- **How to identify:** n/a (process).
- **How to use:** Do it once per week (weekend) and again each pre-market; screenshot/annotate levels; keep chart on New York time (he stresses all his teaching fails if charts are on local time).
- **Example in this video:** Weekly: this week's candle trades up into premium; the weekly candle sequence leaves a buy-side-only inefficiency (week of Sep 9 high to week of Sep 23 low) which is the target zone; he notes CE and quadrants of the Sept 23 weekly candle. Daily: relative equal lows, consecutive volume imbalances, cleared a high, went into a SIBI, traded back up to the CISD (open of the up-close candle). 60m: big wick = discount wick, CE marked. 15m: relative equal lows over sell-side, plus NQ/ES SMT at Sunday 8 PM.
- **Timestamps:** [0:02:52](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=172) — avoids weekend price, only marks weekly opening gap; [0:10:07](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=607) — lists the questions the plan must answer; [0:17:45](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=1065) — skips 4H, goes weekly → daily → 60m; [0:55:48](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=3348) — "this is my pre-market analysis approach"; [0:56:35](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=3395) — why the weekly chart is needed
- **Nuance / caveats:** He says he writes levels on a notepad in price order (as they would sit on a chart, not in the order found) and logs each hour's high/low as a numerical picture of the daily candle, but insists you do not need it and should just use the charts (a 30-year habit from when he could not watch real-time price). Specific weekly numeric levels he reads aloud ("883 and a quarter" etc.) are garbled in the captions (caption unclear).

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Premarket Concepts \ September 30, 2024
head: Higher-timeframe inefficiencies as draws: weekly BISI/SIBI, volume imbalances, CE of candles  (aliases: weekly inefficiency, "buy side imbalance sell side inefficiency", "sell side imbalance buy side inefficiency", volume imbalance)
body:
- **Kind:** definition / refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - A weekly candle range that "only has buy-side delivery" is an inefficiency that price is reasonably expected to revisit. Here the weekly gap spans the Sept 9 week high down to the Sept 23 week low; he labels it with those dates.
  - He can add CE (midpoint) and quadrants of a candle/inefficiency; the "high of that weekly BISI" sits in the same proximity as the daily/15m relative equal lows, so it adds to the sell-side target zone.
  - When there are consecutive volume imbalances only one candle apart, just box the entire range; the result reads the same as boxing them individually. Because it is a premium array above price, shade it a distinct hue.
  - He does not keep all this on his own chart (it disorients him); he draws it for teaching.
  - Terms in his speech: BISI = "buy side imbalance sell side inefficiency", SIBI = "sell side imbalance buy side inefficiency".
- **How to identify:** weekly/daily candle ranges (gaps or volume imbalances) unfilled on one side; label with the anchoring timeframe/date.
- **How to use:** Treat the nearest relevant unfilled array in the direction of bias as the draw/target; combine with liquidity at the same price (relative equal lows) for a stronger objective.
- **Example in this video:** NQ weekly BISI (Sept 9 high to Sept 23 low) lies below price; daily chart: two volume imbalances separated by one candle boxed as one premium array overhead; price had cleared a daily high and traded into a SIBI.
- **Timestamps:** [0:11:40](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=700) — weekly buy-side-only candle, expects a run to explore the low; [0:14:23](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=863) — adds CE/quadrants; [0:16:09](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=969) — box consecutive volume imbalances as one; [0:48:32](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=2912) — weekly BISI high coincides with the 15m low cluster
- **Nuance / caveats:** He also mentions the September-contract volume imbalance up high that he said in the mentorship was "about as far as I could see for the year" (price went slightly past it and the contract rolled). He is not predicting a top; this is a "best case" framing.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Premarket Concepts \ September 30, 2024
head: Wick consequent encroachment (discount wick / premium wick)  (aliases: 60m CE, hourly discount wick CE, "mid-wick")
body:
- **Kind:** definition / refinement
- **What ICT says:** Any big wick on the hourly (or other HTF) chart at a high/low or near market price gets annotated with its CE (midpoint). A wick below current market price is a discount wick; above current price it is a premium wick. He abbreviates on his notepad e.g. "60m CE" with a small "D" for discount.
- **How to identify:** a long wick near a swing low/high or near price; mark the half of the wick.
- **How to use:** A lower-risk, nearer objective on the way to the main target: price may go to the wick CE, perhaps dip a bit below and come back, then continue toward the liquidity beneath. Also usable as a stop reference: if the third candle of an FVG has a wick and the range is small, use the CE of that wick (see FVG concept).
- **Example in this video:** 60m big wick with a swing low; with NQ at 20,525 the wick is below price (discount); its CE is the first objective, then NQ would reach for the sell-side near 19,953 ("worst case" price dips below the CE then comes back, then dives to the sell-side).
- **Timestamps:** [0:18:35](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=1115) — marking wicks; [0:19:37](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=1177) — discount wick vs premium wick; [0:54:57](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=3297) — anticipated path to CE then sell-side
- **Nuance / caveats:** Level 19,953 is read from captions ("19953"); treat the exact digits as slightly uncertain.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Premarket Concepts \ September 30, 2024
head: Premium / discount  (aliases: premium array, discount array, "100% strike rate" claim)
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:** If you are not viewing price relative to premium and discount you are "doing it wrong". Every profitable short was entered in a premium and moved to a discount; every profitable long left a discount and traded to a premium. He says this has a "100% strike rate" regardless of whose method it is, and calls anyone who says to ignore it a "clown". You must be able to frame a short on the basis of a premium and a long on a discount.
- **How to identify:** relative to the range you expect price to expand from to the target; for a candle/FVG, the part above the middle of the range is premium. In the live example he draws the range from the high of one candle to the low of another and checks which wicks/FVG are above the midline.
- **How to use:** For shorts, take FVG/wick entries above the midpoint of the range being traded; for longs, below it. For the OR gap, once price is below its CE, treat the CE as a premium to sell from.
- **Example in this video:** the 15m inefficiency above price (Sunday 8 PM area) sat in a premium, so short entries in/around it were appropriate; wick tops inside that FVG were all valid short entries.
- **Timestamps:** [0:19:37](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=1177) — "absolutely doing it wrong" statement; [0:20:26](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=1226) — 100% strike-rate claim; [0:45:11](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=2711) — why this FVG wick is a premium; [1:02:55](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=3775) — FVG must be in a premium relative to the range expanding to the target
- **Nuance / caveats:** Presented as an absolute; treat as emphatic teaching rather than a measured statistic.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Premarket Concepts \ September 30, 2024
head: Relative equal lows / sell-side liquidity stacking on multiple timeframes  (aliases: "relative equal lows", SSL, resting stops)
body:
- **Kind:** definition / example
- **What ICT says:** Sell-side liquidity rests under relative equal lows; the Sept 23 weekly low is also the 15-minute relative equal lows, so you can annotate them together as "weekly low + 15m relative equal lows sell-side". On the 15m chart he first notes there are NOT clean equal lows because each low is followed by a lower low ("probing lower") until a later zoom-out shows the daily relative equal lows and the weekly BISI high clustered together.
- **How to use:** these are the objective for the short; they are also where smart money would cover shorts and accumulate longs, hence a plausible narrative turning point.
- **Example in this video:** NQ sell-side at the 15m/daily relative equal lows near 19,953 below the hourly discount wick CE and the weekly BISI high; later the first-hour trade targets the intraday relative equal lows below the open.
- **Timestamps:** [0:26:19](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=1579) — 15m lows keep being undercut (not equal lows); [0:48:32](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=2912) — daily relative equal lows + weekly BISI; [0:49:23](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=2963) — stating the sell-side below them
- **Nuance / caveats:** None stated beyond "if it isn't obvious you are straining".

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Premarket Concepts \ September 30, 2024
head: Fair value gap — entry and stop placement  (aliases: inefficiency, FVG, "candle one, two, three")
body:
- **Kind:** rule / refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - The inefficiency is always candle number two; the stop, if affordable, goes above candle two (for a short). If the range is small, use the body of candle three, and if candle three has a wick use the CE of that wick.
  - "Always err on the side of the smallest risk": while learning, he wants the smallest risk and smallest leverage and consistency rather than big wins; that "cookie-cutter" is what you multiply later.
  - Not every price run has a propulsion block, institutional order-flow entry drill or breaker, but there will always be a fair value gap; you may get in late in the run, which is fine as long as the FVG is in a premium (short) relative to the range that expands to the target.
  - A return to a PD array must be on a new candle: price must move away, create a new candle, then trade back into the array. Retracing into the array on the same candle that moved away is "never ever ever" an entry.
- **How to identify:** three-candle gap; for entries choose wicks/FVG in the correct half of the dealing range.
- **How to use:** entry inside the FVG (CE/lower half for bearish iFVG, see below), stop above candle 2 or tighter references above; small risk first.
- **Example in this video:** the 15m premium FVG above Sunday's gap (SMT area), and the 1m first FVG at 9:31.
- **Timestamps:** [0:46:04](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=2764) — candle two / stop rules; [0:46:52](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=2812) — smallest risk and leverage; [1:02:55](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=3775) — FVG is always there; [2:06:16](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=7576) — must be a new candle
- **Nuance / caveats:** He mentions entering "if it could be afforded to you" i.e. the candle-two stop may be too wide for small accounts, so the fallbacks (candle three body, wick CE) apply.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Premarket Concepts \ September 30, 2024
head: SMT divergence (NQ vs ES; Dow check)  (aliases: SMT, "T Divergence" in captions, bellwether timeframe)
body:
- **Kind:** refinement / example
- **What ICT says:**
  - SMT is checked on the 15-minute chart, which he calls the "bellwether" timeframe: on a 15m chart you can see 60-minute and 4-hour highs/lows, so it alone gives enough to day trade (bias, draw on liquidity, reversals, continuations, stops to aim for). You may add 1H–4H charts if you want more information, just not so much that you get conflicting analysis.
  - He has used SMT only two or three times in the whole 2024 mentorship; it is not needed to trade profitably, only helps him decide whether to use the largest leverage. It also is not needed to validate an entry: a well-placed FVG is already the setup.
  - Forex needs one extra step: always refer to the dollar index and expect the mirror image in GBPUSD/EURUSD/USDJPY.
- **How to identify:** at the 8:00 PM Sunday (Asia) 15m highs, ES made a higher high while NQ made a slightly lower high → NQ is the weaker one; NQ "built-in heaviness".
- **How to use:** supports shorting the weaker index; he notes "NQ −" and the time on his notepad rather than drawing it on the chart.
- **Example in this video:** 15m NQ vs ES, Sunday 8 PM ET: ES higher high, NQ lower high → bearish SMT, supporting short in the premium FVG overhead.
- **Timestamps:** [0:36:31](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=2191) — 15m as bellwether timeframe; [0:41:16](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=2476) — NQ lower high vs ES higher high; [0:42:04](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=2524) — note on notepad; [0:45:11](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=2711) — "don't need SMT to tell you the trade is good"
- **Nuance / caveats:** Contradicts the habit of treating SMT as mandatory; it is a leverage-sizing aid. (Today he also expands SMT-style comparison into the three-average decoupling concept below.)

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Premarket Concepts \ September 30, 2024
head: Change in State of Delivery (daily order block reference)  (aliases: CISD, "my order block")
body:
- **Kind:** definition / example only
- **What ICT says:** In a bearish context the CISD level (his "order block") is the opening price of the up-close candle; on the daily chart price traded back up to it after going into a SIBI. Later intraday, three up-close candles' opening price is "the last line in the sand": he wouldn't want price to trade above it while short.
- **How to use:** invalidation reference for the short and a reaction level on the way down.
- **Example in this video:** daily chart: price cleared a high, traded into a SIBI (sell-side imbalance, buy-side inefficiency), then returned to the open of the up-close candle (CISD) — "a really nice delivery". Intraday: opening price of the three up-close candles = line in the sand.
- **Timestamps:** [0:23:08](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=1388) — daily CISD/order block; [2:25:37](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=8737) — line in the sand
- **Nuance / caveats:** None stated; he explicitly equates CISD with his order block here.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Premarket Concepts \ September 30, 2024
head: Narrative — framing both sides (smart money vs retail)  (aliases: "best case scenario on both sides", cannibalizing retail, confederate)
body:
- **Kind:** definition / process
- **What ICT says:**
  - Bias is not enough; you need a narrative for how price will be used on participants: how will sentiment or sudden movement entice traders to buy/chase, unseat them, and let deeper pockets take their seats.
  - Frame the best case for both sides: shorting from the daily FVG down to the sell-side below relative equal lows is not "picking the top"; after a month-plus rally, falling to sweep sell stops below relative equal lows lets smart money cover shorts and accumulate longs, which is constructive for the higher-timeframe bullishness. If smart money sold short in last week's daily FVG, why take profit early when they can take it to the weekly inefficiency and also onboard longs.
  - Ask who is in the trade right now and who would regret being long; put yourself in their shoes when price moves toward an old low/high.
  - Smart money is like a "confederate" in the audience; the algorithm is the price engine that goes to liquidity or reprices to inefficiencies — only two things happen algorithmically.
  - He is not infallible: don't impose your will; have a contingency (if wrong, price may take buy-side first, entice buyers, then break down again; wait for the first FVG value to form and break down).
- **How to use:** your heaviest leverage goes on the trade that fits the narrative; take less leverage on the counter-trend side, "giving yourself permission to be wrong".
- **Example in this video:** narrative that NQ consolidates in a bull-flag like shape to draw in buyers while ES takes buy stops above its equal highs, then sells off toward the 9:31 FVG/ORG then sell-side near 19,953. Retail looks for breakout higher; buy stops above the flag are used by shorts to sell against.
- **Timestamps:** [1:06:58](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=4018) — what narrative is; [1:08:34](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=4114) — both sides framed; [1:10:59](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=4259) — confederate analogy; [1:27:06](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=5226) — contingency if wrong; [2:22:46](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=8566) — who is trapped
- **Nuance / caveats:** "I'm not trying to pick a top"; the weekly analysis was "high 90s accurate" in his private mentorship but he always keeps a contingency.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Premarket Concepts \ September 30, 2024
head: Terminus / One Shot One Kill (weekly) and leverage allocation  (aliases: Terminus, OSOK, "heaviest handed leverage")
body:
- **Kind:** refinement
- **What ICT says:** The sell-side target (relative equal lows + weekly BISI high area) is his Terminus for the week. If a short trades into it, his "weekly one shot one kill has been satisfied", and any other trading that week is just scalps. His heaviest leverage is reserved for being a short seller aiming for that sell-side; longs get less leverage. It may not trade there today.
- **How to use:** one big objective per week, everything else smaller; stop trading for the session once the Terminus is reached.
- **Timestamps:** [1:01:22](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=3682) — heaviest leverage on the short; [1:02:08](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=3728) — "my real good one shot one kill setup"; [1:02:55](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=3775) — Terminus satisfied → scalps only
- **Nuance / caveats:** Uses "one shot one kill" as a weekly-scale idea here, not the 2022 intraday one.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Premarket Concepts \ September 30, 2024
head: News drivers: the 15-minute rule and Judas swing expectation  (aliases: medium-impact news, Chicago PMI, smoke screen)
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:** After any high- or medium-impact news driver wait at least 15 minutes ("a minimum criteria"); trading within 15 minutes means you are in a rush. The Chicago PMI at 9:45 is medium impact, but inside the opening range (9:30–10:00) so it can be more animated; he anticipated a Judas swing between 9:45 and 10:00. News is used as a "smoke screen": the market is not reacting to the number but going to where the stops are. He looks at ForexFactory calendar for this.
- **How to use:** don't predict the delivery; let the news hit, let traders get stopped out or kicked into ideas, then assess.
- **Timestamps:** [0:06:07](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=367) — Chicago PMI at 9:45; [0:06:54](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=414) — wait 15 minutes; [0:26:19](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=1579) — Judas swing 9:45–10:00 expectation; [1:43:34](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=6214) — news as smoke screen
- **Nuance / caveats:** None.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Premarket Concepts \ September 30, 2024
head: Fed chair / FOMC days: manual intervention vs algorithmic delivery  (aliases: Powell speech, manual intervention, "back to algorithm delivery")
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - Algorithmic delivery only does two things: run to liquidity or reprice to inefficiencies. When it is not delivering that way, manual intervention is in play (last week's FOMC, today's Powell speech).
  - Do nothing while the Fed chair talks and for 15 minutes after he stops. Then check whether PD arrays are being respected "to the tick" (price reacts off them or trades into them and leaves right away) — that means algorithmic delivery is back. If not yet, don't trade.
  - Before the speech the market is "fickle" and better left to novices; on days with a testimony in the 9:00–10:00 hour, trade before 8:00 AM; if the speech is in the afternoon, trade only in the morning and the first hour. He calls trading near speeches "the worst time to be in the marketplace".
  - Today's plan: no afternoon trading because of Powell; he expects manual intervention "guaranteed".
- **How to use:** rules say when you can, not "when you might". Don't carve out little exceptions.
- **Timestamps:** [0:03:43](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=223) — Fed/FOMC days: trade early; [1:11:47](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=4307) — algo vs manual, 15 min after speech; [1:15:49](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=4549) — wait 15 minutes and check PD arrays; [1:18:11](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=4691) — don't trade the afternoon session today
- **Nuance / caveats:** The 15-minute-after-speaker rule matches the news rule; a speech often keeps indices out of sync for the first 15 minutes (see decoupling).

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Premarket Concepts \ September 30, 2024
head: Time windows and no-trade rules  (aliases: pre-market session, first hour, opening range, lunch, Monday rule)
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - Pre-market = anything before 9:00 AM ET; the pre-market session starts at 7:00 AM ET; the opening range is 9:30–10:00. If a Fed chair testimony is 9:00–10:00 trade before 8:00.
  - Today (NFP-week Monday with Powell in the afternoon): find the setup in the first hour of trading, 9:30–10:30; if there is no setup, no trade. He tells "Caleb" he can trade only inside that first hour (he jokes about a silver bullet).
  - Lunch is a 2-hour window, 11:30–1:30 PM, and afternoon trading becomes more dangerous as the speech approaches.
  - New students are told to sit still on Mondays because Monday sets the initial parameters of the weekly range and you get chopped up (the transcript wording about "outside of nonfarm payroll" is garbled; he himself always trades the Monday of NFP, i.e. this day; caption unclear). Start trading Tuesday.
  - Be much more rigid about when you don't trade than when you do; turn the charts off if you feel impulsive.
- **Timestamps:** [0:05:18](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=318) — pre-market definition, before 9:00; [0:06:54](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=414) — session starts 7:00 ET; [1:12:36](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=4356) — Monday rule; [1:13:25](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=4405) — first hour 9:30–10:30, lunch 11:30–1:30; [1:27:53](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=5273) — "no entry, no trade"
- **Nuance / caveats:** Distinct from the usual Silver Bullet window (10–11); here the first-hour limit is 9:30–10:30 because of the Fed speaker.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Premarket Concepts \ September 30, 2024
head: Decoupling — Dow / S&P 500 / NASDAQ (symmetry filter)  (aliases: decoupled market, symmetrical market, "canary in the coal mine", Dow theory)
body:
- **Kind:** new coinage / rule (taught earlier in 2016–2017 core content, per him)
- **What ICT says:**
  - The only element of Dow theory he uses: when bearish or bullish you want all three averages (Dow, S&P 500, NASDAQ) to move in the same direction; this is a "symmetrical market" and the ideal environment. When they do different things the market is decoupled.
  - He credits the idea to a book author whose name is garbled in the captions (caption unclear), not to Dow theory.
  - A decoupled day is a "sit still and wait": you are likely to get "sand kicked in your face" because manual intervention is coming. You can trade decoupled markets, but you probably will not reach your targets.
  - The Dow can be the "canary in the coal mine" (30 stocks, "dirty 30"): when it refuses to do what the other two are doing, that may foretell something.
  - Fed speeches and FOMC cause decoupling; waiting 15 minutes after the speaker lets things re-sync, and if they have not synced, keep waiting.
  - Forex equivalent: a "symmetrical triad" — GBPUSD and EURUSD positively correlated, DXY the opposite; e.g. if DXY is flat, GBPUSD up and EURUSD down means a EURGBP short. Futures are easier because everyone gets the same price, while FX brokers' quotes/spreads differ.
- **How to identify:** compare the three averages around the open; check that highs/lows are being taken together.
- **How to use:** if they disagree, stay out or accept a lower probability; stick to a single instrument so you are not tempted to "pick the right one".
- **Example in this video:** 9:30–9:45 ET: NQ and ES go higher (ES with buy-side/equal highs left to take), Dow drops and holds lows; NQ builds a bull-flag type consolidation in the opening-range gap; he says he is comfortable sitting out because of the decoupling, and plans to watch ES to run its equal highs then sell.
- **Timestamps:** [1:31:57](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=5517) — decoupling defined; [1:34:22](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=5662) — Dow divergence, sandbox of manual intervention; [1:41:59](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=6119) — canary analogy; [1:53:24](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=6804) — Forex triad; [2:09:53](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=7793) — how to anticipate it
- **Nuance / caveats:** He stresses he has no preference for the Dow (he has lost more trading it).

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Premarket Concepts \ September 30, 2024
head: Market profiles to avoid: high resistance liquidity run, seek & destroy, decoupling  (aliases: HRLR, low resistance liquidity run, "three bases")
body:
- **Kind:** rule / recap
- **What ICT says:** Characteristics of a high resistance liquidity run: deeper retracements, targets reached later, and smaller inefficiencies. He summarizes the three adverse conditions taught recently: high-resistance runs are tradable but need a wider stop and a stop held near the entry (partly garbled, caption unclear); seek & destroy cannot be traded; decoupled markets are tradable but targets probably won't be reached. Low-resistance runs are "easy" — price runs to targets, entries and stops are easy and low risk. The point of the mentorship is avoiding conditions where trades are less likely to work.
- **Timestamps:** [2:24:40](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=8680) — characteristics of HRLR; [2:32:04](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=9124) — the three conditions; [2:33:42](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=9222) — low resistance runs are effortless
- **Nuance / caveats:** None.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Premarket Concepts \ September 30, 2024
head: First-presented FVG → bearish inversion FVG, CE entry, and "reclaimed bullish FVG" correction  (aliases: iFVG, first presented fair value gap, inversion fair value gap)
body:
- **Kind:** entry model / refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - The model he gives Caleb: the first presented FVG after the 9:30 open on the 1-minute chart (earliest 9:31). If you are bearish, an up-close-candle FVG (BISI) is the one to focus on, because after price trades down through it and away, it becomes a bearish inversion FVG.
  - The retest is expected to hit the CE of that FVG to the tick; the lower half is the entry zone and the upper half should remain untouched. After it has reacted from CE and left it and taken out a low, it is "properly classified" as an iFVG — it need not reach the target.
  - He deliberately corrected himself: if price instead goes back above and into the gap and then comes down into it, it is a reclaimed bullish fair value gap because it is an up-close candle; last week he mislabeled one as an inversion FVG when it should have been called reclaimed bullish FVG (although what he expected price to do was accurate).
  - Using the 9:31 FVG as an iFVG: it should react the first time price returns; a second return (back into it) is not as good.
- **How to identify:** 1m, first FVG after 9:30; in a bearish bias select the up-close-candle gap; wait for displacement below it, then a return to its CE.
- **How to use:** enter at the CE (stacked with NWOG, see below); target relative equal lows; stop back inside/above the gap.
- **Example in this video:** 1m, ~9:31 ET: large first FVG forms; NQ shifts structure, piercing a swing low, trades up into a fair value gap "beautifully" (called in advance), then delivers down to half of the first presented FVG's candle; trades down, away from the orange-shaded 9:31 FVG, returns exactly to its CE "to the tick" and offers a short toward the sell-side beneath the low. Price then trades back up inside the FVG a second time, which he says is weaker.
- **Timestamps:** [2:15:33](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=8133) — MSS, FVG delivery, drop to half of first FVG; [2:17:08](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=8228) — first presented FVG at 9:31 used as bearish iFVG; [2:18:47](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=8327) — retest to CE to the tick; [2:19:34](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=8374) — correction of last week's mislabel
- **Nuance / caveats:** His reclaimed-vs-inversion sentence is hard to follow in the captions (caption unclear). Updates last week's live-stream labeling.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Premarket Concepts \ September 30, 2024
head: Opening range gap / new week opening gap as entry confluence  (aliases: ORG, NWOG, yellow box, purple dashes)
body:
- **Kind:** refinement
- **What ICT says:** The purple dashes are the new week opening gap (Friday settlement to Sunday 6:00 PM open); the yellow box is the opening-range gap (he describes it as Friday's settlement to today's open). Price opened in the lower quadrant of the ORG; once it trades below the ORG CE treat that midpoint as a premium and sell from there. He wanted price to drop, form a new candle, then return into the lower part of the ORG/NWOG overlap; a repeat touch of the first FVG or the ORG low is "not enough time" in the first hour.
- **How to use:** layer the first-presented FVG CE with the NWOG for the entry (as in the Caleb example).
- **Timestamps:** [0:47:40](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=2860) — NWOG marked; [1:37:31](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=5851) — ORG CE as premium; [2:04:41](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=7481) — wanted path through ORG low
- **Nuance / caveats:** ORG definition wording is loose in the captions.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Premarket Concepts \ September 30, 2024
head: The example trade plan for "Caleb" (entry, partial, stop)
body:
- **Kind:** example only
- **What ICT says:** Entry at the CE of the first presented FVG (inversion) with the NWOG lying over it; target the relative equal lows with a large portion (he says in your notes mark this as "first partial or majority" because you are in a decoupled market). The next target further down didn't pan out; you would be stopped when price went back into the first FVG. Annotating this as a trade, the profit taken happened at the relative equal lows and the remainder was stopped. He sticks to the rule that a return into the FVG/ORG low consumes too much of the 9:30–10:30 window so no re-entry.
- **Timestamps:** [2:27:14](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=8834) — entry at CE, target relative equal lows, notes on partial; [2:28:01](https://youtu.be/l7eu9yvUUtg?t=8881) — remainder stopped, stick to the rules
