head: Opening Range Gap (RTH opening gap) — high, midpoint (CE), quadrants, as initial draw  (aliases: "opening range gap", "mid gap", "new week opening gap" mentioned separately)
body:
- **Kind:** rule | refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - "Always starting the opening range with that initial bias": the first 30 minutes of the session he frames price toward the opening range gap midpoint, which he calls the "mid gap" (the consequent encroachment of the gap). It is "always the initial draw for the first 30 minutes."
  - The gap here was a discount-side gap: price had been trading below Friday's settlement ("we kept lower than Friday's settlement price"), so the mid gap (CE of the discount opening gap) is the upward objective. Full gap closure is above the mid gap; he also mentions upper and lower quadrants of the gap and the previous Friday settlement as further levels.
  - Captions give the opening range gap high at "2222.5", the mid gap near "2,179.5"/"21795" (garbled; consistent magnitude would be NQ ~20,xxx but the caption digits are unreliable — caption unclear). Do not use these numbers literally.
  - He keeps his bias to one side of the market: because he does not want to see it as a shorting opportunity, "if it goes lower it's going to go without me."
  - He notes price "traded back to the lower quadrant of the opening range gap" and later says any movement above the mid gap takes price to the new week opening gap low and its CE.
- **How to identify:** Mark the gap between the previous RTH close (settlement) and the 9:30 open; split into quadrants with the midpoint (CE) as the central target; note which side of the gap price is on relative to Friday's settlement.
- **How to use:** Use the mid gap as the initial draw on liquidity for the first 30 minutes; only take longs (in this bias) after a specific model sequence (see next concept); do not sell just because price drops below the gap or trades lower, unless other information provides a bearish read.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 7 Oct 2024. Bias: reach for the mid gap of the opening range gap. Price instead trades below, tags the minor sell side, bounces, spends the first 30 minutes (9:30–10:00) not reaching it, then later in the session rallies to the mid gap after tagging a volume imbalance low.
- **Timestamps:**
  - [0:01:39](https://youtu.be/DzJpkxI057g?t=99) — opening range gap high noted; "initial bias" starts here.
  - [0:09:53](https://youtu.be/DzJpkxI057g?t=593) — full gap closure vs. mid gap; "always the initial draw for the first 30 minutes."
  - [0:54:19](https://youtu.be/DzJpkxI057g?t=3259) — mid gap = CE; beyond it the next references are the new week opening gap low and its CE.
  - [1:01:44](https://youtu.be/DzJpkxI057g?t=3704) — keeps focus on the mid gap/CE of the discount opening gap; filters shorts.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** He says it does not need to be reached within the first 30 minutes for the bias to be valid; "by 10:00 ... I'm filtering": a failure to hit the target early does not flip the bias.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ NQ High Resistance Liquidity Conditions Tape Reading \ October 07, 2024
head: One-minute First Presented FVG + Inversion + Subsequent FVG entry model (opening range, tape-reading version)
body:
- **Kind:** entry model
- **What ICT says:** Entry conditions he sets for himself (and for "Caleb") on the 1-minute and 15-second charts:
  1. Identify the FIRST PRESENTED fair value gap on the one-minute chart formed in the opening range (the first FVG after 9:30; he defines the specific one by a candle's high and another candle's low).
  2. Wait for price to trade above that FVG, come back down, react off it (treat it as an inversion/support), and "displace higher."
  3. That displacement must leave a subsequent fair value gap (he looks for it on the 15-second chart).
  4. THAT subsequent FVG is the entry, "not just trading back into" the first one; trading into the first FVG and sitting in it is "not the entry."
  - Price "just can't be sitting in it and trade away from it." It has to displace away.
  - The entry is a run to the mid gap (opening range gap CE).
  - Optionally: after trading below it, price coming back up to treat it as inversion; displacing lower and creating an FVG on the 15-sec chart would be how he'd trade the afternoon short side if bearish, but he stresses he is not bearish now.
- **How to identify:** (a) first presented FVG on 1m marked; (b) price trades above, returns, reacts; (c) displacement higher; (d) fresh FVG on 15-sec; (e) all of this inside his one-sided bias.
- **How to use:** Enter at/in the new 15-sec FVG after the displacement, target the mid gap. No FVG = no trade. He says explicitly "no FVG formed, no trade, if/then or else."
- **Example in this video:** NQ 7 Oct 2024 — price gives "a little bit of a run" off the first presented FVG but no FVG forms on the 15-sec chart, so he does not trade; later he highlights that a 1m FVG formed around 9:31–10:00 (shaded orange) and that price traded above it without the required inversion + FVG sequence.
- **Timestamps:**
  - [0:18:25](https://youtu.be/DzJpkxI057g?t=1105) — first presented FVG on 1m, treat as inversion, subsequent FVG after that = entry.
  - [0:24:29](https://youtu.be/DzJpkxI057g?t=1469) — "that's the trade ... not the trade" (distinguishes entry from merely trading into the gap).
  - [0:32:45](https://youtu.be/DzJpkxI057g?t=1965) — wants an attempt to get back into the first presented FVG; if no run above, no inversion and no FVG = not touching it.
  - [0:36:57](https://youtu.be/DzJpkxI057g?t=2217) — "no fair value gap formed, no trade."
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** In low resistance conditions he says this would deliver precisely: price trades above the gap, comes back down touching it (maybe to the mid gap), displaces higher and creates an FVG on the 15-sec chart (that would be Caleb's setup). In high resistance that sequence is unlikely, so you do not force it.

head: Volume Imbalance as a magnet / "least rigid" PD array
body:
- **Kind:** refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - Volume imbalances "are the least in terms of rigidness" — price is expected to trade through them and then return above/below, not necessarily respect them hard. "I mentioned this to you many times that means you've got to let it trade through it, then come back above it."
  - In the example, he flagged a volume imbalance inside the move (5-minute volume imbalance) and said price could "spike down into that"; price did spike into it, making the very low of the volume imbalance — the candle's low hit 2163.25 (caption), the imbalance's boundary, i.e. a one-tick variance — then rallied to the mid gap.
  - He used the volume imbalance because, in high resistance conditions, price was not likely to come back down to the first presented FVG ("already proven ... the absence of precision"), so he redirected attention to a nearer inefficiency (the shaded volume imbalance) where bodies stopped and a small wick below it was "the damage," followed by a rally into the CE of the opening gap.
  - Relative equal highs were noted just above the imbalance as the next liquidity.
- **How to identify:** Open space between candle bodies where wicks overlap (volume imbalance); watch how closes (bodies) behave relative to it; look at the close/low of the candle that tags it.
- **How to use:** Use it as a nearby reference in high resistance when the "perfect" FVG is too far away; expect it to be traded through with a wick before the move.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 1m/5m, 7 Oct 2024, late in the morning: price rallies, makes relative equal highs, pulls back into a 5-minute volume imbalance, wicks to its low within one tick (around "2163.25" caption value), then rallies to the mid gap (CE).

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ NQ Tape Reading \ October 15, 2024
head: Overnight Range Grading (overnight range quadrants)  (aliases ICT uses: "grading" / "grading price", "overnight range", "the Fib on the overnight range", "defining the range")
body:
- **Kind:** new coinage / refinement (a specific, repeatable way to pre-locate PD arrays; he links it to price-grading teaching in the 2016/2017 mentorship)
- **What ICT says:**
  - Range is defined by time: midnight New York to 5:00 a.m. New York (12:01 to 4:59). Take the highest high and lowest low BETWEEN those two times. Do NOT count the midnight candle or the 5:00 a.m. candle.
  - Chart time zone must be New York local time; "if your time is set to anything other than that you're doing it wrong."
  - Draw a Fib from the high to the low (or low to high) with levels 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1. 0.5 = equilibrium; 0.25/0.75 = lower/upper quadrants. He draws these as dashed lines (to distinguish from the dotted quadrants of the daily SIBI).
  - Purpose: predicts the general location, "in close proximity", where PD arrays will form so you are not surprised by them.
  - ONLY use it when the overnight is part of a larger consolidation (price has been held inside the prior day's range, no new significant high/low). If the Asian session started running one-way and kept going (a "market protraction"/trend), do NOT use it; he has other tools for that but did not teach them here.
  - Applies to Forex as well as indices, not only stock index futures.
- **How to identify:** (1) Is overnight one-sided from Asia through London? If yes, skip. (2) If it is rotating inside yesterday's range, mark the 12:01–4:59 high/low, grade it.
- **How to use:**
  - First get a higher-timeframe bias. If bullish: look for PD arrays to form BELOW the graded levels (below equilibrium = discount; below the lower quadrant is even better); expect price to react at the lower levels and displace up away from them. Every bullish FVG below these gradient levels is "high probability."
  - If bearish: look for PD arrays forming just ABOVE the respective levels for shorts.
  - Upper half in a bullish day: do not expect pullbacks back to the low; the upper quadrant has "less degree of precision" because price is inclined to just rip through/clear the range high and keep going.
  - Use it before the 6:00 a.m. pre-market and act inside the macros (see Macros).
  - Extensions off the overnight range for targets/partials/reversals: first the -0.5 level, then -1 (one standard deviation).
  - If the bias flips (sentiment changes) everything inverts: bullish FVGs below become inversion FVGs, bullish order blocks become bearish order blocks, i.e. "market maker sell model" context.
  - If PD arrays you mark are not respecting price, that is manual intervention: sit on your hands.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 1m, Tue Oct 15, 2024. Bias bullish (election year, daily SIBI above). Overnight range 12:01–4:59 defined and graded. Price made the overnight low into ~4:30, turned up, then at ~5:08 swept down to the daily SIBI CE (see below) and reversed. Rally took out relative equal highs (minor BSL), into an inefficiency, then back down made an FVG below the overnight equilibrium (dash line) in the 5:50–6:10 macro; redelivered into it, ran up to overnight equilibrium, dropped to the lower quadrant, tapped the FVG, then ran above the minor BSL to the overnight upper quadrant (buy stops above the range high). Pullback from there made another FVG; a short-term low sat at equilibrium (SSL) with an FVG just below it = discount. At ~8:30 price spooled up; the upper-half action was less precise. Price then consolidated in the upper area below Monday Oct 14's daily high (BSL).
- **Timestamps:**
  - [0:08:58](https://youtu.be/HMn46vLjKvY?t=538) — defines the midnight-to-5:00 overnight range and excludes the boundary candles
  - [0:10:37](https://youtu.be/HMn46vLjKvY?t=637) — grading the range with Fib 0/.25/.5/.75/1
  - [0:12:12](https://youtu.be/HMn46vLjKvY?t=732) — do not use when market is trending overnight
  - [0:22:49](https://youtu.be/HMn46vLjKvY?t=1369) — why the FVG below equilibrium inside 5:50–6:10 qualifies
  - [0:36:07](https://youtu.be/HMn46vLjKvY?t=2167) — "an MO in the morning": grade overnight range, decide bull/bear, look for PDAs at the levels before 6:00
  - [1:00:12](https://youtu.be/HMn46vLjKvY?t=3612) — how to qualify FVGs: below the gradient levels while bullish = discount = high probability; scaling in
  - [1:04:11](https://youtu.be/HMn46vLjKvY?t=3851) — bias flip: everything inverts (bullish FVG -> iFVG, bullish OB -> bearish OB)
  - [1:05:00](https://youtu.be/HMn46vLjKvY?t=3900) — extensions -0.5 and -1 (one standard deviation)
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** He frames this as "how I pick the right fair value gaps": the qualification is premium/discount relative to a time-defined range, not chart patterns. He says there are other refinements but this is "the easiest go-to." It is not a standalone signal: bias comes first, time (macro) second, PD array location third.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ NQ Tape Reading \ October 15, 2024
head: Daily SIBI (Sell-side Imbalance Buy-side Inefficiency) as higher-timeframe draw, with quadrants and CE  (aliases: "civy"/"CBI" in captions = SIBI, "daily SIBI")
body:
- **Kind:** example only (with a rule on gradient levels)
- **What ICT says:** The objective since the 2024 mentorship started was to draw up into the daily SIBI formed around July 17, 2024 (a single down-close candle on the daily). Its range gets the same 0 / 0.25 / 0.5 / 0.75 / 1 grading as the overnight range, drawn as dotted lines. Levels quoted: low 20410, lower quadrant 20489, CE/midpoint 20568 (low printed 20567.75), upper quadrant ~20646.75. (High not stated; by symmetry roughly 20726 -- derived, not quoted.) Because he is bullish, price should react to these levels and displace away upward; "we're not trying to short."
  - Consequent encroachment of a gap/inefficiency is the midpoint of the gap; for an order block it would be the mean threshold. He clarifies this daily level is CE because it is an inefficiency.
  - Perfect delivery to a CE level: price trades ONE TICK BEYOND it (e.g. buy at 20568 CE requires price to trade at least one tick lower, 20567.75), because a smart-money buyer needs to be filled; so don't expect the exact CE tick to be the low.
  - Being inside the upper quadrant of the daily SIBI while bullish means consolidation is likely (don't over-expect expansion); price "rebalances" an old gap only when it leaves the range higher/lower after trading in, merely touching it is "redelivery", not rebalance.
- **How to use:** Treat daily-level quadrants/CE as targets/reaction points while you hunt for lower-timeframe PD arrays; do not abandon the bullish daily narrative because of a pullback on the intraday chart.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 1m, Oct 15: the ~5:08 sweep traded exactly to the daily SIBI CE, 20567.75, one tick under 20568, then reversed (during the 4:50–5:10 macro/Asia close). Later price swept relative equal highs, hit the upper quadrant of the daily SIBI, and Monday's high BSL sat above.
- **Timestamps:**

  - [0:17:53](https://youtu.be/HMn46vLjKvY?t=1073) — low of 20567.75 vs. CE 20568 explained on daily
  - [0:19:32](https://youtu.be/HMn46vLjKvY?t=1172) — "one tick below" for perfect delivery
  - [0:32:23](https://youtu.be/HMn46vLjKvY?t=1943) — touch vs. rebalance
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** The 4:50–5:10 window is called "Asia's close" and he describes a shift Asia -> London crossover -> NY pre-market; London "still active until around 11."

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ NQ Tape Reading \ October 15, 2024
head: Macros (algorithmic time windows) and why they exist  (aliases: "macro", "launch macro", "the 8:30 algo")
body:
- **Kind:** rule / definition (with rationale)
- **What ICT says:**
  - A macro runs from 50 minutes past the hour to 10 minutes past the next hour (a 20-minute window every hour). During it price "spools" to run liquidity or reach into an inefficiency.
  - Pre-market (6:00–9:30 ET) macros: 5:50–6:10, 6:50–7:10, 7:50–8:10, 8:50–9:10 = four, plus the 8:30 algo = five opportunities, "the equivalent of the last hour of trading" and not a coincidence.
  - 8:30 is separate: the algorithm "comes online" and runs price around for the first hour before 9:30 regardless of news; a medium/high-impact news release at 8:30 just exaggerates it. It creates a sentiment-driven response that gets traders chasing and revved up before the open ("cheerleader" analogy). He says there has never been a need for an economic calendar.
  - Why: large institutions (funds, insurers) must push big blocks through; they cannot dump an order at once. Their dealer feeds the order through in staggered pieces, targeting an average price, during these high-traffic windows. This is not what moves price direction; price goes where it goes and the order flow just prints as time and sales. He says the sensitive windows are more prone to deliver price because of increased order flow.
  - He explicitly rejects numerology/odd time numbers (e.g. "8:11") as irrelevant.
  - "Time has to be the time for the market to move, otherwise it will stay stagnant or retrace against you."
- **How to use:** Combine macro timing with the graded overnight range and bias; the pre-market (6:00–9:30) alone offers enough opportunities; you never need to trade the morning session, launch macro, PM session or last hour if you can't or don't want to.
- **Example in this video:** The Oct 15 FVG below overnight equilibrium formed in the 5:50–6:10 macro (the second retest at 5:55) and delivered up to equilibrium of the overnight range. 4:50–5:10 macro ended at the daily SIBI CE reversal.
- **Timestamps:**

  - [0:37:47](https://youtu.be/HMn46vLjKvY?t=2267) — counts the four pre-market macros plus 8:30

  - [1:30:48](https://youtu.be/HMn46vLjKvY?t=5448) — 8:30 is the outlier; dealers and order flow explanation
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** 6:00 a.m. is described as the changeover to the "pre-market" (6:00–9:30). Consistent with his statement elsewhere that the 8:30 algo is not news-dependent.

head: Opening Gap Size Filter (NY opening gap / RTH opening range gap size)  (aliases: "anemic gap", "opening range gap")
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:** In the 2024 mentorship he taught that a small RTH opening gap implies a lackluster, low-impact morning session, no easy run from entry to target. Today's gap (previous close 4:14 p.m. settlement vs. open) was "anemic" (numbers around 20631.75 vs ~20662.75 stated, caption unclear which is which).

  - With a tiny gap: no excitement/displacement at the open, so the morning delivery is 50/50. Sit still and wait for 10:00 (10:00–11:00 Silver Bullet) for an FVG that gives liquidity in line with bias; if it isn't clear, do nothing. Defer trading to lunch macro, PM session or last hour (e.g. come back at 1:30, watch the first 30 minutes into 2:00, trade PM; or sit down ~2:45 and trade the last hour).
- **Example in this video:** Oct 15 NQ: gap from the 4:14 p.m. close to the 9:30 open was too small to trade the opening; he waited for 10:00.

It sets up the initial direction/liquidity of the afternoon; price is likely to draw back into it. Like 8:30 and 9:30–10:00, "very specific elements of time" the algorithm always references.

head: Old Highs/Lows of Previous Days and Week -- "endless supply of setups" (not support/resistance)  (aliases: "daily highs and lows", "old highs and lows")
body:
- **Kind:** rule / example
- **What ICT says:**
  - Know each daily high and low of the last five days, at least last Friday's high/low, and the previous week's high and low. These are where order flow will come in; if bullish, wait for displacement.
  - He is not a support/resistance trader: price trading above an old high and returning to it does not mean it bounces from the line. He learned as a 20-year-old that textbook S/R doesn't reliably work that way.
  - Process (using last Thursday Oct 10 daily high): price rallies above the old high, dives back into the range, goes above again, drops again but does NOT take the relative equal lows (leaves the "bait"). That tells you it is unwilling to go lower; since you are already bullish ("in a buy program"), expect protraction higher. Do not buy just because it touched the level. Look for an inefficiency on the way down that acts as an inversion FVG; if it is good, price won't even touch it before leaving.
  - Assignment mindset: put the Oct 10 high on your own chart and watch how it gates above and returns; he leaves parts out deliberately for an interactive study.
- **Example in this video:** 30-second NQ chart, Mon Oct 14: price above the Thu Oct 10 daily high, back below, back above, below once more, then rallied; relative equal highs left behind (minor BSL). He went long on the inversion FVG formed on the drop, add-ons at the discount FVG at the 8:30 launch (see Volume Imbalances).
- **Timestamps:** [1:07:30](https://youtu.be/HMn46vLjKvY?t=4050) — yesterday's session; [1:09:59](https://youtu.be/HMn46vLjKvY?t=4199) — five days + last week's high/low = endless supply; [1:11:35](https://youtu.be/HMn46vLjKvY?t=4295) — watching how price gates above the old high; [1:13:08](https://youtu.be/HMn46vLjKvY?t=4388) — iFVG on the way down.

head: Volume Imbalance (the PD array he calls most flexible)  (aliases: "volume imbalances", "little separations between bodies")
body:
- **Kind:** definition / refinement
- **What ICT says:** A volume imbalance is the absence of overlap between one candle's body (open/close) and the next candle's body, with the wicks still touching, i.e. a tiny gap between bodies. It is "the most flexible" PD array in his repertoire: it measures whether price is willing to sustain a run; can be used as an entry, a partial, or for managing the stop. Its midpoint (CE) is also respected. Read the bodies, not the wicks: price "respecting" the imbalance between bodies is algorithmic delivery.
  - Timeframe: he used a 30-second chart because 15-second is "spotty" (too many volume imbalances) and 5-second gives too many to choose from; he wants a sub-1-minute chart with only a few imbalances. He stresses he is "a time-based price delivery trader," not a one-minute/five-minute chart trader.
  - An FVG below a volume imbalance on a bullish day is in discount and valid for entry.
- **How to use:** Enter as price trades down into the imbalance (when the candle is trading against your direction), not after the candle has started going your way; add more if price is inside the imbalance and runs away; use a limit order if you want a finer entry. Risk: he must keep a stop loss in every execution, being managed.
- **Example in this video:** See execution review below.
- **Timestamps:** [1:13:55](https://youtu.be/HMn46vLjKvY?t=4435) — body-to-body definition; [1:16:19](https://youtu.be/HMn46vLjKvY?t=4579) — "look at the bodies"; [1:21:03](https://youtu.be/HMn46vLjKvY?t=4863) — why 30-second; [1:21:52](https://youtu.be/HMn46vLjKvY?t=4912) — fewer imbalances = better timeframe.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ How To Navigate Decoupled Markets \ October 16, 2024
head: Decoupled Markets (index averages not in agreement)  (aliases: "decoupling", "mixed direction on all three averages")
body:
- **Kind:** rule / new coinage (market-condition filter)
- **What ICT says:**
  - For stock-index trading all three averages (NQ, ES, YM/Dow) should be moving in the same direction. If you trade NQ and want to be long, you want to see support for the idea from ES and Dow as well, "all three bullish".
  - Decoupling is common when no news is due that morning. It makes precision harder; you trade at lower probability. He has traded it, but a new trader/new student should not.
  - Reading price becomes "fuzzy", "out of focus": candles overlap the previous candle's range, a lot of revisiting of the same prices (seen in ES) versus the clean, refined ranges and imbalances in NQ.
  - Choices when decoupled: (1) sit and wait for the averages to come into agreement and move in tandem (sometimes within the same session, sometimes only after the morning, so the afternoon becomes better); (2) worst case they stay decoupled all day and are very problematic, tradable only by very short-term scalpers, which he does not teach.
  - Even when price still delivers to PD arrays and liquidity, that does not make it a high-probability trade; delivery to the sell side happened and still "shouldn't have" been traded.
  - Write in your notes: as soon as you see decoupling, expect an SMT-type divergence later in the session after which they go back in sync.
- **How to identify:** compare the three charts; Dow going one way while ES and NQ do something else; on 10/16 at 9:00 ES dropped while Dow went higher and NQ also dropped (so NQ and ES shared direction briefly but Dow did not).
- **How to use:** Be extra selective; treat these days as observation/teaching; "give yourself permission" to let a trade pan out without you when precision is unlikely; accept some days offer no low-risk entry or no entry at all. If instead all three were in agreement, price returned to the first presented FVG and then showed displacement, "then it's easy": drop to a 15-second chart and take the next FVG in that direction.
- **Example in this video:** NQ/ES/YM 1m, Wed Oct 16, 2024 AM session. Dow was going higher/consolidating ("unruly brat"), NQ weak, ES shrugging off weakness. Opening range gap anemic again. NQ took sell side, never traded back up into its first presented FVG initially, then after the sell side run made a lower low while ES held and returned into the range.
- **Timestamps:**
  - [0:06:46](https://youtu.be/xUWonBnfYOk?t=406) — first spots the decoupling; why you shouldn't try it as a new student
  - [0:07:34](https://youtu.be/xUWonBnfYOk?t=454) — all three averages should move together; trading NQ wants ES and Dow agreeing
  - [0:12:11](https://youtu.be/xUWonBnfYOk?t=731) — two options: wait for agreement or accept all-day decoupling
  - [1:02:44](https://youtu.be/xUWonBnfYOk?t=3764) — definition and note to write down
  - [1:05:13](https://youtu.be/xUWonBnfYOk?t=3913) — loss of resolution in NQ and ES when Dow decouples
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** He notes many wanted to see "NQ-only" focus; he prefers NQ for volatility (only 100 stocks vs ES's 500, "more exaggerated"), calling ES slower; he explained this to students who ask why he never talks about ES. He admits he gets it wrong "a lot" when decoupled.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ How To Navigate Decoupled Markets \ October 16, 2024
head: SMT Divergence between NQ and ES (Dow excluded)  (aliases: "SMT", "unwillingness to go lower", "shrugging off weakness")
body:
- **Kind:** refinement / example
- **What ICT says:**
  - When NQ makes a lower low and ES fails to make a lower low, that is SMT divergence and signals the bulls' side: price will return up into its range. Called "shrugging off any weakness" = failing to take the sell side.
  - He forecast it before it happened: "if es fails to shrug off ... I'm sorry, if it fails and shrugs off weakness, that means it fails to drop down", then NQ would go back into its range and return to the first presented FVG.
  - He does NOT count the Dow in SMT: the Dow's 30 stocks "are not that impactful overall." If Dow makes a lower low and ES does not, he doesn't consider that SMT. Normally the Dow bends to the will of ES and NQ ("all boats rise in high tide"); when it doesn't, that is the decoupling signal.
  - Conditions for return to agreement: Dow either holds/consolidates or keeps going higher (doesn't lose ground), ES fails to make a lower low, NQ makes the lower low then comes back into its range.
- **How to use:** Used as the catalyst for the long-side (return into range) and to decide where to anchor risk. Also it conditions the iFVG: if ES refuses to go lower, the NQ FVG that forms below becomes an inversion FVG.
- **Example in this video:** NQ took its sell side (a small low), went a little under it to make a lower low, ES stopped above its low ("low here at 9:51" caption unclear), NQ then returned up above the sell side into the opening range gap/first presented FVG.
- **Timestamps:**
  - [0:38:23](https://youtu.be/xUWonBnfYOk?t=2303) — "sets the stage for SMT divergence" explanation
  - [0:39:11](https://youtu.be/xUWonBnfYOk?t=2351) — how the indices could come back into agreement
  - [0:56:03](https://youtu.be/xUWonBnfYOk?t=3363) — "I forecasted an SMT divergence before it happened"
  - [1:06:00](https://youtu.be/xUWonBnfYOk?t=3960) — recap; Dow excluded from SMT at [1:07:35](https://youtu.be/xUWonBnfYOk?t=4055)

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ How To Navigate Decoupled Markets \ October 16, 2024
head: Inversion FVG entry: entering before it "proves itself"  (aliases: "iFVG", "inversion fair value gap", "breakaway gap")
body:
- **Kind:** entry model / refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - A bearish FVG (formed on the way down, an imbalance in the down leg) becomes an inversion FVG when price trades back up through it while bullish. Here he pointed out the FVG in NQ was bearish and might invert because ES would not go lower.
  - Caveat: if the market is very strong, price can accumulate in/near it and "run right out" without ever coming back down to touch it (it then acts like a breakaway gap). He says he has no rule for knowing when that happens; it's an experience "knack". "I don't know how to teach that" (a limitation as a mentor).
  - His workaround when convicted bullish: enter INSIDE the iFVG as price first touches the candle that enters it (top of the candle/gap), or at the CE of the gap and watch the bodies at that midpoint. First 6 contracts at that level, and a further 4 if price drops to the gap's high (the low of the candle). He would rather do that than wait for price to leave and come back ("last to the dance floor"), because sometimes there is no second chance and you miss both the fill and the pyramid.
  - If very bullish, why wait to buy a retrace after price has moved away? Take the cheap price inside the iFVG.
  - Also wanted the gap above to "stay open" (preferably unfilled) as that fuels a run (breakaway) rather than a pullback.
- **How to identify:** look for the down-leg inefficiency (bearish FVG/volume imbalance) that price subsequently trades above after a sell-side run + SMT; mark the midpoint (CE); watch candle bodies open/close at that midpoint.
- **How to use:** Entry at the first touch of the iFVG's top or at the CE; add on a return to the gap's other edge; objective: first presented FVG and the opening range gap / buy side above; stop below the low (he said no entry for shorts as no way to frame risk).
- **Example in this video:** NQ 1m, Oct 16, after the sell side was taken and the lower low printed, price reclaimed back into the range, traded up through the bearish FVG; later he noted a bearish order block (two consecutive up-closed candles) price traded back into, and the bodies landed on the CE. Price never returned to touch the iFVG; the gap stayed open and price broke away higher, so the "second entry" didn't occur. Objective was the first presented FVG, plus the buy side/old highs above.
- **Timestamps:**
  - [0:39:59](https://youtu.be/xUWonBnfYOk?t=2399) — enters at the candle that touches the iFVG; 6 contracts then 4
  - [0:40:46](https://youtu.be/xUWonBnfYOk?t=2446) — it may just run away; no rule for when
  - [0:45:43](https://youtu.be/xUWonBnfYOk?t=2743) — "last to the dance floor" argument; midpoint where bodies deliver
  - [1:09:09](https://youtu.be/xUWonBnfYOk?t=4149) — recap of iFVG and why he wanted the gap to stay open
  - [0:59:30](https://youtu.be/xUWonBnfYOk?t=3570) — "I'll enter it at the candle's high; if not, at the CE" as a breakaway gap
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Extends the 10/15 point that FVGs in discount qualify; here the iFVG is the entry and the caution is about whether price returns. The 6 + 4 contract split repeats his scaling style from M24-044. He says he wouldn't teach what he can't explain to his kids.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ How To Navigate Decoupled Markets \ October 16, 2024
head: First Presented FVG + Opening Range Gap as objective  (aliases: "first presented fair value gap", "opening range gap", "gap closure")
body:

Price delivered to sell side without trading back up into the first presented FVG, then later reached back up to it (after SMT). Opening gap here was again "anemic" (settlement price vs. open drawn on RTH view). He wanted the FVG to remain open so price could go back into the opening range gap and first presented FVG, and buy side above (ES: two highs, one lower than another).
- **Example in this video:** NQ 1m 9:30–10:30. First FVG formed near the opening range gap area. Price took sell side, made a lower low, returned into the opening range ("two blue lines"), then up to the first presented FVG, with bodies respecting it ("completely random isn't it? no it's coded"). Phil's request to do it before 10:30 is just the time boundary of the stream.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ How To Navigate Decoupled Markets \ October 16, 2024
head: Bodies vs. Wicks: CE of wicks, volume imbalance, and body behavior inside FVGs  (aliases: "bodies stay at consequent encroachment", "wicks do the damage")
body:
- **Kind:** refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - In a clean FVG/order block the candle BODIES stay at the consequent encroachment or on one side of it; the wicks are allowed to do the "damage". If bodies stay out of the gap, the level is respected.
  - Volume imbalance: price body stops at the high of the imbalance/at the open, doesn't breach it; when a body starts in an imbalance and leaves without coming back that is weakness.
  - Marking the midpoint (CE) of a gap or wick with a rectangle highlights where to watch bodies.
  - Time-based candles (open/high/low/close) are the "advantage": range bars, Renko, Heikin-Ashi hide the algorithm and hide intervention; "price is the same price on any timeframe."
- **Example in this video:** NQ 1m (about 9:45–10:00): bodies of a pair of bearish-order-block candles settle at the CE of the gap; the wick pierces CE ("damage"), then price rotates out of a volume imbalance toward sell side.
- **Timestamps:** [0:14:38](https://youtu.be/xUWonBnfYOk?t=878) — bodies stay at CE or lower; [0:37:35](https://youtu.be/xUWonBnfYOk?t=2255) — body stops at the volume-imbalance high; [0:46:29](https://youtu.be/xUWonBnfYOk?t=2789) — bodies close/open at the midpoint; time-based candles advantage.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ How To Navigate Decoupled Markets \ October 16, 2024
head: Change in State of Delivery (CISD) via the open of consecutive up-closed candles  (aliases: "change in a state of delivery", "order block")
body:
- **Kind:** definition / example
- **What ICT says:** When price has been delivering with two (or more) consecutive up-closed candles (buy-side delivery), use the OPEN of the lowest/first of those up-closed candles as the reference. A move back below that open = change in the state of delivery (price was delivering higher, now delivers lower). He ties it to an order block ("your order block or change in state of delivery").
- **Example in this video:** NQ 1m ~9:35–9:40 ET: two consecutive up-close candles; open of the lowest is the CISD line; price returned to it, traded lower, then delivered to the low of a candle with a 1-tick overshoot (levels read as ~20,37x, caption unclear).
- **Timestamps:** [0:22:49](https://youtu.be/xUWonBnfYOk?t=1369) — CISD defined as the opening price of the lowest of the consecutive up candles; [0:23:38](https://youtu.be/xUWonBnfYOk?t=1418) — perfect delivery to candle low plus one tick.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** "Plus one tick per spread" — he mentions spread as the reason price trades one tick past the exact level (consistent with the "one tick beyond CE" idea from M24-044).

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ News Release Tape Reading \ October 17, 2024
head: News drivers: trade the price reaction, never the data  (aliases: "news release tape reading", "smoke screen")
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - The numbers in high/medium impact reports are "already baked in"; trying to infer intraday volatility from what the data "fundamentally means" is useless. Markets often do the opposite of what data suggests; he learned this in the 1990s.
  - "Price is going to tell me everything I need to know, and if I'm wrong, price will tell me." Do not put your opinion on what the data suggests.
  - News events at 8:30 are a "smoke screen": sometimes they help run price into a layer of liquidity he has already outlined; other times they drop price to make everyone think sentiment is bearish and then at the 9:30 open they make the run up. Either way, watch what price does at 8:30 and then judge the open.
  - With a single report at 8:30, the first run is usually the Judas swing. With MULTIPLE reports at 8:30 (as today), the initial rally or decline is staggered ("feels like it's done, it's not"); give it a couple of seconds, there may be another impulse, and give it a chance to take both sides of the marketplace.
  - Normally he likes to hold a position before the 9:30 open on a high/medium impact news day, but today there was nothing he would have entered on, so he sat still.
- **How to use:** On a news day, outline liquidity pools beforehand, observe the 8:30 delivery, mark the range/volume imbalances created, and decide on the plan for 9:30 from that.
- **Example in this video:** NQ, 17 Oct 2024. The 8:30 reports "didn't do very much"; price stayed in a range created at 8:30 (this low not taken, this high not broken) with wicks and volume imbalances; "nothing in here that I would want to be buying."
- **Timestamps:**
  - [0:08:08](https://youtu.be/z2t62hgjLXo?t=488) — hold plan / election-year bias; [0:09:00](https://youtu.be/z2t62hgjLXo?t=540) — news as smoke screen
  - [0:10:39](https://youtu.be/z2t62hgjLXo?t=639) — data is baked in; "never interested in what the data is suggesting"
  - [0:18:52](https://youtu.be/z2t62hgjLXo?t=1132) — multiple 8:30 reports: staggered moves; Judas swing is the first run only when there is one report
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Consistent with his long-standing line that fundamentals are not used for intraday direction; the new detail is the "multiple reports = staggered impulses" observation.

head: Draw on liquidity: nested relative equal highs and prior-day high as targets
body:
- **Kind:** example | rule
- **What ICT says:** On the daily chart there is sell-side liquidity "still building underneath" and buy side above, including Tuesday 15 Oct's daily high. On the 60-minute chart the area is "too clean" (begging to be run). He anticipates a run up to the "640s at the minimum," then Tuesday's high (caption: 20,659), then a higher high (caption: ~680) — digits are caption-derived. On the 15-minute chart he points to "two nested relative equal highs" (a high, then a higher-but-nearly-equal high, then a high above both): when the targets are that obvious, "it's easy to just side with that as the initial draw until price proves it's not interested," which he reads at 8:30.
- **How to use:** Treat obvious relative equal highs as the initial draw. Ignore nearer minor buy-side (the "first pass up here I would completely ignore that") and focus on the two relative equal highs. If price runs through them it can visit the next high; alternatively it can only reach the consequent encroachment of the range between the relative equal highs and the high above (about halfway) and then roll over to take relative equal lows.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 15m, 17 Oct: price consolidates after 8:30; ICT wants an up move to the CE of the relative-equal-highs-to-next-high range; wicks do reach that CE but candle bodies stop below it ("bodies respecting the level while the wicks are tossed above it"), and then price snaps down. He wanted it to come back down, disrupt the lows, and work down into a volume imbalance, and said he would NOT be interested in being long yet.
- **Timestamps:** [0:06:34](https://youtu.be/z2t62hgjLXo?t=394) — 60-min "too clean"; [0:09:49](https://youtu.be/z2t62hgjLXo?t=589) — nested relative equal highs; [0:24:28](https://youtu.be/z2t62hgjLXo?t=1468) — ignore minor buy side, focus on two equal highs; [0:31:59](https://youtu.be/z2t62hgjLXo?t=1919) — CE of range between REH and higher high works; [0:32:48](https://youtu.be/z2t62hgjLXo?t=1968) — wicks vs bodies "horseshoes" analogy.
- **Nuance:** Wicks tag a level while bodies decline to close beyond it — he calls this the horseshoe-tossing idea (orders tossed around a general area; bodies show real acceptance). He jokes that the correct read of the CE reaction looked like "time travel."

body:
- **Kind:** example only (with entry-model content)

The breakout above the high is "going to be long above this high" — and he loves seeing false breaks in London where breakout traders would get in long or short: because it is an election year the market is predisposed higher, so breakout buyers buy the high, price runs down and stops them out, then takes the market higher again ("ripping their guts out") — "beautiful setup." What he waits for: does the market give him the chance to get in while price is dropping into an obvious discount array? The consolidation before looks like first-stage accumulation. He enters in the fair value gap (bid-side/BISI efficiency, volume imbalance included) as price approaches the 4:50–5:10 ET macro (caption "450 to 510 macro"), accumulating an early position.

head: Volume Imbalance — how to draw it when there are indecisive candles (new refinement)
body:
- **Kind:** refinement (drawing rule)
- **What ICT says:** When a fair value gap is accompanied by two candles with small bodies/indecisive (open ≈ close) next to it, the naive way to frame the inefficiency is not accurate enough. The correct framing: use the LOWEST open/close (the lowest body price) among those candles — here the same price as the low of the volume imbalance — and extend the zone from there across the whole group so it covers the gap and the volume imbalances entirely. "It's not technically wrong but it's not as accurate as it needs to be." Then you can use the consequent encroachment of that zone. Reason: with indecisive candles there are many reasons for price to drop into the volume imbalances, and it would otherwise overshoot the standard FVG you assumed would be used.
- **How to identify:** An FVG sitting next to doji-like/indecisive candles; take the extreme body price (lowest open/close) as the boundary.
- **How to use:** Draw from the lowest body price, then use CE of the whole inefficiency as the reference.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 5m, ~8:30 range: below the lows there is an FVG plus two small-body candles; he draws the zone from the lowest open/close (same as the low of the volume imbalance) up over the cluster.
- **Timestamps:** [0:20:26](https://youtu.be/z2t62hgjLXo?t=1226) — "something you've never learned about"; [0:21:13](https://youtu.be/z2t62hgjLXo?t=1273) — use lowest body, then CE.
- **Nuance:** Presented as new material ("something you've never learned about").

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ News Release Tape Reading \ October 17, 2024
head: Volume Imbalance — behavior, the "paint roller" analogy, and when it becomes a Balanced Price Range  (aliases: "most flexible PD array")
body:
- **Kind:** definition | rule | refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - The volume imbalance is "the most flexible PD array" — it is normal for price to go through it back and forth. Just because it is there does not mean it stops price to the tick. You cannot demand the precision you expect from a bullish FVG's CE or high.
  - First expectation: price trades THROUGH it. A body gets laid over it.
  - How it gains meaning: the imbalance is created between two candle bodies (an up candle's close and the next candle's open). If an up-closed candle goes through that range (buy-side delivery) and later a down-closed candle lays a body over the same range (sell-side delivery), then both sides have delivered and it is "efficiently delivered." He then treats it as a (small) Balanced Price Range, and the imbalance becomes more meaningful. He says he does not hang much on tiny, insignificant ones.
  - Paint roller analogy: roll paint onto a wall; the first foot delivers ample paint, then pockets appear as paint runs out; you roll back over to fill the pockets. Price does the same inside a volume imbalance — delivers one direction first, then returns to deliver the other side.
  - After both sides have delivered and price leaves it, the balanced price range acts as a DISCOUNT array (support) if price returns to it from above; as a premium array if the reverse. If long, you can roll your stop loss to just below that volume imbalance, because "it's done its work in framing out a balanced price range."
  - Contrast: a volume imbalance with NO body ever laid over it — only wicks — behaves like a breakaway gap: price traverses it with a wick and rips away in the same candle; this is not the same as being delivered on both sides. "Two different dynamics."
  - It is not "liquidity" in itself; the buy-side/sell-side delivery means the market has been offered on the up and the down, not that stops are resting there.
  - Practical: annotate the volume imbalances inside the 8:30 delivery range, extend them to the right, and keep referring to them while price is inside that range. One example is not enough; collect many instances in your charts.
  - Management: he often uses volume imbalances to start positioning (as in London); then when time (a macro) kicks in and price displaces and "spools" toward the target, he can use the volume imbalance again as a new entry or as a way to manage the stop. It needs management ("a little bit of management is required").
  - He criticizes people who teach volume imbalances improperly or monetize his material without fully understanding it.
- **How to identify:** (1) Find the gap between two candles' bodies with overlapping wicks; (2) check whether later candles have laid bodies over it from above (sell-side) and below/through it (buy-side); (3) both delivered then left behind = BPR; wicks only = breakaway-gap-like.
- **How to use:** Don't demand a tick-precise reaction; let it trade through then come back; use a delivered one as support/discount and trail your stop beneath it; use as an entry when the macro time kicks in.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 1m/5m, 8:30–9:00 ET range 17 Oct 2024: a bullish body was buried in one volume imbalance (buy-side delivery), later a down-close candle laid over it (sell-side delivery) — he calls it efficiently delivered/BPR (small); price then went back above it, and he wanted price not to dip back below. A second volume imbalance had only wicks (a single candle traversed it down and back up) — treated like a breakaway gap, not delivered.
- **Timestamps:** [0:34:26](https://youtu.be/z2t62hgjLXo?t=2066) — extend 8:30 volume imbalances; "most flexible PD array"; [0:35:15](https://youtu.be/z2t62hgjLXo?t=2115) — bodies laid over it; [0:37:34](https://youtu.be/z2t62hgjLXo?t=2254) — paint roller analogy; [0:40:49](https://youtu.be/z2t62hgjLXo?t=2449) — BPR on discount basis, roll stop below; [0:41:36](https://youtu.be/z2t62hgjLXo?t=2496) — wick-only imbalance = breakaway gap.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Refines the earlier statement (repeated in the Oct 7 video) that volume imbalances are the least rigid; adds a criterion for when they gain weight (both-side body delivery) and a stop-management use.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ News Release Tape Reading \ October 17, 2024
head: Staying still when the algorithm is "held in a range" / manual intervention
body:
- **Kind:** rule (execution/psychology)
- **What ICT says:** When price holds a range (low not taken, high not broken, many wicks, volume imbalances, no cleanness) it is a holding pattern: the "algorithm" is not doing anything; "the hands in there" are stirring the pot. Sit still. You are competing against an entity that can take both sides of the market and still go nowhere, and by entering you relinquish your "power of stillness" and are at the mercy of the outcome. This is manual intervention (repricing) by the market maker rather than the algorithm running on script. Observation/tape reading is what you do before you even use a demo/paper account: study what you feel and how you perceive price, and look for signatures that the algorithm is on script vs. interfered with.
- **Timestamps:** [0:29:31](https://youtu.be/z2t62hgjLXo?t=1771) — holding pattern; [0:30:21](https://youtu.be/z2t62hgjLXo?t=1821) — power of stillness; [0:31:11](https://youtu.be/z2t62hgjLXo?t=1871) — tape reading precedes demo trading.
- **Nuance:** If price takes off without you, "it left without me; it's fine ... I'll catch the next bus stop."

head: Opening Range Gap 50% (mid gap) probability, and Judas swing scenario planning for 9:30  (aliases: "RTH opening gap", "gap closure", "premium gap")
body:
- **Kind:** rule | refinement
- **What ICT says:**
  - Reference points: yesterday's 4:14 PM ET RTH settlement (he says "4:14 p.m. eastern time ... in regular trading hours" — the last RTH reference) versus the 9:30 opening price; set charts to RTH so the opening range gap shows. Price pre-open was at roughly 20,545 (caption "4 545"), about two handles from settlement.
  - Drop a Fib on the gap: the 50% level is a "70% likelihood in the first 30 minutes" that price trades there. (This is the one quantified claim.)
  - If price gaps higher at the open (a premium gap), the likelihood of coming down to 50% of the gap is high; that would run below the lows of the 8:30 range and into the inefficiency below, and retail would be reluctant to be long on that; then he could switch gears and work toward the higher-time-frame buy-side draw.
  - What he wants before the open: price staying close to the 8:30 range, "hugging around it," not running up; then a small initial Judas swing higher at 9:30 taking a short-term high left before the bell, then a drop to a discount to trade to half the gap range.
  - Counter-scenario: if price gets above 600 (caption; likely 20,600) before the open, he'd be less likely to expect a full or half gap closure before higher; instead the Judas swing would be the run between ~600 and ~660 at the open, sweeping that, and then a sell-off to a gap-closure event: mid gap or 3/4 of gap closure.
  - He does not know the opening price until 9:30, so he gives the scenarios; the opening price "tells the story" for which scenario applies, and sets his draw on liquidity and setup.
  - Also: Judas swing "9:30 into 9:45" is the window he expects.
  - He stresses to students that he is not saying "up is right and down is right"; his stated preference is that price does not run up yet; if it does, he is wrong, and he would not chase.
- **How to use:** Compute the RTH settlement-to-9:30-open gap; 50% line is the expected first-30-minute target; adjust by where price is at the open and whether it has already run to the next liquidity.
- **Timestamps:** [0:44:14](https://youtu.be/z2t62hgjLXo?t=2654) — premium gap in the making; [0:46:36](https://youtu.be/z2t62hgjLXo?t=2796) — 50% = 70% likelihood first 30 minutes; [0:47:23](https://youtu.be/z2t62hgjLXo?t=2843) — if >600 pre-open, less likely to fill; [0:49:00](https://youtu.be/z2t62hgjLXo?t=2940) — Judas swing 600–660 then sell-off to mid-gap / 3/4 closure.
- **Nuance:** Garbled price digits; treat levels as approximate. The "70%" figure is stated once; no source or test cited.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Premarket Tape Reading NQ Futures \ October 21, 2024
head: Opening Range Gap (previous RTH settlement to 9:30 open): how to mark it
body:
- **Kind:** definition | how-to
- **What ICT says:**
  - Switch the chart from electronic trading hours (ETH) to regular trading hours (RTH) to find the previous day's settlement. On the 1-minute chart, the last RTH candle is the 4:14 ET candle (it settles at 4:14; there is no 4:15 candle because RTH is closed). On a 5-minute chart the 4:10 candle is displayed instead, which is why he tells you to drop to the 1-minute chart to read the exact close/open when marking any gap (new week or new day).
  - Previous day for Monday is always the previous Friday (unless Friday was a holiday; then use the last settlement).
  - Label convention: always label by the day you are trading, not the date of the data: on Monday it is "Monday's opening range gap high/low", not "Friday's." Until the 9:30 first print you do not know which side is high/low: if the market opens BELOW the prior settlement, the settlement is the opening range gap HIGH and the 9:30 open is the gap LOW (discount gap). If price travels back above it before 9:30 (here he notes it would have to traverse over 100 handles), relabel: the settlement becomes the low and the 9:30 first print the high.
  - Trading sessions context: ETH resumes Sunday 6:00 p.m. ET; Friday ETH stops at 5:00 p.m. ET.
- **How to identify:** Previous day RTH close (1m, 4:14 ET) to today's 9:30 first print.
- **How to use:** Mark the settlement now; pre-open label it provisionally; once the 9:30 open prints, set the FIB across the gap and take the 50% level (see below).
- **Example in this video:** NQ, Monday 21 Oct 2024: Friday's RTH settlement line (caption value ~20,494.25) annotated in black as "Monday's opening range gap high"; pre-market price ~20,39x (caption: "20,39 even") below it, so it is a prospective discount gap.
- **Timestamps:** [0:05:08](https://youtu.be/CQk-5lAirn0?t=308) — ETH vs RTH toggle; [0:05:55](https://youtu.be/CQk-5lAirn0?t=355) — use the 1-minute chart, 4:14 last candle; [0:10:57](https://youtu.be/CQk-5lAirn0?t=657) — labeling convention and relabel scenario.
- **Nuance / caveats:** Price digits in the captions are inconsistent; do not rely on them. Reinforces the Oct 7 and Oct 17 videos ("mid gap" = 50% of this gap).

head: Session highs and lows as the default draw on liquidity (no-news protocol)  (aliases: "previous session highs and lows", "four opportunities per day")
body:
- **Kind:** rule | entry-framing model
- **What ICT says:**
  - When there is no significant data (empty economic calendar, no volatility injection at 8:30), aim for session highs and lows: the high/low of London, Asia, the previous day's PM session and AM session (not just the daily high/low). Four sessions per day = four chances to frame a setup: Asian, London, NY AM, NY PM. He does NOT want people trading every session, but if your schedule allows, tape-reading them all makes you a well-rounded trader.
  - It also applies on news days; it is just his "usual reach."
  - Use these finite reference points ("not something that's always morphing") to anticipate where the next premium/discount array forms, including pre-market without being present for the bell.
  - London's range: use the "overnight dealing range" (taught last week). Midnight NY time is the true day open; the London killzone is 2:00–5:00 a.m. ET; the highest high and lowest low in that window are the London session high/low (the algorithm looks for liquidity and PD arrays in that window). If price is in a clean protraction in one direction, don't grade the range; if there is a consolidation, grade it.
  - Which buy side matters? He asks which is more likely the draw for the morning: the London session high (a cluster of relative equal "smooth" highs) or a single nearby candle high. His answer: the London session high is the more salient; the single-candle high is a minor objective on the way, and he wants to see price accelerate through it to reach the London session high ("before they take their stops out").
  - The NY AM window referenced: 9:30 to 11:00 (London close) going into noon.
  - Applies equally to Forex, bonds, currency futures: "time is universal" across asset classes except crypto (he has not investigated crypto) and he has no experience with the Nifty 50.
  - On any day, these references mean "you'll never run out of setups," including on high resistance liquidity run days; on low resistance days they are "absolute bangers" for easy low-hanging objectives.
- **How to identify:** Mark Asian, London, previous NY AM/PM highs/lows; annotate relative equal highs/lows; Thursday's/Wednesday's Asian lows can be older sell-side targets (he shows Thursday 17 Oct's Asian session sell-side low, at about 8:30 p.m. ET, and Wednesday's Asian session SSL with relative equal lows).
- **How to use:** Pick the nearest significant session level on the side of your bias, framed with the opening range gap and the 9:30–10:00 window. Annotate minor liquidity thinly (ghosted) and the major reference levels bold, so your eye goes to the impactful level; minor buy side "top left" is noted as a stop-trail level of shorts.
- **Example in this video:** NQ 5m, Mon 21 Oct pre-market: Thursday's opening range gap low and Thursday's Asian session sell-side lie below; the London session high (relative equal highs) is above; the current range between a minor high and minor low is "either it stays in the range or runs for the buy side or the sell side."
- **Timestamps:** [0:13:22](https://youtu.be/CQk-5lAirn0?t=802) — session highs/lows when no data; [0:15:00](https://youtu.be/CQk-5lAirn0?t=900) — four sessions per day; [0:19:49](https://youtu.be/CQk-5lAirn0?t=1189) — midnight true day, London killzone 2–5 a.m., London high/low; [0:21:32](https://youtu.be/CQk-5lAirn0?t=1292) — which buy side is the real draw.
- **Nuance / caveats:** Forms the bridge between the "overnight dealing range" (last week) and the opening range gap rule below.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Premarket Tape Reading NQ Futures \ October 21, 2024
head: Opening Range Gap 50% rule — discount gap = bullish first 30 minutes  (aliases: "mid gap", "half gap", "gap closure", "70% likelihood")
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - If the market opens at 9:30 BELOW the previous RTH settlement (a discount gap), the bias for 9:30–10:00 ET is bullish, expecting at least 50% of the gap's range to be traded to. He states there is a "70% likelihood of half the gap being traded to during the first 30 minutes of trading, 9:30 to 10:00 Eastern."
  - The 50% level does not make the bias bearish afterward: "it just means that 70% of the time that's what's usually unfolding." If it does not reach 50% within 30 minutes, he still looks for it later; this is an immediate bias to study/tape-read, not a guarantee.
  - Implementation: take the first 9:30 print as the gap low, drop the Fib to the previous settlement (gap high), read the 50% level. (He says this is for a gap lower; the converse for a premium gap is implied but not restated here.)
  - Beyond 50%: price could go to a full gap closure or 3/4 gap closure; the 50% level is the minimum expectation.
  - "I'm never ever ever going in there on the basis of simply 'I'm going to go short because we open lower'" — worst thing to do, retail-minded.
  - Hypothetical he builds: assume the next tick opens at ~20,408 (caption "408", also rendered "20,480" — caption unclear; likely 20,40x given pre-market ~20,39x), annotated as Monday's opening range gap low; the Fib to the gap high (caption "494 and A4" ≈ 20,494.25) gives a 50% level near the top of the London relative equal highs, so the mid gap AND the London session high buy side agree as the draw.
- **How to identify:** (a) 9:30 open below prior RTH settlement; (b) measure the gap; (c) 50% level; (d) check what session highs lie in the path.
- **How to use:** Be long-biased until the 50% is traded; look for a partial near the first session high/relative equal highs, but aim for the draw above if the relative equal highs sit close to the 50% level, because the other half of the gap remains (3/4 or full closure). Use "any fair value gap, the first presented fair value gap" for the entry; if it wins, you're done; if it loses, don't do it again, sit still.
- **Example in this video (hypothetical, not a live trade):** NQ 21 Oct 2024: if price opens ~20,40x, 9:30–10:00 bias is long; first target the 50% level; pre-open he suggests a "modest little tiny Judas swing lower" taking out a short-term 1-minute low after 9:30, then a rally to attack the London session highs/mid gap. If instead price sells off first and takes out the London low, he'd look for a change in direction and then target the London session high.
- **Timestamps:** [0:26:21](https://youtu.be/CQk-5lAirn0?t=1581) — hypothetical open and gap labeling; [0:27:09](https://youtu.be/CQk-5lAirn0?t=1629) — 70% likelihood, 9:30–10:00; [0:29:32](https://youtu.be/CQk-5lAirn0?t=1772) — bullish until 50% traded; [0:31:09](https://youtu.be/CQk-5lAirn0?t=1869) — confluence of mid gap and London highs; [0:36:46](https://youtu.be/CQk-5lAirn0?t=2206) — not bearish afterwards, just usual 70% behavior; [0:39:08](https://youtu.be/CQk-5lAirn0?t=2348) — scenario if sell-off first.
- **Nuance / caveats / changes:** Same 70%/50% statement as the Oct 17 video (M24-046). Here he adds the explicit "never short just because we opened lower" prohibition and the idea that this alone "could be your entire model."

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ Premarket Tape Reading NQ Futures \ October 21, 2024
head: Retail vs. professional perspective on the opening price  (aliases: "opening price = rough-cut sentiment")
body:
- **Kind:** definition | psychology
- **What ICT says:** Retail looks at yesterday's close versus today's open ("we're way down"), sees weakness, chases shorts and then gets wiped out when the gap starts to fill — even a quarter or half of the gap is enough to stop out over-leveraged traders. The professional perspective is today's close relative to today's open (open-to-close), which is actual accumulation/distribution. The opening price is "rough-cut sentiment" meant to inspire or discourage less-informed, impulsive traders. He challenges indicator builders to plot cumulative close-to-open (retail view) vs open-to-close (professional view).

head: Daily handle goals and the "one good setup then stop" discipline
body:
- **Kind:** rule (risk/psychology)
- **What ICT says:** A new trader should not aim for 100 handles a day. First-rung objective: 5 handles per day on S&P (ES) and 10 on NASDAQ (NQ); later grow to 15–20 handles NQ and 10–15 ES. Once you have the day's objective, stop and tape-read the rest. Pressing the button on every impulse is not following a model; look for the one setup that has "a plethora of things" supporting the idea at the PD array you trade, and build accountability around trading only that setup. The way to find it is knowing the likely candidates for draws on liquidity (framed by session times) rather than only nearby swing highs/lows.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ How ICT Picks Winning FVG's & Orderblocks \ October 25, 2024
head: Large-range day anticipation: 3-day average range (and 5-day alternative)  (aliases: "large range day", "range expansion day", "small range day / compression")
body:
- **Kind:** rule / definition
- **What ICT says:**
  - "Large range" is measured against the average daily range of the last 3 days. If the current day's range is larger than that average, it is outside the normal 3-day range.
  - A day that closes with a range smaller than the 3-day average is a "small range day". It is "mathematically defined" and very sensitive.
  - Stricter or more sensitive version: use a 5-day average. If daily ranges start printing smaller than the last 5 days, you are close to a large-range expansion day.
  - Compression precedes expansion. He frames it as twisting a metal spring tighter and tighter until it releases (a borrowed image from Larry Williams). The smaller the ranges get, the bigger the likely expansion.
  - The large day usually comes the very next day, or worst case the second day after. The compression gives no direction on its own; you still need higher-timeframe order flow or the draw on liquidity.
  - He says large-range days are about 90% low-resistance liquidity runs (he first misspoke "high"). If the day is not a large range day, you will probably meet high-resistance runs instead, "not all the time but 90%".
- **How to identify:** compute the average range of the last 3 days (optionally 5). If yesterday's range is below that average, or an inside day, flag the next day as a large-range candidate.
- **How to use:** as a volatility filter that says WHEN an expansion is likely. Direction comes from the DOL (see next concept). On such a day he is willing to trade pre-market and hold, expects little retracement, and expects the day's open to be near the low (bullish case).
- **Example in this video:** Wed 10/23 NQ large down day. Thu 10/24 range sat inside Wed's range, with a higher low and lower high. Fri 10/25 was expected to be the large bullish range day.
- **Timestamps:** [0:07:23](https://youtu.be/svYZKOrWPRo?t=443) 3-day average and what counts as "large"; [0:17:05](https://youtu.be/svYZKOrWPRo?t=1025) spring analogy; [1:37:37](https://youtu.be/svYZKOrWPRo?t=5857) restated as the math for anticipating a large range day; [1:38:26](https://youtu.be/svYZKOrWPRo?t=5906) 5-day version and the 90% low-resistance figure.
- **Nuance / caveats:** he admits an expansion day inside the last 3 days can skew the average. He notes the smallest-range-in-7-days idea (Toby Crabel, from the book "Street Smarts" by Raschke & Connors, 1995) and Larry Williams' inside-day precursor as influences, and says the 3-day average is his own repeating theme.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ How ICT Picks Winning FVG's & Orderblocks \ October 25, 2024
head: Inside day as precursor  (aliases: "inside day", "range contraction", "spring")
body:
- **Kind:** definition / rule
- **What ICT says:** an inside day is a day whose high is lower than the previous day's high and whose low is higher than the previous day's low. It is a precursor to a large-range day (credited to Larry Williams and the Crabel/Raschke material). It does not give direction.
- **How to identify:** compare today's daily high and low to yesterday's. Both must be inside yesterday's range.
- **How to use:** expect the next trading day (or the one after) to expand. Pair it with a DOL for direction.
- **Example in this video:** Thursday 10/24 high lower than Wednesday's high and Thursday's low higher than Wednesday's low. Thursday's intraday was choppy, back and forth, overlapping ("fuzzy price action").
- **Timestamps:** [0:09:01](https://youtu.be/svYZKOrWPRo?t=541) inside day introduced; [0:11:27](https://youtu.be/svYZKOrWPRo?t=687) definition and "it doesn't give you direction"; [0:42:09](https://youtu.be/svYZKOrWPRo?t=2529) restated.
- **Nuance / caveats:** a small-range day is itself a high-resistance, "fuzzy" environment. Compression means a choppy day now and an explosive day next.

title: ICT 2024 Mentorship \ How ICT Picks Winning FVG's & Orderblocks \ October 25, 2024
head: Direction from smooth highs/lows left behind (draw on liquidity after a sell-off)  (aliases: "smooth highs", "unfinished business", "relative equal highs", "single highs")
body:
- **Kind:** rule
- **What ICT says:**
  - After a large drop (Wed), retail expects continuation lower, so shorts defend "smooth" relative-equal highs left above the market. Those stops are the target.
  - Therefore the inside day's direction is solved by looking at where price left smooth highs or lows that have not been engaged, and not at the drop itself. His Thursday tweets said "look up, don't go short". He calls the untouched orders above "unfinished business".
  - A single high also counts; it is not always relative equal highs. Equal highs and lows are just what new students spot easily.
  - Prime candidate on the 15-minute chart: "high, lower high, lower high" smoothness above price.
  - He also leans on the higher-timeframe narrative: primary bull market, election year, "we're not trying to pick the top in a primary bull market".
- **How to use:** if bias is bullish, only look for buy-side draws and bullish PD arrays. He is "not interested in shorts".
- **Example in this video:** 15-minute relative equal highs above price, with unfinished business above NQ roughly 20,659.25 (spoken "659 and a quarter", caption unclear) and 20,680. Both buy-side levels were run Friday.
- **Timestamps:** [0:02:36](https://youtu.be/svYZKOrWPRo?t=156) relative equal highs and the "10 o'clock may use data to go through" idea; [0:15:29](https://youtu.be/svYZKOrWPRo?t=929) "unfinished business"; [1:10:14](https://youtu.be/svYZKOrWPRo?t=4214) bias bullish means only bullish PD arrays; [1:40:54](https://youtu.be/svYZKOrWPRo?t=6054) smooth highs on 15m are the prime candidate.
